# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS
## HIGH AND MIGHTY LORD MAURICE OF NASSAU, BORN PRINCE OF ORANGE, MARQUIS of Veere and Flushing, Count of Nassau, of Katzenelnbogen, Vianden, Diez, Moers, etc. Lord of St. Vith, Doesburg, of the city of Grave and the land of Cuyk, Monster, etc. Governor, Captain, and Admiral General of Guelders, Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht, and Overijssel.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'C' surrounded by floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>

->**C**<- *It is to your* EXCELLENCY *(great Prince) that this* TREASURY *of the world’s languages must first be presented, since you are today one among the Christians who can give it a most assured safe-conduct to have it well received for its utility among the most distant nations of the earth, for whom it was primarily prepared: so that through the various characters (with which it is filled) and the understanding of their scripts, one nation might more easily communicate with another, regarding human society, and especially the treasury of the* HOLY *Gospel of our Lord* JESUS CHRIST *in these final centuries and the end of times. <note>The author uses apocalyptic phrasing typical of the early 17th century, suggesting that spreading the Gospel to the ends of the earth was a prerequisite for the Second Coming.</note> But what nation could one choose in the world today that is more capable of practicing the instructions in the Oriental languages contained in this treasury than the Dutch people? Who, under the blessed leadership of your Excellency, deploy their triumphant and victorious banners by sea and by land through your valor and good fortune, even to the ends of the earth and the most remote regions. It is therefore with good reason (my Lord) that this first copy is presented to your Excellence, so that from you it may receive its universal permit <note>original: "passepartout"; here meaning a letter of safe passage or a general recommendation</note> of your favor, if you judge it useful to the public, to be not only well received by the Dutch: but also to be transported by them to all nations where the various languages contained herein are in use; and where the characters represented here can serve to express their thoughts in writing, and make known the virtues, magnanimity of courage, and valor of your Excellence, to serve the advancement of the glory of the Almighty, and the worship of the Christian religion in those lands: as well as to the blessed memory of the author of this book, the late* Monsieur *the President* DURET, *of Moulins in Bourbonnais, <note>Claude Duret (c. 1570–1611) was a French magistrate and polymath whose work on languages was published posthumously.</note> renowned among the scholars of this time, who, to serve the public in the assembly of this Treasury (after several other works brought to light by him), employed his labor until the final days of his life, which, by the will of God, having been cut short in the middle of its course, he was unable to put the finishing touches on it to polish it further; rather, just as it is, he left it and commended it to Mademoiselle*

<summary>This page presents the formal dedication of Claude Duret's linguistic "Treasury" to Maurice of Nassau, praising the Dutch maritime expansion as the primary vehicle for the book's global use. The text emphasizes the work's role in facilitating international communication and the spread of Christianity.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the formal dedication to Maurice of Nassau, which began on the previous page. It clarifies the provenance of the manuscript and the publisher's motivations for seeking the Prince's patronage.</meta>

FLORIMONDE BERGER, his wife <note>Florimonde Berger was the wife of Pyramus de Candole, the scholar-printer who oversaw this edition.</note>, the honor and virtue of her family, and worthy of all merit, who—having entrusted it into my hands to have it printed by my people, with the authority to grant its protection to whichever Prince I believed would find it agreeable, so that it might see the light of day under his favor—I have taken the boldness to present and dedicate it to your Excellence. This is in the hope I have held that, as you are a benign Prince and a lover of both letters and arms, you would receive with a favorable eye this work, which is diversified not only in characters <note>The author refers to the various exotic typefaces and alphabets—such as Hebrew, Greek, and Syriac—used throughout the book.</note>, but also in the most signal and remarkable histories of the Universe, regarding the corruption of languages <note>In the 17th century, the "corruption" of languages referred to their historical divergence and change over time, often viewed as a continuing process following the biblical Tower of Babel.</note>, and their change and progress through the valor of the great Princes and Captains of past centuries; and also to witness to you, through this little Treasury, the goodwill and zeal I have to be known by your Excellence.

->The most humble and most<-
->affectionate servant,<-
->PYRAMUS DE CANDOLE.<-

<meta>This page contains the Royal Privilege, a formal legal document granting the publisher the exclusive right to print and sell this work. It follows the title page and preliminary front matter.</meta>

** iiij

**Louis** <note>original: "Loys," an archaic spelling of Louis</note>, by the grace of God King of France & Navarre, To our beloved and faithful Councilors, the members of our Courts of Parliaments in Paris, Toulouse, Rouen, Bordeaux, Dijon, Aix, Grenoble, & Brittany: Bailiffs, Provosts, Seneschals <note>Bailiffs, Provosts, and Seneschals were various types of local judicial and administrative officials in pre-revolutionary France</note>, or their Lieutenants, and to all our other Justices and Officers whom it may concern, Greetings. Our well-beloved Pyramus de Candole, merchant Bookseller, has represented to us that he recently recovered a book titled the *Treasury of Languages*, composed by the late Claude Duret, who during his life was our Councilor and President at the Presidial Court <term>Presidial Court: A middle-level court established to handle cases that were too important for local courts but not significant enough for the high Parlements.</term> of Moulins in Bourbonnais. Since this book is worthy of the light and of being shared with the public, he wishes to have it printed; however, as he fears that after incurring the expenses to support the said printing, other Booksellers or Printers of this our Kingdom might do the same, he would be deprived of the profit he expects from it. He has very humbly petitioned us to allow him the sale and distribution of the said books in this our Kingdom, with prohibitions against all Booksellers or Printers from selling or printing them without his acknowledgement and consent, and to this effect, to grant him our necessary letters. For these reasons, inclined toward the prayer and petition of the said de Candole, we have permitted and granted to him, and do permit and grant by these presents, that after having the aforementioned book printed, he may have it sold and distributed in this our Kingdom, lands, and territories under our obedience, by such Merchants, Booksellers, or Printers, or such others as he sees fit, without any other of the said Booksellers or Printers being allowed for six full and consecutive years—counting from the day that the said printing is finished—to print, sell, or distribute the said books without the express permission of the said de Candole, upon pain of confiscation of all copies found, and for all costs, damages, and interests, and a fine of five hundred livres <term>Livres: The primary currency of France from the Middle Ages until 1795.</term>. We therefore command you, and enjoin each of you, each in your own right, that you allow the said de Candole, whether widow or heirs, to enjoy and use our present permission, privilege, and grant, along with everything contained within it, fully and peacefully during the said time, without allowing any hindrance or obstacle to be placed against him; for such is our good pleasure, notwithstanding any edicts, ordinances, mandates, or prohibitions to the contrary.

Given at Paris the ninth day of May, the year of grace one thousand six hundred thirteen:
and of our reign the third.

->By the King in his Council,<-

Signed
->DERDIN.<-

Collated with the original.

# TO THE MOST NOBLE MAN, LORD CLAUDE DURET
## Most worthy President of the Senate of Moulins, <note>Moulins is a city in central France, formerly the capital of the Duchy of Bourbonnais.</note> Claude Faydeau,
### Canon Theologian and Grand Penitentiary <note>An ecclesiastical official focused on matters of conscience and penance.</note> of the Arch-
### episcopal Church of Bourges, <note>original: "Bituricensis". Bourges was a major religious center in France.</note> from the God of peace,
### prays for peace.

<margin>
2 Corinthians 13
1 Kings 10 <note>original: "3. Reg. 10." Following the Vulgate numbering.</note>
2 Chronicles 9 <note>original: "2. Paral. 9."</note>
Matthew 12
2 Timothy 2
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'Q' set within a square frame, adorned with a rose and leaf patterns.</image-desc>JUST AS the Queen of Sheba, driven by an unheard-of desire for learning and the distinguished fame of King Solomon, arrived at Jerusalem (the city of perfect beauty and the joy of all the earth) so that she might attentively hear his incredible wisdom, perfectly understand his admirable knowledge, and intimately secure for herself his singular friendship; and though she endured many hardships in her laborious pilgrimage and dwelt in a foreign land, she heard, knew, and won over King Solomon. She proclaimed those happy who stood always in his presence; and with great eloquence, she declared that God uniquely loved the people of Israel and wished to preserve them,
<margin>2 Chronicles 9</margin>
because He had placed King Solomon there to deliver judgments and exercise justice. So too have I, with an incredible greed for reading and by the exceptional renown of your name (most distinguished President),
<margin>Isaiah 1</margin>
desired to travel to the city of Moulins (a faithful city and full of judgment), my sweetest homeland and the most pleasant place of my birth,
<margin>Genesis 32</margin>
so that I might timely reap and perceive the most abundant fruit of your wisdom, knowledge, and friendship. Then indeed, I would call those blessed who enjoy your eminent presence, and I would declare with the noble humility of the centurion
<margin>Luke 7</margin>
that the Lord (who shall judge the world in justice and the people in equity)
<margin>Psalm 97</margin>
vehemently loves the people of Moulins and guards them wonderfully, since He called you (most distinguished man) to the highest and loftiest office of President.
<margin>Numbers 12</margin>
Once called, He graced you with the gentleness of Moses,
<margin>Daniel 2</margin>
celebrated you with the knowledge of Daniel, and honored you with the equity of Samuel,
<margin>1 Samuel 16</margin>
designating you to declare the laws (which are the bonds of the city) and to judge with righteous judgment.
<margin>Deuteronomy 16</margin>
What then? I cannot help but extol with the highest praise your wisdom in tongue, your learning in speech, and your steadfastness
<margin>Ecclesiastes 4, 11, 48</margin>
in the work of justice, and I proclaim those happy who are honored by your friendship. Shall I not proclaim this **Treasure** <note>Faydeau refers here to Duret’s famous book, "Thresor de l'histoire des langues de cet univers" (Treasure of the History of the Languages of this Universe).</note> of yours, encompassing almost all languages, sought with such study and labor from the most hidden mysteries of the sciences, and produced and arranged with such industry? Shall I not commemorate it, handing it down to the memory of all ages? From this work, [one may learn] the various forms of languages, the different customs of nations, the manifold laws of peoples, the weighty opinions of Doctors, and the most excellent...

<summary>This page contains a formal Latin dedication by Claude Faydeau to the scholar Claude Duret, using the biblical meeting of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba as an allegory for Duret's wisdom and his landmark book on languages.</summary>

--- Page 23 ---
<meta>The catchword "PRE" suggests this page serves as a preface or preliminary approval (Approbation) for the following work. It continues the formal front matter of the book.</meta>

One may extract and most abundantly draw out, as if from the richest mines of the Indies, the purest gold: the examples of magistrates, the foresighted counsels of governors, and the illustrious deeds of princes. By the brilliance of this work, my mind was so refreshed and moved that I did not hesitate to examine it more diligently; and having scrutinized it accurately with the sharp edge of my mind and read it through by day and by night, I have given it my approval. I decided that my approval (which I hope will not be unwelcome to you) should be sent; I send it therefore and come to an end, and I earnestly pray to the Lord, the Creator of all things, that He may preserve you long in safety and health, and adorn you with His heavenly gifts. For it is God who heals all things, not with herbs or poultices, but with His Word <note>original: "sermone"</note>, and bestows the grace of health through His singular goodness.
->At Bourges <note>original: "Auarici Biturigum," the Roman name for the city of Bourges</note> on the 2nd day of June 1607.<-

---

# APPROVAL.

*I, Claude Feydeau, Doctor of Theology and Canon Law, Theological Canon and Grand Penitentiary <term>Grand Penitentiary: a senior priest in a cathedral responsible for matters of penance and confession</term> in the Archiepiscopal Church of Bourges, certify that I have seen and read this Treasury of Languages <term>original title: "Thresor des Langues"</term> composed by the Noble Claude Duret, President at the Presidial Court <term>Presidial: a type of mid-level royal court in Renaissance France</term> of Moulins in Bourbonnais. I have found nothing contrary to the Catholic religion; therefore, I have judged it worthy of being printed, as being useful and necessary to demonstrate and teach the antiquity, dignity, and variety of languages.*
->*Done at Bourges this 2nd of June 1607.*<-

->CLAUDE FEYDEAU.<-

# PREFACE BY CLAUDE
## FEYDEAU, DOCTOR OF THEOLOGY AND
## CANON LAW, DEAN AT THE COLLEGIAL CHURCH
### of Our Lady of Moulins, regarding the Treasury of Languages, com-
### posed by the noble CLAUDE DURET, President at the Presidial Court

If the father of Roman eloquence <note>original: "pere de l'eloquence Romaine," referring to Cicero</note> calls history the witness of the times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the mistress of life, and the messenger of antiquity, it shall also be permissible for me to name this *Treasury of Languages* (composed by the Noble Claude Duret, President at the Presidial Court <term>Presidial Court: a royal court of justice in Renaissance France</term> of Moulins in Bourbonnais) by these same beautiful titles of honor and praise. For, in the first place, it is a witness of times of war and times of peace, and leads us into the knowledge of the Creator of all this round machine <note>original: "machine ronde," a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe or the globe</note>, who changes the times, carries away kingdoms and establishes them, gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who understand discipline, and discovers deep and hidden things. In the second place, is it not the light of truth? For it declares truth to be sweeter than honey and stronger than a lion, saying with the learned Zerubbabel that truth overcomes all things, and is no respecter of persons, while rebuking those who turn their ears away from it and devote themselves to fables. In the third place, one may say that it is the life of memory, when it describes the magnificent works of the Lord, who has made all things in wisdom, and whose greatness fills heaven and earth. In the fourth place, it may be called the mistress of life, because it teaches the path that leads us there, and turns us away from the wide road by which we slide into eternal damnation. In the fifth place, it is the messenger of antiquity, in that it puts forward the wisdom that comes from the ancients and the prudence found through many years, so that we may renounce (as the Apostle says) infidelity and worldly desires, and live in this world soberly, justly, and piously, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God, who will render to each according to his works. Now I wish (dear Reader) to divide this Preface for you into three parts, and to represent to you therein the utility, necessity, and excellence of the three most noble languages that exist, and to draw you to search through this precious and rare *Treasury of Languages*. I shall begin, then, with the first part, to discourse upon their principal utility recognized throughout the world, and not without great mystery, since they were dedicated and consecrated upon the title <note>original: "le titre," referring to the *titulus* or inscription plate placed on the Cross</note> of the triumphant Cross of the Redeemer: so that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. As much as I am able to judge from my very small talent of knowledge, that sentence of Saint James seems worthy of being inscribed on the famous Delphic column <note>The "Delphic column" refers to the ancient Greek practice of inscribing maxims at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi.</note>, where he proclaims that **God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble**: and this very thing is clearly evident in the arrogant builders of the Tower of Babel, whom God, the all-powerful creator of all things, confused and threw into disorder. On the other hand, God, the Lord of knowledge, gathered and restored the humble builders of the "Tower of David" <note>A theological contrast: Babel represents linguistic confusion and pride, while the "Tower of David" (often a metaphor for the Church) represents the spiritual unity restored through the gift of tongues.</note> through the beautiful distinction of languages, filling the Apostles with the Holy Spirit so that they began to speak in various tongues. What more? Saint Paul, that **vessel of election** <note>original: "vas electionis" — a biblical title for Paul indicating he was chosen by God.</note> (who carried the glorious name of the Lord before the nations, kings, and the sons of Israel), puts forward and extols the types of languages among the greatest and most noble gifts of God. Now, in the most flourishing city of Moulins, my sweetest homeland, I honor you (most distinguished President) with priority, I greet you with a holy kiss, and I lift you to the heavens as much as I am able. Truly, I understand that you are one who has not merely broken off a single twig (as many do) from the universal garden of all the sciences, but have reaped a harvest such as no one else has. Yet you have delighted your mind with that sweetest flower of the Apostle: **not to think of oneself more highly than one ought, but to think with sober judgment**, and you have so established yourself that you never turned even a hair’s breadth <note>original: "transuersum... vnguem" — literally "the width of a fingernail," a Latin idiom for a tiny distance.</note> from the line of moderation. The traces of this wisdom are clearly evident throughout your entire life, and especially in the **history of languages** that you have given to posterity. In this work, you describe, explain, and illustrate various figures of letters <note>In this context, "figures of letters" refers to the specific shapes and alphabets of different writing systems.</note>, the ancient customs of nations, the excellent laws of peoples, the fruitful opinions of the Learned, the useful examples of Magistrates, the necessary advice of governors, and the notable deeds of Princes—all expressed for the memory of all generations to follow. Therefore, acting as a representative of the public will (most distinguished President), I beseech you that without any further delay you hand over your extraordinary history of languages to the printing presses. In this work, you describe, explain, and illustrate the various shapes of letters, the ancient customs of nations, the excellent laws of peoples, the fruitful opinions of the Learned, the useful examples of Magistrates, the necessary advice of governors, and the notable deeds of Princes.

<margin>Eccl. 28.</margin>
Wherefore (most distinguished President), obey the excellent counsel of the Wise Man. "Hedge your ears with thorns," and do not listen to a wicked tongue.

Now, having attentively listened to and seriously noted this doctrine—contemplating human weakness and admiring divine power—let us humbly pray to God, who is the Lord of Knowledge, that he give us the knowledge of salvation, so that we may say something that is to his honor and glory, to the edification of the listeners, and to your consolation. Let us devoutly invoke Jesus Christ, so that he, who sustains all things by his powerful word, may sustain our infirmity. Let us further holily implore the Holy Spirit, who is the true comforter of the desolate, to comfort those of little courage and relieve the weak. Therefore, in order to maintain a better methodical order in this funeral oration, we shall divide it into three parts: in the first, we shall treat the death common to all the posterity of Adam; in the second, the honorable life of the Noble Claude Duret, Presiding Judge, illustrated by Prudence, Temperance, Fortitude, and Justice <note>The four Cardinal Virtues.</note>; and in the third, his happy death, illuminated by faith, adorned with hope, and fortified by charity <note>The three Theological Virtues.</note>.

The divine Plato <note>The author is referencing the famous myth of Prometheus and Epimetheus found in Plato’s dialogue, *Protagoras*.</note>, wishing to represent under the cover of a fable the original condition of the human race, imagined that at the beginning of the world the gods were alone, before there were any mortal animals. But when the fated destiny of generation arrived, these gods produced them in the bowels of the earth, and formed them from fire and earth, along with other things mixed with these two. And wishing to bring them into the light, they commanded Prometheus and Epimetheus <note>In Greek mythology, these brothers were Titans; Prometheus’s name means "Forethought," while Epimetheus’s means "Afterthought."</note> to distribute to each their strengths and properties. Then Epimetheus prayed to Prometheus to let him perform this distribution in his presence; and so he moved forward alone to proceed, giving to some strength without swiftness, and to others swiftness without strength. He armed some, and for those who were without arms, he invented other means of help. Those whom he had enclosed in small bodies, he raised into the air with feathers, or commanded them to crawl upon the ground; he equipped those grown to a great mass with their very mass itself. And he proceeded similarly with the others, distributing to each their virtues and faculties. After he had thus equipped and furnished them—so that they would not destroy one another—he gave them the means to defend themselves from each other and to remain in the open, clothing some with thick hair, shells, <term>tests</term> <note>From the Latin *testa*, referring to the hard shells of tortoises or similar creatures.</note>, scales, plumage, or tough skins against the inclemency of winter or summer. And from these same things, he prepared for them natural litters and bedding, adding to their feet spurs, nails, and callosities, and to their heads, horns, teeth, and trunks. Then he distributed food to them, making some graze on the grasses of the earth, others eat the fruits and roots of trees, and others—more gluttonous—to devour one another, provided that those who lived on prey were somewhat sterile, and the others, subject to their gluttony, were more fertile, so that the species might endure. For divine providence was very wise in this, having made all animals that are fearful and good to eat greatly fecund, so that by being frequently eaten, they would not fail; whereas harmful and mischievous beasts produce few offspring. Therefore, the hare is very fertile, and alone among all the beasts of the hunt, overcharges its lit[ter]... <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the bottom of the page; "portée" (litter) is the likely completion of "por-".</note>

Similarly, the female <note>original: "haze," typically a female hare, but here used for rabbits</note> of rabbits is found so full of young that some are still without fur, others are a bit more formed, and others are coming out of the womb; but the lioness, which is the strongest and boldest of all other beasts, in her life bears, according to the Egyptians, only once, and only a single cub. 

Now, Epimetheus being hardly wise, he gave everything to the brute beasts, reserving nothing for man, whom he left alone without strength, without power, without property, completely naked, without weapons, without clothing, without footwear, without suitable nourishment, and lacking all things: so much so that he could not resist the other animals, who were then more excellent than he. For the stags ran more lightly, the lions and bears were stronger, the peacock more beautiful, the fox more subtle, the ant more diligent, and the snail better housed; every beast found a medicine proper to its sickness and injury, of which man was ignorant. From this arose such confusion that little by little men perished in various cruel ways, so that their species would have soon been reduced to nothing without the counsel of the prudent Prometheus. Seeing such a great fault, and to remedy it, Prometheus stole from Vulcan <note>The god of fire and metalworking.</note> and Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom and crafts.</note> their technical wisdom along with fire—it being impossible to acquire or use such skill without fire—and thus distributed it to the human race. 

By means of this, men began, for their common utility, to assemble out of fear of the beasts in order to resist them, giving help to one another and seeking here and there safe places for their habitation. They learned to build houses and make clothing to avoid the harshness of the cold and the force of the heat, to store fruits for necessity, to prepare weapons for their defense, and to find other conveniences for life. These things finally necessity itself—the inventor of all things—made known in detail to the understandings of mortals, to whom were given as aids: hands, speech, and reason. Reason was given to invent, speech to communicate, and hands to accomplish what they would invent for themselves by reason or learn from others through speech. For no other animal truly speaks, because speech proceeds from reason, and no other has any hands, or at most something merely resembling hands. 

Therefore, man first found through reason the most necessary things, such as food, clothes, and weapons; then those which serve pleasure, ornament, and magnificence. He imposed names on all things, invented letters of many kinds and various ways of writing, and established all the mechanical and liberal arts <note>The "mechanical arts" refer to physical crafts and trades, while "liberal arts" refer to intellectual pursuits like grammar, logic, and astronomy.</note>. He proceeded so far as to measure the earth and the sea, and to use instruments to reduce the vast mass of the heavens—which is hardly understood by the mind—and place it before the eyes. 

Furthermore, the same Plato affirms that before men lived in society and spoke together, or before they had begun to invent and practice the arts—since they alone among all animals participated in divinity, endowed with an immortal soul because of this divine kinship—they first thought that there were gods, and honored and prayed to them. From there, religion, government <note>original: "police," referring to the administration of a civil society.</note>, and the judiciary took their beginning; trade by sea and land was introduced, laws established, magistrates created, trades invented, houses built, villages and hamlets constructed, and then cities, towns, and fortresses, and finally empires, kingdoms, and republics.

### LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE, known for his monumental universal history *Bibliotheca historica* (Historical Library).</note>, a Greek author, in the first book of his *Historical Library*, chapter 1—following the opinion of the most ancient pagan and idolatrous philosophers and historians—has left in writing that at the beginning of the world, men had the sound of their voices confused and unintelligible. However, by making distinctions little by little, they named each thing by its own name and designation. And because they were then living in many different parts of this universe, they did not all use the same speech and language; from this, it happened that they also had different, dissimilar, or contrary characters and forms of letters. Regarding this, one should see what G. Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French polymath and linguist who studied the origins of languages.</note> writes on this subject in his treatise on origins, or on the antiquity of Hebrew and the affinity of languages; also Marc Antoine de Muret <note>A renowned humanist scholar of the Renaissance.</note>, book 1, chapter 5 of his *Variae Lectiones* <note>original: "diuerses leçons"</note> on Horace; and F. de Belleforest, book 1, chapter 2 of his *Universal History*.

Marcus Vitruvius Pollio <note>The famous Roman architect and engineer (c. 80–15 BCE).</note>, the Architect, speaking broadly of this matter, believes that while men lived in the woods and forests at the beginning of the world, and trees clashing and striking together had produced and engendered fire, these men assembled near it. Calling out to one another, they came together in these assemblies to produce various voices and words, which were afterwards formed little by little until the origin and beginning of an entire and perfect language.

Herodotus, another Greek author, in his *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus's *Histories*, named after the Muse of music.</note>, speaking of this matter, said these words: the Egyptians, before Psammetichus was their king, believed they were the first and oldest of all the men in the world. But Psammetichus, having entered the Kingdom and having a certain curiosity and desire to know who were the oldest of men, found that from that time the Phrygians <note>An ancient Indo-European people of central Asia Minor.</note> thought themselves to be earlier than the Egyptians. For Psammetichus, having inquired who were the first and oldest of men, and perceiving there was no way to know it through inquiry, decided to deliver two small children from a lowly place to a shepherd, to have them raised with the herds of beasts he led to the fields. 

He commanded him that no person in the world should utter any word in their presence, but that they should be placed in a small rural hut, into which two goats would be brought to nourish and feed them. Psammetichus had commanded this because he desired to hear (after these small children grew a little older) if they would utter any words. This thing happened just as was expected; for after the time and space of two years had passed, the two children, stretching out their hands and prostrating themselves before the shepherd who served them, upon hearing the door open, began to cry, "Bec, Bec." 

The shepherd kept this secret at first, but entering many times toward them and diligently observing that they always repeated the same word, he reported everything to his master. He received a command to bring and present the children. When Psammetichus heard them cry these words, "Bec, Bec," he inquired which nations used those words; searching for this, he found that the Phrygians called bread by this name in their language <note>The word is *bekos*.</note>. By this means, the Egyptians conceded and confessed that the Phrygians were older than they. Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE, known for his monumental universal history, the *Bibliotheca historica* (Historical Library).</note>, a Greek author, in the first book of his *Historical Library*, chapter 1, following the opinion of the most ancient pagan and idolatrous philosophers and historians, left in writing that at the beginning of the world, men had the sound of their voices confused and unintelligible. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

Greeks make mention of similar things invented by them; namely, that Psammetichus <note>Psammetichus I, Pharaoh of Egypt (664–610 BCE), who famously conducted an experiment to find the "original" language by isolating two infants.</note> gave orders that children should be raised by women whose tongues he had entirely cut out. Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note>, a Greek author, says as much as the author above in the explanation of the Greek word <term>Bekkoselenos</term> <note>original: "Βεκκέσεληνε"; a term of mockery meaning an "ancient fool," literally "bread-moonling."</note>, as does the commentator of the Greek poet Aristophanes in the comedy *The Clouds* regarding this Greek word <term>Bekkoselenos</term>. Justin the historian <note>A Latin historian of the 2nd century CE.</note>, in book 2, mentions the debate between the Egyptians and the Scythians <note>Ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia.</note> concerning the antiquity of their nation, but he makes no mention of this story of Psammetichus. Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 CE), an influential theologian of the Christian Church.</note> writes in book 5 of *Grecian Affections* that some of the ancient Pagans asserted that the first men in the world were born in Arcadia, from which comes the Greek word <term>proselenous</term> <note>original: "προσεληνους"; meaning "before the moon," referring to the Arcadians' claim to be older than the moon.</note>.

->*Before Jupiter was born, the Arcadians are said to have possessed the lands,*<-
->*and that race existed before the moon.*<-
<note>original: "Ante Iouem genitum, terras habuisse feruntur / Arcades, & luna gens prior illa fuit." — A quote from Ovid’s *Fasti*.</note>

Several other ancient pagan authors, among whom was the divine Plato (cited above in his *Timaeus* and in book 1 of the *Laws*), held that the first men of this universe came from Egypt. Following Coelius <note>Lodovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), also known as Coelius Rhodiginus.</note> in book 2, chapter 19 of his *Various Lessons*, Gerard Mercator <note>The famous Flemish cartographer (1512–1594).</note> confirms this in his *Paradoxes*. Aristides, a Greek author, maintains in his *Panathenaic* that the Athenian soil was that which first produced and engendered men. M. Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a prolific Roman scholar.</note> in his *Eumenides* mentions the Athenians who called themselves "Aborigines"; Claudian in his poems to Eutropius, Eusebius in his *Chronicles*, St. Jerome on Genesis, Berosus in his *Antiquities*, and others cited by B. Pererius <note>Benito Pereira (1535–1610), a Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note> in his *Commentary on Genesis*, book 15; Polydore Vergil <note>An Italian humanist scholar (c. 1470–1555) who lived in England.</note> in book 1, chapter 3 of *On the Invention of Things*; Loys le Roy <note>A French humanist and professor (c. 1510–1577).</note> in book 4 of the *Vicissitude of Things*; and Guillaume Postel in his book on the *Origins or Antiquity of Hebraism*, together with Gilbert Génébrard in book 1 of his *Chronography*, treat this matter extensively. Pedro Mexía <note>original: "Pierre Messie"; a Spanish Renaissance scholar (1497–1551).</note> in chapter 13 of his *Various Lessons* asserts for certain that two children nourished and raised together will create and compose a language of their own, separate from others. This is further confirmed by Francisco Vallés <note>original: "François Valese"; a Spanish physician (1524–1592).</note> in chapter 3 of his *Sacred Philosophy*, and the late Laurent Joubert <note>original: "I. # LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

The Philosopher *Pythagoras* attributed supreme wisdom to the person who first imposed names on all the things of this universe. Plato, in the *Cratylus* <note>A dialogue by Plato that explores whether the names of things are determined by nature or by social convention.</note>, asserts that this was done by a power more than human; for in truth, man could not have, by himself and without the help of God, discerned the innumerable things contained in this universe by their proper names or terms—things which otherwise would have remained unknown. Namely: the heavens, their parts and movements; the fixed stars and the planets; the elements with their qualities; winds, rains, hail, snow, thunder, and other <term>meteors</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain and snow, not just falling space rocks.</note>; animals, birds, fish, trees, plants, herbs, grains, legumes, minerals, precious stones, pearls, and their natures and properties; seas, gulfs, shores, harbors, ports, islands, rivers, lakes, ponds; lands, nations, peoples, villages, towns, boroughs, cities; the internal and external parts of the body, the senses and their objects, smells, flavors, diseases, and remedies; infinite human actions, food, clothing, laws, magistrates, judgments, policies, ceremonies, military matters, finances, coinage; so many arts and trades with their tools; and so many persons by their names and surnames, as well as the affinities and alliances between them.

Now, there was in former times no small controversy among the learned as to whether words were imposed according to the pleasure and will of the speakers, or by art and natural reason. Regarding this, one may see *Coelius Rhodiginus* <note>Ludovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), also known as Coelius Rhodiginus, author of the *Lectionum Antiquarum* (Ancient Lessons), a massive encyclopedia of classical knowledge.</note> in book 24, chapters 5, 6, 7, and those following, in his *Diverse Lessons*. The variety and continual mutation seen in languages made some think that this naming was accidental and arbitrary, founded on the convention and custom of men. Others said that since names are like instruments established to represent things—which do not change according to our opinions, but rather remain always in the same order according to their nature—likewise, true names should not change at our pleasure. Instead, they should suit the things signified, whose essences and likenesses they imitated, being first conceived in the soul, then expressed by sounds and the voice, and written by letters and syllables. 

To this opinion, some have added so much faith that they wish to inquire into the properties of things through the properties of words; or they meddle with the power and virtue they believe words possess, attempting to perform miracles by uttering them and to completely heal the diseases of both soul and body. What is more, they have affirmed that some names were invented by divine inspiration—meaning, among others, that the name of God is pronounced with only four letters in all the languages of the world. In this, so many people and nations could not agree without a marvelous mystery of the divinity <note>This refers to the "Tetragrammaton" (the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH). Renaissance scholars often tried to prove that the name for "God" in every language—such as *Deus* (Latin), *Theos* (Greek), or *Gott* (German)—could be counted as four letters to show a universal divine design.</note>. 

If the imposition of names, their property, and their virtue is admirable, the invention and use of letters is no less so; having found a means to encompass such a multitude and variety of human sounds and voices in a few notes. Through these letters, the most useful things in the world are written down: such as divine and human laws, sentences, judgments, wills, contracts, public and private treaties, and other such things necessary for the understanding of human life. Those who died long ago live again in the memory of the living, and those far removed from one another communicate with their absent friends as if they were present. <header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF</header>

God, the sayings of wise men, philosophy, and generally all doctrines and sciences are passed down from hand to hand to those who follow. Some have disparaged this invention <note>Referring to the invention of writing.</note>, such as Thamus, King of Egypt, in Plato’s *Phaedrus*, who responded to Thoth <note>The Egyptian god of wisdom, often credited with inventing writing.</note>—who was boasting of his discovery—that he had not found a remedy for memory, but rather for recollection. For this reason, the Pythagoreans and the Gallic Druids wrote nothing; instead, they passed their mysteries to one another without writing, so that by relying on letters, they would not exercise their memory less. However, experience—the mistress of all things—has clearly shown their error. Inasmuch as they wrote nothing, the memory of their doctrine, through the long course of years and because of human frailty, has been totally lost, with not a single trace or ancient mark remaining today. 

Since letters are therefore very necessary, after they were invented, those who considered them more closely divided them into vowels, mutes, and liquids <term>liquids</term> <note>A phonetic term for consonants like 'l' and 'r' that have a flowing sound.</note>, calling "Grammar" the art that could serve to know, discern, and assemble them to make syllables, nouns, verbs, and speech. And although Pliny, relying on the authority of Epigenes, believes the use of letters to be eternal, he is nonetheless contradicted in this by infinite ancient authors, as I will explain more fully hereafter. See the great and strange curiosities concerning this matter by Johannes Trithemius, Abbot, in book 5 of his *Polygraphy* <note>original: "polygraphie"; a Renaissance work on cryptography and secret writing.</note>, and what Polydore Vergil writes on this subject in book 1, chapter 3, of *On the Invention of Things* <note>original: "de l'inuention des choses".</note>.

### CHAP. II.

The great and admirable Hebrew Prophet Moses, in chapter 11 of his history of Genesis, and Josephus, the Hebrew historian, in book 1, chapter four of the *Jewish Antiquities*, have clearly demonstrated that the confusion of languages—aside from the Hebrew language, the first and most ancient of this universe—was first introduced during the construction and building of the Tower of Babel. This is despite what Philo the Jew seems to want to say otherwise in his treatise *On the Confusion of Tongues*, interpreting the words of the aforementioned Moses allegorically in his accustomed manner. Alexander Polyhistor and Abydenus, very ancient authors, and the Sibyl have said as much as the aforementioned Moses and Josephus, according to the report of Eusebius of Caesarea, a Greek author, in book 9, chapter 4, of his *Evangelical Preparation* <note>original: "preparation Euangelique".</note>.

This being presupposed, we shall learn that according to the true and assured calculation of the Hebrews, this confusion of languages (aside from Hebrew) occurred 340 years after the universal flood, as is detailed in the Hebrew book titled *Seder Olam* <note>An ancient Hebrew chronological work; the title translates to "Order of the World."</note> composed by Rabbi Abraham son of David, although Berossus, in book 4 of *The Times*, writes that it was 131 years after the said flood. Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish rabbi and scholar.</note>, a Hebrew author, and some other Hebrew Rabbis and the common chronologists among them, hold that it was one hundred and one years after the said flood; others say it was 150 years after the said flood. The Hebrews say that Noah the Patriarch lived for a long time after this confusion of languages brought about by some of his descendants. The Lord God wished to test him in his patient faith, and in reward, He allowed him to see the effect of His blessings upon the family of Shem, where the Hebrew language remained, along with the doctrine and discipline of the true Church. This is deduced at length by B. Pererius <note>Benito Pereira (1535–1610), a Spanish Jesuit theologian known for his commentaries on Genesis</note> in his commentaries on the 11th chapter of Genesis, following Saint Augustine in book 18, chapter 39 of his *City of God*, and Louis Vives <note>Joannes Ludovicus Vives (1493–1540), a Spanish humanist and prominent scholar of the Renaissance</note> in his commentaries on that chapter. Regarding what is deduced above concerning the division of languages that occurred during the building of the Tower of Babel, as reported by Moses in the 11th chapter of Genesis previously cited, it seems that the 10th chapter of the same Genesis contradicts this entirely, holding that the children of Japheth divided the islands of the nations each according to his own language and family. Noting this, Philaster <note>Saint Philastrius (died c. 397), Bishop of Brescia, who compiled a famous catalog of various beliefs and heresies</note> in his *Catalogue of Heretics*, chapter 106, dared to assert that even before the construction of the Tower of Babel, there were several varieties and diversities of languages among the first men of the world. And it matters not to the contrary (he says) that Moses wrote in chapter 2 of the same Genesis that the earth had but one language, given that this should be interpreted "by excellence" <note>original: "par excellence"; meaning it was the primary or most noble language</note>, as they say, to mean one language understood by all men of the universal earth, even though they spoke other languages.

But this opinion of Philaster has been entirely rejected by the doctors of the Church, notably by Saint Augustine in his book *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture* <note>original: "de mirabil. scriptur."</note>, chapter 9; Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, in book 2, chapter 7 on Genesis; and Alfonso de Castro in book 9 *Against Heresies* for many reasons based on Holy Scripture. All the Rabbis and Hebrew doctors, as well as Greek and Latin theologians, hold it as a most certain thing that at the time of the Babylonian division of languages, the one and only Hebrew language remained in the house of Heber <note>The biblical great-grandson of Shem; traditionally, the term "Hebrew" is thought to derive from his name</note> to be as an inheritance to those who would be of that family. This is confirmed by Josephus in book 1, chapter 9 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, and Saint Chrysostom in his 30th homily on Genesis. 

And to resolve the doubt mentioned above from Philaster—that before the building of the Tower of Babel, the children of Noah divided the islands of the nations each according to his language and family—we shall learn that this must be understood through <term>anticipation</term> <note>Also known as prolepsis; a literary technique where a writer describes an event as having already happened even though it occurs later in the chronological narrative</note>; thus, the matter was first described as it was to happen later. This was very well deduced by Tyconius <note>A 4th-century theologian famous for his "Seven Rules" of biblical interpretation</note> in his understanding of passages of Holy Scripture, which contains several clauses by anticipation that are later arranged in order and sequence. Saint Augustine praises this greatly in the book *On Christian Doctrine*, and in book 16, chapter 34 of his *City of God*; as do Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan teacher whose biblical commentaries were highly influential</note> in his commentaries on the 10th chapter of Genesis cited above; the author of the *Ordinary Gloss* <note>original: "glose ordinaire"; the standard collection of medieval biblical commentaries</note> on this passage; and Felician Capito in his *Catholic Explanations*, part 1, explanation 7. Along with these, one should see what B. Pererius writes regarding these divisions of the earth according to peoples and nations in his commentaries on the 15th book of Genesis, and the refutation of this opinion of Philaster in book 16, dispute 9. ### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

...of the Tower of Babel. This language is the very same that the ancient and modern Jews—and we after them—hold to be contained in the Old Testament written in the Hebrew tongue. It was preserved solely in the family of Heber, son of Peleg <note>original: "Heber fils de Phaleg"; in Genesis 10:24–25, Eber (Heber) is actually the father of Peleg, but the author here reverses the relationship</note>, without any corruption or alteration. From this Heber came the Patriarch Abraham and the Hebrews, because this same Heber and all those of his family were not present at the building of the said Tower of Babel. Because he and his kin did not wish in any way to consent to such a sin, they were not in any way affected by the punishment of the others. Therefore, it is to be conjectured that in Heber alone, and in his family, the ancient and first language of men—namely Hebrew—remained sound and whole, without any alteration or corruption. It remained in use only in this said family, which occupied the land extending from Mesha to an eastern mountain named Sephir in Judea, as Saint Jerome <note>Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate)</note> confirms in his work on Genesis. This language was entirely lost to other men who conspired against God during the building of the said Tower of Babel. For a greater and more ample understanding of what is deduced above, see: Eusebius of Caesarea, book 9, chapter 4 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*; Polydore Vergil, book 1, chapter 3 of *On the Discovery of Things*; Pedro Mexia, chapter 23 of the first part of his *Diverse Lessons*; Paul Constantin Phrygius in the *Chronology* of Funck; Gilbert Génébrard, book 1 of his *Chronography*; Tostatus <note>Alfonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), a prolific Spanish bishop and biblical commentator</note> on Genesis, chapter 11, questions 1 and 2; Theodor Bibliander in his *Commentary on the System of Languages and Letters*; Benedictus Pererius in his *Commentaries* on chapter 16, disputation 8 on Genesis; Louis Le Roy, book 2 of *On the Vicissitude of Things*; and Antoine du Verdier, book 1 of his *Prosopography*.

Following what we have deduced above, we shall say that the great Saint Augustine, in book 19, chapter 7 of *The City of God*, speaking of this confusion of languages, left these words in writing:

> The diversity of languages alienates man from man. For if two people happen to meet, and are forced by some necessity not to pass by but to stay together, and neither knows the other's language, mute animals even of different species associate more easily than they, though both are humans. For when they cannot communicate their thoughts to each other, such a great similarity of nature is of no use for bringing men together because of the diversity of languages alone; thus, a man would more willingly be with his dog than with a foreign man. <note>original Latin: "linguarum diuersitas hominē alienat ab homine..."</note>

Caelius <note>Lodovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), also known as Caelius Rhodiginus</note>, in book 3, chapter 12 of his *Diverse Lessons*, says: "What is that variety of speech, which—although in the beginning the whole earth was of one lip—increased to such an extent that one cannot wonder at it enough? Especially when someone of a dissonant tongue is hardly even considered a man, which gave rise to the proverb that a man goes deaf in a foreign tongue." <note>original Latin: "quid illa loquendi varietas..."</note> This is what moved Pliny to say in some part of his works: "So great," he says, "is the variety of speech that a foreigner is not like a man to a stranger." <note>original Latin: "tāta est, inquit, loquendi varietas, ut externus alieno nō sit hominis vice."</note> On this subject, see Theodor Bibliander in his commentary on the system of languages in the Prophet Jeremiah, chapter 5. There, the great Eternal God used such words full of His ire, wrath, and abomination against the peoples and nations who would be disobedient to His holy commandments:

His divinity had previously declared this in chapter 28 of Deuteronomy:

### C H A P T E R  I I I.

The great and admirable Prophet Moses, after having described in his history of Genesis, chapter 10, very particularly the generations of the children of Noah, and the division of the Isles and the nations by their regions, each one in his own language, according to their children and families among their people, writes in the following chapter 11 as follows: At that time, the whole universal earth was of one same language and speech, and it happened as they departed from the East that they found a plain in the land of Shinar <note>original: "Sennaar"</note>, and they dwelt there and said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks and bake them in the fire." So they had bricks instead of stones, and clay <note>bitumen or mortar</note> instead of cement; then they said, "let us build ourselves a tower, the top of which reaches to heaven; let us make ourselves a name <note>renown</note>, so that perhaps we may not be scattered over all the earth." Then the Lord came down to see the said tower that the sons of men were building. For he said, "behold," and the great Origen in his 11th homily on the book of Numbers dared to write that various Angels operated various languages for each of the men who worked on the construction of this tower. Josephus in book 1, chapter 4 of his *Antiquities of the Jews*, St. Augustine in his *Questions on Genesis*, and Paul Orosius in his writings, assure us that in the very place where the said Tower of Babel was constructed and built by Nimrod <note>original: "Nembrot"</note> and his followers and underlings (of which the heathens and pagans Hestiaeus, Eupolemus, the Sibyls, Alexander Polyhistor, Abydenus, and others mentioned in Eusebius book 9, chapter 4 of his *Preparation for the Gospel*, and after him in P. de Mornay chapter 26 of *The Truth of the Christian Religion*, all speak), the great and populous city of Babylon, also named in the Hebrew language בבל <gloss>Babel</gloss>, was afterwards built and constructed there upon the river Euphrates, from which the surrounding lands and regions named Chaldea and Mesopotamia took their names and titles. The Hebrews write that the word Babel is derived from the root בלל <gloss>Balal</gloss> <note>meaning to mix or confuse</note>.

This word *Shinar* is as much as to say in Latin: *the knocking out of teeth, that is, of speeches or words, which cannot be made without teeth: for the teeth greatly assist in speaking, which were then in a way knocked out of them, when those "toothed" ones—that is, the proud or the strong—lost their accustomed faculty. This name is also interpreted, and rightly said to be, "their stench," because clearly by such a daring and attempt they sent the stench of pride even to the nostrils of God; to whom, just as humility or a contrite spirit is a sacrifice for a sweet-smelling savor: so on the contrary, pride is a horrible stench* <note>original Latin: "excussio dentium, id est, sermonum siue verborum..." translating a commentary by Rupert of Deutz and Benedictus Pererius</note>: Rupert, *Commentary on Genesis*, book 4, chapter 41, and B. Pererius, *Commentary on chapter 11 of Genesis*. And in chapter 16, the Jewish people were led and conducted into a captivity of 70 perfect and complete years in this same Babylon, according to the prophecy of Jeremiah, chapter 25, having been dragged and led there by force by Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosor"</note>, monarch of the Assyrians, as it is written in the 4th book of Kings, chapter 25 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 25</note>. The region where this city was built was afterwards named Seleucia, as Strabo asserts in book 16 of his *Geography* and Stephanus in his treatise on cities. And just as the Latins in their language use the word *latro* <note>original: "latro," meaning a bandit or robber</note> for *latero* <note>original: "latero," meaning one who stands at the side</note>, speaking of a brigand or thief because brigands *latera viatorum obsident* <note>original: "beset the sides of travelers"</note> and accost wayfarers, travelers, and passengers; in the same way, the Hebrews use this Hebrew word ציר *Thaid*, that is to say in English "to dress" or "accost" from the word ער which signifies "side." Saint Jerome and several interpreters of the Bible use *robustus venator* <note>original: "mighty hunter"</note>, because the word *venator* <note>hunter</note> is attributed as much to thieves as to hunters. In fact, Holy Scripture, under the word "trapper" or "hunter," understands the enemies of God and the persecutors of his Church (Psalms 91 & 124, Ezekiel 32, Lamentations ch. 3). Furthermore, Plato and Aristotle have listed among the types of venery or hunting *lēsteian* <note>original: "λῃστείαν," meaning piracy or brigandage</note>, that is to say, banditry.

For if Holy Scripture had intended in this case to speak of true venery or hunting, it would have used the Hebrew word ציד, that is to say, *Irretire* <note>to ensnare or trap with a net</note>, as it always does. This is why Philo the Jew in his works, and Josephus in book 1, chapter 4 of his *Jewish Antiquities*, wrote that Nimrod, a most audacious man, was the first who incited pride and contempt for God among men. And Rabbi Levi ben Gerson <note>also known as Gersonides</note> in his commentaries on chapter 10 of Genesis, Rabbi Gerundensis <note>Nachmanides</note>, Rabbi Ibn Ezra, and other Hebrew Rabbis on the same chapter of Genesis, have confirmed the above, saying that this Nimrod was the first of men to establish tyranny in this world. To this, Saint Augustine adheres in book 16, chapter 4 of the *City of God*, and Saint Jerome in his Hebrew traditions on Genesis ch. 11.

### *Of the Region of the Hebrews, Israelites, or Jews.*

## CHAP. V.

Abraham Ortelius, in his *Synonyms & Geographical Treasury* <note>Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598) was a famous Flemish cartographer and geographer</note>, says: "The Jews, also called Hebrews and Israelites, are a people who once inhabited Judea, or Palestine; now, however, they wander scattered throughout the whole world, possessing no place of their own. They are everywhere hated by all kinds of men and forced to pay tribute." <note>original: "Iudæi qui & Hebræi & Israelitæ, gens quæ quondā Iudęam, siue Palęstina habitauit: nunc verò per totum orbem terrarum diuersa vagatur, nusquam proprium locum possidens. Vbique & apud omne genus hominum odiosa, & tributaria."</note> Manetho, according to Josephus, writes that they were called *Hyksos* <note>original: "ὑϰσὼς" or "ὑοϰσύους"</note>, as read by Eusebius in Book 10 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, which in the sacred language of the Egyptians, according to Josephus, signifies "king-shepherds." Or, as the same author says, Artapanus writes that they were called *Hermiuth* <note>original: "ἑρμιοὺθ"</note>, meaning captives. In the same 9th book of the *Preparation*, Sedulius and Fortunatus call them *Manzeres* from a Hebrew word, as if calling them "bastards" <note>The term likely derives from the Hebrew 'mamzer', meaning a child born of an illicit relationship</note>. Petrus Gyllius and Nicolas de Nicolay say they are called *Chifout* <note>A Turkish derogatory term for Jews</note> by the Turks today. Among Europeans, they still retain their ancient name. For the Germans, Spaniards, Italians, and French call them *Joden*, *Judios*, *Giudei*, and *Juifs*.

Palestine <note>original: "παλαιϛίνη"</note> is a region of Asia according to Ptolemy, which in the Holy Scriptures is called *Pelisthim*, *Canaan*, and the Land of Promise. It is called *Phylistieim* <note>original: "φυλιστιεὶμ"</note> by the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>. Saint Jerome, in his *On Hebrew Places*, says it should be noted among historians that Judea belongs to Palestine, while Galilee and Samaria belong to Phoenicia. Their inhabitants are the *Canaanites*. Today, all Europeans call it the **Holy Land**, using various words according to the difference in their languages, but signifying the same thing. Mention is made of *Palestine I* in authentic documents, in which is the city of *Caesarea of Strato*. The *Book of Notices* <note>A reference to the 'Notitia Dignitatum', a document of the late Roman Empire's administrative organization</note> mentions *Palestine II & Salutaris* and *Palestine III*. See also *Arabia Petraea*. *Palestinian Syria* is mentioned by Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher</note>, where he writes that the "Jewish stone" <note>A fossilized sea urchin spine used in ancient medicine</note> is found; this seems to refer to Judea. For Eusebius, in Book 10 of the *Preparation*, writes that in his time it was so called. *Palestine Petra* is a place near Arabia Felix according to Agatharchides. See *Sittacene & Interamna* <note>Ancient regions located in Mesopotamia</note>.

Those who wish to see how the Holy Land, otherwise known as the Promised Land, was anciently divided and partitioned, should read what Friar Brocard has very learnedly written in his description of the Holy Land, following the ancient authors; or Gilbert Génébrard in Book 1 of his *Chronography*, folios 84 and 85; and Benito Arias Montano in his apparatus for the great Antwerp Bibles, in the treatise *Canaan, or on the Twelve Nations*, and in the treatise *Caleb, or the Partition of the Promised Land*. I treat this matter at length in the following chapter.

But then again, what would either of them do without the help of writing, their common assistant? Writing cannot be restricted by any boundaries, spreading everywhere. Certainly, little could be achieved without it, as can be seen among the savages of the **West Indies**, who are so barbarian, uncivilized, and beast-like, being deprived of its use. Indeed, when the **Spanish** conquered them, the natives held writing in such admiration and respect—seeing that by its means they could make their thoughts understood from one place to another, regardless of the distance—that they thought there was a demon or familiar spirit enclosed within these characters. One could hardly prevent them from worshipping the packets and dispatches placed in their hands to carry. This served greatly to keep these barbarians in obedience and subjection, and to dissuade them from all enterprises, conspiracies, and revolts. Furthermore, as *Pierre Martyr* <note>Peter Martyr d'Anghiera (1457–1526), an Italian-born historian of Spain's explorations</note> recounts in his *Decades*, if it was a question of discussing something secret among themselves, they took great care not to approach a tree that grows in their region called the *Copei* <note>The Copey tree (*Clusia major*), known for its thick leaves that can be written upon</note>, because for lack of paper, the **Spanish** were accustomed to writing to one another on the leaves with a stylus; these leaves are very large and thick, like those of a water lily. For there is not a single small point or accent in the Torah <term>Torah: the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, also known as the Pentateuch</term> that does not signify some great mystery. It was written (so they say) expressly as one continuous sequence, without any separation of words or clauses from the beginning to the end; so much so that the whole work appeared to be only a single word, if it could indeed be that long. This was done so that the common people—even though everyone had it before their eyes and knew it by heart—could not understand its secret significance for fear of it being held in contempt. Instead, it was understood only by those of the council to whom Moses communicated what was necessary for them to exercise their duties, according to what their capacity could handle. Moses reserved for himself the remainder of the sacred secrets, especially those concerning the Trinity. He never wished to reveal these to the Israelites except in veiled words, for fear of leading them into idolatry, to which they were quite inclined because they could not comprehend the high mystery of a plurality of persons in such a perfect union. However, he did share these secrets with Aaron and the seventy of the Sanhedrin <note>The Sanhedrin was the supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish nation</note>, and they with their successors in like manner, as I will describe more particularly hereafter. From this has come the name Kabbalah <note>original: "cabale"; meaning "received tradition"</note>, which is to say a tradition received by ear without anything being committed to writing. The Pythagoreans and the Druids later followed this same practice, according to the words of Julius Caesar in book 6 of his *Commentaries*.

But these Kabbalistic mysteries proceeded from the written law and did not consist so absolutely in a verbal tradition that the Scripture did not contain the better part of them—whether in the form of the characters, their points, accents, order, sequence, and arrangement, or in the transposition, commutation, and pairing of letters. These are what the Hebrews call *Ethbas* <note>original: "Ethbas" (Atbash); a substitution cipher where the first letter is replaced by the last, the second by the second-to-last, etc.</note>, *Tmurah* <note>original: "Tmurah" (Temurah); the process of exchanging letters to find hidden meanings</note>, and *Ziruph* <note>original: "Ziruph" (Tziruf); the art of combining and permuting letters</note>, as well as *Notariacon* <note>original: "Notariacon" (Notarikon); a method of forming new words from the initial or final letters of phrases</note>, numerical equivalences, and *Ghematrie* <note>original: "Ghematrie" (Gematria); a system where letters are assigned numerical values</note>, along with other such devices and observations. Among all authors, a certain Spanish Jew named Rabbi Joseph Cicatilia <note>Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla (1248–c. 1305), a famous Spanish Kabbalist</note> from the city of Salamanca has composed three large volumes on this, titled **גנת אגוז** <note>original: "Ghinat Egoz," which translates to "Garden of the Walnut Tree"</note>. The first volume treats words; the second, letters; and the third, points and accents, as I shall clearly demonstrate hereafter. 

Furthermore, just as writing is more spiritual than the spoken word (which relates more to the body because it falls under the sense of hearing, which is coarser and more material than the sense of sight, upon which writing consists), secret notes or ciphers are also more spiritual than common writing. Therefore, they relate to the mystical sense of the law, hidden beneath the "bark" or shell of the literal letter. Regarding this, the same aforementioned Rabbi, in the first book of the *Gates of Light*, discusses the difference between these two words: **אמירה** <note>original: "Emirah," meaning speech or word</note>, which comes from the verb **אמר** <note>original: "Amar," to say or speak</note>, and **דבור** <note>original: "Daberah," from "Dibur," meaning reasoning or discourse</note>. He posits that the first denotes the law given by mouth to Moses, which is represented by the divine name **אדני** <note>original: "Adonai," meaning "My Lord"</note>; and the other, namely the utterance (*Daberah*), as when one finds in the Hebrew Scripture **מדבר** <note>original: "Medhaber," meaning "He spoke"</note> (it must be understood that God spoke), signifies the written law, denoted by the sacred and holy Tetragrammaton **יהוה** <note>The four-letter name of God, often transliterated as YHWH</note>. Furthermore, the written law, being more spiritual and mysterious, is explained by the law given by mouth, which is the temple and tabernacle of the written law—just as *Adonai* is for the ineffable four-letter name. From what is said above, we therefore learn that just as the Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</term> Yahweh, or Jehovah, as it is more commonly pronounced, is far more sublime than Adonai, or Lord; and the written law more so than that which was dictated by mouth—which is but a bark or shell of the other—similarly, Writing must also be more excellent than speech. Aristotle and his disciples say that speech in man is nothing other than a <note>original: "ῥεῦμα λόγων"</note> stream of words, a flowing brook of reasoning, whose source is the <note>original: "διάνοια"</note> mental discourse, and the stream that flows from this fountain is speech, which accords with God, the source of reason within us. And just as there is no water in the channel or in the pool created by it that does not proceed from the fountain, so no word comes out that was not first conceived internally in the soul. Of this internal speech, words are the signs and marks, just as letters are the signs of words. Upon this, the philosopher Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a Greek philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> said that letters do nothing but express and state, and things are only stated; but words and thoughts express and are expressed. Words are expressed only once, though in two ways: first, when reason flows and distills into the tongue, then when the tongue strikes the air, the sound passes to the intellect and hearing. From there, the things they represent penetrate through the ear to the understanding, where they attach and imprint themselves. On the contrary, the thoughts of things are expressed doubly—namely, by speech and by writing—but they express only once, whether by the living voice or by silent writing <note>original: "Escriture muette de foy"</note>. This variety demonstrates to us the nature of our words, insofar as they communicate partly with the spirit and partly with the body: so much so that they prepare for us an intermediary access to bring us closer to God. This is the cause of the virtue found in certain words and characters.

Furthermore, there are ciphers of certain languages forged for pleasure as well as for writing, such as the jargon of beggars and Gypsies <note>original: "Bohemians"</note> and other similar groups. A large dictionary of this was formerly seen printed in Venice, so ample and complete that there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be said or written in it, much more distinctly than in Genevan, the "Breton-ing" Breton <note>A term for the most traditional, Celtic form of the Breton language</note>, or in Basque, nor perhaps even in Scottish. There are, moreover, ciphers that act as intermediaries between speech and writing, insofar as they are silent like writing, yet at the same time act just like speech; they are attached and joined to the person, who expresses himself through gestures of the fingers, expressions, and winks of the eyes or lips. These are of almost infinite kinds, sharpened by the notes and abbreviations of Cicero <note>Likely referring to Tironian notes, an ancient system of shorthand</note>. For everyone forges them according to their fancy, just like alphabets, sharing them with their confidants—some in one way, some in another, more or less artificial and ingenious according to the dexterity of their mind, or as they happen to be instructed by others. In fact, all writing—both common writing and that consisting of secret notes or ciphers—is little else than anagrams, considering how few letters, through their various transpositions and assemblies, can express so many diverse and dissimilar meanings unto infinity: reduced first into syllables, then syllables into words, and these words finally woven into clauses and complete oratory. Moreover, regarding this script, the Law that God gave to Moses on the two aforementioned tables was written all in one continuous flow, without any separation of syllables or words, and pierced through from one side to the other; so that everyone, as the Rabbis say, read it differently according to their fancy—to the right, to the left, from the front, and backward; from top to bottom and bottom to top; Moses retaining for himself the true hidden understanding, according to what God had revealed to him. The secret of this consisted partly in the form of the characters, and partly in the true and proper distinction of the words; which is not found in the same way in other languages and scripts, as I shall demonstrate visually hereafter. 

This is why the Hebrews have dared to assert that the considerations of all things depend on the 22 letters of their alphabet, which form the true foundation; for before the creation of the world, they were first extracted from the ten <term>Sephirot</term> <note>In Kabbalah, these are the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite is revealed.</note> or divine attributes, which are otherwise most simple above all other simplicities, without any addition of matter, and held until their explanation within the <term>Belimah</term> <note>A Hebrew term from the *Sefer Yetzirah* meaning "nothingness" or "without anything," interpreted here as a divine silence.</note>—the taciturnity or silence of the divinity. These letters are like the parts of the body, and their points and accents serve in place of spirit and life. Because of this, one should not find it strange if they are held to be the Creator's own workmanship, since they are one of the principal instruments to celebrate and magnify Him in the aforementioned *Belimah*, or silence; for they are mute in themselves, and not babbling, so that they have much more emphasis than words. This is well witnessed by that beautiful and excellent gesture used by our Lord in Saint John, chapter eight, toward the Scribes and Pharisees, whom he confounds and astonishes more by writing I know not what...

The straight line, moreover, possesses what Plato calls <term>the same</term> <note>original: "ταυτὸν" (tauton)</note>, which the Hebrews call <term>He</term> <note>original: "הוא" (Hu)</note>; they establish this as the first attributive name of the Divinity, following Psalm 102: "But you are the very same" <note>original: "Tu autem idem ipse es"</note>; and the 24th <note>The author likely refers to Isaiah 42:8 or 48:12</note> of Isaiah: "I am the Lord, He is my name" <note>original: "Ani Adonai Husemi"</note>, meaning the Lord, Himself or myself, is my name. The poet Virgil, in the 10th book of the *Aeneid*, appropriates this to the great god Jupiter: "King Jupiter is the same to all" <note>original: "Rex Iupiter omnibus idem"</note>. This <term>the same</term> is the supreme idea of things that are always of one kind, without receiving any alteration or change. In contrast, secret notes or ciphers relate to <term>the other</term> <note>original: "ἕτερον" (heteron)</note>, which is the form of those things that behave diversely. 

For this reason, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras who saw numbers and geometry as the foundation of reality</note> took "the same" for the good principle: the one, the permanent, the straight, the true, and the finite; and "the other" for the evil: the diverse, variable, crooked, false, and infinite. The Egyptians took the former for Osiris and the Nile, and the latter for Typhon and the sea. This is the reason why Achilles, in the 9th book of the *Iliad*, so strongly detests the "other"—the diverse, varied, and disguised:

> For that man is as hateful to me as the gates of Hades
> Who hides one thing in his heart, yet speaks another.

Just as true writing and the meaning that represents the knowledge of the thing we wish to express and bring to light are hidden under secret notes or ciphers, and just as a supposition of falsehood is sometimes drawn from the truth; in a similar way, the text of the Law, when taken crudely and literally, is like a cipher for the mystery hidden beneath it. This follows what the Cabalists themselves admit regarding the book of *Ecclesiastes*. According to the *Zohar*, this book was composed by King Solomon in the desert during the seven years he remained there, having been transported and held captive by the Demon Asmodeus—the prince of money, luxury, and ambition—who surprised Solomon in the very snare and ambush the King had set for him. The *Zohar* bases this on the words contained in that same treatise: "I was King of Israel in Jerusalem" <note>original: "Fui Rex Israel in Ierusalem"</note>, implying he was no longer king when he composed it. Furthermore, the text of *Ecclesiastes* is "vanity of vanities and all is vanity" <note>original: "vanitas vanitatum & omnia vanitas"</note>; they explain this to mean that the Law itself—since it excludes nothing—was vain and frivolous until the coming of the Messiah.

These are the wheels of Ezekiel, enveloped one within the other. There is a successive communication of light proceeding from the throne of God—where its primary source lies—to the tenth sphere, or the Empyrean heaven, and from there to the sun, from the sun to the moon, and from the moon to the sensible things of the elementary world. For everything that the heavens influence and transmit to us is light accompanied by heat; upon this depend all the various faculties and virtues imprinted from above here below into the variety of species, through the rays of the two luminaries and the stars. Thus, light is that which carries all these effects along with itself. It is not that by such words or characters we can constrain or attract the higher intelligences to us, or move them to perform anything whatsoever according to our will and intention; rather, it is just as when, by strength of arm, we lift ourselves along a rope to some battlement or window, instead of making them come down to us. Or as when, from within a boat with a cable or capstan anchored to the shore, we do not pull the land toward us, but rather, by moving ourselves, we approach it. This is also practiced among divided things, where the figure is called the body, and the word that accompanies and clarifies it is called the soul. With this, the Hebrew book entitled *Habbahir* <note>The *Sefer Ha-Bahir* or "Book of Brightness," one of the earliest and most important works of Kabbalah.</note>—that is to say, the elucidator—clearly agrees when it says that the Hebrew letters are paired with the human body: the accents with the spirit, and the points serving as vowels with the soul.
