And in fact, that which we see—that bodies deprived of the spirit of life which maintained them in their being are demolished and resolved into their elementary parts and principles from which they were first composed—is very well represented to us by a printing plate <note>original: "planche d’Imprimerie"</note>. After the characters have been pulled from it, they are separated from their sequence and assembly and redistributed, each into its own proper place in the type case <note>The wooden drawer where a printer stores individual letters of type.</note>, to be recomposed anew into some other meaning. Thus, letters symbolize the constituent substances of the body. Despite being so few in number, through the variety of their assemblies and mixtures, they procreate so many different species in the triple genres of compounds—minerals, plants, and animals—and individuals as if to infinity. These substances are, moreover, in a perpetual change and permutation of one into another, in the same way that letters, through their different placements, sequences, interlacings, and transpositions, form now one text of writing, then another entirely different one, even though they are the same characters. Beneath these lies the expressed meaning, which takes the place of souls; and once those meanings are formed, they can no longer be perverted into others, but remain always the same, whatever alteration their external covering may suffer—provided that the proportion of their order, which constitutes their difference, is not changed from its due and natural placement. This can be seen by the various transpositions of the Hebrew alphabets, where, through several disguises, the letters having been thrown out of their first structure, it has truly happened that the meaning they expressed openly has hidden itself intrinsically and withdrawn from the knowledge to which it was previously exposed, as if under the cover of a mask. But it is not extinguished or annihilated for that reason; it remains reality in its first being, though in secret and imperceptible at first glance to our apprehension and notice, disfigured as it is. In the same way, once the rational soul is procreated and joined to the body, although the parts of the body may be erased, perverted, altered, and transformed in a hundred thousand ways upon being separated from it, the soul does not cease to subsist permanently apart in its own particular sameness, divided from all others. This is like individuals, even the most similar ones such as flies, ants, and similar insects, or even sparrows and swallows; despite their exact resemblance, they conduct their lives separately, each for itself. For what one projects, feels, and suffers, the other does not project, feel, or suffer for it. By means of this, not without great mystery (any more than all those other ceremonies), the Catholic Church has instituted the beginning of Lent—which is the time of penance—always at the new Moon; and specifically that of the last month, *Adar*, which corresponds to our month of February. It is as if this denotes that just as when the Moon, through the deprivation of the Sun's light from our perspective, is reduced to the final point of its shadowy darkness, it begins from there to be gradually illuminated again by a new reception of its rays. 

In the same case, those souls which have become all tarnished and clouded by the filth of a dark sensuality through their disordered lusts and excesses, receive a light from divine grace and mercy little by little (if it is not their own fault) and from day to day, when they come to repentance for their misdeeds and recognize themselves in this holy time specially ordained for us for this purpose. This continues until finally—through very bitter and piercing contritions of the heart, very long mortifications of the flesh, a displeasure for one's offenses, devotions, prayers, fasts, and almsgivings—they are entirely enlightened by divine splendor at Easter. This always meets the full Moon of the month of *Nisan* (that is to say, the first month, March), and the renewal of the year with the Spring equinox, when the sea here below is at its highest increase, and when the supramundane <note>beyond the physical world</note> sea is filled to the brim with blessings. He shared these with Capnion, Pellicanus <note>Conrad Pellicanus (1478–1556), an early Protestant reformer and pioneer of Hebrew studies in Switzerland.</note>, and others, who by this means were better enticed to the study of this Hebrew language, which was previously unknown to the Germans, Italians, French, and other Europeans. See Theodor Zwinger, volume 4, book 1 of his *Great Theater of the Human World*. 

And so that we do not forget anything worth considering in this place regarding the other names of the Hebrews, we will say that Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian of the 3rd century BCE whose works are often quoted by later writers.</note>, a very ancient author, wrote (as reported by Josephus in his *Jewish Antiquities*) that they were formerly named <gloss>Hyksos</gloss> <note>original: "ὑκσώς"</note>, which signifies in the sacred language of the Egyptians "King Shepherds." Or indeed <gloss>Hyksous</gloss> <note>original: "ὑκουσώς"</note>, according to Eusebius in the 10th book of his *Preparation*, which signifies in the sacred language of the Egyptians, "captives." They were called <gloss>Hermiuth</gloss> <note>original: "ἑρμιούθ"</note> according to Artapanus; or <term>Mamzerim</term> <note>original: "Manzeres"; a Hebrew term referring to children born of forbidden relationships, translated here as "bastards."</note> in Hebrew, as bastards according to Sedulius and Fortunatus. 

As for the Hebrew word "Israel," it carries as much meaning as "prevailing" or "ruling with God," "seeing God," or as St. Jerome maintains in his book of *Hebrew Questions*, "Prince of God" or "Uprightness of God"; or "he who has complete trust in God." This name was given by the Angel to Jacob in Genesis 32 and 33, who with those of his family occupied Palestine over the children of Canaan. This word also signifies the kingdom of the ten tribes of the Hebrews; in fact, the Israelites (commonly called Hebrews from Heber, as stated above) were anciently all the faithful people who worshipped the true, sole, and unique God, thus named after the said Jacob-Israel, as St. Augustine confirms in book 16, chapter 39 of his *City of God*. (Though Cornelius Tacitus in book 21 of his *Annals* <note>Tacitus's *Annals* do not extend to 21 books; the author likely refers to the *Histories* or a specific Renaissance-era edition.</note>, Strabo in book 16 of his *Geography*, and Justin in book 36 of his *Histories* babble otherwise). Since then, these Israelites were named Jews after Judah, one of the leaders of the twelve lineages and families of the Israelite people descended from Jacob, surnamed Israel, as was said. This name was used after the tribes were led into captivity in Babylon and the kingdom remained in the house of Judah, a word which in Hebrew signifies "he who acknowledges God," that is to say, "he who trusts in God, and believes in Him, and follows Him," as noted by...

The Hebrews hold that the word "Israel" is derived from these three Hebrew words: ראה <note>Ra’ah</note>, which is "to see"; אל <note>El</note>, "God"; and איש <note>Ish</note>, "man": so that this word *Israel* signifies "man seeing God." ### CHAP. VII.

It seemed most necessary to me to begin this chapter with the definition of the word *Kabbalah*, which, according to the Hebrews, is the name of their science, doctrine, or tradition given by hearing—otherwise known as the reception by mouth from holy persons through hereditary succession—or indeed the acroamatic science <term>acroamatic: knowledge intended to be heard or passed on through oral teaching rather than written texts</term>, neither put down nor redacted in writing. More properly speaking, it is a symbolic reception or tradition of divine revelation, given or left from hand to hand through succession for the soul-saving contemplation of God and of separate forms <note>In the philosophy of the time, "separate forms" refers to spiritual beings like angels or the "intelligences" of the spheres that exist without physical matter.</note>. Those who are illuminated by the celestial and divine Spirit are called *Cabalici* [the Kabbalistic], and their disciples and followers *Cabalaei*, and those who follow and imitate them *Cabalista* [Kabbalists]. This Kabbalah is named thus in the Hebrew language קבלה, *Kabalah*, from the Hebrew verb קבל *Kibbel*, meaning "to receive" or "to learn," as asserted by: Rabbi Simeon Ben Jochai in the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism.</note>; the Hebrew author of the book *Hacadiua* <note>Likely referring to the "Holy One," as the text follows with the letters of the Divine Name: Vav, He, Yod, and He.</note>, Vav, He, Yod, and He; Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous philosopher Moses Maimonides (1138–1204).</note> in his expositions on the Pentateuch; R. Ha-Kadosh <note>Judah the Prince, traditional redactor of the Mishnah.</note> in the book titled *The Gates of Light* <note>A famous Kabbalistic work by Joseph Gikatilla, here attributed to the "Holy Rabbi."</note>; the author of the *Book of Faith and Expiation*; Josephus in book 10, chapter 10 of his *Antiquities of the Jews*; Eusebius in book 3, chapter 8 of his *Preparation for the Gospel*; Justin Martyr in his *Oration Against the Gentiles*; Elijah Levita, the Jew, in his *Tishbi* on the word *Kibbel*; G. the Venetian <note>Francesco Giorgio (1460–1541), a Venetian friar and prominent Christian Kabbalist.</note> in his *Introduction to the Harmony of the World*, book 2, chapter 7; Porchetus in book 1, chapter 7 of his *Victory Against the Jews*; Paul Fagius in his commentaries on chapters 26 of Genesis and 11 of Numbers in his Chaldean Bible; Paulus Riccius, an Israelite made Christian, in his book *The Balance of the Just*, and in his *Isagoge* [Introduction], and in the books on *Celestial Agriculture*; P. Galatino in book 1, chapters 1, 5, and 6 of his *Secrets of the Catholic Faith*; S. Pagninus in his *Hebrew Treasury* on the word *Cabal*; I. ...that the Apostle intended to speak of this Kabbalah in his first letter to Timothy when he wrote these words, "The saying is faithful and sure, and worthy of all acceptance—or Kabbalah—that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners." <note>original: "Fidelis & certus sermo est, & omni acceptione seu Cabala dignū, quòd Iesus Christus venit in mūdum, vt peccatores saluos faceret." A reference to 1 Timothy 1:15; the author suggests the Greek "apodoxe" (acceptance) refers to the Hebrew "Kabbalah" (reception).</note> The majority of Hebrew authors hold that this Kabbalah—called by Pliny in book 30, chapter 1 by the corrupted word *Ischabela* <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD) mentioned "Iscathelas" in his Natural History, which Renaissance scholars often linked to Hebrew mystical traditions.</note>—was given and taught by the living God to the Prophet Moses on Mount Sinai; since which time, through the succession of ages and years, it was communicated and left solely by word of mouth by the ancient fathers to one another until the later times of Ezra, as we shall explain more specifically hereafter. This is why the Hebrew people, speaking to Moses, said, "Speak you to us and we will hear, let not God speak to us (they said) we will hear" <note>original: "loquere tu nobis & audiemus, non loquatur nobis Deus te (inquient) audiemus." A citation of Exodus 20:19.</note>: which *Onkelos* the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>A 1st-century convert who authored the most famous Aramaic (Chaldean) translation of the Torah.</note> has called *Necabel* <note>נְקַבֵּל - "we will receive."</note>, for which reason in the Hebrew book titled *Pirkei Avot* <note>Ethics of the Fathers, a foundational text of Jewish ethics.</note> it is written thus: "Moses received—that is, Moses heard and accepted—the law from Sinai, whence Kabbalah is named from acceptance through hearing." <note>original: "Moseh Kibel, id est Moses audiuit, & accepit legem de Sinai, vnde Kabala dicitur ab auditu acceptio." Referring to the opening line of Pirkei Avot 1:1.</note> Arukh <note>Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome (c. 1035–1106), author of the Talmudic dictionary "The Arukh."</note>, a Hebrew author, regarding this word משנה *Mishnah* <term>Mishnah: the first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions, known as the "repetition" or "study"</term>, repetition, *deuterosis* <note>a Greek term meaning "repetition," used to describe the Mishnah.</note>, says these words: "Why is it called Mishnah? Because it is second to the law: for the law which all the Israelites heard on Mount Sinai is the written law. But Moses our teacher heard the *deuterosis* from the mouth of Divine Power a second time, and it is the law handed down by mouth." <note>original: "cur vocatur Mischna? propterea quod est secunda à lege: lex enim quam omnes Israelitæ audierunt in monte Sinai, est lex scripta. Moses autem pręceptor noster deuterofin ex ore diuinæ potentiæ vice secunda audiit, & est lex ore tenus tradita."</note> Therefore, according to the Hebrews, the law that Moses received at the top of Mount Sinai from the very mouth of God and the very hand of the Creator consisted of speech and writing; which writing, as the Kabbalists allege, has this advantage over speech: that many secrets and mysteries of the divinity are represented in writing which could not be expressed by the mouth. For there is not a single point or accent in the Torah <term>Torah: the Law of God, specifically the first five books of the Bible</term> or law of God that does not carry some great and marvelous mystery; and this law was written, according to these Kabbalists, expressly all in one sequence, without any separation or distinction of words and clauses, from its beginning until the end, so that the whole seemed to be but a single word, if it could be that long. This was so that the common people—notwithstanding that everyone had it before their eyes and knew it by heart—could not understand its secret significance or interpretation, for fear of scorn and contempt; thus only the Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme council and tribunal of the Jews</term>, or those of the council, to whom Moses communicated what was necessary for the exercise of their duties, and according to what their capacity could bear. This is confirmed by Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>The medieval philosopher Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), also known as Rambam.</note> in book 1, chapter 70 of his *Guide* <note>The Guide for the Perplexed.</note>, following the traditions of the aforementioned Sanhedrin, saying, "The words that I have communicated to you to keep only in your heart, it is not permitted for you to divulge by writing: and a little later, one shall not reveal the secret mysteries of the law to a stranger, but only to those of the council, and then only to those who are wise, discreet, and learned." This same Rabbi in the place cited above also used these words: "This has been observed among us at all times, to record nothing in writing of the secrets of the Law in order to avoid the sects and partiality of opinions that might arise from it, if everyone wanted to interpret them according to their whim, but rather to communicate them only by mouth, to keep them in the heart and in the mind: and still not to all people indifferently, nor to others than those of our nation who are at the same time wise, modest, and learned people."

...and discreet; which was the cause that most of the principal mysteries have perished among us ourselves, as much by the length of time as by the dominion of foreigners, who were both ignorant and incapable of them: so that nothing more of that is found, except some small collections and summaries to gather together learned men and those of understanding, such as the traditions and maxims that can be seen in the Talmud <note>The central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> and other places, which are moreover of two or three kinds, just like the heart of a tree armed on the outside with several barks, or a kernel clothed in various shells: which has troubled many people, who estimated that there was no fruit hidden beneath.

That is how far this figure <note>Likely referring to a specific author cited in the previous page's context.</note> extends when speaking of the Kabbalah. And regarding what was said above of the traditions of the aforementioned Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of ancient Jerusalem.</note>, we shall say that we have a book *on the fearsome coming of Elijah, now to be in the spirit, just as he was in John [the Baptist] in his mind, a work composed in its power and spirit from the ancient doctrines of the 72 elders of the Sanhedrin, auditors of Moses, to teach that by the work of the one and only Messiah or Christ, it is necessary to restore all those things which Satan destroyed in this lower world.* <note>original: "de formidando Eliæ aduentu nunc in ſpiritu futuro, ſicut in Ioanne erat in mēte ſua virtute & ſpiritu compactum opus ex priſcis patrum 72. Thus the Prophet Moses, having communicated to those Sanhedrin or those of the council what was necessary of the divine law for the exercise of their duties, and according to what their capacity was capable of, he reserved for himself the surplus of the sacred secrets and mysteries, especially of the Trinity: for fear of inducing the Hebrews to idolatry, to which they were quite inclined, for being unable to understand this so high and admirable mystery of a plurality of persons in such a perfect union: which was the reason why he never wanted to reveal and demonstrate these things to them except in veiled words: although he did make Aaron and those of the more secret council participants in it. This seems to be confirmed by Gregory Nazianzen in the book of the *State of Bishops* and in book 1 of the *Theology*. Eusebius book 7, chapter 28 of the *Ecclesiastical History*. St. Hilary Psalm 2, page 193, column 1. Michael de Medina book 7, chapter 14 of *Right Faith in God*, Melchior Cano book 3, ch. 3 of *Theological Places*. Giulio Ruggero chapter 16 on the *Senses of Holy Scripture*. Oleaster chapter 11 of his works. Stapleton book 12, controversy 7, chapter 13.

From what has been deduced and discussed above, this name "Kabbalah" has arisen and proceeded, as one would say, a tradition received by hearing, without setting anything down in writing. To which were subsequently conformed the Razenians taught by Janus, the Semnotes by Samothes, the Saronides by Saron, the Druids by Drius, the old Egyptians by Thoth <note>original: "Thoyt"</note> or Mercury, the Bactrians by Zoroaster, the Thracians by Orpheus, the Indian Brahmans <note>original: "Brachmanes"</note> by Abraham, and the Pythagoreans by these same Indians, all of whom taught their doctrine by mouth and by tradition from one to another alone without setting it down in any way in writing in the form of the Hebrew Kabbalah: but these Hebrew Kabbalistic mysteries proceeded from the written law, and did not consist so absolutely in a tradition that scripture did not include the best part of it, as much in the form of the characters, their points, accents, order, sequence and arrangement, as in the transposition, computation and pairings of the Hebrew letters: which the aforementioned Hebrews call in their Hebrew language: *Temurah* <note>Permutation of letters.</note>, *Ziruph* or *Ziruf* <note>Combination of letters.</note>, *Atbash* or *Ethbas* <note>A cipher where the first letter is replaced by the last.</note>, *Gematria* <note>The study of the numerical value of letters.</note>, *Ghilgul* <note>The cycle or rotation of souls or letters.</note>, *Notariakon* <note>A method of forming acronyms or shorthand.</note>, *Rashe Tevot* <note>Headings or initial letters.</note>, etc.

...the *Toph Theuoth* <note>original: "fop Theuoth," likely referring to the Kabbalistic concept of "The Form of the Letters."</note>, and infinite other Hebrew observations deduced hereafter, of which a certain Spanish Jew named Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla <note>original: "Rabbi Ioseph Cicatilia," a 13th-century Kabbalist.</note> of the city of Salamanca composed three large books above all others, titled **Garden of the Walnut** <note>original: "גנת אגוז Ghinaz Egoz."</note>; the first treating of dictions <note>words or speech</note>, the second of letters, and the third of points and accents. In imitation of the aforementioned observations, most of the ciphers of past and future ages have been and will be invented and built. And just as writing is more spiritual than speech—which is more of the body because it falls under the sense of hearing, which is coarser and more material than that of sight, in which writing consists—ciphers are also more spiritual than common writing. Therefore, they relate to the mystical sense of the law hidden beneath the "bark" or "shell" of the letter. To this purpose, Rabbi Ha-Kadosh <note>original: "Rabbi Hacados," referring to Judah the Prince, though the text attributes the following to Gikatilla’s *Gates of Light*.</note>, previously cited in the *Book of the Gates of Light*, regarding the difference between these two words **Emirah** <note>original: "אמירה," meaning speech or saying.</note>—a diction or word coming from the verb **Amar** <note>original: "אמר," to say or speak.</note>—and **Daberah** <note>original: "דברה," from "Dibur," to reason or discourse.</note>, posits that the first denotes the law given by word of mouth to Moses, which is represented by this divine name **Adonai** <note>original: "אדני," meaning Lord.</note>. The other, namely the utterance **Daberah**, as when one finds in scripture **Medaber** <note>original: "מדבר," meaning "He spoke."</note>, referring to God, signifies the written law denoted by the sacred holy **Tetragrammaton** <note>original: "יהוה," the four-letter name of God (YHWH).</note>. Furthermore, that this written law, being more spiritual and mysterious, is explained by the law given by mouth, which is the temple and the tabernacle of the written law: just as *Adonai* is for the ineffable Four-Lettered Name. And as there is no other access to reach this sacred name except under the conduct and direction of that of *Adonai*, which draws all its blessings and effects from it, so there is no other way to be introduced into the mysteries of the written law than by that which was given by mouth, named **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Cabale."</note>. Josephus, in book 4, chapter 7 of his *Antiquities of the Jews*, held that Joshua was first taught by Moses in this Kabbalah, which he then taught to the seventy members of the **Sanhedrin** <note>The supreme council of ancient Israel.</note>, who thereafter communicated it from order to order to the Prophets, and the Prophets to the Sages—that is, to the Scribes and Pharisees, from whom the Rabbis boast of having learned it, as is well noted by the Hebrew author of the book titled **Ethics of the Fathers** <note>original: "Pirke Abot."</note>, chapter 1, in these words:

> Moses received the law from Sinai, and delivered it to Joshua, Joshua to the Elders, the Elders to the Prophets, and the Prophets delivered it to the men of the Great Assembly. <note>original Latin: "Mofes accepit legẽ de Sinay, & tradidit eam Iechochua..."</note> Upon which passage the Commentator has said: By "law" here the Hebrews do not understand the written law, but that spiritual or mystic law, that is, the meaning or explanation of the law. For the opinion of the Jews holds that Moses received a twofold law from the Lord on Mount Sinai: one which they call **Torah She-bi-khtav** <note>original: "Thorach Bicbab," meaning Written Law.</note>, that is, the law which is in writing, or delivered in writing; the other which they call **Torah She-be-al Peh** <note>original: "Thorah fcebealpé," meaning Oral Law.</note>, that is, the law which is in the mouth, or delivered by word of mouth. And they affirm that this latter was derived to posterity through Moses in a certain sequential order, such that Joshua was the first of all to receive it from Moses, which he later passed to the Elders, they in turn to the early Prophets, the early Prophets to the later ones, among whom the very last were Zechariah, Haggai, and Malachi; these delivered it to the men of the Great Assembly, who were Ezra and his company, who restored the law to its ancient splendor; from them the subsequent sages received it...

Moses, in chapter 23 of Numbers, cites the books of the wars or the battles of the Lord, named in Hebrew **Sefer Milchamot Yehovah** <note>original: "Sepher Milchamos Iehoua"</note>; Joshua, in his 10th chapter, speaks of the Book of the Just <note>The Book of Jasher</note>, and of the books titled in Hebrew **Kirjath-sepher** <note>original: "Kirithh Sepharim," literally "City of Books," which Othniel captured</note> which Othniel, under Caleb, conquered. The third book of Kings <note>Known today as 1 Kings</note> mentions the book of the words and days of Solomon. Ahasuerus speaks of the books of memories; Jonathan, in the book of Maccabees, speaks of the holy books and of the Spartans. The book of Chronicles <note>original: "Paralipomenon," the Greek name for the books of Chronicles</note> takes account of the books of Lamentations and the books of Samuel the Seer, along with those of the Prophet Nathan, Gad the Seer, Shemaiah the Prophet, Iddo the Seer <note>original: "Haddo le viuant"</note>, and Ahijah the Shilonite. The books of Jehu, son of Hanani, speak of the books of the traditions of the Jews. All these books are no longer to be found today, being known only by name, having been lost and consumed during the frequent captures of the city of Jerusalem, just as were the books that follow: namely, 204 books of Ezra, of which mention is made in the 4th book of Ezra, chapter 14; the volumes of the histories of Samuel; the sermons of Hozai, Shemaiah, and Jehu the Prophets; the books of the days of the Kings of Judah and Israel; the descriptions of Jeremiah; the commentaries of Judas Maccabeus; the journals <note>original: "ephemerides"</note> of the Priesthood of John; the five books of the histories of Jason of Cyrene, and infinite other books of which particular mention is made by **Johann Reuchlin** <note>original: "I. Reucl. Capnion," Reuchlin was often called by the Greek version of his name, Capnion</note> in Book 1 of *On the Art of the Kabbalah*; **Pietro Galatino** <note>original: "P. Galat."</note> in Book 1 of *The Secrets of the Catholic Faith*; and **Sixtus of Siena** <note>original: "S. Senen."</note> in Books 1 and 2 of his *Holy Library*. Among the number of these books, we shall place those which were also lost during the burning of the library of Darius, which was in Ecbatana, as Ezra says. The great **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** <note>original: "I. Pic de la Mirade"</note>, the miracle of his age, boasted and bragged in his time of having in his power several ancient and antique books composed in this same Kabbalah, amounting to the number of seventy volumes, which have not come to the particular knowledge of the learned and curious men of today. As for the Hebrew book titled **Yetzirah** <note>original: "Ietzirah"</note>, on creation, commonly attributed to the Patriarch Abraham, it is of the composition of **Rabbi Akiva** <note>original: "Akiba"</note>, esteemed in his time as the wisest and most learned of all the Talmudists. The book of **Zohar** <note>original: "Hazoar ou Zoar"</note>, or "of Splendor," is by **Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai** <note>original: "Simeon Ben Ioachai"</note>, who, to compose it, remained in a vast and dark cavern for 24 entire years; and also the book **Bahir** <note>original: "Habair"</note>, "of Brightness" or the "Elucidary." There are also found books in this Kabbalah composed by an **Abraham Abulafia** <note>original: "Alapsia"</note>, and the notable commentaries of **Rabbi Ramban** <note>Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nahmanides</note> under this collective name, being named **Rabbi Moses son of Nahman** on the secrets of the law, who is otherwise called **the Gerundese** <note>of Girona</note>; and the commentaries of the most learned and knowing of all the Rabbis, **Menachem Recanati** <note>original: "Mnahen Racanat"</note>, on the secrets of Ramban; and the *Book of the Perplexed* of the said Rambam <note>The text says "Ramban" but corrects the name in the following phrase</note>, ending in "Mem," that is to say, by **Rabbi Moses son of Maimon**, who is called **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides</note>; and the book of the *Gates of Justice* which **Rabbi Joseph son of Gikatilla** <note>original: "Carnitol," a variation of Gikatilla</note> composed in his life; and the book titled *The Gate* or *Of Clarity or Light* by **Rabbi Joseph Castilian** of Spain; and the *Book of Cruelties* <note>original: "liure des crudelitez," likely a misreading of a Hebrew title or "Beliefs"</note>, of which the author in Asia was **Rabbi Saadia**; and the book of the *Mystery of the Law* that the wise **Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abé Ezra"</note> composed; and the book of **Rabbi Hamai son of Hanina**, which is called the most excellent chief or pillar of the Kabbalah, titled *Of Speculation*; and another book titled *Commentary of Holiness* which **Rabbi Azriel** composed; and the book of names,

...and the book of the explanations of the alphabet and the Hebrew characters by Rabbi Akiva; the book by Rabbi Hama on the secrets of Psalm 19; the singular book of "Union and Collection" mentioned by Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra in the first chapter of *The Mystery of the Law*; the book of mysteries; the book of abstruse and hidden questions; the book of Kabbalah composed by Azariel (otherwise known as Oriel of Girona); the book titled *Of Faith and Expiation*; the book of roots by Rabbi Joseph Albo (otherwise regarding the Kabbalah); and the books titled *Raziel the Great* and *Raziel the Less* belonging to the said Kabbalah. Beyond these books, we possess a most elegant work within this Kabbalah directed against the pseudo-philosophers <note>original: "Philosophrastes"</note> titled *Al Khazari* <note>original: "Alkoster"</note>, written in the Arabic style, composed by Rabbi Judah Halevi, from which these words, among others, are taken:

> That the Kabbalah is good only when accompanied by a good heart.

There are also commentaries within this Kabbalah on the *Book of Yetzirah* <note>The Book of Formation, an early mystical text</note> cited below, composed by Rabbi Jacob Cohen; and further, a composition by Rabbi Isaac entitled by him *Explanation of the Holy Name*; and in addition, a book composed by Rabbi Todros Ha-Levi <note>original: "Tedacul Leui"</note> on the ten Kabbalistic numerations <note>The Sephirot, or divine attributes</note>; and several other books and writings spoken of by Rabbi Abraham the Levite, son of David, in the work titled *Seder Olam* <note>Order of the World</note>, as reported by Sixtus of Siena in book 2 of his *Holy Library*. Some make a point of including among the books mentioned above the work composed by Solomon under the name of Raziel; but this must not be tolerated because it is a work entirely filled with magic, recently invented by wicked men and impostors. And among all the good and excellent books we have today regarding this Kabbalah, the books of Rabbi Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla of the city of Salamanca, titled *Ginnat Egoz* <note>The Nut Garden</note>, stand above the rest, as we have already remarked previously.

As for the division of this Kabbalah, some Kabbalists divide it into only two types: one of *Bereshit* <note>Genesis/Creation</note>, which concerns natural and perceptible things, and the other of the *Merkavah* <note>The Chariot</note> or divine throne, which concerns intellectual things abstracted from coarse matter. The first type is true Physics and natural philosophy, declaring the great workmanship of the world and secret things hidden under allegories, and refuting the opinions of other philosophers contrary to the Law of God. The other type is named *Merkavah*, or the Throne of God after the vision of Ezekiel, wherein the Majesty of God accompanied by His angels is depicted; this is high and difficult, yet it ravishes the intellect in admiration and contemplation of the intelligible world, which the Hebrews call the "upper waters," and Physics the "lower waters." Solomon, in the 22nd chapter of his Proverbs, seems to divide it into three parts: "words of truth" <note>original Hebrew: *imre emet*; Latin: *eloquoia veritatis*</note>, words of truth written "according to the way of truth" <note>original Hebrew: *alei emet*</note>, which is the Kabbalah—as held by the "Egyptian Rabbi" <note>Maimonides</note> and the "Rabbi of Girona" <note>Nachmanides</note> in their writings. Others among the aforementioned Kabbalists divide it into five parts, according to the report of Rabbi Hamai in his *Book of Speculation*: namely, into rectitude, combination, prayer, sentence, and calculation <note>original: "supputation," likely referring to Gematria</note>. To this the great Giovanni Pico della Mirandola seems to adhere in his 90 questions or conclusions, saying: "Whatever other Kabbalists may say, I would distinguish the science of Kabbalah in its primary division into the science of *Sephirot* and *Shemot*—that is, of numbers and names—as into the practical and the speculative," etc. <note>original Latin: "quicquid dicant cæteri Cabaliſtæ, ego prima diuisione ſcientiam Cabalæ, in ſcientiam Sephirot & Semoth id eſt numerorum & nominum, tanquam in practicam & ſpeculatiuum distinguerem &c."</note>

<page-num>56</page-num>
# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

Rabbi *Joseph Bar Abraham of Jerusalem* <note>original: "Salemitain"</note>, and a great many other Kabbalists, follow the opinion of *Solomon* alleged above, in that they believe their Kabbalah can not only be contemplated in three ways: but also fully practiced according to the triple condition, number, figure, and weight of all things. They hold that this entirely allegorical Kabbalah occurs when one thing is understood for another, when one sentence is nevertheless taken for another, and when one word is taken for another word, or one letter for another letter. 

First, a word is taken for another word, either by transposition (which is called <term>Metathesis</term> <note>The rearrangement of letters in a word</note>), or by an equal numerical value included within the words. A letter is taken for a word, at the beginning, at the end, or in whatever part it is placed, by attaching a mark to it. A letter is taken for a letter by a revolution of the Hebrew alphabet, so that every proportion is fulfilled—namely Arithmetic, Geometry, and Music—as the author of the *Sefer Yetzirah* <note>original: "Sepher Iezirah"; The Book of Formation</note> explains at length. 

Some other Kabbalists divide this Kabbalah into the calculation of numbers called <term>Gematria</term> <note>original: "גימטריא"; a system of assigning numerical value to a word or phrase</note>; much like a mutual numerical dimension of earthly characters, which nevertheless depends on that Arithmetic not graspable by the senses because of its abstract simplicity. Consequently, it is not subject to the crude skill of apprentices and novices; this is why this part was called Geometry rather than Arithmetic, although in truth both serve in this Kabbalistic use and art. Furthermore, letters and syllables are sometimes transformed in such a way that the word is also transformed, or the verb is simply converted and changed. 

Secondly, a letter is often put for a word: this is called <term>Notarikon</term> <note>A method of shorthand using the first or last letters of words to form new words or phrases</note>, because of the accents or abbreviations used by scribes <note>original: "notaires"</note>; for in this Notarikon, each letter is adorned at the top with certain Hebrew accents or points to teach that it is a sign of an entire word. 

Thirdly, this use and art consists in the mutation and change of letters, and this is when one letter is ingeniously put for another, which is called <term>Temurah</term> <note>Commutation or permutation of letters</note>. For this reason, Rabbi *Joseph of Jerusalem* titled his books of Kabbalah *Ginnat* <note>original: "גינת"; meaning "Garden"</note>, meaning *garden*, because of the three letters of this word, each of which represents one part of the Kabbalistic art: for *Gimel* <note>G</note> signifies <term>Gematria</term>, *Nun* <note>N</note> signifies <term>Notarikon</term>, and *Tav* <note>Th</note> signifies <term>Temurah</term>. Thus, Gematria (that is, Arithmetic), along with Notarikon and Temurah, form the principal parts of the entire Kabbalistic craft, according to the author of the aforementioned *Yetzirah*; Rabbi *Joseph Gikatilla* <note>original: "Carnitol"</note> in his books of the *Gates of Justice*; Rabbi *Jacob Cohen* in his book on the exposition of holy names; Rabbi *Akiva*; Rabbi *Abraham Ibn Ezra* in the book of the *Mysteries of the Law*; Rabbi *Judah* <note>Judah ben David Hayyuj</note>, the first among the Hebrew Grammarians, in his works; *Marinus* <note>Jonah ibn Janah</note> in his twenty books of literal instruction; and *Samuel ha-Nagid* in his twenty-two books on the same matter. 

Now, among the modern Latin authors who have written on the Kabbalah, *Pietro Galatino* <note>original: "P. Galatin"</note> has spoken of it as follows in his first book of the *Secrets of Catholic Truth*, chapter 1:

> To refute the stubbornness <note>original: "perfidiam"</note> of the Jews through their own Talmudic Scriptures, it is necessary above all to know that there are two types of teachings among them, which their Synagogue has never ceased to hold, both now and in former times...

One of these they call the <term>Written Torah</term> <note>original: "Thorah Sceuichetab"</note>, that is, the law which is in writing, or which was handed down in writing. The other they call the <term>Oral Torah</term> <note>original: "Thorah scebealpe"</note>, that is, the Law which is in the mouth, or which was handed down by mouth. They claim this is nothing other than the explanation of the law itself, which they assert was delivered to Moses along with the Written Law. For as the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> testify in the first chapter of the book called <term>Berakhot</term> <note>original: "Berachoth"; meaning "Blessings"</note>, Moses received both the law and the exposition of that law on Mount Sinai by the same spirit. This explanation of the law tends toward a double sense: namely, the literal and the spiritual or mystical. They affirm that Moses wrote down neither of these, but delivered both by word of mouth. And they say this is the law of which it is read in the <term>Pirkei Avot</term> <note>original: "Pirke Aboth"; meaning "Chapters of the Fathers," a collection of ethical teachings</note>: "Moses received the law from Sinai and delivered it to Joshua; Joshua to the elders; the elders to the prophets; and the prophets to the men of the Great Synagogue." This kind of tradition—as gathered from various volumes of the Talmudists and as reported by Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides</note> at the beginning of his *Deuteronomy*—happened in this order: When Joshua had received this exposition of the law from Moses, he delivered it to Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, who was the grandson of Aaron (whom we call by the corrupted name Phinees). Phinehas delivered it to Eli the priest. Eli to Samuel the prophet and priest. Samuel to King David. David to Ahijah the prophet. Ahijah to Elijah the prophet. Elijah to Elisha the prophet. Elisha to Jehoiada the high priest. Jehoiada to Zechariah the prophet. Zechariah to Hosea the prophet. Hosea to Amos the prophet. Amos to Isaiah the prophet. Isaiah to Micah the prophet. Micah to Joel the prophet. Joel to Nahum the prophet. Nahum to Habakkuk the prophet. Habakkuk to Zephaniah the prophet. Zephaniah to Jeremiah the prophet. Jeremiah to Baruch the Scribe. Baruch to Ezra the priest and scribe. Up to this point, we do not read that the Jews had any other scripture besides the Bible, although they call it the <term>Holy Sanctuary of God</term> <note>original: "Macdesciya"; likely a corruption of Mikdash-yah</note>, since until that time, no one was found to have committed anything regarding the exposition of the law to letters.

**Chapter.** So that it remains hidden from none of us which books the Jews receive as sacred and divine, tell me, I pray, in what way is the <term>Holy Sanctuary</term> <note>original: "Macdesciya"</note>—that is, the Bible itself—distinguished among them?

**Galatinus.** The Jews call the Bible <term>The Twenty-Four</term> <note>original: "Arbaa veefrim"; referring to the 24 books of the Hebrew Bible</note> because it contains that many books. They divide it into four parts. The first part they call the <term>Torah</term> (the Law) or <term>Chumash</term> <note>original: "Humas"; meaning "the five-fold"</note>, which the Greeks call the <term>Pentateuch</term>. It contains five books, which they name from their opening words. Indeed, they call the book of Genesis <term>Bereshit</term> <note>original: "Berescith"</note>, which means "In the beginning." Exodus they call <term>Ve-elleh shemot</term> <note>original: "Veelle scemoth"</note>, that is, "And these are the names." Leviticus is <term>Va-yikra</term> <note>original: "Vaiera"</note>, meaning "And He called." Numbers is <term>Be-midbar Sinai</term>, "In the desert of Sinai." Deuteronomy is <term>Elleh ha-devarim</term> <note>original: "hadeuarim"</note>, that is, "These are the words." The second part comprises four books, which they call the <term>Former Prophets</term> <note>original: "Neuim rissonim"</note>. These are Joshua; <term>Shofetim</term> <note>original: "Sophtim"</note>, which is Judges; Samuel, which among us contains the first and second book of Kings; and <term>Melakhim</term>, which is Kings, comprising what we call the third and fourth books of Kings. The third part also contains four books, which are called <term>Prophets</term> <note>original: "Neuim"</note>...

They call these the <term>Latter Prophets</term> <note>original: "Aharonim"</note>. These are Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the book of the 12 Prophets, whom we call the Minor Prophets. Finally, the fourth part, which they call the <term>Writings</term> <note>original: "Chetuvim," also known as the Hagiographa</note>, contains eleven books, the first of which is titled the <term>Words of the Days</term> <note>original: "Dibre haiamin"</note>, which we call by the Greek word <term>Paralipomenon</term> <note>meaning "things omitted," known today as Chronicles</note>. The second is the <term>Praises</term> <note>original: "Tehilloth" or "Tehillim," or by the shortened "Tillim"</note>, although "Tillim" also signifies "heaps," the singular of which is "Tel." This is not entirely out of place, since the Psalms are, as it were, certain heaps of spiritual maxims; this book we call by the Greek name <term>Psalter</term>. The third is the <term>Proverbs of Solomon</term> <note>original: "Misle Scelomo"</note>, or rather his Parables. The fourth is <term>Job</term> <note>original: "Iiob"</note>, whom we call Job by a corrupted pronunciation. The fifth is Ruth; the sixth is the <term>Preacher</term> <note>original: "Cohelet," meaning an assembly or a sermon</note>, whom we call Ecclesiastes. The seventh is <term>How</term> <note>original: "Echa"</note>, which is titled by us as the book of Lamentations or Threnodies. The eighth is the <term>Song of Songs</term> <note>original: "Scir Hafcirim"</note>. The ninth is Esther; the tenth is Daniel; and finally, the eleventh is Ezra, which they count as one book along with Nehemiah. These 24 books just enumerated are the only ones the Jews hold as sacred and divine. For although they possess the books of Jesus Son of Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and the first book of Maccabees, they do not include them among the twenty-four. As for the third and fourth books of Ezra, I myself have not yet seen them in Hebrew, though some among them say they have been recently found in Constantinople. I have found the second book of Maccabees and the book of Philo the Jew (which is called the Wisdom of Solomon) nowhere among the Hebrews, having only seen them in Greek. Furthermore, the Hymn of the Three Children and the stories of Susanna, Bel, and the Dragon—which we have within Daniel—they do not have at all. Beyond the aforementioned 24 books, it is certain that no scripture existed among the Jews until the time of Ezra. Indeed, the commentaries on the law themselves, both literal and spiritual or mystical, were spread only through a certain order of oral succession from the lawgiver Moses himself down to the Babylonian migration, shared among the Prophets and the wise men. But after the Babylonian captivity, as Ezra himself was rewriting the law which had been burned in the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the Temple, the other wise men began to write down the exposition of that law. They did this lest, if another destruction of the city should happen to occur in which all the wise men might perish, the explanation of the law might perish along with them. This was indeed done so that all those wise men who lived from the Babylonian migration until the first writing of the <term>Talmudic</term> code—who are also called the "Men of the Great Synagogue" in the <term>Chapters of the Fathers</term> <note>original: "Pirke Auoth"</note> and who were known to have taught the law—handed down the exposition of that same law to their listeners both by word and in writing. Their authority among the Jews is so great that their writings, from which the <term>Talmud</term> was later composed, hold the first place after the Prophets. And not without merit, since their doctrine was handed down to them immediately by the Prophets themselves, whose disciples and successors they were.

The teacher of the law himself handed down the exposition to Simon the High Priest, who is called Jaddus. This Jaddus, or Simon, handed the exposition of the law itself to Antigonus of Soko <note>original: "patria sichæo"</note>. Antigonus then to Joseph son of John, and to Joseph son of Joezer. These in turn to Nittai of Arbela, and to Joshua son of Perahiah, whose student the later Jews falsely claim our Redeemer, Jesus, to have been. But it is clearly shown that they lie openly from this: that from the first Hyrcanus <note>John Hyrcanus, the Hasmonean leader</note>, in whose times this Joshua flourished, until Pilate under whom Christ suffered, 110 years passed. These men, Nittai and Joshua, again handed down the exposition of the law to Judah son of Tabbai and Simon son of Shetah. These then to Shemaiah and Abtalion. These indeed to Hillel and Shammai, about whom Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the famous 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> reports many remarkable things in his book of *Antiquities*.

Hillel flourished, as is said at the beginning of the book <term>Sabbath</term> <note>a tractate of the Talmud</note>, 100 years before the destruction of the second Temple; and as is read in the <term>Bava Batra</term> <note>another Talmudic tractate</note>, he had 80 disciples, all endowed with excellent talent and learning. All of these, by reason of their discipline, were called his sons; and they were so outstanding that (as is read in the same place) 30 of them were worthy that the Divine Presence <note>original: "divinitas," referring to the Shekhinah</note> should descend upon them, just as it had for Moses himself; 30 indeed were worthy that the Sun should stand still for them, as it did for Joshua. The remaining twenty were called "mediocre," of whom the greatest was Jonathan son of Uzziel, and the smallest of all was Johanan son of Zakkai, whom the Jews call <term>Rabban Johanan ben Zakkai</term> <note>original: "Rabá Iohaná ben zaccai"</note>. Who nevertheless (as the ancient Talmudists said) did not neglect to know the Scripture, or the <term>Talmud</term>, or anything else, down to the "parables of foxes" and "stories of demons."

If therefore he, who is remembered as the smallest of all Hillel's disciples, turned out to be so great a sage, what must be thought of the others? Hillel and Shammai handed down the exposition of the law to the same Johanan son of Zakkai, and to Simeon the Just, the son of Hillel himself. This order, derived thus far, is drawn from the "chapters of the fathers" called <term>Pirkei Avot</term> <note>original: "Pirke auoth," a foundational collection of ethical teachings</note>. Where the last of all is placed: Simeon the Just, who took Christ into his arms <note>The author here identifies the Talmudic Simeon with the Simeon from the Gospel of Luke who witnessed the presentation of Jesus in the Temple</note>. 

Yet Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>, continuing this order of teaching further, says that the same Simeon the Just had as a student Gamaliel, surnamed the Elder, at whose feet the Apostle Paul learned the law. And so this Gamaliel was that teacher of the law, most highly held in observance by the whole Jewish people. Next, his student was Rabban Simeon his son, who was later killed by Hadrian Caesar. Who finally also had his son named Judah as a student, whom the Jews, for the excellence of his teaching and integrity, surname <term>Rabbenu HaKadosh</term> <note>original: "Rabbenu haccados," meaning "Our Holy Master"; he is credited with redacting the Mishnah</note>. There was, however, another "Holy Master" who flourished in the time of the Roman consuls, both in doctrine and in the spirit of prophecy, and who performed many and indeed wonderful things, which results in the fact that very few are able to grasp a right understanding of him.

If some think they have attained anything from this [knowledge], they soon hide it in their heart as a secret to be revealed to no one, lest because of the holy Trinity of divine persons and other mysteries of Catholic truth shining forth there, some of the Jews might happen to be scandalized. Therefore it is no wonder if this name <term>Cabala</term> <note>Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition</note>, or the faculty designated by that name, has been rarely on the lips of the saints and other wise men until now, and if our ancients did not remember it. Yet among the younger men, some who are skilled in the Hebrew tongue, and outstanding beyond others in their diligent talent and divine philosophy, have recognized the utility and excellence of this science...

The great Pico della Mirandola <note>original: "Picus de la Mirande," the famous Italian Renaissance philosopher</note> in the prologue of his *Apology*:

> After the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus, and the Temple was restored under Zerubbabel, they applied their minds to repairing the Law. Ezra, then the leader of the assembly <note>original: "Eccleſiæ præfectus"</note>, after the book of Moses had been emended, clearly recognized that through the exiles, slaughters, flights, and captivity of the Israelite people, the custom established by the ancestors of handing down doctrine by hand <note>meaning oral transmission</note> could not be preserved. He feared that the secrets of the heavenly doctrine, granted to them by divine favor, would perish, for their memory could not last long without the intervention of commentaries. He therefore decreed that the remaining wise men should be called together, and each should bring into the open what he held in his memory concerning the mysteries of the Law. Notaries were employed to compile seventy volumes—for there were roughly that many wise men in the Sanhedrin <note>original: "Sanhedrio," the supreme council of ancient Israel</note>. Regarding this matter, those who do not believe me should hear Ezra himself speaking thus: "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: The first things you wrote, place in the open, that the worthy and unworthy may read them; but the last seventy books you shall preserve, to hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge." And so I did. These are the words of Ezra, verbatim. These are the books of the science of the Kabbalah <note>original: "Cabalę"</note>, in which Ezra rightly pronounced with a clear voice that there was a "vein of understanding"—that is, an ineffable theology regarding the substantial deity from above; a "fountain of wisdom"—that is, a precise metaphysics concerning intelligible and angelic forms; and a "river of knowledge"—that is, a most firm philosophy concerning natural things. Pope Sixtus IV <note>reigned 1471–1484</note>, who immediately preceded this Pope Innocent VIII under whom we now happily live, took the greatest care and zeal to ensure that these books were translated into Latin for the public benefit of our faith; and by the time he passed away, three of them had reached the Latins. Among the Hebrews in this time, these books are revered with such devotion that no one is permitted to touch them unless they are forty years old. When I had acquired these books at no small expense, and had read through them with the utmost diligence and untiring labor, I saw in them—God is my witness—not so much the Mosaic religion as the Christian. There is the mystery of the Trinity; there, the incarnation of the Word; there, the divinity of the Messiah; there, I read about original sin, its expiation through Christ, the heavenly Jerusalem, the fall of the demons, the orders of the Angels, purgatories, and the punishments of hell. I read the same things that we read daily in Paul and Dionysius, in Jerome and Augustine.

These words are repeated word for word by this author in his *Oration on the Dignity of Man*, and by Crinitus <note>Pietro Crinito, a disciple of Poliziano</note> in book 25, chapter 3, of *Honest Discipline*: saying furthermore in his treatise on magic and Kabbalah:

...does not explain literally; so too Levi ben Gershon <note>Also known as Gersonides (1288–1344), a medieval Jewish philosopher</note> and many others, and before all, Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>original: "Rabbi Moſes Ægyptius," referring to Maimonides (1138–1204)</note>. The anagogical sense <note>the spiritual or "upward-leading" interpretation of scripture</note> is called Kabbalah. This is because that exposition, which is said to have been delivered by the mouth of God to Moses and received through succession in the manner previously described, almost always follows the anagogical sense. This sense is the most sublime and divine of all, leading us upward from earthly things to heavenly ones, from things perceived by the senses to things understood by the mind, from the temporal to the eternal, from the lowest to the highest, from the human to the divine, and from the bodily to the spiritual. It is from this that the most powerful arguments against the Jews are found; for the discord between them and us—as is most clearly evident from the epistles of Paul—depends entirely on this: that they follow the "killing letter," while we follow the "vivifying spirit." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, a common theme in Christian Kabbalah</note>

**Johann Reuchlin**, called **Capnio**, in Book 1 of *The Art of Kabbalah*:
If it is common in human affairs, and even in somewhat lowly and manual crafts, for people to learn by listening and to trust those men they believe to be endowed with singular learning, should we then think that in the science of the highest and divine matters—which we can scarcely reach even in pairs, let alone by our own strength—the tradition and reception of holy men should be despised? This tradition is called **Kabbalah** in Hebrew. For Kabbalah is the symbolic reception of a divine revelation, handed down for the life-giving contemplation of God and separated forms <note>pure spirits or angels</note>; those who obtain this by heavenly inspiration are rightly called **Kabbalists**. Their disciples we shall call by the surname **Kabbalaeans**, and those who otherwise strive to imitate them are to be named **Kabalists**.

And following these words, this personage <note>Reuchlin</note> mentions the revelation made to Adam by the Angel Raziel, which was the principle and origin of this Kabbalah, as we have noted previously in this chapter. Since Adam's time, his children and successors were indoctrinated in this Kabbalah one after another by particular angels and celestial intelligences, as was said above; he also subsequently mentions the ancient authors of the said Kabbalah.

These authors are sometimes, because of Talmudic disputations, called *Thanaim or Dictators* <note>original: "Thanaim ſeu Dictatores," referring to the Tannaim, the rabbinic sages of the Mishnah</note>. Because of their meditations on the highest things—drawn from individual lower things toward the more excellent, received from their elders, and passed to posterity—they lean upon them with all their study and are called *Mekablim* in Hebrew <note>original: "Mekablim hebraicè," meaning 'those who receive'</note>. In our age, following the lead of Count Giovanni Pico della Mirandola—before whom their name was unknown to the Latin language—they are called **Kabalists** or **Kabbalics**.

Then he says:
Whatever lovers of the finest arts learn from natural science concerning Holy Scripture is equal to good gold, and is called the **Work of Creation** <note>original: "opus de Breſith," referring to Ma'aseh Bereshit, the study of physics and Genesis</note>. But that which we receive through spiritual science is called the **Work of the Chariot** <note>original: "opus de Mercana" (a variant of Merkabah), referring to Ma'aseh Merkabah, the study of metaphysics and the divine realm</note>, and it is equal to the finest and purest gold. For the Kabbalists write thus: The Work of Creation is the wisdom of nature, and the Work of the Chariot is the wisdom of divinity. And since each wisdom is concerned in some way with the world and those things that exist in the world, the opinion of the Talmudists and Kabbalists is unanimous on this point: that there are two worlds. The first is the intellectual world, which is called **Olam Ha-Ba** <note>original: "Olam Aba," the World to Come</note>, that is, the world to come for us. The second is the sensible world <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note>, which is called "this present world." This we receive from the words of our wise men, who speak thus of the studious worshiper of the divine name of forty-two letters:

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

Because such a one undoubtedly exists—that is, one beloved both above and below, inheriting two worlds, the present world and the world to come—for this reason, the Talmudists and Kabbalists are divided into two branches, although both arise and emanate from the same transmitted traditions. For both place their faith in the traditions of their ancestors, even when no rational explanation is given. But they are distinguished by this arrangement of their purpose: the happy and blessed Kabbalist transfers and translates all study, effort, counsel, labor, and diligence—indeed, the entire intention of his mind—from the sensible world <note>The physical world we perceive with our senses.</note> finally to the intellectual world.

The Talmudist, however, remains in the sensible world and does not transcend the soul of this universe. If he occasionally proceeds freely toward God and the blessed spirits, he does not approach God Himself as immanent and absolute, but rather as the Architect and Cause of things, occupied with His creations. He assigns angels to daily ministries and to carry out the effects of the divine will, always relating the contemplation of the highest things back to this lower world. Nevertheless, one of these branches often borrows the insights of the other and draws them toward its own desires.

Indeed, Talmudists and Kabbalists sometimes exchange their studies back and forth, much like the active and contemplative lives. Though they often use the same context of Sacred Scripture, one invites toward "servile fear" and the other toward "filial love" <note>original: "timorem servilem... amorem filialem"; a distinction between fearing God as a slave fears a master versus loving God as a child loves a parent.</note> through their own pleasant persuasions. For that Talmudist will be seen residing with sharp study over the precepts and mandates of the Law, explaining them, arranging and directing them, venerating and kissing them. Thus, we might correctly define the Talmud as nothing other than an explanation of the Law according to the author's intention.

Hence the Talmudists are called "Expositors" and Pharisees, who, from the pulpit and the chair of Moses, are always intent on their work, preaching and exhorting the common people, saying with the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note>: *Serve the Lord in fear*, and with Joshua: *Fear the Lord and serve Him.* Furthermore: "Do this in such a way, and omit that with such-and-such moderation," from which they have reduced the 613 commandments—summed up in the single word <gloss>Taryag</gloss> <insert>תריג</insert> <note>The Hebrew letters Tav, Resh, Yud, and Gimmel add up to 613 in gematria.</note>—into two headings: "Do" and "Do not do," which you are accustomed to calling affirmative and negative commandments, which are very helpful to know and quite necessary in practice.

The Kabbalists, however, although they are men who piously observe the Law (as truth bears witness), lean more toward contemplation; therefore, they are called "men of speculation" among the masters of the Law. These men leave to the Talmudists the care of the state and private affairs at home, the rituals and customs of war, and judicial and moral matters along with their history. They have reserved for themselves only those things which pertain to the peace and tranquility of the soul and to the love of God. For they say: "The intention of the entire Law consists of two things: the good disposition of the soul and the good disposition of the body." For the whole Law tends primarily toward the perfection of man, and according to it, we attain two perfections: one of the mind and the other of the body. Truly, that which helps the soul and perpetuates life is far worthier and of a higher preeminence, even though a suitable condition and proper composition of the body comes first in time and nature. Therefore, the Kabbalists must be held in a higher place and a worthier degree, as they follow that exposition of the Law which, through certain symbols, most powerfully impels the elevation of the mind toward the heavens and toward divine matters. The Greeks call this <term>anagogical: a method of spiritual interpretation that seeks to lead the mind from the literal text to a higher, mystical meaning</term> instruction, which not only...

## LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

Philosophy, but also Wisdom [Sophia] itself—from which the "wise" are rightly named, as Solomon the Preacher says—because they travel to where life is; and according to the capacity of mortals, while still dwelling in these small bodies, they ascend from time to eternity and from the lowest things to the highest, and so forth. And toward the end he says: Once the weight of worldly cares is removed and the fallacies of old wives' arguments <note>original: "anilium disputationum sophismatibus"; a common scholarly phrase for trivial or superstitious debates.</note> are despised, the happy Kabbalist, through Kabbalah—that is, the path of what is received and believed—breaks through the darkness and leaps into brilliance, by which he attains light. Thus, he migrates from light into the Light, and through that Light, as much as human nature can grasp, he comprehends that luminous Word under the category of "being," but not of "non-being," unless this occurs through the abstraction of all things that are not the absolutely first Principle. Since the mind of the Kabbalist frequently travels this path through ineffable joy and alacrity of spirit, leaving behind humble and earthly things within the secret of deep silence, it is transferred to super-celestial and invisible things. Transcending all human sense, though still a guest in mortal skin, he nevertheless becomes a companion of the Angels, like a certain inhabitant of a super-celestial home, whose frequent conversation is known to be in the heavens. Then, at times, he walks with them toward higher things as companions of his journeys and visits the soul of the Messiah; at other times, he descends to lower things—both celestial and other virtues of nature—under Angelic guidance, yet not without his own reason. He strives to understand their dignities and operations and to venerate them with singular honor. From this arises the intimate friendship of the Kabbalist with the Angels, through which, sometimes correctly knowing the divine names, he performs wonderful things which the common people call miracles. For example, <term>Rabbi Meyr</term> <note>A famous Jewish sage of the 2nd century, known for his learning and miracle-working.</note>, through a divine name—even when uttered by a Gentile—preserved his own wife's sister from the corruption of a brothel; though she was forced into prostitution, no debauchee <note>original: "ganeorum"; referring to profligate or gluttonous men.</note>, however robust, was able to violate or dishonor her once the word was spoken. These things are recited in the opening of the *Gate of Light* <note>Referring to the "Sha'are Orah," a foundational Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note>, along with many other examples and their authors. Such operation of miracles was so easy in the memory of the fathers for the Kabbalists that they were often ignominiously called "cunning magicians" by the envious and profane—as if <term>Michael</term> <note>The archangel associated with mercy and divine intervention.</note> had not performed those works, but rather, and most especially, <term>Samael</term> <note>In this context, associated with dark forces or the "left side" of the spiritual realm.</note>, namely through Egyptian incantations and certain secrets. Nevertheless, the rod of the Kabbalists always devours the rods of the charlatans <note>A reference to Aaron's rod devouring the rods of Pharaoh's magicians in Exodus.</note>, and anything divine acts healthily, whereas anything demonic tends toward destruction. For the art of Kabbalah always tends toward the salvation of men, whereas the poison of magical vanity always turns toward perdition—the latter through the names of darkness and evil spirits, the former through the names of light and the blessed Angels. In the 3rd book following:

We feel that Kabbalah is nothing other than—to speak in the manner of the Pythagoreans—symbolic Theology, in which not only letters and names are signs of things, but even the things themselves are signs. By this we observe that almost all the philosophy of <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>The Greek philosopher often linked by Renaissance thinkers to ancient Hebrew wisdom.</note> originated from the Kabbalists, as he transferred a similar symbolic method of teaching to the Greeks.

Afterward, speaking of the secrets of the Kabbalists: from this is born that enumeration of the fifty gates of intelligence, over which the studies of the Kabbalists labor so greatly. These were divinely received by <term>Moyse</term> [Moses], the servant of God, whose knowledge he himself also handed down to us, his descendants, as the condition of the universe—

Philosophy, but also <term>Sophia</term> <note>Greek for wisdom; the author equates it with the Hebrew concept of Chokhmah.</note> itself—that is, wisdom, from which they are rightly named "wise men"—as the preacher Solomon says, because they proceed to where life is. This is not the way of "non-being," unless this happens through the abstraction of all things that are not the absolutely first principle. 

Frequently, by this path—through an ineffable joy and alacrity of spirit—the mind of the Kabbalist itself, within the secret of a profound silence, leaves behind humble and earthly things. It is transferred to super-celestial and invisible things that transcend all human sense. Then, although still a guest in a mortal skin, he nevertheless becomes a companion of the Angels, like a resident of the super-celestial dwelling whose frequent conversation is known to be in heaven. Sometimes he walks with them as companions of his journeys to higher places and visits the soul of the <term>Messiah</term>. At other times, he descends to the lower powers of nature—both celestial and otherwise—under Angelic guidance, yet not without his own reason. He strives to understand their dignities and operations and to venerate them with singular honor. From this arises the intimate friendship of the Kabbalist with the Angels, through which, sometimes by correctly knowing the divine names, he performs wonderful things which the common people call miracles. 

For instance, <term>Rabbi Meir</term> <note>A famous Jewish sage of the 2nd century; the story refers to him rescuing his sister-in-law from a Roman brothel.</note>—through a divine name, even one uttered by a Gentile—preserved his own wife's sister from the corruption of a brothel. Although she had been forced into prostitution, no lecher, however robust, was able to violate or defile her once the word was spoken. These things are recited in the preface to the *Gates of Light* <note>original: "Portae Lucis," likely referring to the work *Sha'are Orah* by Joseph Gikatilla.</note> and many other such things are cited with their authors. Indeed, the operation of miracles was so easy for the Kabbalists in the memory of the fathers that they were often ignominiously called "cunning magicians" by the envious and profane. It was as if <term>Michael</term> <note>The archangel associated with mercy and Israel.</note> had not performed those works, but rather <term>Samael</term> <note>In Jewish lore, the main archangel of death and accuser; often associated with dark magic.</note>—namely through Egyptian incantations and certain secrets. Nevertheless, the staff of the Kabbalists always devours the staffs of the tricksters <note>A reference to Aaron's rod swallowing the rods of Pharaoh's magicians in Exodus.</note>, and a healthy divine power does more than any demonic one. For the art of Kabbalah always tends toward the salvation of men, whereas the poison of magical vanity always inclines toward destruction—the latter through the names of darkness and evil spirits, the former through the names of light and the blessed Angels. 

In the following third book:

We feel that Kabbalah is nothing else but—to speak in the Pythagorean way—symbolic Theology, in which not only are letters and names signs of things, but things are signs of other things. By this we observe that almost all the philosophy of <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>Ancient Greek philosopher known for the "music of the spheres" and the mystical significance of numbers.</note> arose from the Kabbalists, as he likewise transferred the symbolic method of teaching to the Greeks.

Afterward, speaking of the secrets of the Kabbalists:

From here arises that enumeration of the **fifty gates of intelligence** <note>In Kabbalah, these are levels of understanding the created universe.</note> about which the studies of the Kabbalists sweat so much. These were divinely received by Moses, the servant of God, and he himself handed down the knowledge of the condition of the universe to us, his posterity.

...those who reflect, guided by the Holy Spirit, could easily select, read, and gather letters from here and there, from above and below, back and forth, and form them into any words they pleased to create a sentence—signifying good things for the good, and evil for the wicked. We have accepted that this art of Kabbalah was divided into three paths, according to the testimony of Solomon, who says in Proverbs 22: "Indeed, I have written to you in a threefold way, with counsel and knowledge, that I might make known to you the certainty of the words of truth." <note>original Latin: "scripsi tibi tripliciter consultò & è sententia, vt notificarem tibi rectitudinem eloquiorum veritatis"</note> For our people are accustomed to speak in this way when mention is made of Kabbalah, calling it the <term>Words of Truth</term> <note>original Hebrew: אמרי אמת (*Imrei Emet*)</note>, that is, the Words of Truth written, to be sure, <term>according to the way of truth</term> <note>original Hebrew: על דרד האמת (*Al derekh ha-emet*)</note>, which belongs to the Kabbalah. This custom was frequent for the "Egyptian" of Gerona <note>referring to Nahmanides, also known as Ramban (1194–1270)</note> and others. But others have presented five parts of the Kabbalah, as Rab Hamai does in the *Book of Speculation*: *rectitude*, combination, *prayer*, *sentence*, and calculation. Your Pico della Mirandola <note>a famous Renaissance humanist who studied Jewish mysticism</note> wrote in his 900 conclusions in these words: "Whatever other Kabbalists may say, I would distinguish the science of Kabbalah in its primary division into the science of <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>the ten attributes or emanations of God</note> and <term>Semoth</term> <note>meaning "Names," referring to the Divine Names of God</note>, as if into practical and speculative branches." Since the whole business is allegorical, and one thing is understood for another by means of a third—so that the meaning itself is one thing in place of another—we will say plainly that either a word is placed for a word, or a letter for a word, or a letter for a letter. First, a word is taken for a word, either by transposition (which is called *metathesis*), or by an equal number included in the words <note>This is Gematria, where words with the same numerical value are linked</note>. A letter is placed for a word, either at the beginning, or at the end, or wherever one pleases by a mark placed above <note>This is Notarikon, using letters as acronyms</note>. A letter is placed for a letter through alphabetic revolution <note>This is Temurah, a system of letter substitution</note>, so that at last every proportion is clearly completed: Arithmetical, Geometrical, and Musical. For example, regarding that phrase from Psalm 21: *Lord, in your strength the King shall rejoice*: we understand this Kabbalistically as referring to the Messiah, saying: "Lord, through the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>the sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>, in your strength the King Messiah [rejoices]"—understand here "comes" or "works"—for the Messiah is the power of God, and works in the power of the Tetragrammaton. **Metatron** is a name equal in numerical value to **Shaddai** <note>One of the names of God in Hebrew. In Gematria, both *Metatron* (מטטרון) and *Shaddai* (שדי) sum to 314.</note>, as found in both terms, which the **Gerund** <note>Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar from Gerona.</note> marvelously embraces in the place cited earlier. Do you see now the two symbolic paths of the **Kabbalah**? Do you also wish to see the third, where a letter is put in place of a word? Read **Isaiah** chapter 65: *He shall be blessed in God, Amen.* And who is this God? The Kabbalists will answer that He is the *Melech Ne'eman* <note>original Hebrew: מלך נאמן, meaning "Faithful King."</note>, that is, the Lord, the Faithful King; for these three words are signified by their first letters, the three letters of *Amen* (A-M-N), as **Recanati** <note>Menachem Recanati, an early 14th-century Italian Kabbalist.</note> wrote on Exodus 15.

This same person makes mention of the <term>Ziruf</term> <note>The OCR reads "Zeoupſz"; this refers to *Tziruf*, the Kabbalistic practice of permuting and combining letters to find hidden meanings.</note> or commutations of Hebrew letters as the third species of this Kabbalah, along with other secrets and mysteries of which we provide an ample description and deduction later in this work, in the following chapters concerning the aforementioned secrets and mysteries of the Hebrew language.

Regarding King **Euergetes** <note>Ptolemy III Euergetes. This passage likely refers to the Prologue of the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus).</note>: after I arrived in Egypt, and when I had been there for a long time, I found books left there of no small or contemptible doctrine. From these words, it is clearly gathered that, besides the Law and the Prophets, other books were also written among the Hebrews long before the coming of Christ; for **Ptolemy Euergetes** himself—during whose time this **Joshua** reports having found such books in Egypt—died nearly two hundred and nine years before the birth of Christ.

This same author, in the following chapters 3, 4, 5, and 6, discourses at length on the Hebrew authors from whose writings the **Talmud** of the Jews was made and compiled, as I shall repeat in the following chapter; and he says the following concerning the Kabbalah:

The name "Kabbalah" is found neither among the holy fathers, nor among the doctors of the Church, nor among our masters. Because of this, the name is rendered highly suspicious. This faculty which they call Kabbalah was, in ancient times, forbidden to be handed down to anyone unless they were most learned and advanced in age. For this reason, it was not permitted to commit even a small part of it to writing; hence, besides those things said to have been handed down by **Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai** <note>Simeon bar Yochai, the 2nd-century sage to whom the *Zohar* is traditionally attributed.</note>, few or no other things written by the ancients are found. As it is said in the book <term>Chagigah</term> <note>original: "Hagiga"; a Talmudic treatise.</note>, that is, of the "solemnity," in the chapter <term>Ein Dorshin</term> <note>original: "Endorfin"; the Hebrew *Ein Dorshin* means "They do not expound," the name of a chapter in the Talmud (Chagigah 2:1) that restricts the teaching of mystical secrets.</note>—which means "they are not preached"—no one was permitted to write anything about the Kabbalah, but they handed it down by mouth only. Therefore, they not inaptly called it **Kabbalah**, which is interpreted in Latin as "reception." 

However, the doctors of more recent Jews, lest that ancestral dogma should vanish, published something of this faculty in writing, though scattered and obscured by certain veils. He wrote concerning Christ; for this reason, more recent Jews, deceived by the similarity of the name, think that he was this person.
