# 68
# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [THE LANGUAGES]

...[it is said that Moses] received a twofold law, both literal and spiritual. By God's command, he wrote down the first and shared it with the people; the second, however, he did not write at all, but communicated it only to seventy wise men. From these men, it was later passed on to others designated for the task by word of mouth alone. From this arose the name **Kabbalah**, which in the language of that nation signifies "Reception" <note>original: "Receptionem"</note>, because through the stages of succession, it was kept intact entirely without written records. In a later time, however, these mysteries themselves were captured in books, in which almost all things are found not to be at odds with our own faith. This is because they are said to have been arranged <note>original: "cincinnati," literally "curled" or "adorned," here implying the organized composition of the texts</note> before Christ by minds free from every biased affection. And because the science of Kabbalah was held among the secrets in ancient times, it became common practice among the Hebrews that whatever is less common and more passive is sanctified by the name of Kabbalah.

In general, however, they are observed to have honored two sciences by that name: the art of combining, which they call "alphabetic revolution" <note>original: "alphabetariam reuolutionem," likely referring to the Kabbalistic practice of Permutation or *Temurah*</note>; and the other, by which the powers of higher things are explained, which is also a form of Magic. But the whole matter was soon thrown into disorder among the Hebrews due to the emergence of some who were hardly different from sorcerers. These people especially claim the name of **Kabbalists** for themselves, preaching that they primarily hold the secret names of God and possess powers that give them authority over demons and the ability to perform miracles. Indeed, they even claim that Christ performed such wonders by no other method than the one they use.

They further maintain that this is the true and twofold Kabbalah said to have been handed down to Moses by God. Indeed, many things seem to support the idea that the Highest God revealed the mysteries contained in the Law to that great Prophet. This is especially true of that prophetic passage in **Esdras** <note>The biblical figure Ezra; the quote is from the apocryphal book 2 Esdras 14:4-6.</note>, where the Lord, speaking of Moses, says: "I told him many wonders, and showed him the secrets of the times and the end; I commanded him that some things he should make public, and others he should keep secret within himself." Furthermore, the great **Origen** <note>An influential early Christian scholar (c. 185–253 AD) who sought to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian theology.</note>, explaining that statement of the Apostle Paul, *first because the oracles of God were entrusted to them*, says we must consider that he did not say the *letters* were entrusted, but the **Oracles of God** <note>original: "Eloquia Dei"</note>. From this, one can perceive that something else, besides the law captured in letters, was granted to the Jews—which Paul calls the "oracles of God." You would call these nothing other than the **Kabbalah** itself: that is, the truest interpretations of the law, flowing from the divine mouth. Moreover, Origen calls the seventy elders, to whom alone the secrets were communicated, "admirable counselors," whose place in our religion is thought to be held by the **Cardinals**.

Five very swift scribes, receiving them from his mouth, wrote them down on boxwood tablets over forty-two consecutive days. Of these, Esdras published one hundred and twenty-six everywhere; but the remaining books, crafted with a more secret wisdom and a more sublime science, he entrusted with greater care only to the wise and the teachers skilled in the law...

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE
<page-num>70</page-num>

That Moses, besides the written law, revealed another spiritual or mystic law—that is, a separate, secret explanation of that same written law—is testified by Ezra, Paul, Origen, and Hilary. Of these, Ezra, in the beginning of the 14th chapter of his fourth book <note>original: "Esdras lib. 4. in principio 14. capit." This refers to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra in some traditions), which was highly influential in mystical circles.</note>, introduces God speaking to him thus: "Revealing, I was revealed to Moses upon the bush, when my people served in Egypt, and I brought him up onto Mount Sinai. I kept him with me for many days, and I told him many wonders, and showed him the secrets of the times and the end, and I commanded him, saying: *These words you shall make public, and these you shall hide.*" 

Origen, agreeing with Ezra when explaining that passage in Romans (that the <term>Utterances of God</term> <note>original: "Eloquia Dei"</note> were entrusted to them), says that not only were the written letters entrusted to the Jews by God, but also these "utterances." From this statement of Origen, it is indicated that besides the literal law, something else was handed down to the Jews, which Paul here calls the "utterances of God." 

Furthermore, Hilary, in his exposition of the second Psalm, testifies to this same thing even more clearly, saying: "It had already been established by Moses in every synagogue that there should be seventy <term>doctors</term> <note>meaning teachers or learned elders</note>. For even though Moses had set down the words of the Old Testament in writing, he had nevertheless separately disclosed certain more secret mysteries from the hidden parts of the law to the seventy elders, who would thereafter remain as teachers." The Lord also mentions this teaching in the Gospel, saying: "The Scribes and Pharisees have sat in the <term>Chair of Moses</term> <note>original: "cathedram Mosis." A metaphor for the authority to interpret the Law.</note>; therefore, observe and do all that they have told you, but do not do according to their works." The teaching of these men, therefore, remained for posterity, having been received from the writer of the law himself and preserved through the service of this number of elders. Thus says Hilary. 

Since, therefore, nothing concerning this more secret explanation had been written down until the time of the Babylonian captivity, Ezra—after the rebuilding of the city and the restoration of the law by his hand—wished to commit this kind of <term>Cabalistic</term> <note>the term "Kabbalah" literally means "that which is received" or "tradition."</note> exposition and explanation of the letters to written records. He did this lest it should perhaps be lost due to the Jewish captivities and dispersions, in which the order and ancient custom of handing down the Kabbalah by hand <note>meaning oral transmission</note> could not be preserved. Having therefore summoned to himself the most faithful scribes, he reduced all the mysteries of the Kabbalah into seventy books, according to the number of the seventy elders of the synagogue, to be shared in the future only with the wise. 

"When I diligently read through these books, which I purchased at great expense," <insert>writes Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, as quoted here</insert> "I found in them many things—indeed, almost everything—in harmony with our faith, with which Christians might run through the Jews with their own weapons, among whom the authority of the Kabbalists is held in great honor and reverence." 

The same Sixtus of Siena, in the book cited above, while interpreting these words, "Traditions of the Jews and traditions of the elders," speaks and discourses even more extensively on this matter.

-> Jacob Middendorp, *On Academies*. <-

Because of the idolatry of the Kings of the Jews and the most grave sins of the people, it happened that after the synagogue was destroyed, the sacred books were lost; they were barely found at last under King Josiah by studious men. However, while Zedekiah was reigning, Jerusalem was again devastated, and the Temple was burned along with the books. Truly, **EZRA** the Priest and Doctor of the law restored the books of Moses and the Prophets after the Babylonian captivity. Once they were brought into order, he interpreted them publicly, doing so every single day from the first to the last, as seen in 2 Ezra 8. 

Then he himself added other books: for Moses, besides the written laws, handed down certain more secret mysteries, just as he had received them from God, only to the wiser men (whom Origen calls "wonderful counselors"). For this reason, these secrets were called **Kabbalah**, or tradition,

...which was received not through letters, but by a certain succession, by hereditary right, one from the other. Just as in the Church of Christ, certain unwritten traditions <note>original: ἄγραφα (agrapha)</note> are believed to have been transmitted to us from the Apostles even until now, as if passed from hand to hand. For the Kabbalah was nothing else than a certain doctrine handed down by living voice, containing the most certain interpretation of the written divine law, which we read that Ezra <note>Esdras</note> reduced into books on the advice of seventy most learned men, lest the secrets of heavenly doctrine should perish if ever the custom of oral transmission established by the ancestors could not be observed due to wars and captivities. That the Jews preserved these so diligently in their synagogue, *Justin affirms in his Oration against the Gentiles*, happened not without the singular providence of God: lest Christians, in bringing them forward, might be seen as presenting forged or corrupted texts, giving cause for slander <note>original: αἰτίαν συκοφαντίας (aitian sykophantias)</note> to the malicious; hence they are called the "porters" or "chest-bearers" of the Christians by the blessed Augustine. *4 Kings 2. Josephus book 10. chapter 10. Eusebius book 3. chapter 8.*

Elias Levita in his third preface to the *Masoreth Hammasoreth*, following Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides</note> in his preface to the *Sefer Hamitzvot* <note>The Book of Commandments</note>, and on the Talmud in the treatise on vows, says: The Great Synagogue succeeded the Prophets, its leaders being Ezra, Nehemiah, Mordecai, Zerubbabel, and Joshua. These presided over a council of 120 men, some of whom were nobles and others commoners, who entered into the work of correcting the sacred books and establishing their canon according to the prescription of the Kabbalah; there they also ordained that Joshua had been so taught by Moses, the Elders by Joshua, and the Prophets by the Elders. The Notary or scribe of the Council—for so he is called in Ezra 7—was Ezra, whom they say was also joined (or rather led) by Daniel, Ananias, Azariah, Mishael, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. *Michael Neander* in his treatise on the Kabbalah of the Jews seems to confirm the above, as curious readers may see; as does Guillaume Postel in Book 1, chapter 3 of *The Harmony of the World* <note>original: "de orbis concordia"</note>. The Hebrews had, besides the sacred scripture, also their own interpreters of it, of two kinds. For from Moses himself until Christ, there were men of remarkable innocence whom they called by the Greek word <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>original: συνέδρους / סנהדרין (synedrous)</note>, as you might say "assessors," because they would meet in one senate or court when the most important matters were to be discussed, and would pass judgment on matters which held the weight of law and precedent. These spoke with two "tongues" (so to speak) when they relied on the authority of sacred scripture.

For between them and the Prophets there was a certain common revelation of mysteries, which they judged a sin to commit to writing. Therefore, they explained it only by word of mouth to their successors, called to that office according to the merits of their lives; and for that reason they called it קבלה *Gabalah* <note>Kabbalah</note>, because it was mutually received. This certainly contained the greatest mysteries, and was very similar to our <term>anagogical sense</term> <note>A spiritual interpretation that leads the mind from literal facts to heavenly or mystical meanings.</note>, by which we lead minds from corruptible things to heavenly ones. The other "tongue" was the interpretation common to all the learned, representing an allegory which was accustomed to be committed to writing and preserved. Thus, the anagogical interpreters were called Kabbalists; the allegorical ones, much later, were called Talmudists. But when Jesus Christ came in the time of Simeon—whom not only the Gospel but also those people call "the Just" and "Holy"—then the teacher and lawgiver failed from Israel. And a foreign king gained power. Then also the Holy Spirit departed from them, nor was there any prophecy or tradition of doctrine among the Jews afterward. Then the wise men and the remnants of the Jews gathered what they could from both interpretations into one body so that it would not perish, and first called it in Hebrew...

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

Repetition of the Law <note>original Hebrew: משנה תורה (*Mishnah Torah*)</note>, that is, the secondary law. Finally, as other opinions were added as time brought forth those authors who were discovered, they first wrote the *Talmud* <term>Talmud: The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah (oral law) and the Gemara (commentary)</term> from the *Mishnah*, having gathered the Jews from everywhere to Jerusalem; they called it the Jerusalem Talmud, approximately 300 years after the passion of Christ. Soon after, as other opinions arose, they composed another Talmud about 70 years later, having gathered the Jews in Babylon, whose teachers they had summoned from the whole world; they use that Talmud now. Many Kabbalistic traditions <term>Kabbalah: The ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible</term> abound in it, yet they are also scattered separately in many volumes.

Gilbert Génébrard <note>A 16th-century French Benedictine scholar and renowned Hebraist</note>, in Book 1 of his *Chronography*, speaking of the first age of the world and of the Kabbalah and the unwritten traditions from Adam and his children and descendants living during this age, said: *In this first age, the foundations of the pure and saving religion transmitted to us—which are to endure to the end of the world—are laid and flourish. The faithful were called the sons of God (Genesis 6); they were ruled by revelations (Genesis 2, 3, 4, 6, 7) and by the traditions of Adam; for traditions are older than the scriptures. Then they were ruled by the prophecies of Enos and Enoch. For it is not probable that Adam would have begrudged his children and posterity the traditions necessary for salvation, since such a thing would be unworthy of any parent, especially concerning God, His word, and the Spirit, whom he had seen and spoken with (Genesis 2) regarding the creation of the world, of which he had been the most noble part, so much so that he gave names to things at God's command according to the nature of each.*

*In the same place: Concerning the divine inspiration and production of the soul according to the image and likeness of God, which he himself had experienced (Genesis 1), and concerning the dignity and dominion of man over the rest of creation, which he himself had received.* 

*In the same place: Concerning the state of innocence from which he had fallen; concerning the fall and the sin he had committed as the source of all calamities. Concerning the garden of delight <note>The Garden of Eden</note>, a type of the future immortal life from which he had been cast out; concerning the angels, some of whom with a flaming and turning sword guarded the entrance of the garden (Genesis 2). Concerning the devils, enemies of the human race, and their temptations, one of whom had deceived him and his wife through the serpent. Concerning the seed of the woman, that is, Christ, who had been promised to him as a medicine for sin and misery (Genesis 3). Concerning the sanctifying of the Sabbath because of the benefit of creation; concerning the sanctity and laws of marriage, of which he himself had prophesied (Genesis 2). Concerning the sacrifices and the worship of God, concerning God's precepts and will, concerning death, penance, and the punishments for sins—all of which he had learned by experience, or through the spirit of God, or had conceived through the excellence and perfection of his own mind, talent, and nature.* 

*Finally, concerning all the mysteries most necessary for salvation, with which God had fully imbued him, not only as a Prophet but also as a man created immediately by Himself. For this reason, He seems to have extended Adam's life into his 930th year—that is, more than half of the first age—so that he might leave behind long-reaching roots of piety. From this time forward, the unity of God was maintained in the invocations and uses of the name YHWH <note>original Hebrew: יהוה (The Tetragrammaton), the personal name of God</note>, which does not take a plural form.* 

This same figure continues afterward with these words: *Traditions, such as those concerning clean and unclean animals (Genesis 7); concerning not entering into marriage with the impious and those of differing religions (Genesis 6); and concerning the sevenfold vengeance to be given for Cain (Genesis 4). For even God's conversation with Cain reached posterity after many centuries. Indeed, Lamech, the sixth from him around the seven hundredth year of the world, said: "sevenfold vengeance shall be given for Cain."* <note>original: R. (likely referencing a Rabbinic source)</note> *In the same place, the words of God were much more received "by hand" <note>passed down through oral tradition</note> to the pious: Adam, Eve, Abel, Enos, Enoch, Noah, etc.*

HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

The second, called <term>Masekhet Ketubot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת כתובות; the title refers to "written contracts," specifically the marriage contract.</note></term>, meaning the treatise on contracts, is divided into 13 chapters. These discuss marriage contracts, dowries, and the legal obligations that a husband must observe toward his wife, and a wife toward her husband.

The third, called <term>Masekhet Nedarim<note>original Hebrew: מסכת נדרים; "Tractate on Vows."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on vows, is divided into eleven chapters, which discuss the vows made by women.

The fourth, called <term>Masekhet Nazir<note>original Hebrew: מסכת נזיר; "Tractate on the Nazirite."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on the Nazirite, is divided into nine chapters. These discuss the vow of the Nazirites—those who "separate" themselves from the vanities of the world. During the term of their vow, they were not permitted, among other things, to drink wine or taste any liquor or product of the vine, nor to cut their hair, nor to touch any dead body.

The fifth, called <term>Masekhet Sotah<note>original Hebrew: מסכת סוטה; historically referring to a woman suspected of adultery.</note></term>, meaning the treatise on diversion or divorce, is divided into 9 chapters. These discuss the diversion or divorce involving a woman and her husband when she marries another. <note>The author uses the term "diversion" (diuersion) likely to describe the legal deviation from a marriage or the specific ordeal described in biblical law for a suspected wife.</note>

The sixth, <term>Masekhet Gittin<note>original Hebrew: מסכת גטין; "Tractate on Bills of Divorce."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on legal documents of divorce, is divided into nine chapters, which discuss the documents of repudiation and the dissolution of marriage.

The seventh, <term>Masekhet Kiddushin<note>original Hebrew: מסכת קדושין; "Tractate on Betrothals."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on betrothals, is divided into 4 chapters, which discuss betrothals and matters pertaining to them.

### THE FOURTH PART of the aforementioned Talmuds, named the *Order of Damages*, is likewise divided into seven books.

The first of these is called <term>Masekhet Nezikin<note>original Hebrew: מסכת נזיקין; "Tractate on Damages."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on dangers and nuisances; this section is itself divided into three <term>Bavot<note>original Hebrew: בבות; literally "Gates." The author translates this as "positions."</note></term>.

The first of these is called <term>Bava Kamma<note>original Hebrew: בבא קמא; "The First Gate."</note></term>, meaning the first position; it is divided into ten chapters, which discuss all the dangers and nuisances typically caused by both men and brute beasts.

The second is called <term>Bava Metzia<note>original Hebrew: בבא מציעא; "The Middle Gate."</note></term>, meaning the middle position; it is also divided into ten chapters, which discuss lawsuits, rights, usury, and rentals.

The third is called <term>Bava Batra<note>original Hebrew: בבא בתרא; "The Last Gate."</note></term>, meaning the final position; it is likewise divided into ten chapters, which discuss sales, shared fields, partnerships, and heirs and inheritances.

The second book is called <term>Masekhet Sanhedrin<note>original Hebrew: מסכת סנהדרין; referring to the High Court of ancient Israel.</note></term>, meaning the treatise on Ordinary Judges, and is divided into 14 chapters. These discuss at length the ordinary judges, judgments, and other matters pertaining to legal trials. It also discusses those who have a portion in the world to come under the Messiah, specifically in <term>Perek Helek<note>original Hebrew: פרק חלק; "Chapter Portion."</note></term>—that is, the chapter that begins with the word *Helek*, which means "portion."

The third, called <term>Masekhet Shevuot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת שבועות; "Tractate on Oaths."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on oaths, is divided into 8 chapters, which discuss oaths and especially the guardianship of property.

The 5th, called <term>Masekhet Avodah Zarah<note>original Hebrew: מסכת עבודה זרה; literally "Tractate on Strange Service."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on foreign service <note>A common early modern term for idolatry.</note>, is divided into five chapters. ## THE FIFTH PART of the aforementioned Talmuds named *Order of Sanctifications*, contains eleven books.

The 1st of which is called <term>Masekhet Zevachim<note>original Hebrew: מסכת זבחים; "Tractate of Animal Sacrifices."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on immolations, and is divided into 14 chapters. These treat extensively the immolations of sacrifices and the method and place of sacrificing.

The 2nd, called <term>Masekhet Chullin<note>original Hebrew: מסכת חולין; "Tractate of Profane (Ordinary) Things."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on killings, is divided into 12 chapters. These treat the slaughter and immolation of pure and clean animals <note>This refers to the laws of *Shechita*, the ritual slaughter of animals for food rather than for sacrifice.</note>.

The 3rd, called <term>Masekhet Menachot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת מנחות; "Tractate of Meal Offerings."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on flours, is divided into 13 chapters. These treat the wheat flours which must be offered in the temple.

The 4th, called <term>Masekhet Bekhorot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת בכורות; "Tractate of the Firstborn."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on the firstborn, is divided into 9 chapters. These treat the firstborn of animals—both those that must be offered and others that must be redeemed.

The 5th, called <term>Masekhet Arachin<note>original Hebrew: מסכת ערכין; "Tractate of Valuations."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on prices, is divided into 9 chapters. These treat the prices <note>The monetary value or assessment.</note> of things which people had promised to give to God.

The 6th, called <term>Masekhet Temurah<note>original Hebrew: מסכת תמורה; "Tractate of Exchange."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise of permutation, is divided into 7 chapters. These treat the prohibition of making any exchange of sacrifices.

The 7th, called <term>Masekhet Meilah<note>original Hebrew: מסכת מעילה; "Tractate of Sacrilege."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise of transgressions, is divided into six chapters. These treat the transgression of those who had made use of illicit things <note>Specifically the misappropriation or personal use of property belonging to the Temple.</note>.

The eighth, called <term>Masekhet Keritot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת כריתות; literally "Tractate of Excisions."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on perditions <note>The author uses "perditions" to describe *Karet*, a spiritual punishment where a soul is "cut off" from the community or the afterlife for certain grave sins.</note>, is divided into six chapters. In this, it treats the perdition of souls in the future world after this life for their sins, and others for which souls are lost.

The 9th, called <term>Masekhet Tamid<note>original Hebrew: מסכת תמיד; literally "The Continual [Offering]."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise of the continual or continuation—namely of the sacrifice—is divided into six chapters. In these, it treats the continual sacrifice of the two lambs that was to be performed in the temple.

The 10th, called <term>Masekhet Middot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת מדות; literally "Measurements."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on dimensions, is divided into five chapters. In these, it treats the dimensions and measurements of the temple.

The 11th, called <term>Masekhet Kinnim<note>original Hebrew: מסכת קנים; literally "Nests."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on nests, is also divided into five chapters, regarding the offerings of the young of doves and turtledoves, which the poor were required to offer in the temple.

### THE SIXTH PART of the aforementioned Talmuds, named the order of purifications, is divided into twelve books.

The 1st of these, called <term>Masekhet Kelim<note>original Hebrew: מסכת כלים; "Tractate of Vessels."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on vessels, is divided into thirty chapters. In these, it treats the purification of vessels of whatever kind or material they may be, and of cloths and garments which could be polluted by some contamination.

The 2nd, called <term>Masekhet Ohalot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת אהלות; "Tractate of Tents."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on habitations, is divided into 18 chapters. In these, it treats the purification of houses and other things from the contamination caused by the impurity of a dead body.

The 3rd, called <term>Masekhet Negaim<note>original Hebrew: מסכת נגעים; "Tractate of Plagues."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on wounds or persecutions <note>The author uses "persecutions" here to describe the afflictions of leprosy, which were viewed as a divine strike or "plague."</note>, is divided into fourteen chapters. In these, it treats the purification of human bodies from the impurity contracted as much by leprosy and other wounds, as well as by all other things destined for human use, because of these afflictions.

The 4th, called after the heifer, <term>Masekhet Parah<note>original Hebrew: מסכת פרה; "Tractate of the Heifer."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on the heifer or small cow, is divided into twelve chapters. In these, it treats the ashes of the heifer or red cow, through the sprinkling of the blood of which both men and all other things could be purified which were polluted by a dead human body.

The 5th, called <term>Masekhet Taharot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת טהרות; "Tractate of Purities."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on purifications, is divided into ten chapters. In these, it treats the purification of impurity that occurred by means other than that of a dead human body.

The 6th, called <term>Masekhet Mikvaot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת מקואות; "Tractate of Ritual Baths" or "Gatherings of Waters."</note></term>, that is to say, the treatise on congregations or collections of waters, is divided into two chapters <note>The original French text says "two," though the tractate *Mikvaot* contains ten chapters; this is likely a typographical error in the 16th-century source.</note>. The 7th, called <term>Masekhet Niddah<note>original Hebrew: מסכת נדה; "Tractate of the Menstruant."</note></term>, that is to say, regarding the menstruating woman, is divided into ten chapters. In these, it treats and speaks of the

some who were very tenacious and zealous observers of the divine law and its practice, and this was a little before the time when the Jews were in great wars and civil divisions. These <term>Pharisees<note>A Jewish social group and a school of thought in the Levant during the time of Second Temple Judaism. The author here attempts to categorize them based on their relationship to early Christianity.</note></term>, having abandoned Judea and their own country, wandered as travelers and vagabonds among the Gentiles; and, taking no part in the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, they were considered to be free of any crime or wrongdoing. Regarding this subject of the Pharisees, <term>P. Those who, not wishing to adhere to Christ through faith or work, chose to remain stubbornly in their blindness, just as the blind choose to stay in the dark. Yet they were not able to deny the truth entirely (see how great the power of truth is!). For in explaining the Law and the Prophets, compelled by truth alone, they were unable to remain completely silent about it in many places. This should not be thought to have happened without divine arrangement; it was so that we might have testimonies of that same truth from its enemies and deniers. This does not prejudice the truth simply because they did not believe; rather, it adds weight to the testimony, because even the incredulous and unwilling could not deny it. From their sayings and writings, and from all others who handed down anything in writing after the Babylonian captivity, the **Talmudic code** was assembled and compacted.

**Sixtus of Siena**, in Book 2 of his *Holy Library*, notes that **Epiphanius** <note>A 4th-century bishop and church father known for his works against heresies.</note> frequently cites certain traditions of the Jews without naming the author. On their authority, Epiphanius asserts—against the **Hieracites**—the genealogy of Melchizedek as being from the Sidonian people. Against the **Melchizedekians**, he provides the genealogies of the prophets Elijah and Daniel. Likewise, against the **Antidicomarianites** <note>A sect that denied the perpetual virginity of Mary.</note>, he shows from these same traditions that Joseph, the spouse of the Virgin Mary, had another wife before Mary and had fathered four sons by her—who are named in Mark and John as James, Jose, Judas, and Simon—and two daughters, Mary and Salome. When his wife died, and he was a widower of eighty years, he received the Virgin Mary as his wife. Likewise, against the **Collyridians** <note>A movement that supposedly offered small cakes to Mary as if to a goddess.</note>, he relates that the parents of the Virgin Mary were Joachim and Anna. Again, disputing against the **Manichæans**, he proves from these same sources that Lazarus was thirty years old when he was raised by Christ and lived for thirty more years after his resurrection. Saint Jerome also cites other Hebrew traditions in his *Book of Hebrew Traditions*, which, because they were not written down, are called <term>unwritten<note>original Greek: αγραφα (*agrapha*)</note></term>.

The "traditions of the elders" (which Matthew called in Hebrew <term>decrees of the elders<note>original: גזירות הזיקנים (*Ghezeroth azzekenim*), meaning the legal rulings of the rabbinic sages.</note></term>, meaning the constitutions of the elders; while the Greek text uses the singular, <term>the tradition of the elders<note>original: τήν παράδοσιν των πρεσβυτέρων (*tēn paradosin tōn presbyterōn*)</note></term>) are mentioned in several places in Divine Scripture, especially in Matthew 15. There, the Pharisees, accusing the Apostles, ask Christ: "Why do your disciples transgress the traditions of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread." Christ, rebuking them for a greater crime and asking in return, said: "Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?" And a little later he adds: "In vain do you worship God, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men." God, angry with the observers of these traditions, threatens them through his Prophets, saying in Isaiah 29: "Because they feared me by the commandment and doctrines of men, wisdom shall perish from their wise men." And in Jeremiah 8: "Truly the lying pen of the scribes has lied; the wise are put to shame, they have rejected the word of the Lord, and there is no wisdom in them." The Apostle Paul, mocking these same traditions everywhere and calling them now "Jewish fables," now "old wives' tales," now "foolish questions and profane vanities," deters Timothy from dealing with them with these words: "Do not attend to Jewish fables and endless genealogies, which provide questions rather than the edification which is in faith." Just as some, wishing to be teachers of the law... and again to the same he says: "Avoid foolish and unlearned questions," and again: "Avoid profane and old wives' fables," and repeating the same to Titus: "Avoid questions and genealogies and contentions; for they are unprofitable and vain." Nor is it...

...he warns in vain, having experienced in himself how much the observance of these traditions harmed both him and others: for because of these (as the first epistle written to the Galatians testifies), he himself persecuted the Church of God beyond measure and attacked it, being a zealous partisan of the ancestral Jewish traditions. Since, therefore, both Christ and Paul so sharply attack traditions of this kind, lest anyone should perchance think that all human traditions whatsoever are condemned, it would not be out of place to briefly indicate which are the doctrines and mandates of men rejected by God. The **Manichaeans** <note>A dualistic religious movement founded by the Iranian prophet Mani; the author views them as heretics who rejected the material world and much of the Old Testament.</note> impiously affirmed that all the scriptures of the Old Testament were to be understood as "traditions of the elders," and they said these were what Paul, in 1 Timothy 4, called "Jewish fables" and "profane vanities." But against their madness, Paul himself, writing to the Romans in chapter 7, exclaims: *the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good*; and in 2 Timothy 3 <note>The original text cites 1 Timothy 3, but the quote is from 2 Timothy 3:14-17.</note> he says:

> But you, remain in those things which you have learned, you who from infancy have known the sacred letters, which are able to instruct you for salvation through the faith which is in Christ: for all scripture, inspired by God, is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in justice, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work.

The **Ptolemaeans** <note>A Gnostic sect named after Ptolemy, a disciple of Valentinus.</note>—as **Epiphanius** relates in his first book *Against Heresies*—understood the traditions condemned by Christ to mean not all, but some scriptures of the Old Testament. They divided these into three parts: one part they said was established by God, another by Moses, and a third written by the elders of the Jews and later rejected by Christ when he said:

> Why do you transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your traditions? For God says, "honor father and mother," and "whoever curses father or mother, let him die the death"; but you say, "if a man says to his father or mother: *Korban* <note>original: "Korban"; a Hebrew term meaning a gift or offering dedicated to God.</note>, which is whatever gift comes from me, it shall profit you": and you no longer allow him to do anything for his father or mother, rescinding the word of God for the sake of your tradition, which you have handed down, etc.

But since the words of this "tradition" are found nowhere in the entire Old Testament, it is clear that Christ, under the name of traditions, condemned no part of the divine scriptures, but rather other Jewish rulings, alien to the sacred scripture and contrary to the word of God. **Luther** and the whole foul collection of **Lutherans** interpret all ecclesiastical sanctions—which do not have the open and express testimony of God in the divine letters—as the "traditions and doctrines of men" exploded by Christ. However, it appears they are lying wickedly, because Christ and Paul, in the places already cited, do not condemn good and just human traditions (even if they do not have the express word of God), but only Jewish rulings—that is, those repugnant to the mandates of God. Such was that ruling of the Pharisees in Matthew 15: *Whatever gift is from me shall benefit you*, which destroyed the divine precept regarding piety toward parents. Indeed, Christ wishes ecclesiastical sanctions and the decrees of the fathers, which promote and increase the worship of God, to be observed, so that he says through Paul in 2 Thessalonians 2:

> Stand firm and hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by word or by epistle,

and he himself, establishing the law concerning the observance of the traditions of the Pastors, says in Matthew 23:

> All things whatsoever they tell you, observe and do.

And to the pastors in Luke 10:

> He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me: and he who will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican.

For he deserves no less to be cast out among the heathens who rejects the ecclesiastical traditions...

than he who rejects the gospel: for if the constitutions of the Church are cast aside, it is necessary that the Gospel also be thrown away, which even **Saint Basil** <note>Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), a leading Church Father who defended the use of unwritten tradition alongside scripture.</note> clearly testifies in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27, with these words: <note>original: "Si instituta, cõsuetudinésque non scriptas... ad inane nomen eius prædicationem contrahemus."</note> *If we attempt to reject once and for all the unwritten customs and institutions, as if there were no great power in them, we shall secretly and bit by bit condemn the very established sentences of the Gospel, or rather we shall reduce its preaching to an empty name.* Therefore, I deem it an Apostolic duty to remain also in these traditions which are not written, but we have spoken elsewhere more broadly of these matters.

**Stratonicus**, Bishop of Cumae, in his collected works, asserts that these traditions were the opinions and decrees of Jewish secrets: for as **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide key details on 1st-century Judaism.</note> and **Epiphanius** <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop known for his "Panarion," a catalog of various heresies and sects.</note> write, there were four ways of living among the Jews, one of which the **Pharisees** professed, another the **Galileans**, a third the **Sadducees**, and a fourth the **Essenes**.

The <term>dogmas</term> <note>religious doctrines or established beliefs</note> of the **Pharisees** were of this sort:

<margin>1</margin>That all things are governed by Fate—that is, by the presence and unchangeable decree of God—yet while the free assent of the human will remains: for the best God governs the affairs of men with such a balance that while all things depend on His deliberation, there remains in man an intact faculty for approaching either virtue or vice.

<margin>2</margin>That souls are incorruptible and immortal, and their judgments occur beneath the earth; then rewards come to each according to the merit of their virtue or malice.

<margin>3</margin>That the souls of the pious return from the underworld into this life to new bodies, and from these migrate again into other bodies; but the souls of the wicked are condemned to perpetual prisons and tortured with never-ending punishment.

<margin>4</margin>That elders are to be venerated, and it is not permitted either to talk back to those who give advice or to speak against them.

<margin>5</margin>**GALILEANS**, who took their origin from Judas the Galilean, from the homeland of Gamala, followed the same opinions as the Pharisees, adding only this one thing of their own: namely, that God alone must be held as Lord, and no mortal prince is to be obeyed, but one must suffer every hardship and bitterness to assert liberty. Josephus relates that this kind of men often stirred up the people to cast off the rule of kings and lords and to refuse the payment of taxes (which is a manifest testimony of servitude). There are also those who think that those Jews whom we read about boasting of their liberty were from this sect, when they said to Christ, in whom they had recently believed, <note>original: "Semen Abrahæ sumus, & nemini seruiuimus vnquam"</note> *We are the seed of Abraham, and have never been in bondage to anyone*, and that they had therefore clung to Christ because they hoped he would one day be the asserter and vindicator of Jewish liberty.

<margin>1</margin>**SADDUCEES** held opinions diverse from these: namely, that there is no fate at all, nor any decree of divine declaration: but all things are so within the power of men that each is the author of his own happiness as well as his misfortune.

<margin>2</margin>That souls are entirely extinguished along with the body, and no rewards or punishments remain after this life.

<margin>3</margin>That there is no nature of angels, but only names: by which either the movements which God breathes into men are designated, or those demonstrations of His power which He Himself brings forth.

<margin>4</margin>That besides the Mosaic books and the divine laws contained in those same volumes, there is no other authority of scriptures or of human traditions...

# History of the Origin of the...

...to be received.

The **ESSENES**, distinguished practitioners of piety and not much unlike Christian monks, bound themselves by these laws and sanctions:

<margin>1</margin> All things are governed by fate—that is, by the will of God—and nothing happens to men except by the determination of fate.

<margin>2</margin> Souls are immortal, and after this life, rewards and punishments are repaid for one’s deeds: for the good, indeed, beyond the ocean, where there is a region pressed neither by cold nor heat, but made pleasant by the breathing West Wind <note>original: *Zephyrus*</note>; for the wicked, however, in the underworld, where there are places of hardship and full of lamentations.

<margin>3</margin> Every oath is to be avoided as if it were perjury: because whatever a perfect man says should have the force of an oath; and that man is condemned as if guilty of a lie who is not believed unless God is called as a witness.

<margin>4</margin> The greatest reverence, after God, must be shown to the lawmaker **Moses**, whom if anyone blasphemes, he shall be condemned to death.

<margin>5</margin> Principal study must be applied to the divine scriptures and the writings of the ancient fathers, and from there one must seek what may relieve the cares of the soul.

<margin>6</margin> The leader of the common fellowship must be obeyed in such a way that nothing is permitted to be done without his command.

<margin>7</margin> To lead a continent and celibate life, and to abstain entirely from all marriage throughout one’s whole life.

<margin>8</margin> All resources are to be held in common, and there is one estate for all, which is dispensed by common stewards.

<margin>9</margin> Nothing is to be bought or sold among themselves, but it is free for all to receive whatever is needed from whomever they please.

<margin>10</margin> White garments are to be used, and the clothing and shoes are not to be changed unless they are either completely torn or consumed by long use.

<margin>11</margin> Such care for cleanliness must be maintained even in natural waste, that each person should daily dig a trench for himself in the most secret places with a small axe <term>dolabella: a small pickaxe or tool used by the Essenes for hygiene and work</term>, in which he may relieve his bowels, first having lowered his garment all around for the sake of covering the body, and then returning the earth he had dug out to its place, so that, of course, no injury is done to the brightness of the divine light.

<margin>12</margin> Before the rising of the sun, the author of the dawning light must be celebrated with public praises; after that, however, each must proceed to his own arts and studies.

<margin>13</margin> At the fifth hour of the day <note>approximately 11:00 AM</note>, they must gather in a common dining room, clothed in sacred garments—that is, linen coverings—and there they are to eat sitting in silence from the same bread and food <note>original: *pulmentum*, a thick porridge or pottage</note>; nor is it lawful for anyone to taste anything unless a public prayer precedes and follows the meal, which praises God, the giver of food, both before and after the meal.

<margin>14</margin> After the meal, having laid aside the sacred garments, each must return to his own work until evening.

<margin>15</margin> Those recently approaching the worship of the Essenes are not to be admitted immediately into the fellowship, but, clothed in a white garment and a loincloth <note>original: *perizoma*</note> and girded with a small axe, they are to be tested by their curators for three full years, until they have given proof of their tried virtue.

**Epiphanius** <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note>, in Book 1 *Against Heresies*, says that the "traditions of the elders" are four Jewish expositions of the divine law, devised by certain Hebrew masters: namely, by the Prophet **Moses**, by **Rabbi Akiba**, by **Rabbi Ida**, and by the sons of **Asamoneus** <note>The Hasmoneans</note>, who derived constitutions from the aforementioned expositions.

**Jerome**, in his third commentary on Isaiah, in his tenth question to Algasia, and on the third chapter of the Epistle to Titus, writes that these are certain constitutions of the Jews, called by the Greeks <term>deuteroseis</term> <note>original: δευτερώσεις; meaning "repetitions" or "second laws"</note>; which the first among the Hebrews taught before the coming of Christ: **Shammai** and **Hillel**, whose school was taken up by **Akiba**, the teacher of the proselyte **Aquila**, and after him **Meir**; who was succeeded by **Johanan**, son of **Zakkai**, and after him **Eliezer**, and in order **Tarfon**, and again **Joseph**, and finally **Joshua** until the last destruction of the Holy City.

**THOMAS Aquinas**, in his commentaries on both epistles to Timothy, asserts more than once that by the name of "traditions" is signified that huge and vast work of Jewish traditions, called by the Jews the <term>Talmud</term> <note>original: תלמוד</note>, that is, "instruction" or "discipline"; in which are collected all the decrees of the aforementioned masters—**Shammai**, **Hillel**, **Akiba**, **Joseph**, and the sons of **Asamoneus**—together with countless other statutes of the Rabbis, their opinions, and expositions of both divine and human laws, by which the whole nation of the Jews is now governed. This work had its beginning, as the commentators of the Talmud themselves write, in the year 150 after the final ruin of Jerusalem, by **Judah** son of **Simeon** <note>likely referring to Judah the Prince</note>, who encompassed into one volume the explanations of the law and the Prophets, and all the writings which the above-mentioned Rabbis and other doctors had written until then, both before and after the coming of Christ. This they named the <term>Mishnah</term> <note>original: משנה</note>, that is, "repeated lesson" or "repetition." Then, in the three-hundredth year after that same final devastation of Jerusalem, **Rabbi Johanan**, having taken as colleagues **Rav** and **Samuel**, joined the Mishnah itself and certain other writings into one volume, which they called the **Jerusalem Talmud**, because it was written amid the ruins of the city of Jerusalem. Again, in the year 436 after that same destruction (which was the year of Christ 476), **Rabbi Ashi** and **Rabbi Hamai**, living in the Babylon of Egypt—which is now called **Cairo** <note>a common historical identification of the fortress of Babylon in Egypt with Old Cairo</note>—reduced all the writings of their predecessors into one, and constructed a new body of many volumes called the <term>Babylonian Talmud</term>. Since they were prevented by death from finishing it, **Rabbi Meir**, the son of Rabbi Ashi, put the final hand to the work.

All the above being proven, we will repeat again what we have fully deduced in the preceding chapter: namely, that the Hebrews used two principal sorts of laws and interpretations thereof. The other is <term>Torah she-be-al peh</term> <note>original: Torah scebealpe</note>, that is, the law which is handed down by mouth—the law given by word of mouth by that same Moses. The first is that which is compiled in writing in the Hebrew language in the **Pentateuch**, or five books of that same Moses. The other is partly treated within the aforementioned five books of the Pentateuch, and within the books of the **Kabbalah** <note>original: Cabale</note> previously mentioned by us, and in the Talmuds. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

...in the first place, the two senses or understandings, namely, the literal and the allegorical, otherwise called **Cabalistic** <note>refers to Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition of interpreting the inner meaning of the Torah</note>, which it was not permitted in ancient times for these Hebrews to write down in any kind of letters or characters whatsoever. As for the literal sense or understanding, they could not commit to writing all unique human acts, nor all their laws, because these acts and rights could not be contained in writing due to being immense and infinite, and what is more, changeable and variable according to the diverse moods and fancies of men, the differing occurrences of times and years, and the situations and positions of the provinces or regions where they occur. 

Furthermore, while the allegorical or Cabalistic sense could indeed be somewhat reduced to writing, it was nevertheless not permitted or lawful in ancient times to do so in any way, for fear of giving "solid food and firm meat to infants who still take milk" <note>A biblical metaphor (from 1 Corinthians 3:2 and Hebrews 5:12) suggesting that complex spiritual truths should be reserved for the mature rather than the uninitiated</note>. This is why among the Hebrews it was not tolerated in any way that the divine law, with its understandings—both literal and spiritual—be taught to the common people, whether by word of mouth or in writing. This lasted as long as the people of Israel were governed by their kings. 

But after the destruction of Jerusalem and the ruin of their kingdom, the Hebrews were scattered and divided as foreigners throughout many different parts of the earth. Seeing that through the great and cruel tyranny of the Gentiles and idolaters, their religion and their Hebrew law were in danger of being lost entirely, and its secrets and mysteries forgotten from one day to the next, it seemed most appropriate to the aforementioned **Pharisees** in full synod to record and publish in a book, as far as could be done, the explanation of both the literal and spiritual senses of their law. This book they titled in their Hebrew language <term>Talmud</term> <note>original: תלמוד</note>, which means "doctrine" or "discipline," as detailed specifically by **Elias Levita**, a Jew by nation, in his *Tishbi*, in the explanation of the words *Talmud* and *Talmud Chacham* <note>meaning "Disciple of a Sage"</note>; **Sixtus of Siena** in the second book of his *Holy Library* on the words "traditions of the elders" <note>original Latin: "traditiones seniorum"</note>; and **Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie** in his Syro-Chaldean dictionary on the word *Talmud*, as we have already noted above. 

This **Talmud** openly declares the sense or understanding of the divine Hebrew law, and under an infinity or variety of veils and coverings, the allegorical or **Cabalistic** sense which is hidden and concealed there. And although after the time of **Hillel** and **Shammai**, the Great Pharisees, the sayings and sentences of the Talmudists vary in several constitutions concerning the additions to the divine precepts and commandments, nevertheless, one will find no difference regarding the foundation of the law. 

For no one disputes that one must read the **Shema** lesson in the morning and evening—that is, <gloss>Hear, O Israel</gloss> <note>original: "Audi Israel" (Latin) and "oy Israel" (French); the central declaration of Jewish faith</note>; but whether one is in doubt or uncertain at what hours of the said morning and evening this must be done, whether before sunrise or after sunset, matters not at all. Likewise, no one brings into controversy that around the time of vespers on the day of **Parasceue** <note>the day of preparation before the Sabbath, i.e., Friday</note>, one must light the lamp according to what was ordained in the law; but with what oil it must be filled, each has said what he wished, but that also matters not at all. Of other similar and same things, it has been done in the same...

of the Holy Hebrew Scriptures was formerly hidden beneath various layers of code, much like a kernel within multiple husks, skins, and shells. Thus, the matters now seen contained within the **Talmuds** <term>Talmud: The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</term> were not committed to writing in ancient times, nor was any part of the commentary or explanation of the law recorded. Instead, the Hebrews passed these down to one another by word of mouth and through tradition, as he <note>Referring to Maimonides, mentioned later as "Rabbi Moses the Egyptian."</note> confirms in his *Exodus* on *Deuteronomy*. This was done because of the difficulties that arose until one hundred and twenty years <note>original: "six vingts ans"</note> after the second destruction of the temple, which occurred in the time of the Emperors Vespasian and his son Titus; this brings us to approximately the Year of Grace 190. At that time, the same Rabbi Judah <note>Judah ha-Nasi, the redactor of the Mishnah.</note> was the first to arrange that same *Mishnah* <term>Mishnah: The first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions.</term> into a compendium or summary. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar and Bible translator.</note> discusses this at length in Book 2, Chapter 5 of *The Faith Against the Jews*. The aforementioned Rabbi Judah taught and left the explanation and interpretation of this law—arranged in his own compendium and summary—to another, Rabbi Johanan. Three hundred years after the destruction of the aforementioned Temple of Jerusalem, Johanan, along with his companions Rav and Samuel, expanded and increased that compendium or summary of the aforementioned *Mishnah*. He did so with a clearer and more eloquent style, composing another volume called the **Jerusalem Talmud**. In its beginning, this work was quite small, as asserted by Victor of Carben <note>A 15th-century Jewish convert to Christianity.</note> in his book *On the Life and Customs of the Jews*, Chapter 9 and those following. This Rabbi Johanan had as colleagues and companions Rabbi Rav and Rabbi Samuel; their student was Rabbi Rav Huna, who had as a student Rabba; he in turn taught Rabba Ravan, whose student was Rav Ashi (or Rabbi Assé). Rav Ashi, who excelled in great erudition, modesty of life, and worldly honor and glory, was the first to begin—along with Rabina in the year 436—to compose the **Babylonian Talmud**. It was so named because of the Rabbis who assembled in the city of Babylon to create it. This is confirmed by Elias Levita <note>A 15th-century Hebrew scholar and grammarian.</note> in the preface to his Chaldaic lexicon; by Jerome in Book 2, Chapter 5 of *The Holy Faith Against the Jews* (cited above); and by Guillaume Postel in Book 1, Chapter 3 of *The Concord of the Whole World*. The aforementioned Rabbi could not entirely finish this Talmud because he was overtaken by death before doing so. However, after his death, his son named Mor, with his colleague and companion Moreuar, finished it completely. This is likewise confirmed by Pietro Galatino <note>Petrus Galatinus, a Franciscan theologian.</note> in Book 1, Chapter 5 of *The Truth of the Catholic Faith*, and Sixtus of Siena in Book 2 of his *Holy Library* (both cited above). This Talmud contains the glosses and commentaries on the aforementioned compendium or summary of the Mishnah, along with all the other laws, ordinances, and new constitutions that have been made and promulgated at various times and places. It also includes many secrets and mysteries of the holy Hebrew language, as well as other reveries, fables, wickednesses, and impieties of the Talmudists. All the Jews who are currently scattered throughout every province of this universe receive, hold, and keep these Talmuds with careful observation and veneration, as they are—according to them—filled with wisdom that is at once divine, natural, legal, and political.

The first: they specifically interpret everything that is presented in the **Mishnah** <term>Mishnah: The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions, which forms the core of the Talmud.</term> and carefully examine everything that is ambiguous or doubtful in the authors of the glosses <note>Commentaries or explanations written in the margins or between lines of a text.</note>, and resolve the arguments of other commentators.

The third: they report and teach the things that subsequent Talmudists, one after another, learned from the foundations of these Talmuds; they also resolve the arguments used by those Talmudists and, furthermore, explain all the things that were decreed and ordained after the aforementioned Mishnah was published.

The fourth: they insert, in very appropriate places, dialogues and homilies <note>Known as Aggadah: the non-legalistic exegetical texts in the Talmud consisting of folklore, anecdotes, and ethical teachings.</note> which—if they were viewed only from the outside and taught or understood in a commonplace way—would seem to be entirely trivial and humorous things, even completely removed from the right path of reason. However, by considering them more closely according to the type and figure contained within in the form of a riddle, one truly comes to penetrate sublime matters and the most hidden secrets and oracles of wisdom. These are covered and wrapped in a veil of riddles and allegories, for fear that the hesitant and uncertain, as well as the ignoble common people, might come to defile these sacraments of divine truth and pollute pure and clean things with the foul and filthy. It is also done so that those who are eager for sincere religion and more excellent in spirit might devote themselves more vibrantly to the contemplation of the most hidden and secret things, and raise themselves more ardently toward the heavens and the seat of the existence of divine and eternal wisdom. **Michael Neander** <note>A German educator and humanist (1525–1595) known for his Greek and Hebrew grammars.</note>, in his dedicatory epistle to his *Questions on the Holy Language* <note>original: "Erotemates de la langue saincte," referring to his *Erotemata Linguae Sanctae*</note>, used these words: "The **Talmud**, indeed—that is, the doctrinal and disciplinary work of the Jews, in which the entire Jewish tradition has been gathered with immense effort—possesses a double form, the Jerusalem and the Babylonian. Seeing then that the wine of the law was running out and that only the dregs remained—and that the time was approaching when the Gentiles were to be converted and the Church was to begin among them—God permitted and ordained that all the Holy Hebrew Scriptures be translated into the Greek language, knowing that the Hebrew language was destined to be lost. Now, how such a translation and interpretation came about, I will tell you briefly: you should know that during the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus in Egypt, he established a truly excellent library in Alexandria with more than one hundred thousand books, because he kept at least two hundred philosophers on retainer in his house, and daily sought out with diligence the best books in the world.

And when this king heard that among the Hebrews there were learned men, and that he would find among them very ancient books, he sent his ambassadors to the High Priest Eleazar, praying and urgently requesting that he send him a certain number of the most learned figures in the law of Moses, capable of translating the entire Mosaic law from Hebrew into the Greek language, bringing with them for this purpose all the best books of Sacred Scripture. To satisfy this request, Eleazar chose six of the most learned, wise, and virtuous figures from each tribe, totaling 72 interpreters—the most renowned and esteemed in all ancient and authentic histories; they were even given the name of Prophets. For being inspired by the Holy Spirit, they rendered all of the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek with such diligence and fidelity that, as universal doctrine, their writing is received by the whole Church.

And these figures were so prudent that where their translation touched upon the mysteries of the Trinity or the coming of the Messiah prophesied in the Law—since these were very high and obscure mysteries, and faith was very necessary to understand them well—they placed a small mark in such places, where they left the mystery without declaring it <note>The author suggests that the translators intentionally veiled Christian truths from those without faith.</note>. However, although their writing is true, it is also obscure in some places and diminished in others. Once the translation of the aforementioned Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, a student of Hillel, to whom a famous Aramaic translation of the Prophets is attributed.</note> was condemned, it happened that in the sixth year of the reign of the Emperor Trajan, a great pagan priest—a native of the island of Pontus named Aquila—converted to the law of Moses. This conversion to Judaism was not done to save his soul, but rather to obtain in marriage a very beautiful Jewish woman whom he loved dearly. And as this Aquila was a man very learned in the Greek and Hebrew languages, he found no better opportunity to demonstrate his intellect than to set his hand to the translation of the whole of Holy Scripture from Hebrew into Greek. This was the first translation made after the Incarnation of Jesus Christ, in the year 104 after his birth. You Jews held this translation in little esteem because it was made by a man who had formerly been a pagan, and the Christians esteemed it even less, as it came from a man who had made himself a Jew. 

Fifty-two years after the death of this Aquila—namely, in the eighth year of the wicked Emperor Commodus—there was another Jew named Theodotion <note>original: "Theodose"</note> who later became a Christian; he corrected all the faults of Aquila and made another translation. Thirty-seven years after the death of Theodotion—namely, in the ninth year of the reign of Severus—another translation from Hebrew into Greek was made by a learned and virtuous man named Symmachus, which was approved and well-received by the East. However, a short time later it was rejected; at that time, the heresy of the Ebionites <note>A Jewish Christian movement that insisted on the followings of Jewish law and denied the divinity of Jesus.</note> (of which Saint John speaks in the Apocalypse) reigned in the greater part of Asia. And even if Theodotion and Symmachus had been faithful in their translations and true in their words, our Church nevertheless refused to receive their writings, having no confidence in the faith of their persons. 

Fourteen years after the death of Symmachus—which was the fifth year of the reign of Heliogabalus—it happened that a patriarch of Jerusalem named John Budeos found, in a cave in Jericho, the whole Old and New Testament faithfully written and catholically translated from Greek into Latin. This one, then, is what is called the *quinta editio* <note>The "Fifth Edition."</note>, otherwise known as the Jericho translation (that is to say, it was found in Jericho), the author of which has never been known. In the eighth year of the Emperor Alexander Severus, son of Mamaea—which was nearly ten years after this Jericho translation was found—a doctor of ours named Origen corrected the translation of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, namely by adding where they had been brief and explaining obscure mysteries, placing a small star <note>An asterisk.</note> to mark where he explained something, and where he erased something, he placed a small arrow <note>An obelus.</note>. 

The ancients were accustomed to putting all six translations mentioned above—namely those of the Seventy Interpreters, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Jericho, and that of Origen—into one book, writing six columns on each page; they called this book the *Hexapla*, from the Latin, as if containing six translations within itself <note>original: "hexapla, ab eo quod est ex Latino, quasi sex traductions in se continens"</note>. But since both Rabbi Meir, as well as his predecessors and successors, had collected throughout the individual books of the Talmud not only many and cursed insults and blasphemies against Christ our God, but had also written many sanctions and many precepts against the very Law of Moses which they profess, and against all the law of nations, and every law of nature which they themselves, as men, are bound to keep, it seemed right to the Supreme Pontiffs and other Christian princes that the reading and use of such wicked doctrine should be forbidden to all Jews living under the dominion of Christians, and that all Talmudic books throughout the whole Christian world should be delivered to the fires.

<note>original Latin: "Quod etiam sæpe factum esse... connumerari voluit."</note>
Several trustworthy writers testify that this has often been done. Among them, Bernard of Luxembourg, in the second book of his *Catalog of Heretics*, reports that Pope Gregory IX, in the year of our Lord 1230, condemned all Talmudic volumes to the flames, and that Pope Innocent IV did the same again in the year of our Salvation 1244. Later, when the same volumes had been restored by the Jews and, by the aid of the art of printing, propagated in an almost infinite number, Pope Julius III issued a new edict and ordered them to be sought out; and in the year 1553, while the Feast of Tabernacles was being celebrated by the Jews in the month of September, he ordered them to be burned throughout all the cities of Italy. Pope Paul IV, together with the council of the Holy Roman Inquisition, ordered the same to be done again in the year 1559, and willed that the Talmudic books be numbered among the writings condemned by the Catholic Church.

...received especially from the holy fathers, and among others this tradition of Abraham concerning creation, or formation. Although it was not written down by Abraham himself exactly as it appears here, its meaning is truly in agreement with eternal truth. But the title shows to what category it belongs: for it is of the third type of authority. First are the sacred scriptures; second are the Talmud and Mishnah; and in the third place are the *Baraitot* <note>original: "Bariethoth"; these are "external" teachings or traditions from the period of the Mishnah that were not included in the primary legal code.</note>, that is, external writings, both those that relate to the Talmud and those that pertain to other parts of doctrine.

Therefore, the first of all *Baraitot* is the *Sefer Yetzirah* <note>original: "Sepher Jeſirah"; The "Book of Formation," one of the oldest and most important works of Jewish mysticism/Kabbalah.</note>. It is a book very rare to find and much rarer to understand, in which the logic of the entire creation of the world <note>original: "Cosmopaeia"</note> is set forth—but through the method of reason, whereas in Moses and the sacred books it is explained by way of authority. Thus, although it has circulated among the wise since the very creation of the world, and was set forth by Abraham three thousand five hundred years ago, there was no one who could truly reveal such a great treasure to the world until the force of authority had spent those three millennia confirming the account of creation.

Since faith and pure belief must necessarily be preferred over reason—both in things proven by human logic and in those received through religion—it was so arranged by divine providence that this book remained hidden among its own people for a long time. It remained concealed even while its themes were being explored by Plato, Pythagoras, and Cicero in their treatises on nature and the universe, until sacred matters were divinely revealed and received through authority and pure faith. Now, reason alone may be our guide, acting as the priest of highest wisdom alongside the logic of sacred doctrine.

In this, providence seems most admirable: that those things in the third category of authority so persuasively set forth the primary logic of eternal truth that there will be no one in the whole world who, with reason as their guide, will not agree with them. How much authority this *Baraita* had among the fathers has been recorded in many places; but it was most faithfully received and written of by Rabbi Judah, the author of the book *Bitachon* <note>original: "Bithchon"; Hebrew for "Trust" or "Confidence."</note>. There he teaches that other prophets—all the more so as they were greater—and especially Jeremiah, were so engaged with this book that a revelation was made to him with a command to spend three whole years upon it. He studied it to such an extent that by the power of that knowledge he saw a "new man" formed before him, just as was intended in the first divine plan.

For that figure of a man which was formed before him bore on its forehead an inscription that would show God as man and affirm that he would die. But the purpose of this was that when the twenty-two letters of the alphabet <note>The 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet, which the "Sefer Yetzirah" describes as the building blocks of the universe.</note> were inscribed in the most excellent dust of the earth, according to the holy desires of the human heart, men themselves (who are the most excellent dust) might see and feel the "new man" himself being entirely poured into them.

To this end, then, the study of the mystery of creation and this book tends: that we may know how God created us, and in what way God, having become human, pours himself into us, making us like himself in soul and body, and immortal, so that we may praise him forever for such a great benefit. Deservedly, therefore, we shall call this book a *Baraita*—that is, "creation"—and not a *Beraita*, that is, an "eternal constitution."

For I am of the opinion that although some sacred writings were published much later than Abraham himself, I do not hesitate to believe this work was always present in the records of all the fathers, since it explains the *method* of formation, whereas Moses expressed only the *fact* of it. The book, therefore, belongs to Adam and the holy succession of the fathers; for it is certain that before things existed in themselves, they were arranged in their forms and numbers with God through "Ideas." Genesis <note>The first book of the Bible</note> has hitherto been considered more noble. For just as it is necessary for that work to exist before the things themselves, so it is established that nature was prior to grace, although the latter is more noble; yet grace would have had no place anywhere unless nature had been prior. Thus, unless there had been *Yetzirah* <note>The world of "Formation" in Kabbalistic thought; original Latin: "Iezira"</note>, there could never have been *Beriah* <note>The world of "Creation"; original Latin: "Beriah"</note>.

The learned Gilbert Génébrard <note>A 16th-century French Benedictine scholar and noted Hebraist</note>, in book 2 of his *Chronography*, speaking of Ezra and his writings, said:

> He restored the Scriptures, which had been burned by the Babylonian leader of the army Nabuzardan <note>Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard under Nebuchadnezzar</note>, and returned them to this order which the Hebrews for the most part maintain today. Of him, Rabanus Maurus <note>A prominent 9th-century Carolingian theologian</note> writes in *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, chapter 54: "Inspired by the divine spirit, he repaired all the ancient sacred books when the Jews had entered Jerusalem, and corrected all the volumes of the Prophets which had been corrupted by the Gentiles; and he organized the entire Old Testament into twenty-two books, so that there would be as many books in the Law as there are letters [in the Hebrew alphabet]." Otherwise, it was not within the power of Nebuchadnezzar to destroy all copies, especially since ten tribes were already in the East, outside his jurisdiction. For some make him [Ezra] the author of the points and accents <note>The vowel markings and musical notations used in Hebrew</note> with which the Hebrew Bibles are marked today. But they err, since it is clear from the books of Saint Jerome himself that none existed in his time. They were, however, invented shortly after the time of the Emperor Honorius, in the year 436 from the destruction of the Temple, which is the year 476 from the Passion of Christ, in the city of Tiberias in Galilee. The leaders of this were Aaron ben Asher and Jacob ben Naphtali <note>Famous 10th-century Masoretes who standardized the Hebrew text</note>, who, while they disagreed among themselves regarding the points of certain words, divided the Jews into two parties. For the Easterners, and those who inhabit Babylon by the River Nearda, follow the reading of the latter, while the Westerners follow the former. Forty-one years earlier, the Babylonian Talmud <term>Talmud: the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishna and Gemara</term>, or book of doctrine, began to be collected from the writings of the ancient masters by Rabbi Hina and Rabbi Ashi, and was later completed by Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Ashi's son. It contains the Jewish canon law, which in the time of Christ had not yet been committed to a full writing, but was preserved partly from fragments and partly from oral traditions. It began to be written down by Rabbi Hakkadosh <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, also known as "The Holy Rabbi"</note> in the times of the Emperor Antoninus, in that shorter form called the *Mishna* <term>Mishna: the first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions</term>. And that is regarding the Babylonian Talmud: for the Jerusalem Talmud was written in the year of Christ 300, and the Babylonian about a hundred years later.

The same author, afterwards treating the ruin of Jerusalem that occurred under the Emperor Vespasian, says:

> During the destruction, there flourished Rabbi Johanan ben Zakkai and his disciple Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, who wrote the book *Pirke* <note>The *Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer*, a work of biblical interpretation and astronomy</note>, concerning the arrangement and influences of the spheres of the earth and all the wonders of astronomy; his disciple Rabbi Ishmael the High Priest, Rabbi Joshua, Rabbi Gamaliel, and his son Rabbi Simeon, who was the father of Rabbi Judah Hakkadosh, [author of the] *Cozri* <note>Likely referring to the *Kuzari*, though historically it was written later</note>, and in the treatise *Berakhot* <note>Blessings</note> the final chapter. After the destruction, Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiba [flourished]. Following them, after the Emperor Hadrian, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Jose, Rabbi Simeon ben Azzai, and Rabbi Hananiah. Under Antoninus [reigned] the second Rabbi, Rabbi Hakkadosh, or Rabbi Judah; Rabbi Nathan, Rabbi Joshua ben Gotha. Soon after were the *Tannaim* <term>Tannaim: Rabbinic sages whose views are recorded in the Mishna</term>, the authors of the *Mishna*, or the Talmudic context; and finally the *Amoraim* <term>Amoraim: Jewish scholars who commented upon the Mishna</term>, the authors of the *Gemara* <term>Gemara: the portion of the Talmud that analyzes the Mishna</term>, or the Talmud itself. As for what the Jews did after the exile from Rome, and how the *Talmud*, *Gemara*, *Midrashim* <note>Original: "Derasim"</note>, *Gaonim* <note>Original: "Ghernim"</note>, etc., conducted themselves up to the year 1108 from that same destruction, in which Maimonides—Rabbi Moses ben Maimon—was writing (which is the year of Christ 1148), consult his preface to that book and the Kabbalistic history of Rabbi Abraham the Levite <note>Abraham ibn Daud</note>. And these things indeed concern the ancient people.

### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF <note>original: "HISTOIRE DE L'ORIGINE DES"</note>

...received especially from the holy ones, and among others this tradition of Abraham concerning creation, or rather formation. Although it was not described by Abraham himself exactly as it stands here, the sentiment is truly in agreement with eternal truth. But the title shows to which category it belongs: for it is of the third type of authority. First, indeed, are the sacred scriptures; second, the Talmud and the Mishnah <note>The primary collections of Jewish legal and theological traditions</note>; and in the third place are the *Bariethoh* <term>Baraita: a Hebrew term for 'external' or 'outside' teachings that were not included in the main Mishnah</term>, that is, the external writings, which pertain both to the Talmud and to other parts of the doctrine.

In this, providence seems most admirable: that those things in the third category of authority urge the primary reason of eternal truth so clearly that no one in the whole world will be found who does not subscribe to it, with reason as their guide.
