# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

The same [author] <note>referring to Gilbert Génébrard, the 16th-century scholar mentioned on the previous page</note>, continuing to speak of the Jews who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity, says:

"Not all returned for the better. For a multitude of exiles (as Josephus narrates in the *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 18, Chapter 12, and as the Talmud records) founded a city on the banks of the Euphrates. They called it Nehardea <note>original: "Nardea"</note>, which in the Chaldean tongue <note>Aramaic</note> means 'the river of knowledge.' This name arose because the Jews who had been led away to Babylon, having been oppressed there by seventy years of exile and servitude, had gradually forgotten the Hebrew language; the elders had died, and the children had drunk in a foreign tongue. Having constructed synagogues and academies there, they flourished in every kind of science for many centuries. From this place, a long time later around the year 476 AD, they published the Babylonian Talmud, which is full of much knowledge. In imitation of them, the others whom Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah had led back into Judea established many schools of literature in Jerusalem. They eventually published the Jerusalem Talmud, which is about four parts smaller [than the Babylonian], through the work of Rabbi Johanan, a hundred years before Rabbi Ashi published the Babylonian version. The text of this work, called the Mishnah <note>original: "Misna"; the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note>, existed thanks to the benefit of Rabbi Akiva; under the Antonines <note>the Roman emperors</note>, Rabbi Moses [Maimonides] mentions this in his preface." The same [author] in Book 3 of his said *Chronography*.

In the year of Christ 188, that part of the Talmud called the Mishnah was completed by the Jews; the other part, the Gemara <note>original: "Ghemara"; the component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishnah</note>, was finished in the year 505. Of the Mishnah (the core text of the Talmud), the first of the sages was Simeon the Just, who received Christ in his arms <note>A traditional Christian identification of the Jewish High Priest Simeon with the Simeon from the Gospel of Luke</note>. The last was Rabbi Hakkadosh <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince</note>, who was dear to the Emperor Antoninus (as mentioned by Elias in *Thesbite*), and who is understood by the name 'Rabbi' in the Talmud. With his death, the Priesthood ceased (according to the book *Bundle of Myrrh* on Genesis 6). He is called Rabbi Simeon ben Yohai in Genesis 9, in whose age it is said that perfect justice flourished (according to Rabbi Solomon Yitzhaki <note>Rashi, the famous medieval commentator</note>). From this time began the teachers called the Amoraim <note>original: "Amoriam"; the scholars who "said" or "spoke" the commentary that became the Gemara</note>, the first of whom was Rabba, and the last was Rabbi Ashi in the year 426, according to Moses [Maimonides]. Hence, Rabbenu Hakkadosh is usually called the author of the Mishnah, and Rabbi Ashi the author of the Gemara. Afterward, in the year of salvation 505, the Babylonian Talmud was completed by Mar, the son and disciple of Rabbi Ashi—specifically that part called the Gemara—about 100 years after the Jerusalem Talmud, and 317 years after the first part, the Mishnah, and 29 years after the [vowel] points. This edition was preceded by the authors of the Midrashoth and Mechilta, and was followed by the Geonim <note>original: "geonim"; the heads of the Talmudic academies in Babylonia</note>, who were the professors and interpreters of the law who illustrated the Talmud, as Maimonides says in his preface. The same author follows by saying that in the year 469, the Jerusalem Talmud was finished by the Jews; Rabbi Johanan presided over the work, which he constructed with nearly the same number of book titles as the Babylonian version, though the books themselves are much more concise, according to the Hebrew Chronicles.

The aforementioned author in the following Book 4:

Around the year 909, the Miramolinus <note>A corruption of the Arabic "Amir al-Mu'minin," or Commander of the Faithful</note> of the Saracens from Cordoba sent naval forces under the leader Avidamaim to harass Christian ships and maritime cities. They captured a Palestinian ship in which there were four distinguished Babylonian Rabbis. One, Rabbi Shemariah, was sold in Egypt to the Alexandrians; Rabbi Hushiel was sold in Africa to the Kairouanians, which was then the most powerful of the western Saracen provinces. There he fathered Rabbi Hananel, who at his death left ten thousand gold pieces in his coffers.

Rabbi Moses and his son Rabbi Enoch were among the Spanish Jews of Cordoba...

...who were not yet practiced in the Talmudic writings. From among them, Rabbi Moses was made the head of the school, whom they called the judge of the Synagogue. And for four hundred years, Hebrew letters began to flourish in Spain, and the primary Academy of the Jews [flourished] while the Babylonian one decreased because of the persecutions of the Ishmaelites <note>A term used here for Muslim rulers</note>, according to Rabbi Abraham Levita in the *Kabbalah* <note>Referring to the *Sefer ha-Kabbalah* (Book of Tradition) by the 12th-century historian Abraham ibn Daud</note>.

The same Gilbert Génébrard <note>A prominent 16th-century French Benedictine scholar and Hebraist</note> a little later:

In the year of salvation 1002. Rabbi Hai Gaon in Babylonia, the most excellent of the *Geonim* <note>original: "Gheonim"; the heads of the Talmudic academies</note>—that is, the Talmudic legal scholars—and the last of the house of David and the royal blood of Jeconiah. He was not, however, the Prince of the Exiles, because neither he nor his parents wished to buy that office with money from the Muhammadan kings in whose region they lived as exiles. He administered the Jewish school for forty years. According to the same Rabbi Abraham in the *Kabbalah*, the Muhammadan king fixed Rabbi Sherira <note>original: "Seriram"</note>, the father of Rabbi Hai Gaon, to a gibbet after confiscating his property. In the same place.

At that time, Rabbi Samuel the Priest, son of Hophni, was famous and wrote many books.

Around the year 1000, there was a distinguished Academy of the Saracens in Babylon, in which disciplines were taught, especially Medicine and the Astrology of the Chaldeans, Arabs, Persians, Egyptians, Jews, and others of the Indians. *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book 3, Chapter 34.

Almansor <note>Al-Mansur, the powerful de facto ruler of the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba</note> reigned in Spain and Mauritania when Rabbi Enoch was teaching the Talmud with great renown in Córdoba, cultivating the Hebrew Academy begun by his father in the year of our Lord 995.

Around the year 1020, Rabbi Hezekiah <note>original: "Zechias"</note> succeeded the school of Rabbi Hai Gaon in Babylonia, but due to the slander of his own people, he was killed two years later by the Saracen king along with his entire family, except for two sons who fled to Spain to Rabbi Joseph the Levite, the *Nagid* <note>original: "Hannaghid"; a title for a leader or prince of the Jewish community</note>, until a persecution was stirred up in the kingdom of Granada. Rabbi Joseph himself perished, as noted by Rabbi Abraham in the *Kabbalah*, specifically in the year of Christ 1064. Rabbi Joseph the Priest in the *Chronicle of the Kings of France and Turkey*.

With this Rabbi Hezekiah, the *Geonim*—that is, the Talmudic legal scholars—ceased, as did the Babylonian schools which were previously so famous that Jews from the West itself, from Spain, Africa, Egypt, and Palestine, sent their sons there for the sake of study.

Then in Spain flourished Rabbi Solomon <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, the philosopher and poet</note>, whom Abraham ibn Ezra (on Genesis 3) calls *Baal Hassirim Hassekulim* <note>original: "Baal Hassirim Hassekulim"</note>, meaning the master of songs with a fixed and constant meter. It seems he refuted certain opinions of Rabbi Samuel, son of Hophni, who then lived in Babylonia. Thus, around these times, Hebrew poetry—which today makes use of the *Yated* <note>original: "Iathed"; meaning "peg"</note>, that is, the iamb, and the *Tenuot* <note>original: "Tenuhoth"; meaning "vowels"</note>, that is, the spondees, along with syllables and rhythms—took its beginning.

In the year of salvation 1121 <note>This date likely refers to a different timeline or is a citation error in the source regarding Hai Gaon's death</note>, Rabbi Hai Gaon died in Babylonia. He was the newest and most skilled of the *Geonim*, the interpreters of the Talmudic Rhapsody, so much so that all students of the law walk in his light from the rising of the sun to its setting. Indeed, with him the Hebrew schools in the East were almost extinguished, to which the Jews formerly sent their sons from Egypt, Palestine, Spain, and finally the entire West; thereafter, they were transferred to Spain, according to Rabbi Abraham in the *Kabbalah*.

Here, therefore, one must note the succession of Jewish doctors: the first after the Prophets and the Babylonian captivity were the Scribes and teachers of the law from the days... <meta>catchword: tas, likely referring to Artaxerxes</meta>

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

From Zerubbabel to Simeon the Just. Second, the **Tannaim** <note>original: "Tannaim", the rabbinic sages whose views are recorded in the Mishnah</note>, the authors of the **Mishnah** or the Talmudic foundation, from Simeon the Just (whom they establish as the first of them) to Rabbi Judah the Holy <note>original: "Rabbi haccados", also known as Judah the Prince</note>, who was the last, when that first part of the Talmud was published in 180 AD under the Emperor Antoninus.

Third, the **Amoraim** <note>original: "Amoraim", the "speakers" or interpreters who commented on the Mishnah</note>, authors of the **Gemara** <note>original: "Ghemara", the rabbinical analysis and legal decisions completing the Talmud</note>, or the completion and decision of the Talmud; from Rabba (who appeared immediately after Rabbi Judah the Holy), the first doctor of that kind, until the death of Ravina, and Rabbi Sama the son of Rabba, and Rabbi Ashi, who finished the latter part. All of these flourished for 827 years. For they count that many years from Zerubbabel until the death of Ravina.

Fourth, the **Savoraim** <note>original: "Seboraim", the "reasoners" or scholastic doctors who followed the Amoraim</note>, who were the speculative, scholastic doctors; the first was Rabbi Jose, and the last was Rabbi Isana, lasting 187 years.

Fifth, the **Geonim** <note>original: "Gheonim", the heads of the great Babylonian academies who acted as supreme religious authorities</note> (corresponding to Practical Jurists); the first was Rabbi Hanina, and the last was Rabbi Hai, up to the year of our Lord 1121. Sixth, the **Rabbis**, who thereafter exercised themselves in the treatment of the Bible and other theological books. And the same [lineage is found in] the **Kabbalah** <note>here meaning "tradition" or "chain of succession"</note> of the *Kuzari*, and the *Tishbi* by Elias Levita.

Around the year 1127, the book of Jewish annals was written, which we have translated, titled **Seder Olam**, that is, the **Order of the World**; it is of the highest authority among the Jews. For this reason, Rabbi Solomon <note>likely Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note>, Rabbi Kimhi, and more recent Hebrews are accustomed to citing it quite often.

Likewise, there is the *Book of Tradition* <note>original: "liber Cabbalæ", specifically the Sefer ha-Qabbalah</note> by Rabbi Abraham Levita the Spaniard, written during the time of King Alfonso VII, who was called the Emperor of the Spains, a man so famous for heroic praise that this Rabbi Abraham called him the "King of Kings." For he frequently triumphed over the **Saracens** <note>original: "Saracenis", a medieval term for Muslims</note>, took Cordoba from them, etc.

At that time, the heresy of the **Sadducees** <note>a sect that rejected oral tradition and the Talmud</note> was troubling the Jews in Castile; for a certain Abben Altras had written a book.

The **Book of Abu Alfaraj** (Abu Alfaraj was his teacher), in which he taught that the Talmud and Mishnah and the other constitutions of the fathers were empty, and that the true Synagogue existed within his own party.

Against him, the aforementioned Rabbi dictated his *Kabbalah* <note>his work on tradition</note>, proving the truth of his Synagogue or Church <note>The author uses "Church" (Ecclesia) here to refer to the established Jewish community</note>, first from **succession**. For he traced his accounts back through 36 generations—all holding the same view—to the Prophets: the last being Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, whose succession could easily be traced back to Moses. For there were ten generations of the Great Synagogue from them to Rabbi Johanan ben Zakkai, who was among the remnants of the Great Synagogue under Vespasian. Then, under the **Tannaim**, the doctors of the Mishnah or Talmudic text, five generations followed; then seven under the **Amoraim**, the doctors of the Gemara or Talmudic decisions; then another five under the **Geonim**, the interpreters of the Talmud; and from the Geonim until his own age, three generations, which makes 36 in number since the Prophets themselves.

Second, [he proves it] from **communion** <note>universal agreement</note>, since Synagogues throughout the whole world feel the same way: in Spain, Africa, Egypt, Palestine, Arabia, Babylonia, Persia, Elam, Greece, Germany, Italy, and Gaul (for our Gaul then abounded with Jews). They commonly receive the Talmud and Mishnah and the remaining traditions of the fathers. Furthermore, he proves this communion from the fact that the fathers and masters never disagree on the **root** of a commandment, but only on the appendices and circumstances. For example, they do not argue whether a lamp should be lit on the Sabbath or not, but rather with what oil it should be lit, or with what it should not...

...debating whether one is bound to recite the *Kiriath Shema* <note>original: "Kiriah Shema"; the central prayer of Jewish liturgy, beginning with "Hear, O Israel"</note> (their confession of the one God from Deuteronomy 6) in the morning and evening, and exactly when in the morning and when in the evening, so that it is done neither too late nor too early; and likewise for the rest.

On the other hand, they <note>Referring to the Karaites, a Jewish sect that rejects the oral tradition of the Talmud</note> cannot be considered a true Synagogue, first because they are without succession. For Anan and his son Saul <note>Anan ben David, the 8th-century founder of the Karaites, and his son Saul</note>, to whom they trace their origin, were disciples of Rabbi Judah and separated from him, following another doctrine out of ambition alone; nor can they say, "behold, we received this from such and such a teacher."

Secondly, because they have few of their own communion, having only one synagogue in the deserts of Spain, and a few in Egypt and Palestine, who are not received by others but are excommunicated <note>original: "anathematizentur"</note>. Thus Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a celebrated scholar of Hebrew</note>, Professor of Hebrew letters at Cologne <note>While the text says "Colongne," Buxtorf was famously a professor at Basel</note> in his *Jewish Synagogue*, or *School of the Jews*, chapter 1, says the following:

"When the city of Jerusalem was captured, the Temple destroyed, the Jews driven out, and captives led away, and no end to their captivity and misfortune could be found, Rabbi Judah the Prince <note>original: "Rabbi Iuda Hannasi"; a 2nd-century CE rabbi and chief editor of the Mishnah</note> (who because of his humility, piety, and holiness was called our holy Master <note>original: "Rabbenu Haccadosch"</note>) found such great favor and kindness in the eyes of Emperor Antoninus, to whom he was very dear and intimate, that by his majesty's permission he gathered the most learned of the Jews from all parts of the empire to deliberate on what should be done. This was so that while the misfortune of the Jews increased more and more, the wisdom of the Jews and their learned men would not be killed or driven into exile, or the law itself perish utterly, but rather be preserved safe among the people. Although the *Kabbalah* or oral law <note>The term here refers to the "received" oral tradition, not the later mystical movement</note> was among them, because it was not lawful to commit the oral law <note>original: "Thorah scebealpe"</note> to writing, yet in consideration of the great misery of the Jews who were scattered throughout the entire world, he wrote down into a certain book everything that had remained in memory concerning the oral law from before and after Christ until his own time. This book is called the **Mishnah** <note>original: "Mischna"</note>, that is, the repeated or second law, called in Greek *deuterosis* <note>original: "δευτέρωσις"</note>, comprising six *Sedarim* <note>original: "sedarim"; the "Orders" or primary divisions of the Mishnah</note> or summaries, subdivided into sixty *Masikhtot* <note>original: "Massichtos"; the individual tractates or chapters</note>, or lower parts, or individual treatises. And thus again up to here these things have been recited by Rabbi Niccotzi <note>Likely referring to Moses ben Jacob of Coucy, author of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol</note>, etc."

To conclude this chapter, we will say that there are several kinds of Talmudists: namely, those who preceded the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and those who were after the said coming until the time the Babylonian Talmud <note>original: "Thalmud Babylonien"</note> was composed, which was in the year of Salvation 477. Both are called Talmudists because the Talmud was woven and composed from their writings. For this reason, the ancient Hebrew doctors were also not inappropriately called by this name, Talmudists; but the recent or younger doctors have been commonly named Talmudists, who, having lived a long time after the others, tried to pervert and destroy the testimonies of the law and the Prophets concerning the Messiah against the Christian law, so that they might retort against the opinion of the aforementioned ancient Talmudists. And it is very certain that these recent or younger Talmudists can easily be convinced of falsehood, both by the aforementioned ancient Talmudists who preceded the coming of our said Lord Jesus Christ, and by those who lived after the aforementioned...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jewish scholarship and the transition from the compilation of the Mishnah to the various sects and titles of leadership within the Jewish community.</meta>

### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE...

André Osiander <note>A 16th-century German Lutheran theologian</note>, in chapter 15 of his *Evangelical Harmony*, speaks of seven types of Pharisees according to the Jewish Talmud. The author of *The Bundle of Time* <note>original: "Faiſceau des temps," referring to the *Fasciculus temporum*, a popular world history by Werner Rolevinck</note> also adds the Arboneans and Genistes, as confirmed by François de Belleforest in book 2, chapter 4 of his *Universal History*. Carlo Sigonio, in book 5, chapter 11 of his *Republic of the Hebrews*, provides a list of other sects among the said Hebrews, distinct from those previously mentioned. A certain individual named Otthon Henonius, in his *Antiquities of Barbarian Philosophy* (the treatise titled *Indicus*, chapters 21 through 25), discusses this quite extensively, even speaking of the Rechabites <note>original: "Recabees"</note> and their successors the Essenes or Hossians; Gilbert Génébrard does the same in book 2, pages 197 and 198 of his *Chronography*.

As for the Hebrew Rabbis, we learn that the Hebrews have always named those of the greatest and most eminent knowledge among them Rabbanim <note>original: "רבנים"</note> or Rabbis, which is to say masters or persons of great dignity. In fact, he among the Hebrews who possesses great learning in the Holy Scripture is always called Rabbi <note>original: "רבי"</note>, meaning master, and among the Chaldeans, Rabbon <note>original: "רבון"</note>, which means the same. These words come from the root *Rab* <note>original: "רב"</note>, which in Latin means "great" or "much" <note>original: "multus"</note>. The power and virtue of this word is explained in several places in the Talmud, in the *Tishbi* of Elias Levita <note>A famous 16th-century Hebrew grammarian</note>, and in the discourse of Angelo Canini on the explanation of passages from the New Testament.

For a specific explanation of the words mentioned above, we refer to the statement of Porchetus <note>Salvagus Porchetus, a 14th-century Genoese monk who wrote against Jewish doctrines</note> in part 1, chapter 2 of his *Victory Against the Jews*, where he notes that Rabbi Nathan says the following in the Talmud: "The word Rabbi is attributed to the Sages of the land of Israel, upon whom hands were laid in the assemblies and councils of the Hebrews." This is said because of the "imposition of hands" by the elders and ancients, who place their hands upon someone and name him *Rabbi*, "my master." These Hebrews grant power to this created and initiated Rabbi to judge cases that deserve punishment—a ceremony which is still practiced today in the promotion of Jewish Rabbis.

Furthermore, we find in the same Talmud the terms *Rabban*, *Rabbana*, and *Rabbó*. The word *Rabbó*, which is pure Syriac, does not merely signify a simple master or Lord, but one who is called by the Greeks *Kyrios* <note>original: "κύριος"</note> <gloss>Lord <note>original: "x κύριος"</note></gloss> and by our legal scholars "he who possesses absolute power" <note>original: "ille qui habet merum imperium"</note>. Indeed, when the Hebrews mention God in the Mishnah, they use the word *Ribbon* <note>original: "ריבון"</note>. This is why Mary Magdalene saluted our Lord Jesus Christ, raised from death to life, by the name *Rabboni* in chapter 20 of the Gospel of Saint John; in the Syriac language, this carries the weight of "My Lord who knows God." Before the resurrection, no one had called him *Rabboni*, but only *Rabbi*. Be that as it may, one finds in some parts of the Talmud that *Rabbi* is a more excellent title than *Rab*, and *Rabbá* or *Rabbó* is more excellent than *Rabbi*. For this reason, it is said that our Lord Jesus Christ forbade Christians from calling any mortal by the name *Rabbon*.

Many great and curious investigations worthy of note on this matter are recited by Sebastian Münster in his Hebrew and Chaldean dictionaries and in his annotations on chapter 21 of Genesis; by Sante Pagnini in his *Hebrew Treasure* under the word *Rabbi*; by Guy Le Fèvre de La Boderie in his preface to the Syriac New Testament and in his Syro-Chaldean dictionary under the words *Rab*, *Ebed*, and *Ray* <note>original: "רב עבד ריי"</note>; and also by Johannes Mercerus in his booklet on abbreviations.

Génébrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard, a 16th-century French Benedictine scholar and Hebraist</note> at the end of his annotations on the Hebrew book *Seder Olam Zuta* <note>original: "Seder olant zuta," a small medieval Hebrew chronicle</note>, both of whom assert that the word **Rab** was in olden times attributed to the sages and doctors of Babylon; the word **Rabbi** to those of the land of Israel; **Rabban** or **Rabbana** to the sages of the house of David; and **Mar** or **Mor** to the sages of Babylon who were patriarchs and governors of the exiles. Elias Levita <note>A famous 16th-century Hebrew grammarian</note> in his *Tishbi* <note>original: "Thesbite," a dictionary of Talmudic and Midrashic words</note> [says]: "The Rabbis say that Rab and Mar are used for everyone who is from Babylonia, but Rabbi for anyone from the land of Israel; and there are those who are accustomed to pronounce it *Mor* with a *Holam* <note>a Hebrew vowel point</note>; but if it is so, I wonder then how it happens that it is not written with a *vav* <note>the Hebrew letter often used to indicate the 'o' sound</note>." <note>original: "Mar, dicunt Rabbini, Rab & Mar dicitur omnis qui est de Babylonia, Rabbi vero quicunque est de terra Israel, & sunt qui pronunciare solent Mor cum Holem quod si ita est, miror ergo quî fiat quod non fcribatur cum vau."</note> See the same author in the interpretation of the words **Rab** and **Rabaz**. F. Ricold <note>Ricoldo da Montecroce, a 13th-century Dominican missionary</note> or Richard of the order of Preaching Friars, in his confutation of the law of the Saracens [writes]: "For the Chaldean Christians and all Easterners call Bishops and monks, honoring them as **Rabban**, which is interpreted as master, or my elder; in the Arabic language, however, **Rába** is a name of God, which is interpreted as Lord absolutely." <note>original: "Christiani enim Chaldei, & omnes orientales vocāt Episcopos & monachos, honorantes cos Rában, q͂ interpretatur magister, vel maior meus: in Arabica autē lingua Rába, est nomē Dei, quod interpretatur Dominus absolutè."</note>

As for the synagogue of the Jews, it must be understood according to the saying of **R. Manahem** that anciently on **Mount Zion**, outside the city of Jerusalem, seven synagogues were introduced, in which the divine laws were taught indiscriminately without the possibility of using arguments or disputes regarding them, according to the report of **Optatus of Milevis** <note>original: "Optatus Mileuitanus," a 4th-century bishop and saint</note> in his third book. At the time of our Lord Jesus Christ, the synagogue of Jerusalem flourished, which **Alexander the Great** favored with several privileges, according to the words of **Josephus** and **Eusebius** in their works. **Epiphanius** in his book *On Weights and Measures* mentions that the synagogue of the Jews did not cease to be continued after the destruction of Jerusalem. **St. Jerome**, writing to **Pammachius**, writes that **Pompey**, after the Mithridatic War, held the synagogue of **Antioch** in great reverence, and that he was taught in Antioch by one **Apollinaris of Laodicea** <note>A significant 4th-century Christian scholar</note> from this synagogue, which is mentioned in the **Acts of the Apostles**, chapter 13.

Besides this, there was another of equally great honor and authority in the city of **Ephesus**, in which, besides the **Rabbins** and **Archisynagogues** <note>heads of the synagogue</note>, there were very great and excellent doctors in the interpretation of Holy Scripture, as **Justin Martyr** confirms in his dialogue against the Jew **Trypho**. There was also a synagogue in **Caesarea**, which the Romans exempted from tutelage and public burdens, as can be seen in the law *but also to reject* [regarding] the excuses of guardians <note>original Latin reference to the Roman Digest: "sed & reprobare d̃ excusationibus tutorum"</note>, and in this place **Origen** taught the Holy Scriptures, according to **Eusebius** in book 6, chapter 10.

The first beginning of the institution of these synagogues among the Jews was during the **Babylonian Captivity**, as **C. Sigonius** <note>Carlo Sigonio, a renowned 16th-century Italian humanist historian</note> writes in book 2, chapter 8 of the *Republic of the Hebrews*, since which beginning they were continued both in Judea and in several other regions for many centuries, according to the account of the same author in book 5, chapter 10 and those following. At present, when the Jews wish to depart from their synagogue, their service being completed in all points, in place of our *Benedicamus Domino* <note>Let us bless the Lord</note>, the Minister is accustomed to say this: "He who makes peace on high, in His high dwelling, may He also make peace upon us, and upon all the people of Israel," to which the assembly responds **Amen**; and while taking three steps backward—at the first of which they bow toward the right hand, at the second to the left, and at the third forward—which denotes nothing other...

Regarding the סנהדרין **Sanhedrin**, according to the testimony of Rabbi Moses Hadarsan in his commentaries on Genesis, these were 72 old and ancient personages—otherwise ordinary judges—established and ordained by Moses among the Jews in every city under their power and dominion (as seen in Numbers, chapter 11). They dispensed justice to those who requested it at the gates of said cities, as stated by Elias Levita in his *Tishbi* <note>a famous dictionary of the Talmud and Midrash</note>, and Pietro Galatino in Book 4, chapter 5 of the *Secrets of the Catholic Faith*. These Sanhedrin taught and explained to the common people the most arduous and difficult causes and trials to judge, and exercised justice in various ways, as is amply contained in the Hebrew book titled *Sanhedrin*, of which Porchetus <note>Porchetus de Salvaticis, a 14th-century monk</note> makes ample mention in Part 1, chapter 2 of his *Victory Against the Jews*. They were first ordained and instituted by the Prophet Moses, as can be seen in Exodus chapter 17, Numbers chapter 11, and Deuteronomy chapter 16; and they were anciently called in the Hebrew language סנהדרי **Sanhedar**, a word proceeding from the Greek term—for the Greeks call benches (upon which judges sit) <gloss>synedria</gloss>. Regarding this, the aforementioned Elias Levita, a Jew by nation, in his *Tishbi* in the explanation of this word Sanhedar, said the following words:

Nor is it found in the singular number. And it is clearly a Greek word: for the Greeks call the benches (on which judges sit) <gloss>synedria</gloss>, to which Psalm 122 alludes: "For there are set thrones for judgment."* <note>original: "Sanhedar, septuaginta, Sāhedrin, sic vocabantur septuaginta seniores consistorij magni..."</note>

## Of the origin of the Hebrew language and of its Characters.

### CHAPTER X.

Josephus, the Hebrew author, in his book on the *Antiquities of the Jews*; Cedrenus, a very ancient Greek author, in his works; and the Hebrew Rabbis in their writings, have all asserted that Seth and Enos—or, as is more likely, the nephews of our first father Adam, the children of Seth—constructed two columns long before the universal flood (which they had predicted and announced beforehand). One column was made of stone and the other of fired clay. On these, they wrote or engraved in their Hebrew characters and their Hebrew language all the arts, sciences, and knowledge of God and mathematics, together with the promises of the coming of the Messiah or Son of God, Jesus Christ. The aforementioned Josephus affirmed that he had seen one of these columns still standing in Syria in his time. Suidas, another Greek author, writes on this matter that Seth was the first who invented Hebrew letters and the names of the stars, planets, and celestial bodies. <margin>1</margin>
Certain other authors report that the ancient Hebrews had several and diverse types of characters: the first being those that were very old and ancient, used and practiced by Moses and the Prophets, which must not be divulged or demonstrated to mortal men.

<margin>2</margin>
The second are those called "celestial," because the Hebrews show them figured in the sky, just as astrologers show their signs composed of certain stars. Following the aforementioned Hebrews, this view was taken by the late Guillaume Postel <note>A 16th-century French polymath and mystic obsessed with universal language and world harmony.</note> in his commentaries on the book titled in the Hebrew language *Sepher Ietzirath* <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah* or "Book of Formation," an ancient and foundational text of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) that describes the world's creation through the Hebrew alphabet.</note>, which is very inappropriately attributed to the Patriarch Abraham, and other modern authors.

<margin>3</margin>
The third sort are those called the letters of the Angels, named in Hebrew *Malachim*, or *Melachim* <note>From the Hebrew *mal’akh*, meaning "messenger" or "angel." This refers to a specific occult alphabet used in ceremonial magic.</note>.

<margin>4</margin>
The last are those given to the Patriarch Abraham at the crossing of the river, when he departed from Chaldea to come into the land of Canaan.

The Hebrews assert that these characters were found on a statue on the banks of the Jordan River, upon which were engraved the names of the children of Israel when they crossed that same Jordan River, as is related in the Book of Joshua. This is confirmed by Abraham de Balmes <note>original: "Abraham de Palmis," a famous Italian-Jewish physician and grammarian (c. 1440–1523).</note>, a Jew by nation, in his *Grammatical Observations*, as reported by Teseo Ambrogio <note>original: "Theseus Ambrosius," an Italian canon and linguist who published an influential work on various alphabets in 1539.</note> in his *Appendix on Several and Diverse Languages*, stating:

> Agostino Panteo, a Venetian priest, records four Hebrew alphabets in his *Voarchadumia* <note>A work on alchemy and metallurgy published in Venice, 1530.</note>: namely, the common one used everywhere by everyone; a second given by Almighty God to Moses on Mount Sinai; a third granted to Abraham at the crossing of the river; and a fourth, which is older than the rest, handed down to Enoch. This last one, related to the order and number of our own alphabet, contains three extra aspirated letters, namely *Ch*, *Ph*, and *Th*. Abraham de Balmes, a Hebrew doctor, in his grammar printed long ago by Daniel Bomberg <note>One of the most important printers of Hebrew books in 16th-century Venice.</note>, knew only two Hebrew alphabets: the common one and the "Crossing the River" script. Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, in his books on *Occult Philosophy*, reported that the Kabbalists have various modes of creating characters. Besides the two aforementioned alphabets, he says there is another celestial script among the Hebrews, whereby—just as astrologers are accustomed to drawing the images of signs from the lines of the stars—they show the letters of their alphabet placed and shaped among the constellations. There is another which they were accustomed to calling *Malachim* or *Melachim*, which means the "Angelic" or "Regal" script. Having thus related six types of Hebrew letters, I judged it a worthwhile task to add in this Appendix of ours other Hebrew characters that are by no means to be despised, excerpted from various authors of no small reputation. Among the books of Antonio de Fantis of Treviso, formerly a most excellent philosopher and astrologer, I remember seeing the works of Raziel <note>Refers to the *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh*, a practical kabbalistic grimoire.</note>, the *Picatrix* <note>A famous medieval grimoire of astrological magic.</note>, *Bailum*, Hermes <note>original: "Mercurij," referring to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, Peter of Abano <note>original: "Petor Apponis," a 13th-century philosopher and reputed magician.</note>, Solomon, and that interpreter Apollonius <note>Likely Apollonius of Tyana.</note>, and many others. From these, as if from a living and flowering meadow, I gathered the flowers of various letters and diverse characters. I read those books quite diligently before they fell into the power of Vulcan <note>A classical idiom meaning "to be burned" or "destroyed by fire."</note> at the hands of our fathers, into whose possession they had come by testament, for no other reason than to copy out those characters—that is, the various shapes of the letters. He asserts that the Angel Raphael, in the book called the *Book of Fire*, gave them in written form to Adam, the First-Formed <note>original: "Adæ Protoplasto."</note>, and for that reason the children of Adam cannot reject them. Here is yet another [alphabet] which was likewise brought a long time ago from those regions to Venice, when the Christian Princes and Barons were making war there against the infidel Muslims <note>original: "Mahometistes"</note>. It consists of very beautiful and pleasing characters, quite different from the common ones, and copied from those of a significant and ancient inscription that was in Jerusalem. These are distributed into three rows, each of nine characters, where the first begins at the bottom from the right hand toward the left, in the Hebrew fashion; the second, namely the middle one, follows from left to right as it rises; and the third, the one at the top, goes from right to left once again. 

As can be seen here, it is highly noteworthy that the sixth letter, which is *Vau*, is entirely similar to a cross, like the Samaritan *Vau* shown below. This alphabet is attributed—according to the previously mentioned Agostino Panteo <note>An Italian priest and alchemist (c. 1440–1535) whose work explored the mystical properties of letters.</note> in the second part of his *Voarchadumia* <note>original: "Vuarchadumie," an alchemical treatise published in 1530.</note>, following the account of the said Teseo Ambrogio <note>An Italian linguist and scholar of Oriental languages.</note>—to Enoch, who served as scribe and secretary to Adam himself, as the Kabbalists <note>original: "Mecubalistes," from the Hebrew *Mekubbalim*, meaning those who receive the tradition.</note> say. 

It is claimed that these were the characters with which Enoch and Seth <note>The third son of Adam and Eve.</note> engraved the two columns mentioned in Book 1, Chapter 4 of Josephus's *Antiquities of the Jews*: one of marble or stone, and the other of fired bricks. Upon these they recorded everything they had been able to learn of the secrets of the Stars and the elements, to preserve them from the universal accidents of conflagrations and floods that were destined to occur. And indeed, how could it have been possible that in the short span of three hundred years between the Flood and Abraham—in whose time astrology was in its greatest vogue in the land of Chaldea—one could have established the rules and maxims of [astrology if not for these records]?

### Portrait of the characters of Enoch.

<image-desc>A rectangular frame containing three rows of mystical, occult symbols or "Characters of Enoch." These characters are bold and angular, bearing some stylistic resemblance to archaic Hebrew or Greek scripts but unique in their specific forms.</image-desc>

Even today, it is well enough known that there is still in *Ethiopia* a treatise on divine things attributed to this same *Enoch* <note>Referring to the "Book of Enoch" (1 Enoch), which was preserved in Ge'ez (Ethiopic) and considered canonical by the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.</note>, held there in very great respect and recognized as Canonical. And certainly, we are more enlightened by the slightest understanding we can conceive of the celestial substances and the <term>intelligences</term> <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, these were spiritual beings or angels thought to guide the movement of the planets.</note> that assist them, than if, through all our reasonings and discourses, we had reached all the deepest effects of nature in this low elementary world. For since from all eternity the dispositions of all things to come are immutably ordained in God, it follows from this that those who—by a supreme intensity and rapture of thought, and by a sovereign [devotion] toward Him from whom everything proceeds—strive to approach Him most closely, will be the ones nearest and most apt to foresee them. 

And yet our Spirit is more suited and fit for this during the body's sleep than while awake, because its affections are then more brilliant and unbridled, so that they prevail over the contemplative part. By means of which the predictions of the Hebrews relate to these ecstasies and transportations to the third heaven <note>A mystical state of divine revelation or paradise.</note>, which is the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure ideas and spiritual truths, as opposed to the physical world.</note> and the book of life, together with the Shining Mirror, where all things are seen clearly and distinctly, without any veil or covering, and consequently in the Hebrew letters and language also better than in any others. This is what the *Zohar* <note>original: "Zoar"; the foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah.</note> and other more distinguished Kabbalists interpret as the mediating and driving power of the whole universe: namely, the intellect of the Messiah or the Word, the "Mind of minds" <note>original: *Mens mentium*</note>, as they call it, through whom the sovereign Father moves all things. Those [disciplines] of the Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses who were believed to possess divine knowledge of the future.</note> were dedicated to the elementary and lower world, for the conduct and regulation of human affairs; this was the reason why the Romans embraced them more willingly, as they were entirely focused and inclined toward such matters. Thus, there were three principal disciplines among the wise Ancients:

The first is that of the Hebrews, which tends only toward conforming our thoughts, actions, and behaviors to the right path, prescribed by divine ordinances and precepts. These express how God wishes to be honored and served, and how we must maintain ourselves through a mutual and reciprocal charity from neighbor to neighbor, for the preservation of human society. There is nothing on earth more pleasing to the great Monarch and Ruler of the whole Universe than this, by the very testimony of Cicero, notwithstanding that he was a Gentile and Pagan.

The second concerns the effects proceeding from the heavens and the variety of diverse influences here below, the foresight of which is granted to us so that we may prepare for, accommodate, or prevent them. "A wise man shall rule the stars" <note>original: *vir sapiens dominabitur astris*</note>, says the astrologer Ptolemy. This discipline was more specific to the Chaldeans, then to the <term>Brahmans</term> <note>The priestly and scholarly caste of ancient India.</note>, the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>A group of ancient Indian philosophers who lived as ascetics and were known for their "naked wisdom."</note>, and other Sages of the East who followed the first rays of the Sun daily at its rising from the Ocean, as if it had come to refresh itself from its bed and reinvigorate itself with new strength, just like a stag leaving its resting place.

The third was of things established under the heavens, within the elementary world, of which the earth serves as a base and foundation. In this realm, omens and presages cannot be better assigned than in that which, in animals, is most closely joined from the spirit of life to the material mass of the body—such as the heart, liver, and other <term>internal organs</term> <note>original: "precordes"; the viscera around the heart believed to be the seat of emotions and life force.</note> where this spirit has its principal seat and dwelling. This was used for the interpretation of wonders and similar signs, which warn us of some significant disaster or calamity to come. This was the specific domain of the Egyptians and Etruscans, who were excellent in <term>haruspicy</term> <note>original: "aruspicine"; the ancient practice of divining the future by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals.</note>. From these three disciplines mixed together, the Magi composed their own fourth one.

In this there appears a certain "crossroads" of the world, in which the Hebrews hold the center, the Chaldeans and Indians the end of the East <note>original: "Leuant"</note>, the Celts and Etruscans the West, the Egyptians and Ethiopians the South <note>original: "Midy"</note>, and the Scythians the North <note>original: "Septentrion"</note>, like the four principal hinges of the earth, to which all the rest relates.

Some other authors have said that Moses had and used only two kinds of characters: one being those in which the two tables of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> were written or engraved by the very hand and finger of God, as we will deduce very particularly hereafter. These characters are full of great and profound mysteries in their shapes, all depending on the *Iod* <note>The Hebrew letter *Yod* (י), the smallest letter of the alphabet, often viewed in Kabbalah as the point from which all other letters and the universe itself originate.</note>, as will be said hereafter. Priests and Levites for spiritual matters only—though the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council or court of justice in ancient Israel</note> were not excluded from it either—which one should in no way doubt was the same script we have today. This is evidenced by these two Hebrew letters, **ס**, *Samech*, and **ם**, *Mem* finals, which were preserved whole within the fragments of the first tables of law that were broken because of the Golden Calf <note>According to Jewish tradition, because these letters are closed loops, they were held in place miraculously when the Ten Commandments were engraved through the stone</note>. This writing was afterwards released indifferently to the public by Ezra upon the return from the Babylonian captivity. The other set of characters, which are said to be those of the Samaritans, served for profane <term>profane: here meaning secular or non-religious</term> purposes, such as justice, civil administration, trade, and similar worldly affairs. Consequently, the script used by the ancient Chaldeans was vulgar and used by all the Jewish people; it was later shared with the Phoenicians. Just as Syriac and Arabic arose from Hebrew, the Greek script was born from the Phoenician, and consequently the Latin script, which consists entirely, or nearly so, of Greek capital letters, as we shall demonstrate hereafter.

Berossus and Saint Jerome, in his prologue to the Galatians and on Chapter 9 of the Prophet Ezekiel, and in his preface to the Book of Kings, along with the Hebrew author of the *Massekhet Sanhedrin* <note>original: "Masechet Sanhedrin" — a tractate of the Talmud dealing with the law and the priesthood</note>, write that after the capture of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Temple under Zerubbabel, Ezra found the Hebrew letters which the Jews and we ourselves still use today. This seems to be confirmed by Philo the Jew in Book 2 of *The Life of Moses*. Some modern scholars agree with this more readily than with all that has been said above, seeing as the Hebrews and Jews before this Ezra used Samaritan characters, which I treat at length hereafter in a separate chapter on the Samaritan language. Some among the Rabbis themselves agree with this, holding for a certainty that these Samaritan characters were the first in the world. They allege certain reasons for this, among others that these Samaritans always possessed the Torah, or Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>, in this, their own particular Samaritan script. Furthermore, the most ancient medals and coins of gold, silver, and other metals—which have been found from time immemorial in the ruins and countless locations of Jerusalem and Palestine—were inscribed and engraved with Samaritan letters. This is confirmed by Benito Arias Montano in Volume 3 of the *Apparatus*, in the chapter on the Shekel near the end, and after him by François Louis in his *Globe of the Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*, Chapter 1. This is a thing which denotes that the Hebrew letters of today are not the same as the first and most ancient ones.

So it was that the Hebrews or Israelites, during the revolt of the ten tribes when they split from the crown of Judah under Rehoboam, son of Solomon—with whom only Judah and Benjamin remained—went to establish themselves under Jeroboam in the midst of Judea, in the region of Samaria at Shechem, the capital city of their entire state. They declined into idolatry, and because they kept the ancient Hebrew characters, Ezra (or Jeshua his son, the High Priest) and the other Jews who had remained in the true religion of the Great God, wishing to have nothing in common with them, chose to use and serve other letters and scripts that were entirely different, which they invented from that time on. The Samaritans, together with their descendants and posterity until today, have always kept the ancient characters of their fathers and ancestors.

However, Rabbi Simeon, son of Eleazar, maintains that the language and script of the aforementioned Hebrews and Israelites were never changed, and were no other than those practiced even to this day.

### Alphabet of Apollonius of Tyana.
<note>Apollonius of Tyana was a 1st-century Greek Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker whose life became a subject of legend and occult fascination in the Renaissance.</note>

Several other matters of consideration in this subject are treated in the work of Cardinal Egidius <note>Egidius de Viterbo, an influential Renaissance Humanist and Hebraist</note> in his book *On the Hebrew Elements* <note>original: "de Hebraicis Elementis"</note>, by Paulus Riccius in his *Miscellany* <note>original: "farrago"</note> drawn from the book of the Talmud of the Jews, by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in his *Epistle addressed to his unknown friend*, by Pietro Crinito in book 25, chapter 3, *On Honorable Learning* <note>original: "de honesta disciplina"</note>, by Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa in his treatise *On the Vanity of the Sciences* <note>original: "de la vanité des sciences"</note> chapter 2, and in his book *On Occult Philosophy*, by Benito Arias Montano in volume 3 of the *Apparatus, in the chapter on the Shekel, at the end* <note>original: "apparatus cap. de Ciclo in fine"</note>, by Andreas Masius *On Genesis* <note>original: "in Genesim"</note>, and by Friar Louis Vives, a Portuguese <note>This likely refers to a different Louis Vives than the famous Spanish humanist Juan Luis Vives, or reflects a geographical confusion by the author</note>, in book 1 of his *Globe of Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*, chapter 1.

There are also other Hebrew characters besides those represented in the figures above, which are always written without any <term>points or accents</term> <note>referring to the niqqud, or vowel markings, used in biblical texts but omitted in daily or rabbinic writing</note>. These are practiced and used by the majority of Hebrew Rabbis in their commentaries and traditions; this is what is called <term>running letter</term> <note>original: "lettre courante," known today as Rashi script or cursive Hebrew</note>, because it is written more quickly than the preceding type, being less square and more rounded. For this reason, it does not possess such grace or pleasure for the eye. It is called the "small" or "fine" script, or *Masquet*, a word which signifies "thin" and "slender" in the Arabic language, as Elias Levita <note>A famous 16th-century Hebrew grammarian</note> has very well noted in his *Tishbi* <note>original: "Thesbite," a dictionary of Rabbinic Hebrew</note>, in the interpretation of this word *Mashket*. Here are the figures for these: the first used by Jews dwelling in Germany <note>Ashkenazi script</note>, and the other by Jews dwelling in Spain <note>Sephardic script</note>, as confirmed by Sebastian Münster in his *Chaldean Grammar*.

As for what the late G. Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581) was a French Renaissance polymath and linguist who sought to find a common mystical foundation for all languages.</note> had written about it in his treatise on Phoenician letters, it is not to be wondered at, given the inconstant and changeable nature of men, who every day shift and change their scripts—and even their printing styles—writing and printing their books in one way at one time, and in an entirely different way at another, seeking a style more proper, beautiful, and elegant. And because the Hebrews have no vowels arranged in alphabetical order, and instead the consonants must perform that office when adorned and illustrated with points according to their various positions and pairings, one rarely finds a sequence of letters in this Hebrew language from which some meaning cannot be drawn, in whatever way they might be reversed or turned about. Furthermore, these letters are all square and without any ligatures, unlike those seen in Syriac and Arabic scripts, which are very graceful yet of a displeasing aspect <note>The author likely refers to the "displeasing" complexity of cursive ligatures compared to the perceived "purity" of the isolated Hebrew square script.</note>. This is to demonstrate that this Hebrew language has never had any communication with those of other peoples and nations, but has always remained apart, as something separate from the rest of the generation of men. It is quite certain that from the beginning of the world until the present, it has never received any alteration or corruption in its dialect or manner of speaking.

On this subject, see St. Jerome <note>original: "S. Hierosme"</note> in his prologue on the Prophet Jeremiah, in his last Epistle to Paula Urbica, and in his exposition on chapter 3 of Zephaniah; Abraham Balmensis <note>Abraham de Balmes (c. 1440–1523), a Jewish-Italian physician and grammarian.</note> in his treatise on Hebrew letters; Carretius <note>Ludovicus Carretus, a 16th-century Jewish convert to Christianity.</note>, a Jew converted to Christianity, in his Hebrew Epistle addressed to his children; Johannes Reuchlin, called Capnion <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a German humanist and a key figure in the study of Hebrew and the Kabbalah.</note>, in his books on the Kabbalah of the Jews; Sebastian Nozenus in his treatise on the first lesson of the Hebrew tongue; Agostino Steuco <note>original: "Augustin Steuchus"</note> in his annotations on chapter 37 of Genesis; Pedro Mexía <note>original: "P. Genebrard"</note> in book 2 of his *Chronography*; and Blaise de Vigenère <note>B. de Vigenere (1523–1596), a diplomat and cryptographer famous for the "Vigenère cipher."</note> in his treatise on ciphers.

And concerning the explanation or interpretation of the meanings and mysteries contained beneath the surface of the preceding alphabets, we shall say that Eusebius in book 10, chapter 2, and book 11, chapter 4 of his *Preparation* <note>original: "Preparation Evangelique"</note>, together with St. Jerome to Urbica and in his preface to the commentaries on Lamentations, rightly mock the Greeks. For the Greeks, with all their skill and bravado in the exaltation of their language, could not find any meaning in their own Alphabet, whereas the children of the Hebrews can in that of their Hebrew tongue. If these children are asked what א **Aleph** signifies, they immediately answer that it is "discipline"; ב **Beth**, "a house"—understanding by these words "the house of discipline," as if one were saying a discipline of doctrine, of economy and stewardship; ג **Ghimel**, "Fullness of voice"; ד **Daleth**, "books"; ה **He**, "the whole together" which was said before—namely, the discipline of the house and the fullness of voice and of books; ו **Vau**, "in it"; ז **Zain**, "he lives"; ח **Heth**, "the living"—that is to say, he altogether lives living within it; ט **Teth**, "the good"; י **Iod**, "Principle"—these two letters together signifying "a good Prince"; כ **Caph**, "nonetheless"; ל **Lamed**, "aid"—learn all together, and nonetheless learn the מ **Mem**, "from them"; נ **Nun**, "the everlasting help"; ס **Samech**, "Base"; ע **Ain**, "of the Fountain" or "eye"; פ **Pe**, "of the mouth"; צ **Tzade**, "justice"—this last period carrying these words: "the Fountai..."

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THINGS
<meta>catchword: finale</meta>

...heavenly beings, those who are called the *Hasmalim* <note>original: "Hasmalim," an order of angels often interpreted as "shining ones" or "amber ones"</note>, and by the power of God, they are influenced through the medium of the third intelligence, and by that same power they influence those below them. **He** [ה] designates the essence or superior beings of the fifth emanation from God himself, which are the *Seraphim* <note>the "burning ones," among the highest orders of angels</note>; they are influenced by the power of God through the medium of the fourth intelligence, and by that same power they influence those below. ***Vau*** [ו] marks the essence of the heavenly beings of the sixth emanation, who are called the *Malachim* <note>meaning "Messengers" or "Angels"</note>, that is, Angels; they are influenced by the power of God through the medium of the fifth intelligence, and by that same power they influence those below. ***Zain*** [ז] is the seal of the blessed superior spirits of the seventh emanation, who are named *Elohim* <note>a name for God or "divine beings"</note>, that is, Gods; they are influenced by the power of God through the Angels of the sixth order, and by that same power they influence those below. ***Heth*** [ח] is the sign of the superior beings of the eighth emanation, and these are the Angels called the *Beni Elohim* <note>meaning "Sons of God"</note>, that is, the sons of the Gods; they are influenced by the power of *El* <note>a primary Hebrew name for God</note> through the Angels of the seventh order, and by that same divine power they influence those below. ***Theth*** [ט] is the mark of the Angels of the ninth emanation, who are called *Cherubim* <note>celestial beings often associated with wisdom and the presence of God</note>; they are influenced by the power of God through the medium of the intelligence of the eighth order, and by that same power they influence those below. ***Iod*** [י], the tenth letter, signifies the essence of the intelligences of the tenth emanation; they are called the ***Isim*** <note>meaning "Men" or "Individuals"</note>, the noble and patrician ones. They are lower than all the other hierarchies and are illuminated by the power of God through the ninth Choir; by that same power, they influence the children of men with knowledge, the science of things, and marvelous skill. From this, those endowed with such a faculty are called "sons of *Ish*" <note>Hebrew: אישׁ, meaning "man"</note>, that is, men of noble intelligence, of whom Psalm 49 speaks: "Both low and high," <note>original Latin: "Quique terrigenæ & filij hominum"</note> which is properly read as "both the sons of the Commoners and the sons of the Patricians," as if to say, both the rustic and the noble. We ourselves take this name from this order of intelligences. For there is within us an "active intellect," the highest part of the soul, which Aristotle calls <term>νοῦς</term> <note>Greek: "nous," meaning mind or intellect</note>, that is, the mind; which alone comes to us from the outside. From this proceed prophetic visions and all great and holy things; it is called the *Sekhel Ha-Poel* <note>Hebrew: השכל הפועל, the "Active Intellect"</note> by which the angelic world is bounded.

Next is ***Caph*** [כ]; this letter designates the *primum mobile* <note>the "first moved" sphere in classical astronomy that carries all others</note> from *El Shaddai* <note>original: "El Sadai," a name for God meaning "The Almighty"</note> himself as the immediate first cause, though moved communicatively through the spirit of rational life, which is the Angel *Metattron* <note>a high archangel in mystical traditions, often called the Prince of the Countenance</note>; he is called the active intellect of the sensible world, providing a way for all things below through the penetration of forms; thus he influences by divine power everything that is movable. ***Caph* finale** [ך] signifies the circuit of the fixed stars, which is called the eighth sphere in relation to us, but in relation to the higher realms, it is the second orb divided into the twelve signs of the Zodiac, which we call the *Galgalim* <note>Hebrew: גלגלים, meaning "spheres" or "wheels"</note>; it is influenced by the power of God through the medium of the intelligence of *Caph* itself, and similarly influences those below. ***Lamed*** [ל] is the sign of the first sphere of the planets, and they are called *Kokhavim* <note>Hebrew: כוכבים, meaning "stars"</note>, as if they were wanderers, whom the Latins call *errones* after the Greeks, who for this reason assert they are <term>πλανῆτας</term> <note>Greek: "planetas," meaning "wanderers"</note>. It is called the seventh orb attributed to Saturn, whom we name *Sabathai* <note>Hebrew: שבתאי, derived from the word for Sabbath or rest</note>; it influences and is influenced. **Open *Mem*** [מ] marks the sphere of Jupiter, which is named *Tzedek* <note>Hebrew: צדק, meaning "Justice" or "Righteousness"</note> by us, and is influenced by the power of God through the medium of the higher intelligence, and by that same power it influences those below. **Closed *Mem*** [ם] is the symbol of the sphere of Mars, which we call *Madanim* <note>Hebrew: מאדימים, usually spelled Ma'adim, meaning "the red one"</note>, the fifth orb; it is influenced by the power of God the creator through the Angel immediately above it, and by that same power it influences those below. ***Nun*** [נ] signifies the greater light, which is called *Shemesh* <note>Hebrew: שמש, the common word for the Sun</note>, that is, the Sun, and its sphere is called the orb of *Hammah* <note>Hebrew: חמה, a poetic name for the Sun meaning "the hot one"</note>; it is influenced by God through the medium of the sixth intelligence, through which it also influences the lower things. ***Nun* finale** [ן]...

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE

...the final [form of the letter Nun] <note>original: "finale"; refers to the letter Nun [ן] in its final position, following the sequence from the previous page</note> indicates the sphere of Venus, which is called *Nogah* <note>original: "Nogah," meaning "shining brightness"</note> by us and consists of the power of God, and it flows down through the medium of the seventh intelligence. **Samech** [ס] is the symbol of the Chancellor, who is called *Cochab* <note>original: "Cochab," the Hebrew name for Mercury, meaning "star"</note>, known as Mercury in Latin; it is influenced by the power of God from the higher realms and, by that same power, it influences the lower realms. **Ain** [ע] is the mark of the Sphere of the Moon, which is called *Iareah* <note>original: "Iareah," the Hebrew word for the Moon</note> by us, and it appears like the left eye of the World. It is the last of the spheres among the stars, and because of its whiteness, it is sometimes named *Lebanah* <note>original: "Lebanah," meaning "the white one"</note>. All these things we entrust to the skill of Astrology.

**Pe** [פ] signifies the intellectual soul, both individual and universal, and is directed by the separate intelligences into which it is poured by God, as much in the spheres as in the stars, and in all higher and lower living things of the spheres and elements. **Final Phe** [ף] denotes the animal spirits, which are directed by the higher intelligences by the power and command of God. **Zade** [צ] symbolizes matter—both that of the heavens, which is intelligible, and that of the elements, which is sensible—and all mixed things. These are directed by divine power through the separate intelligences and through their own forms. **Final Zade** [ץ] shows the forms of the elements, which are fire, air, water, and earth. They are ruled by divine power through the angels called *Issim* <note>original: "Issim," or the "Ishim," the angelic order closest to humanity, often associated with the souls of the righteous</note>, and by the power of the heavens, and by the power of "prime matter," which is the source and origin of all elements.

**Koph** [ק] is the symbol of inanimate things and minerals, and those things which are called "elemented" and mixed. They are directed by divine power through the celestial spheres and the separate intelligences called the *Issim*. They also influence lower things in the region of the four elements. **Res** [ר] signifies all growing things, fruits, crops, and the plants of the earth; they are influenced by the power of God through the celestial bodies and the separate intelligences named *Issim*, and likewise by the combinations of the elements. **Schin** [ש] designates all sentient things, including the reptiles of the earth and walking creatures, the fish of the waters, and the birds of the air together; and those which, though irrational, have vital movement, which are ruled by the power of God through the celestial bodies and the intelligences called *Issim* and the combinations of the elements.

**Thau** [ת] is the symbol of man and human nature, which is the perfection and end of all creatures. It is directed by God through the combinations and qualities of the elements according to the influences of the heavens and through the peculiar offices of the separate intelligences, the *Issim*, which are of an angelic condition. And just as they are the end and completion in the world of angels, so man is the end and perfection of creatures in the world of elements—or rather, he is established in the world of the universe. For he is made of two worlds, just as it is written:
> The Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.

These matters are treated more abundantly by our ancestors, in whose descendants there clearly appears a most ardent love for the sacred scriptures; they have studied to give an account of everything, even the smallest details. For example, concerning **Aleph** [א], it is written in the *Book Bahir* <note>original: "Libro Habair," referring to the Sefer Ha-Bahir or "Book of Brightness," an early Kabbalistic text</note>—that is, "of brightness"—where Rabbi Amorai sat and disputed: Why is *Aleph* placed at the head of the Alphabet? And it is answered: because it was before all things, even before the Law <note>The Torah</note>. Menachem Recanati <note>original: "Mnaen Racanat," a 13th-14th century Italian Kabbalist</note> mentions this concerning Rabbi Ruhumai, the author of that book, in the first section on Genesis.

Furthermore, why does **Beth** [ב] follow next? Certainly because it was the beginning of the Law <note>The first letter of the first word of the Bible, *Bereshit* (In the beginning), is Beth</note>. And why is **Ghimel** [ג] not named *Gidel*, since in the sacred scriptures the root "to grow" [גדל] is placed before the root "to wean" [גמל] in Genesis 21, where it is written: *And the child grew and was weaned* <note>original: "ויגדל הילד ויגמל" (Vayigdal hayeled vayigamel)</note>. Truly, wise men did not disdain to scrutinize such things and others like them...

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE [LANGUAGES]

There are also a certain number of scholars who, for the sake of brevity, have bypassed the detailed reasoning of others and written only what simply pertains to the matter, since they have always strived with all diligence and zeal to hasten toward more sublime things. One such example is Rabbi Jacob Cohen <note>A 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist known for his work on the mystical properties of the Hebrew letters.</note> in the book titled *Exposition of the Holy Name*. Regarding the alphabet, he speaks briefly as follows: 

**Aleph** signifies Air <note>original Hebrew: אויר (*Avir*)</note>, **Beth** signifies Life <note>original Hebrew: חיים (*Chayyim*)</note>, **Gimel** signifies Peace <note>original Hebrew: שלום (*Shalom*)</note>, **Daleth** signifies Wisdom <note>original Hebrew: חכמה (*Chokhmah*)</note>, **He** signifies Sight <note>original Hebrew: ראיה (*Re'iyah*)</note>, **Vau** signifies Hearing <note>original Hebrew: שמיעה (*Shemi'ah*)</note>, **Zain** signifies Smell <note>original Hebrew: חריח (*Reach*)</note>, **Heth** signifies Speech <note>original Hebrew: דיבור (*Dibur*)</note>, **Teth** signifies Infusion <note>original Hebrew: יציקה (*Yetzikah*); likely referring to the pouring of influence or fluids</note>, **Iod** signifies Cohabitation <note>original Hebrew: שכיבה (*Shekhivah*); literally "lying down," often referring to rest or sexual union</note>, **Caph** signifies Wealth <note>original Hebrew: עושר (*Osher*)</note>, **Lamed** signifies Labor <note>original Hebrew: מלאכה (*Melakhah*)</note>, **Mem** signifies Water <note>original Hebrew: מים (*Mayim*)</note>, **Nun** signifies Walking <note>original Hebrew: הלוך (*Halokh*)</note>, **Samech** signifies Spirit <note>original Hebrew: רוח (*Ruach*); can also mean wind or breath</note>, **Ain** signifies Laughter <note>original Hebrew: שחוק (*Sechok*)</note>, **Pe** signifies Seed <note>original Hebrew: זרע (*Zera*)</note>, **Zade** signifies Suspicion <note>original Hebrew: חריז (*Chariz*); possibly "investigation"</note>, **Koph** signifies Sleep <note>original Hebrew: שינה (*Shenah*)</note>, **Res** signifies Grace <note>original Hebrew: חן (*Chen*)</note>, **Sin** signifies Fire <note>original Hebrew: אש (*Esh*)</note>, and **Thau** signifies Power <note>original Hebrew: ממשלה (*Memshalah*); dominion or rule</note>. 

He listed them with these words: Air, life, peace, wisdom, sight, hearing, smell, speech, infusion, lying down, wealth, business, water-course, spirit, laughter, seed, suspicion, sleep, grace, fire, and power. These and other remaining things that you have heard, I have gathered as briefly as possible from the monuments of the Fathers, so that I might offer you at least a small taste of the literary profession. Indeed, the distinguished author Rabbi Akiba wrote about these things with great care, and many of our most learned men have followed his example, whom we deem worthy of much honor. They said that many meanings lie hidden in the exposition of the alphabet. 

Rabbi Abraham Aben Ezra <note>A celebrated 12th-century scholar and polymath</note> says of this in the book titled *The Secret of the Torah* <note>original Hebrew: סוד תורה (*Sod Torah*)</note>: "It is true that it is good for this to be understood, because wisdom is said to come from them; however, we should not labor in the literal art for the entirety of our lives." He himself says that we should not be tormented day and night in the volumes of Rabbi Judah <note>Judah Hayyuj, the father of Hebrew grammar</note>, who is said to be the first grammarian of the Hebrews, nor in those twenty books that Marinus <note>Jonah ibn Janah, a famous medieval grammarian</note> composed on the instruction of letters, nor those twenty-two books which Samuel Nagid <note>Samuel ha-Nagid, a prominent statesman and scholar in Islamic Spain</note> published on the same subject. Thus far speaks Abraham Aben Ezra, nor did this most prudent man and expert in letters feel this way in vain, for we were born for greater and higher things.

Beyond all that we have deduced above, we will report that certain other Rabbis have given a simple interpretation to their aforesaid alphabet in this manner:

**Aleph**: Ox. **Beth**: House. **Gimel**: Camel. **Daleth**: Door. **He**: of a hook <note>original: "verpunique"; an obscure term, perhaps referring to a lattice or a specific type of fastener</note>. **Vau**: Pointed nail. **Zain**: Arrow. **Heth**: Four-footed beast. **Teth**: Enveloping. **Iod**: Hand. **Caph**: Palm. **Lamed**: Goad. **Mem**: Stain. **Nun**: Fish. **Samech**: Base. **Ain**: Fountain. **Pe**: Mouth. **Tsade**: Fishhook. **Coph**: Monkey. **Res**: Head. **Schin**: Tooth. **Thau**: Voice, term, or boundary. 

[Alternatively:] **Aleph**: The principle of the world, God. **Beth**: Life. **Gimel**: Peace. **Daleth**: Taste. **Iod**: Congregation. **Caph**: Riches. **Lamed**: Operation. **Mem**: Mother. **Nun**: Walking. **Samech**: Wrath. **Ain**: Laughter. **Pe**: Grace. **Tsade**: Suspicion. **Koph**: Sleep. **Res**: Lineage. **Thau**: Empire and power. 

Many and infinite other observations on this subject—very beautiful and curious—are deduced within the Kabbalah following Rabbi Akiba, Rabbi Judah, Marinus, Samuel Nagid, Rabbi Abraham Aben Ezra, and Rabbi Jacob Cohen in their Kabbalistic works. Also: Jean Cheradame in his *Alphabet of the Holy Language*; Pagninus in *Institutions*, Book 1, Chapter 3; Martinus Gilbertus on Hebrew letters in the chapter on significance from the nature of letters; Cornelius Bertramus in his *Institutions*; Paulus Scaligerus in the *Catholic Epistle*, Book 12; Paul of Venice in the *Book of Problems*, Volume 1, Section 1, Problem 51; Goropius in his *Hieroglyphics*; by Guillaume Postel in the *Book of the Affinity of Languages and the Excellence of the Hebrew Language*; Louys Carretus, a Jew made Christian, in his *Epistle to the Jews*, otherwise known as *Divine Visions*; and Jean Boulesse:

->*On the etymology of Hebrew letters and others.*<-

### CHAP. II.

The Hebrews call a letter in their language אות *Oth*, which is to say, as it were, a "sign." In fact, this word אות <gloss>Oth</gloss> is a sign, as can be seen in Ezekiel, Chapter 4. The plural of this word is אותות *Hothijoth*, which means "letters"; it is defined as being a sign of will imposed upon the human voice. Regarding this, Saint Augustine, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, said that the signs of words—which pass suddenly through the beaten or struck air—were established by letters. And rightly so, Isidore, in Chapter 3 of his *Etymologies*, wrote that these are the indices and marks of things, and the signs of words. The same Saint Augustine, in Book 2 of *On Order*, Chapter 13, asserts that Grammar, because of the letters of which it makes profession, was named *Literatura* <note>Literature/Learning</note>; and in that passage, this holy personage treated excellently the occasion for the invention of Grammar, and the distinction between letters, syllables, and verbs. Among the Latins, according to the aforementioned Isidore in Chapter 3 of the *Etymologies*: "A letter is so called as if providing a path for readers, or because it is repeated in reading" <note>original Latin: *litera dicitur quasi iter legentibus præstans, vel quod in legendo iteratur*</note>; or else, according to Priscian: "A letter is named from erasures, for they are written and erased" <note>original Latin: *litera à lituris, cùm scribuntur, & delentur, dicta*</note>. On this subject, one may see Caelius Rhodiginus in Book 24, Chapters 5 and 6 of his *Various Readings*; Johannes Goropius Becanus in his *Heremathene*, Book 3, page 34 and following; and Pierre Grégoire in Book 16, Chapter 3 of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art*. Letters are also called Elements <note>original: *Elemēta*</note>, after the likeness or similarity of the physical elements: "For just as elements are the first thing in the composition of any natural thing, and no resolution can be made except back to the elements, so too any language is composed of letters as if from elements" <note>original Latin: *nam sicut elementa sunt primùm quod est in compositione cuiusque rei naturalis, nec fieri potest resolutio, nisi vsque ad elementa, ita etia quodcumque Idioma ex literis tanquam ex elementis componitur*</note>. Moreover, an element—witness Aristotle in Book 1 of the *Poetics*, Chapter 7—is an indivisible sound, not just any sound, but only that which is by its nature an intelligible sound consti—

Elements, truly, are called the first letters of any language because of their pronunciation, inasmuch as they intrinsically compose the voice itself. They are also called "letters" <note>Latin: *literae*</note> because they are read <note>Latin: *leguntur*</note> and written <note>Latin: *scribuntur*</note>, as Abulensis <note>Alonso Tostado, Bishop of Avila</note> noted in *On Galatians*, question 6. ### CHAPTER XII.

The Hebrew Doctors assert with good and just cause that their Hebrew writing is more excellent, miraculous, and divine than any other writing that has ever been, is now, or could ever be in this universe, as much in the shape of its characters and the points serving as vowels as in the peaks and summits of its flourishes <note>apicules; the decorative "crowns" or tittles on Hebrew letters</note> and accents. It is as if the language consisted of matter, form, and spirit, having been first figured and engraved in the heavens by the positions of the stars; after this model, as the Rabbis and Cabalists recount, the Hebrew characters were formed, filled with celestial mysteries—both through their shape and form and by their numbers and various harmonic combinations. Because of this, the Jewish <term>Mecubales</term> <note>Kabbalists; practitioners of the received mystical tradition</note> boast (as reported by Rabbi Ramban <note>Nachmanides, a major 13th-century Jewish scholar</note> in his commentary on the beginning of Genesis, and as I have said before) that by the position, situation, assembly, signature, simplicity, composition, separation, crookedness, direction, deficiency, abundance, minority, majority, coronation, and revolution of these characters—as well as their points, flourishes, and the calculation of numbers signified by them—they can easily explain and express everything that can be seen by the eye and believed through faith; in short, all things that can be found in this world. To achieve this, they divide the letters of their alphabet in several ways and sorts, drawing from them an infinity of diverse and marvelous effects, saying that just as all things in the world are produced and engendered from the aspects of the planets and signs of the heaven, together with the elements and the acting divine spirit, so too...
