Kimbi"; David Kimhi (Radak), a medieval biblical commentator and grammarian</note> on Psalm 84 and Haggai; namely, the Ark of the Covenant, with the mercy seat and the Cherubim; the fire that burned continually upon the bronze altar, where the sacrifices were burned in the open air, and which was never extinguished by any rain, snow, winds, or other atmospheric conditions. This fire, having been sent from heaven upon a burnt offering in the time of Moses and Aaron (Leviticus 9), was maintained without dying out until the building of the first temple by Solomon; for then it was renewed again from heaven and lasted until the time of King Manasseh at the Babylonian captivity, when the Priests hid it in the depths of a well. Upon their return, their successors, hoping to draw it out, found in its place a thick water, which, when spread over the sacrifices, caught fire, as is contained in 2 Maccabees, chapter 1. The third thing was the presence of God, called in Exodus chapter 40 <gloss>שכינה</gloss> *Shekhinah* <note>The Divine Presence or indwelling of God</note>, which manifested around the ark; then <gloss>נבואה</gloss> *Nebuah*, or Prophecy; and finally the Oracle of the Urim and Thummim. Furthermore, inside the Ark were contained the tables of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, Aaron's rod still adorned with its leaves, flowers, and almonds, the vessel filled with Manna, the cruet of holy oil for anointing the Kings and Prophets of Israel, and the chest of the Philistines' offering (1 Kings 6). Also, the fragments that remained of the first two Tables that Moses broke (Exodus 32), which were engraved all the way through, so that they could be read from both sides, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval French commentator</note> confirms. However, they were read differently, their ancient traditions speaking of it thus: *Mem, Setumah, Vefamech, Beluchth Beniasaion hauu*, meaning that the closed or final *Mem* <gloss>ם</gloss> and the *Samech* <gloss>ס</gloss> were held in great admiration for being closed all the way around. Consequently, it was necessary for them to be as if suspended in the air, without holding onto anything. This manner of the Oracle of Urim and Thummim—where it was necessary to rearrange the letters until some sense was obtained—was not far removed from that of the Pythian Apollo at Delphi, and many other pagan oracles, where it was necessary to organize the confusion of their tangled and muddled responses into distinct and meaningful words. Therefore, from all the points deduced above, we learn that the Hebrews hold that <gloss>אורים</gloss> *Urim* signifies the truth and perfection of things, as they take from the subsequent passages of the Bible; some interpret this word as "Doctrine," or more properly "illustrations of truth" and all kinds of perfections, as George of Venice <note>Francesco Giorgio, a Venetian monk and author of *De Harmonia Mundi* (1525)</note> does in several places in his *Harmony of the World*, deriving this word from <gloss>אור</gloss> *Or*, which signifies light. In this, Sebastian Münster and Santes Pagninus <note>Prominent 16th-century Christian Hebraists</note> agree in their Hebrew dictionaries regarding this word, which, along with that of <gloss>התמים</gloss> *Thummim* mentioned in Exodus 28, Leviticus 8, and Deuteronomy 33—deriving from <gloss>תם</gloss> *Thom*, which signifies integrity or perfection—are pure Hebrew words translated by the seventy-two Interpreters <note>The Septuagint</note> as "declaration of truth," or "illuminations and perfections." The Chaldean Paraphrast <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> left them without translation, because the Hebrews were accustomed to hiding and concealing their secrets in meaningful words. ### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF...

The Holy Spirit <note>Latin: *Spiritus Sanctus*</note>, according to P. Costus <note>Petrus Costus, a 16th-century scholar</note> in his *Type of the Messiah*, and to put it briefly, this Urim and Thummim was a certain tablet in which twelve precious stones were set, and the names of the twelve children of Jacob were engraved. This tablet, named <term>Hofchen <note>original: חשן; the *Hoshen* or Breastplate of Judgment worn by the High Priest</note></term>, hung by two small chains upon the chest of the High Priest, as can be seen in Exodus 28 and Leviticus 8. It contained several peculiarities and mysteries detailed by Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous medieval commentator</note> and Nehemidas <note>Nachmanides, another prominent medieval scholar</note> among others: that this Urim and Thummim was a work of the Eternal just as much as the tables of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, both having been given together by God to Moses upon Mount Sinai, as I have noted before. This Urim and Thummim was used in this way: if the thing being asked of God through the High Pontiff <note>The High Priest</note> was to succeed well, the stones of the *Hofchen*, at the inquiry being made, gave off a light; or the Priest himself, inspired by God, would say what would happen, as can be seen in the places cited above: in Numbers 27, 2 Esdras, Nehemiah 7, and more openly in Josephus <note>The Jewish historian Flavius Josephus</note> Book 3, chapter 9; Book 6, chapters 7 and 15; and Book 8, chapter 2. The Greeks called this *Hofchen* <term>logion <note>original: λόγιον; meaning 'oracle'</note></term>, while the Latins called it the *pectorale* <note>breastplate</note> or *rationale*. Some Talmudists interpret "Urim" as the sacred names by whose power the hidden letters in the said tablet came to be elucidated; and "Thummim" as those which made the said letters visible and apparent. 

The Kings of Israel were accustomed to seek counsel from God through this Urim and Thummim in all their important actions; and if no answer was drawn from it, it was a sign of God's ire and wrath. For this reason, Saul, having forsaken the Eternal, found no answer either by Prophet, or by dream, or by Urim and Thummim, as is contained in the 1st book of Kings, chapter 28 <note>In the author's time, 1 & 2 Samuel were often called 1 & 2 Kings</note>. Then the same Saul said that an enchantress should be found for him who had a diabolical spirit to know the outcome of the battle in which he died. On the contrary, David always had an answer by Urim and Thummim, by the vision of some Prophet, or by dream, as is contained in the 2nd book of Kings, chapters 2 and 5. It is a very certain thing that in former times among the Hebrews, God declared his will and deliberation through three principal means: namely, by Urim Thummim, vision, and dream. We even read in the Hebrew Doctors that although the Oracle of the Urim and Thummim ceased after the return from Babylon, the Jews nevertheless confess that a certain divine voice was always heard in the temple, which Yehoshua son of Levi, Joseph Albo, and others called in their Hebrew language <term>Bath kol <note>original: בת קול; literally "daughter of a voice"</note></term>, which the Greeks call <term>echo <note>original: ηχω</note></term>. This was the resonance of a voice which, being formed and reflecting within certain cavities suited for it, used to emerge from there with the air it struck. <note>original Latin: *pore secundi templi, postquam videlicet, iam desierat Prophetia...*</note> ...time of the second temple, after prophecy had already ceased, as had the Urim and Thummim. For five things were lacking in the second temple which were present in the first temple: namely, the Ark, the Mercy Seat <note>The gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant</note>, the Cherubim, the Perpetual Fire, the Presence of the Divinity <note>original: *praesentia Diuinitatis*; often referred to as the Shekhinah</note>, the Holy Spirit, and the Urim and Thummim. However, in the New Testament, we read more than once that the <term>Bath Kol <note>Hebrew: "Daughter of a Voice"; a divine echo or heavenly voice that guided scholars after the age of the Prophets ended</note></term> came from heaven and bore witness to Christ, such as in Matthew 3, when he was baptized by John in the Jordan: "And behold, a voice from the heavens saying, 'This is my beloved son, in whom I am well pleased.'" Similarly in Matthew 17, when he was transformed <note>The Transfiguration</note> on the mountain before his disciples. Likewise in John 12, a voice came from heaven, saying, "I have both glorified it and will glorify it again," and so on. Who does not see the mystery here? Namely, that God, by this voice which they call *Bath Kol*, wished to prepare the world and accustom it to that true heavenly voice, which is Christ our Savior, in whom God the Father wished to be heard from then on, according to that very command: "Hear him." Guy le Fèvre de la Boderie <note>A 16th-century French Orientalist and poet</note>, in his Syro-Chaldean dictionary, speaks of this at length in his interpretation of this word.

And so that we leave nothing noteworthy in this place without explaining it, we shall say that there were ten preeminences and honors in the first temple, as it is written in the book of the <term>Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial council of ancient Israel; here referring to a tractate of the Talmud</note></term>, chapter *Ellu en Haggolin*, under the assertion of Rabbi Samuel and others mentioned in the Hebrew book <term>Pirkei Avot <note>original: *Pirke Abath*; "Ethics of the Fathers," a collection of ethical teachings from the Mishnaic period</note></term> cited above. These are as follows:

1. Never did a woman miscarry because of the smell of the meat being sacrificed in the sanctuary.
2. This meat never spoiled after being sanctified.
3. No fly was ever seen in the house of slaughtering.
4. No nocturnal accident <note>A reference to ritual impurity or "nocturnal emission"</note> of bad illusion ever happened to the High Priest on the Day of Atonement.
5. The rains never extinguished the fire that burned the burnt offerings.
6. The wind never dispersed the column of smoke mentioned in Exodus, chapters 13 and 33.
7. No defect was ever found in the <term>Omer <note>A biblical unit of dry measure</note></term> of Manna (mentioned in Exodus chapter 16) or in the showbread <note>original: *pains de proposition*; the twelve loaves kept on a table in the Tabernacle</note>.
8. When all the people stood, they were somewhat crowded, yet when they knelt to adore, they had plenty of space.
9. No snake or scorpion ever did harm in Jerusalem.
10. No one ever said to his companion: "The place is too narrow for me to stay here in Jerusalem."

This is confirmed by Porchetus <note>Salvagus Porchetus, an author who wrote against Jewish doctrines in the 14th century</note> in part 1, chapter 2 of his *Victory Against the Jews*, and in the subsequent chapter 7. Sebastian Münster <note>A famous German cartographer and Hebraist</note> mentions it in his dispute on the Messiah, following the commentary of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> on the word *Veccaba*, based on the missing letter *He* <note>original: ה; a common mystical/philological argument in Hebrew exegesis regarding the word "and I will be glorified"</note>, and P. Costus in his *Type of the Messiah*. Previously, Samuel Marrochianus <note>Samuel of Morocco, a Jewish convert to Christianity</note>, in his book on the coming of the Messiah, had treated these things, having drawn them from the Babylonian Talmud in the *Shevu'ot* <note>original: *Scebagnat Tomin*</note> (meaning "seven days"), and from the Talmud in the book *Yoma* (or "the days") in the chapter *Tereph Vekalpi*, and from the Hebrew book titled the *Mishnayot* <note>The written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note> in the treatise on measures.

Whoever wishes to see more on this may read the Talmud in the tractate *Yoma* (the treatise on days), chapter 6; the *Midrash* on the Song of Songs, chapter 8; Rabbi Gerundese <note>Nachmanides, or Ramban</note> in his commentaries on Exodus 25 and 28; Porchetus, part 1, chapters 2 and 7 of his *Victory Against the Jews*; Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria</note>, book 3 of the *Life of Moses* and the book on *Monarchy*; Pietro Galatino, book 4, chapters 5, 9, and 17 of his *Secrets of the Catholic Faith*; Sebastian Münster in his commentaries on the Hebrew Bible, Exodus chapter 28; J. <note>original: "fuit inferius"</note> [The second Temple] was inferior: For it lacked five things which previously provided a wondrously majestic and venerable character, according to <term>Tractate Yoma</term> <note>A book of the Talmud concerning the Day of Atonement</note>, chapter 1; Kimhi on Psalm 84; and Haggai. **First**, the divine presence, which gave answers and oracles at the <term>mercy seat</term> <note>original: "propitiatorium"; the gold cover of the Ark of the Covenant</note>. **Second**, the spirit, or holy inspiration, which formerly seized the Prophets: for from Malachi to John the Baptist of Christ, no Prophets existed. **Third**, the sacred fire, the guarding of which Moses so anxiously commanded in Leviticus 6: for it never appeared again after it was submerged in a well by the priests—so that it would not fall into the hands of the impious—as told in 2 Maccabees 1. **Fourth**, the <term>Urim and Thummim</term> <note>Sacred objects or stones used by the High Priest to determine God's will</note>, which were stones in the High Priest's breastplate; by looking at them, the priests understood hidden things and announced them to the people whenever the stones radiated more than usual. For if they retained their natural appearance and color, it was taught that nothing should be changed. Thus, the former oracle <note>in the First Temple</note> was vocal, while this one <note>the Urim and Thummim</note> was silent, consisting of motion and signs. **Fifth**, the Ark itself and its <term>propitiatory</term> covering, and the two Cherubim attached to the Ark, where God was said to dwell because of the abundance of His presence which He there granted to the High Priests; by the name of the "Ark," I understand both the one constructed by Moses to receive the sacred monuments and relics, and the other by Solomon. In its place, however, they set a stone protruding three fingers from the ground, which held the censer, according to Rabbi Jacob from the first part of the <term>Talmud</term>, page 106. Yet, God had not abandoned His people for all that: for so they might be led to Christ, oracles were often given through the <term>Bat Kol</term> <note>Hebrew: "daughter of a voice"; a divine echo or heavenly voice</note>, which is a thin voice sent down from heaven into the ears of the gathered multitude; and other signs continued among the people, which are recounted by the Talmudists in the tractate <term>Avot</term> <note>Ethics of the Fathers</note>. Such was the voice in the Gospel which descended from the Father to glorify the Son, as in 2 Peter 1.

->*Of the gifts of prophecy, visions, and dreams of the Hebrews.*<-

### C H A P T E R X X I I.

IN the preceding chapter, we spoke in passing of visions and divine dreams without explaining them particularly, reserving the full treatment of them for this chapter. To enter into the matter, we must say that we must turn to the Hebrew prophets to find the true sources of all philosophy and the occult sciences. This is because they read (according to St. Augustine in the first book of *On Free Will*) in the "Book of Life." Because of this, Eusebius, in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, not only prefers them to the Greek philosophers, but even prefers the simple Hebrew theologians. In comparison to the Hebrews, he says, the others—though there are some very excellent ones among them, even admirable for a superficial subtlety of understanding—appear very insignificant regarding the solid foundation. Such was the foundation upon which the visions of the Hebrew prophets were placed and established: they gazed without any obstacle or hindrance, as if in a very certain mirror, at the first model and original of all created things in their real and true existence. Whereas the reasonings of the natural philosophers depend on the bodily senses, which are most of the time uncertain and deceptive; this is what moved Democritus to speak of a certain deep well where he said truth was hidden.

### LANGUAGES

Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and geographer.</note> agrees with this when he says that only those who are breathed upon by the divine spirit know how to predict specific details. This is because these details depend on universal truths, which exist in the first exemplar and the original plan of God. And it is there that the <term>Kabbalists</term> <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of thought in Jewish mysticism concerned with the nature of the divine.</note> occupy themselves: namely, in deciphering the words of the Prophets who spoke through these enigmas and profound obscurities. They did this so as not to reveal the secret wonders of God to the unworthy; furthermore, these mysteries can hardly be manifested through human words, as there are no terms sufficiently proper or emphatic to express them. Therefore, they restricted themselves in this matter to certain types of ciphers—not just in writing, but in figurative speech, removed from common usage. This is similar to when one transposes or exchanges one letter for another, causing the context to change so that it is no longer legible except to those who possess the alphabet.

As for the <term>Bath Kol</term> <note>Hebrew for "Daughter of a Voice"; it refers to a heavenly or divine echo.</note>, or the "daughter of the voice" mentioned above: it was like a type of vocal cipher, rather than a silent one. It is similar to what one might arrange for the ear using certain trumpet blasts or similar loud instruments that can be heard from afar, used in place of letters. This is just as signals are made for the eye, using lights by night and smoke by day, by which means one can make their thoughts understood to those under siege, or from one place to another. This artifice is quite common and has been used for a long time; for Polybius, the Roman captain, mentions it, as reported by Girolamo Cardano <note>A 16th-century Italian polymath.</note> in Book 12, Chapter 61, *On the Variety of Things*, where he recites some of these techniques, and again in Book 17, *On Subtlety*.

This *Bath Kol* was therefore like a sort of Echo, or the resonance of a voice (as I amply noted in the preceding chapter), which, upon being funneled and beaten back into certain concavities suited for it, emerged from there with the air it struck, multiplied into several repetitions. It is like a ball which, for one strike against the ground, will bounce many more times. In a similar case, these visions are like images that, proceeding from the archetype, come to reverberate in His creatures, neither more nor less than the rays of the Sun. When these rays are scattered through the air, they are gathered in a curved mirror or a vial full of water into a shape similar to the Sun itself, and from there they dilate again by reflection as before. And when they pass through stained glass, they appear to take on the color imprinted there. This is exactly how the Divinity acts through its <term>Sephirot</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> or "ornaments." Although God is hidden within them as to His essence, He communicates with His creatures, who could perceive nothing of Him otherwise.

There is yet another type of vision, called "intuitive," which looks into the proper mirror of the Great Workman. The Hebrews call this *Be-aspaklaria* <note>original: "Beſpeculariot" — from the Hebrew term for a looking-glass or "speculum."</note>, because it is double: the "shining mirror," which is the Sun or <term>Tipheret</term> <note>The Sephirah representing Beauty and Compassion, often associated with the sun.</note> (Saint Augustine calls it the "morning sacrifice," which was spoken of at the beginning of this work), and the other, the "non-shining mirror," which is the Moon and <term>Malchut</term> <note>The Sephirah representing Kingdom or the physical world, associated with the moon as it reflects the light of the higher Sephirot.</note>. This is otherwise known as the "celestial sea," which contains within itself a full fecundity and the generation of all these lower elementary things. It gives them life immediately as it receives it from the influxes of the sacred <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God.</note> יהוה <note>YHWH</note>, eternally generated by the Father, who remains up there in perpetual rest within his <term>Ein Sof</term> <note>The Infinite or Boundless nature of God prior to any self-manifestation.</note>, or infinity, which Anaximander <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.</note> himself claimed to be the first principle...

Saint Augustine briefly encompasses all the dreams and divine visions of which the above-named Hebrew theologians have spoken into five species, including both human dreams and others, all being understood by the word **dream** <note>original Hebrew: חלום (*halom*)</note>, which is the same as the Greek **dream-vision** <note>original Greek: ἐνύπνιον (*enypnion*)</note> and the Latin **Dream** <note>original Latin: *Somnium*</note>; and the **visions** <note>original Hebrew: מראה (*mar'eh*)</note>, which are the same as the Greek (according to Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene, a 4th-century philosopher-bishop who wrote "On Dreams."</note>) **visions seen while awake** <note>original Greek: καθ’ ὑπαρ θεάματα (*kath’ hypar theamata*)</note> and the Latin **Visions** <note>original Latin: *Visiones*</note>. The difference between the two is great: the true divine dream is received while sleeping, and the vision occurs while slumbering, with an impression upon the imaginative soul that represents things as if one saw them with the eyes. These are entirely different from human dreams and those of brute beasts, which have nothing but the natural impression in the imagination as things were seen while awake.

Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman author famous for his commentary on the "Dream of Scipio."</note>, regarding the "Dream of Scipio," identifies five species of dreams: the first, the **ordinary dream** <note>original Greek: ὄνειρος (*oneiros*); Latin: *somnium*</note>, which is ordinary and common; the second, the **vision** <note>original Greek: ὅραμα (*horama*)</note>; the third, the **oracle** <note>original Greek: χρηματισμὸς (*chrematismos*); Latin: *oraculum*</note>; the fourth, the **nightmare or insomnia** <note>original Greek: ἐνύπνιον (*enypnion*); Latin: *insomnium* (the text uses "somniũ" likely in error for *insomnium*)</note>, which is between a dream and a vision; and the fifth, the **apparition** <note>original Greek: φάντασμα (*phantasma*); Latin: *visum*</note>.

And one must well note what I have cited from the 12th chapter of Numbers: that God did not communicate with men except in sleep—excluding Moses—using dreams and visions only for the Prophets. This demonstrates the difference between a vision and a dream, and between a divine dream and human dreams, or those which occur through illness. Among these divine dreams and visions, there are several degrees: the first degree being the revelation in a dream to devote oneself to good; of this, the Hebrew Scripture says that the Spirit of God "rested upon" someone, or else that "God is with him." The second degree is when someone perceives while awake something that enters his soul and pushes him to speak in praise of God and His works—just as it is said that David then composed his Psalms, and Solomon his books of Parables <note>The Book of Proverbs.</note>, which are filled with such great and beautiful mysteries. <meta>This page continues the systematic classification of divine revelations, moving from the general types of dreams discussed on the previous page to a specific hierarchy of prophetic degrees as defined by Hebrew tradition and Renaissance scholars.</meta>

->### 234<-
->#### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF<-
<meta>catchword: citing</meta>

Whenever it is found in Holy Scripture that God speaks to *David* or to *Solomon*, those same Hebrews interpret this as happening by means of the Prophets, who had visions from God in order to declare them to *David* and to *Solomon*. Furthermore, they maintain that what was said to *Solomon*—that he would be the wisest man who ever lived—was not through a vision, but rather a **divine dream**. Likewise, when it is said that God appeared to *Solomon*, they say it was not a vision. 

The **third degree** is when the spirit, purified and cleansed, sees some figure in a dream and at the same time understands what it wishes to express, just as it is written in *Zechariah*. 

The **fourth** is when one hears words without seeing any figure of any kind. 

The **fifth** is when one sees a man while sleeping who speaks and reveals divine things. 

The **sixth** is when it seems that one perceives an Angel speaking while sleeping. 

The **seventh** is when it seems during sleep that God speaks, as is contained in *Isaiah* chapter 5, and in *Ezekiel*, *Micah*, and other Prophets. 

The **eighth** is when the vision of prophecy comes with the word of God, and in this degree the ancient Hebrews place the visions of *Abraham*, except for the one in the valley of *Mamre* mentioned in *Genesis* 18, which they place in the **ninth degree**. 

The **tenth** is when one perceives the Angel face to face, speaking, as at the sacrifice of *Abraham*. 

The **last**, which is the greatest and most excellent of all others, is to see and speak to God face to face while awake and without any intermediary; this was unique to *Moses* alone, as I have already stated above. Therefore, when *Isaiah* writes in chapter 6 that he saw God, we must understand this as a vision, and not while awake; and when we read in *Ezekiel* that he was transported to a field between heaven and earth, that took place while sleeping. 

In fact, all theologians agree that the holy Prophets did not all possess the gifts of prophecy in the same way: some never had more than one vision of God, or two or three divine dreams, while others possessed these gifts of prophecy throughout their entire lives, such as *Samuel*, *Elijah*, *Elisha*, and others. 

*Rabbi David Kimhi* <note>A prominent medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian, often known by the acronym RaDak.</note> in his preface to the Book of *Psalms* has very well shown the difference between prophecy and the mission of the Holy Spirit. For this, I refer curious readers to him, as well as to the following authors: the *Zohar* on Genesis; the third book of the Hebrew commentaries entitled *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "nemore habebuchin," a phonetic corruption of the Hebrew title *Moreh Nevuchim*</note> by *Rabbi Moses Maimon* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note>; the author of the *Nizzahon* <note>A title referring to Jewish polemical works (literally "Victory") defending Judaism against Christian critique.</note> on the *Pentateuch* <note>The first five books of the Hebrew Bible.</note>; the author of the Jewish Creed <note>The "Thirteen Principles of Faith" formulated by Maimonides.</note> extracted from the Spanish Breviary; Saint Paul in the fourteenth chapter of the First Epistle to the Corinthians; *Giovanni Pico della Mirandola* in book 2 of *On the Foreknowledge of Things*; *Raphael Volaterranus* in book 30 of his *Philology*, the chapter on divination; *Caelius Rhodiginus* in book 27, chapters 8 and 9 of his *Various Lessons*; *Polydore Vergil* in book 2 of *On Prodigies*; *Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's* treatise *On the Vanity of the Sciences*, chapter 99; *Caspar Peucer's* book on the *Principal Types of Divination*; *Jean Bodin* in book 1 of his *Demonomania*, chapter 4; *Guy Le Fèvre de La Boderie* in book 3 of his *Galliad*; *Agathius Guidacerius* of Calabria in his *Commentaries on Daniel*; *Sigonius* in book 5 of *The Hebrew Republic*, chapter 9; *Andreas Osiander* in chapter 11 of his annotations on the *Gospel Harmony*; and *Laurent de La Barre* in his commentaries on chapter 27 of *Tertullian's* book *On the Soul*.

> There were formerly three types of Prophets among the Hebrews. The first was of those who, whenever circumstances required oracles, visions, or prophetic dreams, obtained them—such as Moses, Samuel, and others, whom the ancient age called "Seers" <note>original Latin: *Videntes*</note>, but whom the common people of the Jews usually call the "Prior Prophets." The second type was of those who, though they could never elicit oracles, visions, or prophetic dreams at their own will, yet whenever it seemed good to God to teach, warn, or rebuke the people through them, they prophesied by divine inspiration. The Jews call these the "Later Prophets," because the majority of them lived after Solomon under the idolatrous Kings—such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the twelve who are called the "Minor Prophets"—whereas that better [first] type largely ceased around the time of David. The third type are those who, although they never obtain oracles, visions, or prophetic dreams from God, yet, having been educated by the prophets of the superior type as if by teachers, and taught by the internal anointing of the Holy Spirit, they rightly understand prophetic writings. They are able to explain them to others, give right counsel to those who ask, and perceive what necessarily follows from these sayings through right reasoning. The ancient age called these the "Sons of the Prophets," but Paul, writing to the Corinthians, calls them simply "Prophets." And while the prior types left in writing for posterity whatever was divinely revealed to them concerning the future kingdom of Christ—and it is to be believed that all these things remain intact and safe to this day—the latter type, though very much engaged in teaching, almost always abstained from writing, especially in the Old Testament.

The learned Gilbert Génébrard <note>A French Benedictine scholar and leading Hebraist (1535–1597).</note>, mentioning in the first book of his *Chronography* the gifts of Prophecy, visions, and the aforementioned dreams of the Hebrews, used these words worthy of being recited by us in this place:

> In the time of Saul and Samuel, the era of the Prophets began (as Peter says in Acts 3). Then the prophetic profession, which had almost died out since the death of the Elders, began to flourish again, with many coming together into the same college and devoting themselves to this institution, with Samuel presiding (1 Samuel 19). It must be known that this prophetic vocation was not [only] extraordinary <note>In this context, "extraordinary" means a miraculous or rare divine intervention outside of the normal order.</note>, since it is clear that men devoted themselves to this profession of their own accord, so that they might more conveniently spend their time in prayer, contemplation, the interpretation of scriptures, preaching, and study. From among these, God sometimes raised up certain individuals who would perform the duty of foretelling events before Kings and Peoples. Sometimes He also elevated others to this prophetic gift from other ways of life, but in those cases their vocation and mission were extraordinary. Such was Amos, whom He raised from the pasturing of cattle to the honor of prophecy.

<header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE</header>

Prophets indeed existed from the beginning of the world <note>original Latin: "ab orbe"</note>, but more rarely and outside the common order. From Samuel onwards, they became more frequent, regular, and in a perpetual succession. For this reason, the Hebrews consider him the founder and author of the Prophets, or rather of the prophetic colleges. Outside of these, there existed forty-eight most celebrated Prophets—some men, others women—whose names consequently appear in various places in scripture. From among these, I will enumerate the Prophetesses here; for the men will be named in their proper place and century further on. The Prophetesses are therefore Sarah, Miriam (the sister of Moses), Deborah, Huldah, Hannah (the mother of Samuel), Abigail, and Esther. Thus says the Hebrew in *Seder Olam* <note>A 2nd-century CE Hebrew language chronology</note> chapters 20 and 21.

See the aforementioned author treating, along with the succession of the Hebrew Kings and High Priests, the perpetual order and number of the Prophets until the Babylonian captivity, through all the subsequent books of the said Chronography. In these, namely in the second book, he says: "The Great Synagogue <note>original: *synagoga magna*—a council of 120 sages who transitioned the Jewish tradition from the era of prophecy to the era of the Rabbis</note> succeeded the Prophets; its leaders were Ezra, Nehemiah, Mordecai, Zerubbabel, and Joshua. These presided over the council—consisting of one hundred and twenty men, some of noble birth and others commoners—who met to correct the sacred books and establish their canon according to the prescription of the Kabbalah. There they also decreed that Joshua had been so taught by Moses, the Elders by Joshua, and the Prophets by the Elders. The notary or scribe of the council (for so he is called in Ezra 7) was Ezra, who is said to have been attended or rather presided over by Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi." See Elias in the preface to the *Masoreth*, titled *Hammasoreth* <note>referring to Elijah Levita, a famous 16th-century Hebrew grammarian</note>; Rabbi Moses in the preface to the *Book of Commandments* <note>Maimonides' *Sefer Hamitzvot*</note>; and in the Talmud in the treatise on vows.

On this subject, one may see what we have treated above in chapter 7 regarding the Kabbalah of the Hebrews.

### CHAP. XXIII.

ALL Hebrew words and utterances are entirely deprived and destitute of vowels, consisting of consonants and letters alone, without action or movement—much like a body deprived of a soul. Considering this, the Hebrews, in order to make these letters (which are mute and immobile of themselves) live and move, decided to place beneath and above them certain points. For this reason, these points have been named by them <term>תנועות</term> *Tenu'ot* <note>The author writes "Tenungot," a phonetic rendering of the Hebrew word for "motions" or "vowels"</note>, "motions"—that is to say, movements by which the letters are moved and uttered—derived from the verb <term>נוע</term> *Nu'a* <note>original: "Nuang"</note>, which means "to move." These are of two different kinds. Those placed beneath the letters are for the most part called in the Hebrew language <term>נקודות</term> *Nekudot* <note>original: "Nekoudoth"</note>, because of their thinness, smallness, and littleness, from the verb <term>נקד</term> *Nakad*, which means "to point" or "to puncture" (as in Song of Songs 1:11); otherwise

These accents denote the Holy and Divine Spirit, which sanctifies and returns to God. This was well noted by those great Kabbalists <note>The text refers to "Cabalistes," practitioners of Jewish mysticism whose ideas were adopted by Christian scholars during the Renaissance</note> Francesco Giorgio of Venice in Chapter 4 of the 2nd Canticle of the 4th book of his *Harmony of the World*, and Jean Cheradame in his *Alphabet of the Hebrew Language*, and after them Guillaume Postel near the end of his discourse on Phoenician letters. Thus, each Hebrew word, usually constructed of three consonants as a sign of matter, form, and composition, consists of points or movements of its elements, much like a changeable soul and a body. The accents contemplate and harmonize the vowels, giving rules and forms to their motions, representing the rational spirit and thought; for, as the Kabbalists say, the office of the spirit is to govern and moderate the blinded impetuosity of the animal part. And just as life is to composite things, the same are the points to the letters and characters of the Hebrews; just as all things flow and receive favor and nourishment from supra-mundane fountains, likewise the words and statements uttered in Hebrew proceed from and retain the vigor and efficacy of the understanding. Upon this understanding is imprinted the image and beauty of the Eternal Word, where these divine properties are unspeakably arranged and placed.

### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

...assured that this great Ezra <note>The biblical scribe and priest Ezra, who led the second group of Jews returning from Babylon.</note> invented them after the Babylonian captivity; without the benefit of these, we would find the Hebrew books to contain more confusion than edification, were it not that from our earliest youth we were accustomed to the ordinary reading and understanding of them, as Sebastian Münster <note>A German cartographer and Hebrew scholar (1488–1552).</note> confirms in his preface to the Bible. Regarding this, Pietro Galatino <note>Pietro Colonna Galatino, author of *The Secrets of the Catholic Truth*.</note> in Book 1, Chapter 8 of *The Hebrew Secrets*, has left a record that after Ezra, Rabbi Jacob ben Naphtali and Rabbi Aaron ben Asher—shortly after the empire of Honorius in the year of Christ 476—were the first who applied the points and accents to the Hebrew letters and consonants. To this opinion adheres Elias <note>Elias Levita (1469–1549), a renowned Hebrew grammarian.</note> in the second section of his *Book of Hebrew Accents*, and in his preface to the *Masorah*. So too do Porchetus <note>Porchetus Salvago, a 14th-century Genoese monk.</note> in part 1, chapter 15 of his *Victory against the Jews*; Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano, editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> in *Reason and Use of the Masorah*, volume 3; Lilio Giraldi in his *History of the Poets*, Dialogue 1; Sixtus of Siena in Book 2 of his *Holy Library*, chapter "Iota and Tittle"; and Gilbert Génébrard in Book 3 of his *Chronography*. In that work, following the authority of Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (Radak), a medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note> on Psalm 60, Génébrard remarked that the first figures of this invention—who were called *Ansie Teuaria* <note>original Hebrew: *Anshei Teveryah*, meaning "Men of Tiberias"</note>, that is to say, men or inhabitants of Tiberias—left to the Hebrews a double reading and mode of interpretation when there was a doubt or question among them. Because of this, the Westerners <note>Referring to the Palestinian or Sephardic tradition.</note> have since entirely followed the points of Rabbi Aaron ben Asher, and the Easterners <note>Referring to the Babylonian tradition.</note> near the River Nehardea have followed the points of Jacob ben Naphtali, though Pietro Galatino (in the aforementioned Book 1, chapter 8) and Gilbert Génébrard (in the second book of his *Chronography*) seem to want to hold the opposite. 

The largest and most sound portion of the Jews, including among others Rabbi Abraham and Rabbi Ibn Ezra, write that in the year of the world's creation 4573 (or as Gilbert Génébrard has it in Book 3 of his *Chronography*, which corresponds to the year of Christ 476 or 478 according to their reckoning, and according to ours the year 229), the *Masoretes*—otherwise known as masters of tradition or of the concordances among the Hebrews dwelling in Tiberia or Tiberias, a province in the land of Israel—invented these points. In Tiberias, the most eloquent and polished Hebrew was spoken, according to the words of Elias Levita in his preface to the *Book of the Masorah*; they called it in their Hebrew tongue מקדשיה <note>original: *Maqdashiya*, likely a reference to Tiberias being a "holy place" or "sanctuary."</note>. Nearly a thousand years after the said Ezra, they invented these points which are found today applied to Hebrew texts. These same Masoretes, by the same means, were the first to distinguish and divide the entire Bible or Hebrew Holy Scripture. Previously, it consisted of one continuous *Pasuk* <note>term: *Pasuk* — a verse or linguistic unit.</note> without any distinction of chapters and verses; they divided it into chapters and clauses that this author calls *Pesukim* <note>term: *Pesukim* — the plural of *pasuk*, meaning verses or sentences.</note>, verses and sentences. Because of this, they were called Talmudists and masters of the *Masorah* (that is to say, of the tradition), as recounted by Saint Jerome in his *Hebrew Questions* and on chapters 23 and 41 of Genesis and in his *Letter to Evagrius*; Elias Levita in his preface to the said book of the *Masorah*; Martin Gilbert in his *Discourse on Hebrew Letters*; Raphelengius in his works, chapter 5; Sebastian Münster in his *Grammar* and in his preface to his Hebrew Bible; and Matthias Flacius Illyricus in his dispute added to the treatises on the *Sermon of the Sacred Letters*. Also Matthew Flacius in his treatise *On the Speech of the Holy Letters*; J. Cheradame in his *Alphabet of the Holy Language*; and Michael Neander, pages 179 and 180.

And because it is necessary to know the multiplicity of these Hebrew points and accents, it seemed good to me to deduce what follows here. We shall learn that there are several sorts and differences among them. Some serve the office of simple vowels, nine in number: *Pathath*, *Cametz*, *Tzere*, *Segol*, *Scheua*, *Sirec*, *Solem*, *Schurec*, and *Meloppé*. The compounds are three in number: *Hateph-pathath*, *Hateph-cametz*, and *Hateph-segol*. Others do not signify or denote any vowels but suggest the qualities of the letters in a dual way, by moving and changing the natural voices of the letters, or demonstrating how they should be taken and pronounced. The diversity of these cannot be known by the varied shape of the figures, but by the property of the places where they are placed and located. They are four in number: namely *Dagesch*, *Raphe*, *Holem*, and *Mappic*, as can be seen in the Hebrew grammars of Clenard, Quinquarbre, Cornelius Bertramus, and others cited below. As for the Hebrew accents, they are commonly distinguished into two orders: some are named "Kings," fifteen in number, and the others "Ministers," seven in number, according to Elias Levita in his Hebrew grammar and *Book of Canticles*, and Sebastian Münster in his Hebrew grammar. Some modern authors assert that up to 34 are found, specified in this fashion: *Dagges*, *Rebia*, *Tebir*, *Zakef*, *Little Zakef*, *Great Zakef*, *Segolah*, *Macaf*, *Rafé*, *Pessif*, *Legarme*, *Meteg*, *Gaiah* with *Sheua*, *Sof*, *Passuf*, *Gheress*, *Gheressin*, *Meaielah*, *Simple Merca*, *Double Merca*, *Tifca*, *Pasta*, *Ietif*, *Mahpach*, *Munach*, *Hilni*, *Mercabel*, *Iarcah ben Iomo*, *Athnach*, *Darga*, *Zarchaz*, *Salseceleth*, *Talissa*, *Talfa*, *Carne*, *Parah*, *Pazer*. « Meanwhile, it must not be overlooked that just as the Hebrews (as we have learned from their grammarians) use the *Rebia* <note>original: "Rebia"; a Hebrew accent mark denoting a minor pause.</note>—which is a single point placed above a word, though it does not appear as a *Holem* <note>original: "Holem"; a Hebrew vowel point representing the "o" sound.</note>—to indicate a sub-division of speech. In the division called *Zatephraton* <note>A variation of the term "Zaqef qaton," a Hebrew accent marking a short pause.</note>, they use two points above the word. In the phrase-member called *Athnahhta* <note>original: "Athnahhta"; a major pause mark in Hebrew cantillation, shaped like a small crescent.</note>, they use a semicircle, much like a rainbow, placed below the word; and they use the *Pasek* <note>A vertical line used to separate words for clarity.</note>, which is a line or stroke written below the word after a number at the end, to signal a full and perfect sentence, as is their custom. The Greeks and Latins also have their own types of points, invented to demonstrate what has been spoken, which are to be sought from the Greek and Latin grammarians. The Macedonians also, and the Russians, as well as the inhabitants of both Moesias <note>Ancient regions in the Balkans, roughly modern Serbia and Bulgaria.</note>, along with the Illyrians and Dalmatians, indicate the incomplete and complete senses of their sentences through punctuation, as can be seen in their books published long ago by printers in their own letters and language. It is also the custom of the Indians <note>In the 16th century, "Indians" often referred to Ethiopians; the description of punctuation here matches the Ge’ez script.</note> to write two points between individual words of a sentence, and to indicate the end of a line and the conclusion of a sentence with four points. The Chaldeans <note>Often used to mean Aramaic speakers.</note> and the Syriacs have only two types of points: for an incomplete or suspended sentence, they are accustomed to using only a single point. But at the end and conclusion of the sentence, they are used to adding four points, depicted in black and red colors. The Arabs also have four types of points: either two points between words, like our caesura and the Greek comma—similar to the Hebrew *Sheva* <note>A vowel mark consisting of two vertical dots.</note>—or only one point, or three in the shape of a *Segol* <note>A Hebrew vowel mark of three dots in a downward triangle.</note>, which point they use in three ways: either extended straight toward the sky, or with the head turned toward the arctic or antarctic pole. They also use a quadrangular form with four points, placed in such an order that one seems to face the sky, another the earth, a third the South, and a fourth the North; these they use in sub-divisions, divisions, members, and the ends of sentences. In these, it must be noted that every Punic <note>Here referring to Arabic or Moorish script.</note> word that contains *Aliph*, *Ce*, or *Quiph* <note>Likely the letters Alif, Kaf, and Qaf.</note> with *Manuben* <note>A reference to "Nunation" or *Tanwin*, a grammatical suffix in Arabic.</note> marks the end of a part. For *Manubé* always stands at the end of a part of speech. Likewise, if *Aliph*, *Ce*, or *Quiph* follows after *Geu*, it is the end of a part; and even if a point is sometimes not added, it is always understood by this general rule. In questions and—if it is permitted to say—answers, the Arabs use various methods, as could clearly be known to us from the Gospel of John, chapter 9, if it were written here in Arabic letters. But since we lack those typeforms, we shall try to express it in Latin words, with the points added in their proper places: "And Jesus said for Judgment, I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind: and some of the Pharisees who were with him heard, and they said to him, are we also blind? Jesus said to them, if you were blind, you would not have sin: but now you say, because we see, your sin remains." * And let these things said of the Arabs suffice for the present. «

### CHAP. XXIV.

The Hebrews, taught by their Cabala <note>The Kabbalah; the ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible.</note>, constantly maintain that the first and oldest Laws of this Universe, which were given by God to their first and oldest Hebrew Fathers, were and have been for all time and Eternity in the *Ensoph* <note>original: "Ensoph"; refers to the *Ein Sof*, the Infinite or the Divine Origin in Kabbalistic thought.</note>, towards the Divine Word <note>original: "Verbe diuin"; the Logos or the creative expression of God.</note>, although these were only promulgated in a certain period and moment of time. This is much like how, several thousands of years later, the Law of Grace <note>In Christian theology, the new covenant established by Jesus Christ.</note> was promulgated in its turn within the same *Ensoph* through the incarnation of that same Divine Word. For this reason, Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note>, interpreting the words of chapters 9 and 10 of Deuteronomy in his book *The Guide* <note>original: "Directeur"; referring to *The Guide for the Perplexed*.</note> chapter 65, and in his exposition of the *Mishnah* <note>original: "mischne"; the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</note>, has assured us that the tables of the Divine Laws were one of the works of the Creation, along with Repentance, Gehenna <note>original: "Gehenne"; a place of spiritual purification or punishment.</note>, the Sanctuary, the Throne of Glory, the Garden of Delights <note>Eden.</note>, and the name of the Messiah, as is confirmed in the Hebrew book titled *Pirkei Avot* <note>original: "Pirke Auoth"; a collection of ethical teachings and maxims from the Rabbis of the Mishnaic period.</note>. Indeed, these Hebrews—as noted by the author of the *Seder Olam Rabbah* <note>original: "Seder Olam Rabba"; a 2nd-century CE Hebrew language chronology detailing biblical history.</note> chapter 5—go much further when they affirm that our first Father Adam, being in the earthly Paradise in the state of innocence, received from God in the Hebrew language the Laws or precepts of the institution and blessing of marriage; the Laws or precepts of power and dominion over all the animals and things of the whole earth; the Laws of obedience and temperance to abstain from tasting and eating of the fruit of the Knowledge of Good and Evil; and the Laws of the sanctification and celebration of the Sabbath. According to Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), an influential Franciscan teacher and biblical exegete.</note> on chapter 7 of Genesis, as noted by Gilbert Génébrard <note>A 16th-century French Benedictine scholar and archbishop.</note> in book 1 of his *Chronographia*, once Adam was expelled from that Paradise by his sin, both he and his children and descendants observed during their lives these same Laws and several others yet given to them by God—such as the Laws of the sacrifices of fruits and pure, clean, and undefiled animals of the earth, and the abstinence from strangled animals and their blood, and other things mentioned in chapters 8, 9, 17, and others following in Genesis. This seems to be verified by the great St. Augustine in book 18, chapter 38, of his *City of God*, reporting that in the primitive Church there were books composed in the Hebrew language by Adam himself dealing with these things; indeed, it is held for certain that the works of Enoch, composed in the said Hebrew language, treated the Laws given by God to the first and oldest Hebrew Fathers at the beginning of the world, which Sixtus of Siena <note>Sixtus Senensis (1520–1569), a Dominican theologian and scholar of the Bible.</note> notes at length in book 2 of his *Bibliotheca Sancta* under the entry "Enoch," as I have already noted before in chapter 10. Since those times and centuries, the same Eternal God wished to entrust into the custody of that great and admirable Hebrew Prophet Moses these same Laws, and several others besides, which He engraved in pure Hebrew characters and pure Hebrew language with His own hand or His own finger, upon the two tables written all in one continuous flow, without any separation or distinction of words,

in his ark of the covenant, as it is written in chapter 34 of Exodus, along with a vessel filled with manna, and Aaron’s rod that budded in the presence of the Lord, chapter 17 of Numbers, which Saint Paul confirms in Hebrews 9; so that through these three things, he might preserve the principal monuments to the ingratitude of the Jewish people. Specifically: by the manna, he made known to posterity the insatiable gluttony or greed of the Jews, who, having been nourished three times in the desert by manna, murmured against God, and greatly provoked and angered him; by Aaron’s rod, he made known to future ages with what insolence of soul and defiance those same Jews rose up against the great and sovereign High Priest, chosen divinely by his Eternity; and by the tables of the Law, he would forever prove the infidelity and inconstancy of the said Jews. Furthermore, after the death of Moses, after Aaron's rod and the vessel of manna had been removed from the ark of the covenant and hidden away with a copy of the divine Mosaic law in the Tabernacle, those tables remained alone in the ark. For when the ark was carried into the Temple by the command of King Solomon—as it is written in chapter 8 of the 3rd book of Kings <note>Known in modern Bibles as 1 Kings.</note>—only the tables were inside the ark at that time. Inside the ark, there were only the two Tables of stone, which Moses had placed there at Horeb, when the Lord made a covenant with the children of Israel when they came out of the land of Egypt. This is confirmed in book 2, chapter 5 of <term>Paralipomenon</term> <note>The traditional Greek title for the books of 1 and 2 Chronicles.</note>. About a thousand or so years later, the prophet Jeremiah—as it is contained in chapter 2 of the 2nd book of Maccabees—was warned by God at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem to take them from the temple and carry them with the ark to Mount Nebo, opposite the city of Jericho (the mountain Moses climbed shortly before his death). There he hid them in a deep cavern unknown to anyone, having predicted and announced that these tables will be brought to light at the end of the ages, when all the Jewish people shall be converted to the Christian faith. Some authors have asserted that these tables were still inside the Temple of Jerusalem at the time of its final ruin under the Roman Emperors, and that they were carried in triumph to Rome by the Emperor Titus among infinite other spoils from the city of Jerusalem. This seems to be true because of the representation of the triumph over the Jews depicted in Rome on the marble triumphal arch of the same Titus; in this arch, one sees among the spoils being carried in triumph the two tables of the Law, the ark of the covenant, and the golden candlestick. However, it is true that Josephus, who described the pomp and magnificence of this triumph at length, mentions only the golden candlestick, the golden table, and the volume of the Law of Moses, and not those tables. The same Josephus and Philo the Jew assert that in each of these two tables there were 5 chapters of the divine laws. In the first were those mentioned hereafter, namely: the Monarchy of the one God, to adore him alone, saying, *I am your God*; the second, regarding the statues, idols, and other images which had to be rejected; the third, not to take the name of God in vain; the fourth, the religious observance of the seventh day; and the fifth, to honor one's parents. In the second table were the subsequent five in number: the first, according to Philo, was to not commit adultery <note>original: "paillarder," an archaic term for lewdness or adultery.</note> at all, and according to Josephus, not to kill or commit homicide; the second, according to Josephus, was to not commit adul-

Saint Augustine and some ancient Latin Fathers divide the precepts of these tables into a group of three and a group of seven. They state that in the first table, before all the precepts, there was a brief prologue to the whole law, namely: *I am your God* <note>original Latin: "Ego sum Deus tuus"</note>, which the Hebrews consider to be the first precept. Saint Augustine divides this into two, namely: the interdict prohibiting the concupiscence of riches, which is the sixth precept [of the second table], and the interdict of the concupiscence of the flesh, which is the seventh and final precept. Moses called these tables in the Hebrew language Tables of Testimony <note>original Hebrew: לחת העדות "luchoth hahedut"; Latin: "tabulas testimonij"</note>. The authors of Oriental law have written concerning these laws as follows:

> Moses completed the law with three types of precepts: moral, judicial, and religious or ceremonial. These were of such weight that the moral ones are still binding even in the Gospel, because they are of natural and divine law. The judicial ones are mostly retained, though a few are abandoned, corrected, or softened, as they were laws polished for a specific people and time. The ceremonial ones are received partly according to the spirit—that is, through secret understanding and sense—and partly according to the letter. For there are two types: some are figurative, bearing the shadow of the future Christ and the Church, such as circumcision, sacrifices, Sabbaths, and unclean foods. Others are purely ritual, pertaining simply to the worship of God. The former have been abolished, having been imposed only until the time of reformation <note>original Latin: "correctionis tempus"</note>. Others are still used so that the solemnity of divine worship may be perpetuated, such as temples of dedication, choirs, vows, lustral water, blessings, religious garments, genuflections, ecclesiastical orders, tithes, firstfruits, processions, visitations of sacred buildings and places, the spreading of hands, the feasts of Pentecost and Passover (once the use of animal sacrifices was removed), singing, images, organs, fasts, etc.

Michael Neander, in his commentaries on the Talmud of the Jews, mentions the fourteen books of Rabbi Moses, son of Maimon—called by the Jews "Ramban" <note>The text here likely confuses "Rambam" (Maimonides, author of the fourteen books of the Mishneh Torah) with "Ramban" (Nachmanides).</note>. The Jewish masters count from the Law of Moses 613 commandments of God that must necessarily be observed. One part consists of affirmative commandments or orders, which number 248, corresponding to the number of members in the human body. The other part consists of negative commandments or prohibitions, which number 365, corresponding to the number of days in the solar year. All of these are explained in the Talmudic books, along with certain other commandments later handed down by the house of judgment <note>The Bet Din or Sanhedrin</note> and the Prophets according to various times and causes. The highest doctor of the Jews after the holy Moses—who is himself called "the Egyptian" although he was Spanish, as he himself writes and names himself—Moses, I say, the son of Maimon (briefly, Ramban), divided the treatment of all these precepts into 14 books.

In the first, he treats in five chapters the articles of faith: what must be believed about God; the doctrine of the law; idolatry; and repentance.

In the second, he treats the love and worship of God; the reading of the *Hear, O Israel* <note>The "Shema Yisrael" (Deuteronomy 6:4), the central declaration of Jewish faith.</note>; sacred vestments; the blessings of the priests; and circumcision.

In the third, the precepts of the festivals according to the seasons, such as the Sabbath and Passover; where he also treats leaven and unleavened bread, Pentecost, the Feast of Tabernacles, as well as shekels <note>the half-shekel temple tax</note>, the new moons, fasts, and the feast of dedication <note>Hanukkah</note>.

In the fourth, marriages and divorces; a brother's widow <note>Levirate marriage</note>; young virgins; suspected wives; dowries; and betrothals.

In the fifth, forbidden unions; permitted and forbidden foods; and the slaughter of animals.

In the sixth, oaths, vows, the Nazirite vow, excommunication, and communion.

In the seventh, doubtful seeds or those of two species <note>laws of "Kilayim," or the prohibition of mixing different species of seeds</note>; and sacred donations.

### CHAP. XXV.

The Hebrews maintain that Moses is one of the first and most ancient writers to have ever existed in this universe, in any language whatsoever, after Enoch. Books by Enoch are mentioned by Saint Jude in his Canonical Epistle, Tertullian in his treatise on idolatry and in his treatise on the apparel and culture of women, Origen in his 28th homily on Numbers, in his *Anacephalaeosis* <note>A summary or recapitulation of main points.</note> in Book 4 of *On First Principles*, in his 5th book against Celsus, and in his Commentaries on Saint John; Saint Augustine in Book 15, chapter 23, and Book 18, chapter 38 of *The City of God*; and Saint Jerome on Chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus, and in the catalog of Church writers. This is also repeated at length by Gilbert Genebrard <note>A French Benedictine scholar and Hebraist.</note> in Book 1 of his *Chronography*. These books of Enoch are said to be found today in Ethiopia, the kingdom of the great Padescha Prester John <note>original: "Padescha Prestegiani," a title combining "Padishah" (Great King) and "Prester John," the legendary Eastern Christian monarch.</note>, composed in the Ethiopic or Abyssinian language, along with the *Book of the Battles of the Lord* mentioned in chapter 21 of Numbers. These two books were found in the primitive Church according to Saint Augustine in Book 18, chapter 38 of his *City of God*. It is true that we read in a certain Greek canon, and in the Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> of Muhammad, that Abraham also wrote and composed books in former times; if they ever existed, they have been entirely lost and gone. The Hebrew book we have today in our hands attributed to this Patriarch, titled *Sepher Yetzirah* <note>The Book of Formation, a foundational work of Kabbalah.</note>, was not composed by the biblical Abraham, but rather by a certain Abraham the Kabbalist or Hebrew doctor.

Indeed, these Psalms contain, in the form of praises and thanksgivings according to the testimony of St. Denis the Areopagite, everything contained in the other books of Holy Scripture, or rather they are an abridged manual of the two Testaments, it being a most certain and established thing that there was never a book or scripture which, through such a long succession of centuries, had such a vogue, circulation, and credit throughout the whole compass of the earth as the Psalms of this Prophet. For the Jews, wherever they are spread and scattered, read and sing them, both in their private orisons in their homes and public prayers in their synagogues in the pure Hebrew language, having held them as their own from all time and antiquity under the name of *Sepher Tehillim* <note>original: *Sepher Theillim*; Hebrew for "Book of Praises."</note>. The Arabs, Turks, Moors of Arabia, Egypt, and Barbary—indeed, all Muslims and Mahometans—hold them in such great account and esteem, as was commanded to them by their Prophet Muhammad in Surahs <note>original: *azoares*; referring to the Surahs or chapters of the Quran.</note> 11, 27, and 64 of his Quran, maintaining that these Psalms were dictated to David from the very mouth of God, and contain all the acts of the world, both great and small, so that they employ them with wonderful devotion both in their orisons and public prayers in their mosques, which are held around the hour of midday—named for this reason in the Arabic language *Pfaltir*—as well as in their secret prayers in their homes and oratories, translated for this purpose from Hebrew into the Arabic language, their grammatical language, and also into their common and vulgar Turkish and Moorish tongues, being called by them in their language *Zebur* <note>original: *Zebur*; the Arabic name for the holy book revealed to David.</note>, a word derived from the Hebrew words *Sepher Tehillim* mentioned above, having used this word *Zebur* in place of *Sepher* which signifies "book," as if this book of Psalms deserved by excellence to be named "The Book." The Persians or Persians under the rule of the Sophy <note>The Safavid Shah of Persia.</note>, King of Persia, also being Mahometans, have likewise turned them into their Persian language, which has great currency throughout all Asia. The Great Khan <note>original: *Cham*; refers to the Mongol/Tatar ruler.</note>, sovereign Emperor of the Tartars, with all the Hordes and Cantons scattered and sown in several places of the North and the East, although idolaters and Pagans, together with the inhabitants of Cathay <note>A historical name for Northern China.</note>, China, Japan, with the adjacent islands and the mainland, likewise have them in their languages. The Great Negus, called Prester John <note>original: *Prestigiani* or *Preste lean*; a legendary Christian monarch often identified in this period with the Emperor of Ethiopia.</note>, King of the Ethiopians and Abyssinians, also has them in his language, in his southern Christian Church. Likewise all the Greeks, the Muscovites, Armenians, Georgians <note>original: *Zorzaniẽs*.</note>, Jacobites, Maronites, Copts, Syrians in each of their languages, together with all the Catholics of the Latin Church, with the branches and offshoots of the particulars and subdivisions of one and the other in the Latin language proper and particular to them, so that there is no place on earth today, nor any religion, that does not use, each in its own faith, the Psalms of this David, which constitute the greatest part of the services of the Christian Churches—Greek, Latin, and Ethiopian—which are of wonderful extent. And it is held that Saint Jerome <note>original: *S. Hierof.*; likely a printer's error for *S. Hieron.* (Hieronymus).</note>, urged by the prayers of Pope Damasus, arranged the Psalter into 7 parts according to the days of the week, so that each day would have certain specific Psalms that would be sung there.

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

<page-num>258</page-num>

...reciting the canonical hours <note>The fixed times of prayer in the Christian liturgy.</note>, and the <term>Psalter</term><note>A book containing the Psalms, used for liturgical worship.</note> being thus divided and partitioned, the aforementioned Pope commanded that it be read throughout all Christian Churches. He was the first to decree that the Psalms should be sung alternately and by two choirs <note>original: "Cœurs"</note> in the Church. It is true that there are some who—according to the account of Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century Byzantine church historian.</note> (Book 13, Chapter 8)—attribute this to Saint Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, who was living in the time of the Apostles; this was because, while dozing, he had heard the Angels singing these Psalms in the very same manner as they are now sung in the Church, with one choir responding to the other. On the contrary, Theodoret (Book 1 of his *History*, Chapter 24), the *Tripartite History* <note>A famous collection of early church histories compiled in the 6th century.</note> (Book 5, Chapter 32), and the author of the *Bundle of Time* <note>original: "feseau des temps"; likely the *Fasciculus temporum*, a popular world history by Werner Rolevinck.</note> write that Flavian and Deodatus, or Diodorus, were the first to divide the choirs of singers in the Church of Antioch into two parts. Socrates (Book 6, Chapter 8) and Sozomen (Book 8, Chapter 8) attribute this to Saint John Chrysostom <note>Known as the "Golden-Mouthed," a prominent Early Church Father.</note> regarding the practices of the Church of Constantinople. 

G. Genebrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard, a 16th-century French scholar and archbishop.</note> in Chapter 17 of his *Apostolic Liturgy*, treating several rare matters concerning this subject, wrote that those clearly err who have written that Pope Celestine, in the time of Saint Augustine, "ordained that the 150 Psalms be sung in order with Antiphons" <note>original: *150. Psalmos cum Antiphonis cantari per ordinem instituisse*</note>, as Platina, Polydore Vergil, and the Centuriators <note>Protestant historians who wrote the *Magdeburg Centuries*.</note> have claimed, having taken it from common authors of divine offices. Instead, it should be said that he had instituted, or rather permitted, that the Psalms be left whole in the celebration of the divine liturgy, despite the lack of devotion and impatience of the people, and that certain verses be drawn from them for the entrance of the sacrifice <note>The Introit of the Mass.</note>, for the graduals, for the offertories, and for the communions, leaving there only the "Glory be to the Father" <note>original: *Gloria Patri*</note>. From this, Saint Gregory afterwards—as a supplement and composition for so many omitted verses—substituted the "Lord have mercy" <note>original: *Kyrie Eleizõ* (the Greek *Kyrie Eleison*)</note> from the Greek Church as the summary and epitome of all the Psalms, as the aforementioned Genebrard deduces at length in the chapter cited above and those following. 

Polydore Vergil <note>An Italian humanist historian who lived in England.</note> in Book 6, Chapter 2 of *On the Discovery of Things*, treats this matter at length and asserts that this manner of singing the Psalms alternately in the Church was drawn from David, who, according to Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> (Book 7 of the *Antiquities*, Chapter 10), instituted seven ranks of singers; as they sang first, he followed and sang after them when the Ark was carried to Jerusalem. Or perhaps in this they imitated Asaph, master of the singers, who was the author among the Hebrews of the order of those who sang before the Ark (2 Kings 6 and 1 Chronicles <note>original: "paralipomen"; the Greek and Latin name for the Books of Chronicles.</note>). See George the Venetian <note>Francesco Giorgio, a Venetian Franciscan and scholar.</note>, Volume 3 of the *Oracles of the Prophets*, Section 1; Theodoret, Books 2 and 5, Chapters 24 and 32 of the *Tripartite History*; Sabellicus <note>Marcantonio Sabellico, an Italian historian.</note>, Book 7, Chapter 7; G. Genebrard, Books 1 and 3 of his *Chronography*; René Benoist <note>A prominent 16th-century French theologian.</note>, Book 1, *Stromatibus Bibliorum*; Sixtus of Siena <note>original: S. Senensis</note>, Book 1, Chapter on the Psalter and Book 2 under the word "David," and in Book 8, Heresy 5 of his *Holy Library*; André Thevet, Book 18, last chapter of his *Cosmography*; René Choppin, Book 1, Title 3, *On the Sacred Forensic Polity*; and Blaise de Vigenère in the introductory epistle of his version of the Psalms.

### CHAPTER XXVII.

->*That the Angels and celestial intelligences, and the souls of the blessed*<-

The Hebrew Prophet Zephaniah <note>original: "Sophonias"</note> in his prophecy or prediction, chapter 3, promises with divine inspiration that the Eternal will restore and re-establish at the end of the world the "chosen lip," or the idiom and chosen speech, so that all may invoke the name of the Lord Jehovah and all serve Him with "one shoulder" <note>An idiom meaning to serve with one accord or unanimously.</note>. These words the Chaldaic Paraphraser <note>A reference to the *Targum*, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> has translated into the Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note> language in this manner: "At the end of the world, I will distribute among all Peoples and Nations a single chosen speech, so that all may pray in the name of the Lord and serve before Him with one shoulder." On this passage, the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> in their commentaries write that this "chosen lip," or idiom, or chosen speech, must be interpreted as the Hebrew language, which God formerly elected and chose above all others to communicate and speak with Adam and the ancient Fathers and Patriarchs, and to give them His divine law. This is also because this language speaks holily, chastely, and honestly of all things, however immodest or foul they may be, as one can see by reading the context of the Hebrew Bible, and as Maimonides <note>original: "Rabbi Mose"</note> confirms in Book 3, Chapter 9 of his *Guide* <note>The *Moreh Nevukhim* or *Guide for the Perplexed*, a seminal work of Jewish philosophy.</note>. Saint Jerome in his commentaries on this Prophet, Saint Augustine in question 108 on Genesis, and Origen on the 11th chapter of Numbers and homily 11, have all written that the largest and most sound part of the Hebrew authors have asserted that the Hebrew language—as the mother and womb <note>original: "matrice"</note> of all other languages—was born at the very beginning of the world. Just as it was the first, so shall it be the last of this Universe; for its use is of all time and shall be in the future in Heaven, while the saints and blessed, as the Psalmist says, praise God from age to age. For this reason, Pietro Galatino <note>original: "Pierre Galatin," a 16th-century Italian scholar and Kabbalist.</note> in several places in Book 12 of his *Secrets of the Catholic Faith*, reciting the Hebrew words of this Zephaniah, wrote that the Hebrew Kabbalists and Talmudists held the opinion that after the final Day of Judgment, at the end and consummation of the world, the souls of the blessed enjoying eternal bliss, together with the Angels and celestial intelligences, will sing and chant psalms of praise to God in the one and only Hebrew language. This is because, just as before the division of languages that occurred at Babel, the entire world was of only one language, likewise in the general resurrection, all the men of the world will speak only that same Hebrew language, which was familiar to Adam in the terrestrial paradise. Thus it is that the prophet Isaiah, in the sixth chapter, writes that he heard the Seraphim Angels singing before the Throne of God in the Hebrew language these words: *Kadosh, Kadosh, Kadosh, Yehovah Tzabaoth, Melo khol ha-aretz kevodo* <note>original: "Kadosch, Kadosch, Kadosch, Iehoua Tzabaoth, Melochal, haaretz, Cebodo"</note>,

> *Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts, the whole earth is full of his [glory].*

### CHAP. XXVIII.

King Solomon was thus called in the Hebrew language שלמה <note>Hebrew: *Shelomoh*</note>, which is to say "sweet and peaceful." # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

The discourse above must be considered all the more marvelous and admirable considering that in what remains to us of so many works or books that can be seen or read today in any language whatsoever, we can only observe seven primary and principal very ancient languages: namely Hebrew, Assyrian, Egyptian, Chaldean, Arabic, Greek, and Latin. This moved Raphael Volaterran <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a humanist scholar from Volterra</note> in book 33 of his *Commentaries* to write these words: "Therefore, seven dialects <note>original: 'catalecti'</note> and as many types of letters are found. The Assyrians or Babylonians are the oldest; then the Arabs. The Jews do not differ much from the Arabs in their characters and language. The Egyptians and Ethiopians, though very ancient, used figures of animals and other things more truly than letters, which they call hieroglyphs <note>original: 'hieroglypha'</note>—no one has yet understood them. The Ethiopians, however, have used Babylonian letters until the present day. After these came the Greeks, then the Latins, and finally the Dalmatians from corrupted Greek. I have also seen books written in the Armenian language, which, however, almost agree with the Chaldeans, being distinguished by very little. The Saracens today, as well as the Tartars and Turks, although their dialects differ slightly among themselves, all use Arabic letters; the Turks also use the Greek letters of those they rule." <note>original: 'Igitur catalecti septem... quibus dominantur'</note>. The other languages which have had fashion and credit after the said confusion of Babylon <note>The biblical story of the Tower of Babel, where God divided human speech into many tongues</note> during ancient centuries until the present time, took their origin and beginning after that confusion, which brought infinite movement and change across the entire world. Pierre Crinit <note>Pietro Crinito (1475–1507), a scholar and disciple of Poliziano</note> on this subject in book 17, chapter 1 of *On Honorable Discipline*:

"Moses first carved the Hebrew letters; the Phoenicians with a wise mind established the Attic letters, which we Latins frequently write; Nicostrata <note>In Roman myth, Nicostrata (also called Carmenta) was a prophetess who adapted the Greek alphabet into the Latin one</note> published [the Latin]; Abraham produced the Syrian ones, and he also discovered the Chaldean; Isis with no less skill brought the Egyptian; Gulfila <note>Ulfilas (c. 311–383), the missionary who created the Gothic alphabet to translate the Bible</note> promptly gave the Gothic <note>original: 'Getarum' — the Goths were often historically confused with the ancient Getae</note> ones, which we see as the last." <note>original: 'Moyses primus Hebraicas... quas videmus vltimas'</note>. See what Jerome Cardan <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and physician</note> writes of this matter in book 17, chapter 90 of *On the Variety of Things*, and J. Caesar Scaliger in the said Cardan, exercise 259.

On this subject, I remember having read in the Quran of the Prophet Muhammad <note>original: 'Mahomet'</note> that when he was carried up to heaven by the Angel Gabriel, he saw there a multitude of very great and very large angels, and said: "The vastness of each single Angel was many thousands of times greater than the world; each of them had seventy thousand heads, and in each head seventy thousand mouths, and in each mouth, one thousand seven hundred tongues, praising God in seven hundred thousand languages." <note>original: 'Prolixitas vniuscuiusque Angeli... septingintis millibus idiomatibus'</note>. These words are repeated by Friar Richold <note>Riccoldo da Monte di Croce (c. 1243–1320), a Dominican missionary famous for his accounts of the East</note> or Richard of the order of Preaching Friars living in the year of Grace 1210, in his book *Confutation of the Law Given by Muhammad to the Saracens*, chapter 14.
