Just as all things that can be spoken and written are comprised and contained within these 22 letters, so too are there 22 divine books in which are comprised all things that can be known and proclaimed. This was the view held among Christians by Origen, Epiphanius, Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note>, Saint Jerome, and Rufinus. Some among the aforementioned Hebrews—namely Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra and Rabbi David Kimchi—count 24 books according to the same 22 letters of the said Hebrew alphabet, adding to them three times the letter י [*Yod*] in honor of the four-letter name of God <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note>. Out of reverence for this name, these Hebrews have the custom of expressing it only in writing and not by voice or word, using three *Yods* in the manner of the Kabbalists <note>Mystics of the Jewish tradition</note> in this way: ייי. This division was followed by some of the ancient Greeks, as it was very suitable for the 24 letters of their Greek alphabet; it was also adopted by some ancient and modern Latins, based on the mystical number of the 24 elders worshiping the Lamb who opens the book sealed with seven seals, which no one could open in heaven or on earth, as mentioned by Saint John in Revelation, chapter 5. Some other Hebrews count 27 books, equal to the number of characters resulting from the 22 simple elements that make up the whole Hebrew alphabet, plus the five final letters <note>Known as *sofit* letters, which change shape at the end of a word</note> repeated or doubled from it, which are formed differently at the beginning, the end, or the middle of Hebrew words. On this subject, one may specifically consult Saint Jerome in his prologue to Galatians, Epiphanius in his books on weights and measures, Abulensis <note>Alonso Tostado</note> on Galatians, Rabbi René Benoist in books 1 and 2 of his *Miscellanies* <note>original: "stromates"</note> on the Bible, Sixtus of Siena in his *Library*, book 1, section 1, and Brother Louis in book 1, chapter 3 of his *Globe of the Canons of the Holy Language*.

The same Hebrews call all these same books *Magdaffa* in their language—that is to say, "sanctification"—otherwise written as מקדשיה *Macdescya* <note>original: "Macdescya"</note>, "Holy thing of God," according to P. Galatin in book 1, chapter 1 of *The Secrets of the Catholic Faith*. This is because it makes its readers holy and enemies of all injustice, as well as despisers of this world who desire nothing other than eternal bliss. The Greeks name them in their language βιβλία <note>original: "βιβλία"</note>, which is to say "Books," *κατ' ἐξοχήν* <note>original: "κατ' ἐξοχήν," a Greek phrase meaning "par excellence" or "preeminently."</note>, because these books alone are such that there are no others like them on the whole earth, and because within them the voice and word of the living God are contained and comprised, according to Porchetus in chapter 8, part 1 of his *Victory Against the Jews*. The aforementioned Hebrews have constantly held that the great Ezra—called *Josedech* the Priest in the first book of the Sacred Annals <note>original: "Annales sacrees"</note> and *Malachias* by the said Hebrews—was the last of all their Prophets. Upon his return from the Babylonian Captivity, being illuminated by the Holy Spirit, he dictated two hundred and forty books of words that were contained in the Holy Scriptures which had been burned during the destruction of Jerusalem. These books were set down in writing on boxwood tables by five excellent and swift scribes during forty entire days, just as this figure dictated them from his mouth. Of these books, he brought 126 to light; the others, composed of secret wisdom and more excellent science, he gave to be read only by the sages and doctors of the law. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE [PROPHETS]

The division of the Hebrew Bibles into chapters and verses, as we currently have them in the Hebrew Bibles printed in Italy, Germany, France, Spain, and other places, is recent and modern. In fact, the Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and other authors found to have written five hundred years ago did not specifically cite any chapter or verse of the Old Testament in their works, except for the Psalms. Regarding the Psalms (as appears in the Acts of the Apostles), from the beginning of the nascent Church, these authors were accustomed to mentioning them by the numbers added to them. These numbers, as Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a prominent Latin theologian.</note> confirms in the preface to these Psalms, were attached to the Psalms by the seventy-two interpreters <term>Seventy-two interpreters: The legendary group of Jewish scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek, creating the Septuagint.</term>. But as for the divisions of these chapters and numbers that we see today in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin copies, they were drawn from the Latin copies. This is shown by the fact that the ancient doctors and interpreters of Holy Scripture spoke of, divided, and also cited the Holy Scriptures not by chapters and numbers, but by citations of specific stories. Saint Augustine reports having done this himself from the beginning of Genesis up to the expulsion of our first Parents from the earthly Paradise, and Saint Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604 AD).</note> did so from the beginning of the Book of Kings until the anointing of King David. Furthermore, these same ancient Hebrew doctors and interpreters of Holy Scripture divided and interpreted that Scripture by "places," or periods, or verses, or small verses, or sentences, which they sometimes called chapters or headings. This was observed by the ancient Jews, whose books were partitioned and divided by sentences, points, and members, and distinguished by certain intervals, according to the report of Saint Jerome <note>The scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> in his preface to Chronicles <note>original: "Paralipomenon"</note> and Isaiah. Jerome asserts that for the convenience of the readers of the Holy Scripture, he used in his translation the same partitions and divisions of points, members, verses, and intervals that he had found in the Hebrew copies. These were distributed into *Parashiyot* and *Sedarim* <term>Parashiyot and Sedarim: Traditional Jewish systems of dividing the Torah and other biblical books into portions for weekly reading or thematic study.</term>—sections and orders: fifty-four for the number of weeks in the Embolic year <term>Embolic year: An intercalary or "leap" year in the Hebrew calendar that adds an extra month to align the lunar year with the solar cycle.</term>, expressed by three large Hebrew letters ס [Samekh], or ס; then into *Sitthoth* <note>Likely referring to paragraphs or stylistic line arrangements.</note>, or paragraphs represented by three small ס, or ס; and then into verses designated by intervals, or commas, or two points. On the contrary, Elias Levita <note>A famous 15th-16th century Jewish grammarian and Masoretic scholar.</note>, a Jew by nation, in his preface to the book *Masoret Ha-Masoret* <note>original: "Masoreth, Hammastoreth"</note>, asserts according to the opinion of the Rabbis that all the Hebrew Holy Scripture was anciently written as or by a single *Pasuk* <note>original: "Pafuk"</note>, that is to say, a single sentence, to which all the words of the Holy Scripture were entirely joined and assembled without any distinction of verses. But he claims that four hundred and thirty-six years after the final destruction of the city of Jerusalem, this same Holy Scripture was divided by the Jews of Tiberias <note>The Masoretes of Tiberias, who standardized the Hebrew text, vowels, and accents.</note> into *Pesukim* <note>original: "Pefukim"</note>, that is to say, verses and sentences. The author of the book of Hebrew questions on the Book of Kings, whom Saint Thomas believes to have been a Jew turned Christian, writes that the Jews partitioned and divided the books of the Holy Scripture into a certain number of sentences or verses, when he says that among those of his nation the Book of Proverbs contains 915 verses. Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), also known as Radak, a medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note>, in his dictionary of the paths of the Holy language, asserting that the Bible among the Hebrews was written by verses, writes that in the Law <note>The Torah or Pentateuch.</note> or books of the Law there were 5,845 verses; in the Prophets...

...Hebrew Prophets, 9,294 verses, and 8,064 in the Hagiographa <note>The Hagiographa, or "Holy Writings," is the third section of the Hebrew Bible, including books like Psalms and Proverbs.</note>. But to avoid error in this calculation, one must know that the partitioning and division of verses is different among the Jews than it is among the Greeks and among us. In fact, the ancient Greeks and Latins distinguished verses by an equal number of words <note>original: "dictions"</note>, writing almost always in each verse six words, partly monosyllables. St. Augustine demonstrates this in his book *Mirror of Holy Scripture* <note>original: "miroüer de l'Escriture saincte"</note>, in which, frequently noting the number of verses previously collected by him but omitted from holy books, he gives as an example of one verse this saying from Psalm 99: *His people, and the sheep of his pasture* <note>original Latin: "Populus eius, & oues pascuæ eius"</note>. As an example of two verses, he gives this sentence from Psalm 118: *How many are the days of your servant; when will you execute judgment on those who persecute me?* <note>original Latin: "Quot sunt dies serui tui, quãdo facias tu de persequentibus me iudicium?"</note>. And as an example of three verses, he provides these words from the 148th Psalm: *Let them praise his name in the dance; let them sing praises to him with the timbrel and harp, for the Lord takes pleasure in his people* <note>original Latin: "Laudent nomen eius in choro, in tympano, & psalterio psallam ei, quia benè placitum est domino in populo suo."</note>. If one wishes to count the distinctions in these passages, one will find in the first, six voices, or words, or utterances; in the second, twelve; in the third, eighteen. Following this calculation, one must understand the division of Holy Scripture made by the ancients, who were accustomed to showing the size and bulk of holy books by the number of verses. Saint Jerome does this when he writes that Origen had composed nearly twenty thousand verses on the Song of Solomon, and that Saint Gregory had completed all his works in thirty thousand verses.

As for those Jews, in distinguishing their verses, they do not take account of the number of words, nor do they follow the divisions of the <term>Colons</term> <note>A rhetorical unit of a sentence, often used in ancient manuscripts to denote a breath or pause.</note> or points of speech, but only follow a certain ancient custom based on the authority of their elders and predecessors, and the tradition of their Rabbis. They offer no other reason for their partitioning and division than this: namely, that Ezra the Great and the Masters of their Great Synagogue, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, thus partitioned and divided their Holy Scripture. From this it has come to pass that among them the <term>Pezukim</term> <note>A Hebrew term meaning "verses."</note>, that is to say verses, are almost all equal, as appears at the beginning of Genesis where the <term>Pasok</term> <note>The singular form of Pezukim, referring to a single verse.</note>, or first verse, is: *In the beginning God created the Heaven and the Earth* <note>original Latin: "In principio creauit Deus Cœlum & Terram"</note>. The second is a little longer: *And the earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the Spirit of the Lord moved upon the face of the waters* <note>original Latin: "& terra erat inanis & vacua, & tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi, & spiritus Domini ferebatur super faciem aquarum"</note>. After which verse the third follows, which is shorter: *And God said, etc.* <note>original Latin: "dixit Deus &c."</note>.

Thus the ancients used the partitions and divisions of the Hebrew Holy Scripture as we have reported above. Whoever wishes to see more of this, let him read what I write hereafter in the subsequent chapter on the Chaldean language. But as for an Ammonius of Alexandria, or Eusebius of Caesarea, or Tatian, who particularly divided the four Evangelists into chapters—namely, the Gospel of St. Matthew into 355 chapters, that of St. Mark into 235 chapters, that of St. Luke into 343 chapters, and that of St. John into 232 chapters—they did not do this to introduce a certain partition and division of Holy Scripture, but only to teach the concordances and harmonies of the Evangelists. After those mentioned above, one finds no numerical division of the aforementioned Holy Scripture in ancient authors, except in Hilary, who partitioned and divided the Gospel of St. Matthew,

David, having thus driven out the Jebusites, called Jerusalem the "City of God," making it the head and capital city of all Judea. During the reign of this King, this city was highly renowned and in great triumph among all nations because of the great and notable victories David obtained; after his death, the wise *Solomon*, his son, succeeded him. And although this King applied himself to living in peace, Jerusalem nevertheless continued to grow in renown, wealth, and most sumptuous buildings. For Solomon expanded its walls and had great fortifications constructed there. Moreover, he built several very magnificent buildings there, and most significantly that Temple so renowned for the craftsmanship of its structure and its riches—so much so that there never was, and never will be in this world to come, a temple that can be equaled or compared to it. Shalmaneser <note>Shalmaneser V, King of Assyria</note> therefore, coming to the aid of the King of Judah, defeated the King of Israel: and nevertheless led away with him a great number of Jewish prisoners, to whom he gave the Region of Itene <note>This likely refers to Halah or Gozan, regions of Assyrian exile</note> to inhabit, and this was the first captivity and dispersion of the Jews since they miraculously left Egypt: indeed, a short time after that, the Assyrian King constrained the Kings of Israel to pay him a tribute every year. In that time, the Prophets Hosea, Isaiah, Amos, Micah, and Jonah were in power.

After the death of the unfortunate Ahaz, Hezekiah his son succeeded to the crown. This Prince was quite different from his father, for he was prudent, just, religious, and God-fearing. Thus Jerusalem regained its former prestige in his time: for he so reformed the government and restored the service of God to such perfection that, as the Holy Scripture bears witness to him, the Kingdom of Judah never had such a King; he also lived in great prosperity and obtained great victories.

This Prince, not content with uprooting all idolatry—to which he saw the people strongly inclined—and wishing to fully restore the service of God, summoned the other ten tribes of Israel to live according to the Law that God had given them by the hand of Moses. To this several condescended, coming to sacrifice in Jerusalem and celebrate the Passover according to the ordinance of Moses; and nevertheless, according to what one can see in the holy writings, the others persevered in their idolatry and mocked his summons, despite whatever warnings the Prophets gave them. Because of this, they were often punished by the rods of God, both by Shalmaneser and by Sennacherib, who greatly oppressed them. In the first year of the reign of Hezekiah—even the fourth year of the reign of Hoshea <note>original: "Osias"</note>, King of Israel—this Assyrian Prince waged such a strong war against the seven <note>The text specifies seven tribes here, though traditionally ten tribes made up the northern kingdom</note> tribes of Israel for the space of three years that he constrained them to abandon their homeland and go to live as slaves among the Medes. And that is how the Jews were dispersed here and there among foreign nations, without ever returning to their homes, so that one cannot say what became of them afterward; this was the ruin and the end of the Kingdom of Israel, which had lasted three hundred and seventy years.

Shalmaneser, on the contrary, sent Assyrians to Samaria to inhabit it; these people, seizing all the country formerly inhabited by the Israelites, took the name of Samaritans. Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note>, however, takes this name as essential <note>meaning inherent to their nature</note>, but his opinion does not seem acceptable to the most learned and scholarly, who hold that they were called Samaritans for and because of Samaria, the capital city of that region. These Assyrians mixed the law of the Jews with their idolatry; thus, they were held in abomination as excommunicated people.

After the defeat and ruin of the Israelites, the Kingdom of Judah alone remained standing: for the good King Hezekiah, to save his people from the fury of King Shalmaneser and to maintain his people in peace, gave him great sums of gold, buying by this means peace for a long time. However, this unfaithful King broke his word to him and came with a large army with the intention of ruining the Kingdom of Judea as he had done that of Israel: but God, wishing to preserve his people, sent the

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE

The Prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah to comfort him (for this Prophet lived at that time), and in one night the Angel of the Lord destroyed one hundred and eighty <note>original: "octante," a regional term for eighty</note> thousand men in the Assyrian camp; this carnage forced the others to retreat. And thus Hezekiah, having escaped this peril along with his people, lived the rest of his days peacefully in his kingdom. And after God had clearly demonstrated great miracles for the sake of the said King, he died peacefully, leaving Manasseh his son and successor to the kingdom.

This Prince did not follow the path of his father, but instead gave himself over entirely to all forms of idolatry, committing several abominable things against the law of God, into which he also led the people. Because of this, God was offended and stirred up the Assyrians against him, who chastised him so thoroughly that, besides the defeat of his men, he was made a prisoner and led captive to Babylon. However, he repented of his sin, which caused God to deliver him from the hands of the Assyrians, such that he returned to his estates and died there peacefully. Amon his son succeeded him, who, being wicked and iniquitous, was miserably killed; in his time lived the Prophets Joel, Nahum, and Habakkuk. After him succeeded Josiah his son, who was a God-fearing Prince and very vigilant in the reformation of his people. For he drove all idolatry out of his kingdom—which was nonetheless deeply rooted in the hearts and souls of men—and repaired the temple, performing several other acts worthy of a holy and just king.

Despite this, the wrath of God could not be appeased against the Jews because of the idolatries committed during the time of Kings Amon and Manasseh. Nevertheless, for the sake of Josiah (who died poorly through his great folly <note>Josiah was killed at the Battle of Megiddo after intervening in an Egyptian military campaign that did not concern him</note>), God deferred the punishment of the Jewish people, as He did afterward. This King died of a wound he received on the day he fought against Necho <note>Pharaoh Necho II</note>, King of Egypt; in fact, this was well-deserved, for Necho asked nothing of him, but rather sought his friendship as much as he could, having no other intention than to employ his forces against the King of Assyria. Nevertheless, Josiah went against him out of a certain recklessness of heart, which cost him his life. His death was greatly regretted, even by the Prophet Jeremiah, who composed his *Lamentations* because of it.

Jehoahaz his son succeeded him, who was given to all iniquity and wickedness; therefore God did not permit him to reign more than three months. For Necho, who had already defeated his father, deprived him of his kingdom, making the land of Judea tributary for one hundred talents of gold and one of silver every year <note>Biblical accounts in 2 Kings 23 usually cite 100 talents of silver and one of gold; the author has likely inverted the metals</note>. Jehoahaz thus being deprived of his estates and led prisoner to Egypt, where he died, Jehoiakim his brother was installed in the kingdom, where he behaved very badly; for he was entirely given to idolatry and induced the people to do the same. Because of this, God raised up as an enemy against him King Nebuchadnezzar, who had already reigned 44 years in Babylon. This King, having obtained victory over the Jewish people, led away as slaves the greatest men of the whole country and carried off the vessels of the temple. The cause of this was that Jehoahaz <note>The author likely means Jehoiakim here, based on the context of the 11-year reign</note> gave aid to the King of Egypt against Nebuchadnezzar, against the advice of Jeremiah. Jehoiakim, having then reigned 11 years and remained a prisoner for three years, died in great poverty. He was succeeded by Jehoiachin, or Jeconiah, who followed the path of his father, being wicked like him; also in his time God began to deploy the very rigorous rods prepared by Him long ago against Jerusalem and deferred for the sake of Josiah.

just as the Prophets had predicted, for Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonofer," referring to the Neo-Babylonian King Nebuchadnezzar II</note> came in person with a great army to besiege the city of Jerusalem. King Jehoiachin <note>original: "Ioachin"</note>, being unable to resist him, submitted to his will along with his mother, his wife, and the principal members of his household. But Nebuchadnezzar, taking all the assurances and oaths of loyalty he could from Mattaniah <note>original: "Mathatias"</note>, uncle of King Jehoiachin, appointed and constituted him King of Judah and named him Zedekiah <note>original: "Sedechias"</note>. This King was one of the most iniquitous and wretched Princes there ever was; for not only was he ungrateful toward God for the great graces He had shown him—turning his back on Him and refusing to listen to what the Prophet Jeremiah <note>original: "Hieremie"</note> predicted to him—but he also broke his promise to King Nebuchadnezzar, who had installed him in the Kingdom, by denying him his friendship.

And despite whatever remonstrances the Prophets Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and others made to this King, his obstinacy nonetheless continued to grow. For this reason, God raised up King Nebuchadnezzar, who, to take vengeance upon this Zedekiah in the ninth year of his reign, came to overrun the land of Judah with a great and powerful army, and held Jerusalem under siege for the time and space of two years, where King Zedekiah had retreated for his safety.

But the besieged, pressed by famine and plague, and unable to endure the siege any longer, were constrained to put themselves at the mercy of the enemy, who, entering the city, put it to fire and blood. This occurred 400 years after the building of the temple by Solomon <note>original: "Solomõ"</note>. He also carried away all the metal that was in the temple and led away the priests and all the principal people, both of Jerusalem and of the entire country, with their wives and children, who remained captive in Babylon for 60 years.

This Babylonian captivity was the one so often spoken of in Holy Scripture and in the writings of the Jews, which occurred approximately 600 years before the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. As for the common people, they were left in the country to cultivate the land under the charge of Gedaliah <note>original: "Godolias"</note>, the appointed governor in Judah. After his death, Ptolemy, one of the princes who seized a part of Alexander's kingdom, came to attack Jerusalem, and this on a Sabbath day. From that time, Jerusalem suffered many hardships during the wars of the Kings of Egypt and Syria, because it was in the middle of those kingdoms, as one can see in the books of the Maccabees. 

Antiochus, also King of Syria, waged a strong war against those of Jerusalem, which he took by force; and having sacked it and the temple also, he had his idols placed there, which he forced the Jewish people to worship. Because of this, these people were troubled by all sorts of afflictions more than any people ever were. However, as they were ready to be entirely ruined, God raised up for them Judas Maccabeus <note>original: "Iudas Machabeen"</note>, who was one of the foremost captains in the world, who, following the path of Mattathias <note>original: "Mathatias"</note> his father, governed the Jewish people in such a way that, having defeated several captains of King Antiochus, he restored his homeland to its former liberty. Having removed and cast down all the idols that were in the temple, he reformed the people according to the law of God. 

This Prince, being High Priest, was of such great renown that the Romans, who then held the first rank in the world, sought to have his alliance and friendship. After his death, Jonathan <note>original: "Ionathas"</note> his brother succeeded him, who was very valiant and bold, and likewise preserved his homeland in its liberties against all. This prosperity of the Jews lasted 50 years for them, though it was not without war; once these years passed, they again desired to have a King, wandering <note>Or "erring," suggesting a moral or political mistake in returning to monarchy.</note> like their predecessors. And thus Aristobulus was elected as King, who was very valiant and bold, but cruel and a tyrant. Jannaeus <note>original: "Ianeus," referring to Alexander Jannaeus.</note>, surnamed Alexander, succeeded him, who was very severe in his time, and nevertheless bore himself valiantly during the 9 years that were his reign. After his death, Alexandra his wife remained as regent, who bore herself very wisely in her regency; she also governed herself by the counsel of the Pharisees. The kingdom of Judea was at that time very great and powerful, for the Jews had defeated the Samaritans and several other neighboring nations that Josephus recounts in his *Jewish Antiquities* and *The Jewish War*, so that it is a very miraculous thing to properly consider the great mutations and changes of this people so loved by God and of this city so great and illustrious, seeing on one hand...

### HOW JERUSALEM, AND THE KINGS THEREOF, CAME UNDER THE SUBJECTION OF THE ROMANS, AND OF THE STATE OF THE JEWS UNTIL THEIR TOTAL DESTRUCTION.

After the death of Queen Alexandra mentioned above <note>Salome Alexandra, who ruled Judea from 76 to 67 BC.</note>, Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, her children, were in great debate and contention for the kingdom. But the Romans, who were very powerful, under the pretext of wishing to involve themselves to bring agreement between these two Princes, seized the kingdom of Judea. For Pompey the Great, being in Asia, was petitioned respectively by these two Princes, each separately to have his favor; but having had very troublesome words with Aristobulus, who was the more powerful of the two brothers, he came with his army against Jerusalem, which he entered by force and sacked, profaning the temple and the *Holy of Holies* <note>original: "Sancta Sanctorum"; the most sacred inner sanctum of the Tabernacle and later the Temple in Jerusalem, which only the High Priest could enter.</note>, where none entered but the High Priest. This having been done by him, he sent Aristobulus as a prisoner to Rome, leaving the title of High Priest to Hyrcanus, and the government of all Palestine to Antipater, son of Herod of Ascalon <note>Antipater the Idumaean, the father of Herod the Great.</note>. And by this means, the country of Judea came under the hand and subjection of the Romans and remained tributary to them. As for Hyrcanus and Antipater, they suffered many setbacks on account of the civil wars of Pompey and Caesar, of Brutus and Cassius, and of Octavian and Mark Antony themselves. Jerusalem was subject to many mutations and changes by reason of these wars; for Cassius seized it by force and carried away the treasures of the temple which Pompey had not wished to touch. Herod of Ascalon <note>Herod the Great.</note> bore himself so valiantly and so wisely in his government that the Romans granted him the Kingdom of Jerusalem, in which he maintained himself in such a way that even though he had given aid and help to Mark Antony against Octavian Augustus, he nevertheless did not fail to acquire his favor, so much so that he confirmed his kingdom.

Jerusalem began to be repopulated and to become a place of trade and wealth, just as it still was in his time. In the year of our Lord 612, during the Empire of Heraclius, Khosrow <note>original: "Cosroé"; specifically Khosrow II, the last great Sassanid king of Persia.</note>, King of Persia, came to overrun Syria and Palestine. Entering Jerusalem by force, he put everything to fire and sword, such that at least thirty thousand Christians, both men and women, remained there <note>referring to those killed in the siege</note>. Having found the Cross of our Lord, which Saint Helena <note>Mother of Emperor Constantine, credited with finding the relic of the True Cross in the 4th century.</note> had left there, he carried it with him to Persia, holding it in great reverence, and took Zacharias, the Patriarch of Jerusalem, as a prisoner. 

Fourteen years later, Kavadh <note>original: "Ciroes"; Kavadh II, who overthrew his father Khosrow.</note>, King of Persia and son of Khosrow, remembering the aid and favor he had received from the Emperor Heraclius in the wars he had led against his father, returned the Cross of our Lord to Heraclius and set the Patriarch Zacharias free. In memory of this, the Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross is held and celebrated on September 14th in the Roman Church. 

Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>, living in the time of this Heraclius, having seized the Kingdom of Persia and Judea, came to assault Jerusalem. Foreseeing this, the Emperor had the True Cross brought with great honor and reverence to the city of Constantinople. This Muhammad, pursuing his goal vigorously, took Jerusalem by force; however, some say it was one of his successors <note>Historically, the city was surrendered to Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab in 637 AD, a few years after Muhammad's death.</note>. But however it may be, this city fell into the hands of the infidels, who possessed it for four hundred and eighty-some years. 

Nevertheless, God having inspired the hearts of Pope Urban II, Emperor Henry IV, and several other Christian Princes—all in a league, at the persuasion of a holy Hermit <note>Peter the Hermit, whose preaching helped ignite the First Crusade.</note>—they crossed into the Levant with a great army to conquer the Holy Land. In this war, there were several great and very renowned Princes and Lords, specifically Godfrey of Bouillon, who, after several notable feats of arms performed by them during this war over three years, finally took Jerusalem in the year of our Lord 1099. By the consent of all, the said Godfrey was elected King for the admirable enterprises he had executed in this war. 

The rest of the country of Syria was distributed among the other Princes and Lords. After the death of Godfrey, the Kingdom passed to his successors through nine Kings, all of whom carried themselves valiantly during their reigns. Registri"</note> and Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish ecclesiastic and writer</note> in book 16, chapter 39; more on this below.

**Rabbi Abraham Levita** <note>Likely referring to Abraham ben David, known as the Ra’avad I, author of *Sefer ha-Kabbalah* (The Book of Tradition)</note> discourses excellently on this matter in his *Kabbalah*, and after him **Michael Neander** <note>A German teacher and humanist</note> in his *Erotemata* <note>A Greek term for a work written in a question-and-answer format</note> on the holy language.

At present, the aforementioned Hebrews or Jews, in whatever part of this universe they may be, do not speak the pure Hebrew language, nor the **Chaldean**, nor the **Syriac**, unless they learn it as we do, through masters, tutors, or long study. Instead, they use the vulgar and familiar language of the places and regions where they are born and where they live. However, the majority of them use Breviaries <note>The author uses the Christian term "Breviary" to describe the Jewish *Siddur* or *Mahzor*</note> in their synagogues composed in pure and grammatical Hebrew. These were transcribed from the written Breviary sent from Babylon to Spain about 600 years ago by one of their Rabbis named **R. Amran** <note>Amram Gaon, who sent his famous *Seder* (order of prayers) to Spain in the 9th century</note>; this Breviary is titled **Mahzor Siddur Tephillot** <term>Mahzor Siddur Tephillot: A "Cycle of the Order of Prayers," containing both daily and festival liturgies</term>. See what **P. Belon** writes of the Jews in the Levant in book 3, chapter 14 of his *Observations*.

## On the Region of the Canaanites or Chananeans.

Palestine <note>original Greek: Παλαςίνη, *Palaistine*</note>, according to **Ptolemy**, is a region of Asia which in the sacred scriptures is called **Pilisthim**, **Canaan**, **Chanaan**, and the **Land of Promise** <note>original Greek: Φυλισιέμ, *Phylisiem*, used by the 70 interpreters (the Septuagint)</note>. **St. Jerome**, in his *Hebrew Places*, says it should be noted among historians that **Judea** belongs to **Palestine**, while **Galilee** and **Samaria** belong to **Phoenicia**. The **Canaanites** are its inhabitants. Today, it is named the **Holy Land** <note>original Latin: *Terram Sanctam*</note> by all Europeans using various terms according to the difference of their languages, but all meaning the same thing. Mention of **Palestine** is found in the authentic records, in which the city of **Caesarea** <note>Caesarea Maritima</note> is mentioned; **Strabo** remembers **Palestine** and **Salutaris** in his book of *Notices* <note>original: "libro Notitiar."</note> as **Palestine the Third**. See also **Arabia Petraea** <term>Arabia Petraea: "Stony Arabia," a Roman provincial name for the area including the Sinai and Negev</term>. **Palestine Syria** is mentioned by **Galen**, where he writes that the **Jew stone** <term>Jew stone: *Lapis Iudaicus*, a fossilized sea urchin spine used in ancient medicine to treat kidney stones</term> is found.

It seems to stand for **Judea**, for **Eusebius** writes in his 10th book of the *Preparation* <note>referring to *Praeparatio Evangelica*</note> that in his time it was so called.

**Palestine Petraea**: according to **Agatharchides**, this place is near **Arabia Felix**. See **Sittacene** and **Interamna**.

**Sittacene** <note>original Greek: σιττακηνή</note> is, according to **Ptolemy**, a small region of **Assyria**, near **Susiana**. According to **Pliny**, this was called **Arbelitis** and **Palestine**, and also **Apolloniatis**, according to **Strabo**. However, **Apolloniatis**, **Arbelitis**, and **Sittacene** are distinct in **Ptolemy**. **Castaldus** now names it **Rabia**. See **Abraham Ortelius** <note>A famous 16th-century cartographer</note> in his *Synonyms and Geographical Treasures* under the word **Interamna**.

## Of the Canaanite Language.

### CHAPTER XXVII.

**W**ithout repeating what we have already deduced regarding the Canaanites in the chapter on the first and most ancient language of the world, we will state that some authors have numbered the *Canaanite* language—called in Latin *lingua Chananaica*—among the distinct languages, relying on the authority of the prophet Isaiah, chapter 19, saying:
> In that day (namely, of the destruction of Egypt) there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt that shall speak the language of the Canaanites, and swear by the Lord of hosts, etc.

Upon this passage, several great Christian personages have held that this Prophet meant by the language or speech of the Canaanites: the Hebrew language. This is what the ancient Rabbis and Hebrew doctors had written before them in their commentaries on the same Prophet, reporting that *Onias* <note>Onias IV, the son of the High Priest Onias III, who fled to Egypt during the Maccabean period</note>, the High Priest of the Jews—based on the authority of this prophet holding that one day five cities of Egypt would speak the language of the aforementioned Canaanites and that there would be a temple in the midst of the land—requested of *Ptolemy Philometor*, King of Egypt, that he be allowed to build in the city of *Heliopolis* <note>Literally "City of the Sun," an ancient Egyptian religious center</note> a temple similar and alike to that of *Jerusalem*. This is what *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> in book 13, chapter 11 of his *Antiquities of the Jews* asserts was done. The prophet *Daniel* speaks of these things in several places in chapter 11 of his Prophecy. And to return to the interpretation of the words alleged above from the Prophet *Isaiah*, we will say that he, through them, wished and intended to speak of the loss and ruin that *Sennacherib* <note>King of Assyria, r. 705–681 BCE</note> would bring upon the Egyptians and Ethiopians who would provide aid and succor to King *Hezekiah*; likewise, he spoke of the salvation that would follow the affliction he would give them, so that the Assyrians and Egyptians, after the death of the same *Sennacherib*—a wicked and impious tyrant—might come to know and worship the God of the Israelites. And this occurred when the religion of those Israelites was entirely introduced into Egypt, in such a way that the five cities thereof spoke the language of the said Israelites. The Prophet used these words, "five cities," to mean "several cities"—namely, using a certain number for an uncertain one—among which cities he notably places *Heliopolis*, that is to say, the City of the Sun, the seat of the Egyptian priests and philosophers, and of Egyptian idolatry. Therefore, the Canaanite language, according to the Prophet above, is called so not as the language used by the Canaanites descended from the wicked and cursed Ham (from whom the Egyptians also originated), but that used by the inhabitants of the land of Canaan—namely, first the Patriarchs *Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob*, and then the Israelites, after having expelled the *Canaanites and Phoenicians*.

*G. Genebrard* <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine exegete and orientalist</note> *in book 1 of his Chronography*: "The Hebrew language not only remained with Eber <note>The biblical ancestor from whom the name 'Hebrew' is traditionally derived</note>, from whom the name of the language and the people is derived, but also in Syria and the land of Canaan, the ancient seats of the Fathers. And when Abraham the Chaldean came into it, both he and his descendants spoke the Tongue of Canaan, which is the holy language itself; around which times, it was corrupted in Syria, so that..."

SAMARIA (Σαμαρεια in Greek) is, according to Ptolemy, a district of Judea, and within it is a city of the same name. ### CHAP. XXXVII.

THE Samaritan language has no other letters or characters of its own than the Hebrew letters and characters, but very ancient ones, as those well-versed in the knowledge of the Hebrew, Syriac, and other very ancient languages—of which we treat particularly in this work—well know. Many Jews today living in Syria, and especially in the city of Sichem <note>Modern-day Nablus; also called Shechem</note>, use this language.

At present, there are three principal sects among the Jews throughout the East: namely, the common ones, who are called *Thalmudim* <note>original: "Thalmudim"</note>, or Talmudists, who firmly embrace in every way the dreams and follies of those who have interpreted the meaning of the Holy Scriptures according to their own opinions and doctrines in their Talmuds <note>The Talmud is a central text of Rabbinic Judaism containing legal discussions and traditions</note>. Then there are the *Caraim* <note>Karaites</note>, meaning "literals" or "men of the letter," who, entirely rejecting all the Talmuds, glosses, and other doctrines and interpretations of men, embrace and observe only the pure and single text of the Hebrew Holy Scripture. These are otherwise very wealthy and opulent people, but so hated by the common Jews that the majority of their daughters remain unmarried all their lives, being unable to find a match among them due to the proximity and small size of their own kinship. Furthermore, those common Jews assert and affirm that if a Karaite and a Christian were both ready to be drowned and submerged in a river, and if it were necessary to make a bridge or a plank from the body of one of them to save the other, they would sooner make a bridge or plank from the body of the Karaite to save the Christian. The third sect is that of the Samaritans, of whom the great Saint Jerome made mention in the proem or preface to the Book of Kings, nearly thirteen hundred years ago.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Hebrew alphabet and its symbolic significance, following the previous page's discussion of the Samaritan script. Here, the author shifts focus to the letter Thau (Tau) and its mystical connection to the sign of the cross and the completion of the Law.</meta>

<page-num>317</page-num>
<header>LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.</header>

From Ezekiel, that this **Thau** was marked by the Angel on the foreheads of people who were mourning and contrite, can also have another interpretation, which even our own authors do not reject: that it was primarily to denote the regret, pain, and sorrow that good people felt seeing the observance of the Law, which in Hebrew is called **Torah**, of which the first letter is the **Thau**. In this way, it represented the word itself; this is a practice quite familiar to the Hebrews through the method of their <term>Notariacon <note>A Kabbalistic system of shorthand where a single letter represents an entire word or phrase.</note></term>, of which we have discoursed at length previously, and also to the Greeks and Latins, to represent an entire word by its first letter. But on the other hand, in confirmation of what Origen and St. Jerome propose, it is well worth considering that the Greek **Taph** <note>The letter Tau (T)</note>, which imitates the Hebrew **Tau**, and which follows **Rho** and **Sigma** just as the latter follows **Resh** and **Shin**, is—in both the capital **T** and the small letter **τ**—altogether similar to a gallows called St. Anthony's cross. It closely resembles a cross, lacking only the crossbar above where the head of the sufferer was placed and where the sign containing the cause of his death was attached. For it is well known that the Greek characters were borrowed from the Samaritan Hebrews, as we shall say hereafter in the chapter on the Greek language. Furthermore, what is also to be noted here is that since this word תו **Tau** signifies "sign," by a certain figure of speech <note>The original uses the term "antonomasia," meaning the substitution of an epithet or title for a proper name.</note> one can say that it must have been that of the cross, which even the Persian Magi and the Egyptians held to be the most excellent figure of all others. They saw it as consisting of two lines intersecting at four right angles, than which nothing can be found firmer or more solid, such that it cannot waver anywhere any more than a cube. Its four ends denote the four parts of the world: East, West, South, and North; the top and the bottom, the right side and the front, the left and the reverse or back, according to the <term>Yetzirah <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah* or "Book of Formation," an ancient Jewish mystical text.</note></term>. But with more authority, the Apostle says to the Ephesians: "so that you may be able to comprehend with all the Saints what is the breadth and the length, the depth and the height." So much so that, not without mystery, the blessing of the Jews was performed by this sign here, as is contained in the first book of the Talmud, in the *Massechet Berachot* <note>Tractate Berakhot, the first tractate of the Talmud, dealing with prayers and blessings.</note>, a treatise on blessings and prayers. There is a great likelihood that the **Tau** was meant to resemble this sign, since it even signifies it; just as this letter is the last of the alphabet, the cross was to be the end and fulfillment of the **Torah** or the Law, designated by that letter, which was its first character. And when we say that תו **Tau** means "sign," it must be understood as a boundary or limit—in Greek "boundary, limit, and end" <note>original Greek: "ὅρος τέρμας & τέρμα"</note> and in Latin "limit or boundary" <note>original Latin: "limes ou terminus"</note>. This was considered in two senses: one from the rising to the setting sun, which was called **Decumanus**, and the other from South to North, **Cardo**, as Pliny states in Book 18, Chapter 34. Thus, it was nothing other than a crossing, which was produced by two lines coming to intersect at a center. But what is more to be admired: just as not only the character of the **Tau** represented a cross, but the word תו also signified it, the second letter of that word, which is ו **Vau**, shows the shape of a nail. Thus, the word composed of these two together, תו, signifies it. Several other things worthy of note concerning this sign of the cross are deduced in Rufinus, Book 11 of his *Ecclesiastical History*; Pietro Crinito, Book 7 of *Honest Discipline*; and Pedro Mexía, Book 1.

As for Samaria <note>original: "Sarmatie"; likely a printer's error for "Samarie," as Sarmatia is a region in Eastern Europe, while the description here perfectly fits Samaria.</note>, it is, according to the aforementioned authors, situated between **Judea** and **Galilee**, but it should not be considered equal in size to either of them. It has the Mediterranean Sea to the West, Galilee to the North and East, along the lake or Sea of **Tiberias**: and crossing the Jordan, it extends its borders as far as the deserts of Arabia.

This region was formerly part of the inheritance of the two families of **Ephraim**, **Simeon**, and part of **Manasseh**, and was separated from the kingdom of Judea by the conspiracy of **Jeroboam** against his prince **Rehoboam**, tyrannically abusing the goods of his subjects as I have detailed above. And because the royal city of Israel was in **Samaria**, and it was named thus, as we shall see, it happened that the Kings were more renowned as being of Samaria than of Israel. And because Jeroboam had corrupted the order and manner of serving God in Israel, and because the factions of the Kings had caused the division of the people—added to the fact that the Jews returning from the Babylonian captivity, intending to rebuild the temple, were troubled by the Samaritans who, according to **Ezra**, chapter 4, did not want the Jews to have the honor of having the true and pure way of serving God, and that the City of **Jerusalem** should be called the head of all the seed of **Abraham**. 

And this was why the Jews detested the Samaritans, and why the latter held the Jews in abomination, as witnessed by the sacred history of the Holy Gospel in **St. John**, chapter 4. And what caused even greater and mortal hatred between these two peoples was the contention and envy between **Jaddua** <note>original: "Ladde"; refers to Jaddua, the Jewish High Priest mentioned by Josephus.</note>, High Priest of the Jews, and **Sanballat**, High Priest also of the Samaritans. For the latter, unable to bear the glory and insolence of the Jew, and wishing to do something that would be profitable, glorious, and honorable for his posterity, obtained from the Great King **Alexander** permission to build a temple on the mountain called **Gerizim**, where he installed as high priest the brother of Jaddua named **Manasseh**, who set up altar against altar, and first introduced a schism into the synagogue of the Jews, which **Josephus** discusses in Book 11, chapter 10 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*. 

So that while the Jews claimed, and rightly so, to have the true Church and the succession of the priesthood, and the Samaritans boasted of the possession of the lands where **Jacob** had formerly lived, this division remained immortal between them, until Evangelical truth removed this cloud and joined this division, making one single wall out of two sides. Now, although these Samaritans said and confessed that they adored and knew only one God, they nevertheless confusedly mixed the false gods of the Gentiles into the service of Him who asks for no companion; and for this reason, the Jews would not associate with them, nor enter into marriages with them. This kingdom of Samaria, having begun (as I said) under Rehoboam, lasted 250 years, until King **Nebuchadnezzar** ruined both the kings and the kingdom, without there ever being a king to command there since, but rather they lived under the Kings of **Assyria** and **Persia**, who sent their governors there, until the successors of Alexander established a kingdom in Asia, the seat of which was in **Syria**; and thus the Samaritans were included among the pagans and idolaters, although they call themselves observers of the Religion and Mosaic Law. > » <note>original: "lib.Panor.capit.13." — Referring to the *Panarion* by Epiphanius of Salamis.</note> (Book 1, Chapter 13) they rejected the Prophets, and some of them took only a single wife, and after her death, they fled marriage forever; others, entirely averse to marriage, embraced lifelong virginity. There also thrived among the Jews another kind of men, which, having borrowed some things from the Pharisees and others from the Sadducees, had fashioned a kind of monster. For in other matters, the followers of this sect agreed with the Pharisees, but with the Sadducees they denied the resurrection of the dead. The main point of their practice was that in Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter, they were baptized daily, thinking that men could not live unless they were immersed in water every day and by that means sanctified. For this reason, according to the same Epiphanius (Book 1, Chapters 17 and 18 of the *Panarion*), they were called **Hemerobaptists** <note>From the Greek for "daily baptizers."</note>, to whom were added the **Nazareans**, who neither accepted the books of Moses nor held sacrifices in common with the rest, and avoided the eating of living creatures as if they were unclean.

Those who have traveled to the Levant <note>The Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East.</note> know well enough that there are today Jews in that country who possess very ancient medals and gold and silver coins engraved around the edges with Samaritan letters praising the city of Jerusalem. These represent, on one side, a vessel full of manna with the inscription in Samaritan letters *Sekel Israel* <note>original Hebrew: "Shekel Israel," meaning Shekel of Israel.</note>, and on the other side, the rod of Aaron, with the inscription *Ierusalem Kedusa* <note>original Hebrew: "Yerushalayim Ha-Qodeshah," meaning Jerusalem the Holy.</note>, as things greatly memorable in the divine law. These Jews maintain that these pieces are a very great treasure, even though they hate the Samaritans and their memory more than the plague. This is because, through the mere sight of these coins, they contemplate their ancient characters and letters, which their first and most ancient Fathers used from the beginning of the world. **Rabbi Moses of Gerona** <note>Also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270).</note> in his *Commentaries* near the end of the Pentateuch, asserts that he saw and handled one of these coins in the Holy Land in his time, as is recounted at length by **Benedito Arias Montano** in his *Apparatus* for the Bible in the chapter on the Shekel. What is more, among those Samaritans currently in the Levant, there are some called *Chus* or *Chussebarich*, who are Samaritans in name only, being descended from the people of the ancient colony sent from **Cuthah** and Babylon into Samaria some years after the destruction of Samaria, according to the 4th Book of Kings, Chapter 17 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 17.</note>, and Book 9, Chapter 15 of the *Antiquities* <note>Referencing Flavius Josephus.</note>. For this reason, they are Samaritans only by their religion, but Cuthites by their nation, as reported by **Elias Levita** in his *Tishbi* in the interpretation of the word *Cuth*, **Gilbert Génébrard** in Book 1 of his *Chronography*, and **Joseph Scaliger** in Book 5 of *The Emendation of Time* in the chapter on the first year of the Samaritans. These Cuthites or Samaritans assert that, commonly, when digging the earth around Jerusalem, such coins are often found, bearing the aforementioned words in Samaritan letters as a mark of great antiquity. Now, it should be noted that the Samaritans have not entered the city of Jerusalem at all since the time of King Solomon, and they have not deigned to call it by the title "Holy," because they worshipped idols as semi-Jews and Gentiles on a mountain outside the aforementioned city; they would have been very far from wanting to honor that city with their own letters, as they regarded it as their adversary and enemy. On this subject, see **Josephus**, Book 13, Chapter 6 of his *Jewish Antiquities*. In conclusion, the Samaritans

at present, they receive only—as they did in the time of Saint Jerome—the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible, attributed to Moses.</note> or five books of Moses written in their own characters, and they hold all the other Prophets and Holy Histories to be fables. And what further strengthens what we have deduced above is that this great and ineffable name of God, the **Tetragrammaton** <note>original: "Tetragrammatum"—the sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note>, corresponds closely in Greek copies to **$\pi$ $\pi$** <note>The Greek letters Pi-Pi (ππ) were often used by those who did not know Hebrew to represent the visually similar Hebrew letters of the name of God (יהוה).</note>; for two **$\uparrow$ $\uparrow$** <note>Likely referring to archaic or Samaritan letter forms.</note>, with which they also depict the ineffable name of **Jehovah** or **Adonai**, were considered among them to be the same as **$\pi$ $\pi$**, by which they presently represent the name Tetragrammaton. This Samaritan language differs in nothing from the Hebrew language except in its characters, as confirmed by the same Guillaume Postel in the aforementioned place, and in his pamphlet on *Phoenician Letters*. **Theodore Bibliander**, in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, and **Joseph Scaliger**, in book 2 of *The Emendation of Time* in the chapter on the year of the Samaritans, state that it is equal and similar to that of the Hebrews. In these they rely entirely upon the literal letter alone, rejecting all human traditions and interpretations, as did also the **Sadducees**, who for that reason were called **Textuaries** <note>Those who strictly follow the written text.</note>, according to the words of **Gilbert Genebrard** in book 1 of his *Chronography*. Furthermore, the alphabet of these Samaritans, just like the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic, proceeds inward, in imitation of the course and movement of nature, from the right hand toward the left, or from the outside pulling toward the stomach.

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

We have recovered, some years since, a Grammar composed in this Samaritan language and characters by a certain priestly figure named Jacques, son of a Mugiaassin. A similar copy was brought back from the Levant by the late Guillaume Postel (previously cited) upon his return to this Kingdom of France; regarding this copy, he wrote the following: <note>original Latin: "In Grammaticis Hebraicis nihil habeo pretioſius vno Samaritanæ Grammatices, hoc eſt, veræ Hebraicæ libro à Sacerdote Iacobi filio Mugiaſſin olim ſcripto, in quo poſitis exemplis Samaritanis, Arabice methodo explicatur Grammatica hebræa priſca."</note> "In the study of Hebrew grammar, I possess nothing more precious than this single volume of Samaritan grammar—that is, of the true Hebrew—written long ago by the priest Jacques, son of Mugiaassin. In this work, by providing Samaritan examples, the ancient Hebrew grammar is explained using the Arabic method."

Juan Bautista Villalpando, <note>A Spanish Jesuit architect and scholar known for his massive commentary on Ezekiel and reconstructions of the Temple of Jerusalem.</note> in the second part of the third volume of his *Apparatus of the City and Temple of Jerusalem* (dispute 4, chapters 20 and 21), has illustrated another Samaritan alphabet even more ancient than the two preceding ones. In this version, the letter *Tau* is marked thus: ת X, in the form of a cross. It is with the letters of this alphabet that all the ancient coins and pieces of money of the Hebrews were inscribed and engraved—those which have been found and are still being found in the Levant—as the aforementioned author explains at length.

<gloss>Chaldaea</gloss> Chaldaea, <gloss>Chaldaea</gloss>, a region of Babylonia in Asia. Pierre Belon <note>A French explorer and naturalist.</note> writes that it is called Azamia in this day and age.    They were previously named <gloss>Arphaxadaeans</gloss>. According to Strabo, the Chaldeans are also a people in Asia Minor, located above Trebizond, whom he testifies were called Chalybes in antiquity and Halizones by Homer. Johannes Leunclavius teaches that Chaldaea is today called Kurdistan, and the Chaldeans are called Kurds by the Turks; he also writes that the region is called Keldam by the Arabs. This is according to Abraham Ortelius in his *Synonyms* and *Geographic Theater*.

### CHAP. XXXVIII.

The Hebrews and Egyptians anciently called wise and learned persons <note>original Hebrew: חכם</note> *Hacham* (meaning "Wise"), or *Chefem Mehonem*, or *Nabi* (meaning "Prophets" or "Seers"—refer to 1 Kings chapter 9, and 2 Kings chapters 15 and 24). This was because, in seeing God, they delivered their responses. Otherwise, they were called Prophets, *Hachamim*, Masters, *Magon*, *Jannes and Jambres* (or as the Syrians say, *Jambarils*), Heliopolitans, or Hierophants. They were also known as Pharisees or Cabbalist Priests. The Assyrians and Babylonians named them Chaldeans. The Indians and Ethiopians called them Hermans, Samaneans, Brahmins, and Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian ascetics known for their wisdom and renunciation of clothing.</note>—who are described at length by Strabo in his *Geography*, Philostratus in his life of Apollonius, and Porphyry in his fourth book *On Sacrifices*. The Hebrews hold it as quite certain that Arphaxad, son of Shem (of whom it is spoken in *Genesis* 10), whose name in the Hebrew language means "healing" or "releasing the prey," was the first from whom these Chaldeans—named in the Hebrew language *Chasdim*, from the singular *Chasdi*, from the word *Chascat*—took their names and titles. Regarding their antiquity, we will report what follows, drawn from several ancient Hebrew and Chaldean books. **Chasceddim**, which is to say the name of the Chaldeans—under which title are included both generally and specifically all the sects of the sages of Babylon—properly and particularly signifies in the Book of Daniel, according to Saint Jerome, a type of men whom the common Latin speakers call in the Latin language *Mathematicos* and *Genethliacos*. <note>Mathematicians and "Genethliacs," or those who cast birth charts to predict a person's fate.</note> Pliny says these men took their beginning from Belus Jupiter, father of Ninus, King of the Assyrians and the first inventor of the science of the stars. These Chaldeans diligently observed the celestial movements and devoted themselves entirely to the rules, canons, and predictions of Astronomy established by them according to the observation of the stars. Philo the Jew, in his work on Abraham, speaks of them in these words:

> The Chaldeans, being exceptionally trained in astral science, attributed everything to the movements of the stars, by which they believed the powers of the world were governed, which consist of numbers and their proportions. They worshiped visible things, not perceiving the invisible and intelligible, searching only for their order; and thus from the circuits of the Sun, the Moon, the wandering stars <note>planets</note>, and the fixed stars, and the cycles of the year divided into four seasons, and the harmony of celestial and terrestrial things, they thought the world itself was God, making the creation equal to the creator by their profane opinion. <note>original: "Chaldæi, cum primis exercitati syderali scientia... creaturá facientes creatori similé."</note>

This is how Philo speaks of these Chaldeans; whom Saint Jerome, in his epistle to the Hebrews, says affirmed that the matter of this visible world was eternal and not produced by anyone. **Asaphim** signifies those who were called "Philosophers" by an old Latin translator; the "Magi" by the seventy Greek translators <note>The Septuagint</note>; and "Magi" by the aforementioned Saint Jerome. They philosophized on all things divine and human. According to the opinion of Origen, the author of these Magi was Balaam, son of Beor, whom Balak, King of the Moabites, called to himself to curse the people with his magics and incantations.

> If the prophecies of Balaam were inserted into the sacred volumes by Moses, how much more were they recorded by those who lived then in Mesopotamia, among whom Balaam was held in great magnificence, and who were known to be disciples of his art? From him, it is said, the race and institution of the Magi flourished in the regions of the East. Having everything recorded among themselves that Balaam had prophesied, they also held this in writing: *that a Star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall arise out of Israel.* <note>original: "orietur Stella ex Iacob, & exurget homo ex Israel"</note> The Magi had these writings among themselves; and therefore, when Jesus was born, they recognized the star and understood that the prophecy was being fulfilled—more so than the people of Israel, who had come to despise the words of the holy Prophets. They, therefore, recognizing from these writings left by Balaam that the time was at hand, came and, seeking Him, immediately worshiped Him.

The author of the imperfect work <note>This refers to the *Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum*, an ancient commentary on the Gospel of Matthew once attributed to St. Chrysostom.</note> on Saint Matthew, chapter [X], says:
> I read in a certain place that these Magi received the knowledge of this appearing star from the books of Balaam the diviner, whose divination is recorded in the Old Testament: *a Star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall arise out of Israel, and he shall rule over all Nations.* <note>original: "orietur ex Stella Iacob... dominabitur omnium Gentium"</note>

Diogenes Laertius, in Book 1 of *The Lives of the Philosophers*, writes that Zoroaster was the Prince of these Magi. These men, acting as priests, were entirely devoted to the service of the gods and were accustomed to being the only ones to offer and present their prayers, vows, and sacrifices, as if they were the only ones heard and understood by the divine. They dressed entirely in white and had only the hard earth for a bed; for their food, they ate only herbs, cheese, and bread. In place of a staff, they used a reed, at the end of which they placed their cheese to eat it. They held as doctrine and religion that there was one first and Eternal God—which Zoroaster had also taught during his life, according to the report of Eusebius in Book 1 of his *Gospel Preparation*. 

These men also posited other secondary gods or Spirits, whose substance they held to be either fiery, watery, or earthly. They rebuked or disapproved of images and statues of the gods and rejected the opinions of those who considered them male and female. They judged that souls, after the dissolution of their bodies, were immortal, and said that all things here below endured through their prayers and supplications. They believed that men must be resurrected, and that the bodies of the wicked and iniquitous deceased must be burned by the fire of damnation. They discussed and treated infinitely beautiful matters concerning justice and other virtues, and they had no use for gold or silver among themselves.

Philo the Jew, previously cited in his *Book of Special Laws*, speaks of this Wisdom in these words:
> That true Magic—which is to say, the speculative science through which the works of nature are seen more clearly—is sought after as honorable and desirable not only by common people, but even by the greatest Kings of Kings, especially those of Persia. They are so curious about these arts that it is not permitted to reign unless one is intimately familiar with the Magi. <note>original: "Veram quidem illam Magiam... nisi cum Magis versato familiariter."</note>

St. Jerome on this subject:
> Magi are those who philosophize on individual things; however, common custom takes "Magi" to mean those who practice sorcery, but they are regarded differently among their own people, for they are the Philosophers of the Chaldeans. Even the Kings and Princes of that same nation do everything according to the knowledge of this art; thus they were the first to understand the birth of the Lord Savior at His nativity, and coming to Bethlehem, they worshiped Him.

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE

...mandi <note>This is likely the conclusion of a term like *Chasmandi*, a transliteration of a Hebrew or Chaldean word for a specific class of sage.</note>, that is to say in Latin *Incantatores* <note>original: "Incantatores"; enchanters or spell-casters</note>, or as Saint Jerome would have it, *Harioli* <note>original: "Harioli"; soothsayers or diviners</note>. These individuals were entirely dedicated to the enchantments of demons. According to the authority of Pliny, Justin, and Saint Augustine, they claimed to have taken their origin from Zoroaster, King of the Bactrians, a magician and the first corrupter of true Magic. He was the only mortal who began to laugh on the very day he was born into this world; it is said his brain pulsated so strongly that it would entirely repel a hand placed upon it—a certain omen of his future madness, by which he declined into the follies of incantations. Having learned these things from his predecessors, he was, by a just judgment of God, defeated in battle and driven from his kingdom by Ninus, King of the Assyrians. The most ancient historians who have spoken of him have written that this Zoroaster—whether he was Ham himself, the son of Noah, or his grandson the son of Ham—was the first who, having learned the science of the stars from Noah, began to abuse it. He converted it into evil omens and mixed it with the conjuring of spirits. He instructed the Chaldeans in those superstitious observations that they practiced thereafter. Those who followed him established two principles, according to Laërtius: one good and the other evil. The good was the God of Heaven, from whom all blessings come, and the evil were the inferior gods, from whom all evils proceed—a belief that, among Christians, the Manichaeans seem to have held. Among the doctrines they believed, they maintained that the air was full of demons who appeared to them in a very subtle manner, like certain vapors. They placed great value and esteem on their divinations and predictions through these communications, which they summoned. They also believed that it was no sin to have carnal relations with one's mother or daughter, which is a most wicked and impious thing.

<margin>*Mecasphim*, in Latin *venefici* <note>original: "venefici"; sorcerers or poisoners</note></margin> **Mecasphim**: those who are called by the seventy Greek Interpreters <note>The Septuagint</note> in the Greek language *pharmakoi* <note>original: "φαρμακοι"; those who use drugs or potions for sorcery</note>, and in Latin *venefici*, or by Saint Jerome *malefici* <note>original: "malefici"; evildoers or practitioners of harmful magic</note>. These people, by observing and contemplating the blood and intestines of sacrificial victims, divined future things; they also did this by observing dead bodies.

<margin>*Gazarim*, in Greek *gazarenoi* <note>original: "γαζαρηνοι"</note></margin> **Gazarim**: those whom the same seventy Greek Interpreters named in their Greek tongue *Gazarenos* <note>original: "γαζαρηνοι"</note>, and Saint Jerome in the Latin tongue *Haruspices* <note>original: "Haruspices"; diviners who interpret the entrails of animals</note>. Having contemplated the intestines of victims and sacrifices, they would divine the future. Some ancient authors understand by this word *Gazarim* the "augurs"—that is to say, those who boast of predicting the future by the flight, song, or feeding habits of birds.

Therefore, under the King Nebuchadnezzar mentioned above, the categories, types, and divisions of the wisdom of the Chaldeans were such as we have described here. Although the prophet Daniel had been fully instructed in these by Chaldean teachers (as noted in Daniel chapter 4), just as Moses in more ancient times was taught all the wisdom of the Egyptians, nevertheless, according to Justin Martyr in his book of questions objected to by the Gentiles, Daniel never wished to use them nor approve of them. He abhorred them entirely as being completely contrary to Divine Law, which is why he was exposed to the lions. Anyone who wishes to see what the Greek and Latin authors have written about these Chaldeans should read Eustathius on the first book of Homer's *Iliad*; Suidas on the word "Chaldeans"; Strabo in books 4 and 15 of his *Geography*; Marcus Varro in book 2 of *On Agriculture* <note>original: "de re rustic."</note>; Seneca in book 2 of his *Natural Questions*; Cicero in books 1 and 2 of *On Divination*; Eusebius in book 6 of his *Gospel Preparation*; Saint Augustine in book 4, chapter 23, and book 12, chapter 10 of *The City of God*; and Petrus Crinitus in book 9, chapter 1 of *On Honest Discipline*.

->On the Chaldean Language.<-

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

Diodorus Siculus, a Greek author in his histories, following Herodotus in his *Euterpe*, recounts the history of the debate and contention previously reported by us in chapter 1 of this discourse concerning the antiquity of the first tongue <gloss>langue</gloss> of this Universe, which occurred between the Egyptians and the Phrygians. He maintained that the Chaldeans were the first who invented the characters of letters, even though the Egyptians boast and brag of having done so first. On this subject, the divine Plato wrote that those Egyptians do not trace their source and origin to Egypt, but to an Asia, and to those Chaldeans. Pliny writes these words in book 7, chapter 56:

> I am of the opinion that letters were always Assyrian, but others wish them to have been discovered among the Egyptians by Mercury, and others among the Syrians. <note>original: "Literas semper arbitror Assyrias fuisse, sed alij apud Ægyptios à Mercurio, alij apud Syros repertas volunt"</note>

This led Aulus Gellius in his *Attic Nights* to hold that among those Egyptians, the aforementioned Mercury was the first who invented these letters, and among the Syrians, those same people; this demonstrates to the naked eye that the Hebrews and Chaldeans were those who first invented and used letter characters in this Universe, which are called Hebraic. For the Chaldeans are none other than the Assyrians. In fact, it is a certain thing that before Eber <note>The biblical ancestor from whom the term "Hebrew" is traditionally derived.</note>, from whom the name of the Hebrews and the Hebrew language first proceeded (as I have extensively touched upon before), both of these two peoples were one and the same kind of people, from whom was first chosen the great Patriarch Abraham, so celebrated in the writings of ancient authors. The same Pliny, in book 5, chapter 12, confirms this opinion, saying:

*The race of the Phoenicians itself (the author meaning by this word all the Syrians of whom I speak here) was held in great glory for the invention of letters and the stars, as well as for naval and martial arts.* <note>original: "Ipsa gens phœnicum... in gloria magna literarum inuentionis & syderum, naualiúmque ac bellicarum artium fuit."</note> Thus, according to sacred and profane authors, the first and most ancient characters of letters, and the first and most ancient language of the world, were those of the Hebrews or Chaldeans. Moses himself even recognized the people of those Chaldeans as older and more ancient than that of the said Hebrews, as Josephus <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Jewish historian whose works are central to understanding the history of the Jewish people in antiquity.</note> seems to confirm in his books of *Jewish Antiquities* and *Against Apion the Grammarian*; as does Eusebius of Caesarea <note>A 4th-century scholar and bishop, known as the "Father of Church History."</note> in several places in his *Evangelical Preparation*; and Guillaume Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French Renaissance linguist and mystic who traveled the East and believed all languages derived from a single source.</note> in his treatise on the *Origins, or the Antiquity of Hebraism, or the Affinity of Languages*. But so as not to confuse our discourse, we shall take this matter from its very first source and origin, and assert that the Hebrew language was called from all antiquity the "holy tongue," because it was that in which, at the beginning of the world, God the Creator spoke with His own mouth to Adam, and taught him to name all the things of this universe by their true and proper name; *For whatever Adam called every living creature in this Universe, that was its name,* <note>Genesis 2:19.</note> Genesis chapter second. This language, therefore called "descended from Heaven to earth," maintained its purity and clarity until the confusion of Babel, where this Hebrew language was altered and corrupted into 72 entirely diverse and dissimilar languages—as many as there were already names, powers, and principalities established in the world, as I have previously detailed in the preceding chapters. Since this confusion of Babel, it did not cease to remain always in its entirety with the holy Patriarchs and faithful men, such as with Abraham and his successors until the Prophet Moses, to whom God gave His Law by voice on Mount Horeb with the Hebrew characters, language, and writing—both being such as they still are today, as affirmed by Rabbi Simeon son of Eleazar in the Talmud <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, recording centuries of legal and ethical debates.</note>. From there, it continued in the synagogue or Church of God until the Babylonian captivity in the land of Chaldea. During the seventy years that the Hebrews remained there, the language came to be altered into the aforementioned Chaldean language <note>Specifically Aramaic, which became the common spoken language of the Near East and the Jewish people during and after the exile.</note>, which those same Hebrews always used thereafter as their common tongue. The aforementioned Hebrew language was then neither practiced nor known except by the Priests, Doctors, and Scholars of the Divine Law, and by lettered men. It is a very certain thing that during this Babylonian captivity, these Hebrews retained three things: namely, their Hebrew language, the dress of their country, and their names, according to Elias <note>Elijah Levita (1469–1549), a renowned Hebrew grammarian and teacher of Christian humanists.</note> in his preface to *Methurgeman* <note>A dictionary of the Aramaic translations of the Bible (Targums).</note> according to the Talmud. Even still today, the Jews, in whatever country or region they reside, have no notice or knowledge of this Hebrew language unless they learn it in schools, just as we do the same with the Greek and Latin languages; thus they speak and use the common tongue of the places where they dwell. Nevertheless, they do not fail to use the pure Hebrew language in all their prayers made in their synagogues, which they practiced even in the time of our Lord Jesus Christ according to
