Even in the time of Ezra, nearly five hundred years before the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, this same Ezra and the Levites read to the Hebrews and translated for them the forms of their prayers and orations in the temple and divine service in pure Hebrew, although by then it was no longer understood by the common people, as may be seen in the 8th chapter of Nehemiah in these words:

> *The priest Ezra brought the book of the Law before the multitude of men and women, and all those who could understand; that is to say, before the common people who understood nothing of Hebrew, and the learned who knew it, as he explains immediately after: that he read therein from morning until noon in the presence of the men and women, whom he takes there for the multitude; and that he, with Nehemiah and the Levites, interpreted it to all the people.*

This is what Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and grammarian of the Middle Ages.</note> touches upon somewhat in his exposition of the 5th chapter of Ecclesiastes, concerning not speaking rashly of divine things, where he tacitly attacks some lyric poets of his nation who mixed Median, Persian, Spanish, and other vulgar tongues into their hymns and canticles, demonstrating that one should not even employ the Syriac and Arabic languages in these matters, even though they are very close to the Hebrew language. And ever since then, until now, the Jews—as contained in the 13th and 15th chapters of Acts and in Josephus, Book 2 *Against Apion*—have been accustomed every Saturday, while performing their divine service in their synagogues (which are to them as parishes are to us), if no other solemnity occurred, to have read aloud from the pulpit one of their *Parashah* <note>original: "Pareschah"; a designated section of the Torah read weekly.</note> or sections, each of which contained 136 verses of the five books of Moses, which are partitioned and divided as follows: namely, Genesis into 12, Exodus into 11, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy into 10 each, making 53 in total, as many as there are weeks in the year; so that in the revolution of the year, the entire Law is finished being read, as Saint James well noted while at the assembly of Jerusalem in these words inserted in the 15th chapter of the Acts of the Apostles:

> *Moses from ancient times has some persons in every city who preach him in the synagogues, where he is read every day of rest,*

In imitation of this, the office of the *Anagnost* <note>The "Reader," a minor clerical order in the early Church.</note> was introduced into the Greek Church, and the Matins lessons in the Latin Church. King Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes (r. 175–164 BC), the Seleucid king who attempted to suppress Jewish religious practices.</note>—according to the report of Elias Levita <note>Elia Levita (1469–1549), a prominent Jewish grammarian who taught many Renaissance scholars.</note>, a Jew by nation, in his *Tishbi* <note>original: "Thesbite"; a dictionary of Rabbinic Hebrew.</note> on the Hebrew word *Patar* <note>meaning to dismiss, release, or conclude.</note>—having in his time forbidden the Jews from reading the divine Hebrew Law in their synagogues, they instead read one of the *Parashat*, or a text from the Prophets that most closely conformed to that of the Law which fell on that Saturday. To finish, [the reading] was not interrupted by the Jews; rather, after the lesson of the Law and <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible, the Torah</note>, they have always added some passages from the Prophets that are most consistent with and approaching the subject of the <term>Parashah</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion read in the synagogue</note>. To this conforms our own manner of employing, in our lessons of Matins for the extension of the Gospel text cited there, the singing of one of the Homilies of the ancient Fathers. A great figure of this time, interpreting the Greek word *archipheréktai* <note>original: α’ρχιφερέκται; literally "chief of the sections"</note> which the Emperor Constantine used in his decree—*that it be permitted for the Hebrews, according to the handed-down law, to read the scriptures in Latin or Greek, or another language, etc.* <note>original: "vt liceat Hebræis ſecundùm traditam legem ſcripturas Latinè vel Græcè, vel alia lingua legere &c."</note>—wrote the following: *The word is a hybrid, partly Greek and partly Hebrew; their duty was to read and interpret those sections of the Law or Prophets which the Hebrews call Parashiot and Perakim, and to adapt to them the sub-divisions of the greater treatises of the Talmud, which the same Jews call Perakim. For what our fifty books of the <term>Pandects</term> <note>The Digest of Roman Civil Law compiled under Justinian</note> are, so are the sixty greater treatises of the Talmudists; as many as we have Titles, they have Perakim. Therefore, these archipheréktai are like masters of the titles, to whom the titles of the Talmud are known to a hair.* <note>original: "Vox eſt hybrida, partim Græca... ad vnguẽ noti Thalmudis tituli."</note>

With these remarks made, we shall say that the ancient Chaldean language was the Babylonian tongue—Babylon being, according to the Prophet Jeremiah in chapter 21 and Ezra in book 1, chapter 5, at that time the head of the entire dominion of the Chaldeans. In this regard, Berosus <note>An ancient Babylonian priest and historian</note> attests that a short time after the universal deluge, there were several books written in this language concerning the state and disposition of the world, and the various columns and cities that were constructed before said Deluge. This is confirmed by Sebastian Münster in his *Chaldean Grammar* and Guy le Fèvre de la Boderie in the preface of his *Chaldean Grammar*. 

Regarding the characters of the letters of this language, some hold that they were the Samaritan characters previously represented in the figure in the preceding chapter; others hold that they were those said to have been given to Abraham at the crossing of the river when he left Chaldea to come to the land of Canaan—since called Palestine, Judea, and the Holy Land—which are also represented in the figure in the preceding chapter on the origin of the Hebrew language and its characters. Some Hebrews do confess that the Chaldeans had letter characters proper to themselves, which the Prophet Daniel seems to declare in his works when he says that Ashpenaz taught him and his companions the letters of the Hebrews and the Chaldean tongue. Indeed, the Hebrew <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Mystics following the Kabbalah tradition</note> have assured that over the characters of the letters and the Chaldean language presided what they call *Bat Kol* <note>original: Bat hcol; literally "daughter of a voice," often referring to a divine echo or heavenly voice</note>, the universal voice, which the *Zohar* and other most distinguished Kabbalists interpret as the mediating and moving power of this universe—namely, the intellect of the Messiah or of the Word, the "mind of minds" <note>original: mens mentium</note> as they call it, through whom the sovereign Father moves everything. 

Even Saint Jerome, in his preface to the Book of Kings, held that the Chaldeans had twenty-two letter elements with the same sound as those of the Hebrews, but diverse and dissimilar, as I will show hereafter. But to say and affirm in truth what these letter elements were is entirely impossible to do, because the Jews themselves, before the time of the same Saint Jerome, were accustomed to writing and copying Chaldean books in Hebrew characters. This is believed to have been done and practiced in the books of Daniel and Ezra which are in our hands.

But regardless of that, it is a very certain thing that both this language and the ancient writing have suffered several mutations and changes. For during the seventy years that those Hebrews remained captive in the city of Babylon, there occurred a mixing and commingling of the Hebrew and Chaldean languages, such as we can visibly see through the writings of the Prophet Daniel, which are woven from both the Hebrew and Chaldean languages. This was well noted in his time by Saint Jerome in his preface to this Prophet, as well as in the Writings of Ezra—which nonetheless closely approach the dialect of the Syriac language—along with the writings of Tobit and Judith, as the aforementioned Saint Jerome confirmed in his prefaces to them. 

This is seen even better and more clearly in the **Targums** or Chaldean Paraphrases of **Onkelos**, who is held to have been the son of the daughter of the Emperor Titus. This Targum was first translated into the Latin language at Strasbourg in the year 1546 by Paul Fagius. It is also seen in the Targums or Paraphrases of **Jonathan son of Uzziel**, one of the disciples of **Hillel** (the great Hebrew teacher) and a fellow student of **Simeon the Just** (who received our Lord Jesus Christ in his arms). Regarding him, the Jews in the *Bava Batra* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning civil law and the history of scripture</note> assert that while this Jonathan was composing that Targum, if a fly or any other bird happened to fly over him or his paper, it was immediately burned and consumed by fire from Heaven, without any damage to the said paper. 

One finds this also in the other Targums or Paraphrases by the Chaldean translators or **Talmudists** of the books of the Hebrew Bible, regarding whom one should consult **Lyranus** <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan teacher whose literal biblical commentaries were highly influential</note> in his commentaries on the eighth chapter of the Prophet Isaiah, and Paul Fagius in his versions of these Targums or Paraphrases. They state that the Targum of Joseph the Blind on the **Hagiographa** <note>The third section of the Hebrew Bible, including the Psalms, Job, and Proverbs</note>, the Psalms of David, Job, the Proverbs of Solomon, and others, is not easily found today, according to the report of Franciscus Raphelengius in his various readings and annotations. 

Furthermore, according to Benito Arias Montano in his preface to the Chaldean Paraphrase in the first and second volumes of the great Bibles printed at Antwerp by **Plantin** <note>The "Antwerp Polyglot" Bible, a masterpiece of 16th-century printing</note>, it is still uncertain among the Jews who the authors were of the Targums or Paraphrases for the other Hebrew books of the Bible. This is explained by Pietro Galatino in Book 1, Chapter 1 of *The Secrets of the Catholic Faith*, where he says:

*About forty-two years before the birth of Christ, Jonathan (or Jonathas), son of Uzziel—a student of Hillel and a fellow student of Simeon the Just, who took the infant Christ in his arms—translated the entire Old Testament into the Chaldean language and explained it. He translated the sense of the passages and explained all the most obscure words, so that whatever was doubtful or hiddenly written concerning the Messiah, he rendered certain and very clear. Indeed, his edition seems not so much a translation as a gloss and exposition, which the Hebrews call a **Targum** <note>Hebrew: תרגום</note>, that is, a translation. It is of such great authority among them that not only [did they not] contradict it...* <note>original Latin: "Anno ante Christi natalem circiter secundo & quadragesimo Ionathan aut Ionathas Vzielis filius, Hillelisque auditor atque Simeonis iusti, qui Christum infantulum suscepit in brachiis, condiscipulus, totum vetus Testamentum, in Chaldeam vertit linguam... id est, translationem nuncupant. Without doubt, *Jonathan* translated the entire Bible into *Chaldean* (as I said before, and I think it is not unknown to you). Here also, *Onkelos* translated and explained the entire Bible in *Chaldean*. They also call it the *Targum*, because it is also in *Chaldean*, just like the other; even if both are written in Hebrew characters. Furthermore, the edition of *Jonathan* himself on the Psalter is in the possession of very few people. His excellent sayings are found scattered in the *Talmudic* books. From the sayings of all these men, therefore, and many others who at that same time wrote upon the Law and the Prophets and openly showed that our Lord *Jesus Christ* was both the only almighty Son of God and the true *Messiah*, almost the entire *Talmud* is composed.

The other Paraphrast, whom they call Jonathan son of Uziel, to whom they attribute the Prophets, wrote his works before the devastation of the temple; although there are those who would have it that both translated the entire Bible into the Chaldean language. A second reason is that almost all passages in the Hebrew Bible which seem to have some obscurity and difficulty are beautifully explained in the Chaldean Paraphrase, with all obscurity removed, especially where there are prophecies concerning the kingdom of Christ. For wherever in the Hebrew truth <note>original: "veritate hebraica"; a term used by scholars of this era to mean the original Hebrew source text</note> Christ is dealt with under a hidden name, there in the Chaldean truth the name of the Messiah is always expressed in plain terms, as is easily seen by those inspecting and comparing both original texts. Through very affectionate letters he sent to me, he gave me hope that this Treasure might one day come to light. I wish with all my heart, night and day, that this happens soon, doubting not that great light will also be added to the writings of the Evangelists." See what F. The old translation says, "truly that which is called by them the second edition." Alas, what a meager explanation! "Second edition" and *Deuterosis* <note>The Greek term for the Mishnah, meaning "repetition"</note> differ by the whole of heaven. The "second edition" is nothing other than the version of the Bible produced by Aquila <note>A 2nd-century convert to Judaism who made an extremely literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> which in Greek is called the "second edition" <note>original: "δευτέρα ἔκδοσις" (deutera ekdosis)</note>; but *Deuterosis* is a part of the Talmud. When I name the Talmud, I mean the civil law of the Hebrews, which has two parts: the **Mishnah** and the **Gemara**. The Mishnah in Greek is called *Deuterosis*, which the Emperor forbade entirely; it contains many obscenities, and many things that are old wives' tales and fables, as Jerome testifies in his *Letter to Algasia*, question 10, writing thus: "I cannot unfold how great the traditions of the Pharisees are, which they today call *Deuteroses* <note>original: "δευτερώσεις"</note>, nor how many old wives' tales they are; for the size of the book does not allow it, and many things are so foul that I am ashamed to speak of them. I will, however, say one thing to the shame of this enemy nation: they have the wisest men appointed to the synagogues for a loathsome task—to taste the blood of a virgin or a menstruating woman if they cannot discern it with their eyes." Let it be noted here that the Pharisaic traditions are called *Deuteroses*; and *Deuterosis* is the tradition of these things, like a body and a compilation <note>original: "σύσταλμα" (systalma)</note>. 

Nor will it be out of place to bring forward the proper word in this matter, which Jerome mentions in the same place: whenever on certain days they explain their traditions to their disciples, they are accustomed to say *the wise men teach the second traditions* <note>original: "οἱ σοφοι δευτεροῦσιν" (hoi sophoi deuterousin)</note>, that is, the wise men teach the traditions. *The wise men teach the second traditions*, that is, *Shano Hakhamim* <note>original: "Sanu Hahachamim"; Hebrew/Aramaic for "The wise have taught"</note>: which in the Syrian <note>Aramaic</note> language they more frequently say *Theno Rabbanan*, *our teachers teach the second traditions* <note>original: "οἱ διδασκαλοὶ ἡμῶν δευτεροῦσιν"</note>: from this verb the Pharisees were called *Deuterotae* <note>Students or teachers of the Mishnah</note>. Jerome in his tenth *Commentary on Isaiah* says: "It seems to us that the prophetic word cries out against the judges of the tribes of Judah and Jerusalem—namely, the scribes and the *Deuterotae*." I know nothing if he does not mean the Pharisees; the following makes it clear: for God saying, "Honor Father and Mother," they on the contrary warned sons to say to parents, "Whatever gift is from me shall profit you." <note>A reference to the 'Corban' practice criticized in the New Testament, where resources were dedicated to the Temple to avoid using them to support parents</note>. 

Elias Levita in his book *Thesbite* under the word *Thana*: From *Thana*, a legal verb which in Greek is *deuterein* <note>to repeat or teach</note>, they call the wise men *Deuterotae*, or *Tannaim* <note>The rabbinic sages of the period of the Mishnah</note>. The first of these was Simeon the Just, and the last was Rabbenus Hakkadosh <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince</note>, that is, our holy teacher, so named for the sanctity of his life, otherwise called Judah by his proper name. They were followed by the *Amoraim* <note>Sages of the Talmudic era who commented on the Mishnah</note>, whose leader was Rabba; and later Rabbina and Rabbi Ashi, who composed the Talmud. See on this subject Rabbi Moses son of Maimon <note>Maimonides, the great medieval Jewish philosopher</note> in his *Massekhet Avot* <note>Ethics of the Fathers</note>, or the prologue to the *Seder Zeraim* <note>Order of Seeds</note> which is a part of the Jewish Talmud. 

Some of the Talmudists hold that this *Mishnah* was first begun and published by one Meir <note>Rabbi Meir</note>, who, from being an Idumean necromancer, was made a Jewish proselyte; and that it was afterwards illustrated and augmented with several volumes by Rabbi Monoa, according to James of Valence in his commentaries on Psalm 81. It was finished by Rabbi Judas, or Judah ben Simon, son of Gamaliel, disciple of Simeon the Just—otherwise surnamed Rabbi Hakkadosh, the "Holy Doctor"—around the Jewish year 3949 or 3952, which corresponds to the year of salvation 188. This *Mishnah* was forbidden by the Emperor Constantine <note>Though citing Justinian's Novel 146 earlier, the author here names Constantine</note> cited above in his "Authentic" <note>A collection of laws</note>, so that it might be permitted for the Hebrews, according to the handed-down law, to read the sacred scri[ptures]...

The first of these was Simeon the Just, and the last was that same Rabbi Hakkados <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, known as "The Holy" (Hakkadosh)</note>, called the "Holy Doctor" for his holiness of life, according to Moses Maimonides in his *Massecheth Avot* <note>Tractate Avot, or "Ethics of the Fathers"</note>, or his prologue to the *Seder Zeraim* <note>The "Order of Seeds," the first major division of the Talmud</note> part of the Talmud. The Sophists of the Talmud having been named אמוראים **Amorain** [Amoraim], or "speakers of maxims," so called from the sayings they pronounced, which in Hebrew are called *Amirot* [sayings], or in Latin *Scita* [Decrees]; their leaders were Rabba, and the last were Rabbena and Rabbi Ashi. These are those called Amoraim, speakers of maxims <gloss>words of oracular response</gloss>; they were succeeded by the **Tannaim**, the Magnificent ones <note>The author's chronology here reverses the historical order, as the Tannaim (repeaters/teachers) preceded the Amoraim (interpreters)</note>, although in the Holy Bible *Tan* is always a noun, as Elias Levita says in his *Tishbi* <note>A famous dictionary of Rabbinic Hebrew published in 1541</note>. Whoever wishes to see more of this should read Pietro Galatino, book one of the *Secrets of the Catholic Faith*, and Guy Lefèvre de la Boderie in his *Syro-Chaldean Dictionary* in the interpretation of the word *Tan*, and the same Elias Levita in his *Tishbi* on the word *Talmudhaca* and the word *Thana*; also G. All these books are also called "Talmuds" by the Jews, although in truth the Talmud is only the Mishnah itself, according to Jean Mercier in his book on the abbreviations of the Hebrews. Following him, one may consult Elias Levita in his *Tishbi*, and Guy Lefèvre de la Boderie in his *Syro-Chaldean Dictionary* on this word *Gemara*.

In conclusion, this Chaldean language <note>Early modern scholars often used "Chaldean" to refer to Aramaic</note> is even better deduced and described in the two Talmuds, both the Jerusalem and the Babylonian. The first was begun since the Year of Salvation 300, according to common opinion, and according to the Dionysian calculation from the Year of Salvation 372, or rather 370, by Rabbi Yochanan, assisted by some other Rabbis, and finished in the Year of Salvation 436 with its perfect and entire completion. However, this one is more corrupted than the Babylonian. The second, namely the Babylonian, was begun according to common opinion in the Year of Christ 400 by Rabbi Ashi from the digests of Rabbi Simeon the Just and Rabbi Yochanan named above, one hundred years after the start of the first; and according to the aforementioned Dionysian calculation in the Year of Christ 508 by the aforementioned Rabbi Ashi, and was entirely perfected and finished by Rabbi Mor and Maremar in the Year of Christ 605 or 606, according to Porchetus in his preface to the first book of his *Victory against the Jews*, Pietro Galatino in book 1, chapter 5 of the *Secrets of the Catholic Faith*, Johannes Reuchlin (also called Capnio) in his *Eye-Mirror* and in his defense against his calumniators, Paulus Burgensis in his addition to chapter 34 of Isaiah and in his book titled *Scrutiny of the Faith*, Alfonso the Jew (who became a Christian) in his book *The Wars of God*, Peter Niger in his books on the Messiah, the author of the book titled *Fortress of Faith*, Jean de Podio, and Master Raymond in his *Dagger [of Faith]* <note>The *Pugio Fidei*, a famous 13th-century polemical work by Raymond Martini</note>, Jerome...

There are several other works and books among the Jews of today composed in this Chaldaic <note>The author uses "Chaldaic" to refer to Aramaic</note> language, whose characters are nevertheless pure Hebrew, but the paraphrases are more vulgar and familiar in their style than the Prophets mentioned before, and do not possess as much of an air of antiquity. For since the Holy Scripture was not anciently read to the common Hebrew people in the Hebrew language, but instead through Paraphrases <note>The Targums, or Aramaic translations/interpretations of the Hebrew Bible</note> which were for the most part explanatory, the authors of these Paraphrases strove to accommodate the intelligence and capacity of the simple populace. This populace spoke a language less polished and eloquent than the Hebrew language—roughly similar (if a proper and relevant comparison can be made) to the relationship of the Italian or rather the Spanish language to Latin. This was the first alteration of the Hebrew language and the ancient Chaldaic; many others followed, affecting both the language and the writing, which are still used today by several nations spread here and there through Asia and Arabia. These people live under the rule of the Grand Turk <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note> and have retained the name of Chaldeans, or under the Sophy, King of Persia, who tolerates them in his lands. Though they are Christians, they are all tainted by the heresy of one Nestorius <note>Nestorius, 5th-century Bishop of Constantinople, whose followers were prominent in Central and East Asia</note>, formerly Bishop of Constantinople, whose error was condemned in the third Synod of Ephesus. They place two persons in our Lord, one divine and the other human, and do not acknowledge the Virgin Mary to be the Mother of God, but only the mother of Jesus Christ as a man. Furthermore, they deny the presence of his body in the Eucharist except when it is being consumed; they consecrate leavened bread like the Greeks and provide communion in both kinds <note>Offering both the bread and the wine to the laity</note>, even to small children. But the bulk of their residence is in Tartary <note>A historical region covering Central Asia and parts of Russia</note>, in a very vast expanse of land containing more than all of France and Italy combined, as confirmed by Hayton <note>Hayton of Corycus, a 13th-century Armenian monk and historian who wrote about the East</note>.

[Euphrates] Mesopotamia <note>The text likely reads "Euphrantis Mesopotamia," referring to the region of Mesopotamia near the Euphrates.</note>, <gloss>Mesopotamia</gloss> <note>original: "Μεσοποταμία"</note>, a region of Asia according to Ptolemy and others, which the old Latin interpreter of Dionysius—be it Priscillian or another—called **Medamna**. Stephanus also calls it **Adiabene** <gloss>Adiabene</gloss> <note>original: "ἀδιαβηνὴ"</note>. In the sacred scriptures, it is called **Aram** or **Charam**, according to the testimony of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. Aurogallus <note>Matthew Aurogallus (1490–1543), a scholar of Hebrew and geography.</note> noted that in the scriptures it is also called **Syria of the Plains** <note>original: "Syriam Campestrem"</note>. Moletius calls it by the more modern names of **Azamia** and **Halapia**. To Mercator <note>Gerardus Mercator, the famous cartographer.</note>, it is called **Diarbech**. To Postel: **Meredin**. To Leunclavius, it is **Black Turkey** <note>original: "Turcia nigra"</note> and **Caraoliuo**; in another place, he calls it **Diarbekir**. Are there other names in other languages? According to Belon, Mesopotamia is today included by the Turks under the single name of **Azamia** along with Assyria. A certain part of Mesopotamia, namely that which pertains to Amida <note>Modern-day Diyarbakır, Turkey.</note>, is called **Armenia** by some, according to the testimony of Procopius in the first book of the *Persian Wars*. There is also a prefecture of Mesopotamia which, according to Pliny in Book 5, chapter 24, draws its origin from the Syrians. It appears from Book 6 of Tacitus's *Annals* that the same area is inhabited by Macedonians; for the cities of **Anthemusia** and **Nicephorium**, which Tacitus ascribes to the Macedonians, Pliny attributes to this prefecture. See also the entries for **Plaga** and **Osrhoena**, as well as **Messana**, which it is also called.

**Assyria** <gloss>Assyria</gloss> <note>original: "Ἀσσυρία"</note>, a region of Asia which was later called **Adiabene**, according to the testimony of Pliny; likewise according to Theodoret in his *History of the Saints*. The barbarians, changing the 'S' into a 'T', call it **Attyria**, according to Dio. Niger writes that it is called **Adrinza** by the natives; Girava calls it **Acimia**; Pinet calls it **Mosul**; and Castaldo calls it **Arzerum**. Mercator calls it **Sarh**. Suidas writes that the Assyrians were called Persians. The Assyrians were those who were later called Syrians, as Trogus says in Book 1. Xenophon, in Book 4 of the *Cyropaedia*, places the Assyrians as neighbors to the Hyrcanians.

**Euphrantis**, a region identical to Syria according to Stephanus, named thus after the nearby Euphrates river; it is the same as **Comagena** <note>Commagene, an ancient kingdom in south-central Turkey.</note>.

->*Of the Syrians.*<-

The Hebrew authors write that the word **Aram**, which is the proper name of one of the children of Shem in Genesis 10, signifies in the Hebrew language—just as it does in French—height, elevation, or sublimity. They note that the Eastern Syrians were in ancient times called by this name, **Arameans**, as confirmed by Josephus in Book 1, chapter 6 of his *Antiquities*. In fact, the Province of Syria neighboring Babylon is named **Aram** in the Hebrew language because Aram was the founder and father of the Arameans, whom the Greeks call **Arimaeans**. Arimaeans or Syrians, according to the report of Strabo in the sixteenth book of his *Geography*; and from there, the Region or Province of Syria is distinguished by several and diverse names in Holy Scripture, as reported particularly by Aurogallus in his works, Santes Pagnino <note>A prominent 16th-century Hebraist and author of a major Hebrew dictionary.</note> in several places of his great *Hebrew Treasury*, Bonaventure Corneille Bertram in his comparison of the Hebrew and Aramean languages, and Benedictus Arias Montanus <note>A Spanish Orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> according to *Phaleg* <note>Referring to Montanus's work on biblical geography and genealogy.</note>, chapter nine. Furthermore, this Syria was anciently one of the largest provinces of Asia, as is amply confirmed by Strabo in the 16th book of his *Geography* cited above. <margin>“</margin>
> The name of Syria is sometimes used by Geographers and other authors, both Greek and Latin, to designate the largest tract of the Eastern region. Such it appears to be when starting from the **Desert of Shur** <note>original: "Sur deserto." A biblical wilderness between Egypt and Palestine.</note> (which lies between Egypt and Assyria at the limits of the Ishmaelite territory), measuring westward through Palestine, it enters toward the North the Mediterranean Sea and the Island of **Cyprus** (once torn away from the upper continent); then, crossing the sea again, it traverses all of **Cilicia** and all of **Cappadocia**, and finally flows down into the **Euxine Sea** <note>The Black Sea.</note>. From there, having crossed the Euphrates and Tigris to the East, it permeates all of **Assyria** and ends at **Persia** and the Persian Gulf itself; to the south, it skirts **Arabia**. At other times, however, it is used to signify any one of these regions included in that upper tract. The origin of the name is variously handed down. Some believe Syria was named after **Syros**, an island of the Mediterranean Sea; others from a certain **Syrus**, son of Apollo; others from **Mount Hermon**, which is called **Sirion** <note>original: "Schirion."</note> by the Phoenicians, who were certainly among the most principal and ancient Syrians. To me, however, the name of Syria seems to be derived from the same source where we traced the beginnings of that region in the description above: namely, from the **Desert of Shur**, for the very same reason that **Assyria** is named after **Assur**. Certainly, the ancient Hebrews do not use the name Syria, but in its place they use **Aram** <note>original: "ארם"</note>, from which they name many of the regions and languages of that upper tract. Therefore, to them, the Region of Aram in that tract is said to be that which stretches straight from **Antilibanus** toward the Euphrates, and having crossed it, skirts the Tigris, and [includes all of] Mesopotamia.

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF...

» traversed entirely as far as the borders of Damascus, and ending at Arabia Petraea itself, all that Royal land, I say, is called **Aram** by the Hebrews in the Holy Scriptures: yet in such a way that different locations within that region are distinguished by various additions.

» **Mesopotamia**, therefore, the greatest and oldest of them all, is sometimes even called simply **Aram** *preeminently* <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν (kat’ exochēn), meaning "par excellence" or "by way of distinction"</note>, and the inhabitants of that region are called **Arameans**. Sometimes it is called by a more proper and peculiar name, **Paddan Aram** <note>Hebrew: ארם פדן</note>, that is, the **Yoke of Syria**, as if you were to say Syria joined under a yoke—meaning placed under the "yoke" of two rivers. For this reason, it is also sometimes called **Aram Naharaim** <note>Hebrew: ארם נהרים</note>, or "Syria of the two rivers," or "between the rivers." Indeed, it is even sometimes signified by the addition of **Paddan** alone.

» The region which is first at the river Eleutherus is called **Aram Zobah** <note>Hebrew: ארם ציבא</note>, which is perhaps Sophene <note>An ancient province of the Armenian Kingdom, later a Roman province</note>. In this tract there appears to be **Lower Hamath**, which is called by the name **Hamath-Zobah** in 2 Chronicles 8. David seems to have conquered Hadadezer <note>original: Adarezer</note> there in 1 Chronicles 18, and thus achieved the limits of the land promised by God, which are commonly placed at **Lebo-Hamath** <note>Hebrew: חמות לביא</note>, that is, "the entrance to Hamath"; for the lower tract of that region is thought by some to be Iturea.

» In the vicinity of that tract, it is certain there was **Aram Beth-Rehob** <note>Hebrew: ארם בית רחוב</note>, located not far from that place on the Euphrates called **Rehoboth** <note>Hebrew: רחובות</note> in Genesis 36:37.

» The fourth Aram, which is called **Aram Maacah** <note>Hebrew: ארם מעכה</note>, was not so far from those areas, as appears from the second book of Samuel <note>original: "Schem," for the Hebrew Shemuel</note>, chapters 8 and 10.

» The fifth Aram is called **Aram Damascus** <note>Hebrew: ארם דמשק</note>, which is enclosed by the territory of Damascus, that is, between Lebanon and Arabia: or as others (who suggest the Anti-Lebanon and Lebanon ranges end in Arabia) advise, it is situated between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon: that is, **Coele-Syria** or "hollow Syria," as if bounded by the valleys of those two mountains. And these five regions are explicitly called by the name of Aram in the Holy Scriptures.

» Furthermore, there is a certain sixth Syria, which although not so explicitly called Aram by the sacred writers, there is nevertheless no doubt that the name Aram—by which secular writers honor it—passed from the former to the latter. Thus **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BC – 24 AD)</note> testifies that the inhabitants of **Commagene Syria** or **Antioch** were called **Arimi** (that is, Arameans) by ancient writers, saying: *The Armenians, Syrians, and Arabs are very closely joined, whether you consider their language, their rites of living, or the features of their bodies.* And a little later: *For they call those Arameans whom we call Syrians.*

» Certainly, the Scripture makes honorable and magnificent mention of this Antiochian Syria. It calls such territory the **Land of Hamath** <note>Hebrew: חמת</note>. It attributes to it a distinguished kingdom among others conquered by the Assyrian Monarch: indeed, even a metropolitan city, which they call **Hamath the Great** <note>Hebrew: חמת רבה</note> or the Greater. Some also add that this same city is called **Riblah** elsewhere. Therefore, this part of Syria also deserves the name Aram, not only for those names we designated above, but especially for this grace: that in later times, such a region brought the six upper regions under its yoke, and ennobled them with its privileges and even its language; which, before we demonstrate it, seems necessary to define entirely, from where it was derived...

This Syriac language was written in the time of our Lord Jesus Christ in Hebrew characters, just like the Chaldean language; but since then, it has had its own characters, unique and particular to itself. Although these characters are read from right to left like those of the Hebrews, Samaritans, Chaldeans, and Arabs, they are nonetheless not written by the Syrians from right to left as those of the Hebrews, Samaritans, Chaldeans, and Arabs are, but from top to bottom toward the stomach, as this Latin verse denotes:

They first taught it to Theseus Ambrosius <note>Teseo Ambrogio (1469–1540), an Italian priest and a pioneering scholar who published one of the first Western introductions to Syriac and Chaldean.</note> mentioned above, who afterwards shared it with posterity, as is asserted by the aforementioned Agathius <note>Agacio Guidacerio (c. 1477–1542), a scholar of Hebrew and Greek from Calabria.</note>, Guidacerus the Calabrian in his Commentaries on the Song of Songs, and the same Theseus Ambrosius in his introduction to the Chaldean, Syriac, and Aramaic languages. <note>The following section is translated from the author's Latin citation.</note> The language of the Arameans is not only called <note>original: "ארמיא"</note> Aramaic: but is also called <note>original: "לשון כשדים"</note> the language of the Chaldeans. One might rightly doubt whether the use of the Aramaic language began among the Mesopotamians or the Chaldeans; but if conjecture from the above holds weight—and from the fact that the first mention and traces of the Aramaic language appear in the history of Laban the Mesopotamian or <note>original: "ארמי"</note> Aramean—it seems to have reached the Chaldeans and Assyrians toward the East from Mesopotamia through the descendants of Nahor <note>The brother of the patriarch Abraham.</note>. Whether it was first carried Westward through the same descendants of Nahor to other tracts of Aram across the Euphrates is not equally clear for all. Certainly, in later times, with the expansion of the Chaldean Empire, their language not only pervaded all those regions of the Aramaic tract but also Judea itself, Palestine, and Phoenicia: so much so that the Aramaic language seems to have antiquated and almost obliterated Hebrew in some way—not just once, but quite often, and with its various dialects.

For the Aramaic language and its dialects made marvelous progress: for, having spread from Mesopotamia among the Chaldeans, it was so refined in Babylon among the Babylonian nobles and philosophers that it achieved the greatest possible purity there. Rightly, therefore, we make the first and principal dialect of the Aramaic language the **Babylonian**: in which Daniel, and likewise Ezra, being educated, wrote several pages of their writings. We shall call its second dialect the **Chaldaic or Syriac**, which the earlier Paraphrasts <note>Scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic to make it accessible to the common people.</note> of the Bible used, such as Onkelos in the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>, and Jonathan in both the former and latter Prophets. We establish the third dialect as the **Jerusalem** dialect, in which the later paraphrases of the Law and the book of Esther were written. This is called the "Jerusalem" dialect because the common people of the Israelites returning from the Babylonian exile mixed many Ammonite, Moabite, Persian, and Greek words into the Chaldean language. We make the fourth dialect of the Aramaic language a certain **middle** dialect between that second Chaldaic one and this third Jerusalem one: in which were written the paraphrases or <term>Targumim <gloss>Aramaic translations or interpretations of the Hebrew Bible</gloss></term> of the five volumes, as they are called: the Psalms, Proverbs, and Job. And from this difference between the aforementioned Aramaic dialects, a double Targum is established by the doctors of the Hebrews: the Babylonian and the Jerusalem. They call both by these names, not because the former was written in the Babylonian language, but because...

From this, it seems entirely likely that the Jews then used the second Aramaic dialect, in which Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Aramaic Targum of the Prophets.</note>, who lived about forty years before Christ, explained the Old Testament to the Jews of his time. Indeed, the paraphrase of the New Testament proves such antiquity of this language that I would dare to attribute it to that early Church of Antioch, and to those who were first called Christians there. And this ensures that I believe knowledge of this Aramaic dialect is more necessary for us Christians than any of the earlier ones. For besides the various uses it has in common with all those others, it provides certain specific and proper ones necessary for a Christian Theologian. No one surely doubts that there are very many places in the context of the Bible that have exercised the wits of many, either because of the various meanings of words or even the ambiguities of sentences. The Syriac dialect can explain all these so sincerely that you would require nothing else for its interpretation.

We now understand that the Aramaic regions were more neighboring to Judea. Indeed, even from this proximity, the Hebrew language was sometimes so varied that the Aramaic dialects succeeded into the original place of the Hebrew language.

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

For other discussions of this language, let the reader consult Emmanuel Tremellius in his *Chaldaic and Syriac Grammar*; Andreas Masius in his *Syriac Grammar* and in his *Syriac Treasury*; Jean Mercier in his *Tables on the Grammar of the Chaldaic Language called Syriac*; Angelo Canini in his *Institutions of the Syriac Language*; Bonaventure Corneille Bertram in his *Comparison of Hebrew and Aramaic Grammar*; Guillaume Postel in his *Alphabet of Twelve Different Languages and Characters*; and Theodore Bibliander in his book *On the Common System of All Languages and Letters*. Also, Gilbert Génébrard in book 4 of his *Chronography*; Benedictus Arias Montanus in his *Admonition on the Books of the Syriac New Testament*; Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie in his preface to that same *Syriac New Testament* printed in Antwerp; and André Thevet in book 11, chapter 18 of his *Cosmography*. Regarding books written in this Syriac language, we shall say that a certain Peter, a Priest of the Church of Edessa, composed Syriac verses on the Psalms in his time, according to the report of Gennadius in his writings. Furthermore, Ephrem the Syrian, a Deacon and Monk, delivered many beautiful sermons in that language during his life concerning various books and passages of Holy Scripture; these were later translated into the Greek language, from which were made the Latin and French versions of this figure’s work that we currently have in our hands. What is more, I remember having seen some time ago, in the possession of a Jew highly learned in ancient languages, books composed in this same Syriac language and in its own characters, dealing with the journey and travels of Saint Peter to the city of Rome. In short, curious readers should be advised that today one finds books written and composed in this language printed in the city of Vienna in Austria. The late Guillaume Postel, in the place cited above, writes that he saw in the hands of a physician to the Grand Turk in Constantinople <note>The capital of the Ottoman Empire, modern-day Istanbul.</note> named Moses Almuli, a book of Kabbalah <note>A tradition of Jewish mysticism.</note> written in this language. Some time ago, a certain Syrian person named George Avira the Maronite, a Bishop in his own country, composed a grammar in this language, as noted by Juan Bautista Villalpando in volume 3 of his *Apparatus of the City and Temple of Jerusalem*.

And because we mentioned above that a certain Tremellius <note>Emmanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a Jewish convert to Christianity who became a leading Reformed (Calvinist) scholar.</note>—a Calvinist Jew and Sacramentarian <note>A term used by Catholics for those who denied the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist.</note>—erased from the aforementioned Syriac New Testament in the Geneva edition the titles of the Epistles and Gospels for the Day, or the subject matter which Christians must celebrate (such as the Cross, the fasts of the saints, holy orders, marriages, Lent, the deceased, and other ceremonies of the Church), we shall report what Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie left in writing in one of his letters regarding the Table of Titles for the entire Syriac New Testament printed by Plantin in Antwerp:

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [LANGUAGES]

I am adding this great man's own words here to shed more light on understanding this Index and to provide greater evidence to everyone regarding the agreement between the Eastern and Western Churches; the testimony of such a significant figure carries great weight. He says:

"I believed it would be a worthwhile task at present to separate the chapter headings interspersed throughout the text of these books and to arrange them according to the annual feast days. The Syrians observe these days according to an ancient tradition derived from the teachings of the Apostles. I have also placed a Latin translation alongside them at the end of this work <note>original: "Latinoſque è regione factos, huius operis fini applicarē"</note>. My goal is that those who dislike the rituals of the Latin [Western] Church might easily see from this that among the Syrians—who were the very first of all Christians—nearly the same rituals and customs have existed to this day. At the very least, these traditions are not foreign to the ones over which some have recently broken away from the common agreement of the Church."

"To make this clearer, I would like to briefly discuss a few matters that came to mind as I hurried toward the end of this work, specifically regarding these indices of days and events. Other matters are explained at length in the book titled *The Treasury* <note>original: "Ærarium"</note>, which is based on the authority of Ephrem, Jacob, Balai, Coco, and other Syrians excellent in holiness of life and doctrine. The Syrians set the start of the <term>Ritual Year</term> <note>The liturgical calendar</note> around the first of November, so that eight Sundays precede the birth of Christ the Lord."

1.  On the first Sunday, they celebrate the **Dedication of the Temple**.
2.  On the second, the <term>Encaenia</term> <note>A festival of dedication or renewal</note>.
3.  On the third, the **Annunciation to Zechariah the Priest** regarding the birth of his son, John the Baptist.
4.  On the fourth, the **Annunciation to the Virgin Mary** regarding the Son of God who would enter this life through her.
5.  On the fifth, the **Journey of the Virgin Mother to Elizabeth** <note>The Visitation</note>. Pope Urban VI introduced this celebration into the Latin Church while the Apostolic See was suffering most severely from the Great Schism, which was finally ended by the authority of the Council of Constance.
6.  On the sixth, the **Birth of John the Baptist**.
7.  On the seventh, the **Oracle given to Joseph** regarding his pregnant wife, whom he was told not to put away despite his surprise.
8.  The eighth Sunday they call the **Sunday Before the Nativity**.

Then follows the 25th of December, the **Birth of Jesus Christ**. The next day is the feast of the **Virgin in Childbirth**, and on the third day after that, the celebration of the **Holy Innocents**. This is followed by the Sunday closest to the Nativity, and then the feast of the **Circumcision of Christ** (unless it falls on that same Sunday).

On the sixth day following, **Epiphany** succeeds, which the Syrians also call the "Feast of Lights." They celebrate it with a frequent use of lamps. On that night, water is consecrated with a solemn prayer; this water is traditionally kept in the sacristies for the entire year. On the following day, they celebrate the **Beheading of John the Baptist**. From Epiphany, they count several Sundays, which are followed by three days of <term>Rogations</term> <note>Days of prayer and fasting</note> which they call the **Nineveh Fast**.

Next follows the day of **Christ’s Presentation in the Temple**, and in their proper order, two Sundays for the dead. The first is dedicated to priests, and the second to all other deceased Christians; on these days, they are accustomed to visit the graves with established ceremonies. The six Sundays that follow are reckoned under the name of the **Fast** [Lent]. The 40th day is marked by the special devotion of the Syrians; the 20th day is also notable as the midpoint of the forty-day fast. This concludes on the Friday after the sixth Sunday. Then follows the Saturday of **Lazarus raised from the dead**, and soon after, **Hosanna Sunday**, which we call **Palm Sunday**.

The continuous week following is named after the **Passion and Rest of Christ**. In this week, Thursday is called "The Day of Secrets" because of the mysteries of the holy <term>Synaxis</term> <note>The gathering for the Eucharist</note>. On this day, the <term>Chrism</term> <note>Consecrated oil used in sacraments</note> is blessed by the bishops because the priesthood was instituted on that day, and the ceremony of the washing of the feet is performed. The Saturday of that week is called the **Saturday of the Annunciation** because...

<meta>This page continues the scholar’s argument that Syrian Christian traditions are deeply aligned with the Roman Catholic Church. ->## LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE<-

...because Christ announced to the patriarchs dwelling in the underworld <note>original: "patrib. apud inferos agentibus"</note> that, through his final suffering, their salvation had now been won. The day of the Lord’s Resurrection is called the "Great Day" by the Syrians, and the eighth day after it—the ninth day including the first, as it falls between two weeks—is called the "Day of the Candidates" <note>original: "Cādidatorū"</note>. This is for no other reason than why the Latin Church calls the Sabbath and this very Lord’s Day *in Albis* <note>original: "in Albis," meaning "in white [garments]"</note>. In the past, those about to be bound by the oath of the Christian military <note>The author uses "military" as a metaphor for the Christian life</note> were washed in the sacred font only during these days and only by Bishops. They testified to their profession of faith by wearing white linen tunics with hoods. On this Lord’s Day, they would present themselves to the Bishop and set aside their white clothes. Furthermore, if they were baptized at Rome by the Supreme Pontiffs, they used to receive sacred amulets as symbols of their baptism—wax seals impressed with the figure of the "Lamb of God" carrying a banner <note>original: "vexilliferi Agni figura"</note>, which were consecrated by being dipped in a mixture of holy water and Chrism. It was also accepted that both the ministers of Baptism and those being baptized should be "candidates" (clad in white); thus, the Bishops, to whom the duty of baptizing was then solely granted, would never go out in public without a white linen tunic, lest they be unable to fulfill their office if an urgent need arose. From this, the use of such a tunic has been retained to this day by the Popes and other high prelates (unless the lesser prelates were called to that rank from a monastic life). In succeeding centuries, this was even permitted to the "Capped Notaries" <note>original: "Pileatis Notariis"</note> once appointed to write the histories of the Martyrs in the city of Rome, serving as a badge of their dignity.

Furthermore, the images of that sacred wax, which they call *Agnos Dei* <note>Lambs of God</note>, still exist in the mosaic work of the apse of the Vatican Basilica, hanging over the pontifical altar, from the structures built by Constantine. These were once shown to me by Pope Marcellus II <note>Marcellus II served as Pope for only 22 days in 1555; the author notes he was still a private citizen at the time he showed him this</note>, a most holy man, as evidence of a ceremony used even before the reign of Constantine the Great.

But enough regarding this "Week of the Candidates." Following this Lord’s Day, on what I believe is the Friday, are the "Feasts of Gold." On these days, the memory of the Apostle Peter healing the lame man at the "Beautiful Gate" is celebrated with solemn rest and worship. They were designated by the name of "Gold" because of Peter’s response, in which he denied having any gold or silver <note>A reference to Acts 3:6: "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee."</note>. The day of the Ascension follows forty days after the Resurrection, and the Lord’s Day of Pentecost completes its own cycle, which is the fiftieth day. On this day, the Syrians pray while resting on their knees, with the upper part of their bodies held erect. They call this ritual the "Positioning of the Knees," a posture they use only on that day. On other days of the year, when showing the form of adorants or suppliants, they either exhibit a downward movement of the body or kiss the earth, from which they rise without delay. In this, they differ from the Muslims, who are accustomed to using that <term>Engonasi</term> <note>original: "Engonaſi," from the Greek for "on the knees"</note>.

They also religiously venerate the Holy Cross; indeed, several Sundays have been named after the Day of the Cross. They call that unbloody sacrifice <term>Qurbana</term> <note>original Syriac: ܩܘܪܒܢܐ; meaning "Oblation" or "Eucharist"</note>, and the things performed before it <term>Qurba</term> <note>original Syriac: ܩܘܪܒܐ</note>, which means the "approach" or "offering." Therefore, those among the Catholics who attempt to remove the mention of gifts, offerings, and sacrifices from the sacred rites seem to promise a false security in their opinions. They are convinced that whatever the Pontiffs of the Latin Church and the Councils of the Fathers decreed in any age can now be revoked at their own whim. Yet, regarding the error of such instability, not only the greatest part of Europe but also the Asian and African Churches stand in judgment. They judge most severely because they maintain prayers distributed at fixed hours—evening, night, morning, and others. They retain the memory of the dead in their sacred rites. They have Priests and Bishops, temples and altars. Finally, on the night of the Epiphany, they consecrate water to be distributed to the people’s homes for the entire year. They observe the laws of fixed fasts with remarkable abstinence, and they tonsure those who are to be devoted to the monastic life. ### *Of the Wisdom of the Egyptians.*

The ancient Hebrews held the wisdom of the Egyptians in very high regard and esteem in their writings, which they called in their Hebrew language <term>the wisdom of Egypt</term> <note>original Hebrew: חכמת מצריים, "Chochemath Mizriim"</note>. The Greeks, in their Greek language, called it <note>original: Σοφίαν Αἰγυπτίων, "Sophian Aigyption"</note>, and the Latins in their language, <note>original: Sapientiam Ægyptiorum</note>. **St. Stephen**, the first Martyr, in the *Acts of the Apostles* chapter 7, attributed this to the Prophet **Moses** as a great praise, saying: "Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was powerful in deeds and words." This wisdom was in ancient times divided into four parts according to the sayings of **Diodorus Siculus**, **Diogenes Laertius**, **Iamblichus**, **Philo the Jew**, and **Eusebius of Caesarea**: namely into natural, divine, and moral mathematics. As for mathematics, it was distinct and separated into Geometry, Astronomy, Arithmetic, and Music. These most ancient Egyptians practiced it, for they engaged in Geometry out of necessity; since the limits and borders of their fields and possessions were blurred by the flooding of the river **Nile**, once it had retreated into its ordinary channel, it was necessary for each owner of these fields and possessions to enter into the enjoyment of them;

To these two parts, they added **Arithmetic**, that is to say, the science of numbers, as a service to those other parts, and without the ministry of which those parts would seem to be entirely lacking and imperfect. They devoted themselves to **Music** as much as was necessary for them to sing the praises of the gods, kings, and **Heroes**. The second part of this Egyptian Wisdom—which deals with the principles, causes, elements, and works of natural things, called **Physics**—does not stray far from **Peripatetic Philosophy** <note>The philosophy of Aristotle and his followers, who famously walked while teaching.</note>, in that it posits matter as the principle of all things, and that from it the four elements proceed, from which all things and all animals originate; that the heavens are round, like a sphere and ball; that all the stars have a fiery heat through tempered mixtures, from which all things are born upon the earth; that the planets have their own souls; and that rains are made and caused by the changes of the air. The third part of this said wisdom, containing divine things and called **Theology**, contains other precepts: namely, that the world had a beginning and is mortal by its own nature; that humans, at the beginning of all things in this Universe, were first produced in Egypt, partly because of the temperate nature of the sky and partly because of the **Nile**, which makes Egypt very fertile in all goods by its overflowing; that the human soul is perpetual, passing by <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>The transmigration of the soul from one body into another after death.</note> from body to body; that God is the sole and unique Father and Prince of the other gods; that the Sun and the Moon are gods, one called **Osiris** and the other **Isis**; that it was necessary to make images and statues of various gods in the temples in different forms and figures, because the true images and forms of these gods were unknown; that a great part of these gods had first been mortal men, then, for their virtues, merits, and the excellent benefits that flowed from them among mortals, had acquired a divinity and had been divinely honored by the living. The Egyptians were accustomed to carry representations of animals into war on the tops of their helmets and shields against their enemies, by the command of their kings and leaders; and after the victory obtained by them against their said enemies, they placed these animals in the rank and number of the gods, as if they had been the sole cause of their victory. Regarding their **Theologians**, they had a certain form of **mystic and secret writing**, by which they hid the most excellent mysteries of their Theology and divine service, which they did not want to be divulged to the common people. ...for writing ordinary letters, into <gloss>priestly writing</gloss> <note>original: "ἱερογραμματικὴν" (hierogrammatikēn)</note>, that is, the sacerdotal style used by those who write on sacred matters; and into <gloss>hieroglyphics</gloss> <note>original: "ἱερογλυφικήν" (hieroglyphikēn)</note>, which is to say, the sacred script that is carved. Of this latter type, there are two species: one is <gloss>literal</gloss> <note>original: "κυριολογικὴ" (kyriologikē)</note>, meaning properly-speaking, which is written with the letters themselves and alphabetic elements in mystical and figurative words; the other is true <gloss>symbolic writing</gloss> <note>original: "συμβολική" (symbolikē)</note>, which signifies through signs. This symbolic type is threefold: namely, imitative, metaphorical (or figurative), and enigmatic. The "imitative" type is that which designates things through characters very similar to the things themselves. The "metaphorical" or "figurative" type is that which transfers various forms and shapes of different things—especially animals—to signify the dignities, fortunes, characters, virtues, vices, affections, and actions of gods or men. The "enigmatic" type is that which results from the combination and mutual interplay of these images. This is why the poet Lucretius said:

> *Not yet did Memphis know how to weave the river-reeds into books;* <note>The "river-reeds" refer to papyrus, which Memphis in Egypt was famous for producing.</note>

Pherecydes of Syros <note>A 6th-century BCE Greek thinker, often cited as one of the first to write in prose.</note> asserts in his histories that the Scythians <note>A nomadic people from the Eurasian steppes known for their prowess in warfare.</note> once used this kind of symbolic writing when he says that Idanthyrsus, King of the Scythians, sent a certain symbol in place of written letters to Darius, King of the Persians (who had declared war on him if he and his people did not submit to his rule). This symbol consisted of a rat, a frog, a bird, a dart, and a plow <note>original: "aireau," a primitive type of plow or ard.</note>. The Scythian King intended the Persian to understand—not as Orontopagas, a tribune of the Persian guards, claimed, who guessed that Idanthyrsus meant he and his people were submitting to the Persian Empire, assuming that by the rat they gave their dwellings, by the frog their waters, by the bird their air, by the dart their arms, and by the plow their fields and possessions—but rather as Xiphodres said to the contrary: that these Scythians meant that unless the Persians flew away quickly like birds, and hid themselves inside the earth like rats, or entered the waters like frogs, they could not avoid their darts and weapons; and finally, being killed and slain, they would fatten the fields and possessions of the Scythians with their bodies and carcasses; or in any event, being their captives and reduced under their yoke and servitude, they would labor in those same fields and possessions.

The fourth and final part of the aforementioned Egyptian wisdom belonged to morals and the political way of life. Diogenes Laertius attributes their laws and precepts to Mercury, whom the Greeks call <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Meaning "Thrice Great." This figure, Hermes Trismegistus, was a legendary fusion of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth.</note>, meaning "thrice great," because he was a very great philosopher, a very great priest, and a very great king. Under his name, we have two dialogues titled the *Poimandres* and the *Asclepius*, in which he predicted and announced several things to come regarding God, the Trinity, the advent of Jesus Christ, and the Last Judgment; thus he should not only be esteemed as a philosopher, but rather as a prophet of future things. Iamblichus, in his book on the mysteries of the Egyptians, holds that this Mercury was not only the author and prince of philosophy, but also of all Egyptian wisdom. > Moses, therefore, received numbers, and Geometry, and all Music—whether Rhythmic, Harmonic, or Metric, and whether contemplative or produced by voices and instruments—in various modes from Egyptian teachers; and especially the occult philosophy, described in letters, as they call them, Hieroglyphic, that is, by the signs of animals, which they themselves worship as divinities. From neighboring regions, the summoned Chaldeans taught the science of the stars, which he also learned from the Egyptians. <note>original: "Moses itaque numeros, & Geometriā, vniuersámque Musicá... accepit ab Ægyptiis doctoribus, maximè verò occultam philosophiá, descriptá literis, vt vocant, Hieroglyphicis... Ex propinquis autem regionibus euocati Chaldęi docuerunt, syderalē scientiam..."</note>

Justin, Philosopher and Martyr, contradicting slightly the aforementioned Philo, says in his book of questions posed by the Gentiles, that Moses, having omitted the study of all Mathematics, which were then common and base in Egypt, turned his mind only to the Hieroglyphic disciplines, which alone were then in honor and value among the Egyptians, and were taught secretly only to the most distinguished and approved men in hidden places. Though Moses learned these, he never did or said anything according to them that was contrary to the worship of the one true God. As for what Saint Stephen the Protomartyr <note>The first Christian martyr, whose speech in the Book of Acts mentions Moses' education.</note> [says] immediately after those words, *Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Chaldeans*, and adds, *and he was powerful in words and deeds*, this should not be understood as if we believe Moses performed miracles by the power of Egyptian wisdom, but that he performed wondrous works solely by the power of the true God. Clement, in the 5th [book] of the *Stromata*, writes that Moses, following this custom of Hieroglyphic teaching, secretly handed down many precepts of moral life under the tropes and mystical symbols of animals, intended only for the lovers of the divine law, such as that one must eat neither Pig, nor Eagle, nor Hawk, nor Raven (Leviticus 11). For the Pig, being an animal devoted to pleasure and unclean, is a symbol of gluttony and lust, signifying a craving for food, and deceitful intemperance in sexual matters, and a defiled life lying in the mire of vices, which is fattened for slaughter and destruction. By the prohibition of the Eagle, Hawk, and Raven, he shows that those who neither know how nor wish to provide for their own food through labor and virtue should not be invited; instead, they live by plunder and iniquity. For the Eagle signifies plunder, the Hawk injustice, and the Raven greed.

See what is written of this Egyptian Wisdom by Cælius Rhodiginus in book 16, ch. 4 [and] book 29, ch. 25 of his *Various Lessons*; Augustinus Egubinus in book 7, ch. 8 of *Perennial Philosophy*; M. Neander in his book on the testimony of the ancient Hebrew Rabbis, Talmudists, and Cabalists; Sixtus of Siena in the first book of the *Sacred Library*; Horapollo <note>author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs that was highly influential in the Renaissance.</note>, Heinrich Glarean, Pierius Valerianus, and Goropius Becanus in their works on Hieroglyphics.

From what we have deduced above, we shall learn that in ancient times, the Egyptians—before the use of letters or character sets—were accustomed to declare and make their concepts understood through the representation or portraiture of certain forms and figures of animals, trees, plants, herbs, and by some of their specific members or parts. ...Egyptians were a very ancient people, and very renowned in all kinds of arts and sciences, and so powerful besides, that it is read that in the past there were as many as twenty thousand inhabited cities, whereas today there are barely five or six to be found, along with ten or twelve small towns; and furthermore they were so warlike that they extended their conquests and gave the law to the greater part of the earth. For this reason, one should in no way doubt that they also had a separate language and a script—not only the signs and marks called Hieroglyphics, serving them as a secret cipher reserved for Kings and Priests, but common letters as well, from which a text could be formed expressing in detail, letter by letter, all sorts of ideas, just like Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, as is sufficiently inferred by the following passage from Apuleius:

The ancient Egyptians had books marked with unrecognizable letters, partly suggesting the condensed words of spoken language through the figures of animals, and partly with knotted marks, twisted like a wheel and packed together like vine-tendrils, so that the reading was protected from the curiosity of outsiders. <note>Original Latin: *Veteres Ægyptij libros habuere ignorabilibus literis prænotatos, partim figuris animalium concepti ſermonis compendioſa verba ſuggerentes: partim nodoſis, & in modum rotæ tortuoſis, capreolatimque condenſis apicibus à curioſitate perſonarum lectione munita.* This comes from Apuleius's *Metamorphoses*, describing the sacred scrolls used in the mysteries of Isis.</note> Tacitus, in the eleventh book of his *Annals*, says on this subject that the Egyptians were the first who, through figures of animals, represented their thoughts and conceptions—very ancient marks of which are still seen in memory of these people, engraved in marble—claiming themselves to be the inventors of written characters. And in the second book, he says: From there, Germanicus <note>A popular Roman general and the nephew of Emperor Tiberius.</note> went to visit the remains of ancient Thebes, where there were very remarkable things remaining, and in large masses of stone, carved Egyptian letters containing their great power and might in past ages. Upon being commanded, one of their oldest priests interpreted what they meant in their language, recounting that formerly in this city there would usually have been seven hundred thousand fighting men, with whom King Ramses <note>The author refers to Ramses II, also known as Ramses the Great.</note> had conquered Libya and Ethiopia, the Medes and the Persians; he also conquered the province of Bactria and Scythia, along with all the lands possessed by the Syrians, Armenians, and their close neighbors the Cappadocians, having extended his Empire along the coast from the sea of Bithynia to that of Lycia. Furthermore, one could read of the tributes imposed on these nations: the weight of gold and silver they were to provide each year, the number of arms and horses, the ivory, the spices and perfumes to offer in the temples, the quantity of grain and other provisions, utensils and munitions that each country would contribute—all of this no less magnificent than what the Parthians today levy by force upon their subjects, or the Roman domination over the peoples they conquered. Egyptians were a very ancient people, highly renowned in all kinds of arts and sciences, and so powerful, moreover, that it is read that there were once as many as twenty thousand inhabited cities, whereas today barely five or six are found, along with ten or twelve small towns. Furthermore, they were so warlike that they extended their conquests and gave the law to the greater part of the earth. Because of this, one should not doubt that they also had a language of their own and a system of writing—not only the signs and marks called Hieroglyphs, which served as a secret code reserved for Kings and Priests, but also common letters. From these, a written context could be formed, expressing every kind of concept letter by letter in detail, just like Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, as is sufficiently inferred by the following passage from Apuleius:

> The ancient Egyptians possessed books marked with mysterious letters; partly using the figures of animals to suggest abbreviated words of the language they had conceived; partly with knotted marks, twisted in the manner of a wheel, and packed together like vine-tendrils, so that their reading was protected from the curiosity of the uninitiated. <note>Original Latin: "Veteres Ægyptij libros habuere ignorabilibus literis prænotatos, partim figuris animalium concepti sermonis compendiosa verba suggerentes: partim nodosis, & in modum rotæ tortuosis, capreolatimque condensis apicibus à curiositate personarum lectione munita." This quote is from Apuleius's *Metamorphoses* (The Golden Ass), describing the initiation into the mysteries of Isis.</note>

Tacitus, in the eleventh book of his *Annals*, says in this regard that the Egyptians were the first who, through figures of animals, represented their thoughts and concepts—of which very ancient marks of remembrance to the memory of persons are still seen, engraved in marble—they maintaining themselves to have been the inventors of writing characters. And in the second book, he says: From there, Germanicus <note>A popular Roman general and the nephew of Emperor Tiberius, who visited Egypt in 19 AD.</note> went to visit the remains of ancient Thebes, where there were very remarkable things remaining; and on great masses of stone were carved Egyptian letters, which contained their great power and might in ages past. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

the ancient Egyptians did not use letters and distinct writing as we do, but only certain signs that represented a whole meaning, according to the two examples he <note>Likely referring to a previously mentioned author like Horapollo</note> provides: the **Vulture**, which signified nature, because among this kind of bird no males are found, but only females, who at a certain season of the year are impregnated by the wind; and the **Honeybee** denoted the King, together with the two conditions he ought to possess: one of kindness and sweetness, conforming to the honey, and the other of severity and vigor, represented by the sting.

T. Bibliander <note>Theodor Bibliander (1506–1564), a Swiss orientalist and linguist</note> in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*: <note>original Latin: "Porrò quod Volaterranus negat Hieroglyphica nulli adhuc cõperta..."</note> Furthermore, regarding what Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), also known as Volaterranus, a humanist scholar</note> denies—claiming that Hieroglyphics have not yet been understood by anyone—this, in my judgment, conflicts with published books in which authors of no small repute describe what the sacred letters of the Egyptians were like and what their use was. Furthermore, Diodorus in Book 4 of his *Fabulous Deeds* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian; the reference likely refers to the *Bibliotheca historica*</note> testifies that the Egyptians received the forms of their letters from the Ethiopians—namely those that were commonly used. Since that language has been completely destroyed in Egypt, first by the Greeks, then by the Romans, and later by the Saracens and Arabs, and since few words remain in literary monuments, it cannot be easily judged, nor can anything be pronounced with certainty concerning the language of the Egyptians. Nevertheless, from those things which have come to our knowledge—from the origin of the people of *Mizraim* <note>The Hebrew name for Egypt, often used in a biblical-genealogical context</note>, which was common with the Ethiopians and the descendants of Nimrod in Babylon, and from the proximity of the Edomites and Israelites and the commerce among these peoples—it can be gathered that it was no less related to the **Hebrew** dialect than the Ethiopian, Chaldean, or Phoenician languages. Even if it were as remote as Latin or Scythian, it could still be compared in each of its parts with Hebrew, and therefore fit the same standard of art and science.

Of these Hieroglyphics, one sees more than enough remains even now on large and small obelisks, bases, sphinxes, and other marbles brought from Egypt to Rome, of which **Pliny** makes ample mention in the 36th book, chapter 9, of his *Natural History*; and likewise **Ammianus Marcellinus**, in the previously cited passage, inserted in Greek letters and language the explanation of the largest one, under the name of the aforementioned **Rameses**. With regard to the common speech or language and the writing, we have nothing certain. Consequently, these two Alphabets attributed to these Egyptians have made the most curious scholars of antiquity uncertain and suspicious; moreover, the first seems to hold some trace of that <term>Capreolatin</term> <note>Likely referring to a convoluted or "goat-like" script style mentioned by Renaissance occultists</note> of **Apuleius**, and the names of the letters conform to it, such as you see hereafter, twenty-four in number, just as there are in the Greek Alphabet. Nevertheless, **Plutarch** in his treatise *On Osiris* puts them at 25, according to the square multiplication of five <note>5 x 5 = 25</note>, which is the number of years he <note>Apis, the sacred bull</note> lived. Here are the two Egyptian Alphabets represented in figures by **Theseus Ambrosius** <note>An Italian linguist and author of the first comprehensive work on non-Latin scripts, *Introductio in Chaldaicam linguam* (1539)</note> in his appendix on the Chaldean, Syriac, and Armenian languages.

If the two Alphabets above are somewhat suspicious and doubtful, those that follow should be no less so: for it has been well known for a hundred years now what the true Characters of the **Abyssinian Ethiopians** are (whom some call **Indians** and **Nubians** <note>In the 16th century, the term "India" was often used broadly to include Ethiopia, which was frequently referred to as "Middle India."</note>), as well as their manner of writing, which goes from left to right like our own. However, this first Alphabet assigned to the said Indians in the **Grimani Library** <note>The famous library of Cardinal Domenico Grimani (1461–1523), a major center for humanist research in Venice.</note> proceeds in reverse from right to left, just as Hebrew, Syriac, and Arabic do. It is indeed true that the Ethiopian, Abyssinian, Indian, or Nubian language is almost entirely derived from those languages; nevertheless, it cannot be their script, nor that of **China** or **Cathay** <note>An archaic name for northern China, popularized by Marco Polo.</note>, who write from top to bottom, as we shall discuss hereafter. Nonetheless, the names of the letters of this Alphabet conform to those of the other which follows, specifically assigned to the said Abyssinian Ethiopians by the Author of the *Voyages Overseas* <note>Likely referring to Bernhard von Breydenbach's "Peregrinatio in Terram Sanctam" (1486), which included some of the first printed alphabets of non-European languages.</note>, where he asserts he obtained it from their Embassy when they came to offer obedience to the Holy Apostolic See under **Sixtus IV** around the year 1482.
