### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [ALPHABETS]

These Ethiopians, Abyssinians, Indians, or Nubians have for a long time possessed an alphabet of their own, containing twenty-six characters. The last four of these are letters joined into syllables as a form of abbreviation, in which this writing greatly abounds, as we shall discuss in the following chapter. This alphabet proceeds not in the manner of the Hebrews, Samaritans, Syrians, and Arabs—from right to left—even though they have taken the greater part of their language and writing from them and call themselves <term>Chaldeans</term><note>In this period, "Chaldean" was often used broadly to refer to various Semitic languages, including Ge'ez, the liturgical language of Ethiopia.</note>. Instead, they write like the Greeks and Latins, from the left hand toward the right, following the specific course of the planets, of which the Sun is the principal, contrary to the <term>primum mobile</term><note>original: "premier mobile"; in the Ptolemaic system, this was the outermost sphere of the heavens which moved from east to west, whereas planets were thought to have their own motions from west to east.</note>. For because of their <term>adustion</term><note>A Renaissance medical/geographical term referring to the "scorching" effects of the sun on the body and temperament.</note>, which is evidenced by their complexion, which is so black, and because of their close proximity to that luminaire which roasts them incessantly, they consider themselves as its children here below.

Master Giambattista Palatino, toward the end of his book on the manner of teaching how to write all sorts of ancient and modern letters, represents an Egyptian alphabet which is entirely diverse and dissimilar from the preceding ones; curious readers may see it there, as it is not necessary to include it in this place at present. Master Marco Polo the Venetian, in the accounts of his travels, relates that in the province of <term>Arcandan</term><note>Likely "Zardandan" or "Carajan" (modern Yunnan), described by Marco Polo.</note>, subject to the Great Khan, there are no letters or characters, but the inhabitants make their contracts and obligations using small tablets which they divide in half. They later come together to compare them, matching their signs and marks against one another, and thus recognize the terms of their aforementioned contracts and obligations. Olaus Magnus, in Book 1, Chapter 36, and in his book on the Northern Nations, maintains that the Goths used these hieroglyphic letters.

Francisco López de Gómara, a Spaniard, in Book 2, Chapter 75 of his *General History of the Indies*, writes that the inhabitants of New Spain, at the time they were discovered, used certain letters made in the form of specific figures. With these, they marked, recorded, and understood all things. By means of these letters, they preserved the memory and remembrance of ancient and past events, and these letters resembled the hieroglyphic letters of the Egyptians; although they did not contain such a profound meaning, nor did the people pronounce these letters as we do ours.

As for the most copious, elegant, pure, and excellent language of this New Spain, it is the Mexican language called <term>Nahuatl</term><note>original: "Ynahuatl"</note> in that country. The lovers, thieves, and robbers of that region use certain whistles and signs in their behavior, by which they understand each other as easily as if they were pronouncing and speaking a true, pure, and entire language. In this regard, the narratives of the West Indies report that at <term>Tenochtitlan</term><note>original: "Thamiftitan", referring to the Aztec capital (Mexico City).</note>, during the conquest made by Hernán Cortés for the Emperor Charles V, certain memoirs or records were found. These contained, through figures of animals, trees, plants, herbs, birds, and fish, and by their limbs and parts, the deeds and feats of the kings of that region. 

And some ten or twelve years later, on another side in Peru, a great quantity of cotton cords were found in the cabinet of King <term>Atahualpa</term><note>original: "Atabalipa", the last Inca Emperor.</note>, which the Indians in their language called <term>Quipucamayoc</term><note>original: "Quippos Camaios"; the author conflates the records (Quipus) with the officials who kept them (Quipucamayoc).</note>. These were knotted in the manner of <term>paternoster beads</term><note>Rosary beads used for prayer.</note>, in various colors according to the things the Indians wished to represent; the number of these knotted cords marked and denoted...

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

the years that their <term>Incas</term><note>original: "Iugnes"; likely a phonetic misspelling of "Yngas" or Incas, the rulers of the Andean empire.</note> or <term>Caciques</term><note>A term used by early explorers to describe indigenous chiefs or leaders in the Americas.</note> had reigned: this is confirmed by Peter Martyr of Milan, the historian of the discovery of the new lands made by the Castilians, who recounts that the inhabitants of the province of <term>Colhuacan</term><note>original: "Collacuane"; likely referring to the region of the Colhua people in central Mexico.</note> write upon very thin and delicate bark of trees whatever they wish and desire, using characters of letters resembling hooks, loops, files, stars, and other such similar forms. With these they arrange lines in our own fashion and style of writing, representing between these forms the figures of animals, birds, plants, herbs, and other things of this Universe—likewise of the men who came before them, and principally of their Kings, Caciques, and Lords, reciting their acts and deeds. They also write their laws, sacrifices, ceremonies, and observations both of the stars and of agriculture, in books of pleasant and delightful craftsmanship; this is confirmed by Paolo Giovio in book 34 of his histories. We have, moreover, learned recently—notably from this embassy from Japan, which in the year 1585 in the month of March came from as far as five or six thousand leagues to offer obedience to the <term>Holy Apostolic See</term><note>The central government of the Catholic Church in Rome.</note> of Rome—that in the East Indies, and even two thousand leagues beyond, in China and <term>Cathay</term><note>An archaic name for Northern China, popularized by Marco Polo.</note> (from whence the art of Printing first proceeded), there are two kinds of writing, just as Apuleius, cited above, recounts of Egypt: one of hieroglyphic letters, and the other of common letters, which by their combinations can form all the words one wishes to express. Both proceed not across, as with the Hebrews in one way and ourselves in another, but from top to bottom. The first, which they call the writing of China, is generally common to all the regions of the Indies, both of the Islands and the mainland: but it is employed only for spiritual things and non-vulgar doctrines by the <term>Bonzes</term><note>A term used by early European travelers to describe Buddhist monks.</note>, as they call them. These are the younger sons of Kings, Princes, and great Lords, and other principal personages who are placed in monasteries with great revenues and great respect and authority, to prevent the dismemberment of the state and internal factions. To these Bonzes belongs the administration and conduct of everything depending on the spirituality and religion of their country, according to their ancient idolatrous traditions, which are of infinite sorts, and they themselves are almost infinite in number—such as the six or seven thousand of their monasteries formerly on a single mountain near the city of <term>Meaco</term><note>The historic capital of Japan, now known as Kyoto.</note>. and though the majority are vicious and ignorant people, there are nevertheless always found some of greater understanding and knowledge than the others. This is not through a doctrine acquired by them in schools, nor by the reading of books (for despite the fact that neither paper nor Printing are unusual to them, they do not have such convenience as we do), but rather by an inveterate routine and such assiduous meditations that there are those who have given themselves to it for thirty or forty years consecutively, without communication with any person who could disturb their conceptions. This is much like Aristomachus of Soli, who remained fifty-eight years amusing himself with nothing else but observing the nature of honeybees, so as to write of them more surely and truly. By which means these personages forge in their brains strange and very bizarre fantasies, being held back in this by no bridle of Religion,

### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF...

» **Carthage**, in Latin, which is *Karchedon*<note>original Greek: καρχηδὼν</note> in Greek, and which **Ptolemy**<note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), a Greco-Egyptian writer, mathematician, and geographer.</note> surnames "the Great," was once the capital of Africa and the rival of the Roman Empire; it later became a Roman colony. Nothing of it remains today except ruins. **Stephanus**<note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary.</note> writes that it was also named *Oenussa*<note>original Greek: οἴνυσσαν, likely meaning "rich in wine."</note> and *Caenepolis*<note>original Greek: καινήπολις, meaning "New City."</note>; **Eustathius** says it was called *Caccabe*<note>original Greek: κακκάβη, often associated with a horse's head.</note> and *Cadmeia*<note>original Greek: καδμεία</note>. By **Suidas** it is called *Africa*<note>original Greek: ἀφρική</note> and **Byrsa**<note>A reference to the legend of Queen Dido, who purchased as much land as could be covered by an oxhide (byrsa).</note>. **Lado. Marmolius** reports that even today it is called *Berfabk* by some Africans. The mountain that was once surrounded by this city, on which the citadel of **Byrsa** stood, is today called *Rocca de Mastinaces* by Christians and *Almenara* by Africans. Its port is now called *Marzia* according to the same witness. **Spartianus** recorded that the Emperor **Hadrian** named it *Hadrianopolis*. The Emperor **Commodus** ridiculously named it *Alexandria Commodiana Togata*, as **Lampridius** testifies. **Solinus** says it was first called *Chartada*, then later *Junonia*, which is confirmed by **Plutarch**, who writes that it was so named by **C. Gracchus**. "Here was her armor, here her chariot," as the Poet<note>A reference to Virgil's *Aeneid*, describing the goddess Juno's love for Carthage.</note> says. I do not favor the opinion of **Isidore** nor that of **Servius** in his commentary on the 4th book of the *Aeneid*, where he teaches that this city was also once called **Tyre**; for contrary to Virgil's intention, he makes Carthage and Tyre the same city. However, **Saint Augustine**, in *On the Unity of the Church*, thinks that Carthage was designated under the name of Tyre by the prophet **Ezekiel**. Yet this is used figuratively rather than literally. According to **Balsamon**, it was named *Justiniana* by the Emperor **Justinian** because he restored it to the Roman Empire. **Hermolaus** and others testify, based on **Suidas** and **Eustathius**, that it is called *Tharsis* in the Holy Bible. **Byrsa**, according to **Appian** and **Servius**, is not a name common to all of Carthage, but only to the citadel. *Megara*<note>original Greek: μεγάρα</note> was also a place within it surrounded by walls, according to the same Appian. Authors call the inhabitants of this city *Poeni* [Punic] and the region the *Punic* land. Regarding the name of this city, see what **L. Drusius** has in chapter 8 of his *Sacred Observations*, book 7. **New Carthage** in Spain (Tarraconensis) is a maritime city of the Contestani; a diligent description of it by Ptolemy and others exists in **Polybius**, book 10. Authors such as **Pliny**, **Antoninus**, and **Appian** surname it *Spartaria*<note>original Greek: σπαρταζίνην, referring to the esparto grass used for making ropes.</note>. The same Appian thinks it was previously called **Saguntum**, but was later destroyed by **Hannibal** and made into a Carthaginian colony. That it was called *Carthage Spartagena* is well known even to "the bleary-eyed and the barbers"<note>A Latin idiom (*lippis et tonsoribus*) meaning something is common knowledge or obvious to everyone.</note>, as the saying goes, yet this Carthage and Saguntum are two different towns. But this error must be forgiven in a Greek man and a foreigner to whom Spain was less known—just as one might write that the **Ebro River** flows into the Northern Ocean, when in fact it exits into the Mediterranean. **Stephanus** writes that this Carthage was also called *Caenopolis*, like the Libyan one. **Polybius** in book 3, and **Polyaenus** in book 8 regarding Scipio, call it *Phoenissa*. Today it is named **Cartagena**. **Old Carthage**, according to Ptolemy, is a city of the Elarcaones in Spain (Tarraconensis). **Pliny** surnames it "of the Punic people." **Cicero** also mentions it in *On the Agrarian Law*. The **Bishop of Girona** writes that it is today called *Villa Franca*. **Varretus** and **Bentherus** write that it is *Cantavilla*. **A. Augustinus** reads it as *Cantaveia* in his 8th Dialogue on Ancient Coins; so also does **Juan de Mariana** in his *History of Spain*. **Stephanus** and **Plutarch**'s *Lucullus* (who calls this the work of Hannibal) also place a **Carthage** in Armenia; see *Carchedon*.

### CHAP. XLIII.

The most ancient historians assert that some time after the universal deluge, the coast of Africa (or Barbary) and Spain was populated by the Phoenicians, who are said to have long been lords and masters of the sea. They state that the so renowned Republic of Carthage, which extended so far, was one of the colonies of Tyre, the capital of Phoenicia bordering Judea. Tyre sent half of its people there, which is why it was called in the Hebrew language <term>Kartagaa</term><note>original: קרתאדא. The author interprets this as "superb and magnificent city," likely connecting "Qart" (city) with a root for grandeur.</note>; others say *Chartago*, from the word *Charta*, which in the Syriac language signifies a city, and *Go*, middle, as if one were saying *Media urbs*, "middle city" or "half-city." The first people who populated it entered through that species of isthmus called the **Catabathmus**<note>A geographical feature—a "slope" or "descent"—historically marking the boundary between Egypt and Libya.</note> or the "descent" that joins Palestine with Egypt. This could still be seen in the time of the historian **Procopius**<note>Procopius of Caesarea (c. 500–565 AD), a prominent Byzantine historian.</note> by a column in the city of **Tingit**<note>Modern-day Tangier, Morocco.</note> in Africa, bearing witness to the inhabitants of Canaan who fled before the face of **Joshua**. This is confirmed by the Greek author **Suidas** in his explanation of the word <term>Canaan</term><note>original Greek: χάנהאן</note>. For this reason, **Saint Augustine** held in several places in his works that the Punic and Carthaginian language was nothing other than a dialect of the Hebrew language, or the Canaanite language; this was well noted by **Otthon Heurnius** in his *Chaldaic*, citing **Salvianus**, book 7 of *On the Judgment and Providence of God*. <meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the linguistic origins of Carthage, specifically focusing on the Phoenicians as the primary transmitters of the alphabet and the eventual destruction of African records during the Islamic conquests.</meta>

<header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [LANGUAGES]</header>

[they were the] first who taught the Africans and the Greeks letters, which these Greeks did not know (according to some) at the time of the Trojan War, as their names themselves show. Against these views stands **Dictys Cretensis**<note>A legendary chronicler of the Trojan War; his "journal" was a popular source for medieval and Renaissance scholars.</note> in Book 1 on the Trojan War. The Hebrews likewise taught the Phoenicians, who according to all cosmographers are the inhabitants of the sea of Palestine. Consequently, what the very ancient Greek historian **Eupolemus** says is found to be true: that the Prophet **Moses** was the first of all mortals who taught Grammar—that is, the art of reading—which **Philo the Jew**, however, attributes to **Abraham**. The Phoenicians received it from the Hebrews, and the Greeks from those Phoenicians, which is why the letters were formerly called Phoenician. This is why the Poet said:

->The Phoenicians were the first, if report is believed, who ventured<-

In the aforementioned passage, a judgment was made regarding the characters of the letters and the Punic, Carthaginian, and Arabic languages.

> I suspect that the forms of the Punic, Carthaginian, or Arabic elements are so various and different that no proof is needed; indeed, I have more than thirty chapters of books, both small and large, and two scrolls which, when unrolled, extend to nearly five arms' length. They are written with such diverse and distant letter shapes that reading them is of no small difficulty. Just as we see in our own Latin, where there is sometimes such a difference that reading them requires complete guesswork; for one who has only dealt with the various Italian letterforms will not be able to read the writing of the Germans, French, Spaniards, or even the English, or the characters of many merchants, though they be Latin, without difficulty. So it is in Punic and Arabic: and what we have said regarding the diversity of letters must easily be believed regarding grammatical rules. Since the Tartars, or Persians, and Turks teach grammar in one way, and the Punic, Numidian, and Baetic <note>Baetica: a Roman province in southern Spain, corresponding roughly to modern Andalusia.</note> in another. As can be seen by those who have read the books of that Monk (who, after the Kingdom of Granada <note>The text says "Grauatæ," a likely OCR error for "Granatæ."</note> was captured by the Kings of Spain, immediately wrote Arabic grammatical rules) or those in the introduction recently published by Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French polymath and one of the first European scholars to study Arabic systematically.</note>, about which I believe I have already said something in the previous discussion of letterforms. We know from the words of Priscian <note>Priscian (fl. 500 AD), the most influential Latin grammarian of the Middle Ages.</note> that the Punic and Arabic languages have only two genders—namely masculine and feminine—and are entirely ignorant of the neuter, when he says: *And especially since the language of the Phoenicians, which is similar to Chaldean or Hebrew and Syrian, does not have a neuter gender.* Later, that same Spanish monk also affirmed this in his introduction to reading Arabic. They have three numbers in declining nouns: singular, dual, and plural. And the names of their masculine gender end in *l*, or in *v*, and in all consonants, but not in the five vowels; feminine nouns are those that do not end as stated above. Indeed, masculine names have only a single termination in the singular and a single one in the plural, in the manner of the Chaldeans, Hebrews, Syrians, and Indians. In the dual, however, it retains a unique ending distinct from these, as can be made clear to the reader by this example: *Raiul*, that is, man in the nominative singular; in the dual, *Raiulai*, two men, and this type of addition is general across all duals. Sometimes, however, the syllable *en* is added, and we say *Raiulen*, two men, which is common to both feminine and masculine names. In feminine names, however, before *Ay* or before *En*, the letter *t* is interposed, which is proper and (so to speak) formative of feminine names in the plural and dual number; for example: *Duſſæ* <note>original: "Duſſæ"</note>, that is, Gate, *Duſſeray*, two gates; *Xamaa*, Camel, *Xamaatai*, two camels; *Mara*, wife or woman, *Maraten* or *Maratay*, two wives or women; in the plural, however, feminine names of birds, herbs, fruits, animals, and other seeds, as well as materials and metals, are declined defectively from the nominative singular by adding the last letter, as *Dabora*, *Dabar*; *Diziia*, Hen, *Dizij*, Hens. And just as these are declined by apheresis <note>The removal of a sound or letter from the beginning of a word.</note> of a letter, so verbals and participles are declined with the addition of *in*, such as *Hhabiz*, Baker, *Hhabizin*, Bakers. *Raiul*, Man, then through apheresis and metathesis <note>The transposition or rearrangement of sounds or letters in a word.</note> of letters, makes in the plural *Rigil*, or even *Regil*, several men...

"Punic has only two modes for verbs, namely the Indicative and the Imperative; they also recognize only two tenses: the present and the preterite perfect, such as *Nignedder*, I punish, and *Gneddebt ani*, I have punished." <note>original Latin: "Duos tantùm verborum modos habét Punici... André Thevet, in Book 1, Chapter 12 of his *Cosmography*, writes that the language of the ancient inhabitants of the Island of Malta—indeed, not so long ago—remained the old and ancient Punic or Carthaginian language. "As for the Island of Malta, although it is included under Europe because it has long obeyed the Romans, it is nevertheless entirely African, even though it is a neighbor to Sicily, inasmuch as it has always kept its ancient Moorish and African language—not such as the Moors use today, but as the inhabitants of Carthage once spoke. As proof of this, the Maltese understand some verses of the comic poet Plautus, which are in the Carthaginian language." <note>Plautus’s play *Poenulus* contains a famous passage of Punic speech.</note> A certain Quintinus Haeduus <note>Jean Quintin (1500–1561), a French priest and author who wrote a description of Malta.</note>, in one of his letters dated from Malta on January 20, 1533, sent to a friend of his named Sophus, says:

"This island of ours, Malta, is sixty miles distant from Sicily across a rather dangerous sea toward Africa; it was once under Punic rule and still uses the language of the Africans. Some stone steles inscribed with Punic letters still exist; in shape and with certain small dots applied, they closely resemble Hebrew. And so you may know that the idiom they have now differs little or not at all from the ancient one, the Maltese understand many Punic words of a certain Carthaginian named Hanno in Plautus, or of Avicenna and similar figures, although that speech is such that it cannot be well expressed in Latin letters, much less pronounced by any mouth except those of their own nation. Also of the same language are those words in the Gospel: *Eloi, Epsta, cumi*. Now it is under Sicilian law and sea." <note>original Latin: "Nostra hęc Melita Insula est... Nunc siculi iuris est ac maris."</note>

Some modern authors have held in their writings that the Punic people had 23 letters and elements in ancient times, though, to speak accurately, they have only 17 letter shapes. These vary in sound and power by means of points placed above them, so that they reach more than thirty in number. Plutarch, in his *Lives* of Fabius Maximus, Hannibal, and Scipio Africanus, demonstrates that this Punic language was entirely different and dissimilar from the Greek and Latin languages. However, he does not specifically explain in those places what language this Punic language was, nor does Titus Livy in the 3rd Decade, Book 9, when writing that Hannibal—that dreaded and valiant African Captain—while spending his summer in a temple of Juno surnamed Lacinia, had an altar built there. ### Of the Region of the Arabs.

->C H A P T E R XLIV.<-

Abraham Ortelius, in his *Synonyms* and *Geographical Treasury*, said the following concerning the region of the Arabs:

Arabia <gloss>Arabia</gloss>, second to no nation and of vast extent: from Mount Amanus in the region of Cilicia and Commagene, it descends to our sea <note>the Mediterranean</note> and the Egyptian coast, says Pliny in Book 16, Chapter 28. The same author, citing Juba, writes that the Arabs reach the Nile River from Syene to Meroë, and it extends beyond the Tigris to Charax toward the east. Heliodorus, in Book 8, makes the Arabs neighbors to the Troglodytes <note>cave-dwellers</note>. Their peoples are also enumerated by Pliny: the Aroei, Ascitae, Autei, Azarei, Catabani, Eldamarii, Esbonitae, Cnebadaei, Mardani, Masaei, Orei, Rhetani, and Scenitae <note>tent-dwellers</note>. Strabo adds these: the Chaulotaeans <gloss>Chaulotaioi</gloss>, Agraeans <gloss>Agraioi</gloss>, and Chatramotitae <gloss>Chatramotitai</gloss>. Read the description of Arabia in Xenophon's *Cyropaedia*, Book 1. The Arabs inhabiting Mauritania <note>North Africa</note> are today called Alabares or Alarbes.

Arabia, according to Pomponius Mela, Ptolemy, and Arrian, the latter of whom also adds the surname "the Happy" <note>Arabia Felix</note>: a town of Arabia Felix, at the Arabian Gulf. Today it is Aden according to Peter Apian; but this seems to be Ocelis to Ionius, though he is mistaken.

Desert Arabia <gloss>Eremos</gloss> according to Ptolemy, which Servius calls "Lower Arabia" and Aristides calls "Rugged Arabia"; in the *Egyptian Oration*, it is called "Hollow" <gloss>Koile</gloss>. Lucian, in his *Apology for those hired for wages*, notes that they are the Scenitae <note>tent-dwellers</note> according to Eustathius, whom he places between the Euphrates and Hollow Syria. To the Hebrews, it is Cedar <note>Kedar</note>, or Beriara, and today Villanuanus calls it so.

Happy Arabia <gloss>Eudaimon</gloss> to the Greeks, is called "Blessed" by Solinus following Pliny, and "Prosperous" <note>Eudaemon</note> by Pomponius. Virgil calls it "Pachaian," as Servius notes; Pliny writes that its inhabitants were once called Sabaeans; today it is called Aiman <note>Yemen</note>; in more recent maps, Pinetus reports it is called Marmotta by the Saracens. Stony Arabia <gloss>Petraia</gloss> according to Ptolemy, "Rocky" according to Servius, which is Nabataea to Strabo and Pliny. In Holy Scripture, it is inhabited by the Amalekites. It is a region of Asia, bordering Palestine. This is the same as the Ancient Arabia, and is called "Third Palestine" by Procopius and Stephanus. Stephanus calls this "Mountainous Arabia" under the word <gloss>Parrattammata</gloss>. It is called "Second Arabia" by William of Tyre in Book 11, Chapter 26; and the same author in Book 13, Chapter 3, and likewise Book 15, Chapter 21, also names it "Petracensis" after its metropolis Petra. This is confirmed by L. Ant. Therefore, it is a most certain and assured thing that this language currently has great currency and vogue throughout this universe, occupying entirely two parts of it (it being divided into three parts), namely throughout the Levant and the South, as far as the Molucca Islands, and as far as Nubia and Ethiopia commanded by the Padishah Prester John <note>original: "Padescha Prestegiani." Many have shown the same in their commentaries on the Song of Songs, chapter 8. The Arabs long ago organized this language into grammatical rules, and recently Guillaume Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581) was a French polymath and linguist who published the first grammar of Arabic in Europe.</note>—a man worthy of a longer life so that he might one day provide us with a complete explanation of the Arabic language—published a Grammar for the great benefit of the Church. I believe his words should by no means be omitted here:

> No language today (he says), nor anywhere in the past, has held a place in so many parts of the world. And again: The Arabic language is the Grammar <note>The standard literary and liturgical form.</note> for all followers of the Muhammadan religion. It is more widespread today than any language has ever been, such that hardly a third part of the inhabited world does not recognize it. For it possesses all of Africa except for the region of Nubia, which is held by Prester John <note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles; here Postel associates him with Ethiopia.</note>, whom they call the "Precious" or "High Ham" <note>original: "Preciosum vel altum Cham"</note>, and whom the common people call Prester John. It possesses all of Asia from our shores through the antipodes even to the western part of our hemisphere. Also the Molucca Islands, which Magellan found beyond America near Tlaxcala <note>original: "Taschaltical"</note>, Colhuacan <note>original: "Curistical"</note>, and Tenochtitlan <note>original: "Themistitam," the Aztec capital.</note>; although the principal part are idolaters, except for certain Indians and those of Narsinga <note>A kingdom in South India, often associated with Vijayanagara.</note>. By the benefit of this language, we shall be able to converse without an interpreter with the Egyptian Moor, the Syrian, the Persian, the Turk, the Tartar, and the Indian. And, to say it once and for all, in almost the entire world, it is so closely related to the Hebrew language that if anyone is diligently practiced in Hebraism, they could understand a good part of that language within two years.

Thus far Postel; it appears therefore that the Arabic language can be compared in all its parts with Hebrew, to weigh what they have in common and what is diverse and peculiar to each—which can only be accomplished through a shared doctrine and method.

Furthermore, these same Muslims <note>original: "Mahometistes"</note> have translated the Psalms of David into this language, along with the rest of the Old Testament and the entire New Testament—though entirely depraved and perverted with the removal of the entire account of the Passion—as well as the Lord's Prayer, the Angelic Salutation <note>The Hail Mary.</note>, and several others. For this reason, the Fathers of the Council of Vienne, held in the year of salvation 1311, rightly ordered that this language should be publicly read and taught in the principal universities of Christendom, as something entirely necessary and useful for the conversion of so many Muslims spread throughout the earth. This was contained in the *Clementines* <note>A collection of canon law named after Pope Clement V.</note>, in the section "On Teachers" (*de magistris*), Book 5 of the *Clementines* within the body of Canon Law. This was also, so they say, ordered at the Council of Clermont in Auvergne, according to the late G. Postel in his book describing Syria.

Our French histories mention that, following the Council, Nicolas Clénard <note>Nicolaes Cleynaerts (1495–1542), a Flemish grammarian and traveler who sought to learn Arabic to peacefuly debate Muslims.</note>—well known to all scholars today through his writings—composed a certain Lexicon in this language for those who wished to learn it, which this figure confirms himself in Book 2 of his Letters.

This language is adorned and embellished with four kinds of points <note>punctuation marks</note>: the high point, like the Greek language; the low point in place of a comma, like the Latin language; the comma in place of the *Sheva* <note>A Hebrew vowel sign indicating a very short vowel or no vowel.</note> of the Hebrew language, serving the same purpose; and for the comma and question mark, three points in the shape of a Hebrew *Segol* <note>A Hebrew vowel mark consisting of three dots in an inverted triangle.</note>. However, it uses these in three ways: with the point turned upward in the manner of a pyramid, or to the right, or to the left. In fact, the late Guillaume Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581) was a renowned French polymath and linguist who traveled extensively in the East.</note>, who was very learned in the Hebrew language, wrote in his *Alphabet of Twelve Different Languages* that while he was in Constantinople, the Turks who taught him the Arabic language called him a **Demon**, because he understood it as soon as it was shown and taught to him—unlike others who ordinarily spend five or six years before knowing its grammar perfectly. This is confirmed by Theodore Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander (1506–1564) was a Swiss scholar who published the first printed Latin translation of the Quran.</note> in his commentary on the common systems of all languages and letters.

The Arabs, Turks, and Persians do not permit any man of their faith to handle the books of their religion—called *Almashaf* <note>original: "Almashaf"; referring to the *Mus'haf*, the written codex of the Quran.</note> in the Arabic language and *Lereteb* <note>original: "Lereteb"; likely a corruption of a Persian term for scripture.</note> in Persian—except for the chief priests, or their officials whom they call the **Qadi** <note>original: "Elcadie"; a judge or legal scholar.</note> or clerks, or indeed the Great Sultan, who is their sovereign King. Thus, no matter what book it may be, it is not placed in the hands of the common people, both because books are rare (printing being unknown in those parts) and because they have a great religious and moral concern that such books might be profaned and exposed to everyone's sight. Consequently, they believe they would fall into the indignation of God and the disfavor of Muhammad, Ali <note>original: "Haly"; Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, central to Islamic history.</note>, and their other Prophets if such a fault occurred. They would believe that everything was lost if any cooks, masons, or servants took the liberty of handling the sacred books that the Great God gave to His holy Prophets and revealed to their ancient fathers.

> It must be known that the Arabic language has the greatest kinship with Hebrew. They place these Arabic letters—*Eliph*, *Lem*, *Mim*, or A, L, M—at the beginning of the book, which they call the "seal of the book" <note>This refers to the *Muqatta'at* or "disjointed letters" that appear at the start of certain chapters in the Quran; Postel/the author provides a mystical interpretation of them here.</note>. By *Lem* <note>Lam</note>, the Majesty of God is designated, and by *Mim* <note>Mim</note>, His empire, so that they may signify that God is Almighty, whose messenger this is, along with His precepts. <note>original Latin: "sciendum quod lingua Arabica maximam cognationē habet ad Hebraicam... vt insinuent Deum omnipotentem, cuius hic nuncius & eius præcepta."</note>

And to be brief, the Arabic language in which the Quran of the Muhammadans is composed is so highly prized and esteemed by the aforementioned people that they have refused to allow any version of it to be made in another language. This language, resembling Hebrew, Chaldean, and Syriac, today has a very wide reach and popularity among many peoples of this Universe. For although the Tartars, Khwarazmians, Persians, and Turks have languages different from Arabic, and the Syrians, Arabs, Moors, and Africans have languages somewhat similar, grammatical Arabic is the common language for religion and scholarly disciplines among the learned Priests and Judges, used by nearly all the inhabitants of Asia, Africa, and a third part of Europe. And so that curious readers may know what difference there is between the Hebrew, Chaldean <note>In the 16th century, "Chaldean" was a common term for Aramaic.</note>, Syriac, and Arabic languages, we have wished in this place to report in Latin characters the Lord's Prayer in each of these languages.

### The Lord's Prayer in the Hebrew language.

> Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen. <note>original phonetic Hebrew: "Abinu aschar basschamaim, iikkadesch schimcha thabo malchuthcha thiheiah reizoncha chemo basschamim chen bearatz z Iahhemenu thàmid tithen lanu haiyō..."</note>

### The Lord's Prayer in the Chaldean language.

> Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us today our sufficient bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who have sinned against us. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. Amen. <note>original phonetic Chaldean (Aramaic): "Abon ascar debismaia nith Kadaschschmech, thatha malchuthach nehuah tzibuach ech debismaia aph beara lahhman desan Kaneniomna..."</note>

### The Lord's Prayer in the Syriac language.

> Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. Give us the bread we need today. And forgive us our debts and our sins, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen. <note>original phonetic Syriac: "Abun dbasmaio nethquadas smoch, tithe malcuthoth nehuæ zzebionoch aicano dbasmaio oph barago hablan lahhmo dsunquanon iaumono..."</note>

### The Lord's Prayer in the Arabic language.

> Our Father who art in the heavens, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth. Our bread of tomorrow give us today. And forgive us that which we owe, as we also forgive those who have sinned against us. And lead us not into the temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. Amen. <note>original phonetic Arabic: "Abana lladhi phi al semeuathi thikuduschu Ismeche thatha malchutheche thechunu mescheitheche chema phi alfamai vealai alardhi..."</note>

The first chapter of this Alcoran or Alfurcan was that which Muhammad asserts was given to him in the cave by the Angel Gabriel; and the last, that of the Fate <note>Likely referring to Al-Fatiha, though the author translates it as "Conquest"</note>, which means the Conquest. And the said Muhammad remaining ten years in Mecca, he made there certain chapters or *Azoares* <note>Surahs</note>, which are called in Arabic *Azoar Mikia*, that is to say, chapters or songs made in Mecca; and staying eleven years in Medina <note>Almedina</note>, during this time he made the other chapters named *Azoar Medina*, Canticles made in Medina. And it must be understood that the said Muhammad never commanded that his Alcoran or Alfurcan be collected or reduced into books, nor into chapters as it is at present; rather, he kept certain schedules or tablets in an ark or chest as he wrote and composed them, and many of these schedules or tablets were lost and were not found after his death. And it is credible that if the said Muhammad had remained alive for a hundred years, he would have continually increased these schedules and tablets, and he did not set down in writing during his life this Alcoran or Alfurcan in the style and manner that it is at present. It is believed by their wise men <note>The author refers to Christian scholars of the time who studied Islamic texts for polemical purposes</note>, and shown by effective reasons, that the first author of the Quran was not a man, but the devil; because through his own envy and by divine permission—due to the sins of the people—he prevailed to solemnly and effectively begin the perfidy of the Antichrist. Seeing, therefore, that the faith of Christ was growing greatly in the Eastern parts and that idolatry was failing (since Khosrow, King of the Persians and an idolater of the Medes, had already been overcome by the most Christian Emperor Heraclius, who destroyed the high tower that Khosrow himself had built of gold, silver, and precious stones for the purpose of idolatry), and because the cross of Christ had already been exalted by Heraclius and was to be exalted further—and since the devil could no longer defend a multitude of gods, nor entirely deny the law of Moses and the Gospel of Christ because they had been spread throughout the whole world—he devised a deception for the world through the fabrication of a certain law, acting as a sort of middle ground between the New and Old Testaments. 

And, to bring this to effect, he took up a certain diabolical man named Muhammad <note>original: "Machumetus"</note>, an idolater by religion, poor in fortune, proud in mind, and famous for sorceries. Indeed, he would have more willingly taken up a man of good reputation if this had been permitted to him, just as he would have more willingly tempted humanity through some other animal in which his malice might be better hidden than through the serpent. But divine wisdom did not permit him to assume any animal but that one, nor to invade the world through any but such a man, so that the world itself might easily consider what kind of law it was that was given by such a lawgiver. 

Therefore, after Khosrow was overcome by the aforementioned Heraclius, and the Holy Cross was translated to Jerusalem with triumph in the six hundred and twenty-second year from the incarnation of the Lord (the fifteenth year of the reign of Heraclius), there appeared a certain Muhammad the Arab. Having first become wealthy through a certain widow whom he took as a wife, and after this having become a leader of robbers, he broke out into such pride that he even wished to become King of the Arabs. But because they did not receive him—since he was of a base family and reputation—he feigned that he was a Prophet. 

And since he suffered from the falling sickness <note>original: "comitiali morbo"; a common medieval interpretation of Muhammad's revelations as symptoms of epilepsy</note>, so that no one would firmly believe he was being seized by it when he constantly fell, he claimed that an Angel was speaking with him. He would afterwards give certain responses which (as I said) he heard as if in the manner of a ringing bell sounding in his ears. 

And because he was an uneducated and illiterate man, the devil gave him his own associates: certain heretics and Jews, and likewise heretical Christians. For a certain Jacobite <note>A member of the Syrian Orthodox Church</note> named Baira <note>The monk known in Islamic tradition as Bahira</note> joined him and remained with Muhammad until death. It is said that Muhammad afterwards killed him. But also certain Jews, namely Phinees and Audia (named Salon, but afterwards called Abdallah <note>original: "Audala"</note>), and Sele, who also became Saracens. And certain Nestorians <note>A Christian sect that emphasized the distinction between the divine and human natures of Jesus</note>, who agree most closely with the Saracens, saying that God was not born of the Blessed Virgin, but rather the man Jesus Christ. 

And then Muhammad composed a certain thing in the manner of a law, taking certain elements from the Old Testament and others from the New Testament through these associates. However, the people did not have the Quran at that time. Yet it is said in their histories that Muhammad said, "The Quran descended to me in seven versions <note>original: "in 7. viris"; likely referring to the 'Ahruf' or seven modes of recitation in Islamic tradition</note>, and whatever is enough, suffices." They say, however, that these were Napse and Eon, Omar, Omra, Eleafar, Asir the son of Cethir, and the daughter of Amer. We asked them, therefore, if they read these things before Muhammad, and they all said no, but before the elders, and so on until Muhammad. 

However, it is certain that these did not agree with the earlier elders in the text that they now hold. This is proven by the fact that the text of the first part is contrary to the second part. For from the time of Muhammad, no one was an expert in the Quran except Abdallah son of Mesetud, and Zeith son of Tamphet, and Ocanā son of Ophyn, and the son of Oeupe.

They also report of a certain powerful man named Al-Hajjaj <note>original: "Elgas"</note> that he removed eighty-five verses from the Quran and added just as many others with a different meaning. Certain histories relate that Muhammad died by poison, and the people did not yet possess a [unified] Quran. And truly, in this book many things are so scattered and disordered—as has already been made clear—that they convey no coherent meaning, but rather mask madness and lies. It happened, however, that they agreed that this would be the Quran they now hold in their hands, claiming that God revealed it to Muhammad and that he wrote it from the mouth of God. 

Yet the jurists <term>Faqih/Fuqaha <note>original: "Alphaki/Aelphocaa"</note></term>—that is, the great doctors and commentators—never agreed on its interpretation, nor will they ever agree. Thus, not only do the Easterners differ from the Westerners, but the Easterners disagree among themselves, and the Westerners among themselves; even within the same schools, there are different sects, so diverse that one condemns the other. For some follow Muhammad, and they are the majority; others follow Ali <note>original: "Hali"</note>, and they are fewer and less malicious, saying that Muhammad used tyrannical power to usurp for himself what belonged to Ali.

Against both groups rose up certain men skilled in philosophy who, beginning to read the books of Aristotle and Plato, abandoned all the Saracen sects and the Quran itself. Realizing this, a certain man from Babylon <note>The author uses "Babylon" to refer to Baghdad, the seat of the Abbasid Caliphate</note> named the Caliph <note>original: "Calyphas"</note> built a school near the Academy and the Mustansiriya <note>original: "Stanzeriam"</note>, which are very costly institutions; he diverted their study back to the Quran and ordained that whoever comes from the provinces to Baghdad to learn the Quran should have housing and necessary expenses provided by the public treasury. He decreed that Saracens who devote themselves to the Quran should in no way study philosophy. For this reason, they do not consider those who study philosophy to be good Saracens, because such people despise the Quran for the reasons mentioned above in chapters 8 and 9.

These people were also called (as indeed they still bear the title today) *Qizilbash* <note>original: "Cuſelbas," from the Turkish "Kızılbaş"</note>, which is to say "Colored Head," because of the colored turban they wear to be distinguished from other Muhammadans. This Musa al-Kazim <note>original: "Muca Cacẽ"</note> having died, his son Junayd <note>original: "Guines"</note> succeeded him, during the time of the great King of the Parthians, Tamerlane <note>also known as Timur</note>, by whom he was so honored and respected that when Junayd asked him for 30,000 captives he held, Tamerlane gave them to him liberally. This false prophet, strengthening himself with these men—just as the Sultan of Great Cairo did with the Mamluks <note>term: Mamluks — a class of warrior-slaves who rose to rule Egypt</note>, and as the Grand Turk does with the Janissaries <note>term: Janissaries — the elite infantry units of the Ottoman Sultan</note>—used them to attack the Christians and ravaged the lands of the Georgians, his neighbors, who refused to receive his false doctrine.

Junayd left as his successor Sheikh Haydar <note>original: "Xech Aidar"</note>, his son, a man of great and lofty enterprises. During his time, a Turk named Amir reigned in Persia, against whom another Turk named Uzun Hasan <note>original: "Cacẽ Bech, autremẽt Vſſucasſá"</note> waged war; the latter reigned in the province of Diyarbakır <note>original: "Diarbech"</note>, formerly called Armenia Major. This Uzun Hasan, having defeated and slain Amir in battle, also made himself King of Persia. But feeling his support was weak because he was born of low station, he gave his daughter in marriage to Sheikh Haydar. He had fathered this daughter by a woman of the blood of the Emperors of Trebizond <note>original: "Trapezõde," a Greek successor state of the Byzantine Empire</note>, so that this valiant man of Ardabil <note>original: "Arduelin"</note> might lend him a hand in his conquests and prevent the Persians from revolting. 

Thus, from this alliance of the Persian with the niece of the Trebizond emperor, it has happened ever since that the Kings of Persia have loved the Christians; even now, they do not reject them as much as other Muhammadans do. When Uzun Hasan came to die, he left as his successor a son of his named Yaqub Beg <note>original: "Iacob Bech"</note>. Yaqub, distrusting the forces of his brother-in-law Sheikh Haydar because he saw him growing greater from day to day and acquiring larger and more ample lordships, did not dare to put him to death because of the great number of his partisans and sectaries. Seeing him entangled in the war against the Georgians and other neighboring Christians of Armenia, Yaqub secretly sent aid to Haydar's enemies, by which means Sheikh Haydar was slain in battle and his forces annihilated. 

He left two sons of a young age, Ismail and Suleiman <note>original: "Solymá"</note>, whom their uncle the King of Persia gave into the custody of one named Mansur <note>original: "Mãçor"</note>, the governor of Shiraz <note>original: "Sirach"</note>, so that he might send them to him whenever required. Meanwhile, Yaqub Beg died, and Rustam <note>original: "Hoſtẽ"</note> succeeded him to the crown of Persia. Some time later, Mansur also died, leaving the Safavid brothers Ismail and Suleiman in the protection of the people of Gilan <note>original: "Geilã"</note>, a people living along the sea of Baku or the Caspian. This was done because he feared that a son of his named Qasim <note>original: "Cacẽ"</note> might betray them and hand them over to the new King of Persia for a sum of money. 

These two children, raised outside the power of their tyrant uncle and far from the furious hands of their cousin, were carefully maintained by Pir Ali <note>original: "Pirraih"</note>, Lord of Lahijan <note>original: "Legiã"</note>, who, along with his people, favored the sect of Ali, of which the Safavids made such strict profession. Furthermore, the eldest of the children of the deceased Sheikh Haydar, named Ismail as stated, became so superstitious that to deceive the people and win the heart of the multitude, he would eat nothing but what was given to him in alms, and what remained he gave to the poor. While these children lived thus in exile and banishment, a strong and furious war broke out among the children of Yaqub, King of Persia; so much so that in less than two years, the state was seen to change five different times.

This division opened the eyes of Ismail, so much so that, desiring to fish in troubled waters, and accompanied by several of his kinsmen and friends, he went into his country, where he was received with extreme joy by his subjects, who attributed to him the name and title of Sophy <note>original: "Sophy," a European corruption of "Safi," referring to the Safavid dynasty</note>, as the principal head of their sect. The arrival of this personage raised the spirits of his subjects, so that taking to the field, he initiated the hatred and war that has since existed, and still exists today, between the Turks and the Persians, as much because of doctrine and opinion as for the cruelties which this young warrior used against the Turcomans <note>The "Turcomans" here refers to the Aq Qoyunlu, or "White Sheep" Turkic tribal federation</note>. For so were called those who followed the party of Uzun Hasan <note>original: "Hoſcen"</note> and were of the false religion of the Ash'arites <note>original: "Leſhari-tes," referring to a major school of Sunni Islamic theology</note>. For Sheikh Ismail Sophy, having taken the city of Shemakha <note>original: "Siniaqua," likely Shemakha in modern Azerbaijan</note> near Ardabil <note>original: "Arduel"</note> from his cousin, sacked it and put it to fire and sword, terrifying everyone by this so cruel and horrible beginning.

It was then that his Ardabil accomplices began to publish everywhere that Ismail was the prophet promised by God, come to plant the Religion of Ali <note>The Shi'a branch of Islam, centered on the lineage of Ali ibn Abi Talib</note> throughout all the Orient by force of arms; and they did so well that the army of the Qizilbash <note>original: "Cuſelbas," meaning "Red Heads" for their distinctive headgear</note> increased, and the Sophy grew bold enough to assault Tabriz <note>original: "Tauris"</note>, the Metropolitan city of the country of the Medes, which he took in the year 1500 from Alvand <note>original: "Aluant"</note> who was its King, and whom he defeated in battle. Entering by force into this city, he committed such strange and furious cruelties upon the Turcomans that from that time on the name of the Sophy has been so odious and fearsome to the Turks, his adversaries, that nothing could be more so. 

And since Jacob <note>Yaqub Beg</note>, his maternal uncle, had been the cause of his father's death, being unable to take revenge upon him because he was already deceased, he commanded that the body of the deceased be pulled from its coffin, which he had burned and its ashes scattered in the air, and the tomb entirely ruined, so as to completely destroy the memory of this prince. This Sophy, not content with having vented his rage upon the bones of his uncle, because his own Mother—the sister of the same Jacob—reproached him for this cruelty, he put her to death, killing her with his own hands. 

Tabriz being won and Alvand in flight, the latter strengthened himself with men to such an extent that, having raised a large army, he came once again against this Sophy, who, standing his ground, defeated him and put him to death in a battle. Succeeding him was Murad Khan <note>original: "Morat Cam"</note>, his elder brother, who, seeing what cruelty the Sophy exercised upon the Turcomans and fearing he would be driven from his seat and lose the crown of Persia, raised the largest army possible. Taking the route to Tabriz, he made himself strong to defeat his enemy and secure his Lordship. 

But however well-armed the Persians of Murad Khan were, and though both they and their horses were covered in mail and breastplates—just as the men-at-arms do in our France—he nonetheless lost the day. All he could do was save himself in the city of Baghdad <note>original: "Bagadet"</note>, built near the ruins of ancient Babylon. The victorious Sophy did not leave a single man alive among those who fell into his hands; however, he was quite courteous to the women, who were (following the Persian custom) in the train of the Royal camp, and whom he gave as wives to his soldiers. It was then that he made himself Lord of the great city of Shiraz <note>original: "Siras"</note>, formerly called Persepolis, the capital of all this great Kingdom, in the Year of Grace 1514 <note>Note: While the text cites 1514, Shiraz actually fell to Ismail around 1503; 1514 is the date of the later Battle of Chaldiran</note>. Thus this Sophy Ismail, from a poor fugitive and exile that he was, having become a powerful and fearsome King, resolved to extend the limits of his Empire as far as Egypt and to the lands of the Turk, who reigned, as he still does, in the city of Constantinople.

This Prince <note>Shah Ismail I, founder of the Safavid Dynasty</note> detested the Jews above all nations, and if he caught any of them, he would immediately have their eyes put out. The Turks likewise were so loathsome to him that as many as fell into his hands, he put to death without any mercy whatsoever. But he was very courteous, affable, and gentle toward Christians, allowing them the free exercise of their religion in his lands, and he often solicited the Emperor Maximilian I, King Louis XII of France, and the Venetians <note>original: "Veritiés," likely a transcription or typesetting error for "Venitiens"</note> to take up arms against the Turk from the European side, promising that he would do the same by overrunning the lands the Ottomans possessed in Asia. And so, in the year 1510 or 1511, the Sophy, having taken to the field, reached Aleppo <note>original: "Alep"</note>, a city in Syria which he besieged, causing great terror to the house and family of the Kings of Turkey. And but for a sectarian pretending to be a new prophet who rose up in Persia—a type of man that the wisest and most prudent Muslim Kings fear and abhor no less than we Christians do heretics—there is no doubt that this Sophy would have struck some remarkable blow in the Asia subject to the Turk and in the lands of Egypt, regardless of the strength of the Mamluks <note>term: Mamelus (Mamluks), the military caste that ruled Egypt and Syria until the Ottoman conquest</note>, so strongly and powerfully had he entered Mesopotamia and Syria.

### On the Prediction or Prophecy of Muhammad Concerning the Duration of His Religion and Empire.

The Turks and other Muhammadans <note>original: "Mahometistes"</note> commonly hold and believe that their religion and empire will last little more than a thousand years. They assert this was revealed to them by their Prophet Muhammad shortly before his death through certain signs and demonstrations. Specifically, while discussing the duration of the religion and empire whose foundations he had laid with his followers, he extended and raised both his hands, spreading his ten fingers wide. His principal disciples first interpreted this as ten years; but once those had passed, they extended the term to a hundred years; and when that period expired, they concluded that each finger signified a hundred years. Many Armenians have learned this from the aforementioned Turks and Muhammadans themselves, and have recounted and revealed it to Christians, as confirmed by P. Camerarius <note>Philipp Camerarius (1537–1624), a German scholar famous for his "Historical Meditations."</note> in volume 2, book 2, chapter 30 of his *Historical Meditations*, and J. Leunclavius <note>Johannes Leunclavius (1541–1594), a leading historian of the Ottoman Empire.</note> in the Preface to his *Turkish Muslim History*.

See what I write hereafter regarding another prediction or prophecy concerning the duration of the aforementioned religion and Empire of Muhammad in the following chapter toward the end, citing T. Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander, a Swiss orientalist who published the first printed Latin Quran.</note> and B. Georgievits <note>Bartol Đurđević, a Croatian writer who spent years as a captive in the Ottoman Empire.</note>. The late Guillaume Postel <note>A renowned 16th-century French polymath and orientalist.</note> writes in the first book, chapter 3 of his *Oriental Histories* that because God gave such great blessings to Abraham and Hagar through Ishmael, as is contained in the Holy Scriptures, it was necessary for the people and nation descended from him to achieve the greatness of Empire seen for the last 900 years among all the peoples descended from Ishmael under the doctrine of Muhammad. In fact, in chapters 16, 17, and 20 of Genesis, it is written that Ishmael shall be great, and that his seed shall be beyond measure or number because of its vast and immense quantity—not on account of his mother Hagar, but because he was the seed and posterity of Abraham, since his seed was blessed within his body.

### On the Al-Furqan or Quran of Muhammad. <note>original: "l'Alphurcan ou Alkoran." Al-Furqan is an Arabic title for the Quran meaning "The Criterion."</note>

A certain person named Peter, Abbot of Cluny <note>Peter the Venerable (c. 1092–1156), who commissioned the first Latin translation of the Quran.</note>, a great friend of St. Bernard, was the first among the Latins to translate the Al-Furqan or Quran of Muhammad from the Arabic language into Latin. He shared it with those devoted to the Latin tongue with the assistance of Peter of Toledo, a Peter who was a monk of Cluny, and Robert of Ketton <note>original: "Robert Kenetense ou Retenense," a 12th-century English astronomer and the primary translator of the first Latin Quran.</note>.

& Herman the Dalmatian <note>Herman of Carinthia (c. 1100–1160), a scholar and translator who produced the first Latin translation of the Quran.</note>, men very learned in the Arabic language living in the year of Grace 1143, in his annotations on this *Alphurcan* or *Alkoran* <note>original: אלכורן</note> (which is commonly interpreted as the Doctrine of Muhammad), writes that this word *Alcoran* signifies in the Arabic language a *Collection* or *recollection* of the precepts or Law of Muhammad, Prophet of the Arabs. This *Alphurcan* or *Alkoran* is composed in very elegant and copious Arabic verse, it being in no way permitted by Muslims and Muhammadans <note>original: "Mahometistes"</note> to translate it into any language whatsoever, as confirmed by the author of *The Fortress of Faith* <note>Referring to the "Fortalitium Fidei" by Alonso de Espina.</note>. This Quran is held and confessed by the Arabs, Turks, Moors, Persians, Tartars, and most Indians, Africans, Egyptians, and countless other peoples and nations of Asia, Africa, and Europe today to be entirely salutary, and that which prepares the way for them to go to the eternal joy of Paradise. It is divided and partitioned into 120 *Azoares* <note>Surahs or chapters.</note>, which we can interpret in French as faces, oracles, clauses, or distinctions. (*For Azoara in Arabic is called "vultus" [face] in Latin; whence what the Latins call a "Capitulum" [Chapter], the Arabs call an "Azoara." For just as the face most clearly indicates who or what kind of man someone is, so the Chapter indicates what the following text intends to say. According to some, Azoara sounds like "oraculum" [an oracle]. For they attribute judgment to it alone.*) These *Azoares* contain many rhapsodies from the Old and New Testaments, from the Talmuds of the Jews, and from many infinite heresies and false doctrines, as is very well known by those who have carefully seen and read this fine book printed in Germany, Italy, and other provinces of this Europe. The Arabs and Turks hold that the Arabic word *Phurcan* <note>original: פורקן</note>, coming from the verb *Pharac* <note>original: פרק</note>, meaning to redeem or to buy back, signifies redemption or liberation. A certain Arab who composed a book in his language so esteemed by the Turks, titled *The Doctrine of Muhammad*, along with John André—formerly a Moor and *Alfaqui* <term>Alfaqui: an expert in Islamic law or a jurist</term>, later made a Christian and Priest—in his *Confusion of the Sect of Muhammad*, interpret the word *Alphurcan* <note>Al-Furqan: "The Criterion," another name for the Quran</note>, by which the doctrine of this Muhammad is titled, as *verses, chapters, parts*, or *figures* and *sentences* discerned and separated from one another as if by articles. Pierre Belon, in book 3, chapter 3, observes that this word Al-Quran signifies a collection of chapters or a mass of Psalms.

They bow and prostrate themselves before it, just as the Jews do before the Book of the Law which is carried in the month of September on a certain feast day around their synagogue <note>Likely referring to the Jewish festival of Simchat Torah</note>. At the return of their journey, they sacrifice this camel publicly, from which everyone in a great crowd takes a morsel of meat <note>original: "lippee," a mouthful or scrap</note> which they keep in place of a most holy and most devout reliquary, as confirmed by J. Antoine Menavino in book 2, chapter 16 of his *History of Turkey*. ### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE [RELIGIONS]

Oriental history speaks of it differently, saying that the Turks hold that God the Creator—after man whom he had created and his posterity had forgotten Him—gave a law to the Jews mixed with two opposites: of good and evil, of great pain and reward, which they did not wish to observe, but instead committed idolatry. Then, He sent another via the greatest of the Prophets, formed of the Holy Spirit, who is Issa, or Jesus Christ (for so Muhammad calls Him in his Alcoran or *Alphurcan* <term>Alphurcan: From the Arabic "Al-Furqan," meaning "The Criterion" between right and wrong, another name for the Quran</term>). This law was filled with sweetness and ease, yet men still did not wish to keep it. For this reason, He willed to send Muhammad, who came with a sword and rigor to make the Peoples and Nations believe in God by force, or else put them to death or make them Tributaries. 

It is a most marvelous thing that the largest and most significant part of the peoples of Asia, Africa, Europe, and several others now embrace the damnable and abominable errors of this wicked and cursed Alcoran. This is detailed by Theodore Bibliander in his *Apology for the Quran*, Guillaume Postel in his *Treatise on the Twelve Languages* and in his *History of the Turks*, Gilbert Génébrard in books 3 and 4 of his *Chronographia*, André Thevet in book 6, chapter 5 of his *Cosmography*, and François de Belleforest in book 2, volume 2, chapter 8, and book 3 of the same volume, chapters 33 and 34 of his *Cosmography*. 

The reason why this Alcoran has been and still is so widely embraced as a religion among so many peoples and nations of Asia, Africa, and Europe, is that it is woven and composed of all sorts and species of religions, sects, and opinions; it permits all effeminate soft living of the flesh and all pleasure, and has loosened the bridle for all its Muhammadans to every corruption of debauchery, as Guillaume Postel confirms in his treatise *On the Configuration of the Celestial Signs*. It is true and certain that there are in Asia and Africa twelve times more Idolaters than Muhammadans, according to the report of André Thevet in book 6, chapter 5, and book 11, chapters 6, 7, and 8 of his *Cosmography*, and Antonio de Torquemada in the second day of his *Hexameron*. 

So that we leave nothing worthy of remark in this place, we shall say that the books of the *Zuna* <term>Zuna: Referring to the Sunnah, the body of traditional social and legal customs and practices of the Islamic community</term>, which we mentioned above in this same chapter, were composed by the disciples of Muhammad after his death. As these books passed through many hands, some added to them while others removed from them as they saw fit, so much so that one finds such great confusion and contradiction in the said books that what Muhammad had said affirmatively was stated negatively. Such division arose in his sect that it became necessary for the *Alcaliph* <term>Alcaliph: Caliph, the supreme religious and civil leader of a Muslim state</term>—that is to say, the King or Pontiff who ruled at that time over this people called by history the Saracens—named Muawiya <note>Muawiya I (r. 661–680), the founder of the Umayyad Caliphate</note>, living (according to Spanish history) in the year of Salvation 674, to command all Muhammadans that wherever learned men of the Quran were found (called *Alfaki* <term>Alfaki: An expert in Islamic law/jurisprudence</term> in the Arabic tongue), they should come to the city of Damascus to hold a Council, and bring all the writings they could recover. 

Once this was done, the said *Alcaliph* or King, out of the two hundred who had come there, chose six *Alfacis* or scholars. Of these six, one named Muszlin <note>The scholar Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj</note> was chosen first, Bochari <note>Muhammad al-Bukhari</note> second, Buhorayra <note>Abu Hurairah</note> third, Annecey <note>Al-Nasa'i</note> fourth, Aternindi <note>Al-Tirmidhi</note> fifth, and Dend <note>Abu Dawood</note> sixth. Among the <term>Muhammadans</term><note>original: "Mahometistes"; a common early modern European term for Muslims</note> one would offer prayers and orations during the month of Ramadan, in March, and in each month one would read the entire Quran. ->***Of the Priests and Ministers of the Arabs and Turks.***<-

AMONG the Arabs and Turks, the Priests and Ministers of their religion, or Muhammadan superstition, are as follows: namely, *Thalismans* <note>likely *Danishmends*, or scholars</note>, *Paracadis* <note>assistant judges</note>, *Cadis* <note>Qadis, or judges</note>, Priests and Judges, *Menissmarls* <note>likely *Müderris*, or professors</note>, and *Imans* <note>Imams</note>, who are well-privileged and exempt from all taxes. At the beginning of the establishment of the Muhammadan law, the Caliphs of this religion were both Kings and High Priests—one in Baghdad <note>original: "Bagadeth"</note>, the other in Cairo. Since then, the Sultans have taken royal authority and have introduced the *Muphtis* <note>Muftis</note>, who are esteemed as sovereign Patriarchs in place of the Caliphs as overseers of religion. They judge sovereignly in matters of the Law, by which not only divine prayers and ceremonies are ordained, but also political and military affairs; they have the power to retract the ordinances of the Sultans and the sentences of their *divans* <note>councils</note> which are not in conformity with, or seem repugnant to, the Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note>. Each Muhammadan Prince keeps one near him or in his principal city with large pensions: the Great Khan <note>original: "Cam"</note> of the Zavolzhye Tartars <note>original: "Tartares Zauolhees"</note> keeps his at Samarkand; the *Sophy* <note>the Safavid Shah</note> at Tabriz <note>original: "Tauris"</note>; there are others throughout Africa at Fez, Kairouan <note>original: "Caroan"</note>, Tlemcen <note>original: "Telmessen"</note>, and elsewhere. The Grand Turk <note>the Ottoman Sultan</note> shows his Mufti more honor and reverence than any other man in his Empire. It is true that today there are still two Caliphs among the Muhammadans: one residing in the city of Baghdad in Assyria, the ancient seat of the Caliphate of Chaldea, and the other in Cairo. These Caliphs, now bearing this title in name only, are kept in possession by the Sultans without interfering at all in affairs of state; in doing so, they receive three thousand *Seraps* <note>gold coins, likely *Ashrafi*</note> because of their pretended right, so as to retain some form of the original religion, the sovereignty of which is no longer governed by them, but rather by the Muftis, as has been said, who act as overseers and Patriarchs of divine things, judging sovereignly in matters of Religion and conscience.

As for the name of *Xeriph*, *Zeriph*, or *Zeriphe* <note>Sharif</note>, a name of great and eminent dignity among the aforementioned Muhammadans after the Caliphs, it is such that, in relation to the Caliph, it is what the *Sincelli* <note>Greek: "Synkellos", a high ecclesiastical office</note> formerly were to the Patriarchs among the Greeks; for after the death of the Patriarch, the *Sincellus* succeeded him and was put in his place. Those who descended in a direct line from Muhammad or from Ali, his son-in-law, are held in great honor among the Turks; they are called *Seithi* <note>Sayyids</note> by them and by the Tartars, and *Zeriphes* by the Arabs. The Ottoman Emperors, to make even their names all the more august and venerable, wish to be called *Zeriphes*.

As for the Priests, Monks, and Hermits of the Turks, one should see what is written of them by Cuspinianus in his works; Sansovino in book 3, chapter 24 of his *History of the Turks*; André Thevet in book 1, chapter 7 and book 11, chapter 7 of his *Universal Cosmography*; Theodor Zwinger in his *Great Theater*; and Pierre Belon in book 3, chapter 22.

### On the Philosopher Averroes or Avenroys & his writings composed in the Arabic language.

SOME authors write that Averroes or Avenroys, an Arab by nation, was so named in the Arabic language because the word *Averroes* signifies an "abyss." However, those who are well-versed in the knowledge of the Hebrew language know well enough that the word בן *Ben* signifies "Son" in that tongue; which the Arabs call in their language אבן *Aben*. Elias Levita, a Jew, in his work *The Tishbi* <note>A dictionary of Talmudic and Rabbinic Hebrew</note>, spells it *Abben*. The majority of Arabs use the word *Aven* for *Aben*, as can be seen in the name *Aué Roys* for *Abé Roys*, or *Aben Ruys*, as noted by Santes Pagnino in his great *Hebrew Treasure*, and Michael Neander in the third part of his *Erotemata* <note>Questions/Lessons</note> *of the Hebrew Language*. It is true that Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie, following the aforementioned Elias Levita, in interpreting this word *Aben* in his Syro-Chaldaic dictionary, writes that the Jews of Spain assert that it is taken as a family name, to which one is entirely referred and related.

Be that as it may, this Averroes—a native of the city of Cordoba <note>original: "Cordube ou Cordone"</note> in Spain, born of a Princely house—was African by nation and a follower of the Muhammadan religion <note>Muslim</note>. He flourished around the year of salvation 1140, when Ali ibn Yusuf <note>original: "Albo Haly Aben Tesfin"</note>, the third *Amir al-Mu'minin* <note>Commander of the Faithful; original: "Miralumim otherwise Miramolim"</note> or King of the race of the Almoravids, reigned over the Moors of Africa and Spain, according to the report of Rabbi Abraham in his *Cabala* <note>likely referring to Abraham Zacuto’s historical work</note>. It is true that Sabellicus, in his 9th *Ennead*, holds that he flourished around the year of salvation 1159, as noted by Gilbert Génébrard in book 4 of his *Chronography*, and Gabriel du Préau in volume 1 of his *History of the State and Success of the Church*.

This Averroes wrote in his life an infinity of books in his Arabic language on Aristotle, with such depth that those of his time and those who came after him held him in such admiration that they almost equaled him to Aristotle himself. They gave him, by way of excellence, the title of "The Commentator"; indeed, some believed that during his life, he was the very soul of Aristotle returned to a body. Abraham de Balmis, a Jew, translated the majority of his books into the Latin language, printed in Venice at the press of the Giuntas. The great Pico della Mirandola, in this regard, said these words in his *Apology* and *Oration on the Dignity of Man*: "There is among the Arabs something solid and unshakable in Averroes; something divine and Platonic in Avicenna; and something weighty and meditated in Avenpace and Alfarabi, etc." <note>original Latin: "est apud Arabes quid in Aueroe firmum & inconcussum, in Auicenna, diuinum atque Platonicum, & in Auenpace & Alfarabio, graue & meditatũ &c."</note>.

This same Averroes also composed several books on mathematics and medicine in his own Arabic language, which have been printed in Venice at various times in the Latin language, and are divided into several parts as can be seen today in those currently in print. Besides these, Bernard Navagero <note>original: "Naugerius"</note> assures us there are others in the hands of the Arab physicians of Constantinople which have not yet come to our knowledge. This personage, for his great depth and subtlety, was given the title of "The Great," and was one of the most eloquent and articulate in...

The histories of the Turks record that the Great Turk Bayezid <note>Bayezid II</note>, being greatly afflicted by gout in his old age, used to take great delight in reading the Arabic writings of this personage. In the time of our fathers, one Ambrosius Leo Nolanus brought to light a thick book of corrections regarding this Averroes, which I have in my possession.

->*On the Physician Avicenna, and his writings composed in the Arabic language.*<-

**Abohaly** or **Albo Ali Abinseni** <note>Ibn Sina</note> was surnamed **Abinsene**, or **Avicenna**, because he was born and descended from the lineage of a Seni Arab, as if one were to say "son or great-grandson of Seni." This is written by Jacopo da Forlì in his commentaries on the first part of the writings of Avicenna. According to Elias Levita in his *The Tishbi* <note>A dictionary of Rabbinic Hebrew</note>, he had for a father an Arab by nation named Eli. He was a physician of Hispalis <note>Seville</note> and wrote during his life a great multitude of books in his Arabic language, as Gerard of Cremona (a native of Cremona in Italy) and other personages maintain in their versions and explanatory commentaries on them, as noted well by Conrad Gessner and Josias Simler in their *Historical Libraries*. This Avicenna was very eloquent in his Arabic tongue, quite modest for a Muhammadan <note>Muslim</note>, and having as good or better a feeling for God than any other Arab. He learned—a miraculous thing—before reaching the age of ten the entire Alcoran <note>The Quran</note> of his Prophet Muhammad by heart, and before the age of sixteen, the *Logic* of Aristotle without commentaries, and what is more, perfectly without any teacher, the books of
