Genebrard** <note>Gilbert Génébrard, a French theologian</note> in book 4 of his *Chronography*. **Nicolas Massa** and **Andrea Alpago** <note>original: "André Apage"</note>, under the authority of the **Arab al-Juzjani**, have assured that this person died at the age of 58 from a great illness that came upon him for having been too debauched in his youth; and that he flourished with **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rafis"</note>, **Albumasar**, and other great Arab figures of the time of **Mansur**, **Marin**, and **Joseph, Moorish Kings of Africa** commanding over **Morocco**, **Fez**, **Tlemcen** <note>original: "Telenfin"</note>, and in **Spain**, excellent in their religion, or rather, Muhammadan superstition. **Some Historians** hold that he was **Bactrian** by Nation, a native of **Bukhara** <note>original: "Baccora"</note> or **Basra** <note>original: "Bazora"</note>, a city in the **Uzbek** Province, or the **Region of the Chagatais** <note>original: "Zagatees"</note> in **Tartary**, and not an Arab; but rather that he was in the pay and service of the **Moorish Kings of Africa** who had come there, and who afterwards passed into **Spain**, as was left in writing by **Giovanni Battista Ramusio** in his preface to the travels of **Marco Polo the Venetian** in **Tartary** and later by **Garcia de Orta** <note>original: "Louys Garcie ab orto"</note> in book 1, chapter 3 of his *Epitome of the History of Spices*. In that place, the Arabian language is called **Araby**, that is to say, Arabian, in which one finds the works of **Galen** and other Philosophers composed in this language. The language of the **Mauritanians** <note>North African Moors</note> is called **Magaraby** <note>Maghrebi</note>, as if one wished to say, the language of those who dwell toward the West, for **Gharbi** <note>original: "Garbi"</note> means West in the Arabian language, and the word **Ma** [means] "of those." This **Avicenna** was the most universal among all the Arabs, and the most eminent in Philosophy, Mathematics, Poetry, and Arabian Theology above all others. Writing several works on medicine in his Arabian tongue, he treated very well, in the judgment of the most learned in this art, the signs and causes of diseases and infirmities, adapting to them several remedies not understood nor practiced by the Greeks, Latins, and others. Rather, these can be easily learned through the reading of his writings contained in four thick volumes translated from the Arabian language into Latin by one **Gerard of Cremona** <note>original: "Gerard Sabion, or Sablonede," an Italian translator known for his work in Toledo</note> and illustrated with commentaries by **Gentile da Foligno** <note>original: "Gentil Fulginate"</note> and others well enough known and leafed through by those who make a profession of medicine, to the great relief of the sick and indisposed. **Nicolas Massa**, cited above in the life of this person, reports that one **Andrea Alpago** <note>original: "André Apage, or Alpage"</note>, a physician by profession, was the first who translated the works of this doctor from Arabic into Latin, having gone specifically to **Syria** to learn the Arabian language. See **Conrad Gessner** and **Josias Simler** in their historical libraries; **André Thevet** in book 16, chapter 21 of his *Cosmography*, and volume 2, chapter 134 of his *Prosopographical History*; **François de Belleforest** in volume 2, book 4, chapter 1 of his *Universal Cosmography*; and **Louis Le Roy** in book 8 of the *Vicissitude of Things*.

### Concerning the Satirical Poet Eldebag, and his poems composed in the Arabic language.

**Eldebag** <note>likely Al-Dabbaj, an Andalusian poet</note>, a satirical poet, Arab by nation and a native of the city of **Malaga** in **Granada**, was well-renowned and known in this province of the **Moors** <note>the Muslim inhabitants of the Maghreb and Al-Andalus</note>. During his lifetime, he was highly eloquent and fluent in his Arabic tongue, and admirable in his ability to disparage others, having been one of the truest satirists to have ever existed among the Arabs. Indeed, this man, passing one day through a very well-walled city situated on the borders of **Numidia** <note>an ancient kingdom in North Africa, roughly modern-day Algeria</note> in a region abundant in walnut trees—through which city flows a great river, and which is located two hundred miles from the Mediterranean Sea on the southern side, named **Tébessa**—the inhabitants of which were very mean-spirited, miserly, and brutish. So far were they from honoring and welcoming strangers that they did not wish to see them in any way whatsoever. He composed these very stinging and biting verses after having been crudely treated by those inhabitants; the substance of these, translated from the Arabic language into Italian, or Tuscan, by **Leo Africanus** <note>original: "Iean Leon Arabe de nation," referring to the famous traveler and geographer al-Hasan al-Wazzan</note> in Book 5 of his *Description of Africa*, is as follows:

> *Nothing else in Tébessa, except for walnuts,*
> *Can be considered precious or worthy.*
> *I was wrong. There are also the walls, and the clear waters*
> *Of the nearby river; and as for virtue, it is empty.*
> *Shall I say it? It is hell, and so many swine*
> *Are the inhabitants of its houses.*
<note>original Italian: "Fuor, che le noci, altro non é in Tebessa. / Che si possa stimar pregiato é degno. / Errai. Et son le mura, & l’acque chiare / Del vicin fiume: é di virtute é sigombra / Dirollo? elle é l’inferno, & tanti Porci / Sono gli habitatori d’elle sue Case."</note>

These verses, thus translated into the French language by **Jean Temporal** <note>a 16th-century French translator known for his editions of travel accounts</note>, signify the following:

> *Tébessa has nothing of value*
> *Except for walnuts; I am mistaken, it has the luck*
> *Of having a river whose crystalline waters,*
> *And the wide circuit of its notable walls,*
> *Give it luster; yet as for virtue,*
> *The people are so stripped of it*
> *That, seeing nature shine in this place,*
> *All vice causes walnuts to grow in abundance,*
> *As if knowing that along with the sweet waters,*
> *Brutish spirits feed themselves like swine.*

The writings of this poet are not easily found today in **Asia** and **Turkey**, despite whatever diligent research I have conducted to recover them. See **Leo Africanus** <note>original: "I. Leon"</note> cited above, Book 5 of his *Description of Africa*, the chapter on **Tébessa**.

## Concerning the poet Ibn al-Farid, and his poems composed in the Arabic language.

**Ibn al-Farid** <note>original: "Ibun Farid"; refers to the famous Egyptian Sufi poet Umar Ibn al-Farid (1181–1234)</note>, a native of the city of **Fez** <note>The author likely mistakes his birthplace, as Ibn al-Farid was born in Cairo, though his work was widely influential across North Africa</note> in Africa, Arab by nation and **Muslim** <note>original: "Mahometan"</note> by religion, was from his childhood a great and admirable Arabic poet. He applied himself to composing a certain doctrine that he followed into very graceful, exquisite, flowing, and fluid Arabic verses and poems, yet all filled with metaphors and allegories. So much so, it seems he treats of nothing other than love. This incited a certain person, also Arab by nation, named **Al-Farghani** <note>original: "Elfragani"; Sa'id al-Din al-Farghani, a prominent commentator on Ibn al-Farid's "Poem of the Way"</note>, to comment on his poems, from which he drew the rules and the degrees—which one must pass through to the number of fifty-two—to arrive at the knowledge of the **Angelic nature**. As he says, once this knowledge is acquired, it is so strong and powerful that man cannot err or sin, even if he were to try, as those of the Muslim faith believe and assert. This poet adorned and enriched his Arabic writings with such great and perfect eloquence that the followers of his doctrine recite and sing no other poems or songs in their private and public festivals and dances than his Arabic verses and poems. For there has not been found anyone in the last four hundred or so years who has written as eloquently and elegantly as he. Those who have followed and do follow his doctrine maintain that the celestial spheres, the firmament, the elements, the planets, and all the stars are gods, and that one cannot err in any faith or law whatsoever, since all men intend to adore that which deserves to be adored; and if they thought they were doing wrong, they would not do it for anything in the world.

**Leo Africanus** <note>original: "I. Leon Africain"</note>, Arab by nation, in Book 1 of his *Description of Africa*, in the chapter on the way of life and customs of the Arabs living in Africa, writes that these Arabs hold poetry in great account and admire it greatly. Devoting themselves to it, they compose poems most often enriched with perfect eloquence, even though their language may be corrupted <note>a reference to the development of regional Arabic dialects compared to Classical Arabic</note>. A poet, however little renowned he may be among them, is very welcome before their Lords, who, for the pleasure they receive from their verses, reward them generously. They go about asserting that it would be impossible to express the great grace they have in their poems. The same author, in Book 3 of the same history, in the chapter on poets in the African vernacular, wrote as follows:

> There are also several<margin>,,</margin>

> contaminate their papers, publishing through them the illicit and disor-<margin>,,</margin>

### On the Region of the Saracens.

## CHAP. XLVII.

Abraham Ortelius, in his *Geographical Treasury and Synonyms*, speaking of this region of the Saracens:

Saracena <note>Σαρακηνὴ</note>, a region of Stony Arabia <note>Arabiæ Petreæ</note> in Ptolemy. The Saracens are in Arabia Felix <note>Happy Arabia</note> according to Ptolemy and Pliny. The Saracens are mentioned in the Panegyric of Maximian addressed to Aurelian, and that of Pacatus addressed to Theodosius. These were formerly called Hagarenes <note>Descendants of Hagar</note> and Ishmaelites, as Sozomen testifies. Also called Arabs and Scenitae <note>From the Greek word for "tent-dwellers."</note>, according to Ammianus; Ptolemy places both in Arabia Felix. To the Hebrews they are the *Chaslubim* <note>The Casluhim, mentioned in the Table of Nations in Genesis.</note>, as Arias Montanus writes. For the Saracens, consult Emperor Leo, chapter 18, number 119. The Council of Chalcedon mentions the cities of the Saracens in the province of Palestine more than once. I consider it the same as Ptolemy's tract of Stony Arabia. These Ishmaelites are called Nomads by Theodoret in *On the Greek Affections*, book 9. See Troglodytes.

Pliny and Ptolemy place the region of the Troglodytes <note>Τρωγλοδύτων, literally "cave-dwellers."</note> in Africa; see the description of these people in Heliodorus, book 8, and Agatharchides, book 5; likewise Strabo, book 16. Today it is called Sirfia by Giacomo Castaldi. To me, it seems to be called Arabia by more recent writers. Eustathius is the authority that these Troglodytes were also once called Erembi <note>Ἐρεμβοὶ</note> and Saracens. They are also called Molgii <note>Μόλγιοι</note> by Diodorus Siculus, book 1, though the reading varies: for it is read as Bolgi <note>Βόλγοι</note> and Bolpi <note>Βόλποι</note> in the Greek Codex published by Henri Estienne <note>Original: "Henrico Stephano."</note>. I see they were also named *Ichthyophagoi* <note>ἰχθυοφάγοι, or "fish-eaters."</note> by Isaac Tzetzes. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

Pintianus <note>Fernán Núñez de Guzmán (c. 1475–1553), a Spanish scholar known as Pintianus.</note> reports that in his preparation, "Troglodytes" <note>original: "Trogodytas." This refers to "cave-dwellers."</note> is always written without an "l" in the works of Strabo; let the credit for that remain with him. Juba <note>Juba II, King of Mauretania and a prolific scholar in antiquity.</note>, cited in Pliny, writes that the Troglodyte tribes are called *Terothioas* based on their skill in hunting. Strabo places Troglodytes above the Caucasian mountains, just as Eustathius places them near the Triballi in Europe; I believe these are the same as those mentioned by Pliny and Ptolemy in lower Moesia <note>A Roman province in the Balkans.</note>. Along the Atlantic Sea in Africa, Hanno and Pliny also record the presence of Troglodytes. The same Juba tells of the island of the Troglodytes, where he says the "hair of Isis" <note>original: "Isidos plocamon." A type of coral or sea plant named after the goddess Isis.</note> originates; see also the Catudaei and Suchae of Barbary.

->## On the Saracens.<-

Ptolemy, Book 6, Chapter 11, Map 6 of Asia, speaks thus of the Saracens: "The entire stretch of the country neighboring the mountains of the Aracene region, located in Arabia Felix <note>Latin for "Happy Arabia," the fertile southern portion of the Arabian Peninsula.</note> toward the North, is inhabited by the Scenites <note>Literally "Tent-dwellers," from the Greek *skene* (tent).</note>; above them are the Oadites, and further toward the South are the Saracens and Thamydetes." Pliny, Book 6, Chapter 28, says these words: "The ancients joined the Thymaneans to the Nabateans, who are now the Tauenes, Suellenies, and Saracens."

Sozomen <note>Salminius Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400–450 AD), a historian of the early Christian Church.</note>, Book 6, Chapter 38 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, writes the following: "This nation took its origin from Ishmael, son of Abraham, and is also named after him; for this reason, the ancients called them Ishmaelites. But in order to wash themselves of this stain of bastardy and to rid themselves of the infamous title of being slaves and commoners, and to put aside the obscurity of the blood of Hagar, Ishmael’s mother (for she was a servant and slave by condition), they usurped the name of Saracens, as if they had been procreated from the legitimate bed of Abraham and Sarah his wife <note>A popular medieval etymology (Sarah-cen) which historians now generally view as a folk etymology. The term likely derives from an Arabic root meaning "easterners" or "raiders."</note>. Taking their lineage from there, they are also circumcised, following the manner and ceremony of the Hebrews; and like the Jews, they abstain from the flesh of the pig and keep several other observations proper to the Jewish nation. If they do not follow all the same rules and laws of living as the Hebrews, it must be imputed both to the long stretch of time they have been separated from their kin, and to the influence of their neighborhood, having always lived among idolaters. And lest I seem to misuse a single country for all the rest, I have good and sufficient authors from whom we gather that all Arabs in general have been named Saracens; for regarding the Hagarenes, we have already declared it before, whether named after Hagar the concubine or the city of Agra founded by the aforementioned woman." Procopius, Book 2 of the *Persian War*, speaking of the King of Arabia bearing the name Arethas <note>Harith ibn Jabalah, a famous 6th-century king of the Ghassanids.</note>, as did the other Kings his predecessors, uses these words: "A short time later, Arethas and Al-Mundhir <note>Al-Mundhir III ibn al-Nu'man, leader of the Lakhmids.</note>, captain of the Saracens, resolved to make war on each other, without seeking help, one from the Romans and the other from the Persians." These two were Kings of Arabia, and yet they are called chiefs of the Saracens. To this agrees Ammianus Marcellinus, Books 22 and 23, when he describes the land of Egypt, saying: "On the side facing the East, there is Elephantine and Meroë, cities of Ethiopia, and the Catadupes <note>The cataracts of the Nile, where the water makes a crashing noise (from Greek *kata-doupein*).</note>, and the Red Sea extends as far as the Scenite Arabs, whom they now call Saracens." In short, this author, wherever in his writings he makes mention of the Arabs, does not name them otherwise...

...otherwise than as Saracens, as if the ancient name of "Arab" had grown old, and this new one were more pleasing and honorable to them, and better received among other nations. This is why Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work was the primary source for herbal medicine for centuries.</note> calls Myrrh "Saracen," not because it grows among the Scenites <note>Literally "tent-dwellers," referring to nomadic tribes.</note> who are properly the Saracens, but in Arabia Felix <note>Latin for "Happy Arabia," the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula.</note>. This gives clear evidence that under the word Saracen, all of Arabia is included, just as since then this same name has embraced all the followers of the Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> of Muhammad, especially since this perverse law received its first establishment among these Saracens.

These people have been known since antiquity and have shown themselves to be enemies of the Romans; likewise, they have hardly ever maintained a firm friendship with anyone. It is true that when Pompey the Great was waging war in Asia, these Arab Saracens took up arms under him and were in his pay; but in the course of time they emancipated themselves, and unable to forget their nature, returned to their raids. This was the reason why Aelius Gallus <note>A Roman prefect of Egypt who led an expedition into Arabia in 24 BC.</note>, of whom Strabo speaks in Book 16, crossed into Arabia and subdued a good part of it. Under Trajan, another enterprise was undertaken by this Emperor against these Saracens. Having been brought to heel, they began once more to run and ravage the borders of the Empire when Odenatus and his wife Zenobia <note>The famous 3rd-century queen of the Palmyrene Empire who challenged Roman authority.</note> held the East as their portion. After this Lady was defeated by Aurelian in the year of Grace 270, according to Vopiscus <note>Flavius Vopiscus, one of the six traditional authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note>, the Saracens remained quiet until the time of Constantine the Great. Having been long unknown, as it were, they then made themselves recognized by their raids and thefts, so that people began to hold them in great hatred. When the war against the Persians was opened by the children of the aforementioned Constantine, the most expedient thing found for the peace of the Empire was to win over the Saracens, although there was never much reason to trust them because of their inconstancy and disloyalty.

This is amply testified by the aforementioned Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian.</note> in Book 14, saying that the Saracens were never good friends to the Romans. Rushing about everywhere, they ravaged in a moment of time everything they could encounter, resembling a predatory kite <note>original: "milan rauiſſant"</note>, which lives only on plundered prey and which, seeing its meat from afar, carries it off and snatches it in a sudden flight; or, if given food, they do not stop to enjoy it on the spot. In short, this figure speaks and discourses on these Saracens and their raids and thefts at length in his 23rd, 24th, and 25th books, always taking these Saracens to mean all Arabs. It must be understood that this people has always been inconstant in its faith and belief, and has never been able to remain in the perfection of one law; above all, they never knew how to settle on the one that was most holy.

For it is to be believed that their father Ishmael <note>According to the Book of Genesis, the son of Abraham and ancestor of the Arab people.</note> had been instructed by Abraham in the fear of a single God, and that he had given instruction to those who took their origin from him. But suddenly they forgot the great God and ran after idols <note>original: "simulachres"</note>, retaining no other part of the Religion of Abraham than the external ceremony of circumcision. And when they became Christians and were baptized, this Christian reformation being against their hearts, as something entirely contrary to their ways of doing things, they also suddenly left it to embrace the heresy diversified by so many monsters that came after Arius <note>A 4th-century priest who taught that Jesus was not co-eternal with God the Father, a belief known as Arianism.</note>, and finally subjected themselves...

Sozomen, in Book 6, Chapter 38 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, discusses at great length how, under the reign of Mavia <note>Mavia (r. c. 375–425) was a warrior queen of the Tanukhids, a confederation of Arab tribes.</note>, their Queen, they received and embraced Christianity. This occurred under the Empire of Valens, who succeeded Jovian around the year of our salvation 382, which was a long time before Muhammad came into the world to infect it with his doctrine. Some time later, Zocome, Prince and Governor of a province of the Saracens, also became a Christian along with his subjects. They remained in the Christian faith until the Persians, ruining the holy places and massacring these Christian Saracens, caused them to forget their faith and doctrine. They then allowed themselves to be led like beasts to the law of the aforementioned Muhammad, which is entirely full of license and concupiscence. Furthermore, as soon as these people were emancipated from the Christian faith, they rushed—during the reign of Emperor Anastasius—upon the lands of Phoenicia and Palestine, around the year of salvation 504, according to the report of Paul the Deacon in Book 15 of the *Roman Deeds*. The leader, author, and conductor of this incursion was one Vadicarim, who succeeded his brother Hagar in the government of the Saracens. He was like a lightning bolt or a whirlwind, passing so suddenly and wasting everything with a cruel and terrifying fury.

These Saracens were tributaries to the Emperor Justinian, as demonstrated by the aforementioned Paul the Deacon in Book 16 of the *Roman Deeds*, where he mentions Arethas <note>original: "Arethe"; likely Al-Harith ibn Jabalah, a King of the Ghassanids and a prominent Byzantine ally.</note>, a Patrician and Prince of these Saracens. He came to the court of the aforementioned Justinian to bring the said tribute and to pray that the Emperor grant him the grace that his children might hold his Kingdom after him. This King Arethas was very loyal to the Romans and greatly aided Justin the Younger against the King of Persia.

But by the time of Heraclius, everything had changed among these Saracens. Some of them were idolaters to please the Persians, others were "Judaizing" <note>Adopting Jewish customs or laws.</note>, and a small number followed the Christian religion. They overran the lands of the Roman Empire and threw themselves upon the country of Syria when Khosrow, King of Persia, took the city of Jerusalem and committed infinite evils and ravages against the poor Christians in the year of salvation 515 <note>The source date 515 is historically early; the Persian conquest of Jerusalem under Khosrow II actually took place in 614 AD.</note>, according to the *Annals of Constantinople*, Book 18.

During the time of this Emperor Heraclius, "Muchamet" or Muhammad commanded these Saracens, as I have noted in this work. This seducer having reigned nine years, he had as his successor "Ebubezer" <note>Abu Bakr (c. 573–634), the first Caliph.</note>. Because he received a pension from Heraclius to guard the borders of the Empire against the Persians, it happened that the man in charge of paying them—when the Saracens asked for what was owed to them—answered them proudly: "What? The Emperor can barely pay his soldiers, and must these dogs ask him for pensions?" These words cost the Christians dearly; for Abu Bakr, informed of the insult done to his entire nation, took up arms and entered Palestine, killing the Roman garrisons. He took the city of Gaza and all the surrounding country. At this time, these Saracens also defeated the Persians and killed their King, Hormizd, bringing an end to that Monarchy.

In the year of grace 719 died Sulayman, and one of his Admirals, namely Umar <note>original: "Haumar," referring to Umar II</note>, son of Abd al-Aziz <note>original: "Habdimazid"</note>, was made Admiral and Sovereign of the Saracens. He, spiteful over the loss received before Constantinople and irritated because he had lost most of his forces, set himself to furiously persecute the Christians, and to constrain them to deny their faith by making themselves Mahometans <note>followers of Muhammad</note>, or else to die without any respite. Those who became Mahometans he exempted from all subsidies <note>the *jizya*, or tax on non-Muslim subjects</note>; but those who remained firm were tormented without rest until death, so that many were massacred under this adversary of the Christians. He also made a Law by which it was not permitted for a Christian to testify against a Mahometan; if he did so, his testimony was without effect or any value, which is observed among the Turks to this day.

This Umar reigned only two years, and upon his death he was succeeded by Yazid <note>original: "Gizid," referring to Yazid II</note>, second of that name. As soon as he was received into his principality, he had business against another Yazid <note>Yazid ibn al-Muhallab</note> who tried to make himself Lord and Tyrant of Persia, where he was a native; but the former sent Maslama against this occupier, who slew him and returned the Persians to their duty. To this Yazid came a Jew, who made him believe that if he cast down the images from the Churches of the Christians, he would be a peaceful King over his people for the space of forty years. Believing this, the foolish Arab set himself to persecute the images <note>this refers to the Iconoclastic movement</note>, in which he gratified the Emperor, but he was deceived in his hope: for he lived as King for only four years.

Yazid was succeeded by Hisham <note>original: "Euclid," a likely corruption of Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik</note> his son, who occupied himself with building palaces and places of pleasure throughout the cities of his obedience, and with erecting aqueducts for the ornament and use of the citizens. He also made war against the Romans <note>the Byzantines</note>, and under him two of his Admirals went to besiege the City of Nicaea <note>original: "Nicie"</note> in Bithynia; but whatever great effort they made, and though their number was infinite, they nevertheless returned without gaining anything. The Prince was afflicted by civil wars, for Sulayman rose against him, but he was defeated and forced to save himself by fleeing to Palmyra, and from there to the land of Persia. Dahhak also revolted, having the citizens of Homs in his favor; Marwan, going before Dahhak in Mesopotamia, broke this revolt, defeated, and killed the man who thought to depose him from his lordship. It was this Salih who was the first among the Saracens to forbid the Christians from building churches, from seeing the cross, and from disputing in any manner concerning religion, or from teaching or discoursing upon their Christian religion before the Arabs. This Salih went to make war upon the Christians in the Roman territories of Asia subject to the Emperor, but hearing that Constantine Copronymus <note>Byzantine Emperor Constantine V, given the derogatory nickname "Copronymus" (meaning "named for dung") by his theological opponents</note> was coming against him toward the land of Cappadocia, he returned without achieving anything.

Abdallah, meanwhile, who was the Great Sultan or Caliph, showed himself hardly any gentler to the Christians, upon whom he doubled the tributes, taxes, and other charges, forcing the monks, the hermits, and the clergy to pay him tax like the laity—something which none of his predecessors had presumed to do. And what is worse, he laid hands upon the relics and jewels of the churches and made the Jews purchase them, which they did easily, being certain that the Christians would not delay long in ransoming them.

It was at this time—namely, in the year of grace 764—that the Scythians, surnamed Turks, passing through the Caspian Gates, rushed upon Armenia and fought a battle against the Agarenes <note>A common medieval term for Muslims, implying they were descendants of Hagar</note>, with a great massacre being made on all sides. It was during this season, and in the year of grace 800, that this Harun, having heard tell of the strength and valor of the great Charlemagne, King of France—who had recently been elected and made Emperor of the Romans—sent him an elephant <note>This was the famous elephant named Abul-Abbas</note> and other great presents. To please him, he released several Christians whom he held in servitude, according to the account of Paolo Emilio <note>original: "Paule Emile," an Italian historian who wrote the *De rebus gestis Francorum*</note> in the third book of the *Annals of France*. 

Nicephorus <note>Emperor Nicephorus I (r. 802–811)</note>, having succeeded Irene as Emperor of Constantinople, made an agreement with the aforementioned Charlemagne so that he could defend himself against the aforementioned Harun, who was making war upon him. Harun defeated him in the land of Phrygia and placed him in such distress that, had Nicephorus not saved himself by a very sudden flight, he would have served as prey to Harun, King of Persia, who had just come from his Persian kingdom to settle some discords that had arisen there. After this, Harun, with 300,000 combatants, entered Asia Minor and took the city of Tyana <note>original: "Thiane"</note>, where he had a mosque built for the exercise of his impiety <note>The author uses "impiety" here from a 16th-century Christian perspective to refer to Islamic worship</note>. Having seen the city, he withdrew without otherwise trying to besiege it or take it by force. This was because Nicephorus sent to beg him for peace, which he accepted from the infidel at the price of 300,000 gold crowns paid once, and a certain annual tribute <term>jizya|a poll tax paid by non-Muslim subjects</term>, both for the head of the Emperor and for his children. This gave a marvelous satisfaction to Harun, who thereby glorified himself for having subjected the Roman Empire, having made a tributary of the man who bore the title of its sovereign. 

But after Nicephorus fortified some places ruined by the Arab, Harun cast them down again; breaking the peace, he came to Cyprus, where he ruined the churches, drove out the islanders, and did infinite evils to the Christians throughout Asia. After this, in the year of our Lord 807, he sent one of his captains named Humayd <note>original: "Chumeid," likely Humayd ibn Ma'yuf al-Hajuri</note> against the island of Rhodes. Landing there, he pillaged it and greatly impoverished it, but he did not take the fortress. Returning, as he touched upon the city of Myra, he saw himself punished by its patron, namely Saint Nicholas, so that he repaired the damages he had done there. Meanwhile, this sovereign Prince of the Arabs died in Khorasan <note>original: "Corasan"</note> in the Kingdom of Persia. 

He had as a successor Muhammad <note>Caliph al-Amin</note>, against whom his brother Abdallah <note>Caliph al-Ma'mun</note> rose up. From this followed a division among the Arabs and the diminishing of their power, which caused both ruin among themselves and great persecution for the Christians subject to their rule. From this it happened that the churches in the Holy City were both ruined and deserted, and the monasteries scattered throughout Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and the surrounding places felt the fire of this storm. In that same season, and in the year of grace 826, the Hagarenes <note>original: "Agarenes," a medieval term for Muslims, referring to their traditional descent from Hagar</note> crossed into Crete <note>original: "Candie"</note>, plundered it, overran it, and made it their home. And Abdallah, having reigned 17 years, died and left the Sultanate <note>original: "Saltanie"</note> to Muhammad, third of that name, who held it for the space of 40 years. Under him, the affairs of the Hagarenes did not go very well in Syria, inasmuch as the Emperor Theophilus beat them several times and conquered several cities from them. 

So it was that as the glory and strength of the Hagarenes vanished in the East, they regained vigor in Africa—as we shall say at another time, for fear of confusing the order of history and mixing the African Saracens or Hagarenes with those of Syria, Egypt, Arabia, Mesopotamia, or Persia. In short, this Muhammad was the last of the Admirals descended from the lineage of the four Captains and Impostors who followed the Pseudo-Prophet Muhammad <note>original: "Mahometh"</note>, when he planted his Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> and his doctrine with the sword. These lineages held their Monarchy for the space of about 250 years, from the false Prophet until the end of the reign of this Muhammad, successor to Abdallah. It seems that this Monarchy was greatly shaken because suddenly the Turks began to raid, the Egyptians to establish their Sultanate, the Persians their empire, and the Arabs strove to remain free, with every city in Syria seeking to have its own Prince. 

To Muhammad succeeded Amer <note>Umar al-Aqta, the Emir of Melitene</note>, but the histories make no mention to assure you of which lineage he came from; nonetheless, it is likely that he was of an illustrious house, since that people then accepted no one unless he was among the greatest and most distinguished of the men of war. He was attacked by the Emperor of the Greeks, Michael <note>Michael III, r. 842–867</note>, son of Theophilus, who went to besiege the city of Samosata. But the Hagarenes, feigning fear, made no show of defending themselves, but kept themselves closed inside their city. This gave the Greeks too much confidence, so much so that they no longer bothered to keep watch, nor set up guard posts or sentinels, but went wandering aimlessly here and there through the countryside. Seeing this, the Hagarenes fell upon them with such vehemence that, putting them to flight, they ruined the entire army, and the Emperor himself narrowly escaped being among the prisoners. Twice this Emperor was handled by the Arabs in this manner. But at the third time Petronas, his uncle, undertaking the charge of the war, thrashed those Hagarenes so well that Amer their Prince was slain there, and the rest put to flight. To this Amer succeeded—

[an]cient language is spoken there, or if it is used, it is only with a corruption as great as that seen when the Goths, Vandals, and Lombards corrupted the natural languages of the nations they conquered, or as the Romans practiced in the past in the lands they subjected. Now, whatever alteration of faith there may have been, both in the time of the Arians <note>A group of early Christians who held specific beliefs about the nature of Jesus that were later declared heretical by the mainstream Church.</note> and in the time of the Arabs and Mohammadans <term>Mahometistes: an archaic term for Muslims</term> in Africa, God always left himself some chosen and elect families who followed the ancient faith of the Church. 

Such was the case in Morocco, where there was a race of Christian gentlemen called *Farfanes*, good knights, who came to King John I of Spain while he was at Alcalá de Henares, as is recounted in Book 15, Chapter 27 of the history of Spain. In our own time, there were still seen in Tunis, when the Emperor Charles V <note>The Holy Roman Emperor who captured Tunis in 1535.</note> went there, certain Christians who had their church separate from those of the Moors; they were called Rabatins. So that they might more freely devote themselves to divine service and enjoy the holy Sacraments of the church, this great Emperor had them move to Naples, granting them great favors and privileges.

In the year of grace 707, Abdemelic <note>Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan</note> having died, Walid <note>original: "Vlid"</note> was called to the crown under the name of Walid I, issued from the blood of Muhammad and the family of Aben Humcia. His lordships were so great that he commanded all of Africa, from the Strait of Gibraltar to the Red Sea, and even extended into the East, striking great fear into everyone. But from where he drew his greatness, he also saw its diminishment and decline. 

For it happened in the year of our Lord 712 or 718, according to Esteban de Garibay (Book 16, Chapter 16 of the history of Spain), that Roderic, the Visigoth King in Spain, seduced Cava, the wife <note>Though historical legends often identify Florinda "La Cava" as the daughter of Count Julian, this text identifies her as his wife.</note> of the Count of Ceuta <note>original: "Septe"</note> called Julian. He, grieved by such an insult, prompted Musa <note>original: "Muça"</note> Aben Zair, an Arab by nation and Lieutenant of Walid in Africa, to cross into Spain. Having informed his Master and Lord Walid, he was given permission to give a light troop to the Count to raid the lands of Spain and Portugal. 

Seeing that matters were succeeding as desired, he sent greater forces, and finally Aben Zair crossed himself with more power than ever. These Mohammadans conquered Seville and forced the Christians to retreat to Asturias and Biscay, where the Spanish nobility preserved themselves for many years for the defense of the Christian faith and the repopulation of the Spains. Inasmuch as the Arabs call their Kings Miramolins, that is to say, "the greatest of the believers." 

The histories of the Saracens state that a certain Saracen person named Abd al-Rahman <note>original: "Abedramon"</note>, descended from the ancient Caliphs of Damascus, was the first among his people who, having retired to Mauretania Tingitana <note>A Roman province located in what is now northern Morocco.</note>, had himself named and called *Miralmumin*, which is to say in the Arabic language, "Prince of the Believers." The Christians, unable to suffer this insult, took up arms and began the war, which did not cease until our time, when the Mohammadans were entirely driven out of Spain.

This Ayyub lived five years in his principality, and was succeeded by a Mohammadan Lord called Alhor <note>Al-Hurr</note>, who, while practicing his grandeur, saw the death of Suleiman <note>original: "Culema," likely referring to Caliph Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik</note>, who ordained as his heirs two of his cousins called Omar <note>Omar II</note> and Yazid <note>Yazid II</note>, sons of the King Walid <note>original: "Vlid"</note> mentioned above. Upon his death in the year of grace 720, the two aforementioned came to the Crown, and when Omar died, Yazid (or Gizid), second of the name and third Moorish King over Spain, held the whole empire. He sent Adha as governor to Spain, whom some call Al-Samh <note>original: "Azá"</note> and others Abraham son of Melit. Being the third Prince and governor of Cordoba, he built there the bridge that is seen today over the River Baetis <note>original: "Bethis"</note>, which is now called the Guadalquivir; and it was also he who, first among the Moors, began to raid the Gauls <note>Modern-day France</note>, and who tried to make himself Lord of the lands the Goths had possessed in Languedoc and Gascony. But before arriving there, being at Tortosa, a city seated on the River Ebro in the country of Catalonia, he died. He was substituted in the government by Zaman <note>As-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani</note>, who crossed the Pyrenees mountains and, taking the city of Narbonne, dared not rush upon Toulouse, which had been the royal seat of the Gothic Princes. In this war Zaman died, and in his place was put one whom Yazid sent, called Abderrahamen <note>Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi</note>, otherwise Abdirame. At this time, which was the year of grace 722, Pelagius <note>Pelayo, founder of the Kingdom of Asturias</note>, a Christian King in Spain and of the blood of the Goths, conquered the city of Leon. Two years later died Yazid, sovereign King of the Moors, succeeded by Hisham <note>original: "Hiscan"</note>, who was the most powerful King who had yet been among the Mohammadans, as he had under his Empire part of Asia Minor, Syria, the Medes, Hyrcanians, Persians, all the Arabias, Judea, Egypt, some part of Ethiopia, then Africa, Sicily, Apulia, and Calabria, and many lands in Gaul, and all the Spains, so well that he could boast of being the greatest Prince in the world. And of this lineage was a man named Abd-ar-Rahman <note>original: "Abderrahamé"</note>, of the Umayyad line <note>original: "Abé Humeya," referring to the Banu Umayya</note>, who came to Spain with the intention of making himself King there and standing against the Abbasid lineage <note>original: "race d'Alabeci," the dynasty that overthrew the Umayyads in the East</note>. No sooner had he arrived in Spain than he made war against Joseph <note>Yusuf ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Fihri, the last governor of Al-Andalus</note>, and he did not cease until he had put him to death and made himself King of Spain. Thus was the Muhammadan Empire divided: there was one King over the Arabs <note>The Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad</note>, another over the Africans, and the third in Spain.

Abd-ar-Rahman, therefore, the first King of Cordoba and the tenth in number among the Muhammadan usurpers of Spain, resolved to keep his court at Cordoba. But because Toledo was, as it were, the capital of the Spanish kingdom, he desired that his son Sulayman <note>original: "Culema"</note> of the Umayyad line should be governor there. He then set about making war against the Christian King of Spain, against whom he gained nothing but blows, and worse still befell him: for as soon as he called himself the Prince of the Believers <note>original: "Miramomelin" or "Miramolin," a corruption of the Arabic title *Amir al-Mu'minin*</note> of Spain, the Moors who were in Valencia refused to obey him, saying instead that they were subjects of the Abbasid blood. But this Abd-ar-Rahman went to besiege Valencia and took it; nonetheless, divisions continued in Spain, in as much as Ibn al-Arabi <note>original: "Hibduabala," likely referring to Sulayman ibn al-Arabi</note> made himself King of Saragossa. However, he was soon deposed by Abu-Tahir <note>original: "Abautar"</note> and Denisez, his Moorish captains. This was the reason he came to France to see Charlemagne <note>original: "Charles le grād"</note>, who restored him to his kingdom in the year 778, on the condition that the Christians would live in freedom of conscience and have the free exercise of their religion in his lands.

Abd-ar-Rahman having died in the year 780 <note>Modern historians date his death to 788</note>, he had as successor Hisham <note>original: "Hisé"</note> his son, the first of that name. Although he was a younger son, he usurped the state, which gave occasion for another division in the Kingdom, as most of the neighbors gave their obedience to Sulayman, who established his royal seat at Toledo and had himself called Prince of the Believers. It was from this that the kingdom of Toledo took its beginning, just as the rest of the kingdoms in Spain have their foundation in the divisions of the Moors. The two brothers went to war together and fought near Vilches, where King Hisham was victorious. From there, he went to besiege Toledo, which surrendered by agreement without a blow being struck. Sulayman, despairing of recovering his heritage, went to Africa to draw help from there and recover his losses. Hisham <note>original: "Hisen"</note> then made war to retake Languedoc, which had been conquered by some of his predecessors; but having performed some successful exploits there, in the end, by the help of the Emperor Charlemagne, this Moorish King was so thoroughly defeated that most of his cities paid tribute to the aforementioned Emperor, from which Hisham died of vexation in the year 794.

To this valiant King succeeded his eldest son Al-Hakam <note>original: "Hali Hatā" or "Alhacan"</note>, who was the first to order a guard of renegade Christians at his gate; he kept five thousand of them as a regular force to be near his person, just as the Grand Turk currently does with the Janissaries <note>The author compares the elite guard of Cordoba to the Ottoman Janissary corps familiar to 16th-century readers</note>. While he was occupied with his grandeurs, his cousin Sulayman plotted with the citizens of Toledo, and passing with forces from Africa into Spain, he made himself lord of Valencia and regained Toledo. But his joy was not great, for Al-Hakam went to meet him and they came to blows; Sulayman lost both the battle and his life. His brother Abdallah, whom he had brought from Africa, was taken and well-treated by Al-Hakam, who was nine years without being able to recover the city of Toledo. But in the end, he took it by a clever ruse, pretending to want to make peace and offer good treatment, but finally putting to death five or six thousand of the principal citizens <note>A reference to the "Day of the Foss" in 807</note>. During that time, the Christians, aided by the French, were making great conquests in Catalonia <note>original: "Cathelogne"</note>. Abd-ar-Rahman <note>original: "Abderahamen," referring to Abd-ar-Rahman II (r. 822–852)</note>, the second of that name, marched upon Barcelona and took it from the Christians. However, he did not enjoy it for long. During the reign of Louis the Pious in France, Aymon, the Governor of Guyenne <note>Aymon of Aquitaine, who rebelled against Louis the Pious</note>, revolted against his King and joined this Muhammadan King. Together, they besieged Barcelona once more, but it was in vain; they were forced to retreat without achieving anything. He also witnessed the revolts of Zaragoza and Toledo. Thus, the King of Toledo continued <note>The text implies a period of independent rule for Toledo</note>, and a Moor named Musa ibn Hazm <note>original: "Muca Aben Heazin," likely referring to Musa ibn Musa of the Banu Qasi family</note> was made King, being the second ruler of that seat. Leaving his son to govern his lands, he went to wage war against the Christians in Navarre and on the side of Catalonia. However, he was so thoroughly beaten there that, losing his army, he was mortally wounded. He left his son, Lubb ibn Musa <note>original: "Aben Lopé"</note>, as the third King of Toledo, who, fearing Abd-ar-Rahman, formed an alliance with Ordoño, King of Galicia and the Asturias <note>Ordoño I (r. 850–866)</note>.

Upon the death of Abd-ar-Rahman, his son Muhammad succeeded him, the second of that name if one includes the false Prophet Muhammad in the count. He felt the revolt of his subjects against his Kingdom, who were aided by the Christians. However, this cunning Muhammad defeated them by a ruse, killing thirteen thousand Moors and eight thousand Christians. Being unable to take Toledo, he placed garrisons at Coria <note>original: "Corite"</note>, Alcalá de Henares, Talavera, and Calatrava. Finally, he held the city so pressed by famine that it surrendered by agreement in the year 844. Then, giving himself over to pleasures, he died in the year of grace 874 <note>Historical records typically date Muhammad I's death to 886</note>, having reigned for thirty-five years.

Al-Mundhir <note>original: "Almudir"</note>, the first of that name and son of this Muhammad, came to the crown, obeyed by those of Cordoba, Seville, and all of Andalusia. This Al-Mundhir was devoted to pleasures and bodily filth, leaving several sons and daughters, though none succeeded him. He waged no war against the Christians, just as he was never attacked by them, and he died in the year 876. He had as his successor Abdullah <note>original: "Abdalla"</note>, the third of the name and seventh King of Cordoba, who was his brother, or, as others say, his nephew. He also passed his time in peace with the Christians and died in the year 889.

He was succeeded by Abd-ar-Rahman III <note>r. 912–961</note>, whom some call Almanzor <note>original: "Almançor," meaning "The Victorious"; a title later famously used by the vizier Ibn Abi Amir</note>, the son of Abdullah. As soon as he became King, he took the title in his records of *An-Nasir li-Din Allah* <note>original: "Ananzer Ledin Alla," meaning "Defender of the Religion of God"</note>. In his time, the Christians laid siege to Talavera in the Castilian kingdom of Toledo. He sent reinforcements which the Spaniards defeated, taking the city and the general of the Muhammadan army. This so incited and moved the heart of this King that he sent to Africa to King Al-Mutarrif <note>original: "Almotaraph"</note>, who commanded over the <term>Tingitane</term> <note>Referring to Mauretania Tingitana, the Roman name for the region of Morocco</note>, namely over Fez and Marrakesh, who sent forces. Thus the Moors, Africans, and Spaniards <note>Meaning the Hispano-Moors</note> rushed into Christian lands along the Douro <note>original: "Duero"</note> and the town of San Esteban de Gormaz. There, the Muhammadans were defeated, and the generals of the two Moorish armies were slain in the year 894.

Then King Ordoño <note>Ordoño II</note> abruptly entered the Moor's lordships and, crossing the Tagus <note>original: "Tajò"</note> and Guadiana rivers, came as far as Badajoz. Abd-ar-Rahman crossed into Galicia, and the Christians followed him, where the battle was cruel and bloody, lasting from morning until evening without anyone knowing who had the upper hand, and each of the Kings boasting of victory. This Abd-ar-Rahman tormented the Christians more than any of the Muhammadan Kings of Spain, for he overran as far as Navarre, and afterwards Castile, which was then only a County. The Count of that country asked for help from Ramiro <note>Ramiro II</note>, King of Spain, who defeated the Moors near the city of Osma. He was succeeded by Hisham II <note>original: "Hiſen"</note>, the second of that name, whom others call Yxecà. He served for nothing more than to bear the title of King, for there was a Moorish Lord called Almanzor <note>original: "Aben Hamar," referring to the powerful vizier Al-Mansur</note> who commanded everywhere and handled affairs according to his whim. Under this King, there was a Count of Galicia named Rodrigo Velázquez who invited the Moors to come into Galicia. Passing through, they reached Compostela and tore down part of the Church of Saint James <note>The Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela was famously raided by Al-Mansur in 997.</note>. However, at that hour his troops were struck by strange diseases, so that he returned without achieving anything. Nonetheless, there was later a general for the same King Hisham who overran the country of León and Galicia, performing great feats of arms and making himself terrifying to all those Christians, whose private hatreds were the cause of these disasters. Consequently, the greater part of Catalonia was once again subjected to the Muhammadans.

Among the Moors, divisions also arose following the example of the Christians. There was a Moor named Sulayman <note>original: "Culema," referring to Sulayman al-Musta'in</note> who seized the kingdom from Hisham, whom he put in prison, and made himself <term>Miramomelin</term> <note>From the Arabic *Amir al-Mu'minin*, or "Commander of the Faithful," a title for the Caliph.</note> of Córdoba, having come there from Barbary <note>North Africa</note>, from whence he drew support. But another powerful lord opposed him, drove him out, and usurped the lordship; he was called Muhammad <note>Muhammad II al-Mahdi</note>. As he persecuted the friends of his predecessor, some revolted, including a Moor from Toledo named Abd Allah, who restored the royalty in the city of Toledo in the year 993, 149 years after it had last been subjected to the Kings of Córdoba. From then on, it had its own kings, and it never again returned to the hands of the Kings of Córdoba. This King of Toledo allied with the Christians to gain advantage against the forces of the King of Córdoba. Meanwhile, Sulayman, having been driven from his kingdom and favored by the Christians, made war on King Muhammad, whom he defeated, and returned to his seat. This caused him to release Hisham—whom we said above had been driven from his kingdom by Sulayman—who, as the legitimate king of the succession and royal family, was also received by his subjects. He took several cities of Andalusia which, during the civil wars, had been usurped by tyrants and rebels, and he waged war against the Africans <note>The Berbers</note> who defended the party of his adversary Sulayman.

He also had war against Ubayd Allah <note>original: "Obeydalla"</note>, King of Toledo, in which the Toledan was defeated and killed; he was succeeded by Hayrà, the seventh King of Toledo. But just as Hisham thought to enjoy his states peacefully, he saw himself attacked worse than ever by a Moor named Ali <note>Ali ibn Hammud al-Nasir</note>, favored by the Africans, who also deprived him of his seat in the year 1011. But he was not King for long, for another, Al-Hakam <note>original: "Halyhatan"</note>, unseated him and had him treacherously massacred in the year 1031. This angered the Moors, so that they elected as king a cousin of Ali named Al-Qasim <note>original: "Cacin"</note>, having on his side the Moors of Africa called <term>Berberuzes</term> <note>Berbers</note>. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

Zaragoza, and Al-Mundhir <note>original: "Almadar"</note>, King of Al-Sahi, and through the cities of Tortosa and Valencia—which, although part of the domain of Córdoba, were held by other Muhammadans who occupied the principal cities of Spain—he made himself Lord of a part of the Cordovan Kingdom. But betrayed by his own men, he was slain in an enterprise undertaken against the city of Granada, and his head was carried to Al-Qasim <note>original: "Cacin," referring to Al-Qasim al-Ma'mun, a Caliph of the Hammudid dynasty</note> in Córdoba.

Upon his death, this Al-Qasim was succeeded in the year 1027 <note>original: "107"</note> by Yahya <note>original: "Hiayà"</note>, son of the aforementioned Muhammad; but he was king for hardly any time, having reached the throne by means of the Berbers <note>original: "Berberuzes"</note>. So it was that the Spaniards called upon Badis <note>original: "Buz"</note>, Lord of Granada, and through his intrigues Yahya was slain in the city of Málaga. The crown then fell to Abd-ar-Rahman <note>original: "Abderrahamé"</note>, fourth of that name, who reigned for only one month and 17 days. He was succeeded by Muhammad IV <note>Muhammad III al-Mustakfi</note>, whose wealth and avarice were the cause of his ruin; for his own people, desiring to possess his treasures, put him to death by poison after he had reigned only one year and 4 months. He had as his successor Hisham <note>original: "Hilé," likely Hisham III</note>, third of that name. At that time, Spain was entirely filled with petty kings <note>original: "Royteles," referring to the *Taifa* period where the central Caliphate fractured into small, independent city-states</note>, there being almost no city or provincial capital that did not have a King who commanded it. This brought low the glory of the Kingdom of Córdoba, whose Kings had been the great sovereigns over all the Moors of Spain. This King was also not of long duration, not because his subjects hated him, but because he had a lieutenant of low birth who treated the people cruelly. For this reason, they punished the King for the fault of his officer, driving him out and deposing him from the crown. They gave him as a successor Al-Mundhir II <note>original: "Almũdir"</note>, who came to present himself to the Cordovans to be their King, as one descended from the blood of their false Prophet <note>The author uses "false Prophet" to refer to Muhammad, common in 16th-century Christian historiography</note>. He was received and listened to, but those who loved him advised him to give up this crown, seeing the perils that were suffered within it. They told him that as the city was in arms and the moods and affections of the citizens were driven in different directions, it was better for him to abandon his enterprise than to expose himself to the danger of losing his life. But this foolish Prince, instead of following their advice and thanking them, replied to them: "Make me King today, and hold me as such, and tomorrow kill me if the desire takes you." He did this with his children and family, going to one of his fortresses. It had happened quite a long time ago that his son, named Muhammad <note>original: Mahomet</note>, the fifth of that name and the last Moorish King of Córdoba, [reigned]; this kingdom came to an end in the year of our Lord 1027, having begun in the year 758. Following the decline of this kingdom, the kingdom of Toledo gained strength, which we must discuss, since reason dictates that having removed the Moors from Africa, we now see them withdrawing back there again. The downfall of the house of the kings of Córdoba was the reason that the Christian kings of Spain extended their borders and recovered many lands from the Muslims <note>original: Mahometans</note>, especially on the side of Portugal, Galicia, and Catalonia. The kingdom of Castile was established in the year 1034, having previously been only a County; its king was Ferdinand, son of Sancho, King of Navarre, surnamed "the Great," who married the heiress of León and sister of King Bermudo. This Al-Mamun was succeeded by a son named Hisham ibn Umayya <note>original: Hisé Aben Humeya</note>, under whom very learned men flourished in Toledo, as did many Christians living in liberty of conscience, who were called Mozarabs <term>Mozarabs: From the Arabic 'musta'rib', meaning 'Arabized'; these were Iberian Christians who lived under Muslim rule and adopted Arabic language and culture while maintaining their Christian faith</term>, just as I have fully described previously. During the final years of Ferdinand, this Toledan king and several other kinglets <note>petty kings of small territories</note> who held the kingdoms of Aragon and Valencia were constrained to return to their former obedience. While these things were passing thus in Spain, there was great division in Africa between the Kings and Princes; for just as those of the blood of Umayya <note>Humeya</note> held Spain (as we have seen), and those of the house of Al-Alawi <note>Aben Alaueci</note> were lords of Africa—both families having descended from two daughters of the impostor Muhammad—there arose a very rich and powerful family of Moors in Africa bearing the name of the Almoravids <term>Almoravids: An imperial Berber Muslim dynasty that emerged in the 11th century</term>. This family drove those of the Al-Alawi race and the blood of the false Prophet out of the African kingdom. The leader of these Almoravids was named Yusuf ibn Tashfin <note>original: Joseph Aben Tesfin</note>, after whom a river in Barbary <note>North Africa</note> is named, in the land and kingdom of Tlemcen. The Spanish and African Moors who did not like the races of Umayya and Al-Alawi placed themselves under the power of this Almoravid. Upon the death of the King of Toledo, Al-Mamun, his only son Hisham succeeded him, which occurred in the year of Grace 1074; those of Córdoba made war against him, but he, aided by his friend the King of Castile, punished them so well that they no longer had the boldness to overrun his lands to harm him.

Now, not to leave out the rest of these Muslims, at that time there were kings in Seville named Al-Mu'tamid <note>original: Almucamuz Aben Amet</note>; in Granada, Al-Muzaffar <note>original: Amundafar</note>; and Abu Bakr in Valencia. However, this last one was a subject of the King of Toledo. This caused the governor of Valencia, named Abu Bakr, to revolt, and led both the Mozarab Christians of Toledo and the Moors to pray—some to King Alfonso of Castile, the most powerful of the Christians—[for aid].

Once this was done by Yusuf, he returned to Africa and went to stay in the city of Morocco <note>Marrakesh</note> in the year 1089. Being old, Alfonso sent his son to the war, who was killed there, and the Christians were defeated. However, the Moors did not advance further, fearing the good fortune of the good King Alfonso. ## **Monarchy of the Moors.**

This young man was of humble origin and the son of a potter, though he possessed a noble heart and a drive reflecting the ambition that smoldered in his soul; he was named Abdelmon <note>Abd al-Mu'min (r. 1130–1163), the first Caliph of the Almohad Empire</note>. He placed such faith in the words of this philosopher, Thumert <note>Ibn Tumart, the spiritual founder of the Almohad movement</note>, that he addressed himself to a Muslim cleric highly learned in the Quran. He revealed Thumert's prediction to him and begged him to provide help and aid, promising that if the affair succeeded as the stars promised, he would make him the greatest among the followers of Muhammad. Almohadi <note>Likely referring to Ibn Tumart's claim to be the 'Mahdi' or 'Guided One'</note>—for so this Muslim cleric was called—resolved to help him. He could find no finer or faster way to sow novelties in their religion than by beginning to interpret the Quran against the sense of all the other doctors of law, adapting everything to the temperaments of the Africans. These people, astonished by this doctrine, gave him their ear and accepted it, holding this man in great reputation for holiness.

Seeing that his plan was progressing according to his desire, he moved further and proposed that Abdelmon was a person chosen by God, who intended to plant His holy Al-Furqan law <note>The author uses "Alphurcaniste," derived from *Al-Furqan*, an Arabic name for the Quran meaning "The Criterion" between right and wrong</note> throughout the whole world. This was the reason that this same Abdelmon was honored and respected as something sent by God. It was then that Almahadi began to reveal himself and to preach against the race of the Almoravids <note>The ruling dynasty prior to the Almohads</note>, calling them tyrants and usurpers, as those who had chased away the family of Alabeci <note>The Abbasids</note> and the blood of their prophet Muhammad.

Going further, he attacked the person of the Caliph of Baghdad <note>Original: "Baldac"</note>, the sovereign pontiff of their law, and spoke against the rest of the *Alfaquis* <note>term: Faqih; an Islamic jurist or expert in religious law</note> and ministers of their sect. In short, by saying that Abdelmon was of the blood of Muhammad, he won over the greater part of the nobility. In this, he was greatly favored by Aben Thumert with his predictions and astronomical figures. With such forces, this son of a potter became great and fought often against the sovereign King of Africa and the Moors of Spain <note>Original: "Hespagne"</note>. Thus was the African state divided into Almoravids and Almohads. It was necessary to recite this history here in order to clear up several doubts that are commonly found in the histories of Africa and Spain.

The matter went so far that when King Albo Aly Aben Tesfin <note>Ali ibn Yusuf ibn Tashfin</note> was killed in battle, this noble potter Abdelmon was made King and *Miramomelin* <note>term: Miramomelin; a European corruption of the Arabic title *Amir al-Mu'minin*, or "Commander of the Faithful"</note> of Africa. The Almohad heretics held the Lordship and government over everything, since the King was of their sect and had been advanced by them; this occurred in the year 1147. During these divisions, Alfonso, the first King of Portugal, won several places that the Moors held in Lusitania <note>The Roman name for the region comprising most of modern Portugal</note>, as did the Count of Barcelona, knowing well that it was good to fish in troubled waters. 

But Abdelmon, not content that Africa obeyed him, prepared also to pass into Europe and subjugate the Moors of Spain who obeyed the Almoravids. However, it was Almohadi who made this journey, while Thumert stayed with the King. Through the diligence of this preacher, Abdelmon was made monarch of the Moors of Africa and Spain. There, these Almohads began to use strange tyrannies and cruelties, as much against the Christians as against the Muslims who were not of their opinion. This was done by Abdelmon, who, forgetting his origins, practiced insupportable insolence against the Christians, over whom he made great conquests. After these were put into effect, he returned victorious to Africa, where he established his seat...

royal <note>The catchword from the previous page was "royal," completing the description of the court in Marrakesh.</note> court in Marrakesh, governing as a gentle and gracious Prince by the counsel of Thumert and Almohadi <note>The author refers here to Ibn Tumart (c. 1080–1130), the spiritual founder of the Almohad movement. When Abdelmon <note>Abd al-Mu'min, the first Almohad Caliph</note>, the first Almohad King, came to die, he had as his successor his son Aben Jacob <note>Abu Yaqub Yusuf (r. 1163–1184)</note>, who, like his father, held the Muslim Kingdoms of Africa and Spain. Then he went to Andalusia and from there to Africa to his city of Marrakesh, where he died full of riches and victories in the year of our salvation 1200. This rout greatly diminished the authority and credit of Aben Muhammad the Almohad; whereas many had previously feared and respected him, they now left him. Among others, his own brother Zayd Abu Zayd seized Valencia and made himself its King and Lord. In the year 1252, four years after the capture of this city <note original="cefte cité">Referring to Seville, which fell to the Christians in 1248.</note> which had remained for 534 years under the subjection of the Moors, Mahomet <note>Muhammad I ibn al-Ahmar, founder of the Nasrid dynasty.</note>, King of Granada, renewed the peace and alliance with Don Alphonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile, known as "The Wise."</note>, King of Castile, whom he went to visit as far as Toledo. All of Andalusia did not obey this King Mahomet, for there was a King in the Algarve named Aben Mosad; and without fail, if the Moors had not thus divided their power, the Christians would hardly have so quickly regained possession of the Kingdom lost by the Goths. <note>A reference to the Visigothic Kingdom, which fell to the Umayyad conquest in 711 AD.</note> In Jerez and Niebla there was another petty king named Aben Amet, both vassals of the King of Castile, who in the year 1261, along with the King of Granada, revolted against the Castilian and took several towns and fortresses from him. To support this King, Mahomet summoned a thousand horses <note original="mille cheuaux">Meaning a thousand cavalrymen.</note> from Morocco, the soldiers who came upon them calling themselves ***Merins*** or ***Marins*** <note>The Marinids, a Zenata Berber dynasty that replaced the Almohads.</note>, all from the same family and sent by Iucep <note>Abu Yusuf Yaqub.</note>, King of Morocco. These were so well favored by Mahomet that his subjects, feeling envy and spite, revolted and caused much harm to the lands subject to their Princes. I have spoken here of Iucep, King of Morocco, descended from Jacob <note>Yaqub al-Mansur.</note>, and father of this Mahomet surnamed "the Green" <note>Muhammad al-Nasir, who wore a green caftan; he was defeated at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa.</note> who was defeated in Spain. Upon his death, his nephew Caid Arrax <note>Likely referring to the Almohad Caliph al-Murtada.</note> reigned in Morocco, the fifth of the Almohad race in Africa, governing the whole country from the Atlantic Ocean as far as Egypt. Among other governors, he had one at Tlemcen named Gomarança Aben Zien <note>Yaghmurasen ibn Zyan, founder of the Zayyanid dynasty.</note>, of a race called Abdalnés <note>The Abdalwadids.</note> subject to the Almohads, who, because he did not conduct himself as he should in his government, fell into the enmity of King Caid Arrax, who went to besiege him in a castle called Tremezezic. But a cousin of the besieged man, feigning surrender to the King and offering to show him the weakest points of the place, treacherously slew him; and while the soldiers were troubled and astonished by the death of the King, Gomarança emerged from the castle, attacked them, made a great massacre, and made himself King of Tlemcen, whose lineage lasted a long time. At the same time, there was a lineage or family in Fez called ***Merins***, from a powerful citizen named Merin, who was initially a Christian, but his successors became Moors. One of this race named Bucarben Merin <note>Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Haqq.</note>, being governor of Fez for Caid Arrax, hearing of the success of the Almohads at Tremezezic and how the fugitives had been defeated by his own people, named himself also King of Fez; and another brother of his named Aben Iucep was made lord of Rabat, not without great astonishment to the Almohads. The Almohads then made Almorcada <note>Abu Dabbus al-Wathiq.</note>, a relative of the deceased Caid Arrax, King of Morocco, who immediately made war on the Marinids of Fez. They defeated him, and from then on, the Lordship of these two cities was separated. Aben Bucar Merin, dying, left a son of young age named Hiaya, who was placed under the guardianship of his uncle Aben Iucep. But the child dying, the uncle was made King of Fez and highly esteemed among the Africans, so that he was called "the Great Old Man of the Marinids." To him retired a cousin of King Almorcada of Morocco named Budebus, revolting against his Prince and begging for aid from this Marinid, promising him a great extent of land for the enlargement of the Kingdom of Fez if he would help him obtain the lordship of Morocco. In the year 1252, four years after the capture of this city <note>Likely referring to Seville, which was taken by the Christians in 1248</note> which had remained for 534 years under the subjection of the Moors, Muhammad, King of Granada, renewed the peace and confederation with Don Alfonso, King of Castile <note>Alfonso X, known as "the Wise"</note>, whom he went to visit as far as Toledo. Not all of Andalusia obeyed this King Muhammad, for there was a King in the Algarve called <term>Aben Mofad</term> <note>Ibn Mahfuz</note>; and without fail, if the Moors had not thus divided their power, the Christians would hardly have so soon regained possession of the Kingdom lost by the Goths. At <term>Xerez</term> <note>Jerez de la Frontera</note> and Niebla there was another petty king named Aben Amet, both vassals of the King of Castile, who in the year 1261, along with the King of Granada, revolted against the Castilian and took several cities and fortresses from him. To pursue this war, Muhammad brought a thousand horses from Morocco, the soldiers riding them calling themselves ***Merins*** or ***Marins*** <note>The Marinids, a Zenata Berber tribe</note>, all from the same family and sent by Yusuf, King of Morocco. These men were so well favored by Muhammad that his own subjects, out of envy and spite, revolted and committed many evils in the lands subject to their Princes. 

I have spoken here of Yusuf, King of Morocco, son of Jacob and father of this Muhammad nicknamed "the Green" <note>Muhammad al-Nasir, known in Spanish tradition as "Miramamolín el Verde"</note> who was defeated in Spain. After his death, his nephew <term>Caid Arrax</term> <note>Likely the Almohad Caliph al-Rashid</note> reigned in Morocco, of whom we have spoken above, the fifth of the race of the <term>Almohades</term> in Africa, governing the entire country from the Atlantic Ocean to Egypt. This man, among other governors, had one at <term>Tremissen</term> <note>Tlemcen, in modern-day Algeria</note> called <term>Gomarança Aben Zien</term> <note>Yaghmurasen ibn Zyan, founder of the Zayyanid dynasty</note>, of a race called the <term>Abdalnés</term> <note>The Banu Abd al-Wad</note> subject to the Almohads. Because he did not behave as he should in his government, he fell into the enmity of King Caid Arrax, who went to besiege him in a castle called Tremezezir. However, a cousin of the besieged man, feigning surrender to the King and promising to show him the weakest points of the fortress, treacherously slew him. While the soldiers were troubled and astonished by the death of the King, Gomarança emerged from the castle, charged them, made a great slaughter, and made himself King of Tlemcen; their race endured for quite a long time. 

At the same time, there was a lineage or family in Fez called the ***Merins***, descended from a powerful citizen named Merin, who was originally a Christian, though his successors became Moors. One of this race named <term>Bucarben Merin</term> <note>Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Haqq</note>, being governor of Fez for Caid Arrax and hearing of the Almohads' fate at Tlemcen and how the fugitives had been defeated by his own men, also named himself King of Fez. Another of his brothers, called <term>Aben Iucep</term> <note>Abu Yusuf Yaqub</note>, was made lord of <term>Ribaté</term> <note>Rabat</note>, to the great astonishment of the Almohads. The Almohads then made <term>Almorcada</term> <note>Abu Hafs Umar al-Murtada</note>, a relative of the deceased Caid Arrax, King of Morocco. He immediately made war on the Marinids of Fez, who defeated him, and from then on, the lordship of these two cities was separated. Aben Bucar Merin, upon dying, left a young son named Hiaya who was placed under the guardianship of his uncle Aben Yusuf. But when the child died, the uncle was made King of Fez and was greatly esteemed among the Africans, such that they called him "the Great Old Man of the Marinids." To him fled a cousin of King Almorcada of Morocco named <term>Budebus</term> <note>Abu Dabbus</note>, revolting against his Prince and praying for aid from this Marinid, promising him a vast extent of land for the enlargement of the Kingdom of Fez if he would help him obtain the lordship of Morocco. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the various peoples and languages of the Levant and the Middle East, specifically focusing on the Syrian Christians and the intellectual contributions of the Arabic-speaking world.</meta>

<page-num>477</page-num>
->LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.<-

Pierre de Vitry <note>original: "Pierre de Vitriaco," a 13th-century historian and bishop of Acre</note> in his history of Jerusalem.

The Syrians or Surani lived in Syria, from which they were named, or from Sur <note>The ancient city of Tyre</note>, which was a famous city of Syria; they follow the religion and rite of the Greeks for the most part. They deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as he does from the Father <note>A reference to the "filioque" theological dispute between Eastern and Western churches</note>. They do not allow fourth marriages and do not recognize the Roman Church as supreme over all others. They regard the excommunications and sentences of the Roman Prelates as nothing. They feel all Latins <note>Western Christians</note> are rightfully excommunicated. They wash the altars on which Latins have performed their rites. They show no reverence to the sacraments of the Latins, nor do they stand for one carrying the consecrated host to the sick. They perform the sacrament with leavened bread; priests keep the wives with whom they contracted marriage before taking holy orders. They do not consider the subdiaconate among the holy orders. Their small children, immediately after baptism, are sealed with chrism by a simple priest, without waiting for a Bishop. They judge the Sabbath day <note>Saturday</note> so solemn that it is permitted to fast on it, except for the Sabbath of Easter. On that day they celebrate divine rites and eat meat. They delight in the Saracenic <note>Arabic</note> language; they keep their wives secluded in a similar manner as the Saracens, and emulate other customs of theirs; they do not shave their beards, in the manner of Easterners.

J. de Mandeville, knight, in his travels composed in the Romance language <note>Old Catalan/Provencal in this excerpt</note> in the year 1322.

Also there are other Christians named Syrians, and they hold a middle belief, which is between our law and that of the Greeks; and they all wear beards just as the Greeks do, and they perform the sacrament with leavened bread, and in their languages they use Saracenic <note>Arabic</note> letters, but for the mystery of the Church <note>liturgy</note> they use Greek letters, and they perform their sacrament just as the Jacobites <note>Syriac Orthodox</note> do.

### On the comparison of Arabic and Saracenic knowledge with Egyptian, Chaldean, Persian, Greek, and Latin or Roman.

As the knowledge of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, Persians, Greeks, and Latins or Romans increased with their force and power, so too did that of the Arabs and Saracens. For when they were the strongest and most powerful in the world, they became highly learned and very scholarly, principally in the astrological and demonstrative sciences, as is deduced by the author of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* <note>original: "Chronique Cassinense"</note>, book 3, chapter 34. Among them, Avicenna and Averroes (mentioned above), Albumasar, Geber, and countless others acquired the highest praise. Avicenna was the most universal of them all in Philosophy, Mathematics, and in Arabic Theology and Poetry; he also wrote on Medicine, treating very well—in the judgment of the most learned in that art—the signs and causes of diseases, applying to them several remedies neither understood nor practiced by the Greeks, Latins, or Romans. Averroes subtly explained the works of Aristotle in their entirety. As for Albumasar, he perfectly understood the celestial movements and their effects, having discovered the great conjunctions <note>The alignment of planets used in historical astrology</note> and several other fine things that had remained unknown until his time. Geber, a very expert Mathematician, found faults in the demonstrations of the Al- <note>The text likely intended "Almagest," the influential astronomical treatise by Ptolemy</note>
