majesty of Ptolemy: several others of theirs like Avempace <note>original: "Auenpace," the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Bajja</note>, Al-Ghazali <note>original: "Algazel"</note>, Ibn al-Baitar <note>original: "Benbitar," a famous botanist and pharmacist</note>, Al-Battani <note>original: "Abaten," the astronomer Albategnius</note>, Ishaq <note>original: "Siphac," likely referring to the translator Ishaq ibn Hunayn</note>, the Philosophers. Mesue, Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"</note> otherwise known as al-Mansur, Serapion, Zoar, nicknamed the wise, the Physicians, Aonias, Avenzoar, Al-Farabi <note>original: "Alpharas"</note>, Al-Farghani <note>original: "Alphragan"</note>, Haly, Ridwan <note>original: "Rodoan"</note> and other Astrologers, cited by me in my discourse on the *Truth of the causes and effects of the decays, mutations, changes, conversions, and ruins of Monarchies, Empires, Kingdoms, and Republics* printed in 1598. All of these figures flourished at nearly the same time, having invented many beautiful things in doctrines and sciences, or improving upon those previously invented; composing their works in the Arabic language, and occupying the schools of the West before the restoration of the Greek and Latin languages. Because of this, these Arabs or Saracens acquired such a reputation in Mathematics that when Alfonso, King of Castile <note>Alfonso X "The Wise," who reigned 1252–1284</note>, undertook the preparation of his Astronomical Tables, he had his primary recourse to them, since they alone in that season could teach and restore such disciplines. To them he gave great gifts amounting to four hundred thousand crowns <note>original: "escus"</note>, imitating in this the liberality of Alexander the Great, who spent a similar sum to have the natures of animals truly represented to him by Aristotle.

But the Arabic Caliphs, seeing that their people were too devoted to Philosophy and Mathematics and cared very little for their Mohammedan Law <note>The author refers here to Islamic Sharia or religious practice</note>, founded colleges for the maintenance of those who would teach and learn the Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> of their Prophet, and in some Universities they transferred, or rather transmitted, the lectureship of Philosophy into that of their said law, ordering that whoever from then on studied the Quran would in no way occupy themselves with Philosophy or Astrology. This caused the practice of the other sciences to cool in some places, though not everywhere, considering that in Persia there are to this day very learned Philosophers and Astrologers. 

Regarding the comparison of the Arabic and Saracenic language with Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, we learn that when the Greeks and Romans were in their greatest prosperity, ruling many countries, they extended these two languages along with their Empires and Lordships. Many people and nations studied to understand and speak them, either to please them or to trade with them; then the Christian religion, using these languages, preserved and spread them in many lands and regions. However, these were never understood and spoken in as many places as the Arabic language is now, which is common to almost all the inhabitants of Asia, Africa, and a third part of Europe, as I have remarked previously. Affairs of the Quran are handled in it, along with all other disciplines, just as we use Latin here, separated from the common tongues and understood only by those who have learned it in schools. This language resembles (as I remarked before) Hebrew, Syriac, and Chaldaic, in that it is written like them from right to left, with points in place of vowels, and has several names and words in common, and a phrasing very similar to them; but it has its own letters and characters specific to it alone. In this, it is very different from the Greek and Latin languages, which are also written from left to right, as I demonstrate hereafter in this discourse.

### Concerning the region of the Turks.

Abraham Ortelius, in his geographical synonyms and treasury <note>Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598) was a famous Flemish cartographer who created the first modern atlas.</note>, speaking of the region of the Turks and their various names and titles, says that Aria <note>original: "Ἀρὶα"</note> is a region of Asia. According to Ptolemy and others, they are the Arii <note>original: "Ἄρειοι"</note>; they are the Arrhiani according to Arrian, and the Ariei according to Curtius—or "Arsi," as the edition by Aldus Manutius has it. They are called Arienses by Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary.</note>, and they appear as the Arieni <note>original: "Ἀριηνοὶ"</note> in the works of Dionysius. The merchant [Pierre] Servere calls it Turkestan; Pinet calls it Hetia eirauæ. According to Giacomo Gastaldi, the region is Khorasan <note>original: "Corafan"</note>, and Garcia de Orta reports that its inhabitants are called the Corasones. According to Pomponius Mela, it is an island in the Black Sea <note>original: "Ponti Euxini"</note>, while Pliny testifies it is called by another name, Chanceritis. Pinet interprets Farnasia as Areos Nesos <note>original: "ἄρεως νῆσος"</note>, that is, the "Island of Mars," which is the name Stephanus gives it. The location of the region of Aria is found in Ptolemy; it seems to me, from the Asian tables of Abulfeda <note>A 14th-century Arab geographer and prince.</note>, to be called Burgiam. Aria is also the name of a city in this region, as well as a river, the Arius <note>original: "ἄρειος"</note>, mentioned by Polybius in Book 10 and by Arrian in his *Life of Alexander*.

The Turks call themselves Muslims <note>original: "Mufulmannos"</note>, as Hugo Favolius writes in his *Byzantine Itinerary*. And Leunclavius <note>Johannes Leunclavius, a 16th-century historian specializing in Ottoman history.</note> notes this in his *History of the Muslims*: their seat is described by Pomponius and Pliny as being near the Sea of Azov <note>original: "Paludem Meotidem"</note>. In the *Miscellaneous History*, they are located near the Caspian Gates. Eustathius writes that the Huns are called "Turks" by the Persians; Hermolaus [Barbarus], in his corrections of Pliny, teaches that they are also called Thunni. According to Scylax, as reported by Theodore Gaza, the Turks are those whom Strabo calls the Cyrtians <note>original: "κύρτιοι"</note>; the Romans called them Curcians, or "Curti" for short. The same Gaza cites Gemistus Pletho, who suggests they are the Paropamisadae, though Gaza admits he does not agree with this. Nearly all authors seem to agree with one voice that their origin is drawn from the Scythians who inhabit the Caucasus mountains between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. Laonikos Chalkokondyles reports that "Turk" signifies a man who follows a more rustic way of life. Guillaume Postel thinks they are named Togarmah <note>original: "Togarma"</note> by the Hebrews; Benjamin of Tudela says the same. Mention is made of them in Ezekiel 27 as Togarmah <note>original: "Thogorma or θόργαμα"</note>. I must not omit here that Pintianus, in his corrections of Pomponius Mela, strikes out the name of the "Turks" from Pliny and Mela and substitutes "Iurcae" <note>original: "Ἰούρκαι"</note> in its place, based on Herodotus' *Melpomene*—though by what right he does this, he himself should see. He would certainly have driven them out of our Europe with greater applause than he did from these historical writings. Suidas mentions the Turks, saying that iron is not easily prepared among them. Much more can be found concerning them in the works of Emperor Leo, chapter eight, paragraph forty-five. See also: Huns, Unni, Jaxartae, Sarmatia, Khazars <note>original: "Cafari"</note>, and Hungarians.

The Huns or Unni <note>original: "Οὗννοι"</note> are a people called Thunni <note>original: "Θοῦννοι"</note> by Eustathius, and also by Pliny, as Hermolaus testifies. They are placed after the Scythians by Eustathius. Theophylact Simocatta, as reported by the same, states that they are called "Turks" <note>original: "τούρκοι"</note> by the Persians. The Huns are also called Sabiri <note>original: "σάβειροι"</note>, according to Nicolaus Callistus and Suidas. The same Callistus says the ancients called them Nebrus. They are called Onogurs by Agathias. The Unni, Huns, and Avars are the same people according to Widukind and Eginhard, as are the Hungarians today. The same author also calls the Hungarians Ugrians <note>original: "Vgros"</note> and Magyars <note>original: "Magores"</note>. Jordanes calls them the Aviri. The Huns are also called Chunos...

The nation of the Turks, *Historia Miscellanea*, book 18.

Jean Leunclavius <note>A 16th-century German scholar of Ottoman history.</note> in his *History of the Muslims*.

The *Iurchi*—who are also called *Iurchae* or *Iurkae*, and correctly recorded with the ancient name *Turkai* <note>original: "Τύρκαι"</note> by Herodotus—are those very people we now call Turks. In their own manner, they are called *Tzurcos* or *Tzurucos*, as the letter 'I' is more forcefully expressed as 'Z' or 'Tz'. Indeed, the word *Zurki* or *Tzurki* signifies in their language exactly what the Greek *Nomades* signifies; that is, "derived from pastures" <note>original: "παρὰ τῶν νομῶν"</note>. For it is known that those who use no fixed dwellings and wander here and there with their families, herds, and flocks for the sake of pastures are called *Nomads*. The Turks were once such a people, and today there are *Turcomans* <note>original: "Turcomanleri"</note> scattered throughout Anatolia. Furthermore, the Ottoman <note>original: "Osmanei"</note> soldiers and courtiers now take offense when someone calls them "Turks" or "rustics"; in their comedies, a "Turk" or "Turkman" is always introduced as a peasant, much like the Italian comedies are never without their *Zanni* <note>The 'Zanni' was a comic servant character in Italian Commedia dell'arte, often portrayed as a slow-witted rustic.</note>.

See Raphael Volaterranus, book seven of his *Geography*. C. Augustinus Curio, book three of his *History of the Saracens*. Andrea Cambini of Florence in his book, divided into four parts, on the *Origin of the Turks and the Empire of the House of Ottomans*. Paolo Giovio in his *Commentary on the Deeds and Feats of the Turks*.

## Concerning the Turks, and the Turkish Language.

### C H A P. XLVIII.

Now, the Hebrews or Israelites were transported beyond Media and had uninhabited lands to clear and settle. The region of Turkestan follows the Tarfenses; it is from here that the Turks first came, long ago separated from the part of them that remained among the Tartars, and agreeing only in language. Of all mortals, however, the Turks hold their own name in hatred because it sounds like "forsaken" and "cursed" <note>original: "derelictum & maledictum"</note>—the sort of name earned by the Ten Tribes when they were led away to the furthest borders of Persia, and later departed of their own accord on a journey of eighteen months. For just as the Israelites had made two defections—the first from the house of David at Dan, and the second from the Ten Tribes at Bethel and Dan—so they suffered a double exile: one forced to the eastern borders of the Persian kingdom, and the other voluntary to the borders of the East and Scythia. However, they remained in two parts. For in that region which they called Turkestan, they settled with their herds for the sake of pastures. That region is about a six-month journey from Armenia. Since there was a great multitude there, they crossed beyond Mount Belgia <note>Commonly identified in medieval legend with the Altai or Ural mountains.</note> for the sake of pastures, and there they were enclosed by Alexander the Great, where they were called—and were—the "Enclosed Jews," until, having forgotten both their origin and their law (of which they were once proud), both groups were called Turks because they were forsaken and cursed by God. The Tartars, or *Totar* or *Totari*, are their survivors; it is most certain that they once had commerce—and for a long time after the time of Alexander—through the mountain passes which opened and closed again, because they are very close and almost similar in language. Miraculously, however (as it is very frequently written in the secret doctrine of the followers of Moses that this must one day happen), the Northern Sea opened to them as they were coming from East to West, after thrice-nine prayers were poured out to God the Greatest and Best. Thus, by a double exit, they were led out for the punishment of the world, without them even thinking of it.

Having done this, they subjugated Lower Asia and the provinces of Phrygia, Lydia, and Cappadocia. And, as it is said, one can still see many of these men dispersed through Asia, who live and interact just like the Scythians called Nomads <note>original: "Nomades," from the Greek for "roaming for pasture."</note>, who can be called shepherds or cattle-drivers. Having no other home or certain house anywhere in Asia, they have another conjecture by which they wish to prove that the Turks are descended from the Scythians: seeing that Lower Asia is now inhabited by the Barbarian Turks, and those who stay in Lydia, Caria, Phrygia, and Cappadocia have nothing that differs—whether in language, clothing, customs, or way of life—from the Scythians who stay in that region between the river Tanais and Sarmatia. Others believe that the Turks took their source from the Parthians; for these people, being afflicted by the wandering Scythians called Nomads and unable to prevail against them, went into Lower Asia. There, they also lived as wanderers without any fixed abode, staying in their portable houses inside wagons. Finally, one sees that they spread through the cities where they now live. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

...descended from Hagar, Abraham's concubine, and not from Sarah, his legitimate wife; and that from the ancient Saracens and the ancient Turks, there has now been formed and composed one and the same people, just as I have extensively detailed above according to the opinion of **G. Postel** <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French linguist and polymath known for his studies of Eastern languages.</note> in chapter 10 of his *Oriental Histories*. These people do not enjoy being named or called by any other names than that of **Mussulmans** <note>Muslims</note>, which signifies in the Arabic and Turkish languages "faithful," "circumcised," or "saved by the effusion of their blood shed during their circumcision," as has been well noted by **F. Ricold** <note>Riccoldo da Monte di Croce, a 13th-century Dominican missionary who wrote a famous critique of Islam.</note> or **Richard**, cited above in chapter 7 of his *Refutation of the Law Given to the Saracens by Muhammad*, and the great **Cardinal of Cusa** <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), who wrote the *Cribratio Alcorani* (The Sifting of the Quran).</note> following him in Book 3, Chapter 3 of the *Sifting of the Quran* <note>original: "cribration de l'Alcoran"</note>. And the aforementioned G. Postel in chapter 10 of his said *Oriental Histories*. 

This name of **Mussulman** was first given, according to the Turkish Annals, to one of the sons of **Bayezid** <note>Bayezid I (c. 1360–1403), an Ottoman Sultan.</note>, Great Lord of Turkey, who was defeated and overcome by the great **Tamerlane** <note>The Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur.</note>; in fact, according to several historians of the last century, this name **Mussulman** is none other than that of the younger son of the said Bayezid, brother of **Cyriscebey** <note>Likely Süleyman Çelebi.</note>, called in the common and vulgar histories written of the deeds of the Turks **Calapin** <note>A European corruption of "Çelebi," a title of honor.</note>, as **Chalcondylas** <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles, a Byzantine Greek historian.</note> verifies in Book 4 of his *History of the Turks*, reciting that Bayezid the Great had six children named hereafter: Cyriscebey (or Calapin), surnamed **Joshua**, Mussulman, Mosch, Muhammad, Joshua the Younger, and **Mustafa**. 

The Latin and Italian authors who have described the history of the Turks mention only four children of this Bayezid, namely Cyriscebey, Mosch, Muhammad, and Mustafa, without including Mussulman or Joseph (or Joshua the Younger), whom the greater part of today's writers join, as it happens that this word **Mussulman** is nothing other than that of Cyriscebey, whom the common people call Calapin, and whom the Greek historians knew under the name of Joshua. 

**Sansovino** <note>Francesco Sansovino (1521–1583), an Italian scholar and writer.</note>, in Book 3, Part 3, Chapter 31 of his *History of Turkey*, recounts that the Mahometan <note>Muslim</note> minister who performs and provides the circumcision of the Turks asks the one placed in his hands to be circumcised if he wishes to be a **Mussulman**—that is to say, circumcised—and intends to receive the Religion and law of Muhammad; when he says yes, the minister makes him promise to keep and observe it well forever, to be an intimate friend to those who observe it, and conversely, a mortal enemy to its adversaries. And then he sets about performing his duty and office with several other ceremonies required and necessary for this purpose, described very particularly by **G. Antonio Menavino** in Book 2, Part 2, Chapter 24 of his *History of Turkey*; **Hugo Favolius** in his *Voyage to Constantinople*; and **F. de Belleforest**, Volume 2, Book 2, Chapter 8 of his *Cosmography*. 

What is more, these Turks have themselves called, besides the name of Mussulmans above, by the name and appellation of **Islams**, which is to say "Unanimous" and "Peaceful" among themselves, regularly praying to God that the **Giaours** <note>original: "Gaures", a term used by Muslims for non-believers, specifically Christians.</note>—that is to say, the Christians—be perpetually discordant and enemies among themselves, as reported by **J. Leunclavius** <note>Johannes Leunclavius (1541–1594), a German historian and expert on the Ottoman Empire.</note> in his *Muslim and Turkish History*. 

These preceding discourses will give us to understand that the Turkish language is identical and similar to the **Tartar** <note>Tatar</note> language, according to the words of **Matthias of Miechów**, a Pole, in his *Book of Sarmatia*, especially since the Turks emerged and proceeded (as I have already said) from the same place and origin as the said Tartars, all of whom have the same or nearly identical customs, languages, words, and way of life...

After Turkish, the Arabic language prevails over the rest, because the Quran was written in that language. This is followed by the Greek language, used in Constantinople among the citizens, in Pera <note>A district of Constantinople, modern-day Beyoğlu.</note>, and throughout Greece. Besides these, many others are in frequent use in the Turkish court, according to the diversity of nations subject to the Turkish empire."

Asia Minor, where previously there had been only one appointed by the Caliph from the beginning. This Caliph wished to be recognized by all the new Sultans of Damascus, the aforementioned Aleppo, Hama, Egypt, Jerusalem, Beirut, Antioch, and others, who in the course of time all entered into dissension with one another and separated themselves from the obedience of the said Caliph. At this same time, the Sultan of Alexandria, named Selim, put to death the first Caliph of Egypt and returned to the obedience of the one in **Baghdad** <note>original: "Baudras," a common early modern French rendering of Baghdad, sometimes via the Italian "Baldacco."</note>, in order to have favor and aid from him. These divisions occurred at the same time that the Moors of Africa and Spain were at their strongest, and whoever could seize a city carried the title of King. In the midst of these events, the Turks overflowed as thick as ants throughout all Asia, where they captured all these noble petty kings known as Sultans, without, however, touching the cities and lordships of the said Caliph, out of the honor and reverence they bore him as the head, protector, and defender of their laws, temples, and oratories; they left him in peace in the city of Baghdad. Sadok, King of the Turks, wished to be named by his people Sultan of Asia; but he did not live long thereafter and was killed by three arrow shots before the city of Aleppo. The same author in Book 7, Chapter 4 of the same *Universal Cosmography* writes that the histories of the Arabs, Turks, and common Greeks teach us that before the impostor Muhammad was born, the Roman and Christian Emperors enjoyed peaceful possession of Asia, Egypt, and Greece, without any mention being made of a Caliph or Sultan. But since that Arabian fellow entered his furies and had himself crowned King of Damascus, which was in the year of our Lord 630, after his death, one of his disciples and close associates named **Uthman** <note>original: "Othomar," referring to Uthman ibn Affan, the third Caliph.</note>, whom the Turks pronounce Othmar, succeeded him and was the first Caliph—which means nothing other in the language of the ancient **Mamluks** <note>original: "Mammelus," the ruling military caste in Egypt and Syria.</note> than "heir" or "successor," because he who held this dignity was substituted in the place and authority of Muhammad—and he was the first who bore the title of Sultan. It is true that in the year 660, one **Muawiyah** <note>original: "Mehua Azaricain," likely referring to Muawiyah I, the founder of the Umayyad Caliphate.</note>, which in the same language of the said Mamluks means "Swift-to-Victory," a Sultan and successor to Selim, after having seized and taken by force the Island of Rhodes, found there more than one hundred thousand quintals of bronze that an enchanter had discovered deep within a very profound rock, which the islanders today still call **Triantapente** <note>original: "Trianda pende," from the Greek for "thirty-five," though the text suggests thirty-eight idols.</note>, because this metal, they say, had come from 38 large idols, which, when melted down, were carried into Egypt. It has since been estimated that this was the bronze from that great and terrifying **Colossus of Rhodes**, which was used, according to the Barbary history, in the year 667 by **Abdallah** <note>original: "Abdallach."</note>, King of Egypt, who succeeded the said Muawiyah, to make 25 great, strong, and powerful gates in his palace in Cairo, and three in his great Mosque. Later, he had them gilded with fine gold by a Greek named Triphylliades, a native of the island of **Zante** <note>original: "Lezante," the island of Zakynthos.</note>, one of the most expert in the art of gilding that ever lived in those countries.

...from Armenia, whom they were accustomed to kidnap and send to be sold in <note>original: "grand Caire"</note> Great Cairo, where they were made to renounce their faith, practice military discipline, and learn the Turkish language, which was the language of the Sultan.

The authority and power of the Sultans of Egypt and the Mamluks began at the time when King Saint Louis was captured at Damietta <note>King Louis IX of France was captured during the Seventh Crusade in 1250.</note>. Furthermore, *Mamluk* <note>original: "Mammeluz"</note> in the *Syrian, African, and Moorish* languages signifies servants or soldiers who lived according to the manner of their religion without marriage, in the fashion of the <term>Knights of Rhodes</term> <note>A Catholic military order, also known as the Knights Hospitaller.</note>. And just as there were four *Vizier Pashas* <note>original: "Viſi Baſchas"</note> serving the Great Turk, so too the Sultan had four *Emir Kabir* <note>original: "Emir Quibir"</note>—that is to say, Great Emirs or Admirals—under them; besides these, there was a Great Constable whom they called *Dawadar Kabir* <note>original: "Derdard Quibir"</note>, named by <term>Paolo Giovio</term> <note>A 16th-century Italian physician and historian.</note> the "Great Diadoro." The said Sultan was elected by the Mamluks from among their own number, and most often from among the Emirs. All of these Mamluks, moreover, were renegade Christians or the sons of Christians, like the *Janissaries*. For they would under no circumstances receive a *Turk, Moor, or Jew* into their company. They were almost all *Liveroya*—the name given by the Turks to those anciently called *Iberians and Circassians*, now simply *Circassians*—and those who were *Colchians, Georgians, and Albanians*, and other *Jacobite and Nestorian* Christians living near the river *Baso*, anciently called the *Phasis* <note>The Rioni River in modern-day Georgia.</note>. These people were taken by the *Tartars* and brought in troops to be sold to the Emirs, who bought them, raised them, and made them *Mamluks*, as is confirmed by *Chalcondyles* in the third book of his history of the Turks; *Friar Antoine Geuffroy*, Knight of Malta, in his book on the conquests of the Turks; the aforementioned *Paolo Giovio* in his book on the Turks and in books 17 and 18 of his histories; and *Giovanni Maria Angiolello of Vicenza*, who also affirms having read (like Paolo Giovio) what a *Kazasker* <note>original: "Cadileſcher," meaning a military judge or chief justice.</note>—that is to say, a sovereign Pontiff or Bishop in the *Mahometan* superstition—had written about it, having accompanied the Great Turk *Selim* on the journey he made to ruin the authority and power of *Tuman bay* <note>original: "Tomumbey"</note>, the last of the Sultans of the said Egypt. All the above has been transcribed and repeated by *André Thevet* in book 8, chapter 12 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

Those who wish to see who the *Beylerbeys* <note>original: "Beglierbeys," high-ranking provincial governors.</note> or Lieutenant Generals of the Provinces subject to the domination of the Great Turk are, should read the aforementioned *André Thevet*, book seven, chapter ten of his aforementioned *Cosmography*, and even better, book nineteen, chapter 2 of the same *Cosmography*.

As for the word *Muley*, it signifies in the *Arabic, Turkish, and Moorish* languages "King" or "Lord." From this word, the Kings of Africa have in these times carried the title of *Muleys*, just as the *Arabs and Saracens* from their beginning used that of *Admiral*, and later *Sultan*, which signifies (as has been said) Lord and Prince. But it must be noted that the first *Mahometan* Kings of Africa did not take the names of *Muleys* or *Sultans*; rather, to show themselves devoted to the foolish persuasion of the *Alcoran* <note>The Quran.</note>, they called themselves *Miramolins* <note>A corruption of "Amir al-Mu'minin," meaning Commander of the Faithful.</note>, which signifies defenders of the law, or Princes of the believers, in the said *Arabic* language.

Regarding the Caliphs, it must be known that among the <term>Mahometists</term> <note>A historical term for Muslims.</note> they formerly held such authority and veneration as the Popes do among Christians. They made their residence in the city of <term>Babylon</term> <note>The author uses "Babylon" to refer to Baghdad, a common geographical conflation in early modern European texts.</note>, called by the Persians *Boughedot* or *Baldac* <note>original: "Boughedot ou Baldac"</note>, and were for this reason called the Caliphs of Baghdad throughout the East. But since the Mamluks mentioned above held the Empire of the Levant under the power and authority of a Sultan elected from among them, and had seized Egypt, Arabia, Palestine, and Assyria, they deprived the Caliph of his patrimony and temporal power, leaving him simply the authority in spiritual matters. This method was followed by the Great Turk <note>The Ottoman Sultan.</note> when he defeated the Sultan of Egypt, and by the <term>Sophy</term> <note>The Safavid Shah of Persia.</note>, who drove the Caliph of Baghdad from his seat more discourteously than the Saracens ever did—except for that great and valiant Prince <term>Saladin</term> <note>The 12th-century founder of the Ayyubid dynasty.</note>, who slew the Caliph of Baghdad to take his treasures and invested himself with the possession and lordship of Babylon, transporting the seat of these Caliphs to the city of Aleppo.

It is true that <term>Paolo Giovio</term> <note>original: "Paule Ioue", a famous 16th-century Italian historian and physician.</note>, in the seventeenth book of his histories, speaks of it differently, saying that the Caliph who lived in the time of Amalric <note>original: "almaury"</note>, successor to Baldwin, King of Jerusalem, called for help to defend himself against the said Amalric who was making war on him. He called a very renowned Captain named <term>Shirkuh</term> <note>original: "Sarraco", the uncle of Saladin.</note> who was in the service of the Sultan of Syria. This Shirkuh, having resisted the war efforts of the said Amalric, seized the aforementioned Caliph, put him in prison, and occupied his state. Since that time, the Caliphs lost their power and Empire and thereafter concerned themselves only with spiritual things and the confirmation of the Sultans. From this Shirkuh came Saladin, who in his time waged war for so long against the Christians who had gone to the conquest of the Holy Land. Whoever wishes to see the genealogies and successions of the Caliphs after the false prophet Muhammad should read <term>Johannes Leunclavius</term> <note>original: "I. Leuntclauius", a German scholar known for his histories of the Ottoman Empire.</note> at the beginning of his Turkish Muslim history.

Barthélemy Georgievicz, Pilgrim of Jerusalem, third book of Turkish matters, in his interpretation of the prophecy of the infidels.

*Patissahomoz* <note>original: "Patissahomoz", the Latinized form of the Turkish "Padişahımız," meaning "Our Emperor."</note> is a name of dignity composed with a plural pronoun, and signifies "Our King" or "Our Emperor." *Memleket* <note>From the Arabic 'mamlaka'.</note> moreover signifies a kingdom, although they also have various other words to signify a kingdom, such as *-istan*. For when they mention the kingdoms of Italy, France, or even Spain, they then say *Frankistan*: which signifies the kingdoms of the Italians, French, and Spaniards alike. *Frank* signifies a man from these regions, such as *Frank Gyaur*, that is, an Italian, French, or Spanish Christian. However, when they wish to name Greece, they change the word, saying *Urum Eli*, that is, Greece <note>original: "Vrum Elli"; referring to Rumeli, the "Land of the Romans" or Byzantines.</note>, and not *Urumistan*, that is, the "Greek Kingdom." Sometimes they also say *Urum Memleket*, and then they mean the entire empire of the Greeks. Briefly, this word *Memleket* signifies an empire rather than a kingdom among those nations of the Turks and Persians.

I. Leunclavius <note>Johannes Leunclavius (1533–1594), a German historian and specialist in Ottoman history</note> in his Turkish nomenclature says: *Hunggiar* is a title of dignity attributed by the Turks to their Sultans, just as Roman Princes used to be called Emperors and Caesars, to be pronounced in only two syllables. *Franc-beg* means Italian Prince, or Prince of the Italians. Likewise, the Roman Pope is called by the Turks *Musulin Histor. 16.* <note>Reference to Leunclavius’s work 'Historiae Musulmanae Turcorum'</note> *Rum-beg*, Prince of Rome, or Lord of Rome. Thus in book 16 of the *Musulman History*, the Turks call the Roman Pope what the Persian ambassadors—sent last year while Sixtus V was still alive to solicit aid against the Turks—called *Rum Schach*, or King of Rome. *Rum Schach*, King of Rome: so the Roman Pope was called by the Persians. The same Leunclavius notes that *Megas Aphendis* <note>original Greek: Μέγας Αὐθέντης</note>, meaning Great Lord, is the name the Greeks use for the Sultan of the Turks; following the Italian custom, he is not called anything other than *The Grand Seignor* <note>original Italian: Il grand Seignor</note>.

The Tartars of today call the Pope and all Christians *Dezinthis*, which means Pagans, and *Chaur* <note>Likely 'Giaour', a derogatory term for non-Muslims</note>, that is to say infidels, Dogs, and Idolaters, because they honor wood and stones. This began after they were summoned by Pope Innocent IV to receive the Christian Religion. While they were almost inclined to do so, Satan stirred up the *Mahometans* <note>An archaic term for Muslims</note>, who did not want to lose such a choice morsel. They admonished them to take up the Religion of the *Alcoran* <note>The Quran</note> as the purest, insofar as it taught only the adoration of a single God, while that of the Christians was stuffed with idols. Furthermore, they argued their own religion was spirited and permitted everything to a free man, putting weapons in his hands, whereas the religion of Jesus Christ was only fit for the effeminate and people who ask for nothing but rest. These *Alcoranists* knew how to harangue so well that those who had no certain Religion embraced the worst one; leaving that law which is entirely spiritual, they seized the doctrine of the flesh, apostasy, and abomination around the year of grace 1247. In the Kingdom of Narsingue <note>The Vijayanagara Empire in Southern India</note>, the word *Gurupe* is a title of dignity, as one might say a learned and scholarly Priest; and the word *Delevay* as well, meaning Captain and General of the army, according to *F. P. du Jarric* <note>Pierre du Jarric (1566–1617), a Jesuit missionary and historian</note> in book 2, chapter 21 of his history of the East Indies. In the kingdom of Deccan, the word *Sabaio* is a title of dignity, meaning Captain of the King's personal guards; the word *Idalcan* <note>Likely 'Adil Khan', the title of the rulers of the Bijapur Sultanate</note> is another title of dignity, meaning the King’s lieutenant general throughout all his lands, according to the account of *Edward Barbosa* <note>Duarte Barbosa (c. 1480–1521), a Portuguese writer and explorer</note>, a Portuguese, in his summary of the Indies.

The person commissioned as *Toldan* by the King in the city of Pegu <note>In modern-day Myanmar</note>, the capital of the Kingdom of Pegu, has total authority. No one would dare present themselves before him without a gift, as it is the custom of the country not to approach one’s King, Prince, or Lord without acknowledging his power. But near the person of the King is the *Cobraim*, called *Mattacqui* by the Cathayans <note>People of Cathay, an old name for China</note>, who holds more credit than the *Toldans* and *Haozamants*, because he is the lieutenant general and acts as Regent throughout the entire country and Kingdom of Pegu. After the *Cobraim* and *Toldans* are the *Talcades*, which is to say Captains: one for the port of *Dogom* <note>Dagon, modern-day Yangon</note>, a day's journey from Pegu, and another for *Martaban*, four days away.

In the Island of Taprobane <note>An ancient geographical name, here identified with Sumatra</note> or Sumatra, there are among the Royal officers two of the most notable who oversee the entire state and civil order: namely, the general of the army whom they call *Nacauda-Roua*, that is to say, Royal Captain; and one named *Chambendure*, who is in charge of setting the price for all merchandise brought to the Island, and without whose license no one is so bold as to dare buy or sell, and who collects the tributes and taxes owed to the King. In the Island of Haiti, otherwise known as Hispaniola, there have been Kings who were named *Huibo*, which signifies as much as "Highness"; others *Tureiguahobui*, which is to say a King more resplendent than gold; another was called *Starei*, which means flamboyant; and another bore the name *Duiheiniqué*, that is to say, rich river. Modern Navigators, speaking of the names of the Kings and Princes of the West Indies, write the following: as the languages are different in the West Indies, the Lords of those countries also have various titles; in some places they are called *Queri*, in others *Caciques*, in certain parts *Tibà*, and in some others *Guasirò*. But for the most part, the word *Cacique* is of wide extent, and in many regions the sovereign Prince is called this. Those who are the next most wealthy and powerful after him, and who have a good number of vassals and subjects under them, are called *Sachò*. And just as these are subject to the *Cacique*, they also have under their jurisdiction Lords who possess lands and lordships, whom they call *Cabrâ*, who are like knights or simple Gentlemen distinguished from the common people, and have more authority than the commoners over whom they command. The lowliest can reach the honor of *Cabrâ* by behaving valiantly in war; for just as in our lands the King ennobles those who have conducted themselves as men of merit in combat and makes them knights of the accolade <note>A ceremony of knighthood involving a tap on the shoulder with a sword</note>, so the Cacique makes *Cabra* those who fight fiercely and are wounded in battle while performing some signal act, giving testimony of their bravery. From then on, they no longer mingle with the common people but are honored and respected, and their children succeed to the nobility of their fathers and are named *Cabrâ*, and consequently are obliged to go to war if the Cacique has need of their service. The greatest Lords are called *Morbichatz*. See Joseph de Acosta <note>A Spanish Jesuit missionary and naturalist (1540–1600)</note>, Book 5, Chapter 25, of his *History of the Indies*, treating the titles and dignities that existed among the Mexicans.

In China, the *Tutans* are absolute Governors of Provinces; after them are the *Ponchases*, and under those the *Anchases*; and the Constable or Master of the Men-at-Arms is called *Aitan*, and his Lieutenant *Luitilius*. Some write that there are five orders of dignity in this China: the first being the *Cunixes*, compared to our Princes and Counts, otherwise called *Toans*, as reported by Father Pietro Maffei <note>An Italian Jesuit historian (1533–1603)</note> in Book 6 of his *History of the Indies*.

Persia to Ptolemy, Persis <term>Περσίς</term> <note>original Greek: "Persis"</note>, a region of Asia, once famous for a most powerful Empire, and even today it does not seem to have degenerated much from that under the Safavids <note>original: "Sophys"</note>. That inner Persia is called Khorasan <note>original: "Curasan"</note> is read in the *Miscellaneous History* 24 and 22; it seems to take Khorasan for the same, as well as the Khorasanite peoples.

G. Postel <note>Guillaume Postel was a French linguist and astronomer interested in Middle Eastern languages</note> in his *Oriental Histories* writes that these Persians are called *Kizilbash* <note>original: "Keizil bass", meaning "red head"</note> because of their turban of that color, otherwise known as Sophys, Pharsis, Agemis, Chorasmis, and Tachmas <note>Likely a reference to Shah Tahmasp I</note>.

## Of the Persians.

### CHAPTER XLVII.

->World / Age / Eternity <note>original Hebrew: "עולם"; Greek: "ἠλὼν αἰλὰν"</note><-

AELAM, Ailam, or Elam—meaning in the Hebrew language youth, or virgin, or hidden, or an age <note>The author is connecting the name Elam to various Hebrew words sharing the same root (CLM), such as "elem" (youth), "almah" (young woman), "alam" (to hide), and "olam" (eternity/world)</note>—the son of Shem, son of Noah (Genesis 10), was the one who first gave his name to the region of Persia. This region is not far distant from Mesopotamia, where Susa is situated, according to the testimony of Josephus in Book 1 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, chapter 6, and of Strabo in Book 16. From this name, those Jews living in Elam or the region of Persia are called Elamites. Concerning this, the *Bundle of Myrrh* <note>original: "faisceau de myrrhe"; likely referring to the *Fasciculus Myrrhae*, a medieval devotional or historical commentary</note> reports that the Persians—descended from the blood and race of Japheth—and the Medes entered the region of the Elamites (successors of Aelan or Elam) and imposed the name of Persians upon them. This is confirmed by Benedictus Pererius <note>Benito Pereira (1535–1610), a Jesuit theologian and commentator</note> in his *Commentaries on the Book of Daniel*, Book 9. In fact, in Daniel chapter 8 and in the Acts of the Apostles chapter 2, we find this word "Elamites" being used to mean the Persians, because the Persians are close neighbors of the Medes. Xenophon even makes mention of the Elamite <note>original: "Ælamide"</note> tribe, which he takes to be Persians. In more ancient times, they were called the Elymaeans or Elymeans in Persia—those who were neighbors of the river Elee, or Tiritiri, who are currently called Azamians, and their region Elam. This word encompasses Susiana, what is properly Persia, and the land of the Parthians, as it was formerly like the patrimony of the Kings of Persia, according to the words of Ludovico di Varthema <note>referred to as "Louys Bartheme", a 15th-century Italian traveler</note> in his books of travels.

Today, the Persians or Persans bear the name of Azamians, as do the Parthians. The easternmost part of Persia is that of Molitene and Cabanden, currently Yezd <note>original: "Iecxt"</note> and Luristan <note>original: "Iurestan"</note>, all surrounded by mountains that are more spacious than others in Persia. It is a wonder of nature to see how these mountains form a pass like that of the Caspian Gates, or Thermopylae, which is also called the Gates of Susa. Through this pass, called Luristan, one enters the country of Persia; the place is so difficult that one can only pass through one after another. Josephus, in Book 1, chapter 6 of his *Antiquities*, writes that Shem, the son of Noah, had five children who possessed Asia from the Euphrates all the way to the Indian Ocean; for Elam left his blood to the Elamites, from whom the Persians are descended. But as for the name "Persian," it is not of such ancient origin, as it happened that the Persians were later called Pantheans, after a king bearing that name, then
<margin>Cephenians <note>original Greek: "κηφῆνες"</note></margin> Cephenians, and <margin>Artaeans <note>original Greek: "ἀρταῖοι"</note></margin> Artaeans, and finally Persians, from Perseus <note>original: "perse"</note>, son of Jupiter, according to the fables of the Greeks, as is written in Herodotus, Book 7 of his *Histories*. Along with him, one should consult Strabo, Books 15 and 16 of his *Geography*; Pliny, Book 6, chapter 27; Marco Polo the Venetian, Book 1 of his travels; Sir John Mandeville in his travels; Giosafat Barbaro in his travels in Persia, printed in Venice; and Messer Ambrogio Contarini, Ambassador of the Venetians, in his travels in Persia, also printed in Venice.

### *On the Persian Language.*
## CHAPTER XLVIII.

Plutarch, in the *Life of Themistocles*, and Valerius Maximus, in Book 8, Chapter 7, make a great deal of the fact—and hold it in high esteem—that this personage, Greek by nation, Themistocles, while a fugitive in the kingdom of Persia, learned to speak the Persian language within a year. Agathias and Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> would have us believe that it is recorded in the memoirs of the ancients that Khosrow <note>original: "Cosroes"</note>, King of Persia, had the works of the philosophers Plato and Aristotle translated from the Greek language into his own Persian tongue. This clearly demonstrates that this Persian language, in the time of that great Greek Captain and the aforementioned King Khosrow of Persia, was quite different and dissimilar from the Greek language.

Those who have carefully read the most ancient authors know very well that the Persians in former times—during their great and flourishing Monarchy or Empire, founded by the force and valor of Cyrus the Great, and continued thereafter for many long years in all perfection, excellence, and prosperity until the last of their Monarchs or Emperors named Darius, who was vanquished by Alexander the Great, King of Macedon—used the Chaldaic or Assyrian language <note>The author likely refers to Aramaic, which served as the *lingua franca* or administrative language of the Achaemenid Persian Empire</note>. This was like a natural, maternal, and ordinary tongue to them in their speech and writing, both common and familiar. Nevertheless, according to Herodotus in Book 3 of his *Histories* and the Book of Esther, chapters 1, 2, 3, and 8 in the Bible, they made use in their state affairs sometimes of their aforementioned language, sometimes of the Greek language, and sometimes of other foreign languages toward their subjects and tributaries, depending on how they understood and spoke said languages. This can be seen in several fine passages cited in the first book of *The Sovereignty of the Kingdom of the Persians* <note>original Latin: "Regio Persarum principatu"; a work by Barnabé Brisson published in 1590</note>. Furthermore, we find in ancient histories that Alexander the Great, having found the tomb of Cyrus, King of Persia, uncovered and ransacked, put to death the one who had done it. And having read the inscription which was in Persian letters and language, he ordered it to be written also in Greek letters and language underneath; the substance of the inscription being as follows:

> *O man, whoever you are, and from wherever you come: for I am certain that you will come: I am Cyrus, he who conquered the Empire for the Persians; I pray you, do not envy me this small bit of earth that covers my poor body.*

Nicolas Chalcondyle, in Book 3 of his *History of the Turks*: The Persians are called Arzamians <note>original: "Arzamiens"; likely a corruption of "Ajam," a term used by Arabs and Turks to refer to Persians</note>, because all those who speak Arzamian are

Barthelemy Georgeuitz <note>Bartholomaeus Georgievicz, a 16th-century Croatian writer who spent years as a slave in the Ottoman Empire</note>, who was for a long time a slave in Turkey, asserts in his travels that the Persian language of today is the same as the Scythian or Tartar <note>original: "Tartaresque"</note> language, saying: The Persians and the Turks use Arabic letters and characters; the Persian language is the easiest of all the other languages of this Universe, and whoever knows and speaks it can use it throughout all the regions of Persia and Turkey, whether negotiating or conducting business with Persians, Turks, Greeks, Armenians, and Christians of whatever condition they may be living in these provinces and regions. The Turks use this language, but in an altered and corrupt form, which is clearly known through the usage of all the other languages. The courtiers of the Sophy <note>original: "Sophy"; a common European term for the Safavid Shah of Persia</note> or King of Persia most often speak the Slavonic <note>original: "Esclauonique"; referring to the Slavic languages spoken by many elite converts and soldiers in the Eastern courts</note> or Slavone language in the court of their Prince, even on the borders and marches of Slavonia. This same Georgeuitz noted and taught some grammatical observations on this Persian language. It even has its own peculiar and proper force or elegance, like the aforementioned Greek and Latin languages." And it is quite credible that the language used in olden times by the more ancient Persians and Medes—descended from Shem the Patriarch—was very close to the Hebrew and Syriac languages. This is visibly demonstrated by the origins of both races and nations, and by the following words: *Gaza, Mandy, Chondy, Ginza, Maddo, Chad*, and infinite other words, which are pure Hebrew and Syriac. And no one should have any doubt in believing that the languages of the most ancient Persians and Medes were the same as, or similar and like, the Hebrew language, if they would carefully consider and compare the edicts and ordinances of the Kings of Persia, inserted at length in the Hebrew books of the Prophet Daniel, alongside the Hebrew words of that same Prophet. But the Persians who are in Persia today are descended from the Parthians, who came and proceeded from Scythia, as modern historians assert. The Persian language of today is widely current and in vogue throughout the greater part of Asia, and has as much credit and reputation as the Latin language has throughout the West. This language has proceeded from the mixture and commingling of the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, Saracenic <note>referring to Arabic-Islamic influence</note>, Arabic, Turkish, Moorish, Tartar, and other languages used throughout Asia. ->Of the Monarchy and Kings of Persia.<-

Those who have seen the Greek and Latin histories know well enough who the Monarchs and Kings of Persia were, of whom, after the ancient authors, F. de Belleforest <note>François de Belleforest (1530–1583), a French historian and encyclopedist</note> has made ample mention in Volume 2, Book 3, Chapters 8, 9, and 10 of his *Universal Cosmography*, and J. This being presupposed, we shall say that the histories of the Saracens report that these Saracens, otherwise called Arabs, held Persia under their domination for a very long time, from the year of salvation 633 or 640—in which Umar <note>original: "Homar"; the second Caliph of the Rashidun Caliphate</note>, a disciple of Muhammad, first taught the follies or ravings of the Quran among them and the Arabs—until the time that the Tartars <note>referring here to the Mongol Empire under the successors of Genghis Khan</note> drove them out and made themselves lords in the year of grace 1260. Then these were driven out by that great Tamerlane <note>original: "Tamburlá, ou Tamerlan, ou Tamerlanes"; Timur, the Turco-Mongol conqueror</note>, who made himself King of the greater part of the East, having defeated in pitched battle Bayezid <note>original: "Baiazet ou Paiazet"; Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I</note>, Emperor of the Turks. After the lineage of this Tamerlane and of one Gempsa, a Turk, as is recorded in the *Asiatic Epistles*, and of Uzun Hasan <note>original: "Vſſuncan"; ruler of the Aq Qoyunlu Oghuz Turkoman tribal federation</note>, named Sultan Hasan Beg <note>original: "Saltam Aſſambey"</note> and Almut, or Alvan, Kings of Persia, Ismail Safi <note>original: "Iſmael Suphy"; Shah Ismail I, the founder of the Safavid Dynasty</note>, son of Haydar <note>original: "Harduel Sechaydar Suphy"</note>, who had married the daughter of the said Uzun Hasan and the daughter of Kaloyan, King of Trebizond <note>John IV or David of the Empire of Trebizond; this reflects the marriage alliances between the Safavids, the Aq Qoyunlu, and the Byzantine Komnenos dynasty</note>, from whom was born this Ismail Safi, as I have already touched upon earlier in the chapter on the life, manners, and religion of the pseudo-prophet Muhammad <note>The author uses standard polemical language of the 16th century regarding Islam</note>; (this Haydar being of the sect or heresy of the Sophies <note>original: "Sophyens"; referring to the Safaviyya Sufi order</note>) seized this Persia around the year of Jesus Christ 1499, not yet having reached the age of twenty years, by the means amply detailed by Joannes Maria Angiolello <note>original: "Iean Maria Angelo"; an Italian traveler who served the Persian Shah</note> in his narration of the life of Uzun Hasan, Jean Lemaire de Belges <note>A 16th-century poet and historian from the Low Countries</note> in his history of the Sophy, Duarte Barbosa <note>original: "Odoard Barboſſe"; a Portuguese explorer and writer</note> in his travels, a certain unknown merchant in his voyage to Persia, and Paolo Giovio <note>original: "Paul Ioue"; an Italian physician and historian</note> in Book 5 of *Illustrious Men* and Book 13 of his *Histories*.

Of this Ismael Sophy, the successors—the Kings of Persia in the time of our ancestors—have held by hereditary succession from father to son the name and title of **Shah Ismail** <note>original: "Xa-ismael"</note>, a word derived from **Shah** <note>original: "Xa"</note>, which in the Persian language means "King," and from that of Ismail, mentioned above, their first and most ancient father. The <term>Sophy</term> <note>A title used by Europeans for the Safavid Shah of Persia, derived from the name of the dynasty's ancestor, Safi-ad-Din</note> is richer, more powerful, and a greater landowner than the <term>Grand Lord of Turkey</term> <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note>, as described at length by André Thevet in book 10, chapter 11 of his *Universal Cosmography*; and after him by <term>Abraham Ortelius</term> <note>A famous Flemish cartographer and geographer</note> in his great *Theater of the World*, and the magnificent Jacques Eava in his reports from the year 1559 concerning Saphan, King of Persia.

The Persians cite several reasons among themselves for why they have always been mortal enemies of the <term>Mahometist</term> <note>A historical European term for Muslims</note> Turks and others. To this point, in the year 1538, the aforementioned Sophy—whom the common people of the country today call <term>Corasini</term> <note>Likely 'Khorasani,' referring to the region of Khorasan</note>, otherwise known as <term>Kezil-bas</term> <note>Qizilbash, or 'Red-heads,' named for their distinctive twelve-gored red hats representing the Twelve Imams</note>—commanded all his priests, ministers, and others, under pain of death, not to dispute in any way with the Turks. This Sophyen Prince made such a decree because of a scandal that occurred a year earlier in the city of Essa, near the mountains of Armenia. Eight Turkish ministers, dogmatizing and preaching in his lands, acted as new reformers of conscience and so stirred the souls of the poor people that, instead of placing faith in the books of <term>Haly</term> <note>Ali ibn Abi Talib, the central figure of Shia Islam</note>, the books of his doctrine were completely overturned. They claimed that he was truly an impostor who never understood the secrets of God nor of his Arabian companion. Consequently, when the Emperor was informed of the blasphemies and insults directed at the said Haly, the sovereign Prophet of the Persian people, he ordered the seizure and arrest of the said ministers and a good number of officers and governors of the towns and provinces who had given them entry and assisted in their new doctrine. Without any form of trial, they were condemned to death—some burned, others impaled—and even their wives, children, and families did not escape, but were put to death as well. This is confirmed by A. Thevet in book 5, chapter 7 of his *Universal Cosmography*, where he also mentions in the subsequent tenth book, chapter 13, a certain Persian heretic named <term>Azelcon</term>, who invented during his life a certain heresy entirely contrary to the Quran of Mahomet, the interpretation of Haly, and the Sophyen sect.

This book had been previously printed in Paris, specifically in the year 1538, in Greek and Latin by <term>Lodovic Tiletan</term> <note>Eloi Tibault, a noted Parisian printer</note>; in addition to these, I shall bring forward this citation from Abbot Serenus, found in <term>Cassian</term> <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435), a monk and theologian</note>, Conference 8, Chapter 21:

"The knowledge of all celestial and sublime things, which Adam had received from God, he passed on to his son Seth. Seth's descendants kept this knowledge untainted, and as long as they remained divided from the sacrilegious lineage of Cain, they exercised that doctrine for the worship of God and for the utility of common life. But when they became mixed with that impious generation, they turned the things they had piously learned toward profane and harmful ends, through the instigation of the Devil. From this source, they boldly established the inquisitive arts of sorcery and delusions, as well as magical superstitions. As for how this inquisitive and malicious doctrine did not perish in the flood, the cause was Ham, as ancient traditions tell us. He was infected by superstitions and sacrilegious arts; yet, since he did not dare bring those arts into the ark (into which he was to enter with his most righteous father Noah and his holy brothers), he engraved them on plates of various metals which would not be ruined by the damage of the waters, and on the hardest stones which would not feel the force of fire. Once the flood had passed, seeking them out with the same curiosity with which he had hidden them, he transmitted a seed-bed of sacrilege and perpetual wickedness to posterity. Thus, by this reasoning, the common opinion—which believes that Angels passed on either sorceries or various arts to men—is fulfilled in truth." <note>original Latin: "Scientiam omnium rerum... in veritate completa est."</note>

<term>Lactantius</term> <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325)</note>, in the second book of his *Divine Institutes*, and Saint <term>Cyprian</term> in his book *On the Vanity of Idols*, attribute the invention of this Magic to the devil and to evil spirits. Pliny, cited above in Book 30, Chapter 2, recognizes several sorts or species of it, taught long ago by <term>Hostanes</term>, a Prince and doctor of that art. <term>Iamblichus</term> in his *Book of the Egyptian Mysteries*, <term>Proclus</term> in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*, and <term>Porphyry</term> in his book *On Sacrifices*, distinguish two types: namely, <term>Theurgy</term> <note>Magic performed with the help of beneficent spirits or gods</note>, which is the good and laudable Magic; and the other, <term>Goetia</term> <note>Magic involving the invocation of demons or "low" sorcery</note> and <term>Necromancy</term> <note>The practice of communicating with the dead</note>, which is wicked and damnable. <term>Suidas</term> <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> divided it into Goetia and <term>Pharmacy</term> <note>The use of magical potions or drugs</note>. <term>Hugh of Saint Victor</term> <note>A 12th-century philosopher and theologian</note>, in Book 6, Chapter 5 of his *Didascalicon*, writes these words, which are worthy of being recited at length in this present chapter:

"Zoroaster, King of the Bactrians, is believed to be the first discoverer of Magic; some assert that he is Ham, the son of Noah, but with a changed name. Ninus, King of the Assyrians, later killed him after he was defeated in war, and had his books, which were full of the arts of sorcery, burned in fire. Aristotle writes concerning this man that up to two million lines of his on the magical art, as dictated by him, were passed down by his books to the memory of posterity. Democritus later expanded this art at the time when Hippocrates was held in high renown in the art of medicine. Magic is not accepted within Philosophy; rather, it is an outsider with a false profession, the mistress of all iniquity and malice, lying about the truth, and truly wounding souls..." <note>original Latin: "Magiæ repertor primus... lædens animos"</note>

...leads away from divine religion, persuades the worship of demons, brings about the corruption of morals, and impels the minds of its followers toward every crime and wickedness. Generally speaking, this encompasses five types of evil arts: <term>Mantice</term> <note>From the Greek *mantike*, meaning the art of divination</note>, which signifies divination and vain "mathematics," <term>Sortilegia</term> <note>Divination by lots</note>, <term>Maleficia</term> <note>Harmful magic or witchcraft</note>, and <term>Præstigiæ</term> <note>Illusions or sleight of hand</note>. 

The art of <term>Mantice</term> contains five species within itself. First is <term>Necromancy</term>, which is interpreted as divination through the dead; for in Greek <note>original: "νεκρὸς"</note> it means "dead" and in Latin a "corpse" <note>original: "νεκρὸν"</note>. This is the divination performed through the sacrifice of human blood, for which demons thirst and in which they delight when it is poured out. Second is <term>Geomancy</term>, which is divination by the earth. Third is <term>Hydromancy</term>, that is, divination in water. Fourth is <term>Aeromancy</term>, which is divination in the air. Fifth is divination in fire, which is called <term>Pyromancy</term>. Indeed, <term>Varro</term> <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a prolific Roman scholar</note> stated there were four elements in which divination consists: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. Therefore, the first type—Necromancy—seems to belong to the underworld, the second to the Earth, the third to Water, the fourth to the Air, and the fifth to Fire. 

The category of <term>Mathematica</term> <note>In this context, it refers to "mathematical" arts like astrology rather than modern arithmetic</note> is divided into three species: <term>Aruspicina</term> <note>Haruspicy</note>, <term>Augury</term>, and the doctrine of horoscopes, which they call <term>Horospica</term>. The <term>Haruspices</term> are so named as if they were "observers of hours" <note>original: "Horaspices"</note>, who observe the specific times for performing tasks; or they are named from "inspecting the altars" <note>original: "haras inspicientes"</note>, as they consider future events within the entrails and fibers of sacrificial animals. <term>Augury</term> (or <term>Auspicium</term>) sometimes pertains to the eye and is called "auspice" (as if "looking") because it focuses on the movement and flight of birds; sometimes it pertains to the ears and is then called "augury" (as if the "chirping of birds") because it is perceived by the ear. <term>Horoscopia</term>, which is also called "constellation," occurs when the deeds of men are sought in the stars, just as the <term>Genethliaci</term> <note>Casters of birth charts</note> do, who observe births; these were formerly called <term>Magi</term> in a specific sense, of whom we read in the Gospel <note>A reference to the Three Wise Men in Matthew 2</note>. 

The <term>Sortilegi</term> are those who seek divinations through lots. The <term>Malefici</term> are those who, through demonic incantations, bindings, or other execrable types of "remedies," perform wicked deeds by the cooperation and instinct of demons. <term>Præstigiæ</term> occur when, through fantastic illusions regarding the transformation of things, human senses are mocked by demonic art. 

In total, there are eleven types: five under Mantice (Necromancy, Geomancy, Hydromancy, Aeromancy, Pyromancy), three under Mathematica (Haruspicy, Augury, Horoscopy), and then three others (Sortilegy, Maleficium, and Præstigiæ). It is said that Mercury first discovered <term>Præstigiæ</term>; the Phrygians discovered Auguries; <term>Tages</term> <note>A founding figure of Etruscan religion</note>, the first Etruscan, handed down Haruspicy and Sortilegy. Hydromancy first came from the Persians.

<term>Cælius Rhodiginus</term> <note>Lodovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), an Italian humanist</note>, in Book 9, Chapter 23 of his *Various Lessons*, wrote these words worthy of being recited: 

"Those who have striven to look more accurately into these matters have discovered two summits of Magic. One is infamous and ill-omened due to commerce with unclean spirits. The other, if you explore it more thoughtfully, is almost nothing else than the very peak of natural Philosophy. The Greeks call the former type <term>Goetia</term> <note>Low or "black" magic</note> rather than Magic; it is sealed by incantations and poems composed with the art of wicked curiosity. Some even dare to call the latter by the more honorable name of <term>Theurgy</term> <note>High magic or "god-working"</note>, yet they wish a distinction to be understood: that some are damnably devoted to illicit arts—of the kind <term>Zabulus</term> <note>A late Latin name for the Devil</note> is remembered to have devised—whom they also call evildoers..."

It also introduces the distinction between "Goetia" (demonic magic) and "Theurgy" (perceived as a higher, natural philosophy).</summary>

...what they commonly call [it]. For they say that <term>Goetia</term> <note>original: "goetiam"; refers to "low" magic or sorcery involving the invocation of spirits, often contrasted with the "high" magic of Theurgy</note> belongs properly to these, about which books are composed of the kind that the <term>Legal Consultant Ulpian</term> <note>Domitius Ulpianus (c. 170–223 AD), a powerful Roman jurist whose writings formed a large part of the Justinian Code</note> calls "prohibited readings," and he determined they should be destroyed immediately, etc.

Julius Caesar Scaliger <note>A renowned Italian scholar and physician of the Renaissance</note> in his *Exercise* 327 against Jerome Cardan <note>An influential Renaissance polymath</note> on the subject of "Subtlety."

Magic is threefold. The first is the lowest, and indeed ours; it is foul and filthy, involving little chants, corpses, and the ropes of the hanged. If anyone dares to touch this, they deserve [punishment]. The second draws powers from the stars into mirrors, seals, rings, and tablets. The third is divine. A flood of impostors has made the name hateful to the common people. But among the Persians, a "Magus" sounds like nothing other than a "wise man"; yet, because of the betrayal and treachery of <term>Smerdis</term> <note>Referring to the "Pseudo-Smerdis," a magus who reportedly usurped the Persian throne in 522 BCE</note>, he made the name of the Magi loathsome for a long time. The Magi who traveled from the most distant regions to worship the Lord Jesus recognized through this Magic that he was the promised King. We have described these things from the books of the Syrians: they say that the powers, methods, and goals of Magic and the transmutatory art <note>Alchemy</note> are very similar. The work and goal of the <term>Chemists</term> is body into body; the work and goal of Magic is spirit in the body. The Magi call their influences "violences" because they exercise their powers beyond those that seem to occur by the order of nature. The Chemists call their work "fortitude" [strength]: for this is what that celebrated <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "philosopher's stone" or "elixir of life" sought by alchemists to transform matter or grant immortality</note> signifies, in whose faith they pledge all of nature. The majority of modern authors divide this Magic into natural and non-natural, the latter of which uses and employs the invocation of demons and evil spirits, as <term>B. Pererius</term> <note>Benedict Pereira (1535–1610), a Jesuit theologian and author of a famous treatise against magic and astrology</note> extensively deduces in his *Treatise on Magic*. A certain modern author in Book 7, Chapter 8 of the *Syntax of the Admirable Art* wrote the following words:

In the Persian language, the name of Magic expresses only wisdom and the peak of the perfection of Philosophy: for the Magi among the Persians are the same as the Philosophers among the Greeks; the <term>Brahmins</term> and Gymnosophists among the Indians; the <term>Druids</term>, Bards, and <term>Semnothei</term> <note>Ancient names for Gallic or Celtic philosopher-priests</note> among the Gauls; the Galertae among the Sicilians; the Priests among the Egyptians; the Etruscan <term>Haruspices</term> <note>Diviners who interpreted the entrails of animals</note> among the Italians; the Wise Men among the Latins; the Prophets among the <term>Cabalists</term>; and the <term>Chaldeans</term> among the Babylonians and Assyrians. However, since almost everything that arose from the most wholesome beginnings has degenerated too far, some disciples—straying from the pure and unadulterated teachings of the Magi and Wise Men, and sometimes being excessively curious or through an affected superstition of wanting to know [too much]—crossed the boundaries of true wisdom. They fell into those vain observations of prohibited Magic, and thus, with the celebrated name of Magic defiled, it fell into hatred: a title previously of honor and excellence was turned into a disgrace, as <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and naturalist</note> teaches in Book 30, Chapter 1. It is clear, therefore, that Magic is loathed because of its abuse; but insofar as it is contained within its own rules, it is the knowledge of excellent things, both divine and human, or natural. One type is upright—namely, natural and divine—while another is improper—namely, demonic, born from the abuse of natural things. Natural Magic is that which works marvelous effects by depending on the natures of things—not known to all, but to the more learned and skilled—either from the entire substance of a compound or a certain mixture of others. It is the consummation of physical philosophy and appears like a miracle to the common people. Therefore, this [art] receives effects from nature and the power of the heavens, stars, elements, animals, metals, plants...

...of [plants] and stones: the science of which is drawn from Astrology, Metaphysics, Physics, and Medicine through experience and observation. This magic may be divinatory, predicting the future and effects that depend on natural causes; or it may be operative, exhibiting wonders to those who are ignorant of the causes and powers of things. There is also Divine Wisdom or <term>Magic</term> <note>The author uses "Magic" here in its highest sense—as a synonym for deep wisdom or "Magia"—rather than sorcery</note>, which consists in the virtue, the name, and the power of God, rather than in natural things. This is seen when the Prophets predict what is to come, or when Christians perform miracles through faith or prayer. From this comes the true <term>Cabala</term> <note>A Jewish mystical tradition. Here, the author distinguishes a "pure" version used by holy men from what he considers the "corrupted" versions of his contemporaries</note>, which—though defiled by the superstition of the Rabbis—was originally composed of the names of the almighty God, either as expressed in the sacred pages, extracted by some art, or received by hand from holy men.

Wicked and demonic, vain and superstitious, is the magic called <term>Theurgy</term> <note>original: "Theurgia"; high ritual magic intended to invoke gods or spirits</note> and <term>Goetia</term> <note>original: "Goiteia"; lower magic or black magic involving the invocation of demons</note>. This is either simple, consisting of the invocation and assistance of demons, or compound—that is, having some deceptive natural power added to it, or colored by a veneer of true religion, so that the unwary are deceived by its pretext. Indeed, this compound magic most often deceives by appearing to be righteous. 

Therefore, this compound magic—which is utterly vain—uses the invocation of demons or silent pacts with them. To hide these frauds and abominations from a Christian man, it adds elements from the four physical foundations: from the earth, whence comes <term>Geomancy</term>; from the water, whence <term>Hydromancy</term>; from the Air, whence <term>Aeromancy</term>; or from the fire, whence <term>Pyromancy</term>. It misuses men, formerly commanding them to perform sacrifices so that their entrails could be inspected. It also misuses men as instruments of its impiety, with the demon bringing forth oracles through their mouths, their chests, their navels, or even their genitals, as written by Plutarch in *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*, Iamblichus in *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, Origen in book 7 *Against Celsus*, Eustathius on the second book of the *Iliad*, St. Chrysostom in his 9th homily on the *Epistle to the Corinthians*, and Caelius Rhodiginus in book 4, chapter 10.

This magic also scrutinizes the lines in the hand, from which <term>Chiromancy</term> was born, as well as the features and proportions of the face—though if these do not exceed the study of bodily temperaments, they are not entirely disapproved; this they call <term>Physiognomy</term>. It even misuses animals, attempting to convince people of a knowledge of the future from the chirping of birds; this they called <term>Augury</term>, as Cicero says in the second book of *On Divination*. Or it divines through the inspection of birds, whence comes <term>Haruspicy</term> and <term>Auspicy</term>, or <term>Oionoskopia</term> <note>original: "οιωνοσκοπία"; Greek for divination by the flight and cries of birds</note>, an invention of Tiresias according to Pliny, book 7, chapter 56. It may also command one to observe the feeding, song, or flight of winged creatures, as if there were divinity or a notion of the future in them, even though the birds know nothing of themselves or their own futures. I would say the same regarding other animals that are observed. 

It even accommodates plants to its infamy, as Pliny says in book 24, chapter 17, as well as stones and metals. From this comes <term>Lekanomancy</term> <note>original: "λεκανομαντία"</note>, which is done with basins full of water after invoking a demon; Strabo in book 15 testifies that this magic was observed among the Persians. Added to this is <term>Catoptromancy</term> <note>original: "κατοπτρομαντία"</note>, which is done through mirrors, and <term>Axinomancy</term> <note>original: "αξινομαντία"</note>, which is done through axes and other iron instruments—whether they are tied to a sieve (whence <term>Koskinomancy</term> <note>original: "κοσκινομαντία"</note>) or whether a key is tied to the Psalms, or if one misuses metals in some other way. 

Horrendous also is that magic which thinks it can disturb and summon the shades of the dead, called <term>Necromancy</term> <note>original: "νεκρομαντία"</note>, which involves conversations with demons. For this, a superstitious and utterly vain use of <term>characters</term> <note>Magical signs or symbols</note>, incense, and ecclesiastical prayers is adapted, and a most wicked abuse of the sacraments occurs. In short, there is nothing holy that the Magician does not usurp and pollute. Therefore, in magic, there is a frequent abuse—I will not say use—of demons, poisons, eye-salves, ointments, potions, love-philtres, bindings, suspensions, rings, images, characters, and metal plates...

...charts, certain numbers, sounding sacrifices, purifications, solitudes, lots <note>original: "fortiū"; likely referring to cleromancy or the casting of lots</note>, bindings, fascinations, thoughts or imaginations, ecstasies of the mind, incantations, wonders, exorcisms, consecrations, devotions, fasts, dreams, prayers, ceremonies, and celestial conjunctions.

Otthon Heurnius <note>Otto Heurnius (1577–1652), a Dutch physician and philosopher who wrote on the "ancient philosophy" of the Barbarians and Egyptians</note>, a very modern author, in his *Indica*, chapter 28, treatise 6, concerning *Asiatic Magic and its author Zoroaster or Zarade the Persian*, speaks of it in these words:

"Magic is threefold <note>original: "Magia triplex est"</note>: one is the lowest and most common among us; it is surely foul and sordid, involving little songs, corpses, and the ropes of hanged men—things that if anyone should dare to touch, they would deserve punishment. The middle type draws strength from the stars into mirrors, seals, rings, and tablets. The third is divine, through which the works of nature are seen more clearly; and because it is honorable and desirable, it was cultivated not only by commoners but also by the greatest Kings of Kings, especially the Persians. They were so curious about it that they did not dare to aspire to the governance of the kingdom unless they were deeply immersed in its core. However, the supreme dictator of Physicians, Hippocrates, shows with this ray of reason that those other two species of magic are by no means arts. Every craftsman is master of his instrument, but the Magician is not master of his instrument, since it is more powerful than himself—namely, the devil, the spirit of greatest power. Therefore, the Magician is not a craftsman, nor is Magic an art. For what the common people believe—that one imbued with Magic can harm another with words—is a trifle. For who taught him those words? Was it another man, and who taught him? It was not a celestial intelligence, for who would dare make such a thing the author of a charm? Therefore, it was an evil demon. He did this not to make the man more powerful, but to deceive him through his own gullibility, and to have him as a companion in both impiety and eternal exile. Thus the demon himself acts, while that foolish and senseless man thinks he acts by his own words. Similarly, the fibers of livers and hearts—inverted, substituted, mutilated, or removed—were once used by the same demon, who had persuaded wretched people through his responses that these things should be done as sacred rites."

Zoroaster, or Zarade the Persian, was the first to skillfully cultivate this filthy imposture. For according to Berosus the Babylonian <note>A Hellenistic-era Babylonian priest and historian</note> and Athercles in their commentaries on the affairs of the Assyrians and Medes, he was endowed by nature with excellent talent, but driven by a detestable spirit <note>original: "genio"; a guiding spirit or demon</note>, he changed the divine and human rites of the ancient Persians.

For the ancient Persians worshiped Belus (or Jupiter), Sandes (or Hercules), and Anaitis (or Venus). Their descendants, however, almost followed the <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>A major dualistic religion that taught a struggle between a good, spiritual world of light and an evil, material world of darkness</note> in divine worship. For they established two principles: one indeed good, producing all the best things from itself, which they called Hormisdate <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of Zoroastrianism</note>, or Oromazen, or Oromagdam. They asserted that his body was most similar to light and his soul to truth. The other principle was evil, the fountain and spring of all adversities, which they named Arimamen <note>Ahriman, the destructive spirit in Zoroastrian dualism</note>. They also celebrated a great festival which they called the "Removal of Evils," in which they killed many serpents and other animals that live in deserted places, offering them to the Magi as a proof of their piety. For by this reasoning, they believed they performed a work good and pleasing to Hormisdate, and unpleasing to Arimani. They especially revered water, to such an extent that they would not wash their faces with it, nor touch it for any reason except for drinking or washing. They considered fire to be worthy of the highest honor and most sacred. For this reason, the Magi kept it perpetually in certain sacred and hidden shrines, and looking into it, they performed secret sacred rites and gave answers concerning future things.
