(Catchword: as if)

...originated from Zoroaster. For he, among other impious and horrifying dogmas, taught that it was lawful and consistent with the laws of nature for a brother to be joined with his sister, a father with his daughter, a grandfather with his granddaughter, and what is most wicked (O laws! O nature!) for a son to be joined with his mother. Two lights of Roman poetry, clearly revealing these rituals, sang of them. Catullus wrote:

> For a Magus <note>A member of the priestly caste in ancient Persia; the word is the root of "magic."</note> must be born from a mother and her son,
> If the impious religion of the Persians is true.

And Lucan in his second book:

> ———Sisters enter
> Into the chambers of brothers; the unfortunate tablet
> Of Oedipodean <note>A reference to Oedipus, the Greek mythological figure who unknowingly married his mother.</note> Thebes condemns among nations the pledges
> Of mothers for a crime committed unintentionally.
> But as often as the Lord of the Parthians is born thus
> From mixed blood, an Arsacid <note>A member of the Arsacid dynasty, the ruling house of the Parthian Empire.</note> who may lawfully impregnate his parent:
> What should I consider a crime?

For this reason, Great Mother Earth herself, the nourisher of all, fleeing such foul and horrifying monsters, refused by any means to receive their corpses into her peaceful bosom (being spurred to vengeance by holy God). So that Zoroaster might veil this disgrace with a cloak of piety, he taught that the most holy rite of burial was not to be enclosed in the bowels of the earth, nor consumed by fire, but to be cast out in the fields to be dissolved by the air—by whose benefit you sustained your life for many years—or to be torn apart and consumed by birds, which you often nourished with your body while you lived.

Hence, all Persians would immediately carry out the body of the deceased and deport it outside the town, exposing it on the bare ground, naked, to be devoured by dogs and obscene birds. In this manner, once the flesh was consumed, the naked bones would rot, scattered across the fields. Furthermore, if birds did not immediately fly to a corpse, or if dogs did not run to tear it apart on the spot, they believed that man’s morals had been impure, his soul unjust and worthy of the abyss <note>original: "barathro," referring to a deep pit or hell</note>, and dedicated to an evil demon. 

Then, with the greatest grief, his friends would mourn him as one truly dead and not a participant in a better fate. However, they proclaimed him who was most quickly devoured to be most happy; they regarded his soul with great admiration as being most excellent, very similar to God, and destined to fly to the blessed seats. 

The common and more obscure crowd, if any among them in the army were afflicted by some sharp disease, were led out while still breathing and conscious. A piece of bread, a jar of water, and a staff were placed beside them, so that as long as they were able to use food, they would not be without it; and with the staff, they might ward off and drive away the attacking wild beasts and the feasting scavengers while they still had some strength. But if they had not yet died, yet the force of the disease had overcome them to the point that they could no longer move their hands, then the miserable wretches, half-dead and already beginning to give up the ghost, were most cruelly devoured, deprived of all sweetest hope of enjoying the breath of life. 

Many also, when they had recovered, returned home like characters in a play or tragedy, returning from the dark gates of the underworld, gaunt and pale, terrifying those they met. If anyone returned in such a state, everyone turned away from him and fled as if from a marked man, as one still dwelling among those below the earth. Nor were they permitted to resume their former way of life until the ritual pollution of their expected death had been expiated by the Magi, and their life...

...as if given anew. A miraculous event also occurred to certain Philosophers returning from Persia to Rome (during the reign of Khosrow <note>Likely Khosrow I, the Sasanian king known as Anushirvan the Just (r. 531–579 AD).</note>, the most powerful King of the Persians) which revealed the same reason for this foul burial rite. For when they were resting in what was once Persian territory, they caught sight of the corpse of a dead man, neglected and cast aside unburied. Pitying the iniquity of that barbarian law, and deeming it in no way just to ignore nature being thus insulted, they had their servants cover the corpse as best they could and buried it, mounding the earth over it.

In the night that followed, while everyone was sleeping, one of them—by Hercules, I do not know which one, for I do not know his name—appeared to himself to see an old man. This man was not known to him, but was grave and venerable, displaying his devotion to Philosophy by both the style of his clothing and his long, flowing beard. He called out to him, as if exhorting and commanding:

> *Leave not the unburied and naked corpse in the tomb*
> *To be torn by dogs and serve as food for birds.*
> *For Mother Earth, who receives all, does not accept him*
> *Who dared to defile his mother with an unspeakable deed.*
> <note>original Latin: "Ne tumulis inhumatum ac nudum linque cadauer... Qui matrem est ausus facto vitiare nefando."</note>

Immediately awakened by fear, he reported his dream to the others; at first, they were uncertain what the dream might portend. However, when they rose at dawn and continued their intended journey, passing through that same field (as the terrain required) where they had provided the sudden burial, they found the corpse naked once more, lying atop the mound, as if the Earth, indignant and acting of her own accord, had vomited it back up in anger. Struck by the miracle of this sight, they continued their journey, performing no further final service for the man. Weighing the dream, they finally came to the conclusion that the Persians suffer this punishment and vengeance because of their shameful unions with their own mothers.

The successors of this Zoroaster embraced nearly these same dogmas: that the Gods should not be represented by any image, and that those who assign the distinction of sex to them sin most grievously. For this reason, Xerxes <note>The Persian King of Kings who invaded Greece in 480 BC.</note> burned all the temples of Greece, deeming it wicked for the Gods to be expressed in images or confined within the narrowness of walls. They asserted that the air swarms with demons who instill themselves into our eyes like miasmas <note>Polluting vapors or contagions.</note>. They wore white clothing; the ground was their bed; their food was vegetables, bread, and cheese, which they would place into their mouths fixed upon the tip of a reed staff. 

They were possessed by a supreme devotion to divination and excelled greatly in it. Thus, when the Parthian throne was vacant and the queen was pregnant—though she was still in the early months of conception—the leading men of the empire ordered them to declare whether the Queen was carrying a male or a female. First, so that their response might be more certain, they brought in a mare near to foaling and pronounced correctly upon its offspring; then they asserted the Queen was carrying a male child. The Princes of the empire, placing faith in this statement, placed the royal tiara <note>cidaris: a high, stiff Persian headdress or diadem.</note> upon the Queen's womb, proclaiming the embryo as King and distinguishing him with a noble name. Thus Shapur <note>Sapores: Shapur II (r. 309–379 AD), the only king in history to be crowned in utero.</note> was born after a few months with his Kingdom, and in it he both grew up and grew old, his life being extended to seventy years. 

Furthermore, those Magi who were in the company of the Parthian ambassadors to Sulla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the Roman general; this meeting occurred around 96 BC.</note> declared (from the marks on his body) that his life and memory would be celebrated, as Velleius Paterculus says in Book 3 <note>Actually Book 2 of Velleius's Roman History.</note>. Likewise, when Artaxerxes had been removed from human affairs and his son Ochus <note>Artaxerxes III (Ochus), reigned 358–338 BC.</note> had seized the reins of the Kingdom, the Eunuchs...

The Suda <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia, formerly attributed to an author named Suidas.</note> also testifies that in his time they bore the name of the Patzinacitæ [Pechenegs], and certain of them were called Gruthungi and Dagci, who are European Scythians; Chalcocondylas <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles (c. 1430–1470), a Byzantine Greek historian.</note> identifies them as those Sachatei.

Nicephorus Callistus also mentions these. Today, however, as Herberstein <note>Siegmund von Herberstein (1486–1566), a diplomat and author of the first major European work on Russia.</note> attests, they are called **Tartars** by foreigners, but they themselves name them *Berfermani* or *Befermani*. Niger <note>Dominicus Marius Niger, a 15th-century Venetian geographer.</note> claims they call themselves *Matius* in their own language. According to Thevet <note>André Thevet (1516–1590), a French explorer and writer.</note>, they are called *Ator Albacaran* by the Arabs. These are the nations of the Scythians in Herodotus: the Anchatae, Arpoxae, Catiari, Traspies, and Paralatae; he adds that the name for all of them is the **Scoloti** <term>skolótēs</term> <note>original: <term>σκολότης</term></note>.

A great many are enumerated by Pliny, such as the Alani, Amordi, Apellae, Aorsi, Antariani, and Arimaspi (who were previously the Calcidiri), the Ariacae, Aroteres, Asaei, Camae, Camacae, Cotieri, Daci, Dahae, Edones, Essedones, Euchalae, Histi, Getae, Hamaxobii, Massagetae, Napaei, Octei, Pesici, Roxolani, Rhymnigi, Sacae, Sarmatians, and Satarchi. Trebellius Pollio, in his *Life of the Emperor Claudius*, also includes these peoples of Scythia: the Peucini, Trutungi, Austrogoths, Virtingui, and Sigipedes.

In the lexicon of Stephanus [of Byzantium] *On Cities*, we read of these: the Aspilas (these are peoples of Colchis in the *Circumnavigation* <note>The *Periplus* of the Euxine Sea, a maritime guidebook by Arrian.</note> by Arrian), the Budini, Daias, Dassas, Heiuros, Euergetas, Edos, Iamas, Iamos, Bechir, Iseros, Lazos (of Colchis, according to Arrian), Matycetas, Maeotas, Myrgetas, Parthyacos, Sanigas (<term>sanígai</term> <note>original: <term>σανίγαι</term></note>, also of Colchis near Sebastopolis, according to Arrian), and Tyrmemenios. Mela <note>Pomponius Mela, a 1st-century Roman geographer.</note> places some of them as Nomads. Likewise, the Suda says they are also called *Hamaxophorei* [wagon-carriers]. Pliny complains, in describing them, of the inconsistency of authors because of—as he adds—the innumerable tribes, so much so that their name (as he says in another place) passes everywhere into the Sarmatians and Germans. Strabo writes in Book 1 that all known regions toward the North were previously called by one name: either Scythians or, as in Homer, Nomads. Likewise in Book 2, he reports that the ancient Greek writers applied the name of Scythians and Celto-Scythians to all the Northern nations; Ptolemy agrees with this opinion in his *Tetrabiblos* [Four Books]. Those older than these divided them such that all who lived above the Euxine [Black Sea], the Ister [Danube], and the Adria were called Hyperboreans, Sauromatae, and Arimaspi, while those beyond the Hyrcanian [Caspian] Sea were called Sacae and Massagetae. Philostratus encompasses the Scythians within the Ister, Tanais [Don], and Thermodon rivers. Trogus bounds them by the Pontus [Black Sea], the Riphaean mountains, Asia, and the Phasis river. Read of the Scythian customs in Theophrastus <note>Likely referring to the Hippocratic work *On Airs, Waters, and Places*, which discusses Scythian biology and culture.</note> on air and waters.

The region which the Scythians now inhabit is said to have once belonged to the Cimmerians, says Herodotus in *Thalia* <note>The third book of Herodotus's *Histories*.</note>. I believe he speaks of the European Scythians. Julius Pollux (in Book 8, *On the Athenian Markets*) noted that the Scythian Archers were called <term>toxotai</term> <note>Greek: "archers".</note>. Even to this day, we interpret the name of the people of the Scandinavian peninsula—among whom are the Celto-Scythians—as "archers." See Scythia Minor, Pontica, Thracensis, and the Scytho-Germans under the entry for *Molsia*.

In Ptolemy, Scythia is twofold; both parts are in Asia, separated by Mount Imaus <note>A name used by ancient geographers for the central Asian mountain ranges, including the Himalayas, Pamirs, and Hindu Kush.</note>. Thus, they are designated as "within" and "outside" the Imaus. Villanomanus <note>Michael Servetus, who edited Ptolemy’s *Geography* under the name Villanovanus.</note> writes in his edition of Ptolemy that the Kingdom of Cathay [China] contains these Scythias. That which is within the Imaus seems to me to occupy a great part of Tartary. That which is situated outside the Imaus is called "Mongal" by the Barbarians and "Ancient Tartary" by more recent writers, according to Marius Niger. Arias Montanus, in his *Biblical Appendix*, believes that Scythia within the Imaus is the land the Hebrews call "Dicla."

Besides these, there is another Scythia in Europe (which Ptolemy calls Sarmatia) found in Herodotus, Pomponius Mela, and other ancient historians. Unless I am mistaken, this is the region Jordanes <note>A 6th-century historian of the Goths.</note> refers to, which he writes the Goths called *Ouim* in their own language; Conrad of Lichtenau reads this as *Ocimnin* from the same author. Strabo calls "Little Scythia" that region located between the Borysthenes [Dnieper River] and the Tauric Chersonese [Crimea]. According to Usuard (for November 3rd), Scythia is also the name of a certain metropolitan city in Phrygia. See also *Indoscythia*.

Ptolemy describes Indoscythia as a region of India stretching along the Indus River; Arrian, in his *Periplus*, names the same region simply "Scythia." The "Southern Scythians" <term>Notioi Skythai</term> <note>Greek: "Southern Scythians".</note> are mentioned by Dionysius Periegetes.

### On the Tartars.

It seemed very necessary to me to report in this chapter what the ancient Hebrew, Greek, and Latin authors left in writing regarding the ancient Scenites <note>From the Greek *skēnē* (tent); a term used by ancients for nomadic "tent-dwellers."</note> and Nomads, before entering into a discussion of the Tartars and their language. The Hebrews assert that Jabal <note>The text mistakenly says "Jabal son of Mathusalem," but Genesis 4:20 identifies Jabal as the son of Lamech.</note>, son of Methuselah, was the first in this universe to invent tents and pavilions, and was the father of those who lived in them (Genesis, chapter 4). This is confirmed by the great Saint Augustine in the eighteenth book, seventeenth chapter of his *City of God*. Regarding this fourth chapter of Genesis, Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] and Rabbi Isaac write that Abel, son of Adam, was the first shepherd of sheep and other beasts <note>The author likely conflates Abel's role as a shepherd with the invention of nomadic infrastructure attributed to Jabal.</note>, having invented carts, tents, and pavilions in order to move and change countries, lands, and habitations often, for the convenience of grass and pastures. For this reason, he was called "the father of those who dwell in tents and pavilions," as confirmed by Gilbert Génébrard in the first book of his *Chronography*. Furthermore, the most inquisitive Rabbis assure us that after the Flood, almost all the children of Noah lived in tents and pavilions. Indeed, in Genesis chapter 9, mention is made of the tent of Noah and the pavilions, tabernacles, or tents of Shem. The word...

The Hebrew word אהל <note>original: *Ohel*</note>, in this chapter, signifies a moving and unfixed tabernacle: a way of living in such tabernacles or tents that was maintained by the Patriarchs who came after the second age, as can be seen in several different places in the Holy Hebrew Scriptures; in *Polydore Vergil*, book 3, chapter 9, *On the Invention of Things*; and in the commentators of *Flavius Vegetius*, book 1, chapter 3, on military matters. This being presupposed, we shall say that the Scenites were anciently certain peoples of Arabia Felix <note>Literally "Happy Arabia," the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula.</note> (just as there are still some today in this province toward the North called Arabs, according to the report of *Ludovico di Varthema* in his *itinerary*). They were named *Scenitæ* in ancient times by the Greeks <gloss>from the word for tents or pavilions</gloss>, in which they lived, as recorded by *Pliny* (book 5, chapter 11, and book 6, chapters 26 and 28 of his *Natural History*), following *Strabo* (books 1, 2, and 16 of his *Geography*). *Solinus* (chapter 36) and *Plutarch* (in the life of *Lucullus*) write that *Tigranes* <note>Tigranes the Great, King of Armenia (reigned 95–55 BCE).</note> forced a change in the way of life of these wandering people, who had no houses other than the tents or pavilions they always carried with them; this King made them settle near him to employ them in the business of trade. The Kurds <note>original: "Cuodes"</note> of today do the same in Assyria, according to the modern Syrian geographers, who note in their works that in the southern part of Mesopotamia there are currently Arabs formerly called *Scenites*. These remain shepherds to this day who rarely stop in one place, but rather change lands and countries according to where they find grass to feed their beasts and flocks.

As for the Nomads, *Herodotus* in several places in his works; *Strabo* (books 16, 7, 10, and 11 of his *Geography*); *Pausanias* in his *Attics*; *Justin* (book 2); *Pomponius Mela* (book 2, chapter 1, and book 3, chapter 5); *Pliny* (book 4, chapters 12, 13, and 17, and book 5, chapter 3); *Sallust* in the *Jugurthine War*; *Solinus* (chapter 29); *Hippocrates* in his *treatise on Air and Waters*; and *Athenaeus* (book 11, chapter 1 of his *Deipnosophistae* <note>A Greek work title meaning "The Banquet of the Learned."</note>) all make ample mention of these peoples. Modern cosmographers hold that the Numidians in Africa currently live in this same manner. Some report that *Homer* had knowledge of these peoples, whom he calls *Ἐνετούς* <note>The Eneti or Heneti, a tribe mentioned in the Iliad.</note>, and whom he places and locates in Paphlagonia. At present, there are several kinds of these nomadic and wandering shepherds in many parts of the earth, such as in our Europe, principally in the Northern countries, named Sargaces and Osyles. In Asia, those who live toward the Caspian Sea were anciently called Parni and Daces; in Africa, those who inhabit the Ammonic region. Modern geographers tell us the Nomads were a people of Africa located in the region of Zeugitana and Mauritania who were eventually called Numidians, according to *Festus Pompeius*. All of them issued and descended from the Persians, and were thus called Nomads <gloss>from the Greek word meaning 'to graze'</gloss>, because they devoted themselves entirely to pasturage, as reported by ancient Greek authors and *Henri Estienne* in his great *Treasury of the Greek Language* under the Greek word <term>nemo</term> <note>original: *νέμω, -εις*; meaning "to pasture" or "to distribute."</note>. Modern authors call them Zuphones. To tell the truth, the Scythian Sarmatians or Sauromatians were the true Nomads and <term>Hamaxobites</term> <note>From the Greek meaning "wagon-dwellers."</note> of the ancients, who have been succeeded by the Tartars of today, living in the same sort and manner. in continual labor and toil, living in tents and pavilions, they have made way for the Arabs and <term>Alarbes</term> <note>A term used historically to distinguish nomadic desert Arabs from settled ones.</note> of today, who live in Asia with a similar freedom of life since the coming of the <note>The author uses "Pseudo-Prophete" reflecting the common 16th-century European Christian perspective on Islam.</note> Pseudo-Prophet Muhammad, carrying and leading with them their houses, villages, and towns which they drag on wagons or on the backs of their camels, following the convenience of grass and pastures through the mountains and deserts, from Arabia and the river Euphrates as far as the Atlantic Sea. These people are very harmful to the plains of Syria, Egypt, and <term>Citerior Africa</term> <note>Nearer Africa, referring to the northern regions closest to Europe.</note>, especially during the gathering and harvesting of grains and fruits: at which time they descend packed and thick in troops like the swallows that come to these quarters in the mild and spring seasons; then, having ravished and carried off all they can, they retreat with such speed that they seem rather to fly than to run, and it is in no way possible to catch them in this flight of theirs. For today, the Scythians have no towns, cities, villages, houses, nor castles whatsoever, each carrying and dragging on a leather-covered wagon—in which they stay with their wives, children, and family—everything they have and possess, wandering and roaming among the deserts, woods, forests, and solitudes. This is what the Muscovites and Tartars of the present still practice toward the <note>original: "Rha"</note> Rha, or Volga, drawing toward the mountains of <note>original: "Iuhira"</note> Yugra <note>A region in the Northern Urals.</note>. Furthermore, the troops of the Scythians, whom we now call Tartars—though formerly two diverse and dissimilar nations, being subjects of different Lords—have a more particular one, and each is called in his principality <term>Cham</term> <note>Khan.</note>; and these are divided into <term>Hordes</term>, or cantons, like the Swiss, the word *Horde* meaning in the Tartar language a multitude, assembly, or lordship. The four principal kinds of these Hordes being in Asiatic Sarmatia are as follows: namely, the Horde of Zavolhen, that of Perekop, of Kazan, and of the Nogais, there being also a fifth, without any Prince, which is named <term>Cazacca</term> <note>Cossacks.</note>; and several others mentioned by <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles (c. 1423–1490), a Byzantine historian.</note> Chalcondyles in book 3 of his history of the Turks; <note>Maciej Miechowita (1457–1523), author of the first printed description of Eastern Europe.</note> Matthias Michou in the first book, eighth chapter of his *Sarmatia*; <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician and historian.</note> P. This is repeated by André Thevet in his Geographical Maps, and François de Belleforest in Book 4, Chapter 5, Volume 2 of his *Geography*, and Book 2, Chapter 10 of his *Universal History*. Regarding the Scythians and Scythias of the ancients, so named after Scythes, son of Shem and Araxa, we must presuppose that it is very certain—according to the accounts of modern geographers and cosmographers—that there are two Scythias, or Sarmatias, divided and partitioned by the river Tanais <note>The River Don in modern-day Russia.</note>: one in Asia and the other in Europe. The Asiatic one is described thus: leaving aside what is on this side of the Tanais or Don toward our Europe, it is that great expanse of land which extends from the said Tanais toward the Caspian Sea, truly and properly called Asian Sarmatia; which, speaking generally of both the East and North, is of very great space and length. The majority of writers who have mentioned Sarmatia have only described the one in Europe; if they touched upon the Asiatic one, they only knew it under the name of the Scythians, since Scythia (now generally called Tartary) is of a marvelous extent, reaching from the Tanais to the easternmost sea, and comprising the northernmost parts on that side down to the Indies. Asiatic Sarmatia, currently called Sargatia or Cumania <note>The land of the Cumans, a nomadic Turkic people.</note> (although Cumania is properly a part of the Colchian country), has for its boundaries to the North <term>Septentrion</term> the unknown land, not yet fully penetrated by anyone, being beyond the Riphean Mountains <note>A legendary mountain range in Greek geography, once thought to be the source of the North Wind.</note> or the "girdle of the world" according to the ancients. To the West <term>Ponent</term> lies the Frozen Ocean and the other Sarmatia—namely, the European one—as far as the Tanais River <note>The Don River.</note> and where it flows into the Black Sea <note>original: "mer noire, ou maiour" (Black Sea or Greater Sea).</note> at the Maeotian marshes <note>The Sea of Azov.</note>. The coast of these marshes as far as the Cimmerian Bosporus is also part of this region. To the South, by a bend in the "Greater Sea" <note>The Black Sea.</note>, it is bounded as far as the place where the Corax River flows into that same sea, extending to the lands of the Colchians and Georgians, and as far as the Sea of Abachu, or Bacchu, or Caspian <note>The Caspian Sea, often named after the city of Baku.</note>, and to where the Erdil River—named Volga or Rhà—discharges into the sea. Toward the East is Scythia, along the aforementioned Volga River, until it turns back toward the West and ends its course in the unknown land. This is how Ptolemy described it in Book 5, Chapter 9, Table 2 of Asia. Adding to this description what Pliny (Book 6, Ch. 17), Pomponius Mela (Book 3), and Herodotus (Book 4) wrote of the northernmost lands unknown in Asia during their times, we learn—according to Giosafat Barbaro in the book of his voyage to Tana, Ambrogio Contarini in Chapter 7 of his voyage to Persia, Hayton the Armenian in his books on the Tartars, Maciej Miechowita <note>original: "M. Michou"</note> in Book 1 of *Asiatic Sarmatia*, Sigismund von Herberstein <note>original: "Sigismond Liber"</note> in his *Commentaries on Muscovy*, Olaus Magnus and Johannes, Bishops of Uppsala in Gothia, in their *Northern Histories*, Paolo Giovio in Book 14 of his *Histories*, and André Thevet in Book 12, Chapter 9 of his *Universal Cosmography*—that these lands are today populated and inhabited by various sorts of people and nations. Those furthest North in Sarmatia do not labor or sow their lands; they have no bread, wine, or ale <term>ceruoise</term>, but live miserably. Keeping to the woods and the grottoes of the earth, they sustain themselves on fish and the meat of wild beasts, of which they have an abundance, quenching their thirst with beautiful pure water and being clothed in the skins of wild animals. And it is quite certain (even though Pomponius Mela in Book 3 and Solinus in Chapter 26 write of these regions that they are very temperate and filled with a pleasant sweetness of air in the depths of the North) that it is a pure fable to say these regions are temperate. For it is certain there is no misery compared to that of those who inhabit them, because they have no bread, wine, nor anything that a man might desire for his life; they are incessantly attacked by the rigors of winter and the harshness of extreme cold. At the winter solstice they have perpetual night, and at the summer solstice continual day—and even then with a very sluggish heat, without strength, because the Sun at that time only casts its rays upon them obliquely and sideways. Nor does one see in these countries—as some ancient and modern authors have believed—men with only one eye, nor those said to have two heads; nor are any such found.

this place, the Tanais <note>The Don River, traditionally considered the boundary between Europe and Asia in classical geography.</note> forming the separation of Europe from Asia: modern writers hold that the Tartars of today, dwelling quite far from one another, possess several provinces and regions of Asia toward the North and East, and of Europe in the said North. They claim that at present, true Tartary extends and comprises all that lies between the Northern Sea, the River Obi, and Lake Kitaye, the river named Volga, and from the side of the said river as far as the Great Sea <note>The Black Sea.</note>, the Caspian Sea, the river Chesel—formerly called the Jaxartes <note>The Syr Darya river in Central Asia.</note>—Mount Imae, now called Vissonte <note>Likely the Himalayas or the Pamir Mountains, referred to as the Imaus in antiquity.</note>, and all that is enclosed within an imaginary line drawn from this mountain to the sea near Capo-Lampo. Thus, all the lands that formerly bore the name of Asiatic Sarmatia, both Scythias, and Serica <note>Serica was the classical name for northern China, the land of silk.</note>, have today changed their name and are presently called Tartary in general. This Tartary also includes several provinces and regions situated further East in Asia, such as the province and region of Tangut, from which comes most of the Rhubarb brought to our Europe. Also those of Cathay, Cambaluc, Quinsay <note>Cambaluc (Beijing) and Quinsay (Hangzhou) were famous cities described by Marco Polo.</note>, and others under the dominion of the Great Khan, sovereign Monarch or Emperor of the Tartars, as can be clearly seen in Abraham Ortelius, map 47 of his *Theater of the World* <note>The *Theatrum Orbis Terrarum*, first published in 1570, the first true modern atlas.</note>.

The Annals of the Ruthenians <note>The ancestors of modern Ukrainians and Belarusians.</note>, according to the assertion of Sigismund von Herberstein in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs* <note>Sigismund von Herberstein (1486–1566) was an Austrian diplomat whose book was the primary Western source on Russia for decades.</note>, carry these words regarding the Tartars, named by them in their language "Besermani" <note>original: "Beſermani"; a term derived from "Mussulman," used to refer to Muslims.</note>. The peoples formerly named Moabites, and later Totars, or Tatars, or Tartars—people entirely different in their ways and customs of living from other nations, whether in language, manners, or clothing—arrived at the beginning as far as the Kalka River <note>The site of the famous Battle of the Kalka River in 1223, where the Mongols defeated the Rus' and Cumans.</note>, without anyone being able to say truly from where they first proceeded, nor of what Religion they were, although some call them Taurimenes, others Pitzeneges <note>Pechenegs, a nomadic Turkic people.</note>, and others by other names. A certain Methodius, Bishop of Patara <note>Referring to the *Apocalypse of Pseudo-Methodius*, a highly influential medieval text attributed to the 4th-century bishop, which prophesied the invasion of "unclean nations."</note>, has them emerging from the deserts of Yatria <note>original: "Ieutriskie"</note>, between the North and East, and attributes the cause of their migrations to the fact that one Gideon, a great Lord among them, struck them with a great fear and terror of the end and consummation of the world. He announced to them that this would soon come to pass, and for this reason, he persuaded them—lest the great riches of this world be lost—to set out in a great multitude toward the surrounding provinces and regions, from the East as far as the Euphrates and the Persian Gulf, to pillage and bandit them. Having executed this, they came to give battle to the Polovtsians <note>original: "Polouutzes"; a nomadic Turkic people also known as the Cumans.</note> and Ruthenians toward the aforementioned Kalka River in the year of the world 6530 <note>The text says 653, but likely refers to the Byzantine year 6530, which corresponds to 1223 AD.</note>.

It is quite certain that the author of *The Two Sarmatias* <note>Maciej Miechowita.</note> has greatly erred in the interpretation of this word "Polouutzes," which he interprets as "hunters" or "venators." It is quite certain that this word simply means "man of the fields," for *Polle* is the same as the French word for a field <note>The Slavic root *pole* means "field" or "plain."</note>, while *Louuats* or *Louutzi* means hunters. The added syllable *tzi* or *kli* does not change the meaning of the word it is in, because that meaning is not taken from the final syllables, but rather from the first ones. Because the general syllable *Ski* is customarily added to Ruthenian words, this gave the aforementioned author the occasion to say what he did, whereas it is quite certain that this word *Polouutzes* means men of the fields, and not hunters. The Ruthenians interpret the Polovtsians as Goths, which is not true. If one wishes to describe...

Regarding the Tartars, one must by the same means describe several and diverse nations greatly separated and distant from one another. The same Annals cited above report that the name of Tartars was imposed upon them because of their sect alone, even though they were greatly distant from other peoples and nations. At present, these Tartars are divided and partitioned into *Hordes*, which is to say, in the Tartar language, assemblies or multitudes, among which the first and principal is that of the **Zavolzhye** <note>original: "Zauolheuse"; the Trans-Volga region.</note>, then that of **Perekop**, then that of the **Nogai** <note>original: "Nahaience".</note> and others, in which the Tartars of today are Muhammadans <note>original: "Mahometistes".</note>, taking no pleasure, but rather displeasure and dishonor, in being called Turks, but instead **Besermans** <note>original: "Befermani"; likely a corruption of "Mussulmans" or the Russian "Basurman".</note>. Sir John Mandeville <note>original: "I. de Madeuille"; the famous 14th-century English traveler.</note>, a Knight living in the year of salvation 1322, writes in his travels that some 160 years before his time, all of Tartary was in subjection and servitude to other neighboring nations, and that it was entirely bestial, knowing nothing other than how to tend livestock. Here are his words in the Romance language <note>The author provides a quote in a medieval Mediterranean dialect, likely Old Catalan or Provençal, common in early printed editions of Mandeville.</note>:

> It has not been 160 years since all Tartary was in subjection and servitude to the other Nations that are around it, for they were all beastly People and knew how to do nothing but guard beasts and lead the shepherds. <note>original: "No ha pas clx anys, que tota Tartaria era en subiugacio è seruitut de les altres Nacions, que estát en torn, car Ells eren tots bestials Gents e no sabien fer si no gardar bisties, e manar als pastors;"</note>

Then he continues:

> But among them there were seven principal nations who were sovereign over all those, of which the first Nation or lineage are called Tartars; these are the most noble and the most powerful; the second lineage are called the Turks; the third Armenians; the fourth Balaar; the fifth Semoch; the sixth Meyer; the seventh Coboch. <note>original: "Mas entre Ells auia vij. Nacions principals qui eren sobirannés de totes aquells de les quals la premera Nacio o linacge son appellats Tartarins, aquest son los pus nobles, e los pus páts, lo secon linacge son appellats los Turchs; lo iij. Erminis, lo iiij. Balaar, lo v. Semoch, lo vj. Meyer, lo vij. Coboch."</note>

That is to say, among them they had seven principal nations, who were sovereign over all, of which the first Nation or Lineage are called Tartars, and these are the most noble and the most powerful, the second lineage are called Turks, the third Armenians, the fourth Balaar, the fifth Semoch, the sixth Menyer, the seventh Coboh. This same author, in the chapter on the city of **Sargun** <note>original: "Surgoine"; likely Shangdu or Xanadu.</note> and the palace and house of the Great **Khan** <note>original: "Cham".</note>, tells and recites several rare things about the Tartars that I will not report to avoid prolixity. Some other authors write that anciently Tartary was inhabited by four peoples, namely the **Yeke-Mongol** <note>original: "Iecha-mongal".</note>, that is to say, Great Mongols; the second, **Sumongal**, which signifies aquatic ones, who also, because they were neighbors of the River Tartar, called themselves Tartars; the **Merkit** was the third people, and the **Metrit** the fourth. Others number seven primary nations of this people, whom they commonly called **Mogles** <note>Mongols.</note>. The first and principal was that of the **Tartar**, from the name of the river, and from which the rest bear the name; the second **Taugor**, and the other **Cunar**; the one neighboring it is **Jalair** <note>original: "Ialait".</note>; the fifth **Sonith**; the sixth **Monghi**, or Mongol; and the last **Tebeth** <note>Tibet.</note>, which is toward the deserts of **Dauvil**, where it is said that evil spirits appear visibly and cause travelers to get lost by showing them the way through paths where they can find neither track nor any trail whatsoever, according to the report of **Hayton the Armenian** in his *Book of the Tartars*, chapter six. A people dwelling somewhat toward the north, namely on the side of Cacia and Bargu <note>original: "Ciezze & Bargu"; regions in Central Asia mentioned by Marco Polo.</note> who were called Tartar, were divided into Hordes or Cantons. A certain Prince [Vncam] afflicted them extremely, seeking to abolish their memory so that he sent them through diverse Provinces to depopulate the country. Nevertheless, these clever fellows, recognizing the Prince's trick, all retreated into the province and Canton that was strongest in their country near a river named Tartar, which signifies "wild" <note>original: "farouche"</note>, and electing a King, they denied tribute to the aforementioned Vncam. And so they began to grow great, and passing the Emaes mountains <note>original: "monts Emaes"; the Imaus or Himalayan/Pamir range</note>, they rushed upon our northern Scythians and subjected them, giving the name of both themselves and their river to Scythia, so much so that since then, this Scythia has been known only by the name of Tartary, from whichever side one considers it, whether in the Orient or in the North. This is what the Baron de Joinville <note>original: "Iainville"</note> in the life of Saint Louis and G. de Nangis in his histories seem to confirm. Others say there was a petty king of the country, who was thought to have descended from a fugitive from Armenia, who gave this name to all these provinces, and who was named Thattafrif, otherwise called by some Cazul. This little Lord gathered a mass of people of every quality, and letting each live at his own discretion, he immediately raised such a formidable army that it was very easy for him to subjugate Scythia, to which he gave his name. Nevertheless, having passed away, the Tartars began to live without a King, each holding himself as a Lord, until **Genghis Khan** <note>original: "Chingis Cham"</note>, otherwise [called] Changi, Chinchis, Cinguic, Caguiste, or Cingiste, or Tzinciscanes and Sitzifcanes, from whom all the Emperors of Tartary have descended until today, was elected by them around the year of salvation 1162.

Ordinarily, for the most part, the Tartars are of small stature, having very broad chests and shoulders, flat faces, snub noses, and are black in color—though not swarthy like Moors—but also not as white as the Sarmatians. For they have no houses, towns, cities, nor castles or fortresses in which to live, staying for a few months in one place, then in another. There are some among them who, tilling the earth with a hoe, sow it with millet to make a sort of paste like porridge called *Bairam* <note>The author likely conflates a food item with the Turkic word for "festival," or refers to a specific regional dish.</note>. Furthermore, they have neither wheat, nor other grain or legumes, and they raise only a great many cattle, especially horses and mares which serve both to carry them and to nourish them. For they eat their flesh, and they make incisions upon their horses and mares to drink their blood; and mixing it sometimes with boiled and soaked millet, they eat the flesh of small white cattle, still bloody and half-raw. Indeed, if a horse dies of disease, they do not fail to feed upon it. They drink water, milk, and a beer made with millet; they call water *Su* or *Suha*, and their beer *Buza*, which the Russians name *Bracha*. They take great pleasure in the taste of sour milk called *Komis* <note>Koumiss: fermented mare's milk, a traditional central Asian beverage.</note>, because it comforts their stomachs and serves them as a purgative medicine. No artisans are seen among them, and they use no money, since their trade is done by permutation and exchange. It is true that some of their Hordes or Lordships are more communicative than others: for those of the Horde of Zavolzhye <note>original: "Zauoclen"; referring to the region "beyond the Volga."</note> are beginning to use a certain Turkish money called *aspers* <note>A small silver coin used in the Ottoman Empire.</note>; those of the Horde of Perekop <note>original: "Precop"; located in the Crimean peninsula.</note> receive ducats. The lands inhabited by these people in Asiatic Sarmatia <note>A classical geographic term for the lands between the Vistula and the Volga.</note> are without hills or mountains, and without forests, trees, or groves, for which they do not care, provided they have pastures for their beasts. They do not guide themselves by miles or leagues when traveling, but rather by days or day-trips, such that from Zavolzhye and the Volga River, they reach the Caspian Sea in thirty days; and they never go on foot as long as they are able to ride. The greatest part of the Hordes of these Tartars living as far as the Ob River, or Kitai <note>An old name for China, here likely referring to the borderlands or Northern China.</note>, obey the Grand Duke of Muscovy <note>The ruler of Russia.</note>; and those toward the Tana <note>The Don River.</note>, and between it and the Borysthenes <note>The Dnieper River.</note>—namely those of the Horde of Perekop—are under the obedience of the Grand Lord of Turkey <note>The Ottoman Sultan.</note>, and these are the Tartars who are ordinarily in his camp. Furthermore, to know if such a great extent of country exists between the Tanais or Don, and the Volga or the Rha <note>The ancient Greek name for the Volga.</note>, to have so many people scattered and spread across it, one must know that from the Tana to the Volga the journey is three weeks, even for a horse that travels very well and very fast. And this Volga is three times larger than the Tanais, and this Volga divides into twenty or thirty branches and arms, the smallest of which is as large as the Tiber at Rome might be, or the Vistula at Krakow. Whoever wishes to see many infinite other discourses on the Tartars, other than those deduced above, should read John Mandeville <note>A famous, though largely fictional, 14th-century travel writer.</note> in his travels; Vincent of Beauvais in book 32 of his *Historical Mirror*; Marco Polo the Venetian in book 1, chapters 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, and 48, and the end of book 3 of his travels in Tartary; Hayton the Armenian in part 2, chapter 33 of his *History of the Tartars*; Bonfini in his *History of Hungary*, book 8, decade 2; and Giosafat Barbaro in

### *On the Tartar Language.*

### CHAPTER 50.

The histories of the Tartars contain that in the year 1212, having crossed the sea under the leadership of their first Khan or Emperor named Genghis Khan <note>original: "Cingis Cham"</note>, or Changius, or Changis, to conquer Western Kingdoms, Lordships, and lands, and to subject them to the rule of their said Khan or Emperor, they were deprived of him by his death. Before his passing, he had his eldest son, the wisest and most prudent of the twelve children he had, named *Hocota* <note>Ogedei Khan, the successor to Genghis Khan.</note>, received as their Khan and Emperor. This man, determined to march further, won the Caspian Gates <note>A narrow mountain pass, historically identified as a barrier against the "barbarian" tribes of the north.</note> placed in that location and continually guarded and closed so as to prevent the passage into Asia of the infinite peoples living beyond them, as if in another world. After this, the Emperor dispatched three armies and placed them in the hands of three of his sons, commanding Jochi <note>original: "Iacchis"</note>, the eldest, to go toward the West; Batu <note>original: "Batho"</note> toward the North; and Chagatai <note>original: "Tagladais"</note> to the South. Abounding in men, he marched with a large and powerful army into the East, conquering all the countries as far as Cathay <note>Northern China.</note>, where he established the very powerful and rich Empire which still lasts there today, possessed by his descendants. He also invaded the Kingdom of Persia, during which journey these Tartars learned letters, the use of which they were previously ignorant. Hethum the Armenian <note>original: "Hayton Armenien"</note>, in the first chapter of his book on the Tartars, writes that the Cathayans, subjects of the Great Khan of Tartary, have and use very beautiful letters, which are somewhat similar in beauty to Latin letters. The same author says in the sixteenth chapter following: The region in which the Tartars first lived is situated beyond the great Mountain of Belgian <note>A semi-legendary mountain range in early modern maps, often associated with the Altai or the borders of the Gobi.</note>, from which—

Then, toward the end of the said chapter, excusing himself because he could not openly declare the conquests and feats of arms of these Tartars, he used these words:

Nicolas Chalcondyle <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles (c. 1423–1490), a Byzantine historian who wrote about the rise of the Ottoman Empire.</note>, in the third book of his history of the Turks, speaking of the power of the Great Khan <note>original: "Grand Cham"</note> of Tartary, writes that this Emperor was among the nine chiefs of the Chagatays <note>original: "Tzacataides"; the Chagatai Khanate was a Mongol and later Turkicized khanate.</note>, who, having passed the Araxes River <note>A river flowing through modern-day Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Iran.</note> in the time of Timur or Tamerlane, overran and subjugated a great part of these countries. Now India is a region very fertile and very abundant in all sorts of goods and conveniences, which it sows and scatters everywhere with full handfuls (as they say), from whichever direction one may turn. But the sovereign authority over all this so great and profound expanse of lands and seas belongs to this Prince here, who, having formerly set out from the country above the Ganges River and the maritime regions of India, together with the Island of Taprobane, came with an armed force to the kingdom of Cathay <note>An archaic name for China.</note> situated between the Ganges and the great Indus River. Having conquered it by the point of the sword, he established the throne and Imperial seat of all the provinces subject to him in the capital city, so that India from that time on has always been ruled under the command and obedience of a single Prince. # LANGUAGES OF THIS WORLD

...have a language related to that of the Tartars. <note>original Latin: "guagium Tartarorum cognatum habent." This fragment likely continues a thought from the previous page regarding the linguistic roots of Northern tribes.</note> The speech of the Tartar and the Turk does not differ except in small measure, as it might be said by way of example, like Italian and Spanish, or Polish and Bohemian. <note>original Latin: "Non differt loquela Tartarus & Turcus nisi modicè velut exemplariter diceretur, sicut Italus & Hispanus, vel Polonus & Boemus."</note> That is to say, that the Turks have descended and proceeded from the Tartars; the very same customs, ways of living, and common language that they share among themselves demonstrate this openly. In fact, both of these peoples and nations use the same and similar dress, and the same fashion of riding a horse with short stirrups <note>original: "à la genette," a style of riding with short stirrups and bent legs, typical of light cavalry in the East and Spain.</note>, and of making war with bows and arrows. And the majority of these Turks use the same and similar speech and language common to one another. Indeed, the Turkish language differs only very little from the Tartar language, just as the Italian language differs from the Spanish, or the Polish language from the Bohemian. Theodore Bibliander <note>A 16th-century Swiss linguist and scholar who attempted to find commonalities among all known languages.</note>, in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, confirms the above. Marco Polo the Venetian, in Book 1, Chapter 8 of his history of the Tartars, reports that in his time the Tartars used principally four different kinds of writing and languages, without taking into account several other different kinds of languages from the infinite provinces and cities of Tartary, of which he makes particular mention in the aforementioned book and others following it.

André Thevet, in Book 9, Chapter 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*, maintains that the Tartars are not so barbaric that they do not have histories as well as their neighbors, which are written by hand, and that their letters are quite fanciful and mixed, and very difficult to read except by means of interpreters <term>Truchements; a term historically used for translators and middlemen between Westerners and the cultures of the Near East and Asia.</term> who understand them. The same Thevet, in Book 12, Chapters 9, 16, and 19 of his same *Cosmography*, speaking of the language of Cathay <note>An archaic name for Northern China, popularized by Marco Polo.</note>, says the Cathayans have a very mixed language, and for that reason it is very difficult for foreigners to understand, but for singing the praises of the gods they have one that is quite specific. The alphabet of the monks of Cathay, Quinzay <note>Modern-day Hangzhou, described by Marco Polo as one of the greatest cities in the world.</note>, Japan, and the surrounding lands has forty-seven letters, just like that of the Maronites <note>A Levantine Christian group; the author is comparing Eastern scripts to the Syriac alphabet used by Maronites.</note>. The characters are nearly similar, but the words are somewhat different, just as the Germans and French have the same letters, and yet the language of one is unknown to the other. Hayton the Armenian <note>Hethum of Korykos, a medieval monk and historian who provided one of the most influential accounts of the Mongols to the West.</note> has written this in his history of the Tartars (as I have already said): *The Cathayans have very beautiful letters, which are in some ways similar in beauty to Latin letters.* <note>original Latin: "Cathaini valde pulchras habent literas, quae Latinis literis in pulchritudine quodammodo similes sunt."</note> In this same history, Chapter 17, he says: *Genghis Khan gave many good examples, which were observed by the Tartars; they are called in their language the Yasa of Genghis Khan, that is, the Constitutions of Genghis.* <note>original Latin: "Multa bona exempla dedit Changius Cham, quae fuerunt à Tartaris obseruata, dicuntur in lingua eorum Iasaclz Changij Cham, id est, Constitutiones Changij." The "Yasa" was the secret written code of laws created by Genghis Khan.</note> François de Belleforest, in Book 2, Chapter 18 of his *Universal History*, confirms this, asserting that these Cathayans use Latin characters in writing, similar in squareness to the Roman letter, by which one sees that they have come out of our Europe, seeing as the Romans never passed beyond Gedrosia <note>An ancient name for the coastal region of modern-day Pakistan and Iran.</note> in conquest.

...assure us that in the Duchy of Lithuania, there live Tartars near the city of Vilnius in certain hamlets or villages belonging to them. Modern navigators and travelers assure us that in the kingdom of Mangi <note>A term used by Marco Polo to refer to Southern China.</note>, which is under the subjection of the Great Khan of the aforementioned Tartars, there grows a certain tree named Tal <note>Likely the Talipot palm, whose leaves were historically used as a writing surface.</note>. The Tartars make use of the leaves of this tree for writing for lack of paper; for in no part of the East Indies, except in Cambay, is any paper to be found. Thus, this leaf must serve in its place for making their writings, as confirmed by André Thevet in Book 11, Chapter 23 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

The Kazanians <note>People of the Khanate of Kazan.</note>, a people of Asiatic Sarmatia who live today in Tartary, were formerly subjects of the Tartar Khan but are presently Muslims, though they obey the Muscovite <note>The Grand Prince or Tsar of Russia.</note>. They nevertheless speak the Tartar language and follow the same and similar way of life as those Tartars, as confirmed by Matthias de Miechow in Book 2, Chapter 4. In short, we are assured by the accounts of the moderns that the Tartar language of today is understood throughout the North and a great part of the East.

->*Of the Great Khan, Emperor of the Tartars.*<-

### CHAP. LI.

The Tartars of today are, for the most part, commanded by an Emperor or sovereign King called the Great Cham or Khan, <term>חן</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Chen," though here used to approximate "Khan."</note>, which signifies as much as <term>מחנה</term>, Mahanah, meaning a Camp or Tent. Marco Polo the Venetian, in Book 1, Chapter 2 of his travels in Tartary, assures us that in the Tartar language the word Cham signifies the "Great King of Kings" <note>original Latin: "magnum Regem Regum"</note>. This is the same as what is meant among the Muslims and Turks by the words <term>שלטן</term>, Sultan, or <term>שלטון</term>, Soltan, meaning Emperor or King; for "Soltan" in Hebrew and Chaldean <note>A term often used in this period to refer to Aramaic.</note> signifies a prefect or governor <note>original Latin: "nam Soltan Hebraicè, & Chaldaicè sonat præfectum."</note>. Some authors hold that the word Cham with an aspiration <note>An "h" or breathy sound.</note> signifies "Lord" in the Tartar language, and without the aspiration, it signifies "blood."

Sigismund von Herberstein, in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs*, writes: "Lake Kytai, from which the Great Khan of Cathay (whom the Muscovites call the Kitayan Tsar) takes his name; 'Cham' however signifies 'King' among the Tartars." <note>original Latin: "Lacus Kitai, à quo magnus Cham de Cathaia, quem Mochi, Czar Kithaiski appellant, nomen habet, Cham autem Tartaris Regem sonat."</note> The names of dignities among the Tartars are roughly these: *Cham*, as I said above, is the King; *Soltan* is the son of a King; *Pij* is a Duke; *Iursa* is the son of a Duke; *Olboud* is a noble or counselor; *Olboudulu* is the son of a noble; *Scid* is the High Priest; and *Ksi* is a private citizen. Regarding offices: *Ulan* is the rank second to the King; for the Kings of the Tartars have four men whose counsel they use most especially in grave matters. Of these, the first is called *Schirni*, the second *Barni*, the third *Gargni*, and the fourth *Tziptan*. Matthias de Miechow, the Pole, in Book 1, Chapter 8 of *Asiatic Sarmatia*, writes: "There are four Hordes of Tartars, and as many Emperors of them..."

So much for the Emperors of the Zavolhensian Tartars, otherwise called Chagatay. The other race of Tartars, called Precopensians <note>The Crimean Khanate</note>—who are nonetheless descended from the aforementioned Zavolhensians, for they were the source and origin of all the others—took its beginning from a certain Vlam, a man of base and unknown birth who first took possession of this point of land called the Tauric Chersonese <note>The Crimean Peninsula</note>. This is because it is almost entirely an island that stretches into the Maeotian marshes <note>The Sea of Azov</note>, above the Great Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, being some 24 leagues long and 15 wide. There are three cities of some note: Solat, Kirkee, and Kaffa, with two castles, Mangup and Azov. The principal city is Solat, which the Tartars call Chrim <note>Staryi Krym</note>, from which the Lord of these Precopensians takes his name, being called the Crimean Emperor. The other, smaller city is Kirkee <note>Qyrq Yer</note>, where there is a castle made of wood and sod at the top of a rock. It is said that in former times there was a dragon there that devoured everything, so much so that the country was in danger of being left a desert, if some Italians who were settled there had not had recourse to the Virgin Mary. For not a year passes that they do not miserably overrun and pillage Russia, Lithuania, Wallachia, Poland, and very often even Muscovy itself. However, they are entirely under the obedience of the **Muscovite** <note>The Grand Duke or Tsar of Russia</note>, who disposes of them as he pleases and gives them such lords as seems good to him. The fourth Horde, the most recent and new of all the others, is that of the **Occaſſiens** or **Nahaiens** <note>The Nogai Horde</note>, who also came from the **Zauolhenſe** <note>The Trans-Volga region</note>; for after *Occass*, a subject of the Great **Cham** <note>Khan</note> but a very valiant and courageous personage, was put to death, his children—who numbered thirty—departed from those of the Trans-Volga and retreated to the surroundings of the Castle of **Sarai** around the year of salvation 1450. And in a short time, they grew and multiplied so greatly that it is now the most populous of all the Hordes. But they are more Northerly than the others, and the region where they live is much colder, neighboring Muscovy on the side of the Levant <note>the East</note>, into which they often enter and cause great harm and ruin, just as the **Procopiens** <note>Crimean Tartars</note> and those from the Trans-Volga do in Russia, Poland, and Wallachia. The successors of *Occass* still rule among them; they have no use for money but trade by the exchange of slaves, livestock, and horses. These are the four principal Hordes of the **Tartars**, so feared and redoubted, not only by their neighbors but also by peoples and nations very far from them, at whose name children still tremble at the breast. And in truth, one can call them one of the true plagues and ruins of the human race. There are still many other branches and offshoots of this vermin who nonetheless were part of those mentioned above and set out to make their own way. For they have very great and spacious plains, or rather wildernesses, which extend as far as **Cathay** <note>China</note> and **China** where the Sun rises. Therefore, that people is without number, almost like the sand of the sea or the stars in the sky. And although they are very brutal and far removed from all civility, they nonetheless still have some order and policy among them, and above all, they bear great honor and obedience to their Emperors, whom they call *Champs* <note>Khans</note>. The other degrees of honor and dignity among them are *Soltan* <note>Sultan</note>, which is the son of their Lord; *Bij* <note>Bey</note>, meaning Duke; *Murſa* <note>Mirza</note>, the son of the Duke; *Olboud*, a counselor; *Olbaudulu*, the son of a Gentleman; and *Seid* <note>Sayyid</note>, their sovereign Priest or Pontiff, of whom they make such great account that even the Emperors, being on foot, greet them and extend their hand without the Priests dismounting from their horses. This they do for no other person whatsoever; for the greatest of their subjects, whether they be Dukes or others, touch them only at the knees, the Gentlemen at the feet, and the common people at the garment. There are also four personages, the first of whom is called *Schioni*, the second *Barni*, the third *Gargni*, and the fourth *Tziptzan*, who are accustomed to assist the Emperor as a council when there is a question of some matter of importance.

Some modern travelers affirm in their journeys that the King or sovereign Prince who commands today over **Turkestan** (so named for the Turks, just as they say *France* for the *Franks* <note>original: "Freiſten"</note>, who were later called *Turcomans* and then *Turquizel*, from whom the said Turks took their name, who at that time had no law nor policy), and who also has power over the Province of **Zagate** <note>The Chagatai Khanate</note>, bears the title of **Sultan Chapar**. He is the nearest of the Northerners to the great Emperor of the Tartars and is so powerful that when it pleases his lord, he will easily lead one hundred thousand men on horseback for him, all men of action and valiant in war. The one who moves more toward the **Tanais** <note>The Don River</note> is called **Sultan Hochtay**, and he approaches **Asiatic Sarmatia** <note>An ancient name for the lands between the Vistula and the Volga rivers</note>, having charge over the **Tartars** as far as **Europe**. He can lead more cavalry than the other, although the men are not considered as brave or as fierce in the business of war, even though they have better horses than all the rest of the **Scythians**. Be that as it may, these people are furious and redoubtable, with whom it is ill-advised to deal; they are proud, cunning, and harmonious in their actions. The **Turks** feel no dishonor in being descended from such a gallant nation, without needing to trace their origin back to the **Trojans**—as some historians have falsely tried to do—to reach all the way into **Scythia** <note>In the Renaissance, it was a popular but incorrect theory that the Turks were the descendants of the Trojans (Teucri), based on the similarity of the names</note>. But the **Scythians** were not so easy to handle that the **Trojans** could have made an entry there; rather, it is they who have made raids as far as **Asia Minor**, and then into **Europe** as far as **Raška** <note>The central region of medieval Serbia</note>, **Poland**, and **Lithuania**. They even keep the **Sophy** <note>The European term for the Safavid Shah of Persia</note> in check, because the **Great Khan** <note>The "Grand Cham"</note> tries from one day to the next to take land from him. This is the thing that most delays the said **Sophy** from expanding against the **Turk**, as he must defend himself against such a powerful enemy as the **Tartar**.

Now, the source of their quarrel came from the greed of **Sheikh Ismail** <note>Shah Ismail I (reigned 1501–1524), founder of the Safavid dynasty</note>, father of the **Sophy**, from the year 1543 until 1552 <note>The author's dates here are historically confused, as Ismail I died in 1524; he likely refers to the reign of his son, Shah Tahmasp</note>. For having heard that **Iesilbas** <note>Likely a corruption of *Kyzylbash* (Red-heads), the nomadic tribes that supported the Safavids, though the author here treats it as the name of a ruler of Samarkand</note>, lord of **Samarkand** and ally of the **Sultan of Chagatai** and **Turkestan**, had entered his lands, he went to meet him, following the fortune that had always accompanied him. It happened that the **Tartar**, hearing what the forces of the **Sophy** were, retreated by a few days' journey and came to pitch his camp on the **Larit River**, now called the **Ezra** (see **Thevet**, book 9, chapter 4, folio 292 of the *Universal Cosmography*).

Thus, coming out from **Lake Khorasan**, the battle given was so furious that the **Sophy** saw himself in danger of losing his life, his men having been twice on the point of being routed. Were it not that, seeing how he exposed himself to hazard, they took such courage that at last **Iesilbas** (or **Kyzylbash**) was taken, along with the General of his army named **Uzbek** and his children. The **Persian** immediately had the heads of these leaders cut off; as for the children, after making them swear obedience, he restored to them the lordship of their deceased father.

Upon being informed of this, the Lord of **Chagatai** <note>A successor state of the Mongol Empire</note> went to his nephews in **Samarkand** and showed them the wrong they did to the **Tartar** name and to the greatness of their **Khan** by having sworn obedience to the **Sophy**, warning that the **Great Khan** might well feel resentful. Consequently, this—combined with the hatred the people of **Samarkand** had against the **Safavid sect** <note>Shiism, which conflicted with the Sunni Islam of the Tartars and Uzbeks</note>—led them to take to the field once more, and the said children of **Iesilbas** took several cities from the **Sophy**. He, irritated by such a revolt, marched against them, but in vain; for having given a thousand raids and skirmishes to his camp, they retired toward **Turkestan**, awaiting new forces from that country and the will of the **Great Khan**, whom they had informed of the war made upon them. Thus, at the same time, the **Sophy** found himself enveloped in two great wars against the two greatest monarchs in the world: namely, the **Turk** and the **Tartar**. This was the occasion that made him come to an agreement with the aforementioned children, relinquishing the obedience he claimed over the city and country of **Samarkand**. Not that the **Tartar** was appeased for having his country overrun; this occurred during the time the **Great Turk Selim** <note>Sultan Selim I of the Ottoman Empire</note> made his expedition into **Persia**, before attacking the **Sultan of Egypt** in the year of salvation 1512. In short, although **Tartary** is the country from which the **Turk** is descended, they are nonetheless different from one another in several...

things, namely in that they have diverse religions: for although the Tartar admits the law of **Mahomet** <note>Muhammad</note>, he nonetheless mixes it with idolatry, taught to him by **Sogomonbar**, one of their Kings, Prophets, and Priests of the gods, as well as some ceremonies of the Christian Religion, as deduced by **Matthias Michovius** <note>Maciej Miechowita, a Polish scholar and physician</note> in book 1, chapter 5 of *Asiatic Sarmatia*, and **André Thevet** in book 12, chapter 18 of his *Universal Cosmography*. Additionally, the **Turk** is quite civil and friendly to everyone, whereas on the contrary the **Tartar** is fierce and wild. Their clothes are also different, even the head ornament; the Turk wears the **Turban**, and the Tartar a pointed cap, around which there is a white band very well furred, along with the rest of his garments. Regarding war, there is also much difference, since the Turk is a good foot soldier, while the Tartar is not, being unable to do anything unless he is on horseback. Furthermore, the Turk has retained the use of the bow which was formerly—and is still—familiar to his brothers the **Scythians**; as for <term>arquebuses: an early form of heavy matchlock gun</term> and pistols, they do not know what they are. As for the Prophet **Mahomet**, the Tartar pays him little mind for lack of religious practice; however, he mocks him and his Prophets, just as most Black **Moors** of Africa do for the most part. Moreover, they despise the general resurrection and many other things that are said in our Religion, as well as in the **Mahometan** <note>Islamic</note> superstition. It is true that the great Tartar King is a bit more scrupulous, and the lords who neighbor him more magnificent than those who stay in the Northern parts, who do not differ at all from the lowest in the country in their clothing or preparation of food, seeing as the people are not abundant in worldly riches. This is also the cause why in the morning you will see a Tartar go to gather some herbs or small fruits in the fields for his life, such pasture seeming very good to them, and they content themselves with beautiful, clear, and pure water. Not that they do not have the means to nourish themselves better than that, given the abundance of animals they kill and those they raise in their pastures, such as oxen, cows, horses, mares, sheep, and ewes, whose meat they eat while drinking their milk—and especially that of mares <note>Kumis, a traditional fermented dairy product</note>, which they find the best, most savory, and healthiest. Also, when one of them is sick, they make him use this milk two or three hours before he takes his meal, saying it is more beneficial to the body than that of a sheep, cow, or other beast. See what **Hayton the Armenian** writes on this subject in his *Book of the Tartars*, **Marco Polo the Venetian** in his *Travels in Tartary*, **André Thevet** in books 9 (chapters 2 & 4) and 12 (chapters 17 & 19) of his *Cosmography*, **François de Belleforest** in volume 2, book 3, chapter 4, and book 4, chapter 1 and following of the same volume 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*, and **Blaise de Vigenère** in his *Description of the Kingdom of Poland*. As for the Titles of the dignities of the Great **Khan**, **John Mandeville** in his travels cited above writes that he is thus called <note>original: "Chá filius Dei excellétissimus omniũ vniuersam terrá colentiũ, sumus Imperator, & Dominus dominantiũ"</note> Khan, most excellent son of God of all those inhabiting the whole earth, supreme Emperor and Lord of lords. And around his small seal there is engraved: <margin>“</margin> <note>original: "Fortitudo omniũ hominũ Imperatoris"</note> Strength of the Emperor of all men; and around his large seal there is: <margin>“</margin> <note>original: "Dominus in cælo, & Chá super terram eius fortitudo omniũ hominũ Imperatoris Sigillũ"</note> Lord in heaven and Khan upon the earth, the seal of his strength as Emperor of all men. Commonly his <margin>“</margin> subjects use these dignities: *By the force and virtue of the great God, and by the <margin>“</margin> grace he has given to our Empire, let the name of the Khan be blessed, and let <margin>“</margin> all those who do not obey him die and be destroyed.*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Tartar culture and religion from the previous page, shifting focus from their general customs to the specific history and religious pluralism of the Great Khans, particularly Kublai Khan and Tamerlane.</meta>

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE

Some modern travelers have reported that the Great Khan of Tartary is called **Tamirlangue** <note>Tamerlane</note> by his Tartar subjects. The seal which this Great Emperor uses in his official letters is such, according to the report of **Marco Polo the Venetian** in book 2, chapter 22 of his travels in Tartary: *God in Heaven, Chuichuch Khan on earth; the Emperor is the strength of God and of men.* **André Thevet**, in book 12, chapter 13 of his *Universal Cosmography*, writes that the inhabitants of the Island of **Cipangu** <note>Japan</note> call the Great Khan **Gogomat**, or **Go-gomat**, and the Indians who live toward the North call him **Aliadath**. **Marco Polo the Venetian**, in book 1, chapter 1 of his travels in Tartary, writes that **Kublai** (or **Cobila**, as he is called by **Hayton** <note>Hethum of Korykos, an Armenian historian</note>), the fifth Emperor of the Tartars, was the first of the Khans of Tartary to make a profession of the Christian religion. He sent his ambassadors to **Pope Gregory X** to obtain from His Holiness doctors of the church in order to instruct him and his subjects in Christianity. In the year of our salvation 1272, the Pope sent them two preaching friars of the Order of Saint Dominic, doctors of Theology named **Nicholas of Vicenza** and **William of Tripoli**, for this purpose. When these men arrived before the Emperor, he received them graciously, but he was not baptized and did not make a public profession of Christianity; **Hayton** (chapter 23) is content to say that he was a Christian only in the sense that he favored the Christians, kept them in his retinue, and followed their counsel. This seems to be stated more fully by the aforementioned **Marco Polo** in book 2, chapter 2, mentioning that during a solemn feast, this Emperor summoned all the Christians to him, wishing them to carry the book of the four Gospels. He had the book censed with great ceremony, kissed it humbly, and commanded his Princes to do the same. He did this at all the great feasts of his Empire—Christian, Muslim, and Idolater alike. When he was asked the reason why he practiced such inconsistency in religion, he replied that there are four Prophets who are adored and in whom the whole world believes and holds in reverence: since the Christians confess Jesus Christ to be their God, the Saracens <note>Muslims</note> hold **Muhammad** to be their sent Saint, the Jews have **Moses**, and the Idolaters recognize **Sogomonbar Khan**, who was the first author of Idols among the Tartars. **F. Antoine Geuffroy**, a Knight of Saint John of Jerusalem, in his treatise on the *Origin of the Turks*, speaks of it differently, saying that **Ögedei Khan** was succeeded by **Güyük** (or **Cni**), his son, who reigned briefly, and after him **Möngke Khan** (or **Mongu**, or **Metho**), his cousin. **Pope Innocent IV** sent to him a Brother **Ascelin** of the order of preaching friars in the year 1266, as stated by **Vincent** <note>Vincent of Beauvais</note> in his *Historical Mirror*, and **Maciej Miechowita** in his histories.

See what **André Thevet** writes in book 12, chapter 19 of his *Universal Cosmography* regarding the homage that the Tartars pay every year to their Great Khan. The Empire of this ruler (according to the reports of modern travelers) extends from the Eastern Ocean or the **Sea of Manzi** <note>The South China Sea</note> to the Caspian Sea toward the West; and following the sea through all the lands along the Northern Ocean as far as **Muscovy** <note>Russia</note> and the **Meotian marshes** <note>Sea of Azov</note>; and toward the south as far as **Calicut** <note>India</note> and the most distant islands. In short, it is not without cause that this Emperor is called the Great Khan, for it is certain that he surpasses in greatness, power, wisdom, governance, revenue, and magnificence all the Princes of Asia, Africa, and Europe—even the Great Turk himself. Then, climbing a tree, he delivers to them I know not what sermon on their foolish opinions; when it is finished, he scatters this liquid over the people in the manner of holy water. The abominable abuse of these **Kirgesses** is that they take and receive this fine sprinkling as their God, and worship or recognize no other, so that their God is foul, ephemeral, and dependent on the will of the one who distributes it to them. 

Furthermore, although the **Turks** are descended from these Tartars, as we have demonstrated before, they are nevertheless different from one another in several things, specifically in that they have different religions: for although the Tartars admit the law of **Mahomet** <note>original: "Mahomet" — the Prophet Muhammad</note>, they mix it with Idolatry; moreover, the Turks are quite civil and friendly to everyone, while on the contrary, the Tartars are fierce and savage. Their clothing is also different, even their headwear: the Turks wear **Turbans**, and the Tartars pointed caps, around which there is a white band, very well furred, along with the rest of their garments. 

In matters of war, there is likewise a great difference, as the Turks are good infantrymen <note>Soldiers who fight on foot</note>, and the Tartars are not, being able to do nothing unless they are on horseback. Besides this, the Turks have retained the use of the bow, which was formerly, and is still now, familiar to their brothers the **Scythians** <note>Ancient nomadic people of the Eurasian steppes</note>; for as for arquebuses <note>An early type of portable long gun</note> and pistols, they do not know what they are. As for the Prophet **Mahomet**, the Tartars hold him in some account for lack of any other religious practice; however, they mock him and his Prophets, just as the black **Moors** of Africa do for the most part. Furthermore, they despise the general resurrection and many other things which are observed and believed both in our Religion and in the **Mahometan** <note>Islamic</note> superstition. 

It is true that the **Grand Chá** <note>original: "Chá" — the Grand Khan</note> is a little more scrupulous <note>Observant of religious law</note>, and the Lords who are his neighbors are more magnificent than those who stay in the Northern parts, who do not differ at all from the lowest of the country in their clothing and preparation of food <note>original: "viádes" (viandes)</note>, seeing as the People are not abundant in the riches of this world.
