...if it is a female, these people say that the faith of the parents suffices, and especially that of the mother, and that the holy communion she received while pregnant has sanctified the child in her womb; which child is carried to the Church as is done here <note>The author is likely referring to European customs of his time</note>, and baptized at the door thereof, and not over the fonts, the water being blessed there. The child is sprinkled with this water with the same words that we say, and they use anointing just as in the Roman Church, on the forehead, the shoulders, and the armpits; and the Priest, holding a ewer of water in one hand, performs the pouring with the other, saying: "I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." In short, they use the same ceremonies as those of our Catholic Church. It is true that they only baptize on Saturday and Sunday, because only on these days do they celebrate the holy Mass, and without it they do not confer the grace of Baptism, because they give the sacred communion to the newly regenerated child. 

In addition to this holy Sacrament of Baptism, all these Ethiopians observe another annual Baptism at the same time as we celebrate the feast of the Epiphany <note>original: "l'apparition de nostre Seigneur," the manifestation of our Lord</note>; during which solemnity they all come to a certain lake, and after some prayers made by a Bishop, they all go down naked into the water and bathe there, being of the opinion that this washing serves to purge those who, having been Christians, had become Moors <note>Used here to mean those who converted to Islam</note>, and then returned through repentance to the Church. Now, throughout all Ethiopia, there are Soldiers and Officers chosen from all parts who are in the King's pay, and who are lightly marked on the skin with a cross using a hot iron; this has been the reason why some have estimated that in Ethiopia this sign was the only thing that served as Baptism. 

What is more, according to the account of Leo Africanus <note>original: "Iean Leon," referring to the 16th-century diplomat and traveler Joannes Leo Africanus</note>, Book 4 of the *Description of Africa*, the inhabitants of the city of Bresk <note>An ancient city in modern-day Algeria</note> in Africa have the custom of painting a black cross on their cheek, and another on their hand—namely in the palm of the hand, under the fingers—this practice being observed by the mountain people of Algiers and Buggie <note>Modern-day Béjaïa, Algeria</note>. This is because, according to African historians, the Goths seized many lands and infinite mountains, by which means a great number were reduced to the Christian faith, for which the Gothic Kings charged their officers to levy no tribute from them. But because at the time of payments they all declared themselves to be Christians, without it being easy to notice and recognize those who were or were not, it was ordained that Christians should be designated and recognized by this cross. Since the lordship was taken from their hands, the whole people returned to the Mohammedan Law <note>Islam</note>. Nevertheless, this manner remained successively from time to time, without many being found who could give a reason for it. The Lords of Mauritania still observe this same custom as well as the nobles, who make a cross on their cheek with a hot iron, and one sees enough of them in Europe thus marked. 

As for the holy communion, they receive it with very great reverence, and honor the bread before it is consecrated in honor of what it is to become, believing firmly in the real presence of the substance of the body of our Lord sacramentally in the Eucharist. Only one Mass is said each day in each Church, and it is not celebrated without incensing, saying...

...[it is believed by] these Ethiopians that it is a sin to do otherwise, and that it shows little respect for such a high and divine mystery. Furthermore, there must be more than one Priest present when the Mass is said, and all those in attendance must receive communion. They are required to observe great fasts, especially the Monks, who fast for more than half the year; during this time, they only say and celebrate Mass at night, and everyone takes communion before going to have their meal. As for which days are designated for these fasts, Francisco Alvarez in his *History of Ethiopia*, chapter 3, and Joseph Scaliger in his *Commentaries on the Abyssinian Calendar* in book 7 of *The Correction of Time*, describe them at great length. The order of the Social Classes is such that the Clergy holds the highest place after the King; then come the <term>Tenquates</term> <note>Likely referring to learned scribes or scholars</note> and <term>Balsamates</term>, which is to say Doctors, and those who make a profession of teaching letters and acting as judges; after them, the Nobility is respected, and finally the Soldiers. 

When someone happens to die, they incense the body and wash it, and afterwards they shroud it and sew it into a linen cloth. The Priests, coming to carry the body to the earth, say several very short prayers, then lift the body and carry it to the Church, the cross always walking before it with the censer and holy water. Being near the Church, they do not carry the body inside it, but rather place it immediately into its grave, having incensed it and thrown holy water inside, without saying any obsequies or vigils <note>Traditional Catholic prayers and watches for the dead</note> except for several chapters of the Gospel of Saint John. They do not sing any Masses for the deceased, just as they do not celebrate any for the private devotion of any living person, since they only sing one single Mass per day in each Church. They mourn their dead for the space of forty days, and as long as their mourning lasts, they are dressed in entirely black garments, which they set aside after this time to resume their ordinary and previous clothing. 

In short, all Christian Ethiopians are uniform in their Religion, without there being any schisms, heresies, or divisions among them regarding their doctrine, because only the Clergy involve themselves in treating and discussing Holy Scripture. Marriage ceremonies are commonly performed there in the same form and manner as in the Catholic, Apostolic, and Roman Church. These Ethiopians, under the authority of Zerah Jacob <note>Emperor of Ethiopia, 1434–1468</note> their Emperor, first pledged obedience to Pope Eugene the Third <note>original: "Eugene troiſieſme"; likely a chronological error by the author referring to Pope Eugene IV (1431–1447), who presided over the Council of Florence</note> residing in Rome, who thereafter sent them a certain rather thick book to serve as instruction for their ceremonies. According to the travels of modern authors, this book is still held and found in Ethiopia today, as stated in the letter inserted at the end of the travels of Alvarez, and as confirmed by Damião de Góis in his book *On the Faith, Religion, and Customs of the Ethiopians*. See what is written at length regarding their customs and religion by Andrea Corsali in his *Epistle and Travels* addressed to Duke Lorenzo de' Medici; Dom Francisco Alvarez in his *Travels in Ethiopia*; Jerónimo Osório in book 9 of the *Deeds of Alfonso* and book 17 of his *History of Portugal*, chapters 20, 21, 22, 23, and 24; Duarte Barbosa in his books of travels; the author of the *Summary of the Kingdoms, Cities, and Peoples of the East*; Sabellicus in his *Rhapsodies* or *Enneads* 10, book 8; André Thevet in book 2, chapter 14 of his *Cosmography*; and François de Belleforest, volume 2.

### Of the Ethiopian, Indian, or Nubian language.

Raphael Volaterran, as reported by Theodore Bibliander in his commentary on the common reasoning of all languages and letters, wrote that the Ethiopians use and employ, up to the present day, the letters and characters of the Babylonians. This author had learned this from those ignorant of the truth of this matter, who, by a common and vulgar persuasion, held that these Ethiopians had learned and received their language, religion, and origin from Abraham the Chaldean. This is not true, given that it is a very certain thing (as we have clearly verified above) that these Ethiopians are descended from none other than Cush, son of Ham, and not from any of the children of Shem. And even though the form and order of writing the letters and characters of the Ethiopian language—which are written from the left hand toward the right—is entirely different from those of the Hebrew language, nevertheless the phonetic power of said letters and characters, the origin of their words, and the forms of declining and conjugating their nouns and verbs approach very closely those of the said Hebrew language. Regarding this, we cite the authority of that great and learned personage Guillaume Postel <note>A 16th-century French polymath and linguist</note>, who, in his treatise on the *Alphabet of the Twelve Languages*, in the chapter on the Indian or Ethiopian language, said the following:

Johann Potken <note>A German priest who published the first printed book in Ge'ez (Ethiopic) in 1513</note>, administrator of the Church of Cologne, was the first who, having had the Psalms of David and the Song of Solomon printed in this our Europe some years ago in the Ethiopian, Indian, and Nubian language, and in its characters, dared—through an ignorance of the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Syriac languages—to assert along with the common crowd, though without much reason, that this language was the same as and similar to Chaldean. This is despite it being very certain that the Chaldean and Syriac languages are nothing other than the two languages which in ancient times issued and proceeded from the purity of the sole Hebrew language; namely, one being Assyrian or Babylonian, and the other Jerusalemite, which in the time of

our Lord Jesus Christ <note>Refers to the use of Aramaic/Syriac in the time of Jesus</note> was common and spoken by the people throughout all Syria, which is apparent from several places and passages of Holy Scripture previously cited by me in the chapter on the Syriac language. The *Targum* <note>An Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> or Assyrian or Babylonian Paraphrase is written and composed in that Assyrian or Babylonian language; and the other *Targum*, or Jerusalem or Syriac Paraphrase, is written and composed in that Syriac language. The reason that induced the said Potké <note>Johannes Potken, a German scholar who published the first printed Ethiopic Psalter in 1513</note> to hold, along with the common and vulgar opinion, what we have deduced above, is that he had heard it said, or had read in the books of antiquity, that the Chaldean language was immediately the first and most ancient in the world after the Hebrew language, and consequently that it was this Ethiopian, Indian, or Nubian language. 

But we must—with the authority of T. Ambrogius <note>Theseus Ambrosius, an Italian orientalist</note> in his introduction to the Chaldean, Syriac, and Armenian languages, and the said T. Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander, a Swiss linguist and reformer</note> in his *Commentary on the common reasoning of all languages and letters*—hold it as most certain that this language is in no way Chaldean, but rather another quite diverse and dissimilar from it. However, it is no less ancient than the other, because the third son of the Patriarch Noah, Ham, to whom and to whose kin fell (by the division of his father for habitation and dwelling) Africa and inner Ethiopia—where his descendants, the Ethiopians, Indians, and Nubians of today, reside—transplanted into these regions the offshoots of Hebraism or Chaldaism. These still endure for the present among the Ethiopian, Indian, or Nubian Christians in the southern or meridional region of Sabachta, from which departed the Queen of Sheba, who came to visit King Solomon in the city of Jerusalem. 

These Ethiopians, Indians, or Nubians assert that they have prayed to and adored our Lord Jesus Christ in this language since they were taught and instructed in the Christian Religion by a Philip, the Eunuch of their Queen named Candace <note>Acts 8:26-40 describes the conversion of the Ethiopian eunuch</note>, wife or daughter of one of their Kings named Alexander—a name common and familiar to the Ethiopian Kings even before the time of Alexander the Great. These Ethiopians, Indians, or Nubians became more particularly known in Christendom from the time of Pope Eugene III <note>Reigned 1145–1153; this likely refers to the arrival of Ethiopian pilgrims or envoys during the Crusades or early councils</note> and currently converse ordinarily in the city of Jerusalem and Rome, as well as in the ports and harbors of Africa, with Jews, Greeks, Italians, Spaniards, Portuguese, and others. 

The poet Virgil, in the 4th book of his *Georgics*, called them "colored Indians" <note>original: "Indos Coloratos"</note>, stating "the Nile is carried down from the Indians" <note>original: "Nilum ab Indis deuexam"</note>; the "Indian color" <note>original: "color Indus"</note> is common to both Ethiopians and Asiatic Indians. It is a word of all Oriental languages, some calling others *Hindi*, others *Hundy*, *Hundiet*, and some *Mundistam* <note>Likely a corruption of Hindustan</note>; he asserts they are called Indians. This is a word or name which, according to the Ethiopian, Indian, or Nubian priests who currently live in both Constantinople and Venice, is common to the Indians and Oriental Christians, as well as to the greatest and most sound part of the other Indians, the <gloss>Gueberes</gloss> <note>original gloss: "Gueberes", likely referring to the Guebres or Zoroastrians, or more generally to non-Christians</note>, which is to say, devil-worshippers. 

And this Ethiopian, Indian, or Nubian language is so similar to the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic languages that there are few words and expressions in those languages that are not found in the said Ethiopian, Indian, or Nubian language. This demonstrates infallibly that these languages, although different in their letter characters and in their points <note>vowel markings</note>, are very close to one another in their

And so as not to keep benevolent readers in suspense any longer regarding the truth of this *Ethiopian* language, we shall say that it is almost entirely composed and woven from the *Hebrew*, *Chaldaic*, *Syriac*, and *Arabic* languages, having emerged and proceeded from each of the aforementioned tongues. It is adorned and embellished in its Alphabet—currently used among the said *Ethiopians*, *Indians*, and *Nubians* (who constantly maintain and affirm they have possessed it for a long time)—with 26 characters or letters, of which the last four are letters coupled into syllables as a form of abbreviation, in which their writing is very abundant. This can be seen in the *Itinerary of Bernhard von Breydenbach* <note>A famous 15th-century travelogue to the Holy Land</note>, the *Indian Psalter* and *Song of Songs* by the aforementioned *Johannes Potken* cited above, and the *New Testament* by *Pietro the Ethiopian* <note>also known as Tesfa Zion, a 16th-century monk who helped print the first Ethiopic New Testament in Rome</note>, an Ethiopian monk and cleric, first printed in *Ethiopian* characters in the year 1548 along with the *Epistle of St. Paul to the Hebrews*, and the concordance of the *Gospels of Eusebius*, together with the *Missal* and blessings of fire, candles, and other ceremonies, with the alphabet written in the language called *Ge'ez* <note>original: "Geetz"</note>, which is to say, "free," because it does not derive its source from any other language. It is commonly called *Chaldaic* by *Leo Africanus* <note>original: "Iean Leon," a 16th-century Berber diplomat and author of "Description of Africa"</note> in book 7 of his description of Africa, in the chapter on the kingdom of *Nubia*; in the treatise on the twelve languages by the late *G. Furthermore, the Alphabet of this language does not proceed in the manner of those of the *Hebrews*, *Samaritans*, *Syrians*, and *Arabs*, from right to left—notwithstanding that these *Ethiopians*, *Indians*, or *Nubians* have taken the greater part of their said language and writing from them, and even call themselves *Chaldeans*—but rather like the *Greeks* and *Latins*, from the left hand toward the right. This follows the course and particular movement of the Planets, of which the *Sun* is the principal, contrary to the *prime mover* <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the "prime mover" (primum mobile) rotates from East to West, while the planets move West to East relative to the stars</note>. For due to their "adustion" <note>scorching or darkening of the skin by the sun's heat</note>, which is evidenced by their very black complexion, and their close proximity to that great light which burns and roasts them incessantly, they hold and repute themselves as its children here below. 

Therefore, based on what has been deduced above, it remains quite certain that this *Ethiopian*, *Indian*, or *Nubian* language is not true *Hebrew*, *Chaldaic*, or *Syriac*, nor any other of the languages described above, but rather a distinct and particular one among them. Nevertheless, it is entirely filled with many *Hebrew*, *Chaldean*, and *Syriac* words and verbs, as confirmed by *Sebastian Münster* in his *Chaldaic* Grammar and *Theseus Ambrosius* in his introduction to the *Chaldaic*, *Syriac*, and *Aramaic* languages. These *Ethiopians*, *Indians*, or *Nubians* commonly place two dots at the end of each word, one above the other in the manner of a colon <note>original: "coma"</note>; and at the end of a clause, four dots in a square. These people came to offer subjection and obedience to the *Pope* and the *Holy Apostolic See* under the Pontificate of *Clement V* in the year of Grace 1306, as written by *Filippo da Bergamo* <note>original: "Phelippe Bergomense," an Augustinian chronicler</note>...

->*Of Prester John, Prest-Ian, Prestian, or Prestegian, great Emperor, or King of the Ethiopians, Indians, Nubians, & Abyssins.*<-

### CHAP. LII.

Génébrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine exegete and orientalist</note>, in Book 2 of his *Chronology*, making mention of the three Kings who came to adore our Lord Jesus Christ, has reported these words worthy of great consideration and remark.

In the 35th year of Herod <note>original: "Herodis 35. tempore"</note>, the Magi, about to adore Christ, came from Persia, which is in the East of the land of Israel (Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 51). Two years later, Herod died of a horrific disease at the age of 71 (Book 2 on the Kings of Israel). He was buried in Herodium, which city was a journey of two and a half days from Jerusalem (ibid.).

More probable is the view of Ammonius of Alexandria <note>A 3rd-century Christian philosopher</note>: that on the 13th day after the birth of Christ, the Magi arrived in Jerusalem, coming under the lead of a certain new star, and proclaimed the King of the Jews born (*In the Harmony*). From this, the Church celebrates the Epiphany on that day. Namely, that they came from Persia or rather another place in the East (of which more soon); in the 33rd year of his [Herod's] reign, the star appeared to the Kings four years before his death (words of Saint Cyprian at the very beginning of his sermon on Baptism). For it is an ancient tradition of the Church that the Magi were Kings and Toparchs <note>original: "Toparchas" — local governors or petty kings of a specific district</note>. Tertullian in his book *Against the Jews*, and Book 3 of *Against Marcion*; Jerome on Psalm 71; Augustine in Book 3 of *The Miracles of Scripture*, chapter four, and in the *Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert*, sermon 43; Hilary in Book 4 *On the Trinity*; Idacius Clarius to Varimund the Arian—not to mention the Greeks—Athanasius in question 2 of *Various Questions to Prince Antiochus*, which Reclinus translated differently from those commonly extant in his volumes. He says: "We call the Feast of the Epiphany the Day of the Three Kings." [See also] Cantacuzenus, *Apology* 1, etc.

Nor indeed were they only Kings, but they also laid the foundation of that very vast Christian Kingdom in India (for they had come from there, from its province which was called Tarsis, and today Tartestan <note>A reference to Tartary or Central Asia</note> according to Hayto), which he who held for twelve hundred years was called **Prester John** <note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles from the 12th to the 17th centuries</note>, being powerful in both Ecclesiastical and secular authority, until around the year 1200 it succumbed to the arms of the Tartars. And from there the Mohammedan empire of the Great Khan arose. (Marco Polo the Venetian in his *Travels*). With the title of Prester John being transferred to 그hat great Christian Emperor of the Abyssinians or Ethiopians (Osório in *The Deeds of Emmanuel, King of Portugal* <note>original: "Osorius in rebus Emmanuelis Reges Lusitaniæ"</note>). Nor is it necessary that they were "great" kings, since God often chooses the weak things of the world to put the strong to shame. But they were all called Kings according to the custom of the East, who could use the scepter and diadem with dignity, whether they were independent or under the law of another: and thus they were distinguished from Dukes, as Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and biblical commentator</note> often notes. This is observed today by the Tartars, Persians, Ethiopians, and other Orientals; for they are not so anxious and concerned in distinguishing between a King and a Prince. Thus Catherine of Alexandria was the daughter of King Costus, that is, a Prince; thus in the Gospel the Lord heals the son of a certain "little king" <note>original: "Reguli"</note>; thus in the Old Testament 30 Kings of the land of Canaan...

The same Génébrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French scholar and Benedictine archbishop</note> in Book 4 of his said *Chronology* writes: In India there was a certain great Christian King; the Land of Caghat <note>likely referring to the territories of the Khanate or Cathay</note>, from which the three Kings came to Bethlehem, was still entirely Christian, but under the Lord Cham <note>The Great Khan</note>, in the year of Salvation 1253. The voyages and navigations of the Portuguese and Spanish report that Pêro da Covilhã and Afonso de Paiva were the first European Ambassadors sent on behalf of Manuel, King of Portugal, to Ethiopia to this great Emperor around the year 1496 or 1497.

Dom Francisco Álvares, a Portuguese by nation, in his travels in Ethiopia writes that the Ethiopian Annals—composed in the Ethiopian, Indian, Nubian, and Abyssinian languages, formerly taken from Hebrew and Chaldean <note>In this period, Ge'ez (Ethiopic) was often associated with Chaldean/Syriac</note>, which he saw in Axum <note>Caxumo</note>, the principal city of Ethiopia—state that the Queen of Sheba, who came from Meroë <note>Meroc</note> to see this great King Solomon in the city of Jerusalem, was named Makeda in her own name (others say Nicaula), and that she had a son by the said Solomon named Meilech, and later David. She established and instituted him as her heir to Ethiopia, from whom is descended the race of Kings of the great Ethiopian Empire. This is confirmed by Marinus Victorinus in his discourse on the Kings of Ethiopia, Andrea Corsali in his letter to Duke Lorenzo de' Medici, and Guillaume Postel in his *Alphabet of the Twelve Languages* and in his work on the noble nations who took their names and appellations from Noah and his children. Because of this, all the Ethiopian Kings hold the memory of Solomon in very great reverence, sending offerings every year to the temple in Jerusalem, as children of the house of David and instructed in the law of Moses; this they also take from the New Testament, speaking of the Eunuch <note>The Ethiopian official described in Acts 8</note> sent to Judea in the time of the Apostles, who was baptized by Philip, one of the seven deacons, and who first planted the Christian Religion in Ethiopia.

As for this word "Prester John," "Prestian," "Prestan," or "Prestegian," a name common and familiar to all the Kings of Ethiopia, Paolo Giovio <note>Paul Ioue</note> in Book 1 of his *Eulogies* maintains that it is corrupted among us, and that the true name of the Kings of this Province is *Belulgiam*, which was common to all the Kings of this country, meaning "Pearl of great price and incomparable excellence." This is confirmed by Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie in his preface to the Syriac New Testament, noting that the Ethiopians call this King and Lord *Ian Belul*, or *Ian* in the Chaldaic language—that is to say, "precious" or "high"—or else as Jean Bodin writes in his *Method for the Easy Comprehension of History*, chapter 5, *Iochan Belul*, "Very precious stone." Some modern authors maintain that Saint Thomas the Apostle, according to what is written in the Acts of the Apostles, went to preach in Greater India, that he died there, and left such a great multitude of people converted to the faith of Jesus Christ that, as they had elected a Lord to govern them, they gave him this name of Prester John—both because all the Lords were clerics, and because they had this name of John in common since the first one who was elected, who was so named. ...who reigned were chosen by the hand of Saint Thomas, in which was placed a dry vine branch. They would carry this in procession, and when it happened that the one who was to be elected passed by, this hand would sprout leaves, branches, and clusters of grapes, which would then ripen. From these grapes, the wine was pressed for the Mass he said that day, and so on. Juan de Torquemada <note>A Spanish cardinal and theologian, 1388–1468</note> in his *Hexameron*, Day 2, leaves 176 and 177. Damião de Góis <note>A Portuguese humanist and historian</note> in his *History of the Ethiopian Religion* writes that the term *Prester John* <note>original: "Preste Ian"</note> signifies as much as "Powerful, Excellent, and Precious King." Others say that *Ian* or *Gian* means precious or excellent. The same Dom Francisco Álvares cited above maintains that this Emperor has two principal names: *Acegué*, which means Emperor, and *Negus*, meaning King. Sebastian Münster, the German, in his *Chaldean Grammar*, in the chapter on Chaldean letters, asserts that the term *Prester John* is corrupted from the word *Priest Cohen* <note>original: "Prestre Cohan"</note>, which signifies—in both the Hebrew and Chaldean languages—a Priest or Pontiff. Concerning this, one should see what Guillaume Postel <note>A French linguist and polymath</note> writes in his treatise on the *Alphabets of the 12 Languages*, and his treatise on the *Renowned Regions Named After the Children of Noah*. Julius Caesar Scaliger, in his 117th exercise against Girolamo Cardano on *Subtlety*, held (in agreement with Álvares cited above) that the Ethiopians call their Emperor *Negus* or *Acegué*, which is to say King and Emperor.

Some other Ethiopians living near Cape Guardafui call him in their language *Thamnat-Hares*, "Image of the Great God"; the people of Calicut call him *Zobeleth*, "Inexpugnable Mountain"; the Javanese, the people of Taprobana <note>likely Sri Lanka</note>, and those of Borneo call him *Cappach Elisua*, "Son of the Great David"; the Persians call him *Cochouet*; the Ethiopians call him *Gerich*; the Moors call him *Soltan Abyssin*, "Sovereign of the Abyssinians," or *Aticlabaffi*, according to the report of Andrea Corsali cited above in his letter to Duke Lorenzo de' Medici. The great Pico della Mirandola, having read it somewhere in his *Apology* (fifth question on Magic and Kabbalah), calls him by a corrupted word, *Prestam*; and Jean Bodin, in his commentaries on the third book of the hunt by the Greek poet Oppian, calls him *Preste*.

But without lingering on all these preceding opinions, we shall hold it as quite certain that this word *Prester John* or *Prestegian* signifies in the Persian language (which is widely current throughout all of Asia, just as Latin is in the West) as much as if one said "Apostolic." In fact, in this Persian language, the word *Prestegian* <note>original Hebrew-script Persian: פֿרסתגאן</note> in the plural number is the same as the Greek word <term lang="grc">Apostoloi</term> (Apostles); and *Prestegiani* <note>original: פֿרסתגאני</note> is the same as the Greek <term lang="grc">Apostolikos</term> (Apostolic).

-> *Padescha Prestegiani* <note>original Hebrew script: פֿרשט פֿרסתגאני</note> <-

Apostolic King, which is to say, Christian. The Arabs call him in their language *Melich Ressuli* <note>original Hebrew script: מליך רסולי</note>, and his subjects call him *Negus Chauuarauui* <note>original Hebrew script: נגוש חררויי</note>, "Apostolic King," or *Gerichauauraich*. On this matter, one should see Marco Polo the Venetian, book 2, chapter 27 of his travels, who was greatly mistaken in his explanation of this word *Chauuarauui*, as it is a very certain thing that it does not signify "holy man," as that author says, but rather "Apostolic," as I have already stated above. André Thevet, in book 2, chapter 13 of his *Cosmography*, reports that this Emperor is called by some Easterners *Gideroth*, "Lord of the Hot Country." This Emperor or King of Ethiopia—who, through the aforementioned Dom Francisco Álvares, wrote letters both to Manuel, King of Portugal, in the year of salvation 1521, and to Pope Clement VII in the years 1533 and 1548—titled his qualities thus: "I, the King..."

Joseph, Patriarch of Constantinople <note>Joseph II (c. 1360–1439), who attended the Council of Florence to attempt a reconciliation between the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches</note>, accompanied by a great number of Archbishops, Bishops, and Prelates of all sorts—among whom also appeared the representatives of the Patriarchs of Antioch, Alexandria, and Jerusalem, all in agreement in the love of the holy faith and Christian religion—by whose means, with the grace of the Lord, the unity of the Church was confirmed and all the difficulties of the past, which seemed contrary and repugnant to religion, were removed: and these things being confirmed and established in good order, the Pope wished for each and every person to rejoice in them.

These letters subsequently carry these words:

"Now we send you this book from Pope Eugene <note>Pope Eugene IV (r. 1431–1447), who presided over the Council of Florence</note>, which we have always kept without corruption. We would have also sent you the treatise on the order and power of the Pontifical blessing, had the volume not been too large, for in truth it is bigger than the book of Saint Paul to the Gentiles <note>The collected Epistles of St. Paul</note>. And to declare to you the personages who brought these things from the Pope: they were Theodore, Peter, Didymus, and George, servants of Jesus Christ; assuring you, Most Holy Father, that you will do very well if you have the registers of your Chancery searched, in which I believe you will easily find some memory of the things I am writing back to you. Therefore, your Holiness may firmly believe that whatever you write back to me will be immediately recorded in our books, so that a memory of it remains for posterity. Certainly, he seems very happy to me whose memory is kept by letters in the holy City of Rome, and at the See of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, Lords of the kingdom of heaven and Judges of all the world."

Sir John Mandeville, a knight living in the year of Grace 1322, in his travels composed in the Romance language <note>The vernacular "Romance" or "Romanesque" language here refers to an early dialect, possibly Catalan or an Occitan-influenced French, used in the manuscript he is citing</note>, in the chapter regarding why the Emperor is called *Prester John*, writes what follows: *“It has been a long time since an Emperor, who was a very valiant prince and had in his company many other Lords and sons, set out to see the manner of the Christian Church... he took in his company only one knight... and they traversed all Turkey, Syria, and Tartary... Arabia, Aleppo, and all the land of Egypt and India... they came to a church, etc. folio 88.”* <note>original: "Elle ha louch temps que vn Emperador qui era molt valent princep... é vndiſapte eſde vngueren a vna Eſgleia"</note> By these words, this personage asserts that this Emperor first took this surname of Prester John because of a Priest named John whom he saw promoted to holy orders during his pilgrimage. > In the year of Salvation 784, Oger the Dane <note>Ogier the Dane, a legendary paladin of Charlemagne</note>, a most Christian Prince, flourished. ...of the Red Sea in the land neighboring Ethiopia, as confirmed by **Paolo Giovio** <note>An Italian physician and historian (1483–1552) famous for his work on contemporary history and geography</note> in Book 18 of his histories. All the subjects of this great Emperor or King constantly affirm that never has any Emperor, King, nor Prince of any other Province in the world overcome or subjugated their country, nor even the Saracens, Arabs, Turks & other Mahometans <note>Followers of Islam; the text emphasizes the empire's survival against surrounding Islamic powers</note> who have ravaged & destroyed the largest part of Asia & Africa, without ever daring to address themselves to the said country. Several other noteworthy and remarkable particularities regarding this great Emperor or King **Prester John** are treated in the book of **Mandeville** in his travels (chapter on Prester John and his state); **Alvise Cadamosto** <note>A Venetian slave trader and explorer who explored the Atlantic coast of Africa for Portugal</note> in part 2 of his *Navigations*, chapter 60; **Marco Polo the Venetian**, Book 3, chapter 38 of his travels; **Francisco Álvares** in his travels in Ethiopia; **Damião de Góis**, a Portuguese, in his treatise on the faith, Religion & customs of the Ethiopians under the Empire of this Prester John; **André Thevet**, Book 2, chapters 13 & 14 of his *Cosmography*; **Joseph Scaliger**, Book 7 of the *Emendation of Time*, in the chapter of annotations on the Calendar of the Ethiopians; **Antoine du Verdier**, Book 2, chapter 1 of his *Diverse Lessons*; **Juan de Torquemada**, a Spaniard, on the 2nd day of his *Hexameron*; **François de Belleforest**, Book 1, chapter 4 of his *Universal History*, & Book 6, chapters 22 & 23 of the 2nd volume of his *Cosmography*; **Abraham Ortelius**, tables 4 & 47 of his *Theater of the World* <note>The first modern atlas, published in 1570</note>; **Louis Le Roy**, Book 9 of the *Vicissitude of Things*; the author of the *Treasury of Politics*, Book 2, the chapter on the great King of Ethiopia; & **Blaise de Vigenère** in his *Treatise on Ciphers*.

The dominion of this great Emperor or King extends in Africa from one Tropic to the other, reaching an extent of 50 or 52 degrees of latitude, which makes more than a thousand leagues of travel. Its length is from the East to the West, namely from the Red Sea, where **Suakin** and **Massawa** are located, to the Atlantic Ocean; that is to say, Egypt lies to his North, and neighbors him toward **Nubia**, so named in the Hebrew language *Nubiah* <note>original: "Nubiah"</note>, meaning "Sprout of God," because the faith was sprouted in the person of the **Ethiopian Eunuch**, and later of **Candace**, Queen of Ethiopia <note>Referring to the story in the biblical Acts of the Apostles where an Ethiopian official is converted, which the author uses to explain the name "Nubia"</note>, according to G. le Fèvre de la Boderie, folio 24. To the east of him is the Red Sea and part of the Indian Sea, and the Gulf named **Barbarian** <note>The *Sinus Barbaricus*, a historical name for the coast of East Africa</note>, as far as the country of **Malindi** and **Benamate**, unknown to ancient authors. To the south, it looks toward the **Mountains of the Moon** which serve as a closure and wall on that side, or rather the Cape of Good Hope. To the West, it has for boundaries and limits the River **Niger** or **Senegal**, and the kingdoms of Nubia and **Manicongo** <note>The Kingdom of Kongo</note>, as confirmed by **Abraham Ortelius**, table 4 of his *Theater of the Universe*.

Regarding the Kingdoms & Provinces that are under the said dominion of this great Emperor or King, the titles and styles of his patent letters sent to Popes Leo X and Clement VII, and to the King of Portugal—included in the travels of **Álvares** mentioned above, and translated into Latin by **Damião de Góis**, a Portuguese knight, in his discourse on the faith, Religion & customs of the Ethiopians—provide ample proof and demonstration. They state that this Emperor or King is Emperor of Great and High Ethiopia, and of very great kingdoms, jurisdictions, & lands: King of **Goa**, **Cafattes**, **Fatigar**, **Angote**, **Baru**, **Balignanzar**, **Adee**, **Vanga**, **Gojjam** <note>original: "Goyame"</note> (where the sources and fountains of the Nile are found), **Amara**, **Begemder** <note>original: "Baguamedre"</note>, **Ambee**, **Vangussi**, **Tigray** <note>original: "Tigremahon"</note>, **Sabaim**, **Saba**, **Barnagas**, and Lord as far as Nubia, which extends all the way to the land of Egypt.

Marius Victorius <note>Mariano Vittori, an Italian scholar and bishop known for writing one of the first grammars of the Ethiopic language</note>, in a book of his entitled *On the Kings of Ethiopia* <note>original: "de Regib. ### Of the several kinds of Christians who are spread and scattered throughout the whole extent of the earth.

Joachim the Abbot <note>Joachim of Fiore (c. 1135–1202), a mystic and theologian who organized history into three ages</note>, in his *Appendix of Christian Nations*, has written the following concerning Christians:

The Christian peoples are divided into ten nations, namely the Latins, Greeks, Indians, Jacobites, Nestorians, Maronites, Armenians, Georgians, Syrians, and Mozarabs <note>original: "Gentes Christianorum diuiduntur in decem nationes..."</note>.

The first nation is that of the Latins, who have the Emperor of Germany and many Kings, namely the Kings of Castile, Aragon, Spain, Portugal, Navarre, etc. In the French nation, there is one King of the Franks, and many Dukes, Counts, and Barons. In the nation of Italy, there is the Pope, the King of Sicily and Naples, many Dukes, Counts, Marquises, and great Communes, namely those of Venice, Lucca, Siena, and others. In the Germanic nation, besides the Emperor, who must be Christian, there are many Kings, namely the King of England, Scotland, Hungary, Bohemia, Poland, Denmark <note>original: "Daciæ"</note>, Frisia, Sweden, Norway, Dalmatia, and many Marquises, Landgraves, Dukes, and Counts; likewise the King of Cyprus, and the inhabitants of the island of Malta <note>original: "insulæ Meltidis"</note>, and of other islands obedient to the Roman Church.

The second nation is that of the Greeks, who formerly had the Patriarch of Constantinople, Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, etc., in spiritual matters, and in temporal matters an Emperor, Dukes, and Counts, etc. However, they are now few in number, because the Agarenes <note>A medieval term for Muslims, referring to descendants of Hagar</note> and Turks have occupied and invaded the greatest part of Greece; and these do not obey the Roman Church, and hold many errors which are condemned by the Church, because they say that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, but from the Father alone, and they also say that there is no Purgatory.

The third nation is that of the Indians, whose Prince is Prester John <note>A legendary Christian monarch said to rule a vast empire in the East or Africa</note>, whose power exceeds all Christians: for he has seventy-two Kings under him, and when the said King and Lord Prester John rides, he always has a wooden cross carried before him. When he goes to war, he has twelve crosses made of gold and precious stones carried as banners: in his land is the body of the blessed Apostle Thomas in greatest veneration, though others say on the contrary that the body of this Saint is in East India.

The fourth nation is that of the Jacobites <note>Members of the Syriac Orthodox Church</note>; so called after Jacob the Heretic <note>Jacob Baradaeus, who reorganized the Monophysite church in the 6th century</note>, a disciple of the Patriarch of Alexandria. These occupy a great part of Asia in the regions of the East, the land of Mamre which is near Egypt, and the land of Ethiopia as far as India, comprising more than 40 Kingdoms: these are circumcised and baptized with a hot iron <note>A reference to the practice of branding a cross on the skin</note>, printing the mark of the cross on their foreheads and other parts of the body, such as on the chest or arms; these confess to God alone and not to Priests, nor to Jews or Agarenes, and they say that in Christ there is only a divine nature <note>The doctrine of Monophysitism, which held that Christ had a single divine nature rather than distinct human and divine natures</note>. Some of them speak the Chaldean language <note>Syriac or Aramaic</note>, some the Arabic language, and others in other languages according to the diversity of their nations; and these were condemned in the Council of Chalcedon <note>original: "concilio Cedensi"</note>.

<meta>catchword: The tenth</meta>

The fifth nation is that of the Nestorians, named after the heretic Nestorius, who was the Bishop of Constantinople <note>Nestorius (c. 386–450 AD) was deposed for his views on the nature of Christ</note>. They alone posit two distinct persons in Christ: one divine and the other human. They deny that the Blessed Virgin Mary is the Mother of God, asserting instead that she is the mother of the man Jesus. They use the Chaldean language <note>original: "lingua Chaldaica," referring here to Classical Syriac</note> in their scriptures and consecrate the body of Christ using leavened bread. They inhabit Tartary <note>a historical term for North and Central Asia, including the Mongol Empire</note> and Greater India, and they are many in number. Their land is as vast as Germany and Italy combined; these are the same heretics who were condemned in the third Synod of Ephesus [431 AD], and having been divided from the Roman Church, they have remained obstinate in their views.

The sixth nation is that of the Maronites, named after a certain heretic called Maro. They posit only one intellect and one will in Christ <note>a doctrine known as Monothelitism, which suggests Christ had two natures but only one governing will</note>. They live near Lebanon <note>original: "Lybiam," likely a transcription error for "Libanum"</note> in the province of Phoenicia in great numbers. They are warrior-men, well-taught and experienced in battle, making special use of bows and arrows. Following the custom of the Latins, they use bells; their Bishops use rings, mitres, and pastoral staffs. In their writings, they use the Chaldean script, but in common speech, they use the Arabic language. At one time, they were under the obedience of the Roman Church—for their Patriarch was present at the General Lateran Council held in Rome under Innocent III [1215 AD]—but they later withdrew from the Roman Church. They were first condemned in the Synod of Constantinople, later returned to the obedience of the Roman Church, and have since returned again to their own opinion, in which they persevere to this day.

The seventh nation is that of the Armenians, who live in the kingdom of Armenia near Antioch. They have their own idiom and a language common to all; they sing the Holy Scriptures and the office of the Church and speak in the vernacular tongue so that they may be understood by all laypeople, both men and women. They have their own Primate, whom they call the Catholicos <note>original: "Catholicum"</note>, whom they obey with great devotion and reverence, just as we obey the Pope. They fast during Lent with great devotion, during which they neither eat fish nor drink wine. However, on Fridays, they eat meat.

The eighth nation is that of the Georgians, named after Saint George, whom they hold as their patron in battle. They live in the Eastern regions; they are a handsome, strong, and refined people, and are greatly feared by the Medes, Persians, and Syrians, on whose borders they dwell. They use the Greek language and perform the sacraments after the Greek custom. The clergy have round tonsures <note>original: "coronas," referring to the shaved circle on a priest's head</note> on their heads, while the laymen have square ones. When they come to the Holy Sepulchre, they do not pay tribute to the Saracens <note>a medieval term for Muslims, particularly those in the Levant</note>, and they enter Jerusalem with banners held high because the Saracens fear them. Their women use arms just as the men do; they also have hair and "beards" <note>likely a reference to heavy veils or perhaps a misunderstanding of local fashions</note> like the men, and they wear tall hats on their heads a cubit in height. When they write to the Sultan, whatever they request is immediately granted to them.

The ninth nation is that of the Syrians, so named after the city of Tyre <note>original: "Sur"</note>, which is the most eminent city in Syria or Assyria. In common speech, they use the Saracen language <note>Arabic</note>, but for the divine scriptures and the office of the Mass, they use the Greek language. They have Bishops and observe the customs of the Greeks, obeying them in all things; they perform the Eucharist with leavened bread and hold the opinions of the Greeks against the Latins. They are followed by certain Christians who are called Samaritans in the Holy Land; these were first converted in the time of the Apostles, but they are not well-grounded in the Catholic faith.

The tenth nation is that of the **Mozarabs**. These Mozarabs were once numerous in parts of Africa and Spain, but now they are few. They are called **Mozarabs** because they followed the customs of the Christians of Arabia in many things. <note>The name "Mozarab" comes from the Arabic *musta'rib*, meaning "Arabicized." It refers to Iberian Christians who lived under Muslim rule and adopted Arabic language and culture while remaining Christian.</note> They use the **Latin language** in their divine services, and they obey the Roman Church and the Latin Prelates. They celebrate the Eucharist with unleavened bread <note>original: "in azymo"</note> like the Latins, but they differ from the Latins in many other respects. Because the natural day is divided into twenty-four hours of day and night, they have just as many offices—including hours, psalms, and hymns—and they have certain prayers that are excessively long, which they do not recite in the Latin fashion; for what the Latins say at the beginning, they say at the end or in the middle. Some divide the Sacrament of the Eucharist into seven parts, and others into ten. This nation is exceedingly devout; in marriage, however, they only unite with people of their own race or nation. Among them, a woman who has lost her first husband never joins with another, but remains in perpetual chastity. 

The cause of such great diversity or division among Christians was that, in ancient times, Christians were restricted from holding general councils; therefore, when heretics arose in various parts of the world, there was no one to apply a remedy. The second cause was the negligence of the Supreme Pontiffs [the Popes], because they did not take care to send envoys to the Christians living in error; for if they had done so, they would have brought many or all back to the one faith and obedience of the Roman Church.

**Barthélemy de Chasseneuz**, in the twelfth part of his *Catalog of the Glory of the World* <note>original: "cathalogue, gloria mundi," referring to the *Catalogus gloriae mundi* (1529), a famous legal and encyclopedic work</note>, consideration 22, writes the following: Of the Christian sects, there are thirteen nations that hold to it, and there are four that are included under the **Latins**, because the Latins are primarily all Christians. And within the Latin nation, there are four other specific nations: namely, the **French** <note>original: "Gallicana"</note>, **German** <note>original: "Germanica"</note>, **Italian** <note>original: "Italica"</note>, and **Spanish** <note>original: "Hispanica"</note> nations. 

But there is one that has held and continues to hold the faith without monstrosities or any error, and without deviation, because it never withdrew from it or strayed in any way: this is the **French nation**, which has always been free of monstrosities, and has always defended, aided, protected, and increased the Catholic faith, and has fought with all its might against almost all other nations [that opposed it]. In this first French nation, the **King of France** is the principal figure, who is called the **"Most Christian"** <note>original: "Christianissimus," a formal title granted to the Kings of France</note> among all the kings of the world. Under him are many Dukes, Counts, Marquises, and Barons obedient to him, as well as the King of Navarre and the King of Yvetot <note>The "Kingdom of Yvetot" was a small, sovereign-like principality in Normandy</note>, although some say the kingdom of Navarre falls under the Spanish nation. 

The second nation is the **Italian**, in which resides the principal figure of all Christendom, who is the **Pope**. He holds the primacy and leadership over the entire Church and the Christian sect, whom everyone obeys, or is bound to obey. In that nation are the King of Sicily, the King of Naples, the Duchy of Venice, the Dukes of Milan, Ferrara, and Urbino, the Marquises of Mantua and Montferrat, and many other Counts, principalities, and lordships, such as Florence, Siena, and Genoa. 

The third nation is the **Spanish**, in which are the Kings of Castile, Leon, Granada, Aragon, and Portugal, along with many Dukes and Counts; the principal kingdom is called Castile and Spain, whose King is called **"The Catholic"** <note>original: "Catholicus," the traditional title of the Spanish monarch</note>. 

The fourth nation is that of the **Germans**, in which is the **Emperor**. There are also many kings, such as the King of England, Scotland, Hungary, Bohemia, Poland, Denmark <note>original: "Daciæ," a common Latinization for Denmark in this period</note>, Frisia, Sweden, Norway, Dalmatia, and Croatia, as well as many Landgraves, Dukes, and Counts. Likewise, the King of Cyprus on the Island of Cyprus. All the aforementioned are obedient to the Roman Church, although many heresies have emanated from this Germany, which were condemned, and...

To these nations, in these most recent days, has risen the **Lutheran sect**, which has stained Christianity in many ways. The **fifth nation** is that of the **Greeks**, who have the **Patriarch of Constantinople**, as well as Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, and others of that kind in spiritual matters. In temporal <note>Meaning worldly or political, as opposed to spiritual.</note> matters, they have an **Emperor**, and they also have Dukes, Counts, Despots <note>original: "Hisbotum," likely a transcription error for "Despotum," a title for high-ranking lords in the Byzantine Empire.</note>, and so on. However, they are now few in number, because the **Hagarenes** <note>A medieval term for Muslims, based on the biblical Hagar.</note> and the **Turks** have occupied and hold the greater part of Greece. These people do not obey the **Roman Church**, although they were at times subject to the Roman Pontiff himself; nonetheless, they have frequently attempted to tear the "seamless tunic of the Lord" <note>A common biblical metaphor for the unity of the Church, referring to the robe of Jesus that was not divided by the soldiers at the Crucifixion.</note>. For this reason, twelve divisions of the Greeks are usually counted, which are listed by **Johann Eck** <note>A prominent 16th-century German theologian and opponent of Martin Luther.</note> in the third book of his treatise *On the Primacy of Peter*, chapter 16. Truly, they now hold many errors and have been condemned by the Church because they say that the **Holy Spirit** does not proceed from the Son <note>original: "Spiritus sanctus nō procedit à Filio." This refers to the "Filioque" controversy, the central theological disagreement between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.</note> and because they do not believe in **purgatory**. 

The **sixth nation** is that of **India**, in which is **Prester John** <note>A legendary Christian king of the East who captivated the medieval European imagination; he was believed to rule a vast, wealthy empire in "India" or Ethiopia.</note>, who presides over that people as a **Patriarch**, and one hundred and twenty-seven Archbishoprics are subject to him, each of which is said to have twenty Bishops. These people are reborn through the fountain of baptism in the Roman manner, in the name of the **Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit**. They perform the sacrament of the **Eucharist** with the same rite, with this sole exception: they chant the *Pater Noster* <note>The "Our Father" prayer.</note> before the elevation of the sacrament. After the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Apostles Peter and Paul, and the Blessed John the Baptist, they especially receive and worship them with honor. They also venerate others with the greatest devotion, particularly **Matthew**, their principal teacher. Furthermore, they follow with the highest devotion the blessed **Paul the First Hermit**, **Anthony the Abbot**, **Macarius**, and two other hermits. Indeed, they say their **Emperor** is most Christian, whom seventy-four Kings and almost infinite Princes obey—excepting only twelve small rulers <note>original: "regulis"</note> who observe the laws of **Muhammad**, yet who nonetheless obey the Emperor's commands in all other things. 

Truly, in the time of **Clement V**, specifically in the year of our salvation 1306, this Emperor is said to have sent thirty legates to the **King of Spain**, offering him aid against the infidels, as a certain Genoese priest, the provost of Saint Mark, declares and wrote in his treatise on the customs of this people, titled *Mappa Mundi* <note>Map of the World.</note>. These legates, approaching the aforementioned Pope Clement V in **Avignon** with reverence, were instructed in many things; with many gifts and Apostolic letters, they came to visit the "thresholds of the Apostles" <note>A traditional term for a pilgrimage to the tombs of Peter and Paul in Rome.</note>, Peter and Paul; and having visited them, they returned to their own lands with joy. However, while waiting in **Genoa** for many days for the time of sailing, they were asked much about their tribes, customs, and regions, and they left a written account, which the same author reported. **Philip of Bergamo** <note>A 15th-century Augustinian friar and chronicler.</note> says these things in the eighth book of his *Supplement to the Chronicles*. Whenever the said Prester John rides, he always has a wooden cross carried before him; but when he goes to war, he then has two crosses carried: one of gold and the other of precious stones. In that land, the body of **St. Thomas the Apostle** is held in the greatest veneration. Extensive refutations of their errors are written by the same Juan de Torquemada. **Philip of Bergamo** <note>original: "Philippus Bergomensis" - an Augustinian friar and chronicler.</note> says in the ninth book of his *Supplement to the Chronicles* that they hold yet another error preached by Nestorius the heresiarch: namely, that living virtuously is of no benefit to human life, as is found in the passage discussing "certain heretics," because he claimed that **predestination** alone brought about salvation or dominion, which is entirely false. One could here adapt the subject of predestination, which belongs to theologians, but I only refer you to **Bernardino de Bustis** <note>A popular 15th-century Franciscan preacher.</note>... where he refutes this error and speaks at length on the matter of predestination.

The **ninth nation** is those called **Maronites**, after a certain heretic Maron, who posits only one intellect and one will in Christ. <note>This refers to Monothelitism, a 7th-century theological attempt to bridge the gap between Miaphysites and the Chalcedonian church.</note> They inhabit **Libya** <note>Likely a general term for the coast of Africa or the Levant.</note> in the province of **Phoenicia** in great numbers; they are skilled and experienced in battle, specifically using bows and arrows. They use bells in the manner of the Latins, and their bishops use rings, miters, and pastoral staffs. In their divine scriptures, they use the **Chaldean** script, and in common speech, they use **Arabic**. They were at one time under the obedience of the Roman Church; indeed, their Patriarch was present at the **General Lateran Council** held in Rome under Pope Innocent III, but they later withdrew. They were first condemned in the **Synod of Constantinople**, then returned to the obedience of the Roman Church, and have since returned again to their false opinion, in which they persist.

The **tenth nation** is those called **Armenians**, who live in the kingdom of Armenia near Antioch. They have their own idiom and common language, and they sing the Holy Scriptures and the Church office in the common tongue so that they are understood by all secular men and women. They have their own primate whom they call the **Catholicos**, whom they obey as if he were the Pope with great devotion and reverence. They fast during Lent, in which they do not eat...

The **Eleventh Nation** of Christians is those who are called **Georgians**, after Saint George, whom they have as their patron in battles. They use the Greek language and practice the sacraments according to the Greek custom. The clergy have round tonsures <note>original: "coronas rotundas" — the shaved part of a priest's head.</note> on their heads, while the secular people have square ones. When they come to the Holy Sepulchre, they do not pay tribute to the Saracens <note>A term used by medieval Europeans for Muslims.</note>, and they enter Jerusalem with banners raised high because the Saracens fear them. Their women use weapons just like the men, and they wear tall hats on their heads, a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm.</note> in height. When they write to the Sultan, what they request is immediately granted.

Philip of Bergamo <note>Philippus Bergomensis (1434–1520), an Augustinian monk and author of the 'Supplementum Chronicarum,' a popular historical compendium.</note> says in the ninth book of his *Supplement to the Chronicles* that the Scots or Hibernians are today called the Georgian people and worship Christ to this day, although they are far from the Apostolic See <note>The Papacy in Rome.</note>, the teacher of truth. He claims they do not preserve the full truth of the Gospel because they are surrounded by barbarian nations. For these (as he says) are established in the Northern part, and in the year of Christ 338, during the time of Emperor Constantine, they miraculously received the covenants of the Word of God and the faith of Christ. 

A certain Christian captive woman provided the cause for this great good. While she led a modest and holy life in that region and spent days and nights in prayer, she became an object of admiration to those nations. When they asked why she afflicted herself so much, she responded that she thus worshipped her God, who is Christ. The barbarians, wondering at nothing more than this (as we know of such novelties), began to hold the little woman in honor. Now, it was the custom of that nation that when a small child fell ill, it was carried around by its mother to the neighboring houses in search of remedies. It happened that a certain mother, after she had carried her boy around for some time and found no healing, went to the captive woman as if drunk with grief and sought her help. The woman replied that she knew of no human remedy, but that the Lord Jesus Christ whom she worshipped could grant the health that men despaired of. Placing the little boy upon her hairshirt <term>hairshirt (cilice): a garment of rough animal hair worn against the skin as a sign of penance and devotion</term> and pouring out a prayer to God Christ, she immediately returned him to his mother healed. Soon the rumor of the deed filled the whole city and even reached the Queen, who, being afflicted with pain, saw to it that the captive was brought to her. When the captive refused to enter the royal house, she poured out a prayer to God for the Queen; immediately, the Queen herself was restored to health and was thus admonished to believe in Christ and to adore Him who had provided her healing. Moved by these benefits and words, the Queen asked her husband to become a Christian. Although he had promised to do so, and despite being moved by signs and the frequent urging of his wife, he did not see to his baptism—not so much because he was an enemy of the faith, but because he was doubtful. However, it happened...

...once, when he went to hunt in the deepest forests, and having arrived there, a sudden storm arose; darkness covered everything so completely that he could see no one, nor could he be seen by them. Not knowing what ought to be done, he remembered the promise made to his wife and then prayed to Christ, asking that if He were God, He might deliver him from such great perils. Without delay, the clearest daylight was restored to the world. Having been brought back to the city, the King explained what had happened to the Queen as a miracle. The captive woman <note>Saint Nino, a slave woman who is credited with bringing Christianity to Georgia (Iberia) in the 4th century.</note> was summoned, and her counsel was heard. She said that idols must be immediately rejected and Christ must be worshiped; she urged that He be supplicated and that a basilica be constructed. 

The King, having called the people together, preached the Gospel and, though not yet initiated into the sacred rites, became the Apostle to his own nation. The men believed through the King, and the women through the Queen. A temple of great workmanship was constructed, and when the circuit of the walls had been persistently raised, the columns were set in place. But though the first and second were erected, the third could not be raised by any machines or any strength. After they had labored until nightfall, everyone withdrew, and only the captive woman remained at the Church in persevering prayer. On the following day at first light, as the people returned, the column was found suspended in the air above its base by the space of one foot. At the sight of this miracle, everyone magnified God and recognized the true faith of the captive woman. While everyone was stupefied, the column was gradually lowered onto the base without anyone touching it. Soon, the remaining columns were erected with great success. 

Once the Church was perfected and the faith of the people confirmed, at the persuasion of the captive woman, an embassy from the whole nation was sent to the Emperor Constantine in Greece <note>Original: "Constantinum Imperatorem in Græciam." Referring to the Eastern Roman Empire centered in Constantinople.</note>, and the events were explained, and priests were requested to fulfill the service begun among them. The Emperor satisfied these requests with a most joyful countenance; so says Philip of Bergamo <note>original: "Philippus Bergomensis," referring to Jacopo Filippo Foresti (1434–1520), an Augustinian monk and historian from Bergamo.</note> in the place mentioned above.

The **Twelfth Nation** of Christians is that of those called **Syrians**, from the city of Sur <note>Tyre</note>, which is eminent in Syria or Assyria. In their common speech, they use the Saracen language <note>original: "lingua Sarracenica," referring to Arabic.</note>; in the divine scriptures and the office of the Mass, they use the Greek language. They have Bishops and preserve the custom of the Greeks, obeying them in all things. They perform the sacrament of the Eucharist with leavened bread, and they hold the opinions of the Greeks against the Latins. Certain Christians follow these, who in the Holy Land are called **Samaritans**, converted in the first era of the Apostles, but they are not well-grounded in the faith.

The **Thirteenth Nation** is that of those called **Mozarabs**. Formerly, there were many of these in parts of Africa and Spain, but now there are few. They are called Mozarabs because they held the customs of Christians according to the Arabic way in many things <note>The Mozarabs were Iberian Christians who lived under Muslim rule; the name comes from "musta'rib," meaning "Arabized."</note>. These use the Latin language in divine offices and obey the Roman Church and the Latin prelates; they perform the Eucharist in unleavened bread <note>original: "in Azimo," referring to the host used in the Western Church.</note> just like the Latins, but they differ from them in many things. For in the divine offices, they have very long "hours," because since the natural day is divided into twenty-four hours of day and night, they have as many offices, each with its own hours, psalms, and hymns, as well as certain prayers, and they are excessively long, which they do not say in the manner of the Latins. For that which the Latins say at the beginning, they say at the end or in the middle. Some divide the sacrament of the Eucharist into seven parts, others into ten. It is a nation very devoted to marriage; they do not join themselves except to persons of their own people or nation. Among them, a woman who has lost her first husband never joins with another but remains in perpetual chastity. 

All these aforementioned sects or nations use three languages, namely Hebrew or Arabic, Greek, and Latin, whence—as it is held in Luke 23 and John 19—the title or inscription of the Cross of Jesus Christ was written in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin...

...from <term>Gratian's Decree</term> <note>The foundational collection of Canon Law; the text here refers to Distinction 9.</note>, who says this: "Just as the reliability of the Old Testament books is to be examined against the Hebrew volumes, so the truth of the New Testament requires the standard of the Greek speech." <note>original: "vt veterum librorum fides de Hebræis voluminibus examinanda est, ita nouorum veritas, Græci sermonis normam desiderat"</note> This is understood to refer to the Old and New Testaments. The text also states in the final chapter of Distinction 20: "Regarding those causes where no authority for loosening or binding <note>A legal and theological term for the power of the Church to forgive sins or make laws.</note> appears in the books of the Old and New Testaments, or in the four Gospels along with all the writings of the Apostles, one should recur to the divine Greek writings." 

However, the <term>Great Gloss</term> <note>The standard 13th-century commentary on legal texts.</note> on the said chapter *Ut veterum* says that Jerome, in his second prologue to the Bible, holds the opposite view. He claims that the Latin copies are more correctly emended than the Greek and Hebrew ones. But Augustine, in the aforementioned chapter *Ut veterum*, was looking back to the primitive Church, when the Greek and Hebrew copies were not yet corrupted. 

As time passed and the Christian population grew significantly, many heresies sprouted among the Greeks. Out of envy for the Christians, both the Jews and the Greeks corrupted their own copies. Thus, it happened that their copies became more corrupted than the Latin ones. Jerome refers to this later period, or perhaps he is referring to Latin copies translated by faithful interpreters. Augustine, on the other hand, was referring to Latin copies translated not by the faithful, but by counterfeiters. In this matter, as the said Gloss states, Jerome is to be believed more than Augustine. 

Among these three—Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory—Augustine is to be believed more in matters of disputation; Jerome in matters of history and translations; and Gregory is preferred in matters of morality. This is because "not everyone is expert in all things, but specific people in specific areas," <note>original: "non omnes in omnibus, sed certi per certa"</note> as is stated in the text of the <term>Digest</term> <note>A massive collection of Roman legal opinions compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note> regarding the clarifying of old laws. "Nor can we all do all things." This is the opinion of the said Gloss, which is cited and followed by Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer.</note> and after him by Felinus in the chapter *Ne initiaris* at the end of the section on constitutions. There, Felinus says that this Gloss was approved by Ludovicus Romanus in his legal commentaries.

However, the <term>Archdeacon</term> <note>Guido de Baysio, a prominent commentator on Canon Law.</note> in the said final chapter of Distinction 20—and after him the Provost and Geminianus—state that when a written text is found to be contradictory or doubtful, one must recur to the Greek language. This is understood according to those times when the integrity of the Catholic faith flourished among the Greeks. But since today they are "headless" <note>original: "acephali"—likely referring here to the Great Schism, meaning they are without the "head" of the Church (the Pope) or lack proper leadership.</note> and their copies are corrupted and full of errors, one should not recur to their volumes. Indeed, it is not likely that those who do not sincerely hold the unity of the Catholic faith would have preserved the integrity of their volumes; rather, they likely corrupted them out of hatred for the Latins (who are the unshakable observers of the faith’s unity). For adversaries and enemies lie easily, as noted in the legal texts where many concordances agree in the commentary on inquiries.

Albericus de Rosate, in his first Constitution and in his dictionary under the word "Language" <note>original: "lingua"</note>, says that among all languages, three are most excellent: namely Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. Of these, Greek is said to be the clearest and most resonant. Its variety is discerned in five parts: the first is called "Mixed" or "Common"; the second, "Athenian," which the Greek authors used; the third, that which the Egyptians and Syrians have; the fourth, "Ionic"; and the fifth, "Aeolic." Or otherwise: one is called Attic, another Boeotian, the third Aeolic, the fourth Doric, the fifth...

<margin>judicial:</margin> How much the Greek language surpasses the Latin is written by <term>Budé</term> <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a famous French humanist scholar.</note> in his treatise *On the As and its Parts*, book one, folio 7. Indeed, it is said there are four types of the Latin language: first, the **Ancient** <note>original: "prisca"</note>, which is the oldest form used by the people of Italy under Janus and Saturn; second, the **Latin** <note>original: "Latina"</note>, used by the Italians from the time of King Latinus and other kings of Tuscany, in which the <term>Law of the Twelve Tables</term> <note>The earliest code of Roman law, dating to the 5th century BCE.</note> was written; third, the **Roman** <note>original: "Romana"</note>, which the Roman people used after the expulsion of the Kings; and fourth, the **Mixed** <note>original: "mixta"</note>, which took hold in the city after the Empire had expanded, along with new customs and people, corrupting the integrity of speech through <term>solecisms</term> <note>Grammatical mistakes.</note> and <term>barbarisms</term> <note>The use of non-standard or foreign words.</note>.

All Eastern peoples clash their words in the throat, such as the Hebrews and Syrians. Mediterranean nations produce their speech in the palate, such as the Greeks and Asians. Westerners, however, break their words against the teeth, such as the Italians and Spanish. I would add that the Northerners and Germans form their words in the chest; we French, however, use the throat, palate, and chest. Hence it is commonly said: **the Italians bleat like goats, the Germans howl, the French sing, and the English shout for joy.** <note>original: "Itali caprisant, Alemani ululant, Galli cantant, & Angli iubilant."</note> This is also stated by Albericus in the place cited below, who says he found in the authentic scriptures on Genesis and in the *Inventory of the Entire World* (in the section on the building of the Tower) the reason for the diversity of languages. <term>Isidore</term> <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential scholar and encyclopedist.</note> says the same in his book *Etymologies*, noting that the speech of the Greeks is more elegant than the others, as I mentioned above. <term>William Durand</term> <note>A 13th-century liturgical writer.</note> in his *Rationale of the Divine Offices* says that the Hebrew language is the mother of all languages because of the Law. The Greek language is the **Teacher**, and the Latin language is the **Interpreter**, owing to the dominion of the Roman Empire and the Papacy. Therefore, it is said that Hebrew was the mother of all tongues, for before the pride of the Tower of Babylon divided them, there was one language for all nations, as held in Genesis 11: "And the earth was of one tongue and of the same speech." And again the Lord says: "Behold, they are one people, and they all have one tongue." Because of that sin, seventy entirely different languages were introduced (as discussed below in the 69th distinction regarding famous towers). Whence Remigius says regarding the passage in 1 Corinthians 14, "languages shall cease": just as before the Tower of Babel there was one Hebrew tongue, so some doctors believe that after the Judgment, that same one shall remain. Thus, as I said, there is variety in many languages, and where there is variety, there is dissention; but in the kingdom of the saints, there will be no dissention, and therefore no variety of languages. Likewise, Bernard says that although many know many things, there will be one language for all: an unwearied shouting for joy, one affection, eternal love; and there will be a common omnipotence, wisdom, peace, justice, and intelligence for all. In that peace, there will be no diversity of tongues. Yet, it is a gift to use different languages, as the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 14: "I thank my God that I speak in the tongues of you all," and the Apostles spoke in various tongues in Acts 2. Regarding the praise of this Hebrew language, see more in the *Margarita Philosophica* <note>An early encyclopedia from 1503 by Gregor Reisch.</note> in the section on Hebrew instruction, where he praises it for its antiquity and priority, since it preceded all others in purity, holiness, abundance of meaning, and utility, excelling all others most elegantly. And Isidore says in his first book of *Etymologies* that the Greek letters, along with their names, were taken from the characters of the Hebrews, just as **A** comes from **Aleph**...
