...[A]leph, Alpha, a, and so on for several others. It is held as an indubitable truth, and certain among nearly all, that the Latin language gushed forth from Greek sources. Whether this is entirely true, I have discussed above in this part, in the 17th consideration, where Gaul is praised for its tradition of letters.

Brother Brochard <note>Burchard of Mount Sion, a German Dominican friar and traveler.</note>, a monk living in the year of salvation 1283, wrote in his description of the places of the Holy Land that in his time, the following peoples and nations were found in Jerusalem and in the Holy Land:

> In the Land of Promise, there are men from every nation under heaven, and each people lives according to their own way of life. And, to speak the truth to our great shame, none in that land are found to be worse or more corrupt in their morals than the Christians. I believe the reason for this is as follows: When someone in Spain, France, Germany, Italy, or other Christian nations has been caught as a criminal—be it a murderer, bandit, thief, incestuous person, adulterer, fornicator, or traitor—and fears that the judge will impose a punishment worthy of his crime, he flees and moves to the Holy Land. It is as if he intends to wipe away the evil he committed; but when he arrives there, he has changed his location, not his soul. Thus, what is written has happened to him: *Can the Ethiopian change his skin?* <note>A reference to Jeremiah 13:23, implying that a change of scenery does not change a person's inherent nature.</note> There are not a few such men in the Holy Land today, who rob pilgrims and their own countrymen who turn to them in good faith, suspecting no evil from them. These detestable fathers leave behind even more detestable sons, who trample the holy places with polluted feet, and by their wicked lives, they cause the holy things of God to fall into great contempt.
>
> Besides the Christians in the Land of Promise, there are also various other peoples, especially the **Saracens** <note>original: "Saraceni"; a term used by medieval Europeans for Muslims.</note>, who preach Muhammad and observe his law. They also recognize Christ as a great Prophet, conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, but they deny that he suffered and died; rather, they say that when it pleased him, he ascended into heaven. They say he sits at the right hand of the Father as a Son. But they say Muhammad sits at the left hand of God, and that he was sent only to them as God's messenger. These followers of Muhammad are greatly addicted to impurity, and they take as many wives as they can feed, in addition to being defiled by the vice of Gomorrah <note>original: "Gomorrhaico fœdati sunt vitio"; a historical euphemism for sodomy or homosexual acts.</note>. Yet they are hospitable and sufficiently humane, a fact I have experienced for myself more than once. For a small service shown to them, they return a generous reward.
> 
> Furthermore, in this land there are **Syrians**, who are indeed Christians, but they keep no faith with the **Latins** <note>original: "Latinis"; here referring to the Roman Catholic Church and Western Europeans.</note>. They live miserably and poorly; devoted to greed, they grant alms to no one. The wealthiest among them lives no more delicately than the poorest. They live among the Saracens and for the most part are bound to their service. In their dress, they differ almost not at all from the Saracens, except that they distinguish themselves by a woolen belt.
> 
> The **Greeks** are likewise Christians, but they are schismatics and estranged from obedience to the Roman Church. They are also entangled in many other errors—may God grant that many follies have not also crept in among the Latins. Among the Greeks, almost all the prelates are monks and practice great abstinence; they are held in great reverence and honor by the common people.
>
> There are also in this land Armenians, Georgians, Nestorians, and Nubians...

<note>original: "labeani"</note> Jabeans, Chaldeans, Maronites, Ethiopians, Egyptians, and many other nations, all of whom indeed confess Christ and have their own Patriarchs. Some are heretics <note>In the medieval Catholic view, "heretic" applied to any group that disagreed with Roman dogma, such as the nature of Christ's divinity.</note> and have taken their names from the founders of their sects, such as the Nestorians, Jacobites, and the like. Yet there are many among these sects who are quite simple, knowing nothing of these heresies; they are devoted to Christ, mortifying their flesh with fasts and wearing the simplest of garments, so that they even far surpass the religious orders of the Roman Church in their devotion.

The Nubians and Jabeans say that they, or rather their ancestors, received the faith from Saint Matthew and were baptized by him. They claim to have received their manner of baptism from him, which they strive to keep inviolable today, relying on this authority: *He shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire* <note>original: "Ipse vos baptizabit in Spiritu sancto & igne," a reference to Matthew 3:11.</note>. For when they are baptized, they brand a cross onto their face or another part of the body with a hot iron, and these are considered the most devout among the Eastern peoples.

There is also the nation of the Midianites, who are now called Bedouins and Turonians, who have filled a large part of the Holy Land. These people devote themselves solely to raising livestock and camels, of which they have an exceeding abundance. They have no fixed dwelling place, but where they find good pastures, they stay there with their tents for as long as it takes for the grass to be grazed, until they are forced to seek another place for their flocks. They are a very warlike people and have filled all of Syria; they have particularly occupied the banks of the Jordan from Lebanon all the way to the desert of <term>Pharan</term> <note>The Wilderness of Paran, a location mentioned in the Bible as a place where the Israelites spent time during the Exodus.</note>. The mountains beyond the Jordan provide the best fodder for sheep, goats, and other cattle. They have rams and wethers so thick and fat that a single tail is enough for three or four men to eat.

The Nestorians live around Beirut and Byblos in the plains of Lebanon toward Iturea.

The Maronites, however, have occupied the region around the "fountain of the gardens" <note>A poetic or local name for a spring near Tripoli.</note> descending from Lebanon toward Tripoli, and they are said to have forty thousand fighting men.

Furthermore, around the fortress of Arcas <note>A Crusader-era castle near Tripoli.</note> past Tripoli live the Saracens who are called Vanni. Associated with them are the Saracens whom they call the <term>Assassins</term> <note>The OCR text uses "Asininos," likely a corruption or pejorative variation of "Hashshashin."</note>, living in the mountains as far as the fortress of Antaradus, possessing many castles and towns and occupying very fertile land. These are said to have originated from Persia, and they have increased so much in number that they are claimed to be able to produce forty thousand armed men. A few years ago, they wished to submit themselves to Roman obedience <note>That is, to convert to Roman Catholicism.</note>, but they were hindered by the Templars and withdrew from their purpose. No Sultan has yet been able to bring these Assassins to order, but they establish their own laws and rights for themselves, using them as they please; they are a terror to all neighboring nations because of their ferocity.

And since I have touched upon these Eastern nations here, it did not seem useless to make more extensive mention of them. For today there are many who, while knowing nothing, wish to know everything, asserting that no Christians are found in these vast regions all the way to India, but that the treacherous Muhammad has defiled all places. This is not true; rather, Christ has his worshippers everywhere in the world, except in Arabia and Egypt, where Christians are rarely found, but almost everyone there has given their name to Muhammad. It is indeed true that all Christians across the sea—namely the Armenians, Cappadocians, Greeks, Chaldeans, Medes, Parthians, Indians, Nubians, Jabeans, Asians, Georgians, and the rest of the Eastern peoples—are not men accustomed to war. Rather, when they are attacked in war by Saracens, Turks, or Tartars <note>The author uses "Tartars" to refer to the Mongols, who dominated much of Asia during this period.</note>, they become their tributaries and allow them every dominion, enduring the tax collectors, provided that they can preserve peace and harmony as far as it lies within them. From this, it happens that those regions which Christians inhabit are thought to belong to the Saracens and to be subject to their treachery, even though almost everyone there is Christian. I experienced this myself in Cilicia <note>original: "Cicilia," a common medieval misspelling of Cilicia in Southern Turkey.</note> and Lesser Armenia, which are subject to the prince of the Tartars; nevertheless, they are purely Christian. They inhabit those regions, frequenting churches, hearing Masses, kneeling, and praying devoutly. They also show great honor to religious persons, which I experienced myself when I stayed there for some time. Furthermore, those whom we judge to be condemned heretics—such as the Nestorians, Jacobites, Maronites, Georgians, and the like—I found for the most part to be good and simple men, living sincerely toward God and men. They practice great abstinence, and during Lent they eat neither fish nor oil. They listen attentively to the word of God, as I saw on the evening of Palm Sunday, when they flocked to the sermon in great crowds. Moreover, they have their own Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, and other prelates, except for the Nestorians, who in place of the Pope have a prelate whom they call the *Iacelichum* <note>original: "Iacelichum," a Latinization of the Syriac "Qatoliqa" or Catholicos, the title for the head of the Church of the East.</note>, whom a great part of the East obeys.

->Truly the Armenians and Georgians have prelates whom they call Catholicos,<-
who have under them Archbishops, Bishops, and other prelates. These men lead the people by their excellent way of life, teaching them equally by word and example. And although they inhabit very well-fortified castles and possess great wealth, they nonetheless dress in cheap and dirty clothes with very wide sleeves. Their outer garment is a coarse and red sheepskin, and beneath it they wear a gray and worn tunic. Their topmost garment is a black scapular, cheap and rough like haircloth. I also attended their sacred rites once on the Day of the Annunciation, and I noticed that they use almost the same ceremonies and prayers as we do in the Mass, except that they use their own language and not the Roman one. Note also that the Catholicos himself and all other prelates are Monks, and no one except Monks is admitted to these ecclesiastical offices. The secular clergy and priests, however, have almost no authority and do nothing else except celebrate the divine offices. At all hours they give the signal with a wooden board <note>A "semantron," a wooden or metal plank struck with a mallet, used in Eastern Christianity instead of bells.</note>, for they do not have bells; and then they rise at night for morning prayers, waking one another so that all may gather. Nor do they go back to sleep after those short prayers are finished, but they sit in the church teaching the people until dawn. All priests are married, and no one is permitted to perform the office of a priest unless he has a legitimate wife. They celebrate Masses only on Saturday and the Lord's Day; on the remaining days of the week, they devote themselves to their wives <note>original: "amplexibus vacant," literally "they are free for embraces."</note>. However, if his wife dies, the priest shall remain continent and cannot marry another wife. If he commits fornication or adultery, he loses his office and his church without any hope of recovery. When a priest dies, his widow must remain continent, and if she presumes to enter into another marriage, she shall be burned; however, if she chooses to live as a prostitute, she suffers no harm, and this often happens among them. This seems to me the primary reason why so many prostitutes are found in those lands; for the wives of such priests, being unwilling to remain continent, become prostitutes. Thieves committing a theft that is not very harmful, and other malefactors who have not deserved death, are castrated, so that they do not father sons who might imitate their father's character. I know that when I was with the King of Armenia, the Queen had more than sixty Eunuchs. When the Bishop performs the service, he has his ministers standing by him—such as the deacon, subdeacon, and acolyte—and he celebrates the accustomed ceremonies with great gravity.

A certain ancient Spanish author has written the following regarding this matter.

Even assuming that the greatest and truest Christendom is in Europe, under our mother the Holy Roman Church, one does not fail to find Christians in all parts of the world, or in the greater part of it. Kingdoms, Cities, & Islands: such as Sumatra <note>original: "Samotre"</note>, Taprobane, Ceylon <note>original: "Zeylan"</note>, Borneo, & the Molucca Islands—from whence come the spices—& several other large and small islands, in which live a great number of Christians, both Portuguese and locals, who by their means have been converted to the Christian faith. Thus, there is a great likelihood that they will go to meet and join with the Christianity that I told you exists in the provinces subject to the **Great Khan**, since they are already arriving so close to them; this will be a great increase for Christendom. Everyone knows that the Christian faith has a place in the Armenias: for in Greater Armenia almost everyone is Christian, and in Lesser Armenia, the majority are. There are also Christians in Syria and in Egypt, where even today the relics or remains of ancient Christianity reside. I well believe that in many other places there are Christians of whom we have no knowledge because they are too far removed from us. I have read in the histories of the Portuguese that when the **Island of Socotra** <note>original: "Zocatore", an island off the coast of Yemen.</note> was found, all its inhabitants were Christians; but of such a sort that they knew nothing other than to worship a cross, because God made man had suffered death upon it. Otherwise, they had few commandments: for the principal one among them was to keep the **law of nature** <note>In medieval thought, the "law of nature" refers to a basic moral sense of right and wrong shared by all humans, even without formal religious instruction.</note>, and they called themselves by the names of the Apostles and other Saints. And know that between those mountains <note>likely referring to the mountains of Lebanon or the Caucasus</note> on one side and the other live many Christians of many and various kinds, and of many names, and all are baptized and have different laws and different customs; but all believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. However, they all usually fail in certain articles of the law. Some are named **Jacobites** because John the Evangelist <note>Medieval writers often confused the Jacobite sect (Syriac Orthodox) with the Apostle James or John; the name actually derives from the 6th-century bishop Jacob Baradaeus.</note> baptized them, and they say that one should make confession to God alone, and not to man, for one should admit guilt to God. Against this, they have strongly erred, because he [God] has not ordained to do any ill according to what the Prophets described to us; as they say, one should not confess to any other but God, just as Moses wrote it in the Bible, and for this reason David said in the Psalter: **I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart** <note>original Latin: "Confitebor tibi Domine in toto corde meo"</note>. In another place: **[I acknowledged] my sin... and I will confess to you** <note>original Latin: "delictum meum & confitebor tibi"</note>. ->*On Greek Christians.*<-

The Greek Christians of today occupy a greater extent of territory than the Christians of the Latin and Roman Church. These Greeks, being separated and divided from those of the Roman Church, have chosen another way of life quite different from the Latin one. ### Of the Patriarchs of the Greeks.

There are four Patriarchs among the Greeks of the Eastern Church: the first and principal is he of Constantinople, the second he of Jerusalem, the third he of Cairo <note>Though titled "of Alexandria," the Patriarch often resided in Cairo during this period</note>, and the fourth he of Antioch. These four Patriarchs have great power over the Greeks, even though they are not very wealthy: for the total income each has for annual living amounts to only two hundred crowns <note>original: "efcus"; the Ecu was a gold coin</note>. Each of them has a certain territory under his rule and Ecclesiastical government: he of Constantinople has the land of Candia <note>Crete</note>, Chios, and all the Greeks of the Empire of Constantinople as far as Philippopolis, and all the land of Athens and of Anatolia <note>original: "Natolie"</note>. He of Jerusalem has all the land of Cyprus and Judea, with the greater part of Galilee. He of Cairo has the land of Egypt, Alexandria, Africa, and other surrounding lands. He of Antioch has the land of Syria, Greater and Lesser Armenia as far as Persia. These aforementioned Patriarchs are elected and elevated to this office of leadership as very elderly men bearing great white beards; furthermore, they possess such honorable gravity and such sweetness of face that they move men to honor them. You will perhaps ask me why the said Patriarch and the common people hate us Christians of the Latin Church so much and do not wish to follow our law? We answer you that they claim to be the first converted to the faith and are totally convinced that we others have added to the Gospel. They err in several points: for in the first place they perform the Supper <note>The Eucharist</note> and communicate under the form of leavened bread, and give the bread separately. Likewise at Easter, both great and small receive under two species <note>Both bread and wine</note>: which Pope Julius, writing to the Bishops of Egypt, reproved, along with several other ceremonies observed by them in various parts. They take no account of the Sacraments of the Catholic Church and pay them no reverence; indeed, if some priest celebrates the Mass upon their altars in the Latin fashion, once the Mass is said, they wash the said altars as if they were polluted and unclean, and as if we Latins were excommunicated. Furthermore, they say, like the Arian heretics <note>The author compares the Greek rejection of certain Roman doctrines to Arianism, a 4th-century heresy</note>, that the good we do for the deceased, such as fasts, alms, prayers, and other intercessions <note>original: "fuffrages"</note>, are in no way profitable to them. And they are also of the opinion, and even affirm, that there is no purgatory, which a well-born Christian will never grant: for that there is a purgatory is an opinion

### *Of the East Indian Christians.*

Ancient histories, according to the testimony of Saint Gregory Nazianzen in his *Oration against the Arians* <note>original: "Oraison contre les Arrians"</note> and Saint Gregory the Great in his 17th *Homily on the Gospel*, record that although the Indians had Saint Thomas as their Apostle—and though he is currently the patron of the Christians in the Orient—apostolic history nevertheless confirms (according to the words of Abdias of Babylon in book 8 of the *Apostolic History*) that Saint Bartholomew also carried the Gospel to the Indies. It is held that he arrived there before Saint Thomas and suffered martyrdom there. However, since the aforementioned Abdias describes three distinct regions of India <note>Medieval geographers often divided the vast East into "Three Indias": India Major, India Minor, and Middle India (sometimes including parts of Ethiopia or Arabia)</note> in the passage cited above, it is not impossible that two Apostles were employed there, as the commission was great and important, requiring two great leaders to accomplish it well. Furthermore, after the Apostles, there were also other figures who carried the word of God to the Indians, who had strayed from the true doctrine learned from the Apostles. Thus, in the time of the Emperor Commodus, there was a holy person named Pantenus <note>Pantenus was a Stoic philosopher who became the head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria</note> who, having withdrawn from the Stoic sect to Christianity and being the principal regent of the school of Alexandria in Egypt, was ordained to announce the word of God to the Eastern regions. This is testified by Saint Jerome in his book *On Illustrious Men* <note>original: "des hommes illustres"</note> and Eusebius in book 5, chapter 10 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. They assert that in these Indies, this holy person found the Gospel of Saint Matthew (which had been received there before he arrived) in the hands of some who made profession of Christianity in those countries. It appears that this Gospel was announced to those Indians by the aforementioned Saint Bartholomew, who left it written in Hebrew letters and language, and it was preserved until the time mentioned above when Pantenus was in India. He notes that many Christians lived there and that the Indians held this Apostle to be a great Prophet, calling him *Avariiam* <note>original: "Auariiam"</note>, which means "holy man" in the Indian language. Joseph the Indian <note>a 15th-century Indian Christian priest who traveled to Europe</note>, in book 2, chapter 142 of his voyages, confirms these last words of Marco Polo, saying further that the temple where the body of this Blessed Apostle lies is similar to that of Saint John and Saint Paul in the city of Venice. John Mandeville, in his travels, speaks of this quite extensively. Duarte Barbosa <note>original: "Odouard Barboffe"</note>, a Portuguese writer, in his work on India, writes these words regarding this fact: "Moving a little away from the city of Quilon <note>original: "Coulan"; modern-day Kollam in Kerala, India</note> in the East Indies, one sees a point of land extending into the sea, upon which sits a beautiful and large church in honor of Saint Thomas. It was built because of a miracle he performed there before dying, which the Christians of the country told me they had described in their books, which they keep and honor with great reverence. And the miracle is this: That the Holy Apostle, finding himself in the city of Quilon very poorly dressed among the crowd of citizens who were heathens and idolaters, sought to win over the people and draw them to the faith of Jesus Christ, having with him some natives of the country whom he had converted and baptized..."

One morning, then, as he was preaching, a large piece of wood was seen appearing at sea, which came to rest against the shore. The King wanted to have it and commanded that by the strength of men and elephants it be brought to land, but it was impossible to move it. The King, annoyed by this, came himself in person, thinking that his presence would further encourage the people, but they gained nothing by it. Seeing this, the holy Apostle, and noting that the King was distressed at being unable to have this wood, said to him: "Sire, will you grant me this favor, if I bring this wood onto the land, that you give me as much land as I shall need to build a temple in honor of my Lord the true God, who made heaven and earth, by whose command I have set out?" The King, looking at this poor man, said to him: "And how could you provide for this, since all my forces could not suffice?" "With the help of the great God whom I announce, I am confident I can pull it to shore, for He is stronger than you and all other men." The King had the land he requested measured and delivered to him, and Saint Thomas, approaching the floating wood, tied it with a cord and belt <note>This refers to the traditional legend where Saint Thomas moves a massive log—intended for a royal palace—using only his priest’s girdle, proving his divine mission.</note>, and pulled it easily toward the place designated for the building of the Church. The King was greatly astonished by this, but nevertheless did not wish to become a Christian. The Apostle used this wood for the construction of the Church, and it sufficed for everything that was necessary there, not without the wonder of everyone. Once the Church was completed, the King gave him a certain income from the pepper produced in the country of Coulan <note>Modern-day Kollam (Quilon) in Kerala, a major center of the ancient spice trade.</note>, which the Christians of Saint Thomas enjoy to this day in memory of such a miracle.

In the end, this King persecuted the Apostle, who, following the command of God, retired elsewhere and went to the Region of Choromandel <note>The Coromandel Coast, the southeastern coast of the Indian subcontinent.</note>, and to the city of Malabar, or Maliapur <note>Mylapore, now a neighborhood in Chennai, traditionally held as the site of Saint Thomas’s death.</note>, where he was killed and martyred, and where his tomb is shown to this day. This is what the aforementioned Armenians still do today, according to the testimony of Manuel Acosta <note>Manuel da Costa (1541–1604), a Jesuit who wrote about the missions in the East.</note>, a Jesuit, in his *Commentaries on the Indies*. Therefore, according to the aforementioned Barbosa <note>Duarte Barbosa (c. 1480–1521), a Portuguese explorer whose writings provided early European accounts of India.</note>, it was in the city of Malabar or Maliapur that this Saint Thomas was martyred. After those of Coulan had (as we have said) persecuted him, he retired to the said Malabar or Maliapur, where, beginning to preach, he made a singular profit, drawing many to the knowledge of the Gospel. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF #

...[he] is no longer in the Indies, inasmuch as his disciples, stealing him away, carried him to the city of Edessa in Mesopotamia; though it is well said, he says, that the tomb remains there, and that from its earth, King Mazdai <note>original: "Mesdee"; a king in Indian tradition associated with the martyrdom of St. Thomas</note>—who had put the Apostle to death—took a small amount and placed it around the neck of his son, who was possessed by a devil, and he immediately received healing.

Osorius <note>Jerónimo Osório (1506–1580), a Portuguese historian known as the "Portuguese Cicero"</note> in book 4 of the *History of Portugal*, and several other modern travelers and navigators, have left in writing that the sepulcher of this holy personage was searched for near the city of Coromandel, by the command of King Manuel of Portugal given to Duarte de Meneses <note>original: "Eduard de Meneses"</note>, his Viceroy in the Indies. In executing this, the aforementioned Duarte commanded Emanuel Frias, Governor of the said city, to carry out this search. Complying with this, he traveled with Priests and Architects toward Mylapore <note>original: "Maliapur"</note>, to a place filled with the ruins of many beautiful and ancient buildings. Among these was found a rather ruined temple, in which, within a very old and ancient stone tomb, were seen the bones of this holy personage, and the iron tip of a lance with a piece of a walking staff, and an earthen vessel. These bones were placed in a silver shrine within the aforementioned temple, which was then repaired by the Portuguese, and later transported with great pomp and magnificence to the city of Goa, as Father Pierre du Jarric of Toulouse <note>A Jesuit historian (1566–1617) who wrote about missions in the East Indies</note> deduces at length in book 2.

He states that if one opposes this history with the authority of the ecclesiastical histories of Rufinus (book 2, ch. 5), Socrates (book 4, ch. 14), and Sozomen <note>Three major historians of the early Christian Church</note> (book six, chapter eighteen), as well as the Martyrologies—specifically the Roman one, which places on the 3rd of July the translation of the body of this holy personage from the city of Calamine in India to Edessa in Mesopotamia, and from there to the city of Ortona <note>original: "Orthone"</note>, which is in the Apulia <note>original: "Appouille"</note> region of Italy—one must first say what Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>original: "D. Halicarnasse"; an ancient Greek historian</note> replied to those who marveled at seeing several sepulchers for the same souls <note>original: "Ames"; likely a reference to the many "tombs of Aeneas" discussed by Dionysius</note>. Being certain that his body was in only one of them, he said that this is a common and vulgar doubt, especially regarding those who were illustrious personages and who traveled through many countries. This is because empty monuments <note>The author is referring to cenotaphs—monuments erected to honor someone whose remains are elsewhere</note> were erected in several places, either in recognition of some good deed received from them in those lands, or because some relics of their lineage remained, or because they stayed there for a long time and showed themselves to be humane and kind toward their hosts.

The same can be answered if one did not know that these monuments or sepulchers were not entirely empty of the relics of this Holy Personage; rather, since the translation of these relics is celebrated, it is necessary to confess that some were there. Thus, it is better to say, along with the learned Baronius <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a giant of Catholic ecclesiastical history</note> in his *Roman Martyrology* for July 3rd, that the transport of a portion of the relics—not only of the said Apostle, but also of several other Saints—has given occasion for some to think that their bodies were in several places. This is not because, in fact, all the relics of the same Saint are in different places, but because one part is in one, and another in another. Very often, a part is taken for the whole by a very frequent figure of speech called <term>Synecdoche</term> <note>A rhetorical device where a part represents the whole, or vice versa; here, a single bone might be called "the body of the Saint"</note>.

<summary>This page addresses the conflicting historical accounts regarding the location of Saint Thomas the Apostle's remains, explaining that while his body was reportedly found by the Portuguese in India, various traditions and "empty monuments" (cenotaphs) led to claims of his burial in Mesopotamia and Italy.</summary>

Now, that the relics of Saint Thomas have been dispersed in several places is testified by Saint Chrysostom <note>Saint John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> in a Homily that he gave in praise of the said Apostle. In that of Saint Thomas, which is the 14th, Saint Chrysostom speaks these words: "The relics of the righteous man (speaking of this Saint) have surpassed the earth; he has shown himself more ample, and has extended further than any other created thing; grace has spread him throughout the whole world. Many other things worthy of note in this history are treated in *Osorius* <note>Jerónimo Osório, a 16th-century Portuguese historian.</note>, book 3 of his histories; *João de Barros* in his 3rd decade of *Asia*; *Pietro Maffei* in the 12th book of his history of the *Indies*; the author of the *History of China*, part 2, book three; *André Thevet*, book eleven, chapter eighteen of his *Universal Cosmography*; and in *Father Gaspar Zelandois* in his *Indian Epistle of the year 1553*.

To be brief, the Indian and Oriental Christians are as follows: Their temples are built like ours, except that there is no image or figure in them, save only for the cross, which is placed everywhere very large and high. All the Indian Christians hold this in honor and reverence. Those who wish to be appointed to the dignity of Bishop must go as far as their <term>Catholicos</term> <note>The title of the patriarch or head of the Church of the East.</note> who is in Armenia <note>The author likely refers to the Patriarch in Mesopotamia, though "Armenia" was often used broadly in this period for the region.</note>. This leader attributes to himself the power to consecrate Bishops, against the authority of the Holy Apostolic See, calling himself—falsely—the substitute of Saint Peter, and holding the place of the Patriarch of Antioch, wearing a crown in the shape of a cross. These Indian Christians do not baptize their children until forty days after their birth, unless they see in them an extreme necessity due to the threat of death. They confess as we do and receive the holy sacrament, which they consecrate if possible with unleavened bread, just as the Catholics do here. Having no wine because their country does not produce it, they use <term>currants</term> <note>original: "raisins de Corinthe"</note>, which they soak in water to extract a substance that they use in place of wine. They do not use holy unction for the sick, but instead pray over the patient and give them a blessing. They use holy water as we do and pray for the deceased. They have the four Evangelists with their Gospels, observe Lent and Advent by fasting and praying during them, and perform and keep many other fine and great Christian ceremonies concerning the service of God and His Church. They make use of both the Old and New Testaments, according to the interpretation of their doctors, both ancient and modern, as described more particularly by *Marco Polo the Venetian* in book three, chapters twenty-eight and twenty-nine of his travels; *Joseph the Indian* in book two, chapters 132, 133, and 134 of his navigations; *Alvise Cadamosto* in book two of his navigations, chapters fifty-six, 57, and fifty-eight; and *Ludovico di Varthema*, book 6, chapter...

1. and 14. of his *Navigations*; Duarte Barbosa <note>A Portuguese writer and officer in Portuguese India between 1500 and 1516.</note> in his book on the Indies in the chapter on the Kingdom of Quilon; Osório <note>Jerónimo Osório (1506–1580), a Portuguese historian.</note> in books 3 and 4 of his *History of Portugal*; André Thevet in the place cited above in his *Cosmography*; Emmanuel Acosta in his *Commentaries on the Brothers of the Society of Jesus*; and the aforementioned Father du Jarric throughout his two books of the *History of the East Indies*. One of their Bishops, from the "Island of Pepper" <note>likely referring to the Malabar Coast of India, famous for pepper production</note> located in the East Indies, came on their behalf to Rome to Pope Gregory XIII to offer obedience to the Holy See on November 24, 1584, and to learn from His Holiness if he would wish and intend for them to continue receiving the Bishops sent by their aforementioned Patriarch, as is confirmed by the *History of China*, parts 2 and 3. On this subject, Gilbert Génébrard <note>A French Benedictine exegete and orientalist.</note> writes in book 4 of his *Cosmography* for the year 1584: 

The Archbishop of Angamaly <note>original: "Angulianensis." Angamaly was the seat of the Saint Thomas Christians in Kerala, India.</note> in that part of India where the Christians of Saint Thomas are, requested from the Supreme Pontiff through the Jesuits the characters of the Chaldean or Syriac language, so that they might not only print their own books (for they celebrate the Mass and canonical prayers in that language or even in Hebrew <note>original: "vel etiam Hebraica." Early modern scholars often grouped Syriac/Aramaic and Hebrew together.</note>) but also translate our own works into that language. This is also noted by Emmanuel Teixeira in his *Epistles*.

Modern travelers assure us that the East Indians recognize that the first Christians among them were the inhabitants of the Island of Socotra, where the aforementioned Saint Thomas first preached and announced the Christian religion. They have had, and still have, temples and altars like ours from ancient times, which are decorated with nothing but crosses and have no images. On fasting days, which they observe very strictly, they abstain from eating anything; they marry only one wife; they observe the same feasts, and on the same days, as we Europeans do—even those of the saints—and they pay the full tithes of grains and fruits to their priests. However, they are still so ignorant, despite professing Christianity, that they do not understand a single word of the Christian religion, according to Osório in book 5 of his *History of Portugal* and Father Maffei <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei (1533–1603), a Jesuit historian.</note> in book 3 of his *History of the Indies*. In short, anyone wishing to report everything recorded about these East Indian Christians here would never be finished. Whoever wishes to see more should read André Thevet, book 11, chapter 18 of his *Cosmography*; then Escalante, chapter 16 of his *Narratives*; I. Acosta in his *Commentaries on the Brothers of the Society of Jesus*; Father Maffei, books 2 and 8 of his *History of the Indies*; Melchior Carneiro, a Jesuit, in his *Epistles*; the notices and *Epistles* of the Jesuit Fathers, and among others, those of Father Nunes from the years 1554, 1555, and 1558; of Father Quadros in the same year; and of Father Perez <note>transcribed as Eroez</note> from the year 1556; the letters of Fathers Pinnerus and Xavier, Jesuits, from August 20, from Lahore, the court of the Great Emperor of the Mughals <note>original: "Mogor." Referring to the Mughal Empire in India.</note> in the year 1595; and the aforementioned Father du Jarric in his books on the *History of the East Indies*.

### CHAPTER 53.

Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais (c. 1184–1264), author of the massive encyclopedia *Speculum Maius*.</note> in books 29 and 30 and Nauclerus <note>Johannes Nauclerus (1425–1510), a German historian.</note> in Volume 2, Generation 42, write that Pope Innocent IV, in the year of Salvation 1245, sent as an ambassador one Ascelin, a monk of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>, along with three others, to the Tatars <note>A historical term used here to describe the Mongol Empire.</note> and their King Baitho <note>likely referring to the Mongol commander Baiju or Batu Khan</note>, to induce them to embrace Christianity; however, they achieved nothing, and this pilgrimage lasted three years and seven months. It is certainly true that they reported having seen many Christians in Tartary, commanded by a Prince named Cuine <note>Güyük Khan, the third Great Khan of the Mongol Empire.</note>, who supported priests and clerics who celebrated and administered sacred and divine things, singing and performing psalms in the manner of the Greeks at certain hours prescribed for this purpose.

Around the year of Salvation 1245, the third Cham <note>Khan</note> or Emperor of the aforementioned Tatars, at the prayer and supplication of the King of the Armenians, was converted to the faith of Jesus Christ and was baptized, according to the report of Hayton the Armenian <note>Hethum of Korykos, a medieval chronicler and member of the Armenian royalty.</note> in his histories of the Tatars. This Khan afterwards undertook the defense of the Christians against the Saracens, having sent forces commanded by Hielon <note>Hulagu Khan, founder of the Ilkhanate.</note>, his brother, who subjugated Persia and a great part of Syria and Mesopotamia. In the year of Salvation 1258, this same man defeated and captured Muftacene <note>Al-Musta'sim Billah, the last Abbasid Caliph of Baghdad.</note>, the Caliph of Babylon <note>Baghdad was often called Babylon in medieval European texts.</note>, who had greatly afflicted and tormented the Christians, proposing various punishments for them under these insulting words from the Gospel: "Say to this mountain and it shall be moved" <note>original: "Dicite monti huic & transfertur". A reference to Matthew 17:20; the legend says the Caliph challenged the Christians to prove their faith by moving a mountain.</note>. Having shut him in a tower with all his treasures, he caused him to die of hunger among them. From that Caliph until the Sophy <note>The Safavid dynasty of Persia.</note>, the people of Persia had no sovereign Doctor of their law. For this reason, in the year of Salvation 1500, these people easily admitted the Sophy as the sovereign Doctor of their said law, tracing his origin and doctrine to Haly <note>Ali ibn Abi Talib</note>, the son-in-law of Mahomet <note>Muhammad</note>; this is confirmed by James Nauarchus in his *Asiatic Epistles*. At that time, while the Christians were in contention with the Egyptians over the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the aforementioned Hielon and Abfaga <note>Abaqa Khan</note>—in the same manner that Tamerlane <note>Timur the Lame</note> did a hundred years later—descended from Tartary into Syria, declaring themselves neither friends nor enemies. Following Pagan superstition, they made profession of neither Christianity nor Islam. Although they were summoned with gifts and presents from Baldwin <note>Baldwin II of Constantinople or perhaps a regional Latin ruler.</note> to embrace Christianity, they nevertheless preferred to follow Islam, according to Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician and historian.</note> in book 2 of *Illustrious Men*, in the chapter on Tamerlane. Saint Louis, King of France, arriving at the Island of Cyprus with his army to go on the conquest of the Holy Land in the year 1249, received Tatar Ambassadors sent to him by a Prince Erchaltans <note>Eljigidei, a Mongol commander.</note>, with letters by which he learned that three years previously the Tatars had made profession of the faith of Jesus Christ and had been baptized, as Gaguin <note>Robert Gaguin (1433–1501).</note> writes in book 7. A copy of the letters mentioned above is inserted in Vincent, book 13, chapter 91. The aforementioned Saint Louis also sent ambassadors to the aforementioned Erchaltans with letters from himself, by which the King prayed this Prince and the Great Khan to remain firm in the said faith of Jesus Christ; he sent him a tent or pavilion of purple made in the form of a chapel, in which with

...a singular art all the deeds and miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ, and others concerning the Christian Religion, as confirmed by the aforementioned Gaguin <note>Robert Gaguin (c. 1425–1501), a French Renaissance humanist and diplomat.</note> book 7, and Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais.</note> book 3, chapters 92 and 94.

Several Tatars came to the Council of Lyon to see Pope Innocent IV; having returned to their country, they made profession of Christianity and were baptized, as held by Biondo <note>Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), an Italian Renaissance humanist historian.</note> and Martin <note>Martin of Troppau (d. 1278), author of the *Chronicon Pontificum et Imperatorum*.</note> in his Chronicle; though it is true that some relate this to the time of Pope Gregory X, according to book 5, chapter 1 of the *Sacred History Continued*.

We read in the travels of Mr. Marco Polo, living in the year of Salvation 1275, that Niccolo, Marco, and Maffeo, Venetians, were sent with Khutughtu <note>originally: "Chotogalus"</note>, a great Tatar Lord, on behalf of Khubilai <note>originally: "Cabyla"</note>, 6th Khan or Emperor of the Tatars, to Pope Clement, to beseech him to send priests or doctors to teach him and his people the faith of Jesus Christ.

In the year 1290, Möngke Khan <note>originally: "Mangu Cam"</note>, 5th Emperor of the Tatars, was miraculously converted to Christianity by his wife, the daughter of Hethum <note>originally: "Haiton"</note>, King of Armenia, and was baptized with his brother Hulagu <note>originally: "Allan" or "Hielon"</note> and all his family. Shortly afterward, Hulagu descended with a great army into Palestine, causing a crucifix to be carried on his banners and standards like the Melkite Catholics <note>originally: "Cathes Melechinees"</note> in order to recover Jerusalem (Guillaume de Nangis). A short time later, these same Tatars returned to their former impiety; and since that time they have been Mahometans, or rather *Sagomorbates* <note>A corruption of "Shakyamuni," referring to Buddhism, which medieval writers sometimes confused with a sect of Islam or a distinct paganism.</note> because of *Sagomor-bar* their Prophet whom they worship, as the Saracens and Turks do Mahomet; this *Sagomor-bar* taught them many things concerning God, governance, and good morals, and among these an edict that the Great Khans of the Tatars, successors of Genghis Khan <note>originally: "Cingis Cham"</note>, swear at the beginning of their reign: not to afflict the Christians, nor to constrain them to pay a larger or more excessive tribute than their other subjects. The aforementioned Hulagu having defeated the Saracens in this same year of Salvation 1290, made himself the peaceful ruler of the kingdom of Syria and Jerusalem: but 3 years later the Sultan of Babylon reconquered it from him, as is contained in the continuation of Nangis and Sabellico <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506), an Italian historian.</note> Ennead 9, book 7.

In the year 1302, Ghazan <note>originally: "Cabagade"</note>, the Tatar King of Persia, having renounced the Christian faith, embraced Mahometism and made his subjects Alcoranists <note>Followers of the Quran.</note>; and from that time the Christian Religion was banished from among the Tatars. The Turks, having defeated the aforementioned Tatars under the leadership and power of Osman <note>originally: "Ottomā"</note> their first great lord, and the Parthians having defeated the successors of this same Ghazan, occupied Persia in the year 1350 under the leadership of Gepsar their Sultan. The rest of these Tatars divided into Hordes across Europe and Asia, each of which established a Prince for itself. For some settled in the Tauric Chersonese <note>The Crimean Peninsula.</note>, now called Gazaria, and those are called Perekopians <note>originally: "Precopites"</note>, whose Prince gave his daughter in marriage to Selim, father of the late Suleiman; others are called Nogais <note>originally: "Mogaues"</note>, who do not obey a single Prince but govern themselves in the form of a Republic, and from those proceeded the Horde of the Jagatais <note>originally: "Hagutaues"</note> or Zavolhenses, whose metropolitan city is Samarkand <note>originally: "Sinarcand"</note>, of which the great Tamerlane was a native.

Brother Antoine Geuffroy, knight of St. John of Jerusalem, in his treatise on the origin of the Turks, speaks otherwise of all the above, detailing at length the lives and conquests of the Great Khans of Tartary.

Marco Polo the Venetian, in Book 1, chapters 47, 49, 62, and 63 of his travels in Tartary <note>A historical name used by Europeans for the vast region of North and Central Asia, from the Caspian Sea to the Pacific Ocean, dominated by the Mongol Empire.</note>, asserts that in his time, Christians were found in many and various provinces and cities under the rule of the Great Khan of Tartary in Asia. These Christians were Nestorians <note>Members of the Church of the East, a branch of Christianity that spread widely across Asia along the Silk Road.</note>; he speaks of them further in the subsequent Book 2, chapter 61, and in the following Book 3, chapter 50, where he mentions certain other Tatar Christians whom he calls Nestorian Ruchenes <note>likely referring to the Rus' or Russians living under the Golden Horde.</note>.

Ludovico di Varthema <note>original: "Louys Vuactoman"</note>, a Roman Patrician, writes in Book 6, chapter 14 of his navigations that there are several Christians in Tartary who are subjects of the Great Khan of the Tatars. They are baptized (as we other Christians are), believe in the twelve Apostles and the four Evangelists, write in the manner of the Armenians, celebrate the Nativity, death, and passion of Jesus Christ, observe Lent and certain feasts of the Saints. This author says he spoke and conferred with these Christians who had arrived in the East Indies; they assured him that in their Tartary, there were several Christian kings near the borders of the Turkish Empire, called by some the Rumes <note>A term derived from "Rome," used in the East to refer to Christians or the Byzantine (Roman) Empire.</note>.

The histories of the Tatars according to Hayton the Armenian <note>Hethum of Korykos, a monk and historian from the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia who recorded the history of the Mongols.</note>, in Book 1 of his history of the Tatars, state that Möngke Khan <note>original: "Mangu Cham," the fourth Great Khan of the Mongol Empire.</note>, the Great Emperor of the Tatars, was the one who so greatly respected the Christian name. Solicited by Hayton, King of Armenia, in the year 1253, he willed that total liberty be granted to Christians throughout all his lands, and that none be so bold as to hinder them in the exercise of their religion. He received Baptism, though his successors cared little for it. He made a law for Christians stating that in all the lands the Tatars had conquered, and those they would conquer hereafter, they would swear to leave Christian Churches intact, and that both clergy and laypeople should live in total liberty, exempt from servitude, and without paying any tribute whatsoever, except according to the taxes imposed by the Kings upon the native inhabitants of Tartary. This law has benefited Christians so greatly that it is a marvel.

The Lord of Joinville <note>Jean de Joinville, the biographer and companion of King Louis IX of France.</note>, in chapter 19 of the life of Saint Louis, recounts this history differently, as reported by Nicolas Vignier in part 3 of his *Historical Library*, citing the book of John of Plano Carpini <note>original: "Iean Capin"</note> of the Order of the Cordeliers <note>The Franciscans.</note>, who was sent by Pope Innocent to this Khan; the book is titled *On the Origin, Manners, Ceremonies, Religion, and Manner of Warfare of the Tatars*.

Formerly, the Abyssinians <note>Ethiopians.</note> were those who once held the Indies under the Empire of their Prester John <note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles from the 12th to the 17th centuries.</note>, whom Genghis Khan <note>original: "Cingis Cham"</note> and his successors entirely drove out from there. By this means, the religion of the Indians—which was the superstition of the Gentiles, worshipping a plurality of gods—was lost, replaced by that of the Tatar who worshipped a single God and honored a certain Prophet of his nation named Sagomonbar <note>Likely a corruption of Shakyamuni (the Buddha), whom some early Western writers confused for a local Tatar prophet.</note>. However, the Christian race was not removed, except for those who were native Ethiopians. This is the reason why the Nestorians, Georgians, and Armenians still worship Jesus Christ there and celebrate the mysteries of our Religion. These Christians know nothing of the Councils celebrated in the Greek and Latin Churches; nevertheless, they hold to most of the ceremonies of the early Church, which was planted in those quarters by some Apostles or their disciples. The Tatar Kings and Princes still support more than ten million Christians today in those countries, who live according to the simplicity of the doctrine

Apostolic <note>Likely referring to the papal legates or missionaries sent from Rome.</note> envoys, who, when one confers with them, say and maintain that since the Easterners began to be divided on the matter of religion, and one believed one thing and another something else, there appeared soon after a Muhammad among the Arabs, a Sagomonbar <note>A corruption of Shakyamuni Burkan, referring to the Buddha.</note> among the Tartars, a Xaqua <note>Shaka, another name for the Buddha.</note> among the more Eastern Indians, a Xaholan among the Bengalis, an Ali <note>Haly</note> among the Persians, a Sharif <note>Cheriph</note> among the Africans, an Azelcon among the Asians, Comassan and Alxamath among the Cephaliens, and Kalmorath among the Abyssinians <note>Ethiopians</note>. These men, under the pretext of preaching the purity of doctrine and speaking of a single God, won over the whole Levant and gained the advantage over the divided Christians. It is held that one of the ancestors of the Great Khan of these Tartars, being asked why he did not become a Christian, since he was so fully informed of the excellence of our religion, replied: "How do you want me to do so, being surrounded as I am by subjects of diverse religions? If I became a Christian, and my ministers did not perform miracles and things as marvelous as those done by the priests and enchanters who serve our idols, I would be spinning the rope that would cause the end of my life." In short, this Tartar acts somewhat like a Christian when with Christians, and follows the Law of Moses or Judaizes with the Jews, and becomes an idolater with his own people; for he celebrates Christmas and Easter with the Christians, as well as other feasts common to them, and carries himself likewise with all the Muhammadans.

->See A. Theuet book 12, ch. 19 of his Universal Cosmography.<-

Hayton the Armenian, in Book 1, Chapter 2, of the Tartars, describing the kingdom of Tarsis <note>Likely referring to the Uighur Kingdom of Qocho.</note> toward Tartary, says that in this kingdom there are people called Iogours <note>Uighurs</note> who since ancient times have worshipped idols, except for ten generations or lineages of those three Kings who came, led by the celestial star, to worship our Lord Jesus Christ in the city of Bethlehem; and that in his time, there were still among the Tartars several great and noble personages of this race who held firmly to the faith of Jesus Christ. This same author in the subsequent Chapter 4 maintains that in his time, part of the inhabitants of the kingdom of Chorasmia <note>Khwarazm, in modern Uzbekistan/Turkmenistan.</note> toward the country of Turkestan were Christians living in the manner, fashion, and religion of the Greeks, and that they were called *Soldini*.

Sigismund Herberstein <note>original: "Sigismond Liber," referring to the author of Rerum Moscoviticarum Commentarii.</note>, in his history of the affairs of Muscovy, describing at length the Tartars and their countries and regions, says that moving from the East toward the South near the Meotide Marshes <note>The Sea of Azov.</note> and the Pontus <note>The Black Sea.</note>, toward the river Cupa which empties into the aforementioned marshes, are the Aphgases <note>Abkhazians</note>. Beyond them are found great mountains reaching to the river Merule, which discharges into the said Pontus; these mountains are inhabited by the Circassians <note>original: "Circasses ou Cikz"</note>, who obey neither the Turk nor the Tartars because their mountains are inaccessible. Rather, they are Christians living according to their own laws and according to the Greek religion, using the Slavonic language in their common speech and in the celebration of their divine service, as the *Ruthenians* <note>Ancestors of modern Ukrainians, Belarusians, and Russians.</note> assert.

Today, in the kingdom of Mangi <note>Southern China.</note>, currently subject to the Great Khan of Tartary, there is a city named Cinghianfu <note>Zhenjiang.</note>, inhabited by people who worship idols, in which there are two Christian churches, though they belong to the *Nestorians*. These were founded in the year 1274 by a man named Marfachis <note>Mar Sarghis, a Nestorian Christian official mentioned in the travels of Marco Polo.</note>, whom the Great Khan of Tartary had placed there as governor.

### Of the Jacobite Christians.

John Mandeville, an English Knight living in the year of salvation 1322, in his travels composed in the Romance language <note>original: "langue Romaneſque"; referring here to the vernacular French in which his famous (and often fantastical) travels were circulated</note>, in the chapter on the law of the Jacobins—that is to say, the Jacobites cited above—speaks ampy of these Jacobites and of their religion. Hayton the Armenian, in book 1, chapter 54 of his history of the Tartars, makes mention of certain Christians named Rapti <note>Possibly a corruption of "Copts"</note>, who lived in his time according to the manner, fashion, and religion of the Jacobites, and who boasted of being the oldest inhabitants of the land of Egypt. In this regard, one should see Leo Africanus <note>I. Leon</note>, book 8 of his *History of Africa*, speaking of Asyut <note>Aſioth</note>. The same Leo Africanus, in the aforementioned book 8, chapter on Alexandria in his same *History of Africa*, says these words regarding the aforementioned Jacobites: "There are in Alexandria, among its inhabitants, Christians called Jacobites, who have their church where the body of Saint Mark the Evangelist used to be, which the Venetians carried off by stealth <note>original: "d’em-blee"</note>, transporting it to their city of Venice. All these Jacobites make a living by trade or practice the arts, paying a certain tribute to the Lord of Great Cairo; in Elchian <note>Likely Al-Khanka, a city north of Cairo</note>, a city situated on the Nile, there are also some of these Jacobites." The author of the *Summary of Kingdoms, Cities, and Oriental Peoples* writes that near Susa <note>Suz</note> dwell certain Christian Arabs, some of whom are circumcised after the manner and fashion of the Jews, and others not; the circumcised being called Jacobites, and the others Melkites <note>original: "Malaquiti"; the Melkites were Middle Eastern Christians who remained in communion with the Byzantine Emperor</note>, who observe two Lents, one at Christmas and the other at Easter as we do. Most of them are hermits and persons of holy life; the others trade at El-Tor <note>Tor, a port on the Sinai Peninsula</note>, Jeddah <note>Zidem</note>, and Mecca, and are held and reputed by all to be men of good character and conscience. Jacques de Vitry, in his *History of Jerusalem*, chapter 37, writes that in the year of salvation 1171, there were a great number of these Jacobites, who were not only scattered throughout Syria, but also through India and Ethiopia, who still retained circumcision along with baptism, as do the Saracens. They confessed their sins to God alone and imprinted a mark of fire <note>a ritual brand or tattoo</note> on the foreheads of their children. André Thevet <note>A. Theuet</note>, in book 11, chapter 18 of his *Universal Cosmography*, says these words about these Jacobites:

"The Christians who live here and there, scattered through the Indies, and who are at the sepulcher of Saint Thomas, are for the most part Jacobites—a people who differ in belief and ceremonies from all other Levantine Christians, and who have been thus deceived by the most malicious heretic who ever was on earth; and it must be noted here, that before he had embraced Christianity, he had been..."

[He was] Jewish, and the son of a father named Azzas and a mother called Arama from the Island of Carpathos <note>Located in the Aegean Sea</note>, situated between Rhodes and Thasos. It happened that he was taken as a slave at the age of 17 and sold to a Greek priest, who had him baptized and gave him the name James <note>original: "Iaques"; likely referring to Jacob Baradaeus, though the details here are semi-legendary</note>, instructing him so well in languages that he earned the rank of sovereign Legate of the Patriarch of Alexandria in Egypt. After the death of the Patriarch, he achieved the dignity of the Patriarchate himself. He lived for eight years in a fairly Catholic manner, but once they had expired, he became a heretic and infected the people of the Orient with his devilish opinion more than Arius <note>The 4th-century priest whose teachings on the nature of Christ were declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea</note> ever did. It was he who first introduced and admitted this sect of "Judaizers," approving of circumcision, which many of them still observe today.

Others, instead of Baptism, have certain characters branded with a hot iron onto the arms of their small children, or others behind the neck or at the temples. They hold that such incisions are equivalent to a baptism that delivers them from original sin, basing this on what is said in the Gospel of Saint John: *He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.* <note>Though the text attributes this to the Gospel of John, these words were spoken by John the Baptist in Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16.</note> And as these people are entirely unlearned <note>original: "idiot"; meaning uneducated in theology</note>, not understanding the mysteries of Holy Scripture, they were also perverted in their affections and excommunicated from the Greek Church by the authority of Patriarch Dioscorus, who was then under the obedience of the Latin Church.

Secondly, these people never confess their sins to a priest. Their bishops, priests, and other ministers are married. All Christians have always detested these people—thus named after the author of such a heresy—and have also held them as schismatics. However, they do not for that reason enter into conflict or controversy through arms or popular sedition, for trade is free and open to them just as it is to others who consider themselves more Catholic.

I do not wish to forget to remind you here that while traveling through the land of Asia Minor, three leagues from the city of Seleucia in a ruined place that the local shepherds call Mellothi, I was shown the tomb of the aforementioned Heresiarch <note>The founder of a heretical movement</note>. Having been banished from Egypt and relegated to the Island of Grabusa <note>original: "Crabusé"</note>—distant from the mainland of Pamphylia by about five leagues—he found a way, with the help of some pirates, to escape to Asia, where he again committed many evils. Having lived in this madness until the age of 74, he was killed in an ambush by an Armenian lord.

Those of this persuasion have a beautiful chapel in Jerusalem, within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where I have often seen them celebrate Mass and other services according to their tradition and custom. I have seen four others: one in Egypt, and the three others in the cities of Suez <note>original: "Zidem"</note>, Tor, and Bubutor, which border the Red Sea. They have a particular language <note>Syriac</note>, which is hardly understood by anyone but themselves, and they have thirty-two letters in their alphabet, which are quite strange.

And as it happened that these people had no support, they turned in the year 1552 toward the Roman Bishop, who was Julius III, sending the Legate of the Patriarch of Antioch, named Moses of Mardin <note>original: "Moses Mardenus"</note>—a learned man born in the land of Syria—to make a profession of their faith. He protested that they held what their churches formerly held in the time of Isaac Comnenus, Emperor of Constantinople, who lived in the year of the world 5020, and in the year of our Lord 1058; this monarch punished them so well that he ran...

### On the Nestorian Christians.

Marco Polo the Venetian, in book 1 of his travels in Tartary, writes that in his time, in several and various provinces and cities under the rule of the Great Khan of Tartary in Asia, there were Christians who were named Nestorians <note>A Christian sect named after Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, whose views on the nature of Christ were condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431 AD</note>. Niccolò de' Conti, the Venetian, in his travels to the Indies, and the author of the summary of the Kingdoms, cities, and peoples of the Orient, maintain that in their time there were many Nestorian Christians spread throughout all of Asia, just as the Jews are in Europe. Giovanni Empoli, a factor <note>A commercial agent or representative</note> for the King of Portugal in his navigations to the East Indies, recounts that these Nestorian Christians are otherwise named Nazarenes. Ludovico di Varthema, in book 3, chapter 2 of his navigations of India, says that these Nestorian Christians are surnamed by four other names, namely: of Saint John, of Saint James, of Saint Matthew, and of Saint Thomas.

André Thevet, in book 10, chapter 14 of his *Universal Cosmography*, maintains that on the Island of Gisire or Giferte <note>Likely Gezira, referring to Upper Mesopotamia/Al-Jazira</note>, located in the Euphrates River in Asia, there are many Armenian, Jacobite, and Nestorian Christians, and that there resides the Great Patriarch of the aforementioned Nestorians, whom some Levantine peoples call *Sid*, and others *Sulaca* <note>Likely referring to Yohannan Sulaqa, the first Patriarch of the Chaldean Catholic Church, who was consecrated in Rome in 1553</note>: whom they hold as head and sovereign Bishop, and who is in such reputation among them as the Pope is among Catholics. He maintains three Bishops in the principal cities of the Persian country, namely one in the noble city which was first founded by Darius son of Hystaspes, 521 years before our Lord, named Arbela <note>Modern-day Erbil</note>, and the others Salmas and Ador Beigani <note>Azerbaijan</note>, situated eight leagues away, where in former times was built, stretching toward the East, the great city of Nineveh mentioned in Holy Scripture, named at present by those of the country Ninimich, otherwise Nisroch. I know well that some have in the past broken their heads <note>A colorful idiom for "struggled greatly" or "worried themselves"</note> trying to know where this city of Nineveh had been—a Hebrew word which signifies nothing other than "beauty"—and have wished to say that it was on the edge of the Mediterranean Sea at a...

### *Of the Maronite Christians.*

We shall advise the benevolent readers in this place that we have previously made mention of the Maronite Christians in the chapter on the Chaldeans and the Chaldean language, in which we represented in a figure the alphabet of the letters of their language: this being presupposed, we shall report in this place only the specific words of Pierre Belon and André Theuet, modern authors speaking of these Maronites. The first of whom, in the second book, forty-second chapter of his *Observations*

of the Levant, wrote what follows.

André Thevet, aforementioned, in the sixth book, twelfth chapter of his *Universal Cosmography*, writes that the Maronites are monks who were formerly heretics, otherwise called Monothelites <term>Monothelites: from the Greek for "one will," a 7th-century belief that Christ had two natures but only one divine-human will</term>, and they bear the name of a certain Maron who said that in Jesus Christ there was only one will, and consequently one operation: an error into which the Emperor Heraclius fell during the time that Muhammad’s soldiers were performing wonders in Syria, pillaging the entire territory of Damascus as far as Aleppo. This Maron was not the inventor of the sect, but rather it was a fellow native of Antioch named Macarius, who was condemned along with him by the Sixth Council of Constantinople, as some Greek Bishops of the country related to me, and have also written in their histories. Others say, which is more likely, that this Council was celebrated in Rome around the year of our Lord 647 under Pope Martin I <note>The author refers to the Lateran Council of 649, which condemned Monothelitism</note>, where two hundred Bishops condemned the error of several Patriarchs of Constantinople who had troubled the faith received in the Church, and above all, they condemned these Maronites and their accomplices. Since the Emperor was infected by this heresy, and the Pope resisted him—using censures appropriate for such an effect, and not for his own private profit—Constans <note>Constans II, reigned 641–668</note>, grandson of Heraclius, had him seized and put in prison, where he died in great misery in the year 652, the seventh year of his Pontificate; but a short time later, while he himself was making war on the Catholic Bishops, he was defeated by the Saracens, and fled like one who did not wish to enjoy the prayers of those who were good people, whom the false prophets who deceived him had ruined with their heresies. Finally, these Maronites, having been separated from the true faith of the Church for a space of nearly five hundred years, recognized their state, and detesting their error by the grace of God, they embraced union and returned to the same faith, opinion, and belief as us, submitting themselves to the legitimate Pastors of the Church of God. As proof of this, and of the obedience they bore to it, their Patriarch came to the General Council celebrated in Rome in the year 1515 <note>The author likely means the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 under Innocent III, or is confusing it with the Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517)</note> under Pope Innocent III, where he abjured the ancient errors on behalf of his people, and protested to live under the obedience of the Roman See. However, being currently scattered as they are, and living more in the mountains than elsewhere—as I have seen while conversing with them, except for those who go as pilgrims to Jerusalem—they know no one to recognize but their own Pastors and ministers. These men celebrate the divine office in Hebrew <note>original: "Hebrieu" — The author likely means Syriac, the liturgical language of the Maronites, which was often confused with Hebrew or called "Chaldean" by Westerners at the time</note>, although in their common speech they speak Arabic for the most part, and follow the customs of the Roman Church in very few ceremonies; they live for the most part at present on Mount Lebanon and the surrounding lands. The same Thevet speaks again of these Maronites in book 11, chapter 18, of his same *Universal Cosmography*. So does Gilbert Génébrard in book 4 of his *Chronography*, speaking of Acurius Joseph <note>Likely Joseph el-Ruzzi, a Maronite Patriarch</note> sent by his Patriarch and the Maronites from the monastery of Saint Mary of Kanubin on Mount Lebanon in the year 1515 to Rome to recognize the Pope as the sovereign head of the Church; and of Siud the Syrian <note>Referring to Shimun VIII Sulaqa</note>, also Patriarch of the aforementioned Nestorians, who in the year 1552 did the same.

Since then, they returned for a second time to the bosom of the Roman Church, but they hardly stayed there; instead, they persevered long enough in their error until our own time when, abjuring their error for the third time into the hands of their Patriarch named Emeris, they call themselves Roman Catholics today. Throughout all time they used bells in their churches, and their Bishops wore miters, rings, and croziers like ours, contrary to the custom of the Eastern Church, as they still do now that they are reunited with our Church, using all our ceremonies, and so forth.

### On the Armenian Christians.

Pierre Belon, in book 3, chapter 13 of his *Observations of the Levant*, writes that at the very beginning of the Turkish conquest, the Armenians were the first to be assailed when those Turks came out of Scythia <note>a vast region of central Eurasia</note>: for the Armenians, who were then Christians, found themselves the weaker party and lost their Kingdom. But notwithstanding this, they have always remained constant in the Christian faith: as it appears that even today they hold the name throughout all of Turkey; for to name an "Armenian" in that country is understood to mean a "Christian." If an Armenian becomes a Turk <note>converts to Islam</note>, he loses his name. One finds them inhabiting towns and villages as far as beyond Armenia, and in Asamie, and in Adiabene <note>an ancient kingdom in northern Mesopotamia</note>, given that the King of Persia allows them to live in his country. They are also a peaceful and humane people, and are commonly poor farmers, good gardeners, and those who dress the vines well. The Priests of these Armenians are married like those of the Greeks, and celebrate the Mass with a chalice like the Latins, and are dressed in the same ornaments of copes and chasubles; they do not consecrate using large bread like the Greeks, but in a small host <note>unleavened wafer</note> like the Latins, and all those assisting respond to the Priests.

For the Turks do not constrain anyone to live in the Turkish fashion, but rather it is permitted for each to live in his own law. This is what has always maintained the Turk in his greatness: for if he conquers any country, it is enough for him to be obeyed, and provided that he receives the tribute, he does not care for souls. Therefore one commonly sees several villages throughout the country of Thrace <note>a historical region in southeast Europe, now split between Greece, Bulgaria, and Turkey</note>, some inhabited only by Bulgarians, others by Wallachians <note>people from Wallachia, a historical region of Romania</note>, others by Serbians, others from Bosnia, and Albanians, Dalmatians, and Slavonians, all holding to their Christian religion. And one sometimes finds along the shore of the Black Sea <note>original: "Pont"</note> such and such villages in which one hears five or six different Christian languages according to the different villages.

### Of the Georgian Christians.

The Georgians, anciently named Iberians <note>not to be confused with the Iberian Peninsula of Spain/Portugal; this refers to Caucasian Iberia</note>, were so called because of St. George, because (according to some writers) most of the Levantine peoples do honor to this martyr and hold him in very great reverence, as confirmed by Nicolas Hué, a Carmelite, in his voyage to the Holy Land, and G. Postel in his treatise on the *Alphabet of the Twelve Languages*. ...the year of Christ 334, for the reasons set forth by Rufinus and Theodoret <note>Rufinus of Aquileia and Theodoret of Cyrus were prominent 4th and 5th-century Christian historians</note> in their books of *Ecclesiastical History*; Nicephorus in book 8 of his history; Socrates in book 1 of his similar history; N. However, these people are steeped in an infinity of wicked and perverse heresies <note>the author writes from a traditional Roman Catholic perspective, labeling non-conforming Eastern rites as "heresies"</note>; for a hundred years they have had no rest, having to please now the Turk who possesses Mingrelia <note>a historic region in western Georgia</note> and Armenia; now the Persian who rules along the Caspian Sea toward the south and the land of the Medes; then the Tartar who is at their back toward the North, and the Alans <note>an Iranian nomadic group of the Caucasus</note> who are numbered among the Scythians. Since the last journey made by the Great Turk Solyman <note>Suleiman the Magnificent, Sultan of the Ottoman Empire</note> against the Sophy <note>the Safavid Shah of Persia</note>, this people who used to pay tribute to the Tartar has been forced to pay it to the Turk, because that great Monarch has extended his borders as far as the Euphrates, indeed even to the middle of the Caspian Sea, and has made himself Lord of both Armenias. He leaves these Georgians in peace, fearing to lose everything and stir up all the Eastern neighbors, who would easily return at the slightest opportunity under the obedience of the King of Persia, which is not as submissive and captive as that of the Tyrant of Turkey.

Several fine and ample discourses on the manners and ways of these Georgians are set forth in Josafa Barbaro <note>Giosafat Barbaro, a Venetian explorer</note>, chapter 14 of his *Voyage to Tana*; Ambrogio Contarini, chapter 2 of his *Voyage to Persia*; Marco Polo the Venetian, book 1 of his *Travels in Tartary*; Haython the Armenian, book 1 of the *Tartars*; André Thevet, book 9, chapter 1 of his *Universal Cosmography*; François de Belleforest, book 2 of his *Universal History*, and Volume 2, book 3, chapter 7 of his *Universal Cosmography*. They observe in every way the ceremonies and errors of the Greeks in their sacraments, and are just as much schismatics as they are. Their priests wear round crowns <note>referring to their clerical headgear</note> and the laypeople wear square ones; and every time they come from their country to Jerusalem to visit the holy places, they enter the Holy City with banners flying <note>original: "l’enſeigne deſployee"</note> without paying any tribute. For the Turks and Saracens <note>a medieval term for Muslims</note> do not dare to molest them at all, fearing that once they return home, they might wish to do the same to their neighbors who are Muslims and of the Saracen law. The women of these Georgians for the most part resemble the Amazons <note>mythical female warriors; the author suggests they are exceptionally fierce or capable</note> in their skill with the bow and in going to war, and their faces and manners show clearly enough that they have a virile and robust courage. The men grow their hair and beards long and wear hats of various colors on their heads. They also speak the Arabic, Chaldean <note>likely referring to Syriac or Aramaic</note>, and Persian languages, and their priests use the Greek language in their Liturgy and divine service. See what I write hereafter regarding the Georgians and the Georgian language.
