Thevet in book 18, chapter 5 of his *Universal Cosmography*, and F. de Belleforest in volume 2, book 3, chapter 6 of his *Universal Cosmography*, asserting that these Albanians <note>the Caucasian Albanians, an ancient people of the eastern Caucasus, distinct from modern Balkan Albanians</note> are otherwise called Zithracois or Garzenians.

## Of the Colchian Christians.

The Colchians <note>an ancient kingdom on the eastern coast of the Black Sea, in what is now Georgia</note>, a people descended from the Egyptians, were formerly circumcised, just like the aforementioned Egyptians according to the report of Diodorus Siculus in book 2, chapter 1 of his *Antiquities*; as I have remarked here before. They presently inhabit the region of ancient Colchis in Asia, which is now divided and split into two provinces: the first bearing the name of Lazia or Laxia <note>home of the Laz people</note> which extends as far as Trebizond and is further inland, and the other named Mingrelia, which is almost entirely coastal. Procopius, in book 1 of the *Persian Wars*, holds that these Colchians were Christians long before his age. But M. Michou <note>Maciej Miechowita, a Polish scholar and author of "Tractatus de duabus Sarmatiis"</note> in book 1, chapter 7 of his *Sarmatia*, writes that the history of Moravia records that the Mingrelians were converted to the faith of Jesus Christ by Cyril and Methodius, sent there by the Emperor of the Greeks, Michael III of that name, in the year of our Lord 861. Consequently, to this very day, these people follow the faith and Religion of the Greeks <note>Eastern Orthodox Christianity</note>, having previously been called Gazares and currently, by the Greeks, Abgazares and Abgazeles <note>referring to the Abkhazian people</note>. And one must carefully consider these authorities, given that between the Empire of Justinian, in whose time the said Procopius lived, and this Emperor Michael cited by the aforementioned Michou, there is a span of about 321 years. This leads some to believe that the Persians, reconquering this country, returned it to Paganism, and it persisted in this impiety while the disciples of Muhammad poisoned the Persian Empire with their Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note>, until the aforementioned holy Figures went there to sow the Christian faith. Since that time, as is probable, these Mingrelians have strayed from the union of the Apostolic Church of Rome. Ambroise Contaren <note>Ambrogio Contarini, a Venetian diplomat who traveled to Persia</note> in chapter 2 of his *Voyage to Persia*, holds that these Mingrelians do not occupy more than three days' travel of land; and even that is all mountainous and full of thickets, where the men are beast-like, wearing their heads shaved. They are Christians, but steeped in various heresies, celebrating divine service in the Greek manner. They are under the domination of the Turk, who is Lord of the Empire of Trebizond, to which they were previously subjects after the crown of Constantinople was fragmented and divided into two different empires. At present, they are often constrained and forced to sell their own children for lack of money to pay the taxes <term>daces: royal or feudal duties</term> and impositions they owe to the Grand Seigneur <note>the Ottoman Sultan</note>.

See A. Thevet, book 8, chapter 12 of his *Universal Cosmography*, and F. de Belleforest, volume 2, book 3, chapter 5 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

# THE SYRIAN CHRISTIANS
->*or Syrians.*<-

## CHAP. LIV.

We have previously, in the chapter on the Syrians and the Syriac language, treated these Syrian Christians or Syrians at length. Referring the readers to that chapter, we will only say that Jacques de Vitry <note>a French historian and cardinal who participated in the Crusades</note>, in his history of Jerusalem, chapter 37, writes that in the year of salvation 1171, these Syrian Christians were divided into several sects. Among these were the *Suriens*, so named after a city called Sur <note>the ancient city of Tyre</note> where they lived. They conformed in ceremonies and doctrine to the Greeks <note>Eastern Orthodox Christians</note>, attributing no superiority to the Roman Pontiff <note>the Pope</note> and taking no account of the ceremonies used by Latin Christians in the celebration of the Sacraments, nor of the ordinances concerning fasts in the Roman Church. On this matter, one may see what I have written toward the end of the chapter on the Saracens and the Saracenic <note>Arabic</note> language, and in the chapter on the various kinds of Christians who are spread and scattered throughout the entire compass of the earth.

The Lord of Villamont <note>Jacques de Villamont, a 16th-century traveler</note>, in book 2, chapter 22 of his *Voyages*, writes the following:

> After the Greeks, you also see in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and elsewhere in the City of Jerusalem certain Syrians who are as Schismatic as the Greeks; they are from Syria near Palestine, a region as beautiful, opulent, and fertile as any neighboring it, and they are named after Sur, or Tyre, the city of the Sidonians. As for those who would make them Assyrians, I reject their claim due to the distance between the two regions, etc.

# THE MUSARAB CHRISTIANS
->*or Mozarabs.*<-

## CHAP. LV.

The Histories of Spain, book 6, report to us that the Arabs, Saracens, Moors, and Africans of the Mahometan <note>Muslim</note> religion, around the year of Salvation 714, spent a full five years conquering the Spains <note>the various kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula</note>. Afterward, all the Regions, Cities, Places, and Castles therein—except for certain areas in the mountains of Asturias, Biscay, and Navarre—were made subject and tributary to these Arabs, Saracens, Moors, and Africans. At that time, these conquerors did not greatly care to force men into their Religion, but rather permitted them to practice it freely, and even granted great privileges to some cities, so that

...not to depopulate the country by charging heavy tributes <note>taxes paid by non-Muslim subjects, known as jizya</note>, which was what they desired most. The city of Toledo, among others, had the favor of obtaining seven Temples <note>churches</note> for the exercise of the Christian Religion: namely, Saint Just, Saint Luke, Saint Torquatus, Saint Mark, Saint Eulalia, Saint Sebastian, and Saint Mary. Furthermore, it was granted that justice would be exercised by judges of the aforementioned Christian religion and Christian nation, and according to the laws of the Gothic Kings <note>the Visigoths</note>, and other privileges. By this means, the aforementioned Arabs, Saracens, Moors, and Africans retained an infinite number of Christian families, who lived and multiplied under them; otherwise, the Spains <note>the various kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula</note> would have remained deserted, for the aforementioned Arabs, Saracens, Moors, and Africans could not have populated them. Those who, being Christians, remained among the said Arabs, Saracens, Moors, and Africans, were called **Mus'Arabes**, because of the name of the governor of Africa, **Musa**, who wished to make himself famous through this rule. These **Mus'Arabes**, otherwise named **Moz Arabes** Christians, celebrated their divine offices according to the manner used in the time of the Gothic Kings, and following the institution of an **Isidore, Bishop of Seville**, or of **Leander**, as was the custom in all the said Spains to serve God at that time. And this continued until the service called **Gregorian** or **Roman** was introduced at the time mentioned hereafter. And this **Mus'Arabe** office is still maintained today as a mark of antiquity in the Chapel of the Company of the Body of God <note>original: "du corps de Dieu"; likely the Mozarabic Chapel of Corpus Christi</note> in the great Church of Toledo, and other places in that city. From this year of Salvation 714 until the year of salvation 950, these Mozarabic Christians lived in great tranquility and rest, not being forced or searched regarding their Religion in any way whatsoever, and justice was administered to them, in exchange for the tributes and pensions imposed upon them; but when **Haly Hatan** came to the kingship, he was such a zealot of his Mohammedan religion, and held such great hatred for that of the Christians, that he had an edict published by which it was commanded that all Christian inhabitants in the lands and cities subject to him leave the Christian Religion and, by being circumcised, take that of **Mohammed**, on pain of death. But notwithstanding this wretched edict, the **Mus'Arabes** or **MozArabes** Christians did not cease to celebrate this office among themselves, both in Toledo and in Castile and Leon, until the time of King **Don Alfonso VI**, in the year of salvation 1121 <note>historical dates for this transition vary; Alfonso VI captured Toledo in 1085</note>. This King, desiring in everything and everywhere to show himself an affectionate son of the holy see of Rome, wanted the rite to be changed, and in its place the office called **Gregorian** (after its author) was received—that is to say, from **Gregory VII**. For this reason, he sent for the Pope's Bull, which commanded that the said Roman office be celebrated from then on in all the Churches of the Spains, just as was done in France; and for this reason, it is called by some Spaniards the **Gallican office**. To ordain this, a legate had been sent to Spain a few years earlier by the said Pope **Gregory VII** (predecessor of **Urban II**): one **Richard, Abbot of Saint Victor of Marseille**, who took great pains for the introduction of the new Gregorian or Roman office and the abolition of the said **Mozarabic** office.

...or Musarabic: For which reason, and to put into effect what had been ordained in this matter, upon the return from Rome of Don Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo, a general council was created and assembled in Spain in the city of Toledo. There, the Clergy, Knights, and people of Toledo, Castile, León, Asturias, Galicia, and Portugal were present, or their deputies in great numbers. With Don Bernard presiding and the King being present, great debates, seditions, and disputes were brought forward, as the Spaniards did not wish to abandon their ancient ways to receive a new <term>office</term> <note>The "office" refers to the liturgy or the specific set of prayers and ceremonies used in the Mass.</note>. So much so that, as the arguments and reasons of neither side were sufficient, they came to the furious and beastly manner of trial by duel, which was quite common at that time. Two Knights were placed on the field of battle: one for the King and those who desired the change of the rite, and the other for the Knights and the people who refused it and wished to retain the Musarabic or Mozarabic rite. Jean Ruis took up arms for the latter and defeated the one who fought for the Roman rite, whose name is unknown. Nonetheless, such was the persistent urging of the King, the Queen, the Archbishop of Toledo, Don Bertrand <note>likely referring to Bernard of Sedirac</note>, and others of that party, that this matter was referred to another kind of judgment and test, namely, by fire. Therefore, having brought two books—one containing the rite and usage of Rome, the other ancient and Musarabic—they threw them both into a very hot fire. From this fire, the Roman book leaped out immediately, so it is said, and the other remained there without being in any way damaged or spoiled. Because of this, it was conjectured that both were agreeable to God; for this reason, it was ordered that they would retain the ancient manner of the rite in the six parishes of the city of Toledo, and that in the great Cathedral Church and others within it, the Gregorian or Roman rite would be introduced and put into use, as well as throughout the remainder of the Kingdom of Don Alfonso. This was settled and agreed upon more by force, and to please the King and obey the Pope (who confirmed and approved it), than out of good will. However, in several monasteries of Spain, the Musarabic rite remained for a long time afterward. Even in the same great Church of Toledo, since that time, a Mass is still sung in Musarabic every day in a chapel called the Body of the Lord <note>original: "Corpus Domini"</note>. The six parishes of this city, in which this rite was held, had been held by the Musarabic or Mozarabic Christians throughout the time that the Moors ruled there; these parishes are: Saint Luke, Saint Just, Saint Torquatus, Saint Mark, Saint Eulalia, and Saint Sebastian. Now, whether the Musarabic rite used in ancient times was the same as that held today, or whether it has been reformed and corrected, is not something that can be doubted: for it is certain that in religion all things have been adapted to the times, inclinations, and affections of those who have lived from age to age, especially concerning ecclesiastical order and discipline. A certain author I have with me named J. Yafee has described at length in Latin the form and manner of this Musarabic rite, and of its Masses and ceremonies. G. In the year of Christ 714, Christians permitted to live in Spain as taxpayers were called Mozarabs <note>original: "Mozarabes"</note>, because they were mixed with the Arabs. Among them flourished Urban of Toledo, Frodoarius, Accitanus, Evantius, and John of Seville. This liberty lasted until the arrival in Spain of the Almohads <note>original: "Almoadûm," a Berber Muslim dynasty</note> (a race of Arabs), who permitted no Christians to live among them, and began to reign in the time of Alfonso VII, around the year 1100.

See what I have written previously concerning the African Christians of the city of Marrakesh called Farfanes, and those of the city of Tunis named Rabatins, in the chapters on the Saracens and the chapter on the African language.

P. Maffei, in book 1 of his history of the Indies, makes mention of certain nations of Africa who are commonly called Moses, who in many things follow Christian institutions, and even in the giving of names, which they most often borrow from the holy Apostles.

->*Of several other Christians.*<-

Pierre Belon, in book 2, chapter 85, of his observations of several singularities and memorable things of the Levant, writes that Christian nations most often send men, more or fewer depending on the region, to inhabit the city of Jerusalem and to stay at the Holy Sepulchre of our Lord Jesus Christ. From this, it happens that one counts twelve languages of the Christian religion, different from one another, and it is reckoned that there are twelve principal ones; however, this author says he finds only eight. Among these, the Latin nation, which they call <term>Frank</term> <note>From "Frank," the general term used in the Levant for Western Europeans</note>, is placed before all the others and includes all those obedient to the Roman Church. The second is the Greek nation, which is called in their language <term>Romæos</term> <note>referring to the Eastern Roman or Byzantine identity</note>, whose obedience is not to the command of the Pope, but they have their own Patriarchs. The third nation is the Armenian, which is closer to our ceremonies than the Greek. Consequently, the other nations include the Jacobites, who are from the region converted to the faith by Saint James the Greater; others are Georgians, which is a nation governed by its own laws, and which is adjacent to the Persians, having their borders at East India, and who have been subjugated by no one; thus they are absolute masters of themselves. Others are named Christians of the Belt <note>A term often applied to Copts or Melkites, referencing the "zunnar" belt they were sometimes required to wear</note>, who have taken the surname of Copts, who were brought to the faith by Saint Thomas. Others are Indians, who are sent there from the country ruled by Prester John <note>A legendary Christian king; here identifying his kingdom with Ethiopia</note>, and are very black, called Abyssinians. And because they are baptized in fire, they wear three branding marks <note>original: "brusleures"</note>: one between the two eyes above the nose, and the other two near the temples; they are not as black as the Ethiopians. Others are Nestorians, and others are called Maronites, who are the same as the Arabs <note>likely referring to their use of the Arabic language</note>. Each of these nations has a chapel of its own, because they all differ in some points, and they are maintained by money sent to them by the princes of their provinces. The Greeks hold the Choir and have custody of the site of Calvary, and the Latins have custody of the Sepulchre.

The religious men of all the aforementioned Christian nations enter there and exit when they please without paying anything. The Church of this Holy Sepulchre of our Lord encloses the entire circuit of Calvary, which is on flat ground and not on a mountain, as many have believed. It is high and round in shape, with an opening for light. And in the middle of this circle, the Holy Sepulchre is below, in the middle of the nave, inside the enclosure of a small chapel covered with a round vault, all of fine marble. The Guardian of the Franciscans <note>original: "Cordeliers," a name for the Order of Friars Minor in France</note> of Mount Sion is accustomed to giving a certification to pilgrims who have been sent by someone, so that it may be a testimony for them that they have been there; it contains all other things that I have not specified in detail here for the sake of brevity. The Lord of Villamont, in his modern travels, speaks extensively of all these particulars.

In the year 1580, a certain *David Chytraeus* <note>original: "Dauid Chythreus," a Lutheran theologian</note>, a Lutheran, had a speech of his printed in Frankfurt entitled, *On the State of the Churches at this time in Greece, Asia, Africa, Ethiopia, Armenia, Persia, etc.* <note>original Latin: "De statu Ecclesiarum hoc tempore in Græcia, Asia, Africa, Æthiopia, Armenia, Perside, &c."</note>, in which he demonstrates that all these provinces and regions, which comprise the greater part of this universe, attend to the Mass, *attend to the Masses* <note>original Latin: "Missis operam dare"</note>, that is to say, to the celebration of Masses. His companions—*Martin Crusius*, a teacher <note>original: "pedant"</note> of Tübingen, in his *Turcogrecia* and *Germanogrecia*; *Gerlachius*, a Protestant Minister; and *Wenceslaus von Ludovitz*, Agent of the Emperor in Turkey—in their epistles, give similar testimony. And even if they wished to deny or conceal it, they would be refuted by the travel books of the Catholics who have been to those countries, according to the report of *André Thevet*, book 6, chapter 9, of his *Universal Cosmography*, which confesses to having often seen, and still seeing today in the city of Jerusalem, on the same day, the celebration of Masses by fourteen Oriental and overseas Christian nations, all diverse and separated by long stretches of land and different languages from one another. This is confirmed by *G. Genebrard* in book 4 of his *Chronography*, and book 1, chapter 4, of his *Apostolic Liturgy*, following *André Thevet*, book 11, chapter 18, of his *Universal Cosmography*, and book 19, chapter 12, following.

At the last Jubilee celebrated in Rome in the year 1600, besides the infinite number of Christians from our Europe, several other Christians from the East—inhabitants of China, the Mughal Empire <note>original: "Mogor"</note>, and Japan <note>original: "Giapan"</note>, and from the ends of the Indies—were found there and attended in devotion, via express embassies from their Emperors, Kings, Sophis <note>The Safavid rulers of Persia</note>, Kwambaku <note>original: "Quabacondons," referring to the Japanese title "Kampaku" or regent</note>, Chins, and other titles they have among themselves, according to their languages and nations. So many from Egypt, and from a great part of the adjacent Libya, also presented themselves there—an infinite number of other Christians—tending toward their conversion, or rather their reversion to the ancient faith of their Fathers, from which they had strayed for a time. This clearly demonstrates that in the end, the Catholic Church will remain victorious over all the upheavals that have come upon it. Even the Grand Duke of Muscovy and the Great Khan of the Tartars sent some of their people there, from which there is great likelihood that God will keep them in His mercy and bring them back with the remnants of Israel, as He knows they are faithful. In the aforementioned country of **Mogor** <note>The Mughal Empire in northern India</note>, which is between the Indus River and the Ganges River, the Jesuits have worked so diligently for the spiritual well-being of the souls of the inhabitants there that the King, named **Mahomet Zelabdin Echebar** <note>Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar (r. 1556–1605)</note>, descended from the lineage of the great **Tamerlam** <note>Tamerlane</note>, now freely allows his children to be raised in Christianity, and attends the divine service celebrated daily by the aforementioned Jesuits with great reverence; this is despite the **Mullas** <note>Mullahs</note>, who are their priests, the **Gioges** <note>Yogis or Jogis, Hindu ascetics</note>, who are their monks, and the **Brachmans** <note>Brahmins</note>, who are their ministers.

Regarding the great and ample kingdom of **China**, situated in the easternmost part of Asia on the continent of the East Indies, modern accounts report that Christianity was first known and heard of there in the Year of Salvation 1575, through the ministry of a certain Father **Martin Herrade** <note>Martín de Rada</note>, Provincial of the Augustinians and native of Pamplona, and one **Hierosme Marin** <note>Jerónimo Marín</note>, a native of the city of Mexico, sent from the Philippine Islands (otherwise called the Islands of the West), which are distant from that kingdom by two hundred leagues. They first entered that kingdom led by a particular captain of the King named **Omoncon**, accompanied by **Synsay**, a merchant of the said kingdom, who unexpectedly arrived at the aforementioned islands, as is fully recounted in the *History of China*. Shortly thereafter—namely, in the year 1579—a certain Father **Pedre d'Alfare** <note>Pedro de Alfaro</note>, a native of Seville and guardian of the aforementioned Philippine Islands, of the Order of Saint Francis of the Province of Saint Joseph; a Father **Juan Baptiste of Pesare** from Italy; Brother **Sebastian of Saint Francis** of Baeza in Spain; and a religious Father **Augustin of Tordesillas**, all priests, made a voyage to this great kingdom by the command of the late King of Spain and his Great Council of the Indies. They remained on this journey for seven months, as is recounted in the second part, book 3, of the *History of China*. Since then, in the year 1583, certain Augustinian monks, and also those of the Observance of Saint Francis, along with Jesuits (called there "Fathers of Saint Paul"), went to take up their residence in the city of **Xauquin** <note>Zhaoqing, then the seat of the Viceroy of Liangguang</note>, where the Viceroy of China resides, where they had a convent and church built, in which they began to celebrate Mass regularly. In the year 1584, a certain Father **Martin Ignace** <note>Martín Ignacio de Loyola</note>, Guardian of the Order of Saint Francis, made the same journey from Spain to this kingdom, where he baptized several inhabitants whom he instructed in Christianity; from that kingdom, he returned to Spain via the East Indies after having made a circuit of the earth, as is recounted in the second part of the third book titled *Itinerary of the New World*. Following these good Fathers, some fifteen or twenty years ago, a good number of **Jacobin** <note>Dominican</note> monks from Spain went to the aforementioned kingdom of China by the command of the aforementioned King of Spain and the Lords of his Royal Council of the Indies, in order to assist in the enterprise of the aforementioned religious men. Serving not a little in the conversion of these Chinese people is the great desire they have to do so because of their books, in which it is written that from the side of the West, the "true law" must come to them, which will raise them to heaven to be angels there. Currently, several Chinese merchants who have become Christians have settled in the aforementioned Philippine Islands to live freely in their religion, being housed in a town called **Mauilles** <note>Manila</note>, having among them many artisans, such as shoemakers, tailors, goldsmiths, blacksmiths, and...

As for **Japan**, a Kingdom 600 leagues long and 30 wide, divided and shared among many Lords, distant from China by about 300 leagues, it was instructed in the Christian Religion by Father **Francis Xavier**. It was first discovered by **Antonio Mota**, **Francisco Zeimoto**, and **Antonio Peixoto** in the Year of Salvation 1542, when [Martim Afonso de] Sousa took the government of the Indies, according to Antonio Galvão’s book on the discoverers of the New World. Despite the rigors of **Taicosama** <note>Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537–1598), the regent who first issued edicts against Christians</note>, the wars in **Korea**, and the troubles of the five Regents against **Daisusama** <note>Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543–1616), the first Shogun of the Tokugawa Shogunate</note>, the current Emperor of **Teuse** <note>Possibly a corruption of 'Tenshi' (Emperor) or a reference to the Shogunate's seat</note>, the principal seat of the Empire of Japan; and even despite the regrettable death of **Lord Augustin** <note>Konishi Yukinaga (1555–1600), a prominent Christian daimyo executed after the Battle of Sekigahara</note>, a great pillar of Christianity in the said Japan, nevertheless the aforementioned Jesuits have not tired of doing good in **Meaco** <note>The old name for Kyoto</note>, **Amakusa**, and among other peoples where they have their residences. Notwithstanding all the oppressions that have been inflicted upon them there, they have sometimes baptized more than twenty-five thousand people from one of these nations alone. The **Tono** <note>from the Japanese *Tono*, meaning 'Lord'</note>, who is the high provost of the said Japan and who persecuted them, was himself converted by them. What caused and served as an argument for the conversion of these peoples was that **Taicosama** was made a **Kami** <note>original: "Came"</note>, that is to say, a God in their language, and his statue was erected like that of Nebuchadnezzar to be adored. On this subject, the aforementioned Jesuits took the opportunity to tell these people that the *Taicosamas* had been nothing but men and could not be *Kami*; this the people recognized through the vivid reasons preached to them. A vision also occurred of a cross, which moved those people to want to be baptized and to renounce the **Kami** and **Hotoke** <note>original: "Cames, & Fotoques"</note>, who are their gods and their saints. And things have progressed so far in the Christian Religion that at present there are seven or eight Christian Churches: namely at **Bungo**, a city situated toward the North at some 33 and a half degrees from the equator; the second at **Kuchinotsu** <note>original: "Cutamé"</note>; the third at **Hirado** <note>original: "Firande"</note>, which is a neighboring island subject to Japan and very rich, where the number of Christians is more than two thousand; the fourth at **Hakata** <note>original: "Facata"</note>; the fifth in the great city of **Kagoshima** <note>original: "Cangoxima"</note>, which is the southernmost of the island and placed at some 31 degrees <note>The OCR reads 21, but Kagoshima is located at roughly 31 degrees North</note> and some hundred leagues distant from Bungo; the sixth is at **Yamaguchi** <note>original: "Almangut"</note>, and this Church and that of Kagoshima are the first that were established on this island around the year of our Lord 1548. The seventh is that of **Meaco**, the capital city of all the Japanese, and where the preachers have also had the most difficulty because of the university and monasteries of the idolaters <note>Refers to Buddhist monks and centers of learning</note> who resisted them; nevertheless, the King supporting our fathers, they preached there freely and converted a great number of people to holy baptism. The last is that of **Sakai** <note>original: "Sacaïa"</note>, a city situated near Meaco, but which lives under its own laws without being subject to any King whatsoever. Throughout all these Churches, one sees the newly converted Japanese so ardent in the Christian faith that it is impossible that any fear of death or torments could turn them away from it. See Father **Torres**, Jesuit, in his letters from Japan; Father **Xavier** in his letters from the said Japan; Father **Frois** in his letters; and Father **du Jarric of Toulouse** in his books on the history of the East Indies.

# ON THE ORIGIN OR INVENTION OF LETTERS, OR
*Characters of languages.*

## CHAPTER LVI.

**M**arcus Tullius Cicero, in the first of his *Tusculan Disputations*, concluded from the invention of letters the divinity of the soul and spirit of man, and argued that human nature was too excellent to be thought of as born and proceeding from corporeal existence alone, saying: <margin>“</margin>What is that power—what is it, indeed—which investigates hidden things? <note>original Latin: "Quid illa vis, quę tandem est, quę inuestigat occulta?"</note> <margin>“</margin>That which is called invention and discovery—does it seem to you to be composed of this earthly, mortal, and <margin>“</margin>decaying nature? <note>original Latin: "quæ inuentio atque excogitatio dicitur ex hac ne tibi terrena mortali que natura & caduca concreta ea videtur?"</note> Or who was the first—as it seemed to Pythagoras, a man of supreme wisdom—to <margin>“</margin>give names to all things? <note>original Latin: "aut qui primus... omnibus rebus imposuit nomina"</note> Or who gathered together scattered men and called them to the society <margin>“</margin>of life? Or who limited the sounds of the voice, which seemed infinite, with a few <margin>“</margin>marks of letters? <note>original Latin: "aut qui sonos vocis, qui infiniti videbantur paucis literarũ notis terminarunt?"</note> This gift, handed down from God to mortals, all <margin>“</margin>wise men endowed with judgment and virtue have pursued with admiration and the highest gratitude <margin>“</margin>of soul. Cælius Rhodiginus <note>Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus (1469–1525) was an Italian scholar famous for his "Antiquarum Lectionum" (Ancient Readings), a massive encyclopedia of classical knowledge.</note> in book 4 of his *Ancient Readings*: <margin>“</margin>For what of that majesty of writing which acquires for us the knowledge of such great things, <margin>“</margin>prolongs it through antiquity, and lets nothing perish? And that time, which consumes all <margin>“</margin>things, it compels to succumb to our hands? <note>original Latin: "Quid enim illa scribendi Maiestas... & quod omnia conterit tépus, nostris cogit manibus succumbere?"</note> What is more magnificent than this? What <margin>“</margin>is equally wonderful: that this was given to man, over which even the greedy <margin>“</margin>rapacity of death has no right? <note>original Latin: "id esse homini datum, in quod ne mortis quidem auida rapacitas ius vllũ habeat"</note> What of those volumes woven from so <margin>“</margin>many and such great laws, which finally display the excellence of a more <margin>“</margin>civilized life? What of the faith of words and agreements <margin>“</margin>preserved in public tablets against the depravity of minds? I would <margin>“</margin>dare to say that if our hands were separated [from the use of letters], we would not only be unarmed, but even <margin>“</margin>unhappier than the beasts. For what use of reason would that divine light have <margin>“</margin>if it were destitute of all help? <note>original Latin: "Quem eum vsum rationis habeat lumen illud diuinum omni ope destitutum?"</note> Hence those seem to me to have acted rightly who <margin>“</margin>pronounced the hands to be the servants of reason and wisdom. <note>original Latin: "Hinc rectè mihi fecisse videntur, qui rationis ac sapientiæ ministras esse manus pronunciarunt."</note> On the contrary, the saying of that cursed Emperor Licinius <note>Licinius was a Roman Emperor (reigned 308–324 AD) and rival of Constantine; he is often portrayed in Christian history as a persecutor and hater of learning.</note>, enemy of the Christians, was considered altogether barbaric and brutal when he held that these letters were the poison and common plague of men. Because of this, Pythagoras, Platon, Cicero, and others have well and soundly judged them when they maintained that they were entirely derived and proceeded from the celestial and divine nature. Palamedes <note>A legendary Greek hero from the time of the Trojan War, often credited with inventing various letters of the alphabet, weights, and measures.</note> attributed the invention of the four Greek letters Θ, Ξ, Φ, χ <note>Theta, Xi, Phi, and Chi.</note>, which he first brought to light, to the immortal Gods. For the Gods are accustomed to bringing such inventions to light through wise men; as for the cranes <note>Ancient authors often claimed the flight patterns of cranes inspired the shapes of certain letters.</note>, they do not know these said letters, but only seem to approve of their order when they travel to Libya to fight the Pygmies.

Plutarch in book 9 of his *Symposiacs* <note>A collection of dinner-table discussions on various philosophical and historical topics.</note> and Cicero in book 3 of *The Nature of the Gods*, have written on this subject that the God Mercury was the first who taught the Egyptians the letters he had invented. Then, speaking of Cadmus <note>A Phoenician prince in Greek mythology credited with bringing the alphabet to the Greeks.</note>, who was held to have been the first to bring these letters to the Greeks, they attribute the invention of them to the Phoenicians, as several other authors, both ancient and modern, have done. The same Plutarch takes the Phoenicians to be the Hebrews; for when the question was raised as to why Alpha held the first rank and order among the Greek letters, Ammonius <note>A philosopher and teacher of Plutarch.</note> is introduced, provoking Plutarch of Chaeronea to the debate with these following words, saying:

> Do you then, as a Boeotian, offer no help to Cadmus, who they say placed Alpha before all others because the Phoenicians call the ox by this name? <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲν οὖν τῷ Κάδμῳ βοηθεῖς ὁ Βοιώτιος ᾗ φασὶ τὸ ἄλφα πάντων προτάξαι διὰ τὸ Φοίνικας οὕτω καλεῖν τὸν βοῦν."</note>
> Do you bring any help or aid to Cadmus, you who are a Boeotian? It is said he placed Alpha in the first rank and order of the letters because the Phoenicians call an ox by that name; which he did not wish to place in the second or third rank among necessary things, as Hesiod did, but rather in the first place—the Hebrews calling the ox *Aluph* <note>The Hebrew word "Eleph" or "Aluph" refers to an ox or a leader; the letter Aleph is anciently derived from a pictogram of an ox head.</note> in their language?

Cyprian Martyr <note>Likely referring to the early Christian writer Cyprian of Carthage, or a text attributed to him.</note> in the 4th treatise on *The Vanity of Idols*: In Crete, one sees the cave of Jupiter and also his sepulcher, and it is held as quite certain in that place that Saturn was driven out by him, and from there Latinus <note>In mythology, the king of the Latins; the author here links his name to the word for "hiding."</note> took his name from *latebra* <note>Latin: a hiding place or retreat.</note>, who first instituted the art of printing letters and of minting money, because of which the term *Aerarium Saturni* <note>Latin: "The Treasury of Saturn," the public treasury in ancient Rome.</note> originated in Italy in former times. Several ancient writers, exalting the invention of these letters as more than human, have reported these words: Diodorus Siculus, book 1, chapter 1: The Egyptians assert that it is they who invented letters, the course of the Stars, Geometry, and several other arts and sciences. And in book 6, chapter 13, following the time when Attin, son of the Sun, having gone into Egypt, had taught Astrology to the Egyptians: finally, Greece having been devastated by the deluge, many thousands of men perished, and the memories of letters fell into oblivion. This provided an argument, after several centuries had passed, for the estimation that Cadmus, son of Agenor, was the one who first introduced letters into Greece; so that the Greeks, led by a common error and ignorance, feel themselves his debtors in that they attribute this invention to him. Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian.</note> says, if one chooses to believe rumor, the Phoenician race was the first to both learn and teach letters. <note>original Latin: "si famæ libet credere, gens Phœnicum literas prima & didicit, & docuit."</note>

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> regarding this matter in his book 5 says: The Phoenician race itself is in great glory for the invention of letters and stars, and of naval and warlike arts; <note>original Latin: "Ipsa gens Phœnicum in gloria magna literarum inuentionis & syderum, naualiúmque ac bellicarum artium"</note> and in book 7, chapter 56, he says that he has always judged that letters were found by the Assyrians, and that Cadmus was the one who first brought from Phoenicia to Greece these sixteen letters <term>α β γ δ ε ζ ι λ μ ν ο π ρ σ τ υ</term> <note>Alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, zeta, iota, lambda, mu, nu, omicron, pi, rho, sigma, tau, upsilon.</note>, to which, during the Trojan War, Palamedes added these four shaped thus <term>θ ξ φ χ</term> <note>Theta, xi, phi, chi.</note>; after him, Simonides Melicus invented four others in this form <term>ζ η ψ ω</term> <note>Zeta (repeated here), eta, psi, omega.</note>, the power of which is recognized among the Greeks.

Aristotle holds that the ancient letters were eighteen in number, namely <term>Α Β Γ Δ Ε Ζ Ι Κ Λ Μ Ν Ο Π Ρ Σ Τ Υ Φ</term> <note>Adding Kappa and Phi to the previous list.</note>, and that Epicharmus, and not Palamedes, added two to them, namely <term>Θ</term> and <term>Χ</term>, or <term>Ψ</term>, as Hermolaus Barbarus <note>An Italian Renaissance scholar (1454–1493).</note> testifies. A certain very ancient Greek author named Anticlides claims that an ancient personage named Menona, or Menon, was the first who invented letters in Egypt, fifteen years before Phoroneus, the very ancient King of the Greeks, which he tries to prove by certain examples and documents. Epigenes, a serious author, teaches on the contrary that the Babylonians had among them observations of 720 years written in letters upon tablets of baked clay; it is true that Berosus and Critodemus do not recognize more than 480 years of these observations, because of which it appears that the use of the said letters is eternal, or at least from all time, or from the beginning of this Universe. 

The Pelasgians <note>A term used by ancient Greek writers to refer to the indigenous populations of the Greek world before the arrival of the Greeks proper.</note> were the ones who first brought these letters to Italy; since then, the tacit consent of peoples and nations was such that they served themselves by and used the letters of the Jovians <note>Likely referring to the Latins or Romans, through a mythological connection to Jove/Jupiter.</note>, according to Pliny, book 7, chapters 56 and 57 of his *Natural History*, saying in the subsequent chapter 58 that the ancient Greek letters were almost the same and similar to the Latin or Roman ones. This was demonstrated by the very ancient Delphic bronze tablet, which in his time was in the palace at Rome, dedicated to Minerva by the gift and liberality of the Roman Princes with this inscription: <term>Nausicrates, son of Pisamenos, an Athenian</term>. <note>original Greek: "Ναυσικράτης πισαμένυ Αθηναῖος"</note>

<margin><insert>to ask; having said</insert></margin> <note>original Greek: "αἰτεῖν· εἰπόντος·"</note> Socrates, in Plato's dialogue titled *Phaedrus*, narrates (according to the testimony of Caelius, book 22, chapter 15) having heard it said that among the Egyptians there was worshipped a God called Theuth <note>The Egyptian god Thoth, often associated with wisdom and writing.</note>, who first invented several arts, together with letters, and taught them to those Egyptians at the time when King Thamus commanded all of Egypt; and that this King, asking one day of this Theuth, as the first inventor of them, what utility and profit these said letters could bring, he replied to him in these words: <term>“This, O King...”</term> <note>original Greek: "τοῦτο δ' ὦ βασιλεῦ"</note>

"This study will make the Egyptians wiser and improve their memory; for a medicine for wisdom and memory has been found." <note>original Greek: "τό μάθημα Αἰγυπτίους σοφωτέρους καὶ μνημονικωτέρους παρέξει μνήμης ἰδοὺ καὶ σοφίας φάρμακον εὑρέθη." > "O King, this teaching will make the Egyptians wiser, more prudent, and

The same Plato, in his *Philebus*, demonstrates that this Teuth was the first Inventor of these letters, and describes how he invented and organized his observations into the art of Grammar. A certain Philo of Byblos <note>Philo Byblius, a scholar who claimed to translate the works of an ancient Phoenician priest.</note>, a Greek interpreter of Sanchuniathon of Beirut <note>Sanchoniaton Berutien</note>—who in the time of Semiramis described the deeds of the Phoenicians in the Syriac language, according to the report of Eusebius—says the following:

> "Sanchuniathon was a

> and increase the things that Theuth had invented; for he was not 
> ignorant that this same Theuth had been the first among mortals to 
> find letters, and by this means dedicated and consecrated to eternity 
> those things memorable and worthy of remark."

The Egyptians called this Teuth, "Thoyth"; those of Alexandria called him "Thoth," and the Greeks called him "Mercury." Diodorus Siculus, in Book 1, speaks thus of the origin of human affairs:

> "From the 
> beginning of this world, the sounds of the mouth being confused, it 
> is held that little by little men formed and separated their voices, and 
> that they imposed names on all things: And because they were in 
> various places of this Universe, they did not use the same and similar 
> words, but diverse and dissimilar ones, as also with the characters of 
> letters: this same author in Book 2 teaches through the deeds of the 
> ancients, that the Egyptians attributed to themselves the invention of 
> these letters:"

St. Augustine, in Question 69 on Exodus, [discusses] who were the *introducers of letters* <note>original Greek: γραμμάτων εἰσαγωγεῖς</note>. The Greeks, having interpreted the word *Schotrim* <note>A Hebrew term often translated as officers or scribes.</note>—that is to say, attendants—as *Teachers who introduce letters* <note>original Latin: "Doctores qui introducant in literas"</note>, used these following words:

> "Here it is certainly signified that before the 
> law was given, the Hebrews had letters; when these began to exist, 
> I know not, nor whether it can be tracked down; for to some it seems 
> they began from the first men and were brought down to Noah, and 
> from there to the parents of Abraham, and from there to the people 
> of Israel; but how this can be proven, I do not know." <note>original Latin: "Hic sanè ſignificatur... ſed unde hoc probari poſſit, ignoro."</note>

Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note>, on this subject under the word "Adam," considering the perfection and great wisdom of the first man before he was seduced by Satan, speaks thus according to the judgment of the Church and its ancient Theologians:

> "Adam, 
> the first man, made by the hand of God, and formed in the image and 
> likeness of the Maker and Creator, who also obtained the honor of 
> inhabiting paradise. He will most rightly be called the first wise man, 
> and the primitive image and likeness described by God himself, 
> since he was copiously adorned with all gifts, and carried about all 
> senses, both of the soul and the body, pure and whole," <note>original Latin: "Adam primus homo Dei manu effectus... pura & integra circumtulit,"</note>

and a little later, speaking of the great praises of the first Father of men:

> "It was he, therefore, who distinguished 
> each thing, and applied to all of them standards, and measures, and

> reason; his are the Prophecies, sacred rites, purifications, laws 
> written and unwritten alike; his, finally, are all things." <note>original Latin: "Is igitur extitit qui diucreuit ſingula... huius denique ſunt omnia"</note>

...inventions, disciplines, and whatever else is useful and necessary for life and community. Josephus <note>original: "Iosephe"; referring to Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note>, in the first book of his *Antiquities*, maintains that Seth, son of Adam, and their children were the first to record astronomy in writing, which they had learned from their first father, Adam. This led the Arabs to attribute Theology and all other sciences to this Seth, son of the aforementioned Adam—which is most true and certain, as we have discussed extensively in the preceding chapters 2, 3, 5, and 9 of this present work. Theodore Bibliander <note>A 16th-century Swiss orientalist and linguist.</note> says in his commentary *On the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, in the chapter concerning the origin of letters:

It is consistent with reason that Adam—who had fallen into sin through the seduction of Satan but was soon after restored by divine grace—depicted his thoughts and the memory of past deeds through letters. This is fitting for the excellence and dignity of the first man. For whom else should we consider that God, or that "divine man" (as Plato says), who first discovered letters? Or to whom should we rather attribute that "divine mind" (as it seemed to Cicero and Pythagoras), who reduced so many distinct voices to certain laws and marked the elements of human speech with suitable signs, than to Adam himself? According to the testimony of Holy Scripture, he gave the most appropriate names to all things, which God also approved. Indeed, since the power of reason is most vast, and puts itself forward and comes under the senses both in words and in works, no work of human reason appears more excellent to me than that which, by the marks and signs of letters, depicts speech—through which reason presents itself—and even depicts itself. It deposits this in books, as if in chests to be preserved, and transfers itself into other minds whose bodies are separated by the greatest intervals of both place and time. And so the mind found an instrument suited to its nature, by which it might grasp with a tool divine and human things, things embodied and things without bodies, and—to put it simply—whatever man can comprehend with his mind, and propose them to others for perception and judgment. Furthermore, it sufficiently refutes the opinions of those who attribute the receipt of letters to Pagan authors, or to Moses, or to Abraham, or to a single writing of the Prophet Enoch <note>A biblical figure often associated with the invention of writing and ancient wisdom in mystical traditions.</note>, who flourished about 800 years before the Flood. It is also pleasing to transcribe here some ancient verses concerning the inventors of letters, which Petrus Crinitus <note>Pietro Crinito (1475–1507), an Italian humanist scholar.</note> testifies to have found in an ancient manuscript in the Library of Septimana, in book 17 of *On Honest Discipline*, chapter 1:

> Moses was the first to carve out the Hebrew letters,
> The Phoenicians with sagacious minds founded the Attic.
> Abraham found the Syrian and the Chaldean as well,
> Those which we Latins write, Nicostrata published.
> Isis, with no less skill, produced the Egyptian,
> Ulfilas <note>original: "Gulfila"; the 4th-century bishop who translated the Bible into Gothic and created the Gothic alphabet.</note> brought forth the Gothic, which we see as the last.

Pliny and Solinus <note>Roman authors Gaius Plinius Secundus and Gaius Julius Solinus.</note> say that the Pelasgians <note>An ancient people who inhabited the Aegean region before the Greeks.</note> were the first who carried letters to the lands of the Latins. Some maintain that Nicostrata, mother of the Arcadian Evander, was the one who first gave letters to the Latins. Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric.</note> relates in book 1 that the Arcadians under Evander—who came to Italy after the Pelasgians—brought letters there. Titus Livius <note>Livy, the famous Roman historian.</note> in the first book of his *Decades* calls this Evander the author of them, writing in this manner: "Evander then, having fled from the Peloponnese, came to these places where he ruled more by authority and majesty..."

this, *Quintilian* <note>A Roman rhetorician from the 1st century AD.</note> says, not inappropriately, that *Claudius Caesar* had added this

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

As for **K**, taken from the Greeks, there is no good author who advises that it be used in any way: the letter **Q** was received because it has a softer sound than **C**. The letter **X** was taken from the Greeks, but we can do without it, as **Quintilian** <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35–100 AD), a Roman educator and rhetorician.</note> remarks, by using these letters **C** and **S**, or **G** and **S**, as in these Latin words *Apex* <note>original: "Apecs"</note> and *Grex* <note>original: "Grecs"</note> which mean **summit** and **flock**. **Y** and **Z** also have their source in the fountains of Greece, but are so adopted by us that we only use them in words that are naturally Greek. **Theodore Bibliander** <note>A 16th-century Swiss scholar and linguist who studied the relationships between languages.</note> says:

> Furthermore, since the **Hebrew letters** are the primary ones from which the letters of other nations and peoples were born and propagated—and this is not obscure if one attentively inspects the forms themselves—I will also add some things regarding at what time such a great benefit was transferred from the family of **Heber** <note>The traditional ancestor of the Hebrews, from whom the name is derived.</note> to other nations, and through which men. For when the entire race of **Adam** used one speech, there was also one common form of letters. But with the introduction of a plurality of languages, diverse writing also followed. And among the children of **Ham** <note>original: "Cham"</note>, **Canaan** prevailed, from whom the **Phoenicians** descend. Their language and letter forms approach the Hebrew most closely in name, form, and order. For among good authors, such as **Serapion** and others, the order of letters is the same as that observed by the Hebrews themselves. Among the sons of **Japheth**, **Javan** <note>In the biblical "Table of Nations," Javan is associated with the Greeks.</note> prevailed, from whom the **Greeks** lead their origin: whose letters likewise agree for the most part with the Hebrew in number, order, names, and power. From them flowed the letters of other nations which are worn by public use, such as those of the **Latins** from the Greeks, and likewise of the **Sarmatians** <note>An ancient people of Iranian origin who lived in what is now Ukraine and southern Russia.</note> and **Teutons** <note>Germanic peoples.</note>. However, the use of writing increased later among some barbarian nations, as **Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author who wrote in Greek.</note> says in Book 8 of his *Various History*, where he cites **Androtion** writing about the ignorance of letters and disciplines among the **Thracians** and other barbarians, noting that none of the ancient Thracians knew letters. Indeed, he would have said it was a disgrace for all barbarians in **Europe** to use letters, yet the **Asians**, as it is told, used them more; whence some dare to say that **Orpheus** was not a wise man, but others fabricated his fables. **Herodotus**, writing about **Cadmus** <note>The legendary Phoenician prince who founded Thebes and brought the alphabet to Greece.</note>—who they say brought letters to the Greeks—writes thus in his book *Terpsichore*: "As I have found by inquiry, there were Phoenicians among those who came with Cadmus to the land now called **Boeotia**, and they inhabited it, having been allotted the **Tanagric** district. Whence the **Cadmeans** were first driven out by the **Argives**, and again by the **Boeotians**; if the **Zephyrians** <note>Likely referring to a specific subgroup or location mentioned in the classical text.</note> were expelled, they turned toward **Athens**. They were received by the Athenians under conditions that they would be citizens among them, many things worthy of memory being imposed upon them. These Phoenicians who arrived with Cadmus, of whom the Zephyrians were part, while they inhabited this region, introduced many other doctrines into **Greece**, and especially letters, which in my opinion did not exist among the Greeks before; and those were first of the kind which all Phoenicians use. Then, with the progress of time, along with the sound, they changed the ancient shape <note>original: "modulum pristinum"</note>, and since at that time their neighbors in most of the surrounding places were **Ionians**, who had received letters by learning them from the Phoenicians, they used them, arranging them with a few of their own; and in using them, they confessed, as reason suggested, that they were called 'Phoenician' because they had been brought into Greece by the Phoenicians. And by an ancient custom they called skins *biblos* <note>A term usually associated with papyrus, but here used to describe writing on animal skins.</note>, because at one time, due to a shortage of books—that is, papyrus—they used goat and sheep skins. Even to my own memory, many of the barbarians write on such skins; indeed, even men themselves in **Boeotian Thebes**, in the temple of **Ismenian Apollo**, saw the Cadmean letters..."

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

...on the tripods where I saw them engraved, for the most part very similar to the Ionian letters. <note>The author is likely quoting the Greek historian Herodotus, who described seeing ancient "Cadmean" inscriptions on tripods in the temple of Apollo at Thebes.</note> One of these tripods bore this epigram:

->Amphitryon <note>A legendary Theban general and the foster-father of Hercules.</note> offered me as a gift from the Teleboan people.<-

A second tripod declared in hexameter verse:

->Scaeus, victorious in the accustomed contest of boxers,<-
->Dedicated me as a beautiful gift to you, holy Apollo.<-

A third tripod stated in hexameter verse:

->Laodamas himself, being the monarch in his city,<-
->Dedicated this tripod as a distinguished ornament to you, great Apollo.<-

> **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BC Greek historian.</note> in his 6th book says it is an error of Greece to attribute the invention of letters to **Cadmus**, son of Agenor; he says Cadmus was merely the first to bring letters to Greece after the great flood, an event which had destroyed previous records of writing. Regarding the time when letters were brought to Italy, judgment was previously rendered using the words of **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author.</note>, to which I will add these few points from the first book of the *Roman Antiquities* of **Dionysius of Halicarnassus**: roughly sixty years before the Trojan War, certain Arcadians led by **Evander** <note>A culture hero from Arcadia who brought Greek pantheon and laws to Italy.</note> arrived in Italy and founded the Palatine settlement. They were the first to bring the use of Greek letters to Italy—letters which had appeared among the Arcadians only shortly before. Some say that **Carmenta** <note>Evander’s mother, a prophetess said to have adapted the Greek alphabet into the Latin one.</note> only changed the forms of the letters. Others say that **Hercules** brought letters to Italy from the Falisci <note>An ancient Italic people.</note>. As **Victorinus** <note>Marius Victorinus, a 4th-century grammarian.</note> testifies, **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian.</note> writes in his 6th book: "The deeds of the Romans from the founding of the city to its capture [by the Gauls], I have set forth in five books; these matters are obscure due to their great antiquity, like objects seen from a vast distance, and also because in those times writing was extremely rare, though it is the only faithful guardian of the memory of past deeds." **Cornelius Tacitus**, writing about the Germans, says they celebrate **Tuisto** and his son **Mannus** <note>The mythical ancestors of the Germanic peoples.</note> as the origin of their race in ancient songs, which is their only form of memory and annals. Regarding the Goths and Franks, we have already spoken in our list of languages. Furthermore, six hundred years ago, the **Turks** embraced **Arabic letters** along with the religion of the Saracens, and long after them, the **Tartars** <note>A general term used here for Central Asian nomadic groups, including the Mongols.</note> did the same. In our own age, the **Hungarian language** has finally begun to be recorded in writing. **Otto Heurnius** <note>A Dutch physician and philosopher (1577–1652).</note> conforms to the above in his work on the Chaldean language.

Those who wish to see many other fine discourses on the invention of letters and grammar—which **Suidas** <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> attributes to **Prometheus**, who lived in the time of the Hebrew Judges—should read **Julius Pollux** in his *Onomasticon*, book 4; **Quintilian**, books 4 and 7; **P. Crinitus**, book 16, chapter 8 of *On Honest Discipline*; **Gregor Reisch**, the Carthusian, in book 1, treatise 1 of his *Philosophical Pearl* <note>original: "Marguerite philosophique," a famous 16th-century encyclopedia.</note>; **Polydore Vergil**, book 1, chapter 6 of *On the Inventors of Things*; **Theodor Zwinger**, volume 2, book 1 of his *Great Theater of Human Life*; **Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa**, chapters 2 and 3 of his treatise *On the Vanity of the Sciences*; **Theodor Bibliander** in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*; **Petrus Ramus**, book 1 of *Grammar Schools*; and **Pierre Grégoire**, book 16 of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art*. As for the parts of this grammar, **Raffaele Volaterranus**, book 32 of his *Philology*—in the chapter on the cyclic sciences, and primarily on grammar, letters, syllables, and feet—has written amply and learnedly on everything one might desire. After him, **Caelius Secundus Curio** in his book divided into three parts entitled *The School, or on the Perfect Grammarian*; and more excellently and profoundly, **Luis de Figueiredo**, the Portuguese, in his preface to his *Globe of the Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*.

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE. On the Region of the Greeks.

**Ortelius** <note>Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598) was a famous Flemish cartographer and geographer who created the first modern atlas.</note> in his *Geographical Synonyms and Treasure* says: "Greece, the most noble region of Europe, and the source and mother of all learning." <note>original Latin: "Græcia, Europæ nobilissima regio, totiúsque eruditionis fons & mater."</note> It was called **Hellas** <gloss>Hellas</gloss> by its inhabitants. We have observed that its dwellers were most frequently called by these names among the most ancient writers: the **Achaeans** <gloss>Achaioi</gloss>, **Achivi**, **Argives** <gloss>Argeioi</gloss>, **Danaans** <gloss>Danaoi</gloss>, **Dolopes** <gloss>Dolopes</gloss>, **Dorians** <gloss>Dorieis</gloss>, **Dryopes** <gloss>Dryopes</gloss>, **Graians**, **Gratugena**, **Hellenes** <gloss>Hellenes</gloss>, **Ionians** <gloss>Iones</gloss>, **Myrmidons** <gloss>Myrmidones</gloss>, and **Pelasgians** <gloss>Pelasgoi</gloss>. But **Nicolaus Gerbelius** <note>A 16th-century German scholar who wrote extensively on Greek geography.</note> noted the same even before us. I understand that those who inhabit it today call it **Romechi**, and the Turks call it **Horomeli**. To **Leunclavius** <note>Johannes Leunclavius, a 16th-century historian known for his studies of the Ottoman Empire.</note> it is **Rumelia**. It is called **Phobel** by the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in Isaiah 61, and **Javan** among the same (where **Saint Jerome** <note>The 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> reads "Greece") in Ezekiel 27 and Zechariah 9.

True Greece is **Achaia**: thus **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman author and administrator.</note> says in his 8th book of letters to Maximus. This same area is called Hellas by **Polyhistor**. On this subject, see **Petrus Fabri**, *Agonisticon*, book 3, chapter 15. In **Xenophon's** *Cyropaedia*, book 1, there are also "Asiatic Greeks." Either he is mistaken, or they are on the coast of the Aegean Sea in Asia Minor, where there were many Greek colonies, or in the region of Galatia where the **Gallo-Greeks** lived: whom **Plutarch** calls "Asian Greeks" in his *Sayings*. According to **Suidas** <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note>, "Greece" was also the name of a village from which the region took its name; see the entry for Achaia.

**Greater Greece**, or *Magna Graecia*, is a region of Italy according to **Ptolemy**. Between the Bruttii and the Salentini, **Pliny** calls Italy "Greece" in book 36, chapter 5, and the "coast of Greece" in book 3, chapter 5. To distinguish it from this, **Livy** in his 7th book calls the area that is true Greece (that is, Hellas) "Further Greece."

**Achaia** <gloss>Achaia</gloss> is a region of Greece which **Ptolemy** also names Hellas. **Pliny Caecilius** calls it "Pure Greece" <note>original Latin: "meram græciam"</note> in his 8th book of letters to his friend Romanus. Today it seems to be called **Livadia**. There is another Achaia in the Peloponnese which is renamed by the same Ptolemy; it is called **Ionia**, **Ias**, and **Olenus** by **Diodorus**. It is called **Aegialos** by **Pausanias** and Pliny. **Herodotus** writes in his book *Polymnia* that the inhabitants were called <term>Pelasgians</term> <note>The Pelasgians were the indigenous people who inhabited the Aegean region before the arrival of the Greeks.</note> Aegiales, which means "people of the coast." **Giacomo Gastaldi** <note>A prominent 16th-century Venetian cartographer.</note> reports that it is now called "High Romania." **Apuleius** calls the entire Peloponnese "Achaia," on which see the entry for Lacedaemon. For **Thucydides**, it is also the name of a city in the Peloponnese. There is an Achaia region, an Achaia village, and an Achaean people in Asiatic Sarmatia near the Black Sea, according to Ptolemy, Strabo, Pomponius, Dionysius, Appian, and the *Circumnavigation* of Arrian.

Some write **Achaea** <gloss>Achaia</gloss> with three syllables; there is also a city of that name on the island of Rhodes, as witnessed by Diodorus and **Athenaeus** in his 8th book. According to **Appian** in his *Syrian Wars*, it is in Parthiene. It is also in Macedonia and even in Crete, unless **Gesner** is mistaken in his entry on the "Achaean Deer." There is also a spring called Achaia in Messenia near the city of Dorium, according to Pausanias. **Aelian** mentions an "Achaean Gulf" in the 1st book of *On Animals*, chapter 12.

**Nicolaus Gerbelius**, in his *Commentaries on the Description of Greece by Sophianos*, in the chapter on the names of Greece, wrote the following:

"Before the Trojan War, which is recorded among the most ancient events by historians, I find that the Greeks achieved nothing worthy of memory under a common name. This lasted until Alexander, son of Priam, also called **Paris**, under the most unlucky omens, seized **Helen**, the wife of Menelaus, as we also said above. For then, in the city of Aulis in Boeotia, a conspiracy was formed by the leaders of the Greeks..."

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE. Concerning the Region of the Greeks.
<sig>Nnnn 2</sig>

**Abraham Ortelius**, in his *Geographical Synonyms and Treasury*, writes: **Greece** is "the most noble region of Europe, and the source and mother of all learning." <note>original Latin: "Græcia, Europæ nobilissima regio, totiusque eruditionis fons & mater." Ortelius was a famous 16th-century Flemish cartographer.</note> It was called **Hellas** <gloss>Hellas</gloss> by its inhabitants. We have observed that its inhabitants are frequently called by these names among the most ancient writers: **Achaians** <gloss>Akhaioi</gloss>, **Argives** <gloss>Argeioi</gloss>, **Danaans** <gloss>Danaoi</gloss>, **Dolopes** <gloss>Dolopes</gloss>, **Dorians** <gloss>Dorieis</gloss>, **Dryopes** <gloss>Dryopes</gloss>, **Graians** <gloss>Graioi</gloss>, **Greek-born**, **Hellenes** <gloss>Hellenes</gloss>, **Ionians** <gloss>Iones</gloss>, **Myrmidons** <gloss>Myrmidones</gloss>, and **Pelasgians** <gloss>Pelasgoi</gloss>. But **Nicolaus Gerbel** also noted the same before us. I understand that those who live there today call it **Romechi** <note>A reference to "Romaioi," the term used by Greeks in the Byzantine and Ottoman periods to identify themselves as Romans.</note>, and the Turks call it **Horomeli**. It is **Rumelia** according to **Leunclavius**. It is called **Phobel** by the seventy interpreters <note>The "Seventy" refers to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in Isaiah 61, and **Javan** by the same (where **St. Jerome** reads "Greece") in Ezekiel 27 and Zechariah 9.

True **Greece** is **Achaia**: so says **Pliny** in his 8th letter to Maximus. This same region is **Hellas** to **Polyhistor**. Add to this **Petrus Faber** in his *Agonisticon*, book 3, chapter 15. In **Xenophon's** *Cyropaedia*, book 1, there are also "Asiatic Greeks." Either I am mistaken, or they are on the coast of the Aegean Sea in Asia Minor, where there are many Greek colonies, or in the region of **Galatia** where the **Gallo-Greeks** are: whom **Plutarch** calls "Asian Greeks" in his *Sayings*. According to **Suidas**, there is also a village called **Greece** from which the region takes its name; see the entry for **Achaia**.

**Greater Greece** (or *Magna Graecia*) is a region of Italy according to **Ptolemy**. **Pliny** calls the area between the Brutii and the Salentini "Grecian Italy" in book 36, chapter 5, and the "Grecian coast" in book 3, chapter 5. To distinguish it, **Livy** in his 7th book calls that which is true Greece (that is, Hellas) "**Further Greece**."

**Achaia** <gloss>Akhaia</gloss> is a region of Greece which **Ptolemy** also names Hellas. **Pliny Caecilius** calls it "Pure Greece" in his 8th book of letters to his friend Romanus. Today it seems to be called **Livadia**. There is another **Achaia** in the **Peloponnese** which is specifically named by the same Ptolemy; it is called **Ionia**, **Ias**, and **Olenus** by **Diodorus**. It is called **Aegialos** by **Pausanias** and **Pliny**. **Herodotus** writes in his *Polymnia* that the inhabitants were called **Pelasgian Aegialeans**, which means "coastal people." **Giacomo Gastaldi** reports that it is now called **High Romania**. **Apuleius** calls the entire Peloponnesus "Achaia"; on this, see the entry for **Lacedaemon**. For **Thucydides** in book 1, it is also the name of a city in the Peloponnese. There is an Achaia region, an Achaia village, and the Achaian people in **Asiatic Sarmatia** <note>An ancient region covering parts of present-day Russia and Ukraine.</note> near the Black Sea, according to Ptolemy, Strabo, Pomponius, Dionysius, Appian, and the *Periplus* of Arrian.

Some write **Achaea** <gloss>Akhaia</gloss> as three syllables. Achaia is also a city on the island of **Rhodes**, as witnessed by Diodorus; and according to **Athenaeus** in book 8, it is in **Parthienae**. According to **Appian** in his *Syriaca*, it is in Macedonia and also in **Crete**, unless **Gesner** is mistaken regarding the "Achaian Deer." There is also an Achaian spring in **Messenia** near the city of Dorium, according to Pausanias. **Aelian** mentions an **Achaian Gulf** in book 1 of *On Animals*, chapter 12.

**Nicolaus Gerbel**, in his *Commentaries on the Description of Greece* by **Sophianos**, in the chapter on the names of Greece, wrote what follows:

> Before the Trojan War, which is remembered among historians as being among the most ancient events, I find that the Greeks achieved nothing of common note at home or abroad. This remained so until Alexander, son of Priam, also known as Paris, under the most unhappy omens, abducted Helen, the wife of Menelaus, as we have already said above. For then, at the city of Aulis in Boeotia, a conspiracy was formed by the leaders of the Greeks...

...and by the common consent of all Greece, war was waged against Priam <note>King Priam of Troy, referring to the Trojan War.</note>. For this reason, Thucydides records that before the time of Hellen—whom the same author identifies as the son of Deucalion, while the commentator on Pindar calls him the son of Prometheus and Clymene, and others the son of Ion—the Greeks were not called by a single name. Instead, he relates that individual tribes, most notably the Pelasgians, each took their own names for themselves. However, once Hellen and his sons gained power in Phthiotis, they allied themselves with neighboring cities for the purpose of commerce. From this shared interaction, they became accustomed to a single language and eventually adopted one name, being called **Hellenes** after Hellen. Yet, this name did not immediately spread to the entire nation; at first, it applied only to the people of Phthiotis who served as soldiers under Achilles in the Trojan expedition.

Therefore, Pliny, with his usual great learning, asserts that Greece frequently changed its name and was most often named after its kings. Because a King **Graecus** was born there, it was called **Graecia** (Greece). Because **Hellen** (as we have said) held the kingdom there, the Greeks were called **Hellenes**. Homer named these same people, though not all in one place, **Myrmidons**, **Hellenes**, and **Achaians**. However, the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator or annotator</note> of Homer affirms that only Thessaly is called "true Greece" by Homer. We shall briefly explain the names that are more common and well-known among authors, which are primarily: **Achaians, Argives, Danaans, Pelopes, Hellenes, Ionians, Myrmidons,** and **Pelasgians.**

### A C H A I A N S.

Xuthus, the son of Aeolus, having taken Creusa, the daughter of Erechtheus, in marriage, fathered two sons by her: Ion and Achaeus. One of them, Ion, took possession of Athens and called the region of Attica **Ionia** after himself, and the Athenians **Ionians**. Achaeus, when he had stained himself with the blood of his own kin, fled to Thessaly; becoming the Lord of that region, he called the Thessalians **Achaians** after himself. Thus, Homer often uses the name through <term>metonymy</term> <note>A figure of speech where a related term or a part is used to represent the whole; here, using one tribe's name for all Greeks.</note> to refer to Greece as **Achaia** and the Greeks as **Achaians**, as in Book 3 of the *Iliad*:

> To horse-breeding Argos and Achaia, land of beautiful women.
<note>original Greek: "Ἄργος ἐς ἱππόβοτον καὶ Ἀχαιΐδα καλλιγύναικα."</note>

And in Book 11 of the *Iliad*:

> But come, let us see if we might somehow arm the sons of the Achaians.
<note>original Greek: "Ἀλλ᾽ ἄγετ᾽ αἴκεν πῶς θωρήξοmen υἷας ἀχαιῶν."</note>

The remaining matters pertaining to the Achaians in Thessaly we shall save for when we discuss that region.

### A R G I V E S.

The **Argives** were named after Argus, the son of Apis and Niobe, as the Scholiasts of Homer prefer. There are some who think the Argives and the region of Argia received their name from the "clarity" or fame <note>A play on the Latin and Greek roots implying "bright" or "shining."</note> of the city itself. We will discuss this more copiously a little later in the section on Regions. But if you have looked closely at the map—which, as I have often advised, you should do—you will see the city of Argos and the region of Argia beautifully and diligently marked in capital letters. Didymus, in Book 18 of the *Odyssey* (if the title is correct), records that all of Greece is called **Argos** because that city is situated in the middle of Greece. Strabo, however, in Book 8, mentions from Euripides that Danaus lived in the citadel of the Argives. Since he far surpassed the previous kings in the greatness of his deeds, he decreed throughout all of Greece that the people previously called **Pelasgiotas** should be named **Danaans** after himself, so that this name might be used publicly thereafter. Virgil used both names in these two verses:

> *Fierce Jupiter has transferred all things to Argos,*

<note>original: "Ferus omnia Iuppiter Argos / Transtulit, incensa Danai dominantur in urbe." These lines from Virgil’s Aeneid describe the moment the Greeks (Danai) finally seized control of Troy as it burned.</note>

### DANAI.

We have already mentioned that the **Danai** <note>One of the primary names used by Homer to refer to the Greeks, specifically those from the region of Argos.</note> took their name from **Danaus**. However, the commentator on Homer has explained this matter a bit more clearly. **Belus** (he says)—the son of Neptune and Libya (after whom the land of Libya was named) and brother of Agenor—married Anthinoë, the daughter of the Nile, while he was reigning in Egypt. With her, he fathered the twins **Aegyptus** and **Danaus**. Belus placed Danaus in charge of Libya and Aegyptus in charge of Arabia; after Aegyptus conquered the **Melampodes** <note>Literally "Black-feet," an ancient name for the people of the Nile region.</note>, the region of Egypt gained its name from him. Aegyptus had fifty sons by various wives, and Danaus had just as many daughters. 

But when the brothers Aegyptus and Danaus disputed over the kingdom (as often happens), and Danaus was warned by an oracle that he would be killed by one of his grandsons, he had his daughters kill his brother's sons, though one or two were spared. Having committed this crime, and on the advice of **Minerva** <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena, who was said to have helped Danaus escape.</note>, he was the first to build a ship. He called it a **pentekontoros** <note>original: πεντηκόντορον; a ship with fifty oars, named after the number of his daughters.</note> because of the number of his daughters (for there were fifty, as we said). Fleeing from Libya in this ship with his daughters, he arrived at **Rhodes**. There, after erecting a statue to **Lindian Minerva**, he moved on to **Argos**. **Elenor**, who was then reigning there, surrendered the administration of the kingdom to Danaus, who then called the people of Argos "Danai" after himself.

### DOLOPES.

The **Dolopes** lived in **Thessaly**; from them, the region of Thessaly itself and the city of **Clymene** were called "Dolopian," as noted by Apollonius of Rhodes. **Peleus** <note>The father of the famous hero Achilles.</note> once held this land, and he granted Dolopia to **Phoenix** when he came to Oeus as a kinsman; he also entrusted his young son **Achilles**, still a boy, to Phoenix to be educated. **Homer** mentions the Dolopes in this verse from the 9th book of the *Iliad*:

> *I dwelt on the frontier of Phthia, ruling over the Dolopes.*
<note>original: Ναῖον δ' ἐσχατιήω Φθίης Δολόπεσσιν ἀνάσσων.</note>

In this passage, Phoenix recounts this entire history in several verses. Therefore, since the **Myrmidons** (whom we shall discuss later) served under Achilles, and the Dolopes served under Phoenix, **Virgil** joined them in these verses from the second book of the *Aeneid*:

> — *Who, in telling such things,*
> *whether of the Myrmidons, or the Dolopes, or a soldier of harsh Ulysses,*
> *could refrain from tears?*
<note>original: "Quis talia fando / Myrmidonum, Dolopumue, aut duri miles Vlyssi / Temperet à lacrymis?"</note>

**Didymus** writes in the 11th book of the *Odyssey* that **Scyros** was a city of Dolopia. And the commentator on **Pindar** has left it on record that the Dolopes were the best **slingers** <note>Light infantry specialized in using slings to hurl stones or lead bullets with high velocity and precision.</note>.

### HELLENES.

We have previously recounted from **Thucydides** the occasion on which the Greeks were named **Hellenes**. However, **Eustathius**, in his commentary on the second book of the *Iliad*, reports that **Hellas** was a city in Thessaly that took its name from a king, and that name was later applied to all Greeks. Homer uses the names **Phthia** and **Hellas** interchangeably...
