...the lives of Homer and Herodotus. Likewise, the specific city in Greece where he was born is uncertain; the debate remains undecided among these seven Greek cities: Smyrna, Rhodes, Colophon, Salamis, Ios, Argos, and Athens, as appears in this Greek epigram:

> Seven cities contend over the roots of Homer:
> Smyrna, Rhodes, Colophon, Salamis, Ios, Argos,
> Athens, etc.
<note>original: "Ἑπτὰ πόλεις διερίζουσι περὶ ῥίζαν Ὁμήρου / Σμύρνα, Ροδος, Κολοφὼν, Σαλαμὶν, Ἴος, Ἄργος, / Ἀθῆναι, &cc."</note>

This uncertainty moved the grammarian Didymus <note>Didymus Chalcenterus, a scholar in Alexandria known for his prolific writing</note> to compose 4,000 books on the contradictions among Greek authors regarding this question, as Seneca writes in book 13 of his *Letters*, Letter 89 <note>Seneca's Moral Letters to Lucilius, typically cited today as Letter 88</note>, recounting many peculiarities of this poet. Cicero had spoken of it previously in his oration for the poet Archias. The desire to know the truth of the matter was such that the grammarian Apion did not hesitate to use <term>magic</term> to summon Homer's <term>manes</term> <note>the spirits or shades of the dead</note> for this purpose, as Pliny remarks in book 30, chapter 2.

The time in which he flourished is also uncertain: for some write that he lived in the year 3150 from the creation of the world; others say 3560. Some say 120 years after the destruction of Troy; according to Herodotus, 168 years after the said destruction; according to Crates, 80 years after; and according to Archilochus, 500 years after. Aulus Gellius in book 17, chapter 21, and Plutarch in his works say it was 140 years after the aforementioned destruction. Cornelius Nepos says 160; Solinus 272. Following Suidas and several other ancient authors—among whose number are Saint Cyril in book 1 *Against Julian*, and Philochorus in book 1 of the *Stromata* <note>a "miscellany" or "tapestry" of various topics</note>—they speak of it quite differently, as Matthew Beroalde <note>a 16th-century French chronologist</note> notes very well in book 4, chapter 5 of his *Chronicle*.

His poems or poetic works are the *Iliad*, the *Odyssey*, the *Hymns*, and the *Battle of the Frogs and Mice*. The *Iliad* was not composed by him all at once, but at several and diverse times, leaving now one book here and now another there. Being thus scattered, they were gathered and put in order, along with the books of the *Odyssey*, by Pisistratus, the Tyrant of Athens (according to Cicero in book 3 of *On the Orator*), or by his son Hipparchus, as reported by Pausanias in his *Description of Greece* and Aelian in book 8 of his *Various History*. Some other authors attribute this to Aristarchus, who, by the command of the aforementioned Pisistratus, corrected the <term>rhapsody</term> <note>the collection of epic songs</note> of this poet and was the first to divide it into 24 parts, corresponding to the number of letters in the Greek alphabet. After all these, Zenodotus of Ephesus—a grammarian, poet, and disciple of Philitas, and tutor to the children of King Ptolemy I—corrected them and put them back in order, according to the aforementioned Suidas.

These poems and poetic works are filled with many Greek words and phrases from every Greek dialect, as Plutarch discusses in his treatise on the dialects found in Homer. We read in this same author, in the *Life of Lycurgus*, as well as in Heraclides’ treatise *On States* and Aelian in the 13th book of his *Various History*, that the first person to bring these poems from Ionia to the Peloponnese—where they were in the hands of the successors of Creophylus—was Lycurgus. Solon, having collected them all, placed them in a public location with an ordinance that each book should be read and recited in order at every Greek festival, as affirmed by Julius Caesar Scaliger in book 1, chapter 41 of his *Poetics*, and Caelius <note>Lodovico Ricchieri, also known as Caelius Rhodiginus</note> in book 7, chapter 29 of his works. As for the other Greek poems or writings by Suidas and Gyraldus...

### On the Philosopher Plato and his writings composed in the Greek language.

Julius Firmicus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman senator and astrologer</note>, having taken the trouble to calculate and draw up the horoscope of the Philosopher Plato, wrote that he found through its computation that this personage was born by nature to be most eloquent, and endowed with a celestial spirit and understanding for comprehending all the secrets of the supreme divinity. To this point, the Greeks have asserted that while he was still in his cradle, a swarm of bees was found to have placed its honey within his mouth; this presaged the future eloquence of this great figure, as recounted by Aelian in book 10 of his *Various History*, Pliny in book eleven, chapter 17, and Valerius Maximus in book 1. It is even said that Socrates saw in a dream a small swan in his lap, which began to clothe itself in feathers, with the help of which, soaring into the air, it came to sing most sweetly and melodiously; and that the following day, when Plato was brought to him to be instructed, he said that this was the fulfillment of his previous dream.

This Plato was first called Aristocles, but because of his broad shoulders, high forehead, and large body—or perhaps for the breadth of his speech—he was surnamed <term>Platōn</term> <note>original: "Πλάτων"; the name derives from the Greek word "platýs," meaning broad or wide</note> Plato, as Suidas and Laertius write. He was called the "Attic honey-bee," because of which Cicero, following the Greeks, said in his *Brutus*:

> Who was more abundant in speaking than Plato? For if Jupiter were to speak Greek, as the Philosophers say, he would speak just so. <note>original: "Quis uberior in dicendo Platone? Iouem sic, ut aiunt Philosophi, si Græcè loquatur, loqui"</note>

The same author in his *Tusculan Disputations* names him the God of Philosophy. Some call him the imitator of Moses, or the "Attic Moses," as he drew many beautiful things from that Hebrew Prophet; as noted (following Numenius the Pythagorean) by Josephus in his rebuttal against Apion <note>The text incorrectly cites "Apollonie Molon," referring to the grammarian Apollonius Molon whom Josephus refutes in "Against Apion"</note>, Suidas in his dictionary, Justin Martyr in his *Exhortation*, Eusebius in his *Preparation*, Theodoret in his book *On Greek Affections*, Ficino in his *Commentaries on Plato*, and Juan Luis Vives in his commentaries on book 8, chapter 11 of Saint Augustine’s *City of God*. 

This Philosopher lived and flourished in the year of the created world 3770 <note>The author uses a chronology dating from the biblical creation, placing Plato in the 4th century BCE</note>, some time after the Peloponnesian War, and lived eighty-one years, dying around the 108th Olympiad. He was so highly prized by the Greeks that Aristocles of Messene composed ten books comparing him and Homer, according to Suidas; for this reason, Cicero calls him the "Homer of Philosophers," and Quintilian says he is filled with divine and Homeric eloquence. His Greek style, according to Aristotle, holds the middle ground between prose and verse or poetry, with such sweetness and eloquence that nothing more divine or miraculous can be imagined. This moved the Father of Latin eloquence <note>Cicero</note> to say that he would rather err with Plato than hold the correct opinion with all the other Philosophers. It is no wonder if a Cleombrotus, or another listener of Hegesias, having heard certain of his discourses concerning the immortality of the soul, killed and took their own lives in order to enjoy—

St. Augustine prized him so much that in his book *Against the Academics* he wrote that if, in the doctrine of Jesus Christ, he had to use reasons and deductions, he would seek them nowhere else but in the writings of this personage: which is more than verified by St. Dionysius the Areopagite, Eusebius, and St. Cyril, saying the Platonists were true Christians, except in a few points. This is confirmed by Symphorien Champier <note>original: "Symphorien Camperius"; a French physician and humanist who sought to harmonize ancient philosophy with Christianity</note> in his book *On the Theology of Orpheus*, supported by the authority of St. Basil, St. Augustine, and others, maintaining that in some writings of this Philosopher, the Gospel of St. John was found transcribed almost in its entirety: indeed, some ancient authors write that inside his tomb was found a plate inscribed with these words, translated into English <note>original: "tournez en François" (translated into French)</note>, *I believe in Jesus Christ who will be born of a Virgin, who will suffer for the human race, and who will rise on the third day.* Many beautiful and excellent discourses of this Philosopher are detailed after Labeo, Varro, Apuleius, and other ancients by the same St. Augustine in book 7 of his *Confessions*, and in his *City of God* book 8, reporting that this Labeo numbered Plato among the demigods, that Varro assured that Plato had felt better of divine and human things than other Philosophers, and that Apuleius had estimated Plato to be not only superior to the Heroes, but equal to the gods themselves, because he alone had entered into the inner chamber <note>original: "cabinet"</note> of the supreme divinity. His Greek writings, almost all divided and split into dialogues in which his master Socrates is always introduced speaking, treating many diverse matters, have been translated from Greek into several languages and dispersed among infinite nations, which teach us the true divine Philosophy. The great Giovanni Pico della Mirandola proposed in his life to accord and reconcile the writings of this personage with those of Aristotle, as Boethius had previously undertaken: but both remained under the burden <note>meaning they died or failed before the difficult task was completed</note> before accomplishing their promise: whoever wishes to see several other things on this matter should read Pausanias in his *Attica*, Plutarch in the *Life of Dion*, Aelian book 13 of his *Various History*, Diogenes Laertius book 3 of the *Life of the Philosophers*, Aulus Gellius book 3 chapter 17 of his *Attic Nights*, Suidas in what he collected of Plato in his Greek works, Valerius Maximus book 8 chapter 7, St. Augustine book 8 chapter 4 of the *City of God*, Cardinal Bessarion in his commentaries in praise of Plato against George of Trebizond, St. Jerome volume 3 in the *Epistle to Paulinus*, Pietro Crinito book 12 chapter 1 and book 24 chapter 1 of *On Honest Discipline*, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in his book *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente et vno"</note>, Marsilio Ficino in his *Commentaries on Plato*, Caelius Rhodiginus in infinite places of his *Various Readings*, Gessner and Josias Simmler in their *Historical Libraries*, Raffaele Volterrano book 18 of his *Commentaries*, André Thevet book 2 chapter 29 of *Illustrious Men*, and Louis Le Roy book 5 of the *Vicissitude of Things*.

->Concerning the historian Herodotus and his writings composed in the Greek language.<-

Herodotus, a Greek historian born of illustrious parents and a native of the city of Halicarnassus—now called Messy <note>Halicarnassus is the modern-day city of Bodrum, Turkey. In the 16th century, it was sometimes referred to as Mesy or Mausi.</note>, located at 57 degrees 50 minutes longitude and 36 degrees 10 minutes latitude, in the country and region of Caria in Asia Minor—flourished around the year 3699 since the creation of the world. <note>This "Year of the World" (Anno Mundi) system, common in Renaissance scholarship, places Herodotus in the 5th century BCE.</note> Cicero, in the third book of *The Orator* and the first of his *Laws*, calls him the **Prince and Father of History** <note>original: "Principem & Patrem historiæ"</note>, because he is among the most eloquent and one of the most ancient historians among the Greeks. Strabo, in his final book, held the opinion that he wrote a false and fabulous history rather than a true and certain one, partly drawn and extracted from the Greek histories of one Xanthus the Lydian <note>A 5th-century BCE historian who wrote a history of Lydia (Lydiaca) and preceded Herodotus.</note>, who was older than he. This work is contained in nine books under the name of the **nine Muses**: which history he began to compose in the Ionic Greek language while living on the island of Samos, where he had been exiled by Lygdamis, the tyrant of Halicarnassus. Besides this history, he wrote a compendium or brief discourse in the Greek language on the **life of Homer**. These works have been translated from Greek into Latin by several and various authors, as taught by Conrad Gesner and Josias Simler in their historical bibliographies. Lucian, a Greek author, in his dialogue titled *Herodotus, or Aetion*, strove to recount how he became known in a short time to all the Greeks. Quintilian, in book 9, chapter 14 of his *Institutes*, following Aristotle’s discourse in his *Poetics*, wrote these words in praise of the Greek Histories of this personage:

> In Herodotus, while everything—as I feel it—flows smoothly, the dialect itself possesses such a charm that it seems to embrace even hidden musical rhythms. <note>original Latin: "In Herodoto cum omnia vt sentio leuiter fluant, tum ipsa dialectos habet eam iucunditatem, vt latentes etiam numeros complexa videatur."</note>

And in book 10, chapter one:

> Many have written history excellently: Thucydides is dense, brief, and always driving himself forward; Herodotus is sweet, clear, and expansive. The former is better at portraying stirred emotions, the latter at relaxed ones; the former is superior in formal speeches, the latter in conversational ones; the former in force, the latter in pleasure. <note>original Latin: "Historiam multi scripsere præclarè, densus & breuis & semper instans sibi Thucidides, dulcis & candidus & effusus Herodotus, Ille concitatis hic remissis affectibus melior; ille concionibus, hic sermonibus, ille vi, hic voluptate."</note>

This personage died having gone into exile at Thurii, one of the colonies of the Athenians, and was buried there. Some hold that it was in the city of Pella or Ieuize in Macedonia. See Cicero in his *Orator*; Strabo, book 14; Plutarch, *On the Malice of Herodotus*; Suidas in his works; Pliny, book 12, chapter 14; Athenaeus, book 12, chapter 14 of his *Deipnosophists* <note>Literally "The Banquet of the Learned," an ancient Greek work detailing a series of dinner table conversations.</note>; Aulus Gellius, book 15, chapter 23; Guillaume Budé in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*, citing Hermogenes; Jean Pontanus in one of his epistles on this author; Henri Estienne in his *Apology for Herodotus*; Victorius, book 28, chapter 21 of his *Variae*; Gilbert Génébrard, book 2 of his *Chronography*; Jean Bodin, chapter four of his *Method of History*; François de Belleforest, volume two, chapter seven of his *Universal Cosmography*; and Antoine du Verdier, book 2 of his *Prosopography*.

### On the Orator Demosthenes and his writings composed
### in the Greek language.

Those who wish to be fully informed of the parents, country, and Greek city from which this great Greek orator Demosthenes was born, should read Plutarch in the *Life of Demosthenes*, and in his treatise on the *Lives of the Ten Orators*, as well as Suidas in his works. <note>Demosthenes (384–322 BCE) is widely considered the greatest of the ancient Greek orators. "Suidas" refers to the Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> This figure, a native of Athens, was aided and served in his life by the Greek orations of a certain Zoilus, or Zethus of Amphipolis, and of a Polycrates and Alcidamas, who were disciples of Gorgias and Isocrates. <note>These men were famous rhetoricians and teachers of the 5th and 4th centuries BCE who shaped the art of persuasion.</note> With these orations, he progressed so far in the oratorical art that he acquired in his time such a reputation as an eloquent man in the Greek tongue that no one before or since has been able to match him. He was a disciple of Plato, whom he heard for some time, and was a friend of Aristotle; he was so accomplished in Greek eloquence that he was esteemed to be the rule and the law of speaking well and orating well in that language. There is such force in his words, and they are so well arranged and ordered, that one could add nothing to them nor take anything away. For in the legal cases he handled and the orations he wrote, one could find no subtlety or cleverness that is not included there, nor anything more lofty, grave, eloquent, or better adorned and set down in writing that is not encountered at every turn, as Cicero maintains in his *Brutus*. <note>Cicero’s *Brutus* is a history of Roman oratory that frequently uses Greek orators as the gold standard.</note> Moreover, there are no principles for governing a Republic that cannot be found within them. These works tend not only toward utility, but toward honor and integrity, so much so that Plato and Aristotle are not found to have philosophized better in their schools than he did in the public assemblies of Athens around the year 3780 from the creation of the world. <note>This "Year of the World" (Anno Mundi) date is a Renaissance calculation placing him in the 4th century BCE.</note> This we can easily see in his beautiful arguments and Greek orations printed in several places, which comprise a large, entire volume remaining from his other writings. This is why a certain person, greatly admiring the orations proceeding from the admirable torrent of eloquence from this man's mind, one day asked Cicero—the most articulate and eloquent man of his century—which of Demosthenes' orations seemed to him the best. He replied that the longest and the greatest was the one most to be prized. Saint Jerome said this brief word about him in Latin: *Demosthenes is said to have spent more oil than wine, and to have always preceded all craftsmen with his nocturnal vigils.* <note>original: "Plus olei quàm vini expendisse dicitur Demosthenes, & omnes opifices nocturnis semper vigiliis præuenisse." This refers to the anecdote that Demosthenes' speeches "smelled of the lamp," meaning they were the product of intense late-night study rather than drunken inspiration.</note> Cicero, cited above, although a great and perfect Latin orator himself, held him in such high regard and esteem that he judged him to have possessed within himself all the arts of speaking well and excellently—which all those who attentively contemplate his writings in the Greek language will confess. See what is written of this Orator by Lucian in his *Praise of Demosthenes*; Libanius the Sophist in the *Life of Demosthenes*; Ulpian the Rhetorician in his prefaces to the *Orations of Demosthenes*; Caecilius Siculus in his comparison of Demosthenes and Cicero; Pausanias in his *Description of Greece*; Quintilian in Book 10, Chapter 1; Cicero in his discourses titled *Brutus* and *On the Orator*; Aulus Gellius in Book 3, Chapter 13 and the last chapter of Book 17; Plutarch in his comparison of Cicero with Demosthenes; Guillaume Budé in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*; and Caelius. <note>Guillaume Budé was a 16th-century French humanist; Caelius likely refers to the scholar Lodovico Ricchieri.</note>

Philosophy—which Cicero in book 1 of *On Duties* and the *Tusculan Disputations* calls the "Love of wisdom" <note>original: "Amour de sapience," translating the Latin *philosophia*.</note> and the desire for it, and that which seeks virtue and drives away vice—was brought to Greece, as they say, by the Greeks who learned it from barbarian and foreign nations. For previously, that which is now called Philosophy was called "Sophia" <note>original: "Sophie," from the Greek word for wisdom.</note>, and those who are now called Philosophers were called "Sophoi" <note>original: "Sophes," from the Greek word for wise men.</note>. But one must not think that there was ever a man so devoted to his particular tongue that he did not mix some words and dialects of other languages among his works. Indeed, the more learned a man was, the more he scattered diverse words, chosen from the most learned of each nation, throughout his writings. Plutarch, in a book on the life of Homer, shows this at length when he gives an ample discourse on the verses of this excellent Greek Poet, whom he praises for the variety of dialects and Greek language recognized in his poetry; so much so that the Ionians, Dorians, Aeolians, and Attics can see therein how excellent this personage was, who, like a honeybee, <note>A classic metaphor for a scholar who gathers the best "nectar" from many sources to create a unified work.</note> had gathered the flowers of all their languages together. I feel the same about all the idioms of the nations to which the Greek language was once spread; for it was celebrated not only in Greece <note>original: "Hellade"</note> alone, but also in Epirus, the Peloponnese, Illyria, Macedonia, Thrace, in Asia Minor, and in Syria—where there were most eloquent men in the Greek tongue, such as Philo, Josephus, and many others. Now, if this Greek language was once held in such high regard, this can teach us: that all the most excellent men of whatever foreign nation under Heaven have striven to possess knowledge of it. Regarding this, Herodotus in Book 2 writes that Psammetichus, King of the Egyptians, brought Greeks to Egypt to teach the children of his subjects Greek letters and the Greek language. Among the Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people from the Eurasian Steppes.</note> (according to Herodotus in Book 4), Anacharsis <note>The OCR reads "Anaxarchis," but refers to the famous Scythian philosopher.</note> the great Philosopher and Prince of a great house, brought the Greek language, knowledge, and the "computations"—or rather superstitions—of Greece to the Scythians. What is more, according to Strabo (Book 4) and Ammianus Marcellinus (Book 5), as Coelius Rhodiginus writes (Book 16, chapter 18), the people of Marseille in olden times were such lovers of this language that they had their contracts written in it. From this, it has happened that the Gallic language has retained several phrases, filled with Greek words and idioms.

The Carthaginians also loved and cherished it, as descendants of the Phoenicians and allies of the Greeks against the Romans, as Livy assures in the third decade, Book 9.

Philostratus, the Greek Sophist, in the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, writes that when this great personage went to visit the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>From the Greek for "naked wise men," these were ancient Indian philosophers who lived as ascetics.</note> or "Naked Sages" of India, he spoke to King Phraotes, whom he found so well-versed in Greek letters and sciences that he was amazed that a man considered a <term>Barbarian</term> <note>In the classical world, "Barbarian" simply referred to anyone who was not Greek or did not speak Greek.</note> had such perfect knowledge of them. He was even more astonished when he heard the philosopher Iarchas <note>The OCR reads "Iaebas."</note> discourse in the Greek language as correctly as those who were native to the land of Greece and most learned in that tongue. Roman histories assure us that Augustus Caesar devoted himself greatly to the study of Greek letters and language, and that he stayed in Greece for a long time to gain a complete and perfect knowledge of it. He succeeded to such an extent that he composed fine and beautiful verses in this Greek language and took great pleasure in speaking Greek when conversing privately with his friends, as Suetonius Tranquillus relates in the life of this Emperor Augustus. The learned Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607) was an influential Italian historian and cardinal.</note> in the first volume of his *Ecclesiastical Annals* confirms this very well, providing sure proof that the Greek language was in common use and spoken in Rome during the time of this Emperor.

And who does not well know that the Romans in general sent their children to study in Athens out of the desire they had for them to learn the Greek language? Titus, son of the Emperor Vespasian, was well-versed in both Greek and Latin letters; the Emperor Alexander Severus, while at rest after hearing petitions and doing justice for his subjects, had no occupation more agreeable than reading Greek books. According to Lampridius <note>Aelius Lampridius, one of the traditional authors of the *Augustan History*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> in his biography, while dining, if something was read to him, he preferred it to be in Greek rather than in his mother tongue. The Emperor Hadrian was devoted to it more than was reasonable; Antoninus and Aurelian, as they were very learned, also had a perfect knowledge of Greek letters. 

And what is most marvelous is what Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric who lived in Rome during the reign of Augustus.</note> recounts: that Romulus, Father of the Romans and the first King of the proud city of Rome, wrote his own deeds and the victories obtained against his adversaries in Greek. In this, one should note the desire that all have had to understand and embrace this language, the most polished and eloquent of all others. What is more, the first and most ancient Romans drew their laws to civilize their Republic from the wisdom of the Greeks; for instance, Spurius Postumius, Aulus Manlius, and Publius Sulpicius <note>These three men were part of the embassy sent to Athens around 454 BCE to study the laws of Solon before the creation of the Law of the Twelve Tables.</note> were sent to Athens to bring back its laws, as well as the ways of life, rights, and customs observed by the rest of the cities of Greece. There were also various legislators, such as the ancient King Cecrops, Draco, and Solon in Athens—one of the Seven Sages, whose laws were sought after by the Romans; Lycurgus in Lacedaemon <note>Another name for Sparta.</note>; Nicodorus in Mantinea; Zaleucus at Locri; and Minos, who gave laws and civil order to the Candiots <note>An archaic term for the inhabitants of Crete.</note>. 

But what use is it for me to say that so many great personages in olden times studied the Greek language, since the Evangelists and Apostles themselves—though Hebrews and Jews by nation, using their own Hebrew or Syriac tongue as their native and common speech—wrote the sacred books containing Christian doctrine and religion for the most part in the Greek language? This was done as much for the sweetness of the language as for the fact that almost everywhere in the world there were men instructed in it, who by this means could very easily embrace and follow the Christian religion. Furthermore, those two great Hebrew personages, Josephus and Philo—Jews by nation and learned in their Hebrew tongue above all others—nevertheless did not hesitate to write their books in Greek rather than in Hebrew, due to the perfection of that language which was so widely embraced and cherished by men of all nations. This is as Saint Jerome assures us in the preface to the second book of his *Commentaries on Galatians*. G. Génébrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine exegete and champion of the Hebrew language.</note>, on this subject in Book 1, Chapter 5, page 25 of his *Liturgy*, reported these words:

Although languages shift and change incessantly like all things in this Universe, and though in the same country and language a great difference in speaking and pronouncing appears in a short space of time, it is nonetheless true that there have always been some more elegant and eloquent than others; such as were the Athenians in Greece, and the Romans in Italy. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE #
<meta>catchword: spoke</meta>

...that of the common people was less elegant than that of men of state and more refined citizens: as one can see in the Latin of Vitruvius, who was a master mason, and of Cicero, a man of Consular rank. This author, in the third book of *The Orator* <note>Original: "De Oratore". Cicero was a Roman statesman and philosopher renowned for his rhetoric.</note>, writes that in his time, the learning of the Athenians was lost in Athens, the city remaining only as a residence for studies, which the citizens themselves did not care for, but which foreigners enjoyed, drawn there somewhat by the name and authority of the city. He notes, however, that an unlearned Athenian still surpassed the most learned men of Asia—not in his words, but in the sound of his voice—and not so much for speaking well, but for speaking sweetly. Similarly (he says), there is a certain voice proper to the Roman people and to the city, in which nothing offends or displeases, and which lacks any hint of foreignness; so much so that the Romans, though studying less than the Latins <note>The "Latins" here refers to the other peoples of the Italian peninsula who spoke Latin but were not original inhabitants of the city of Rome.</note>, surpassed the most scholarly among them through the sweetness of their voices.

The Greeks living in true Greece, Asia, Italy, Sicily, and other islands had four languages <note>The author uses "languages" where we would now say "dialects".</note> as I have said before: Attic, Doric, Aeolic, and Ionic. From these, the Greeks selected words and figures from each as they saw fit, and gave birth to one called "the Common" <note>The *Koine* Greek, which became the lingua franca of the Mediterranean after Alexander the Great.</note>. Afterward, under a single name, they called all five the Greek language.

And although the Athenian dialect was more elegant and fertile than the others, scholars who were not Athenian by birth wrote only in their natural style, fearing perhaps that they could never achieve Attic purity, which was rarely and only belatedly achieved by those born elsewhere. For Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note>, who had resided for a long time in Athens and was reputed to be highly articulate and eloquent, was recognized as a foreigner in his speech by an old Athenian woman. Pollio <note>Asinius Pollio, a Roman orator and historian.</note> likewise charged Livy <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian.</note> with "Patavinity" <term>Patavinity: A perceived provincialism in Livy's Latin, attributed to his upbringing in Padua (Patavium).</term>. And Virgil, who was from Mantua, was reproached because he did not speak "Roman."

Furthermore, the further any language wanders from its natural source, the less pure and clean it becomes. Just as in ancient times the Syrians and Egyptians speaking Greek did not speak it as purely as the Athenians, neither did the Gauls, Spaniards, or Africans speak Latin as well as the Romans. But even if their words were Greek or Latin, they retained the phrasing of their own country. Thus, when speaking Greek or Latin, they were always recognized as foreigners, just as we see today with the English, Scots, Germans, Flemings, Italians, and Spaniards speaking French, unless they learned it while very young.

Now these languages, like all human things, have a beginning, progress, perfection, corruption, and an end. They are first crude, then they become polished alongside the civility of manners and knowledge; and after having lasted some time in purity and eloquence, they are altered and corrupted, and finally they perish, until through the passage of time no trace of their writing remains. In short, the Greeks were at the beginning very coarse, as Plato, Aristotle, and Thucydides say; the first among them to become civilized were the Athenians, who polished their language and brought it to perfection. It did not remain there long, but was corrupted and lost along with the liberty of the country, supplanted by the Macedonians, Syrians, Romans, and other foreigners who ruled there. Consequently, the native character and true elegance and eloquence of Greek, such as was spoken...

## HOW AND SINCE WHAT TIME THE GREEK
### Language was known and learned in Italy, France,
### Spain, Germany, and other surrounding
### Provinces.

The strange and cruel ravages of the Arabs, Saracens, and Turks, in both Asia and Europe, drove out good letters, sciences, and disciplines from Greece, from where they withdrew to Italy and France under the guidance of several excellent individuals. Through the toil, labor, and study of these men, the sciences and doctrines—illuminated by means of the Greek language—returned to prominence and began, so to speak, to live again, having been buried and entombed in profound ignorance since the first destruction the Goths had wrought in Italy. The first who displayed and made known the value of the Greek language in Italy was a certain person named Manuel Chrysoloras <note>Manuel Chrysoloras (c. 1355–1415) was a Byzantine diplomat and a central figure in the introduction of Greek literature to Western Europe.</note>, father-in-law of Francesco Filelfo. This Manuel, having carried out his charge as best he could, stayed in Italy and taught publicly in Venice, then Florence, Rome, and finally Pavia. One can still read today a Greek grammar composed by him, printed by Wechel <note>Christian Wechel was a prominent 16th-century printer based in Paris.</note>; he died in Germany at the time of the Council of Constance. After this man came Bessarion, a native of Trebizond and Bishop of Nicaea, a Greek by nation who was created a Cardinal in Rome in the year of salvation 1438 or 1440 (according to Laonikos Chalcondyles <note>Original: "Nicolas Chalcondyle". Later, under Constantine <note>Constantine XI, the final Byzantine Emperor.</note>, he withdrew to Rome after the city of Constantinople was taken by Mehmed II, Emperor of the Turks. Some modern authors maintain that before the aforementioned Chrysoloras <note>Manuel Chrysoloras (c. 1355–1415), a pioneer in spreading Greek literature in Western Europe.</note>, Constantine Lascaris of Byzantium was the first of all the Greeks who taught his Greek letters in Italy and who composed a Greek grammar there, according to A. The successor to the aforementioned Chrysoloras was George of Trebizond <note>George of Trebizond (1395–1486) was a Greek philosopher and scholar who helped ignite the Renaissance.</note>, who kept the name of his ancestral country instead of his own surname, having been born in Candia <note>Modern-day Crete.</note> to ancestors from Pontus, a very renowned city in Greece. After these came Theodore Gaza, a gentleman of Thessaloniki, expelled from his country by the tyranny of the Great Turk Murad <note>Original: "Amurath." Likely referring to Sultan Murad II.</note>. The aforementioned George of Trebizond and Theodore Gaza were envious of one another; however, Theodore Gaza surpassed George of Trebizond in quickness of spirit, dexterity of judgment, and knowledge of the Greek and Latin languages. For he translated from Greek into Latin Aristotle’s *History of Animals* and Theophrastus’s *History of Plants* in such a way that, by first softening the harshness of the Latin words, he joined them properly and then assembled or coupled them together, following the example of the composition of the aforementioned Greek language, expressing the force and virtue of the Greek words through new Latin words very skillfully, and with such a bold and successful translation that he greatly enriched the Latin language.

He composed grammatical institutions in his language which are still seen today, as well as several other books on rhetoric and other subjects.

John Argyropoulos <note>John Argyropoulos (1415–1487) was a major figure in the revival of Greek learning in Italy.</note>, a native of Constantinople and a friend and companion of the aforementioned Theodore Gaza, was the tutor of Piero de' Medici (son of Cosimo) and of Lorenzo, his nephew; he explained the Greek authors in the city of Florence and then in Rome. Johann Capnion, called Reuchlin <note>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a German humanist and scholar of Greek and Hebrew.</note>, heard him interpreting Thucydides in the city of Rome. Speaking sometimes of the first words he had with this Argyropoulos, Reuchlin would recount the following: that having entered the hall where this great man was lecturing, as an Ambassador followed by several men, he found therein a great number of listeners, including Cardinals and both old and young men, all noble and from good houses. He bowed there to Argyropoulos, deplored the banishment of the Greeks, and told him that he desired to be one of his students. Argyropoulos asked him what country he was from and if he understood the Greek language; to which he replied that Germany was his country and that he had learned something of the Greek language. This caused Argyropoulos to ask him to read a portion of some speech by Thucydides and to explain or interpret it in the Latin language. This man, Capnion <note>Reuchlin.</note>, took the book and began to read it in a loud voice, adding the Latin exposition or interpretation instantly with a very sweet and easy pronunciation, explaining or interpreting...

...it is known that the great wisdom and providence of God ensured that the Greek language had been planted throughout the extent of this great Roman Empire shortly before the time of Emperor Julius Caesar. This occurred for no other reason or occasion than that the Evangelists and Apostles, who were to write, preach, and announce His Gospel in this language, might be more easily understood by the peoples and nations destined to receive them. For this same cause, we must believe that the same wisdom and providence of God allowed the Turks to occupy Greece in the time of our fathers, so that by means of the Greeks exiled and banished from that land—refugees who retreated to Italy, France, and Germany—the Italians, French, and Germans might recognize the most beautiful and excellent discourses and secrets of this Gospel, which was first written and composed in the Greek language. This language they then taught and learned in the form and manner that has been more particularly detailed above in this chapter.

Polydore Vergil <note>Polydorus Vergilius (c. 1470–1555), an Italian humanist scholar and historian.</note> in book 4 of the *History of England*, following Werner <note>Werner Rolevinck (1425–1502), author of the *Fasciculus Temporum*, a popular universal history.</note> in the *Bundle of Times* <note>original: "Faisceau des temps"</note>, holds that Charlemagne was the first to transport the Academy to Paris. Long before, this Academy had come from the city of Athens to that of Rome; it was moved through the ministry of four disciples of the monk Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735), an influential English scholar and monk.</note>, named Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus, a Frankish Benedictine theologian.</note>, Albinus <note>Alcuin of York, the primary scholar of Charlemagne's court.</note>, Claudius, and Johannes Scotus <note>John Scotus Erigena, an Irish Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>. This is confirmed by Erphordiensis in chapter 69 and Cardinal Francesco Zabarella <note>An Italian canonist and cardinal (1360–1417).</note> regarding the *Clementines* <note>A collection of decrees in Canon Law.</note> in the section on Masters, question 5. Gilbert Génébrard <note>A French Benedictine exegete and historian (1535–1597).</note> speaks of it amply in book 3 of his *Chronography* on leaf 519.

Our History of France records that the late King Francis I, at the persuasion of Guillaume Budé and Jean du Bellay, first established public professors of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages in the University of Paris. Specifically, for the Hebrew language, François Vatable; for Greek, Pierre Danés of Paris. To these he added others, namely Agathius Guidacerius, a doctor of the Hebrew language, and Jacques Toussain <note>Jacques Toussain (d. 1547), a renowned French scholar of Greek.</note>, a doctor of the Greek language. Later, upon the promotion of Pierre Castillan <note>Pierre Duchâtel (c. 1480–1552), a humanist who served as the king's librarian and reader.</note>, his <term>Anagnoste</term> <note>A royal reader or librarian who read aloud to the monarch.</note>, he likewise established public professors in the Latin language, according to the confirmation of Carion in book 3 and Jean du Tillet in his *Chronicle*.

...and constrained, but nevertheless diversified—or rather, to speak properly and correctly, entirely significant or mysterious—being able easily, properly, simply, and clearly to express and explain all human and divine descriptions and conceptions, just as the aforementioned Greek language does. This language consists of the beauties, perfections, eloquence, and elegances we have deduced above, principally in that it is easy and effortless to speak and pronounce, greatly satisfying the ear. It is, by the same means, copious and abundant in synonyms and all kinds of words, nouns, dictions, and verbs, with infinite other figures and phrases of eloquence and of speaking well and perfectly. For it is a most certain thing that its pronunciation is incomparably easier and simpler than that of the aforementioned Hebrew language, or any other language whatsoever, greatly delighting and ravishing the hearing with its sweetness and eloquence, and filling it also with its strength and vehemence, far better than any other language. Furthermore, it is so rich and opulent in all kinds of words, nouns, dictions, and verbs—even regarding all the arts, both liberal and mechanical—that it lends to all other languages and borrows from none. What is even more marvelous is that whenever some new thing arises that does not yet have a name, it has the means on the spot to provide and furnish it with one, without waiting for help from any other language whatsoever. This is amply confirmed by many ancient Greek authors, as well as Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist</note> in his *Onomasticon* <note>A dictionary arranged by subject matter</note>, Guillaume Budé <note>A leading French humanist (1467–1540)</note> in the first book of *On the As* <note>original: "De Asse"; a famous treatise on ancient coins and measures</note> and in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*, Henri Estienne <note>A famous French printer and classical scholar</note> throughout his *Treasury of the Greek Language* <note>original: "Theatre de la langue Grecque"; likely referring to his monumental "Thesaurus Graecae Linguae"</note>, Angelo Canini in his *Greek Grammar* printed by Morel, and Aldus Manutius <note>The famous Venetian printer and humanist (c. 1449–1515)</note> in his *Institutions of Greek Grammar*.

Theodor Bibliander <note>A Swiss Orientalist and linguist (1505–1564)</note>, in his commentary on the *Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, making a comparison of this Greek language with Latin, used these words:

> <note>original Latin: "Lingua Græca est erudita admodum & locuplex..."</note> The Greek language is extremely learned and rich; and just as the Latin language can instruct and help others with its own abundance, so Greek augments and adorns both Latin itself and others as well, and is as necessary for the perfection of Latinity as Latin is for Italian or Spanish. Nor has anyone ever been absolutely skilled in Latin speech unless he was imbued with Greek. For from the Greek tongue flowed Latin, and from Latin flowed Italian, Spanish, and French—nations for whom the Latin language was once the vernacular. And we find through usage that the Latin language becomes more fertile and eloquent through Greek, and from Latin the remaining languages of Europe, but especially those three I just listed. It would be most advantageous for these to grow accustomed to Latin speech, both so they might properly understand it (and through it, all the arts), and so they might render their own native speech purer and more opulent from it, like more abundant water derived from a fountain. Furthermore, many things are committed to memory in Greek literature—in history, the nature of things, private and public customs, medicine, and piety—which are drawn from these very sources both more easily and more purely. ❧

Genebrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine scholar and Archbishop of Aix</note>, in the third book of his *Chronography* dealing with the first century of Jesus Christ, says: **"Regarding Apostolic Traditions which, lest they slip from memory, Clement, a disciple of the Apostles, committed to books. This author treats this matter very extensively in the centuries that follow, which curious readers may see and read at their leisure. Now, the Traditions from the beginning were understood as everything passed down from mouth to mouth, from hand to hand, from one to another—much like how, in the infancy of the Church, Adam received from the very voice of his Creator and transmitted it to his successors, notably through Enoch, Methuselah, and Noah, until Abraham; and from Abraham through Jacob and Amram, to Moses. Moses was the first who (as I have already noted) recorded in writing the precepts and ordinances of the divine will, and what God requires of man here below, all within the context of a history continued in sequence from the creation of the World until the hour of his death, when the Israelites entered the land promised to them.

And thus the divine law was, from Adam until Moses, maintained by a verbal tradition from one to another—at the very least its principal points and articles. For it is not to be presumed that God would have wished to leave the human race for so long, especially the gentle and good people, without knowledge of Him; and one see clearly enough through the thread of sacred history that the ancient Patriarchs recognized and worshipped none but the one true God. This is true even though it is said in Genesis 4 that Enos <note>The grandson of Adam</note> began to invoke the name of the Lord—that is to say, more solemnly than had yet been done. And in the 26th chapter, God says in express terms to Isaac: that He will give him such and such blessings, together with his posterity, because Abraham had received His word and added to it an indubitable faith, kept His precepts, and observed His covenants, laws, statutes, and ceremonies without infringing them.

For Circumcision, which is the entrance into the Judaic law, had been practiced by Abraham long before Moses. And that which is ordained in the eighteenth chapter—to instruct his children and household in the ways of the Lord, to practice judgment and Justice—is this not repeated in several places in the law of Moses? Such as in Deuteronomy 11: **walk in the ways of the Lord and cling to Him**; and in the twenty-fourth: **Have Justice in recommendation before your God.** Likewise, there is the distinction that Jacob makes between burnt offerings <note>Holocausts</note> (which were to be entirely burned) in chapters 8 and 22, and peace offerings, of which a portion was reserved for banquetting...

<note>original: "facietis singuli quod vobis rectum videtur"</note> *Each of you shall do what seems right in your own eyes,* as it says in Deuteronomy chapter 12; these [man-made traditions] should have no place unless they serve, so to speak, as entries into the divine Word. Indeed, *every plant that our heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted,* according to Saint Matthew 15. However, this does not apply to those traditions that clarify the obscurity of the Scriptures, bringing to light what is hidden beneath the surface, and helping to imprint more deeply the love, zeal, and fear of God in our hearts—following what is said in Ecclesiasticus 24: <note>Sirach 24:31 in the Vulgate</note> *Those who explain Wisdom shall have eternal life.* For God has left several things to His Church to be perfected and accomplished in due time and at the proper occasion, as circumstances change every day. 

This can be seen in the celebration of Easter, which has been changed so many times, and in the establishment of Sunday in place of the Sabbath day, despite the Sabbath being so strictly commanded in the Decalogue and throughout the entire Mosaic Law. For although nothing is expressly ordained regarding this exchange in the Gospel, it is nevertheless accepted unanimously by all Christian Churches without any contradiction. *I have many more things to say to you,* says the Savior in Saint John 16, *but you cannot bear them now.* And Saint Augustine, writing to Casulanus, posits that in matters where Holy Scripture has specified nothing expressly, or which is not manifest enough, the usage and observation of the faithful and the statutes of the ancients must be held as having the status of Law. Furthermore, in his treatise on the Christian faith, he says that the entire Catholic Church spread far and wide is governed either by the authority of Scripture, by traditions admitted by universal approval, or by particular constitutions adapted to the diversity of places and the temperament of the inhabitants. 

Thus, the Scriptures were not given to us with such a narrow and rigorous restriction that we must receive, believe, hold, or observe nothing unless it is found there in express terms. Rather, they were given to establish an unvarying foundation upon which we can seat and plant a firm and assured bulwark for our belief against all the batteries and assaults of sects, heresies, fantastic inventions, and curious novelties, with which the evil spirit incessantly strives to disturb the peace of our souls and consciences. And are there not many lost books that we could not deny if they were in our sight, from which the ancient Fathers were able to draw the greater part of their traditions? Such as, among others, the Epistle to the Laodiceans by Saint Paul, mentioned by him in the last chapter of Colossians: <note>original: "Ea quæ Luodicentiū est, vobis legatur"</note> *Let that which is from the Laodiceans be read to you.* Also, in the Old Testament in Numbers 21: *The Books of the Wars of the Lord*; in Joshua 10: *The Book of the Just* <note>The Book of Jashar</note>; and in 2 Kings 1. Furthermore, in the first book of Chronicles 29, the books of Samuel, Nathan, and Gad, and several others which I mentioned previously in the chapter on the Kabbalah of the Hebrews. If these were not lost, they would be canonical for us, as they are approved by those who cite them. 

The ancient Fathers also saw fit to remove certain works from the New Testament without being rebuked, such as the Gospels of Saint Bartholomew, Philip, Thaddaeus, and Nicodemus. ->LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.<-

...the infallible promise of our Savior in Saint Matthew 28: *Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the age.* Therefore, it was very wisely ordained at the sixth Ecumenical Council of Constantinople in the year 681—where the Emperor was present and a certain reconciliation and agreement was made between the Greek Church and the Latin Church—that if any dispute should arise regarding the understanding of the Scriptures, no one should presume to interpret them otherwise than the lights of the Church have understood from the explanations given in their writings. We should seek the praise of adhering to them rather than anything that might come from our own workshops and inventions; for fear that in giving ourselves free rein, we might fail to achieve what we intend in our projects.

This conforms to what is expressly ordained in Deuteronomy 17: *If you perceive any difficulty and doubt in the judgment you are to pronounce, go to the place the Lord your God has ordained for you to find the Priests and Levites. Once you have been informed by them, you shall follow their opinion. And whoever is so arrogant and presumptuous as to refuse to obey what the Priest, appointed then to the ministry of the Lord your God, has decided, that man shall be put to death, and this evil shall be removed from Israel.* 

Because the malice of the enemy and the instability of our own brains cast us down at every hour without us knowing where, making us grope against the double-edged blade of the scriptures, we need a sure and faithful escort in this to lead us through this darkness toward the understanding of divine things. In regard to the human spirit, this works much like sight does for the body: if you try to strain it too much to penetrate further, or to reach something smaller and finer than the capacity of your eye allows, not only will it fail to grasp its target, but it will weaken its own strength and remain more sluggish in the future. 

In the same way, those who wish to excessively stretch their thoughts and meditation to reach the knowledge of something will debilitate their understanding; they will even make themselves less capable than they used to be. It is just as if one tried to look directly at the sun with a steady eye, without anything interposed between the two—such as a veil <note>original: "crespe," a thin silken fabric</note> or a cloth sieve <note>original: "estamine," a loosely woven fabric used for filtering</note>—to soften the overly vivid penetration of its rays. Those rays, being incomparably more powerful, would extinguish the light of the eyes. Therefore, we must soberly keep within the barriers of modesty limited for us in the understanding of the scriptures, where each person, according to their capacity and vocation, must seek a middle path. This can be no surer than what the universal consent of the Church prescribes for us, without straying from the obedience we owe it. 

Nor should we be curious to know more than we ought, as says Ecclesiastes 7, and the Apostle in Romans 11: *Do not be high-minded, but fear.* <note>original Latin: "Noli altum sapere, sed time." This is a famous warning against intellectual pride.</note> For once that boundary is broken, a terrible opening is made for infinite erroneous opinions, which then crowd into our souls and consciences—just as enemies would in large groups through the breach of a fortress, or the fury of a torrent across the fields if the dike or sluice holding it back should break, however slightly.

->Concerning the Armenians.<-

### CHAP. LXIII.

Strabo, in book 11 of his *Geography*, left a written record stating that Armenia formerly took its name from a Thessalian named Armen, a native of a city in Thessaly called Armenia. This city was situated between Pherae and Larissa. This Armen followed Jason on his voyage; after returning from Greece, he went back to the Levant <note>A historical term for the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East.</note> and conquered the Provinces of Mingrelia, Georgia, and Albania <note>This refers to Caucasian Albania, an ancient kingdom in the eastern Caucasus, not the modern Balkan country.</note>, which he populated and instructed in the superstitions of the Greeks. After Jason died, this Armen gathered the troupe of Greeks and caused the settlement of this province. From this, it happened that in ancient times the Armenians dressed, armed themselves, and spurred their horses in the manner of the Thessalians, as Justin seems to confirm in book 42 of his *Histories*. Some authors hold that Armenia was so named after the Arameans or Syrians, of whom we have previously spoken at length; they were the first to settle there, according to Guillaume Postel in his discourse on the distinguished regions that took their names from the children of Noah, and André Thevet in book 8, chapter 13 of his *Cosmography*. Others say it was named from these Hebrew words ארם מן יה <term>Aram Min Iah <note>original: "Aram Min Iah"; translating to 'Highland from God' or 'Height of God'.</note></term>, and by contraction *Armenia*, meaning the height of God. At present, this province is still called Armenia, or *Aremnoe*, without having lost its ancient name. It is true that the learned Abraham Ortelius, in his *Geographical Synonyms*, wrote the following words about it:

Arias [Montanus] in his Biblical Appendix testifies that it is called *Arias* in Hebrew. It is called Turcomania by Mercator and Girava. Thevet writes that it is called *Thoura Aremnoe*—that is, the mountains of Armenia—by the Mesopotamians and Persians, and is called *Zelbiodibes* by the Nestorians—that is, mountains inhabited by wolves. I would believe that it retains its ancient name among the Christian inhabitants. Lesser Armenia is nicknamed "the First" in the book of *Notitiae*. ## *On the Armenian Language.*

### CHAPTER LXII.

Theodore Bibliander, in his *Commentary on the Common Reasoning of All Languages and Letters*, speaking of the language and letters of the Armenians, says the following, following Haiton the Armenian, who flourished in the year of Salvation 1300:

The Armenians have Armenian letters, and others which are called Haloen <note>Likely referring to the Caucasian Albanian script, often associated with Armenian history</note>. And because there are a thousand bishops joined to their Patriarch, whom they call the <term>Catholicos</term> <note>The title of the head of the Armenian Apostolic Church</note>, all called Christians; and in order to clearly demonstrate in how many places and provinces the use of the Armenian language extends, I will cite here the very words of Haiton the Armenian in his histories, saying that in the land of Armenia there are four kingdoms, possessed throughout time by one single and unique King. This Haiton, in chapter 9, speaking of these Armenians, says: "They have Armenian letters, and others also which are called Haloen" <note>original Latin: "Literas habent Armenicas, & alias etiam quæ dicuntur Haloen."</note>. That the ancient language of the Armenians agrees closely with the Chaldean and Syriac languages is verified as much by the origin of these Armenians, who are descended from Aram, son of Shem <note>Referring to the biblical table of nations in Genesis</note>, as by the proper names of men, places, and other arguments. Guillaume Postel, a very learned man in this language, speaks thus of this tongue which was in use among these Armenians in the time of the aforementioned Haiton, and which is still used among them today: "Among all the languages of this Universe, Armenian is the most difficult to pronounce, since it has many things in common with the languages of the Orientals, many others with that of the Greeks, and many others still with that of the Gauls <note>Postel was known for attempting to link Armenian phonology to French/Gaulish</note>." Theseus Ambrosius <note>Teseo Ambrogio (1469–1540), an Italian humanist and early scholar of Oriental languages</note>, in his *Introduction to the Chaldean, Syriac, Armenian, and ten other different languages*, chapter 13, writes the following words about this language:

» We believe it is known not only to all those engaged in the literary arena of the Pagans, but also to those who read the volumes of the sacred scriptures of the New and Old Instrument <note>The New and Old Testaments</note>, that Armenia is a province of Asia situated between the Taurus and Caucasus mountains. For, to omit Ptolemy, Solinus, Dionysius, Stephanus, Virgil, Lucan, and many other authors, we have it written in the book of Genesis, chapter 8: *And the Ark of Noah rested in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, upon the mountains of Armenia.* And in 4 Kings 19 <note>In modern English Bibles, this is 2 Kings 19:36-37</note>: *And Sennacherib, King of the Assyrians, returned and stayed in Nineveh, and while he was worshipping in the temple of Nesrach his God, Adramelech and Shareser his sons struck him with the sword and fled into the land of the Armenians, and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.* The Hebrew script calls this land <term>Eretz Ararat</term> <note>original: ארץ אררט</note>, that is, the land of Ararat. And we also have the land of Ararat in the book of the Prophet Isaiah, chapter 37; and what the Hebrew script has in Genesis chapter 8, <term>Galhare Ararat</term> <note>original: על הרי אררט; "upon the mountains of Ararat"</note>, the Arabic text has as follows: <term>Alai Gbal Pharda</term>, "upon the mountains of Pharda." In it is the river Tigris and the Araxes, of which Lucan says in book 6: *The Roman drinks from the Armenian Araxes.* This region is divided into Greater and Lesser Armenia, as the same poet Lucan hints, saying:
» ->Nor you, peoples wandering through both Armenias.<-
» <note>original Greek: Α᾿ρμενία Χώρα πλησίον τῇ Περσῶν</note> "Armenia," says Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century geographer</note>, "is a country near the Persians." For the Armenians obey and are subject in temporal matters to the King of the Persians, who is commonly called *El Sophi* <note>The Safavid Shah of Persia</note>. In spiritual matters, however, they are led by the Patriarch Simas, who pays obedience to Prester John <note>A legendary Christian monarch of the East, often confused with the rulers of Ethiopia or Central Asian tribes</note>, the pontiff of the Indians. Moreover, the Armenians are Christians commonly called "of Saint Thomas of the Belt" <note>original: Sancti Thomae de la Cintura</note>, and they assert that they live according to the rite of the Roman Church. In recent years, the Ottoman Emperor of the Turks took the great city of Armenia, Troisa <note>likely referring to Erzurum</note>, by force, and once captured, he destroyed it, consumed by fire and sword. He cruelly slaughtered all Christians of both sexes over forty years of age like cattle, and led all the others into captivity. He sold some of them under the spear <note>at auction</note>, and some he still holds captive, bound by the promised price of redemption. John, a noble citizen of Troisa, testifies to this; he and those who arrived with him in Italy a little while ago to redeem the captives, prostrated themselves humbly at the feet of the Supreme Pontiff Paul <note>Pope Paul III</note>, and suppliantly beg for alms through the churches and the streets of the cities. This great and learned figure in all languages, Guillaume Postel <note>A famous French Renaissance polymath (1510–1581) who traveled the Levant and wrote extensively on Middle Eastern languages</note>, in his treatise on the twelve different languages and their characters, speaks of this language as follows:

> The Armenian language is not only used for holy matters among the Armenians living today in both Greater and Lesser Armenia (as it is commonly written), but also among all the peoples to whom the Alcoran <note>The Quran</note> of Muhammad is preached and proclaimed. This includes the peoples of all Asia Minor, Syria, Tartary, and Persia; even among the peoples of the Pontic Sea (which is called the Black or Great Sea), and principally among the inhabitants of the Tauric Chersonese <note>The Crimea</note>. These Armenians live today entirely free and independent among the Muslims and followers of Muhammad because they possess (as they say) a certain privilege of complete exemption and liberty, never to serve the aforementioned Muslims. This was formerly granted to them by the Prophet Muhammad, in memory and reward for the kindness he received during his life from those of this nation.

This was because Muhammad was humanely received by the people of this nation, along with his army and veteran soldiers, when returning from the expedition of the son of the King of Persia, Khosrow <note>Khosrow II, the last great Sasanian king</note>, made into Asia by the Emperor Heraclius <note>Byzantine Emperor who reigned 610–641 AD</note>. 
>

At that time, when the monks paraded this privilege too boldly before the Sultan of Egypt (whom the said Selim defeated), the Prince had the privilege brought before him and stripped them of it entirely. This privilege was such (as the Armenians commonly recite and the Turks affirm) that after five or six Arabic words, there was the form or figure of a hand, with its fingers dipped in ink, printed and depicted upon it—just like the one the aforementioned Armenians currently possess.

These Armenians pray to God in the manner of the Muslims, namely on their knees, kissing the earth three times (unlike the Turks, however, who only kiss it twice). They were tainted by the Nestorian error <note>The followers of Nestorius, who emphasized the distinction between Christ's human and divine natures; a common label for Eastern Christians by Roman Catholics at the time</note> until the time of the Pontificate of Eugene III <note>Pope from 1145–1153</note>, at which time, having abjured that error, they partially placed themselves under the subjection of the Roman Church. The Greeks hold them in such capital enmity that they would much prefer, if the law permitted it, to contract a marriage with a Jew or a Turk than with them. They allege two causes for this capital enmity: first, that they were formerly infected with a very great heresy, and second, that they recognized the Roman Church, which these Greeks do not hold or repute to be the true Christian and Catholic Church. Armenia, moreover, as has been said above, has for a very long time been divided into two: the Greater and the Lesser. [...of the] Greeks only one <note>The text likely refers to the "tonsure," a ritual shaving of the head for clergy</note>: and they have a large and wide crown at the top of the head, with the rest of their hair hanging down all around as long as it can grow, and the beard likewise, in the manner of the <term>Nazareans</term> <note>A term used here to refer to those who take a vow to leave hair and beard uncut, similar to the biblical Nazarites</note>: for they never trim anything away except the aforementioned tonsure, which the secular people also wear in the same place, but traced in the form of a cross. This has been the case since the year 744 when, finding themselves greatly harassed by war with the Syrians, they were admonished in a revelation to adopt this style of dress, after which they immediately defeated their enemies. Their priests are very venerable and as reformed as any others: and although their divine service is closer to Latin ceremonies than to Greek ones, even regarding the shape of their chalices and patens, they nevertheless celebrate in their vernacular, and the congregation responds in the same. When the Gospel is sung, they all stand up and kiss one another on the cheek as a sign of reconciliation, peace, and brotherly love, as the ancient Christians used to do when they gave the *Kiss of Peace* <note>original: "Osculum Pacis"</note>. Their Eucharist is <term>azyme</term> <note>unleavened bread</note> like ours—that is to say, made of dough without leaven—in the form of a round host. Once it is consecrated, they place it on the paten and thus raise it and show it to the people, and subsequently the Chalice, which is made either of crystal or of wood, and they add no water to the wine. They have young children confirmed by a simple priest; they do not receive the orders of Deacon or Subdeacon, but only the priesthood. They do not feast on the Nativity of our Lord as we do, but fast austerely on 그날; in return, they solemnize with great devotion the day of Epiphany, which they take for His spiritual birth, believing that on this same day He was baptized by Saint John in the river Jordan. They perform their prayers and orations almost in the fashion of the Turks or Arabs, crouching low on their heels, and they kiss the earth three times; whereas the Turks do so only twice, and the Greeks pray standing upright. Of all the saints, they hold in greatest reverence the Apostle Saint James the Greater, whom they consider their protector and patron. They have a very beautiful church for him in Jerusalem, built near the place where he was beheaded, and others as well, where they assemble in great numbers, as confirmed by the Lord of Villamont in book 2, chapter 23 of his *Travels*. As for Lent, they observe it at the same time as we do, but much more austerely beyond comparison, for they drink no wine and eat nothing whatsoever that has had life—not even butter or oil, nor any other flavorful liquid—but live only on herbs and some thin legume soups seasoned only with a little salt, dried olives (not preserved), and similar things of little taste or appetite. Finally, they have their own separate cemeteries, as do all the other sects and religions. Their common and vulgar speech is <term>Turkish</term>: and their writing is <term>Arabic</term>, because they converse and trade among them. But in their divine service, and in their private talk and business, they use their own particular language and characters, of which there are two kinds, one older than the other, as Josafa Barbaro notes very appropriately in his *Travels to Persia*, chapter 17, saying,

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE

Modern reports coming from the Levant and Italy state that the Primate, otherwise called the Grand Catholicos <note>original: "grand Catholique," referring to the *Catholicos*, the head of the Armenian Apostolic Church</note> of these Armenians, has the custom every seven years of sending a monk to Rome to offer the obedience they have promised and sworn to His Holiness. It is true that if, within the seven years mentioned above, this Primate or Grand Catholicos happens to die and another is created in his place, this new Primate or Grand Catholicos must offer a new oath of obedience for his investiture. In the year 1592, during the time of Pope Clement VIII, the Patriarch of Armenia and the Maronites of Mount Lebanon came to Rome to offer their obedience to the Holy Apostolic See, according to the author of the *Appendix to the Chronography* by Gilbert Génébrard <note>A prominent 16th-century French scholar and Benedictine archbishop</note>.

Whoever wishes to learn this Armenian language should carefully read the introduction by Teseo Ambrogio <note>original: "Theſeus Ambroſius," a 16th-century Italian humanist known for his work on Oriental languages</note> regarding the Chaldean, Syriac, and Armenian languages, chapter 13, *On Armenian Letters and Introduction* <note>original: "de Armeniorum literis, & introductione"</note>.

### The Lord's Prayer in the Armenian Language.

*Chair mer vr hierchins des ſrboi eziſt anoncho ekeſſe archaiotai cho, eziſiu chan Kch vrbis Kierkins ie & chri zachas mer hanaba gſord tour mez ais aur ie touz mer zaabartis mer vrbis ie mech teſſumo bart banas merus ie mi tamir zame zprtz tai ail phirkai zamer i zare. Amen.*

This prayer was taken from the writings of modern travelers and cosmographers, who seem not to have had a true and complete knowledge of this Armenian language, since within it, one must pronounce the said prayer as I have it before me in Armenian characters and language:

*Hair mer or iercins des ſurb, eglizzi anuncho eceſzze archaiuthai cho, eglizzin camch cho orpas iercins eu iercri. Zhazt mer hanapazord tur mez aiſaur eu thogl mez zpaartis, mer orpas eu inech thoglumch inerozi partpanazt eu mi tanir zmezi phorxuthai ail pharceai zmezi zara zi cho e archaiuthai eu zauruthai eu pharch iauiteans. Amen.*

> Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, thy will be done, as in heaven so on earth. Give us this day our supersubstantial bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors, and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen. <note>original: "Pater noſter qui es in cœlis..." This is the standard Latin Vulgate version of the Lord's Prayer.</note>

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF LANGUAGES

...bordering on **Illyria** and **Liburnia**, it is commonly called **Slavonia** by nearly all nations of the world. And whatever fields lie across the Sava river on the way toward Italy are named **Croatia**; the Germans pronounce it *Krabaten*. Tacitus, in the third book of his *Annals*, mentions the **Dalmatian sea** in this vicinity.

**Illyricum** (in Pliny), *Illyris* <gloss>original: "Ιλλυρὶς"</gloss> (in Ptolemy), **Illyria** (in Stephanus), and *Hilluricus* (found on an ancient stone). A coin of Trajan Decius <note>Roman Emperor, r. 249–251 AD</note> mentions the "people of Illyricum." According to geographers, this is a vast region of Europe stretching far and wide. However, Pliny does not see it so, for he constricts it between the Arsia and Titius rivers; that region described by Pliny could today be called **Slavonia** in Italian, and **Windenland** in German. Lazius <note>Wolfgang Lazius, a 16th-century Viennese historian and physician</note> mistakenly imagines it was called *Quirinal Illyricum* based on an ancient inscription, in which he suggests a triumph was held by the Illyrians during the festival of the Quirinalia <note>A Roman festival honoring the god Quirinus</note>. It is common in the books of the *Triumphal Records* <note>The Fasti Triumphales</note> to add the specific day the triumph was celebrated. For more on Illyricum, read Appian, Sextus Rufus, Jordanes, the *Register of Offices* <note>original: "lib. Notitiar.", referring to the Notitia Dignitatum, a document of the late Roman Empire's administrative organization</note>, and Lazius (Book 1, Chapter 1), in whose works you will find many regions included under the name Illyricum; see also **Pannonia**.

**Albania**, a region of Asia <note>referring to Caucasian Albania, located in the eastern Caucasus, not the modern Balkan country</note>, called *Albania* <gloss>original: "Αλβανία"</gloss> by Ptolemy, is called **Zuiria** by Girolamo Ruscelli and Alfonso Adriano, and **Chipiche** by Giacomo Castaldi. Domenico Niger writes that it is called **Zitracha** by its inhabitants and **Garzena** by others.

**Colchis** <gloss>original: "κολχὶς"</gloss> <note>An ancient region on the eastern coast of the Black Sea, famous in myth as the destination of Jason and the Argonauts</note> is a region of Asia whose inhabitants are called **Lazos** <gloss>original: "λαζοὺς"</gloss> by Procopius, Gregoras, Suidas, and Isaac Tzetzes. Lycophron calls it *Ligystican Colchis* <gloss>original: "λιγυστικὴν"</gloss>. Stephanus of Byzantium reads it as *Libystine* with a "B" in this passage of Lycophron. The same Stephanus records the *Libystine* peoples as adjacent to Colchis. Herodotus also places the **Ligyian** peoples in this area, and Stephanus mentions the city of **Ligystice** among them. Marius Niger writes that Colchis was previously called **Arimana**, citing Appian as a witness. He also says it is divided by more recent authors into two provinces: namely **Mingrelia**, where it reaches the sea, and **Laxia**, which is inhabited further down. I believe these are the *Laxios* of Herodotus, or the *Lazas*, and the *Manralos* who are placed in Colchis by Ptolemy. Moletius reports that Colchis, Albania, and Iberia are today called by the single name **Comania**. Ogier de Busbecq <note>A 16th-century Flemish diplomat to the Ottoman Empire</note> writes in his third letter that the Colchians are today called **Mingrellians** by the Italians. He says in the same place that the Albaros and Iberians are called **Georgians**, and he describes Colchis skillfully here. Furthermore, the Sixth Council of Constantinople shows that this was called **Lazica** a few centuries ago, stating: "Theodorus, the unworthy Bishop of Phasis in Lazica." No one is unaware that **Phasis** is in Colchis. Colchis is also a city of Greater Armenia according to Ptolemy. See **Messeuia**.

**Macedonia**, a celebrated region of Greece, was previously called **Emathia** <gloss>original: "ημαθία"</gloss>, as attested by Pliny and Trogus. Livy writes in his 40th book that it was first called **Paeonia**, and then **Aemonia**. It was also called **Edonia** and **Pieria** according to Solinus. Trogus writes that it was once called **Boeotia** (Book 7); Stephanus and Hesychius write that a part of it was once called **Macetia** <gloss>original: "μακετία"</gloss>, and Eustathius reports in his commentary on Dionysius that the whole region took its name from there. The people were called the **Macetae**; Trogus calls them **Pelasgians**. In later centuries, a part of it was called **Salutaris** in the *Register of Offices*, which is ascribed partly to Macedonia and partly to Dacia. Also **Praevalis**, or **Praevalitana**, according to Sextus Rufus. There is also **Maritime Macedonia** in Dio, which he says is inhabited by the Paeonians around Mount Rhodope. This is called the "First Region of Macedonia" in Livy (Book 45), for he there divides Macedonia into four regions. A part also...
