This text, attributed to Pseudo-Clement, describes the "Table of Nations" and the belief that 72 angels govern the 72 legendary nations of the world, with Michael protecting Israel.</note> St. Basil in his third book and St. Dionysius the Areopagite in chapter 9 of his *Celestial Hierarchy*, <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-century theologian whose work on the ranks of angels (Seraphim, Cherubim, etc.) was foundational for medieval thought.</note> and several other ancient Greek and Latin theologians speak of this very well and excellently, just as I noted in chapter 21 of my discourse on the *Truth of the causes and effects of the decays, mutations, changes, conversions, and ruins of Monarchies, Empires, Kingdoms, and Republics*. On this subject, one may also see what was written afterward by Giovanni Pico in book 4, chapter 4 of his books *Against the Astrologers* and in the second prologue of his *Hexaplus*, <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a famous Renaissance philosopher and kabbalist.</note> as well as Gianfrancesco Pico in his book *On the Providence of God*, chapter 6; Guillaume Postel in book 1, chapter 2 of his *Oriental Histories*; and Pierre Grégoire in Volume 4, chapter 11 of his *Commentaries on the Syntax of the Admirable Art*.

These discourses have moved several ancient and modern theologians and philosophers—relying on the passages cited above and according to the assurances of Josephus in book 2 *Against Apion the Grammarian*—to say that one cannot achieve victory over any Monarchy, Empire, Kingdom, Republic, or City unless the *Genie* <term>Genie: A guardian spirit or tutelary deity (from the Latin 'genius') believed to protect a specific person or place.</term> or guardian Angel, protector, and patron of that place has first been "evoked" <term>evocatio: A Roman ritual 'calling out' the protector deity of an enemy city to entice them to switch sides.</term>. Following this example, the Romans—as noted by Pliny in book 3, chapter 5, and more clearly in book 28, chapter 2, following Verrius Flaccus—had a custom during the sieges of cities. Before making any final assault, the priests would evoke the protector God of the place, promising them greater honors in Rome. This is what Furius Camillus did with the Goddess Juno at the capture of Veii, as recorded in the fifth book of Titus Livius <note>Livy (Titus Livius) was a Roman historian; he describes how Camillus invited Juno of Veii to relocate to a new temple on the Aventine Hill in Rome.</note>. For this reason, for fear that the same might be done to them, the Romans kept the true name of their city secret; so much so that Soranus, for having dared to divulge it, died on the spot, as witnessed by Plutarch in his 61st *Roman Question*.

Macrobius, speaking of this entire matter in book 3, chapter 9 of his *Saturnalia*, writes most excellently that he had once read in the fifth book of *Hidden Things* by Sammonicus Serenus the following words used to evoke the *Genie* or guardian Angel, protector, and patron of cities:

> Whether you be a god or a goddess, in whose protection the people and city are, and you especially, who have taken up the protection of this city and people, I pray and venerate you, and I ask pardon from you, that you might desert this people and city; leave their places, temples, sacred things, and city, and depart from them. Cast fear, dread, and oblivion into this people and city; and having betrayed them, come to me and my people at Rome. May our places, temples, and sacred rites be more acceptable and approved by you; be you the leader over me and the Roman people and my soldiers, so that we may know and understand it. If you do so, I vow that I will build temples and hold games in your honor, etc. <note>original: "Si Deus, si Dea est... templa ludósque facturum, &c." This is the formal Roman formula for *evocatio*.</note>

The same is found in the jurist Ulpian in the law regarding sacred places (*De rerum divisione*): "Those who wish to free a sacred place from its religious status are accustomed to evoke the sacred inhabitants from there." <note>original: "Qui sanctũ locũ liberare à religione volũt solet inde sacra euocare."</note> See several beautiful and excellent discourses on this subject...

->On the types of divination and the origin of the Haruspices derived from the aforementioned Etruscans.<-

**POLYDORE VERGIL**, in Book 1, Chapter 24 of *On the Invention of Things*, says the following regarding the matter above: "There are," says **Cicero**, "two types of divination, one of which depends on nature, and the other on art." Now, the natural type occurs in those who do not concern themselves with any reason or conjecture while observing and taking note of signs, but are moved only by a transport of spirit, or a free thought and agitation in the soul, predicting and as if knowing things to come. This often happens to those who dream, and sometimes to those who prophesy moved by a frenzy <note>original: "fureur." In this sort of divination, one must also add the Oracles, such as those of **Apollo** and **Ammon**, and others where men were often deceived, as in things done through the devil's art and by the trickery of pernicious men. But the holy Prophets, inspired not by a mad and diabolical frenzy but indeed by the divine spirit, never deceived with their predictions. And artificial divination is performed by those who, seeking new things through conjecture, learned the ancient ones through their contemplation, under which were formerly comprised **Haruspicy** <term>Haruspicy: the ancient practice of divining the future by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</term>, **Augury** <term>Augury: the practice of interpreting the will of the gods from the flight or behavior of birds</term>, and **Astrology**. -> *On the region of the Latins.* <-

**Latium**, a region of Italy known to all authors, is today called **Campagna di Roma**, taking its name from Rome, its city, as if one were to say the Territory of Rome. Its inhabitants are called Latins, who were previously called <gloss>Apioi</gloss> <note>original Greek: "απίοις"</note> or **Prisci** [The Ancients], as Halicarnasseus <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian who wrote about Roman antiquities.</note> has it. They were properly called *Prisci*, according to Festus, being those who existed before Rome was founded. These same people were called **Casci** <note>An archaic term meaning "ancient" or "primitive."</note>, as Joseph Scaliger believes in his notes on Varro’s *On the Latin Language*, Book 7. Suidas writes that these people were first called <gloss>Cetians</gloss> <note>original Greek: "κετίος"</note>, and later <gloss>Aeneads</gloss> <note>original Greek: "αίνειάδας", referring to the descendants of the Trojan hero Aeneas</note>, and <gloss>Romans</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ῥωμαίους"</note>. Latium is divided into the Old and the New. The Old extends from the Tiber to Circeii; the New from there to the Liris River. The authors are Strabo and Pliny, who calls the inhabitants Latins; he also mentions the **Latinenses** among them, but writes that they have perished. Collemitius writes that Latium is today called Latium, or **Campagna di Roma**, and Maremma. The poet Virgil gives Latium the name **Hesperia**. Livy writes in the beginning of Book 1 that the **Aborigines** <note>In Roman mythology, the oldest inhabitants of central Italy.</note>, the indigenous peoples of Italy, together with the Trojans who had come to Italy under Aeneas, were called by the single name "Latins." According to Strabo, they lived around Rome itself in Latium. Halicarnasseus lists their towns in Book 1. Festus says that they are the most ancient people of Italy and lived in the Roman territory.

**Tuscany**. See what I have written in the previous chapter on the region of the **Etruscans** <note>original: "Hetruriens"</note>.

**Latium** is that part of Italy situated between the rivers of the **Tiber** and the **Liris** (or Garigliano). It was first inhabited by the **Sicels** <note>original: "Siciliés", an ancient Italic people.</note>, and after they were driven out, the **Aborigines** arrived and occupied their seat. Finally, a king named **Latinus** rose among them, from whom the land is called Latium and the inhabitants Latins. Another reason for this is given by the poet **Ovid** in his *Fasti*, when he says:

> I remember Saturn being received in this land,
> He had been driven from the celestial realms by Jove,
> From that time the name "Saturnian" remained for the people,
> The land was called Latium because the God lay hidden there.
<note>original Latin: "Hac ego Saturnum memini tellure receptum / Cælitibus regnis à Ioue pulſus erat, / Inde diu genti manſit Saturnia nomen, / Dicta fuit Latium terra latente Deo."</note>

Showing by this that **Saturn** was once received in this land when **Jupiter**, his son, chased him from his Kingdom; and from this it happened that this country was named Saturnian, and since then **Latium**, because Saturn had been hidden there, which in Latin is said as *latitare* [to lie hidden]. <meta>catchword: Nicostrata (transcribed in OCR as "coftrare")</meta>

I am fully of the opinion that this Latin country takes its name from the word meaning "concealment" <note>original: "absconsement." This refers to the Latin verb *latere*, meaning to hide, from which *Latium* is traditionally derived.</note>; but not because of the Saturnian fable <note>A myth claiming the god Saturn hid in this region after being overthrown by his son Jupiter.</note>, but rather because it is hidden and held tightly between the precipices and high rocks of the Alps and the Apennines, and is enclosed by the sea, the Garigliano river, and the Tiber. The boundaries of the Latian territory were formerly the Tiber on one side and Mount Circeo on the other, being some fifty miles in length; but in the end, it was bordered as far as the Land of Labor <note>The *Terra di Lavoro*, a historical region of the Kingdom of Naples.</note> and the country of Abruzzo where the Sabines, Paeligni, and other inhabitants of the Apennines lived; and this is what is now called the Campagna di Roma.

The language of these people has been so greatly extended over the course of time—by means of the men of spirit and knowledge who have lived among them—that it has been received by men of letters not only throughout all of Italy, but also throughout all of Europe, and a good part of Asia and Africa, as I have declared previously, except for a portion of Greece. And this served well the power of the Romans, by which Gaul, Spain, Britain, Illyria, the borders of Africa, and others mentioned in Roman histories were subjected. Now, when the power of the Romans increased, the name of the Latins began to fade, and in its place, Romulus took up the name of the Romans; consequently, the Latin language began to be called Roman <note>The author notes a shift in terminology from "Latine" to "Romaine" as the city's political power eclipsed its regional origins.</note>. Latium has several cities, among which Rome is the metropolitan center; near the sea one finds Ostia, Astura—where Conrad, the last Duke of Swabia, was killed <note>Conradin, the last Hohenstaufen heir, captured at Astura in 1268.</note>—Saracinesco, Formia, Gaeta, Fondi, and Sinuessa near the mouth of the Liris river, which is today called the Garigliano. And within the Latin country are these cities, namely Laurentum and Alba [Longa], which is said to have existed 300 years before Rome, and which are now called Palestrina and Tremoli; as well as Praeneste, Tivoli, and Aquino. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book 1 of *Roman Antiquities*; Sebastian Münster, Book 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*, the chapter on the Campagna of Rome, called in Latin *Latium*, which was the most renowned as well as the first inhabited in Italy; and after this author, François de Belleforest, Book 3, Chapter 33 of his *Universal History*, dividing this Latium into "Ancient" and "New" according to the descriptions of modern historians.

Ni-costrate <note>The text continues from the previous page's mention of Nicostrata, a prophetic goddess in Roman mythology.</note>, mother of the Arcadian Evander. Other authors claim that this Nicostrata was otherwise named Carmentis or Carmenta, and that she was not the mother, but the daughter of the said Evander, according to the account of the *Author of the Bundle of Times* <note>original: "l’Autheur du faisceau des temps," referring to the *Fasciculus Temporum*, a popular 15th-century world history by Werner Rolevinck.</note>; her son, named Latinus, corrected the Latin language and called the Latins by his name. Some other authors assert that this Carmentis or Carmenta only altered and changed the forms of these Latin letters. Still others claim that Hercules brought them from the Falisci <note>An ancient Italic people living in what is now northern Lazio.</note> into Italy, as Victorius <note>Pietro Vettori, a 16th-century Italian humanist.</note> certifies. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in Book 1 of his *Roman History*, holds that the Arcadians under the aforementioned Evander were the first who, after the previously named Pelasgians, brought these letters from Greece into Italy. Titus Livius <note>Livy.</note>, in Book 1 of his *Roman Histories*, maintains that the aforementioned Arcadian Evander was the first to bestow this benefit upon the Latins, and calls him "Venerable" for the miracle of his letters; Plutarch seems to adhere to this opinion in his treatise *Roman Questions*, as does Cornelius Tacitus in his works when speaking of the Aborigines. Concerning this, a certain very modern author has said:

<margin>cc</margin>
> From Greece into Italy, the Cadmean letters <note>original: "literæ Cadmeæ." The alphabet traditionally introduced to Greece by the Phoenician prince Cadmus.</note> made their way, brought there by Evander the Arcadian in the year of the world 2730, 110 years after the arrival of Cadmus. This was 24 years after the fame of Linus the Theban (the teacher of Hercules), 32 years after Orpheus of Thrace, and 43 years before the fall of Troy—or 60 years, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus computes it. For this Evander, a fugitive from the Peloponnese, obtained royal dignity in those parts of Italy adjacent to the Tiber more through his authority than by power; he was venerable for the miracle of letters, a new thing among men unskilled in the arts, which is why they are called by Ausonius "the black daughters of Cadmus" <note>original: "Cadmi Nigellæ filiæ." A poetic reference to written letters.</note>. Furthermore, very many colonies were led from Greece into Hesperia <note>An ancient Greek name for Italy, meaning "the Western Land."</note> at that time, which is why that part most frequented by Greek colonies acquired the name of Great Greece <note>Magna Graecia.</note>. Later, however, the land was called Italy by them because of the outstanding height of the calves <note>original: "vitulorum."</note> produced there, an etymology which Varro also followed: for to the Greeks, *Italus* signifies a calf.

But regardless of that, the same Titus Livius in Book 6 demonstrated that the aforementioned Latin letters arrived very late in Italy, continuing in his subsequent Book 9 that anciently, the children of the Romans were accustomed to learning only Greek and Etruscan letters. These were taught in days of old to the Etruscans by Demaratus of Corinth, as I well noted in the preceding chapter on the Etruscan language. Cornelius Tacitus, in Book 11 of his *Annals*, confirms the above; as does Raphael Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei, a humanist scholar.</note> in Book 5 of his *Geography*. Among the moderns, Polydore Vergil, in Book 1, Chapter 6 of *On the Discovery of Things*, treating quite amply the invention of letters, pursues these words which he seems to have drawn from the very words of Dionysius of Halicarnassus in Book 4 of *Roman Antiquities*:

<margin>cc</margin>
> "That the ancient Greek and Latin letters were almost similar, as our Latin ones are now, is shown by the golden table brought from Delphi which was consecrated in the Temple of Minerva at Rome. It could be seen inside the library and was still there in the time of Pliny, as he himself confesses, and Raphael Volaterranus has asserted as much in his writings." The same Pliny continues further: "Now, as the Greeks had little by little increased the number of their letters, the Latins, striving also to do the same, added six to their first and ancient ones: namely F, K, Q, X, Y, Z, and H, which last one, however..."

[The letter H] is not a letter; rather, it is only a mark of aspiration, and the letter F they received from the Aeolians. This letter, as Priscian <note>A 6th-century Latin grammarian whose "Institutes of Grammar" was the standard textbook for the Middle Ages.</note> testifies, had among the ancient Latins the same form and vigor as among the Aeolians themselves, who expressed the same sound with their aspirated *phi* [$\phi$] that we make with our F. This is also what we observe in Greek words such as Orpheus. After this, Claudius Caesar <note>The Emperor Claudius (r. 41–54 AD), who famously attempted to introduce three new letters into the Latin alphabet to improve orthography.</note>, successor to Tiberius, as Tacitus writes, wished that instead of F, one should use a Ⅎ <note>A reversed F, known as the "digamma inversum," intended to represent the consonant 'v' sound.</note>, which would be a consonant; and that one should say *Fulgaire* instead of *Vulgaire* [Common], and *sesquit* instead of *vesquit* [he lived]. Regarding this, Quintilian <note>A celebrated Roman educator and rhetorician.</note> says, not without reason, that Claudius Caesar had added this Aeolian letter F for such a purpose. Even in our own time, the Germans have retained a pronunciation following this force when they speak Latin. 

In short, among the Latins, we are accustomed to using F for a *Ph*, as in the words *Fame* [for Renown] and *faire* [to do]. As for the K, among the Greeks, there is no good author who advises that it should be used in any way whatsoever. The letter Q was accepted because it has a softer sound than C. The letter X was taken from the Greeks; without it, we could use (as Quintilian says) these letters: C and S, or G and S, as in the Latin words *Apexs* <note>The author is demonstrating how 'X' functions as 'CS' or 'GS'.</note> and Greek words meaning "summit" and "herd." Y and Z also have their source in the fountains of Greece, but are so usurped by us that we only use them in words that are naturally Greek. 

Theodor Zwinger <note>A Swiss scholar (1533–1588) known for his massive encyclopedia, the *Theatrum Humanae Vitae*.</note>, in volume 2, book 1 of his *Great Theatre of Human Life*, repeats all the above and adds that Spurius Carvilius <note>Spurius Carvilius Ruga, a Roman freedman credited with inventing the letter G around 230 BC to distinguish it from C.</note>, a Roman grammarian, was the first to invent the letter G, the Romans previously using C in its place; and that Appius Claudius the Jurist <note>Appius Claudius Caecus, a Roman statesman famous for his work on the Appian Way and his linguistic reforms.</note> gave the letter R to the Romans so that they would say *Valerii* for *Valesii*, and *Furii* for *Fusii*, according to the report of Pomponius in the *Digest on the Origin of Law* <note>original: "Digestis de origine Iuris"</note>. He also notes that the Latins took the digamma [Ⅎ] from the Aeolians, which according to Priscian had the same force as these two letters among the Aeolians: *Ph*. Theodor Bibliander <note>A Swiss Orientalist and linguist (1509–1564).</note>, in his commentary on the *Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, treats this question very extensively and learnedly in these words:

> In Latin writing, the principle is the same: initially, there were only sixteen letters among the ancients, the same number that Cadmus <note>A legendary Phoenician prince who, according to myth, introduced the alphabet to the Greeks.</note> brought to Greece. Just as there were no more than sixteen letters among the most ancient Greeks, the Latins, having received them, preserved that antiquity forever, as Priscian testifies. Later, two more were added to the sixteen of the ancient Greeks: the Aeolic F or *Vau* [digamma], and X. They also adopted Ypslion [Y] and Z for the sake of Greek names. Varro, Macer, and Censorinus <note>A group of Roman scholars and grammarians.</note> judged that H, K, and Q should not be included in the number of letters. Diomedes also records in his second book that some believe there are seventeen letters in the Latin tongue. For they consider the two Greek letters Y and Z, as well as K and Q, to be superfluous; X to be a double letter; and H to be merely a mark of aspiration. Servius also notes that the Greeks have this mark of aspiration, which they call *Dasian* <note>original: "Daſeian"; the Greek word for "rough breathing," indicating an 'h' sound.</note>; and for its likeness, the *Psilen* <note>original: "pſilen"; the Greek word for "smooth breathing," indicating no 'h' sound.</note>. By joining these, we made our mark of aspiration, H. But it is much more likely that the Greeks changed the aspirated letter H (or 'h') into the mark for the long vowel *Eta*, and having divided it [into Ⅎ and ℣] <note>Referencing the ancient practice of splitting the letter H into two halves to signify rough and smooth breathing marks.</note>, transformed it into the marks for smooth and rough aspiration. These are marked with different signs among the Hebrews, certainly in the verses of the Commentary of Nonius Marcellus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian.</note> on the "Compendious Doctrine" arranged in order...

Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric (c. 60 BC–after 7 BC) who lived in Rome and wrote a history of the city to show its Greek origins.</note>, in the first book of *Roman Antiquities*, maintains that this ancient Latin language was a mixture of both the Greek and ancient Latin tongues, closely approaching the nature of the Aeolic dialect <note>One of the main dialects of ancient Greek, spoken in parts of Greece and Asia Minor.</note>. However, it was not pronounced as delicately due to the mixture of several words and terms from the Opici, Marsi, Samnites, Etruscans, Bruttii, Umbrians, Ligurians, Spaniards, Gauls, and others who were present in said language. Furthermore, Polybius <note>A Greek historian (c. 200–118 BC) famous for *The Histories*, which covered the rise of the Roman Republic.</note> gives us to understand that this language was so altered and changed between the first Punic (or Carthaginian) War and the second, that it was with great difficulty that one understood the meaning of treaties made previously in that language between the Romans and Carthaginians. Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and biographer (c. 46–119 AD) best known for his *Parallel Lives*.</note>, in his *Platonic Questions*, asserts that in his time, almost all the peoples and nations of this world used and served themselves with the Latin and Roman language.

By taking root in the churches and schools, and consequently in the books, public documents, and legal sentences that were written and composed in this aforementioned language, the Church kept and preserved it throughout Europe, in the provinces and regions of Poland, Germany, Prussia, Sweden, Hungary, Bohemia, Italy, Spain, France, England, Scotland, and others. In these lands, this language is understood and spoken by the most learned and hardworking students who learn it in schools, from private masters, or through books written and composed in it. 

But we must know and understand that as the Roman Republic shifted and changed into a Monarchy, and its manners became altered and corrupted, the aforementioned Latin and Roman language changed and decayed likewise, losing its previous strength, vigor, and natural purity under the later Emperors. Then, once the Roman Empire was transferred from Rome to Constantinople, several different foreign nations arriving in Italy altered this language, so much so that people stopped speaking it commonly. Since that time, it has remained only in books which have been shared with us, read, and interpreted in the few centuries since—having been neither leafed through nor understood for nearly eight hundred years prior. Some were lost and gone, others gnawed and eaten by worms, or by old age or rot, until some Italians a few centuries ago (according to Raffaele Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a humanist scholar from Volterra who wrote the *Commentarii urbani*, an influential encyclopedia.</note> in Book 21 of his *Commentaries*) brought it entirely back to life through long and painful study, writing, correcting, and publishing the books written and composed in it that remained in libraries, protected from the rage and fury of the Barbarians. 

And as the said Empire declined in the West, and as the Goths, Ostrogoths, Lombards, and other Northern peoples invaded and occupied Italy—the Visigoths and Saracens taking Provence and Languedoc, along with Aquitaine and the Spains, and other Northern nations occupying other provinces and regions of Europe—this Latin language was altered and corrupted through their victories and through their frequent interactions and conversations. From this corruption—or rather, alteration—proceeded the Italian, Spanish, French, and other common languages of today. And to return to our first topic, we will note that Velleius <note>Velleius Paterculus (c. 19 BC – c. 31 AD), a Roman historian who wrote a compendium of Roman history.</note> wrote in Book 1 that the elegance of this Latin language was, at the time of the poet Accius <note>Lucius Accius (c. 170 – c. 86 BC), a tragic poet of the Roman Republic.</note> (who lived one hundred and fifty or so...

> 
> By the **Priscan**, they understand that with which those contemporary with Janus and Saturn <note>Gods from the earliest myths of Italy, symbolizing the prehistoric era.</note>, and soon even those close to their own people, conversed. > 
> The **Latin** figure of speech is believed to be so named from what they used in Latium when Latinus <note>A king in Roman mythology from whom the Latins take their name.</note> was in power, and furthermore the Etruscan Kings: in which form indeed the Tables of the Ten Men <note>The Law of the Twelve Tables, the foundation of Roman law.</note> were written. ...the Latin [poets], who published—after the peace made with the Carthaginians at Rome—a comedy, according to Cicero in his *Brutus* and the preface of his *Tusculan Disputations*, and Aulus Gellius in the final chapter of the seventh book of his *Attic Nights*. The **Ancient** period lasted from this Livius Andronicus <note>The first Roman poet, a freed Greek slave who translated the Odyssey into Latin</note> until the time of Cicero, during which it reached its **Perfection**. Shortly thereafter, under Augustus and the following Emperors, it began to lose its natural purity and elegance, gradually becoming corrupt along with the majesty of the Roman Empire; then came the **Imperfect** period, until finally it ceased to be spoken altogether, and was succeeded in its place by the common Italian tongue. Pietro Crinito <note>An Italian humanist scholar (1475–1507), author of *De honesta disciplina*</note>, in Book 3, Chapter 3 of *On Honest Discipline*, follows Marcus Varro in distinguishing the Latin language differently: into **Priscan**, **Latin**, **Roman**, and **Mixed**. 

He interprets the **Priscan** <note>original: *Priscum*</note> as the language used by the ancient peoples of Italy living under the kings Janus and Saturn. This was the language used for certain verses or poems seen in those times which were understood by few people, such as those used by the Salii <note>Priests of Mars who performed ritual dances and sang ancient hymns</note> and the Argei <note>A group of religious figures or locations associated with early Roman ritual</note> in their sacrifices. The **Latin** <note>original: *Latinum*</note> was that used by all the Latin peoples under King Latinus and the Kings of Tuscany, in which were composed the Centumviral laws <note>Laws regarding inheritance and property disputes handled by a court of 100 men</note>, the sacred laws, and various public edicts. The **Roman** <note>original: *Romanum*</note> was that used by the Roman people after having driven out their kings; it was held in great esteem by the poets Plautus, Naevius, Accius, Pacuvius, Ennius, and Virgil, and by the orators Marcus Cato, Sisenna, Quadrigarius, Valerius Antias, Caesar, Cicero, and others. The **Mixed** <note>original: *Mixtum*</note> was that spoken during the Empire of the Caesars by the Roman people and by those who were received as fellow citizens of the city of Rome.

Little by little, this language and Roman virtue began to degenerate along with the morals of the Roman people, which was the cause of this common maxim:

->*The Roman state stands by its ancient customs and its men.*<-
<note>original: *Moribus antiquis res stat Romana virisque.* This famous line from the poet Ennius suggests that Rome’s power relied on traditional morality and strong character.</note>

It is a very certain and assured thing that the Latin language is composed of parts of the Latial, Volscian, Oscan, and Sabine languages, and also of Punic and Carthaginian. In fact, the poet Ennius spoke the Oscan tongue, and some Romans spoke the Etruscan tongue, as Titus Livy and Cicero write. The same author cited above, under the authority of Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous Renaissance philosopher known for his vast learning</note>, speaking of writers in the Latin language, said the following in Book 8, Chapter 3 of *On Honest Discipline*: among the Latins there are several sorts of writers. Some of them delight, some teach and move, and there are some who do both, while others do only one. Many among them have been very elegant and eloquent in their language, such as Caesar, Cicero, and Sallust. Others were less elegant and eloquent, as if they had been foreigners and rustics, born under another sky or region where they had learned a different language than their own—such as Titus Livy, Livius Junius, Columella, and Cornelius Tacitus. As for the Spanish [writers], they were very flourishing and sharp, though some of them have a foreign air, such as Quintilian, Hilary, Seneca, Suetonius, and Pliny <note>The author here categorizes these writers as "Spanish" or provincial based on their stylistic departure from the pure Ciceronian Roman standard</note>. The Punic and Carthaginian [writers] were harsh, bold, and contrary, such as Tertullian, Apuleius, Cyprian, Capella, and those who followed. The first and most...

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

ancient writers spoke the Latin language in every way and in every part, and did not wish to permit any defect within it. Those who followed them declined from that standard, and the third group—entirely wandering and straying—preferred defect over virtue. Regarding the Gallic writers, such as Cassiodorus <note>A Roman statesman and author (c. 485–585) who served under the Ostrogothic kings</note>, Apollinaris <note>Sidonius Apollinaris, a 5th-century Gallo-Roman poet and bishop</note>, Fulgentius, Ennodius <note>Magnus Felix Ennodius, a 6th-century bishop and rhetorician</note>, and others of their time, their works composed in the Latin language should be seen and read, but should by no means be accepted for imitation. T. Bibliander <note>Theodor Bibliander (1506–1564), a Swiss scholar of linguistics and theology</note> in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters* writes:

<note>original Latin: "Lingua Romana & Latina..."</note> While the Roman and Latin language had a fixed seat in the city and in Latium, and also held the Empire and flourished greatly in the Roman Provinces, it nevertheless had several distinct variations, and those not obscure. For frequent mention is made of the Latial, Volscian, Sabinian, Opican, and Etruscan languages; even in Titus Livy, a certain "Patavinity" <note>A term coined by Asinius Pollio to criticize Livy’s style as sounding too much like his hometown of Patavium (modern-day Padua)</note> was noticed by Pollio, because he was from Padua and did not retain a pure and unadulterated Roman eloquence in all things. Furthermore, in Augustine, Cyprian, Tertullian, and other Africans using the provincial speech, there is something vernacular and African; in Hilary, Prosper, and other Gallic writers, something peculiar stands out. Likewise, Annaeus Seneca, Lucan, Sedulius, Columella, and even Quintilian himself smell somewhat of the Spanish style <note>original: "Hispaniēse"</note>.

To make it short, if we wish to compare this Latin language—perfect in all elegance and eloquence—with the excellent Greek language, we shall find it (according to the testimony of the aforementioned Cicero, Gellius, and Lucretius) so poor and defective that it cannot even express in many and various words what the aforementioned Greek language can in a single and unique one. To this Quintilian consents, saying that the aforementioned Latin language is much lesser and more sterile than the Greek, being rougher in its pronunciation and derivation of words, as this author proves by several Latin passages cited by him in his works. This moved the learned poet Horace to say:

->*To the Greeks the Muse gave the power*<-
->*To speak with a well-rounded mouth.*<-
<note>original: "Graijs dedit ore rotundo / Musa loqui"</note>

And the poet Martial, holding that the Greeks could express all things in their language very eloquently:

> It is not permitted for us to be so eloquent,
> We who worship the more severe Muses.
<note>original: "Nobis non licet esse tam disertis / Qui musas colimus seueriores"</note>

And we should not accept the aforementioned Cicero in his preface to the *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 2 of *On the Orator*, etc., and *On Ends*, writing that this Latin language is richer and more abundant than the Greek, seeing as the Greek had no proper word to signify the Latin word *Ineptus* <note>Meaning "unsuitable" or "tactless." Cicero argued Greeks lacked a word for this concept because they lacked the social awareness it described</note>, as if, if understood correctly, the Greek word did not signify the same and identical thing. But this great Orator, when writing on Philosophy, finds himself quite hindered in finding and inventing new Latin words corresponding exactly to the Greek words of each art or speculation—which this figure is even forced to confess frankly in the fifth book of his *Tusculan Disputations* and in his speech *For the Poet Archias*. And we shall believe Seneca even less in Book 12 of his *Controversies*, holding that the Latin language <note>original: "Facultatis non minus habere..."</note> "has no less faculty [ability] than the Greek, but less license [freedom]."

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

<note>The author refers to Aristotle's "History of Animals"</note> translated by him from Greek into Latin, claiming that the Latin language is sufficient to represent every Greek word, clause, and sentence. The contrary has been more than sufficiently demonstrated and verified by the aforementioned Theodore Gaza in his preface to the *History of Plants* by Theophrastus <note>A student of Aristotle and the "father of botany"</note>; by Laurentius Valla in his *Elegances of the Latin Language*; by Scipio Carteromachus and Conrad Heresbach in their orations in praise of the Greek language; by Guillaume Budé in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*; by Tusan and Henri Estienne in their *Dictionaries* and *Treasury of the Greek Language*; and after them by Louis Le Roy in books 6 and 7 of the *Vicissitude of Things*, in the chapter on Roman literature and other sciences compared with the Greek, Egyptian, and Chaldean. This is something I have clearly verified through what I have previously deduced regarding the Greek language in the preceding chapters.

It remains to be said that Theodor Bibliander, in his discourse on the common reason of all languages and letters, has said the following regarding this Latin language:

<margin>m „ „ „ „ „ „ „ „ „ „ „ „ „</margin>
> <note>original Latin: "Ea lingua quoniam diffusa est..."</note> Since this language is now spread through many nations of men, and almost all the arts have been entrusted to its writing, it is also copious, having been cultivated and increased by the genius of many writers. It possesses, moreover, a sweet sound, along with a certain gravity—not wild or rustic, as is found in some others—but like that of a strong and prudent man, born and raised in a well-ordered state; it would be a sin not to cultivate and preserve it. If it were lost, a great confusion of all disciplines would follow, as well as great discord and aversion among men due to the ignorance of languages. For indeed, as Saint Augustine says, one would rather spend time with his dog than with a man of an unknown tongue. To the spreading of piety, it is also most useful that men understand one another.

Today, this language has great currency and is in vogue throughout almost all the provinces and regions of Europe, and through the Latin Churches, as well as in the regions and provinces of the earth discovered by the voyages and navigations of the Portuguese, Spanish, English, Flemish, French, and others. What is more, some modern travelers have written that the Cathayans <note>Historical name for the people of China</note> currently use Latin characters in their writing, entirely similar in their squareness to Roman letters. By this means, those with the clearest vision can evidently recognize that these Cathayans originally came and descended from our Europe, seeing as it is very certain and assured by ancient histories that the Romans never passed beyond the country of Gedrosia <note>An ancient coastal region corresponding to modern-day Makran in Pakistan and Iran</note>. Blaise de Vigenère, in his *Treatise on Ciphers*, has endeavored to extract mysteries and secrets from the characters of Latin letters, similar to those that the Hebrews extract from their own characters, which we have previously and extensively declared in the chapters on the Hebrew language. But whoever wishes to compare what the said author writes with what I have deduced above in the aforementioned chapters will find that there is no comparison between the one set of mysteries and the other.

## WHETHER THE ROMANS OF OLD
### *all generally spoke Latin.*

Polydore Vergil <note>Polydore Vergil (c. 1470–1555) was an Italian humanist scholar who wrote a famous history of "firsts" or inventions.</note> in Book 1, Chapter 3 of *On the Discovery of Things*, when treating the first birth of men, the origin of the diversity of languages, and the first division of lands made in the world among men, used the following words:

"But it will not be at all out of place to discourse a little on the ancient controversy among learned men, who inquire whether in the past the Romans all generally spoke Latin, or whether they had two kinds of language—just as both we and the Greeks have two today: one which is called common and the mother tongue, and the other literary and Latin (or, among the Greeks, Attic). And so that we do not labor over a matter that is so clear (as I believe), following Cicero in the third book of *The Orator* <note>original title: "De Oratore"</note>, we shall provide the evident reason for it. Now, he says in that place that in Rome there was a certain and proper language for those of the city. He proves this by a woman named Laelia <note>Laelia was the daughter of Gaius Laelius Sapiens and was renowned for her pure speech.</note>, who spoke so well and had such excellent phrasing that one thought, upon hearing her discourse, that she was a Plautus or a Naevius <note>Titus Maccius Plautus and Gnaeus Naevius were early Roman playwrights known for their mastery of the Latin tongue.</note>. And so that one does not think that this Laelia had learned another language—namely Latin—different from that which was her own and natural, and which she had sucked from her mother’s womb, he adds a little later: 'No one was ever astonished hearing an orator speak Latin; however, if he spoke any other language, they mocked him.' And in *The Perfect Orator*, he says that if on the stage a verse is pronounced in which a syllable is too long or too short, the whole audience begins to shout. And in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations* <note>original: "Tusculanes"</note>, when the vast multitude is present in the theater, including women and children, everyone is moved upon hearing a swelling and well-sounding verse."

These are the words of Cicero, by which it appears that the Latin language was common to all, since even common women and children knew how to speak this language. But he was considered the most learned who chose the most proper words and who judged them with the just weight of his ear, which could not be done without "letters" <note>In this context, "letters" refers to formal education and literacy.</note>. Now, all Romans spoke Latin well, but that all were learned, Cicero testifies to the contrary when, in his *Brutus*, he introduces Titus Pomponius Atticus <note>Atticus was Cicero’s closest friend and a wealthy patron of letters.</note> speaking thus: "You see that Latin elocution is refined, the praise for which does not come or proceed from reason or any science, but rather from good custom." Then he adds: "When we were children, we saw Titus Flamininus <note>Titus Quinctius Flamininus, a Roman general and consul.</note>, who was Consul with Quintus Metellus; it was said indeed that he spoke properly in Latin, but he did not know his letters."

Is there then anyone who, considering that these things are testified to by the prince of the Latin language <note>Referring to Cicero.</note>, can suspect that the Romans had—any more than we do—two different kinds of language? For just as in Rome those who had lived outside the city spoke less purely and with less ornament than the others, likewise among the Latins, barbarism and rudeness of language were introduced in part by the strange and cruel nations who occupied...

Louis Le Roy (c. 1510–1577) was a French humanist scholar whose work "De la vicissitude ou variété des choses en l'univers" explored the cyclical nature of history and culture.</note>, speaking of this matter:<-

But although languages change incessantly, and even within the same country a difference in speech and pronunciation appears in a short space of time, it is nevertheless true that there are more elegant forms everywhere. Such were the Athenians in Greece, the Romans in Italy, and today the Tuscans, the Castilians in Spain, the Saxons in Germany, the Persians in Asia, and the nobles and courtiers in France. By this, the question is settled which has been debated among some learned men: namely, whether the ancient Greeks and Romans had two languages, and whether Plato, Aristotle, and Demosthenes among the Greeks, and Caesar, Cicero, and Sallust among the Latins, wrote in their mother tongues. 

It is certain that in Athens there was only one language, and in Rome another. But that of the common people was less elegant than that of the statesmen and the more refined citizens, as one can see in the Latin of Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the famous Roman author of "De Architectura."</note>, who was a master mason, and that of Cicero, who was of consular rank. This elegance and purity of speech is preserved longer among Ladies, who converse less with foreigners than men do, and are commonly more careful to speak well. Cicero, in the third book of *The Orator*, writes that in his time the learning of the Athenians was lost in Athens, with only the home of studies remaining in that city, which the citizens did not care for but foreigners enjoyed, being drawn somewhat by the name and authority of the city. 

Nevertheless, an unlearned Athenian would surpass the most learned of Asia, not in words, but in the sound of the voice—and not so much by speaking well as by speaking sweetly. Similarly (he says), there is a certain voice proper to the Roman race and to the city, in which nothing offends or displeases by sounding at all like a foreign quality; so much so that the Romans, though studying less than the Latins <note>In this context, "Latins" refers to the other peoples of the Latium region or Italy who spoke Latin but were not original citizens of the city of Rome.</note>, surpassed the most learned among them by the sweetness of their voice. 

The Greeks living in Greece proper, in Italy, Asia, Sicily, and other islands, had four languages: Attic, Doric, Aeolic, and Ionic. By choosing specific words and figures from each as it best suited their purpose, the Poets gave birth to one called "the Common," and later, under a single name, they called all five the Greek language. And although the Athenian (Attic) dialect was more elegant and fruitful than the others, the scholars who were not Athenians by birth wrote only in their natural style, fearing perhaps that they could not achieve that Attic purity, which was rarely and only belatedly achieved by those born elsewhere. For Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note>, who had long resided in Athens and was considered highly eloquent, was recognized in his speech as a foreigner by an old Athenian woman. Pollio objected to the <term>Padouennerie</term> <note>original: "Padouennerie," referring to "Patavinity" (Patavinitas). And Virgil, who was from Mantua, was reproached because he did not speak like a Roman. Likewise, any language is less pure the further it wanders from its natural source. Just as in ancient times the Syrians and Egyptians speaking Greek did not speak it as purely as the Athenians; nor did the Gauls, Spaniards, or Africans speak Latin as the Romans did. # WHAT DIFFERENCE THERE IS BETWEEN
## *Dialect, Speech, Discourse, and Related Terms.*

### CHAPTER LXVIII.

Speech <term>Sermo; conversation or informal talk</term> is explained as conversation by Donatus in that passage of Terence: "He begins a conversation with him." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in Book 3 of *To Herennius*: "Speech is discourse relaxed into the neighbor of everyday talk." The same Cicero in his book *On Duties*: "Since the power of discourse <note>Latin: *orationis*</note> is great and of two kinds—one of conversation <note>Latin: *sermonis*</note>, the other of formal debate <note>Latin: *contentionis*</note>—let debate be assigned to the disputes of the courts, public assemblies, and the senate; let conversation take place in circles, discussions, and gatherings of friends, and also follow along at banquets. There are rules for debate from the Rhetoricians, but none for conversation. Though I do not know if these too might be possible. But while masters are found for those subjects studied by students, there are none who study this; everything is filled with the crowd of Rhetoricians. Nevertheless, the same rules for words and sentences will apply to Conversation." And the rest by which Cicero forms everyday conversation.

The grammarian Diomedes also calls the common speech of man "eloquence" <note>Latin: *eloquium*</note>, so to speak. For he writes in Book 2: "Some designate three functions of the voice: Eloquence, ringing, and sound. Eloquence is the distinct expression of human pronunciation, impressing a happy understanding upon the mind." Though "Eloquence" <note>Latin: *Eloquentia*</note> is rather the perfection of speech.

Utterance <term>Locutio; the act or style of speaking</term> is skilled and artful speech. Cicero in *Brutus*: "Although every utterance is discourse, yet the utterance of a single Orator is marked by this specific name." And again: "You see that the foundation and, as it were, the base of the Orator is utterance that is corrected and Latin." In *To Herennius*: "Speech is neighboring to everyday utterance." Aurelius Augustine, when he titled his books on utterances, intended idioms and dialects to be understood.

Varro, in *On the Latin Language*, testifies that some have called the word we bring forth in speaking "speech" <note>Latin: *loquela*</note>. Cicero, in Book 4 of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*: "From that difficulty..."

...those words of deceitful speech, as Accius <note>Lucius Accius was a Roman tragic poet; only fragments of his work survive.</note> says, are born of malice. Indeed, "eloquence" (*loquentia*), like "loquacity" (*loquacitas*), is categorized among the vices of speech. Aulus Gellius, book one, chapter fifteen. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] gravely and truly detests a foolish and empty abundance of speaking. "Provided," he says, "that this is established: that neither the lack of speech in one who knows a thing but cannot explain it by speaking, nor the ignorance of one for whom the matter is lacking but words are not, should be praised. If one of these must be chosen, I would rather have unspoken wisdom than foolish talkativeness." Sallust [said] of Catiline: <note>original: "satis loquentiæ, sapientiæ parum"</note> "enough talkativeness, but too little wisdom." For so Valerius Probus, the illustrious Grammarian, judged it should be read, as the same Gellius testifies.

Speech (*Oratio*) signifies both common conversation (*sermo*) and artistic expression (*locutio artificiosa*). Cicero, in *On the Orator*, book 1: "This is the orator’s own characteristic, as I have often said: a speech that is grave, ornate, and suited to human senses." "We ought to know this," says F. Victorinus in his commentary on Cicero’s *On Invention*: "in dialogues there is conversation (*sermo*), not a formal discourse (*diction*). Discourse belongs to the orator in civil cases." Or: the philosopher uses conversation, the orator uses discourse. *Speech* (*Oratio*) can also apply to dialogue if the expression is a bit more splendid. Yet it is properly the orator's domain.

*Dialect* <note>original: διάλεκτος / dialektos</note> is defined by John the Grammarian as a *property of language* <note>original: γλώττης ἰδίωμα / glōttēs idiōma</note>, such as Attic, Doric, and the rest. Thus the Stoics define *dialectos*, according to Diogenes in book seven, as "a voice marked by national or Greek character," <note>original: λέξις κεχαραγμένη ἐθνικῶς τε καὶ ἑλληνικῶς</note> that is, a way of speaking established variously among the Greeks and other nations. Furthermore, Aristotle calls human speech *dialectos*; however, that which is commonly called "idiom" and "dialect," Aristotle calls a "tongue" <note>original: γλώτταν / glōttan</note>, as does Galen. For so Aristotle divides the noun in his book *On Poetics*: "every noun is either proper, or from another language [a gloss], etc." "I call 'proper' that which is in use by everyone; 'from another language' that which is used only by some." From which it is clear that such a word can also become proper, so that they sometimes fall into the same category, yet not for the same people. For example, *sigynon*—that is, a spear—is a "proper" word to the Cypriots, but to us it is a *glotta*—that is, a word from their language. And Galen, in the book he titled *Explanation of Tongues*, says that whatever names were once in use but are no longer, they call *glōssas*, that is, "tongues" <note>A 'gloss' originally referred to an obsolete or foreign word requiring explanation.</note>. And in explaining the "tongues" of Hippocrates, he provides not only individual words but sometimes several. Hence the Latins also call brief interpretations—where a word is usually rendered by another word—*glosses*, *glossaries*, and *glossemata*. As Fabius [Quintilian] says in the first book of his *Institutes*: "a boy can immediately learn the interpretation of the more secret 'tongues'—that is, what the Greeks call *glossas*—while doing something else." Furthermore, Aristotle calls discourse or speech both *logos* and *lexis*. Although *lexis* is taken to mean a formal discourse or a single signifying voice by Apollonius and other good authors. Aristotle also calls elocution *lexis* in his *Rhetoric*. This is also sometimes called *diction* (*dictio*) by the Latins, or the "thread" of a speech. Just as Cicero in *The Orator* speaks of the "thin thread of argumentation." It is also called *Phrase*, character, form, and type of speech. *Dialexis* <note>original: διάλεξις</note> is artistic speech, named either from *dialegomai* (I discuss) or *dialegō* (I select and distinguish). As Gellius says, the Greeks use the very significant word *lala* <note>original: λάλα</note> for men who babble foolish and immoderate things. Although *lalia* [babbling] also...

...is properly used for conversation and dialect. And humans have this specific quality, that they are <term>talkative</term> <note>original Greek: "λαλητικοὶ"; meaning prone to or capable of speech</note>, conversational, or more correctly, endowed with speech. Furthermore, "dialogue" and "dialogism" are terms with meanings well known by both the Greeks and Latins; these indeed seemed necessary to distinguish at the outset, because they are often confused even by great authors. Moreover, the tongue, the mouth, and the lip—because they are the "beasts of burden" for the voice—are usually understood through a figure of speech to represent the differences in speech itself. For example, Cicero, in *On Ends*, says that the Latin language seems to some to be more lacking in words than the Greek. And in the 5th book of his *Tusculan Disputations*: "In those languages which we do not understand, we are truly deaf." And Horace, in his *Art of Poetry*:

> Latium [Rome] would not be more powerful in virtue or famous arms
> Than in language, if the labor of the file <note>original: "lima labor"; a metaphor for the meticulous editing and "polishing" of a literary work</note>, and the delay,
> Did not offend every one of our poets.

Moses used this same figure of speech when he writes that God confounded the tongue and the lip in Babylonia <note>A reference to the Tower of Babel in the Book of Genesis</note>.

Indeed, "voice" is used for speech and discourse, not without a figure of speech, as when it is said: "It is a voice unworthy of a wise man to say, 'I did not think [this would happen].'" And these are the related names used for speech.

Discourse and conversation are defined in this way: To speak is to give a sign with an articulate voice. A sign is that which shows itself to the sense and, besides itself, shows something to the mind. I say "articulate" because it can be captured in letters. These are the words of Augustine in his *Logic* <note>Aurelius Augustine's "De Dialectica," an influential text on the nature of signs and communication</note>. Aristotle, in the fourth book of the *History of Animals*, says: <term>speech</term> <note>original Greek: "διάλεκτος"</note> is the articulation of the voice by the tongue. Speech is nothing other than the explanation of the voice through the tongue. And he adds: "Humans do not use the same speech, although they all produce the same voice." In his book *On Poetics*, he calls it <term>diction</term> <note>original Greek: "λέξιν"</note> or discourse, as Grammarians and Rhetoricians do when they speak of certain "figures of <term>diction</term>" and others of "thought." For example: questioning, answering, threatening, narrating, and commanding are figures and species of diction. He establishes one part of it as <term>reasoned speech</term> <note>original Greek: "λόγον" (Logos)</note>. And he defines it in this way: <term>reasoned speech is a composite significant voice, some parts of which are significant by themselves.</term> By this definition, Aristotle shows it is to be understood that both the phrase "rational animal" and the entire writing of Homer called the *Iliad* are "speech." For he explains this in two ways: speech is said to be "one" either as signifying one thing by itself, or by the addition of conjunctions. For example, the *Iliad* will be one speech by conjunctions; but the definition of a human—namely, "an animal endowed with reason"—signifies one thing. In the first book of *On Interpretation* <note>original Greek: "περὶ ἑρμηνείας"</note>, he explains with the same definition. The Stoics say it a little more explicitly: "Reasoned speech is a significant voice sent out from the mind and thought." From this, Democritus acutely defined speech as <term>a flow of the mind</term> <note>original Greek: "ῥεῦσιν τῆς νόου"</note>, a down-flow or, as it were, a derivation of the mind.

Diomedes <note>A 4th-century Latin grammarian</note> defines speech in his first book as the structure of words composed for an ending, terminated at the final clause. Or as others have defined it: a composition of words completing a thought and signifying a perfected matter. Or, according to Scaurus: a pronunciation sent from the mouth and ordered through words. <note>original: "lib.2"</note> In the second book <note>This likely refers to Priscian’s *Institutes of Grammar*, a foundational text for medieval and Renaissance linguistic study</note>, it is stated: **Speech** is the arrangement of words expressing a congruent and complete thought. This is a general definition—that is, one which is divided into specific types or parts. For otherwise, even a book on Rhetoric is called a "speech" <note>original: "oratio"</note>, as is a single word, such as imperative or responsive verbs which complete a thought on their own. Fabius Quintilianus <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a famous Roman rhetorician</note> expresses what he understands speech to be when discussing the parts of Rhetoric in his third book: every discourse by which a specific will is declared must necessarily contain both a **matter** <note>original: "rem"</note> and a **word**. And if it is brief and concluded with a single point, perhaps it requires nothing further. But a longer discourse demands more, and in his eighth book, he states that all speech consists of matter and words. In the matter, one must look for <term>Invention</term> <note>The process of finding arguments or ideas; from the Latin "inventio"</note>; in the words, <term>Elocution</term> <note>The style or manner of expression; from the Latin "elocutio"</note>; and in both, <term>Arrangement</term> <note>The structure and order of the speech; "collocatio"</note>. These are then embraced by memory and commended by delivery. Indeed, it is the role of eloquence to bring forth all things conceived in the mind and convey them to the listeners. And in the twelfth book of his *Rhetoric*: "The work of the Orator is speech, and its forms are many." Cicero also expresses his opinion on speech both frequently elsewhere and in the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*. "Now truly," he says, "how magnificent, how divine is that power of eloquence—the 'mistress of things,' as you are accustomed to say? It first ensures that we can learn those things we do not know and teach others what we do know. Then, through this power, we exhort, we persuade, we console the afflicted, we lead the terrified away from fear, we restrain those who are unrestrained, and we extinguish desires and angers. This power has bound us together in the society of justice, laws, and cities; it has separated us from a cruel and wild life. Furthermore, if you pay close attention, it is incredible to see what great effort Nature has engineered for the use of speech. For first, the windpipe extends from the lungs all the way to the inner mouth, through which the voice, taking its beginning from the mind, is perceived and poured out," etc.

It has seemed proper to propose the opinions of theologians, philosophers, logicians, grammarians, and orators regarding speech, so that it may be seen more clearly whether they have also envisioned a single purpose for discourse.

---
->The Purpose for which Speech is Made.<-
---

Since in the process of knowing and deeply inspecting things, as well as in the undertaking and perfection of any business, a great deal of weight is placed on causes, so too in the treatment of discourse and languages it is of the utmost importance to know the causes—and to know them exactly. Foremost is the "final cause," or the reason *why* each thing exists or is made. This is the good itself: the use of the thing and the end goal for which the movement occurs. When we have rightly contemplated that goal—why Nature, or rather the Creator of Nature, gave to humans the faculty and use of speech; why humans have conversations; why they speak—then we will easily adapt the entire doctrine of using speech correctly toward that goal. In this way, we shall use discourse and languages properly, and we will perceive without difficulty the kinship between the <term>logical arts</term> <note>Traditionally including Grammar, Logic, and Rhetoric</note> and what their purpose is as well. From this, the common reason of all languages and letters will offer itself of its own accord—to show which this book is primarily destined. Furthermore, the goal...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of linguistic definitions, moving from the rhetorical foundations of the previous page into theological and logical definitions provided by St. Paul, St. Augustine, and Aristotle. It establishes speech as a system of signs used for mutual understanding.</meta>

<page-num>780</page-num>
<header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF <note>The header is incomplete in the original, likely continuing from "History of the Origin of Languages"</note></header>

...of discourse <note>original: "sermonis"</note>, so that we may first investigate its definition from the classical authors and the reasons they followed—and this briefly, since our intent in this commentary is to perform the duty of a judge, not of a teacher or master. The Apostle Paul, in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 14, indicates the use of languages and speech when he requires **edification** <note>original Greek: "οἰκοδομὴν"</note>, that is, building up, so that good fruit may return from the speech to the people listening. This cannot happen unless it is perceived by the mind and intellect; and it will not be perceived unless one produces **intelligible speech** <note>original Greek: "εὔσημον λόγον"</note>, which is to say, significant discourse. Just as with a song played by a lyre-player, no one understands it unless the lyre produces distinct sounds. Likewise in war, unless the trumpet sounds clear signals, no one will be roused to battle by its judgment, nor will they perform the military duties that are usually indicated by the signal of trumpets.

**Augustine**, in his book *On the Teacher* <note>original: "de magistro"</note>, establishes that words are signs. A thing cannot be a sign unless it signifies something. And again: He who speaks gives a sign of his will outwardly through an articulate sound. Does it not seem to you that speech was instituted for any cause other than teaching or reminding? You see, therefore, that we seek nothing through speech except to teach. Throughout the whole book, he explains that words are signs of things, and also signs of other words. In **Logic** <note>original: "Dialectica"</note>, speaking also of the nature of discourse, he commands that these four things be held distinctly: the *sayable* word, the *utterance*, the *word*, and the *thing*. 

A **thing** <note>original: "Res"</note> is whatever is either felt (such as physical bodies), or understood (such as spiritual matters), or hidden (such as God and unformed matter). A **word** <note>original: "Verbum"</note> is the sign of each thing which can be understood by the listener when brought forth by the speaker. A **sign** is that which shows both itself to the senses and something beyond itself to the mind. **To speak** <note>original: "Loqui"</note> is to give a sign with an articulate voice. By "articulate," I mean that which can be captured by letters. Indeed, every word makes a sound; for in writing, it is not the word itself, but the sign of the word. Indeed, once the letters are inspected by the reader, that which breaks forth in the voice occurs to the mind. For what else are written letters than voices showing themselves to the eyes and, beyond themselves, to the mind? 

There are also signs of words that are themselves words, as when a Grammarian asks how many syllables the word "man" has, or what part of speech it is; or when a Logician asks whether it is a genus or a species, and what belongs to that genus. Furthermore, words are either **simple**, which signify one single thing (such as individual nouns and verbs), or **joined and coupled**, such as "man lives by his faith." 

The **sayable** <note>original: "Dicibile"</note> is called whatever the mind, rather than the ear, perceives from a word, and which is kept enclosed within the mind itself (just as "sensible" refers to what the senses perceive). It is called an **utterance** <note>original: "Dictio"</note> when a word proceeds not for its own sake, but for the sake of signifying something else. Logic deals with all of these.

**Aristotle**, in the first book of *On Interpretation* <note>original: "de Enunciatione, siue Interpretatione"</note>, says: Those things that exist in the voice are signs of the affections <note>mental states or impressions</note> that are in the soul; those things that are written are marks of those that exist in the voice. And just as letters are not the same among all men, so the voices are not the same; however, the affections of the soul, of which these are signs, are the same among all men. Likewise, the things of which these voices are **likenesses** <note>original Greek: "ὁμοιώματα"</note> and images are also the same among all. Furthermore, no voice is significant except **by convention** <note>The text uses the Greek "φύσει" (by nature) but immediately glosses it as "ex pacto" (by agreement/convention). In Aristotle's original Greek, he argues speech is *not* by nature but by convention (*kata suntheken*). The author here is likely correcting or clarifying the term.</note>, so that it may become a **symbol** <note>original Greek: "σύμβολον"</note> and a common mark of a thing. Therefore, sounds that cannot be written, such as those of wild beasts, are not significant voices. Furthermore, some voices are **composite** <note>original Greek: "συμπλεκόμενα"</note> or joined, such as a sentence; others are without connection, such as individual nouns and verbs.

...words, and other sounds from which speech is constructed. Aristotle discusses all of these at greater length in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original Latin: "de Anima"</note>. Furthermore, he refers to "affections" or "dispositions," not in the sense that we call anger, pain, and other disturbances of the mind "affections," but rather what others call **thoughts** <note>original Greek: "νοήματα"</note>. In this passage, Aristotle calls them **affections** <note>original Greek: "πάθη"</note>, while Themistius called them **signified things** <note>original Greek: "σημαινόμενα"</note> and **images** <note>original Greek: "φαντασίας"</note>—that is, the meanings and images of things residing in the soul. The opinion of Galen is indicated from the ninth book of *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato*; these are his very words: **For we use names and generally the dialogue we have with one another for the sake of declaring the opinions of the soul which we have acquired from the inspection of the nature of things; it is therefore ridiculous to abandon this and contend about names.** <note>The original Greek text: "χρώμεθα γὰρ ὀνόμασι κὴ ὅλως τῆ πρὸς ἀλλήλους διαλέχτῳ χάριν τοῦ δηλῶσαι τὰς κτὰ τὴν ψυχὴν δόξας ὡς ἐκ τοῦ σκοπεῖσθαι τὴν τῶν πραγμάτων φύσιν ἐκτησάμεθα γελοῖον οὖν ἐστ’ καταλιπόντας τοῦτο περὶ τῶν ὀνομάτων ἀμιλλᾶσθαι."</note> In his first book, Diomedes shows the purpose of speech and how it is produced in this manner: **The secret speech of the heart, revealing itself, migrates to the tongue under its own guidance; it is tempered by a certain mobile breath of articulate voice and by the rounded control of its steering; and the air, being struck by sharpness in the inner neighborhood of the chest, and the palate being pulsed gently and little by little, speech is driven rationally through the mouth and discourse, like a messenger and betrayer of the human mind, to express the signs of thought.** For this speech, expressed by the great benefit of reason, separates us from the other animals; nature acknowledges and demonstrates that this belongs to humans alone. Orators also most consistently maintain that speech was given to man to explain the feelings of the mind and for his well-being, not for destruction; nor is anything more contrary to nature than to obscure one's meaning with words. Indeed, they establish the highest perfection of speech as the science of speaking out, or rather the virtue and faculty of <term>Eloquence</term>: which good rhetoricians combine with wisdom in such a way that it can by no means be torn away from it. It will be enough to have revealed this with one or two examples. Next, we shall consider the goals of the arts of speaking along with the goal of speech itself.

Quintilian defines **to speak out** <note>original: "Eloqui"</note> in this way: **To bring forth everything you have conceived in the mind and convey it to the listeners.** Without this, the prior steps—namely, finding and arranging what is to be said—were useless, much like a sword that is put away and sticking inside its scabbard. This, therefore, is what is most taught; this is what no one can achieve except through art. To this, study must be applied; this is what practice seeks, and this is what imitation pursues. Here every age of life is consumed; by this, the orator is especially superior to other orators. By this, the very types of speaking are made better than others. And a little later: **Let there be, therefore, the greatest possible care for elocution, provided we know, however, that nothing should be done for the sake of words, since words themselves were discovered for the sake of things: of which those words are most commendable which best bring out the sense of our mind and produce in the minds of the judges the judgment that we desire.** These should undoubtedly provide an admirable speech—not in the way we marvel at monsters—but a pleasant one, not with a shameful pleasure, but joined with praise and dignity. And again: **What the Greeks call "phrase"** <note>original Greek: "φράσιν"</note>, **we call "elocution" in Latin. We look at it in words either singly or joined together.** In single words, we must see that they are Latin, clear, ornate, and adapted to what we wish to achieve: and that they are as little "foreign" or "external" as possible. In joined words, they should be corrected, well-placed, and figurative. Furthermore, in the twelfth book, defining an orator as **a good man skilled in speaking** <note>original Latin: "virum bonum dicendi peritum"</note>—and this from the opinion of Marcus Cato—he shows that the faculty of speaking well should be granted to no one who is not also a good man. And he proves this from the laws of Nature, which are undoubtedly the best. For thus Quintilian concludes. Truly that...

...that which he [Quintilian] established first, and which is certainly more natural and greater: and this is not only because if this power of speaking were to arm malice, nothing would be more ruinous to public and private affairs than **Eloquence**. We ourselves, who have endeavored to contribute something to the faculty of speaking to the best of our ability, would deserve very poorly of human affairs if we provided these weapons to a bandit rather than a soldier. Why do I speak of ourselves? Nature itself, in that which she seems to have especially granted to man and by which she separated us from the other living creatures, would be a stepmother rather than a parent <note>original Latin: "nouerca fuerit, si facultatem dicendi sociã scelerum... inuenit." A "stepmother" in classical literature was often a metaphor for a harsh or hostile provider, as opposed to a nurturing mother.</note> if she had devised the faculty of speech to be an ally of crimes, an adversary to innocence, and an enemy of truth. For it would have been better to be born mute and lacking the reason of the soul than to turn the gifts of providence into mutual destruction. 

But after a few intervening words: Since therefore the orator is a **good man** <note>original: "vir bonus." This refers to Quintilian's famous definition of an orator: "vir bonus dicendi peritus"—a good man skilled in speaking.</note>, and since such a man cannot be understood to exist without virtue; and even if he takes certain impulses from nature, virtue must nevertheless be perfected by instruction. The character of the orator must be cultivated above all by study, and every discipline of the honorable and the just must be mastered; without this, no one can be either a good man or skilled in speaking. Unless, perhaps, we agree with those who think that character is established by nature and is not aided at all by discipline. Naturally, they might admit that even the most contemptible things made by hand require teachers; yet they believe that **virtue**—than which nothing has been given to man that brings him closer to the immortal gods—is something we encounter effortlessly, just because we were born. Will a man be abstinent if he is ignorant of what abstinence is? And will he be brave if he has not purged the diseases of fear, pain, death, and superstition by any reason? And will he be just if he has not discussed the treatment of the fair and the good, nor the laws—both those given to all by nature and those specifically established for peoples and nations—with some more learned discourse? O, how little they think of this, to whom it seems so easy! 

But I pass over this, about which I think no one who has tasted literature (even "with the tips of their lips" as they say) will doubt. I shall return to the following point: that no one will be sufficiently skilled in speaking who has not both looked deeply into the whole power of nature and formed his character through precepts and reason. For not in vain does **L. Crassus** <note>Lucius Licinius Crassus (140–91 BCE), a famous Roman orator and a main character in Cicero's dialogues.</note>, in the third book of *On the Orator* <note>original Latin: "De Oratore"</note>, affirm that everything said regarding the fair, the just, the true, and the good, and regarding their opposites, belongs to the orator. He notes that when philosophers defend these things with the power of speech, they are using the weapons of Rhetoricians, not their own. Yet he also confesses that these things must now be sought from Philosophers, because it seems they have been more in possession of such matters. From this also comes what **Cicero** testifies in several books and letters: that the faculty of speaking flows from the innermost springs of **wisdom**. And for that reason, for some time, the teachers of character and of speaking were the same. 

**M. T. Cicero** writes in the *Brutus*: "Delivery is, as it were, a certain eloquence of the body, since it consists of voice and movement." And again: "But now the image of that perfect orator and of the highest eloquence must be expressed." The name itself indicates that he excels in this one thing: that is, in speech. For the inventor, or the composer, or the author did not encompass all these things. But he is called a **Rhetor** in Greek from the word for "speaking," and in Latin, he is called **eloquent**. For as for the other qualities found in an orator, each person might claim some part for themselves. However, the greatest power of speaking—that is, of elocution—is granted to him alone. And again in *The Orator*: "But **wisdom** is the foundation of eloquence, just as it is of all other things. For as in life, so in speech, nothing is more difficult than to see what is fitting." The Greeks call this <term>πρέπον</term> <note>original Greek: "prepon," meaning "that which is appropriate" or "fitting."</note>. Let us call it **decorum**. Concerning which...
