...many things are perceived excellently, and the matter is most worthy of knowledge. Through ignorance of this, errors are made not only in life, but very often in poetry and in speech. Furthermore, the orator must see what is appropriate <note>original Latin: "quid deceat." This refers to the concept of *decorum*, or propriety—fitting one's speech to the audience and occasion.</note>, not only in his thoughts, but also in his words. And again: Let it be established then among the first principles—which will be better understood later—that the eloquence we seek cannot be achieved without **Philosophy**. Thus, in the *Oratorical Partitions*, speaking of the virtues and every kind of good in the demonstrative and laudatory genre, he says: "And these virtues are seen in action. But there are others that are like handmaidens and companions of **wisdom**. One of these distinguishes and judges between true and false things in dispute, determining what follows once certain points are granted; this virtue resides entirely in the method and science of disputation. The other is **oratory**. For eloquence is nothing else than wisdom speaking fluently <note>original: "copiosè loquens sapientia." A central theme for Cicero: speech without wisdom is dangerous, and wisdom without speech is useless.</note>. It is drawn from the same source as the former, but it is more abundant and broader in dispute, and more adapted to the movements of the mind and the senses of the common people." 

And so that I may join the judgment of **Aristotle** to the opinion of **Cicero**, I will add one passage from Cicero’s *The Orator*: "I think it belongs to perfect eloquence not only to have that faculty which is its own, of speaking broadly and widely, but also to assume the neighboring and related science of the **dialecticians** <note>Dialectics: The formal logic used in debate and philosophical inquiry.</note>. Although speech seems to be one thing and formal dispute another, and talking is not the same as speaking, nevertheless both consist in discourse. The method of disputing and talking belongs to the dialecticians, while speaking and embellishing belongs to the orators." And after the **Chria** <note>A short anecdote or saying used as a school exercise.</note> of **Zeno the Stoic**, who represented dialectic as a clenched fist and eloquence as an open palm, he adds: "And even Aristotle says at the beginning of his art of Rhetoric that it corresponds, as if from the other side, to dialectic: so that they differ in this way, that the former method of speaking is broader, and the latter method of talking is more contracted." 

Now, after the method and way of teaching dialectic, he adds: "Nor should he be instructed in dialectics alone, but he should have all the topics of **philosophy** known and handled. For nothing concerning religion, nothing concerning death, nothing concerning piety, nothing concerning the virtues or vices, nothing concerning duty, nothing concerning pain, nothing concerning pleasure, nothing concerning the disturbances of the mind and errors—which often fall into legal cases but are handled too meagerly—nothing, I say, can be spoken and explained weightily, grandly, and copiously without that knowledge which I have mentioned. I am speaking of the matter of the speech even now, not of the style of speaking itself." And after the skill in civil law and history, he adds: "**Wisdom** must especially be applied to the eloquent man, so that he may be a moderator of times and persons. For I do not think one should speak always, or before everyone, or against everyone, or for everyone, or to everyone in the same manner. He will therefore be eloquent who can adapt his speech to whatever is appropriate. When he has decided this, he will then speak whatever must be said." 

Furthermore, he shows that there is a difference between being "fluent" and being "eloquent"; likewise Cicero in Book 1 of *The Orator*: "I wrote that I have known several fluent men, but no one yet who was truly eloquent. For I defined the **fluent** man as one who could speak with enough sharpness and clarity before ordinary men according to common opinion; but the **eloquent** man as one who could amplify and adorn what he wished more admirably and magnificently, and who held in his mind and memory all the sources of all things that pertain to speaking." **Fabius** <note>This refers to Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, known in English as Quintilian, the Roman educator and rhetorician.</note> at the end of Book 7 says: "But nature, doctrine, and study provide all these things in speech. Therefore, let no one expect to be fluent by the labor of another alone. One must be vigilant..."

Publilius says: "An eloquent companion on the road is as good as a carriage." <note>original: "Facundus comes in via pro vehiculo est." A famous maxim suggesting that good conversation makes a journey feel shorter and easier.</note> However, as to why a speech is called "articulate" <note>original: "diserta."</note> and other terms of this argument, I shall pass over them, as they do not serve our current purpose quite as well.

For it was necessary to provide these many words from the most illustrious men, which will be read with profit by students. From these I shall now strive to gather summarily those points which most pertain to our project. First, we perceive by the judgment of the most eloquent men that eloquence and a solid knowledge of things divine and human—whether one ought to call it wisdom or **Philosophy**—are most closely joined, so that they should not and cannot be separated. Both of these faculties belong only to the "good man," and conversely, the "good man" shrinks from neither virtue. Furthermore, eloquence—which is wisdom speaking ornately and abundantly—is the vigor and supreme power of speech, or as the Greeks say, *echōn* <note>original: ἔχων, meaning "having" or "possessing" power/influence.</note>. The definitions of all the arts adapted to cultivating and refining speech show that they aim for that same goal of perfect and absolute discourse, for they have destined themselves to achieve a certain correctness in oratory. For what is **Rhetoric**? It is nothing else than the art of speaking well, if we listen to Fabius <note>The author refers to Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (Quintilian), the most famous teacher of rhetoric in Rome.</note> defining it thus in his second book. What, then, is **Dialectic**? Nothing else than the science of disputing well, if we do not reject the opinion of Augustine, which would be wicked. What is **Grammar**? Certainly nothing else, if Asper <note>Aemilius Asper, a Roman grammarian known for his commentaries on Terence and Virgil.</note> is heard, than the art of writing and pronouncing correctly, and interpreting the poets through history, shaped for the use and logic of words. Again, Quintilian in his second book shows Grammar to be twofold: one part being the method of speaking, the other the explanation of authors; or the science of speaking correctly and the narration of the poets, as in his first book. **Dialectic** is defined similarly by Cicero in his *Topics*, namely as a diligent method of discourse. And as we have just rendered it, Dialectic is the method of disputing and speaking, while the Oratorical art is that of speaking and adorning; these do not differ even according to Zeno, Aristotle, and Cicero, except that the method of "speaking at length" <note>Rhetoric.</note> is broader, while that of "speaking concisely" <note>Dialectic/Logic.</note> is more contracted. <note>This refers to the famous "Open Hand and Closed Fist" metaphor: Rhetoric is the open palm, Dialectic is the clenched fist.</note> Therefore, the sciences destined for explaining reason and speech—Grammar, Dialectic, and Rhetoric—agree in their goal and definition. In this respect, nothing prevents there being one common reason for all languages and letters; the arts even agree in their very subject matter, whether you look at the words or the things themselves. For whatever things can come into the mind, both those that have no name and those marked by a certain name, pertain to the logician. The most illustrious orators subject this same material both to the art of Rhetoric and to the craftsman himself. In every speech, whatever the subject may be, the observation of Grammar prevents one from falling into solecism, barbarism, or impropriety,

...or lest anything become faulty through foreignness <note>original: "peregrinitate." Referring to the use of foreign words that might corrupt the purity of a language.</note>, so far as can be avoided. Furthermore, that which is right and concerns the arts destined for speech is the very thing that wise and good men look for in every language: that everything be spoken as correctly as possible, and that nothing be perverse. For when James the Apostle says the tongue is a great and untamed evil <note>Referring to James 3:8, "but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison."</note>, he is certainly speaking of speech which is performed by the tongue as an organ; this does not arise from the proper use of language and speech, but rather from its abuse. For the end proposed by God is altogether good. 

Furthermore, where the same Apostle shows that with one tongue we bless God and curse our neighbor, and where Cicero attributes to it the power of teaching, exhorting, consoling, terrifying, and many other things of that kind, these are indeed the effects of men using speech either rightly or wrongly. They are the effects of the oration, but as an instrument, not as the acting cause. For he who speaks and writes must be considered the craftsman. 

Moreover, so that the goals of speech, the arts of speaking, and the craftsman (whether he wishes to be considered a Grammarian, a Dialectician, or an Orator) may be compared and distinguished—even for one unskilled in the arts—the comparison <gloss>is taken from the understanding</gloss> <gloss>of the science of healing.</gloss> For the end and perfection of the body is health, so that the whole body and its individual parts may perform their functions just as the mind and nature dictate. Yet many who are physically well abuse that good for drunkenness and other foul acts; this is an abuse of good health, not its proper use. 

Furthermore, the art of medicine—which is a quality of the soul, a habit and aptitude for doing something rightly and well—applies all its power and actions to the body so that it may be healthy and rightly perform its natural functions, and so that it may protect good health, preserve it from diseases, and, when diseases have perhaps invaded, call back the lost health once they are driven out. And it does this by means of diet—and is called <gloss>dietetics</gloss> <unclear>dietetics</unclear>—or by medicines, and is called <term>pharmaceutics <note>original: "φαρμακευτική"</note></term>; or by the hand and instruments, which is called <term>surgery <note>original: "χειρουργια"</note></term>; or it even applies itself to curing beasts of burden, and is called <gloss>equine medicine</gloss> <note>original: "ἱππιατρική"</note>, but in Latin, *Veterinaria*. 

But there are diseases, both in humans and in other animals, so violent, stubborn, and deplorable that they reject all medicine. The Physician himself, insofar as he is dedicated to this—to consult the good of health according to his ability, art, and profession—looks to the goal of both the body and the art, just as God himself, the Lord of nature, made and instituted the physician, just as He produced medicinal things from the earth, as the book of Ecclesiasticus says <note>Referring to Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:4: "The Lord created medicines out of the earth, and a sensible man will not despise them."</note>. Meanwhile, he receives a just salary by which he may longer preserve himself for human uses, and he is most worthy of honor and ample rewards. However, when he kills men who could have been kept among the living, he does this not as a physician, but as a bandit, an assassin, and a poisoner. And when he hunts for nothing but money and holds his art for sale, he does this as a trader of commercial goods. By indulging too much in the whims of the sick, he performs the duty of a flatterer, not a physician. 

Let us now look at that same similarity in speech, which is likened to the body, just as by a very frequent kind of metaphor, things belonging to the body are transferred, as if closely related, to the soul. Whence in speech, a certain principal virtue and "health" is observed, attributed most greatly to the Attic orators <note>The orators of ancient Athens, known for a "pure," polished, and unornamented style.</note>. Speech, however, is not a body, nor a quantity, nor an action, nor a thing related and connected to another (though some might suspect all these things), but speech is a **quality**. This is derived from the mind through the breath expressed from the lung by the muscles and sinews of the sides, and passing through the rough artery <note>The trachea or windpipe.</note> into the mouth, where it is articulated by the tongue, teeth, and lips as if into joints; or through the marks of letters traced by the hand and a writing instrument into the mind of another man...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion regarding the purpose of speech. The previous page established that the gift of language is inherently good, but its morality depends on the user (the "craftsman"). This page further defines speech as a messenger of thought and transitions into a bibliography of classical and humanist scholars who have defined the rules of the Latin language, focusing finally on Cicero.</meta>

<header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [LANGUAGES]</header>

<note>original: "...nis"</note> ...is poured out both through the ears and through the eyes. Its function is to express reason and will, and to reveal them to others who are capable of both speech and reason. Hence, John of Damascus <note>An 8th-century Syrian monk and scholar known for his writings on theology and philosophy.</note> acutely defined expressed speech as <term>messenger of thought <note>original Greek: ἄγγελος νοήματος (angelos noematos)</note></term>. And although certain signs of the mind are indeed issued through nods, gestures of the hands, the head, and movements of other parts of the body, this function belongs properly to speech. 

Just as we know that the duty of reason and intelligence—which is the most excellent part or faculty of the soul—is to grasp things that exist, or those which are imagined and produced by thought; to inspect, scrutinize, and explore these perceived things internally and externally; to distinguish things separate by nature and, conversely, to join those which are related; and to perceive truth and goodness as well as their opposites. From there, it suggests counsel to the will and persuades it to pursue those things which are truly good, and rouses the other faculties of the soul and body to action, like an empress. Thus, a man performs his duty in all things that present themselves anywhere or at any time. Truly, a man best fulfills this duty when he acts in a way consistent with his ultimate end—so that he might become as similar as possible to his Creator and Parent, God—by imitating and emulating God, who does all things with the most upright judgment and in the best manner. 

And that alone is the perfection of reason: when it is accommodated as closely as possible to the end of man, and thus to the divine nature, which alone is good of itself. Therefore, there shall be no other fulfillment or proper end of speech than if it attains the end of man. Nothing more excellent can happen to a man than to be joined, related, and made most similar to God, as far as human nature is capable: namely, to be wise, truthful, just, holy, good, a diligent actor of right work, and finally, happy and blessed. This health, this rectitude, this perfection, this is the end of speech, as the opinions of wise men and evident reason have indeed shown me. 

However, to divert speech elsewhere, to achieve other things through oratory—to obscure the truth, to seduce, to put on a false front, to deceive, to use the tongue like a fan to stir up seditions, to attack innocence, to curse men or God, and to accomplish the countless other evils through speech—this is indeed the abuse of a thing given by God to men for the common salvation.

Many other infinite, beautiful, and curious researches concerning this matter are detailed by Fabius Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35–100 AD), a Roman rhetorician.</note> in his twelve books of *Oratorical Institutions*; Aelius Donatus the Grammarian; Agroecius the Grammarian; Priscian; Lorenzo Valla; Despautère; Pellisson; Aldus Manutius in their writings on the Latin language; and by Theodor Bibliander in his commentary on the common reason of all languages and letters. Also Aldus Manutius in his institutions of Latin Grammar; A. Mancinelli in his writings on the Latin language and its properties; and above all others by Valentin Erythraeus in his four books on the figures of the Grammarians.

### Of Gaius Julius Caesar, and of his writings composed in the Latin language.

There are hardly any people today who make a profession of arms and letters who do not know well that Gaius Julius Caesar, the Roman Emperor—so named "Caesar" for having formerly killed an elephant called *Caesar* in the language of the Moors, or else because he had blue eyes, and not for the reason of his mother’s belly being slit and opened at his birth according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, *Natural History*, Book 7, Ch. 9.</note>—was in his life one of the greatest and most excellent Captains among the Romans, for the great prowess and deeds of arms executed by him in a short time, as Plutarch and Suetonius amply report in the *Lives* of this Caesar. As for the writings that he left to posterity in the Latin language, we still have them: namely, the *Commentaries* <term>Commentaries: from the Latin "commentarii," these were originally informal daily logs or journals of military campaigns, rather than polished historical narratives.</term> of the Gallic War and the *Commentaries* of the Civil War. Although some have wished to attribute them—though inappropriately, according to Justus Lipsius <note>A famous Flemish humanist.</note>—to a certain Julius Celsus, they are greatly esteemed and prized by the learned men of today. During the memory of our fathers, the Great Turk <note>A common Renaissance title for the Ottoman Sultan.</note> Selim I had them translated into the Arabic language, to read and leaf through them regularly and to govern and conduct himself in his affairs by his example, in his enterprises and conquests; this is found written in a certain travelogue of an Armenian merchant, composed in the Portuguese language. The books of the Alexandrian, African, and Spanish wars attributed to this Emperor were composed, according to the opinion of some ancient authors, by Oppius or Hirtius. Marcus Tullius Cicero, speaking of the *Commentaries* of this Emperor, wrote what follows in his *Brutus*:

> He wrote commentaries of his own deeds that are indeed very much to be approved; they are naked, straightforward, and graceful, with all the ornament of oratory removed, as if a garment were taken off; but while he wished others to have material ready from which those who wanted to write history might take, he perhaps did a favor to the foolish, who wish to singe those things with curling irons <note>A metaphor for over-decorating prose.</note>, but he certainly deterred sane men from writing. <note>original: "Commentarios scripsit rerum suarum valdè quidem probandos, nudi sunt, recti, & venusti, omni ornatu orationis, tanquam veste detracta, sed dum voluit, alios habere paratam vnde sumerent, qui vellent scribere historiam, ineptis gratum fortasse fecit, qui illa volunt calamistris inurere, sanos quidem homines à scribendo deterruit."</note>

->Hirtius speaking of these same Commentaries.<-

> They are so approved by the judgment of all that the opportunity seems to have been snatched from writers, not offered to them. In which matter, however, our admiration is greater than that of the rest, etc. <note>original: "Adeò probantur omnium iudicio, vt prærepta, non præbita facultas scriptoribus videatur. Cuius tamen rei maior nostra, quàm reliquorum est admiratio, &c."</note>

The Romans held this book in great regard and esteem, as they did that of Cicero, as Pierre Crinit <note>Pietro Crinito, an Italian humanist.</note> remarks in book 7, chapter 7, of *On Honest Discipline*. ->*Of Gaius Crispus Sallust and of his writings composed in the Latin language.*<-

Those who have collected Roman histories assert that *Gaius Crispus Sallust*, the "Prince of Latin History" according to *Martial*, was born of a father named *Sallust* like himself, and that he benefited wonderfully well from the liberal arts. He composed his writings in a Latin style not unlike that of the ancients, yet with a marvelous craftsmanship, being full of sinew, force, and vigor in the manner of *Thucydides* <note>A Greek historian known for his dense and powerful prose</note>, as can be seen in his *Catiline Conspiracy*, the *Jugurthine War*, his *Invective against Cicero*, and in his Latin harangues <term>harangues: formal public speeches, often embedded in historical narratives</term> taken from the books of the civil wars. This is so even though *Asinius Pollio* and *Lenaeus Pompeius* criticized him for being too great a lover of antiquity, and for having taken several words from the *Origins* of *Cato* according to *Filippo Beroaldo* in his commentaries on Chapter 86 of *Suetonius Tranquillus* in the *Life of Augustus Caesar*. He is also accused of having taken many words from *Trogus* and of having used excessively long discourses like *Thucydides*. In addition to these writings composed in the Latin language, this figure composed others during his life which are not to be found today, although in the city of *Venice* in the workshop <term>officine: a printing house or workshop</term> of *Aldus Manutius*, and in that of *Lyon* in the workshop of *Gryphius*, there have been some fragments of them.

### *Concerning Publius Virgilius Maro, and his writings or poems composed in the Latin language.*

**PUBLIUS Virgilius Maro**, also named **Vergile**, according to the reports of Minutianus, Apuleius, Calvus, Donatus, and Priscian, was so called because of the **rods** <note>original: "verges"; a traditional folk-etymology suggests his mother gave birth in a place surrounded by poplar twigs or rods</note> among which his mother gave birth to him, as **Pierius Valerianus** holds in his annotations on this poet. In his youth, he composed several Latin poems titled ***Moretum***, ***Priapeia***, ***Epigrams***, ***Dirae***, and ***Culex*** <note>These are part of the *Appendix Vergiliana*, a collection of poems traditionally attributed to Virgil in antiquity</note>, which demonstrate the great natural inclination of this personage toward Latin poetry. In addition to these poems, he wrote that of the ***Aetna***, according to the word of some; and having begun to write the deeds and feats of the Romans, but being hindered by the grandeur of the subject and the harshness and roughness of the Roman names, he devoted himself to composing the ***Bucolics*** <note>Also known as the *Eclogues*, pastoral poems</note> to praise and magnify **Asinius Pollio**, **Alfenus Varus**, and **Cornelius Gallus**. This work was completed by him in the space of three whole years. After that, he went to the city of **Naples** to perfect the ***Georgics*** <note>A poem on agriculture and rural life</note> over seven years in honor of **Maecenas**. Afterwards, he wrote the ***Aeneid***, a work greatly diversified and expanded as a model or pattern of the verses or poems of the ***Iliad*** and ***Odyssey*** of **Homer** joined into one, as can be clearly seen through the commentaries of **Servius** and **Pomponio Leto** <note>OCR: "Pimpo Vuaillant"; likely referring to Pomponio Leto, a famous Renaissance commentator on Virgil</note> on Virgil. This moved **Quintilian** to believe, in his Book 10, Chapter 1, that among all the Greek and Latin heroic poets, he approached most closely the style of **Homer**—to whom, however, the same **Quintilian** recognizes there is more naturalness. This *Aeneid* was composed by this poet, partly in **Sicily** and partly in **Campania**, during the time and space of twelve years. He was the author of the new Latin edition, which even the Hebrews themselves admitted was true. <note>original Latin: "Auctor fuit nouæ Latinæ editionis..." referencing Augustine's *The City of God*, book 18, chapter 43.</note>

For this reason, his prefaces and arguments are placed at the beginning of each book of this edition, because they were written for it and alongside it; he mentions this himself in his eleventh Letter to Augustine, found among the Epistles of Augustine.

Because of this, even the Hebrews attribute this work to him. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> mentions him quite often, never naming him without a preface of praise, and occasionally citing him for the explanation of certain passages, giving him the title <term>כהן</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kohen*, meaning Priest</note>. Rabbi Joseph Albo, in the third book of his *Ikkarim* <note>"Principles of Faith"</note>, chapter 25, calls him a wise translator. Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and grammarian</note> in his commentary on Psalm 110, and Elias <note>Elijah Levita</note> in his work *Thesbi* and under the root <term>פחש</term> <note>The Hebrew root for "interpretation" or "explanation"</note> in Kimhi's work, refer to him by the name of the Wise or Learned Jerome.

Several things worthy of note on this subject are treated by *Polydore Vergil* <note>An Italian humanist and historian (c. 1470–1555)</note> in Book 6, Chapter 2, of *On the Discovery of Things*.

The same *Gilbert Génébrard* <note>French Benedictine scholar and Hebraist</note> in the aforementioned third book of his *Chronology*, making mention of the Apostle Saint Peter, the first Pope of Rome, said of him and of the other Apostles: *Peter* thundered the words of God in Italy, *Paul* in Greece, *Andrew* in Achaia, *John* in Asia, *Philip* in Phrygia, *James* in Judea, *Bartholomew* in Scythia, *Thomas* in India, *Matthew* in Ethiopia, *Simon* in Persia, *Thaddeus* in Mesopotamia, the other *James* in Spain, and *Matthias* in Palestine (specifically, as they say). <note>Citing Honorius on Psalm 18, Origen's 12th homily on Genesis, and George of Trebizond on the phrase "If I want him to remain..."</note>

*Peter* came to Rome in the second year of the Emperor Claudius to defeat *Simon Magus* <note>A sorcerer mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles</note>, according to Jerome in his *Catalogue*. However, *Calvin* denies in his commentary on Acts Chapter 8 that this Magus was ever in Rome, which goes against all antiquity—specifically *Augustine* in his book on heresies, *Tertullian* in his *Apology*, and *Eusebius*, who also mention a statue erected to him in Rome. *Peter* directed many disciples made Bishops in Rome to various provinces for the sake of preaching, specifically into Gaul. *Paul* first preached in Rome in the year 58 AD.

*James*, the brother of the Lord, and *Mark* the Evangelist [were] in Aquileia (which was once called the second Rome), where at the request of the Romans, Mark wrote his Gospel in Greek, or perhaps in Latin, as *Richard FitzRalph* <note>fourteenth-century Archbishop of Armagh</note> suggests in Book 9 of his *Questions*, as does *Jacobus de Voragine* in his sermon on St. Mark, and all the *Syrians*—not to mention those who believe the Latin archetype is preserved in Venice among the Treasures of St. Mark. Mark then became Bishop of Alexandria and was crowned with martyrdom in the year 63 AD.

See what I have previously written in the chapter on the Syriac language regarding this *St. Mark* the Evangelist, who first composed his Gospel in the Latin tongue, which is held to still be present today in the Treasury of the Church of *St. Mark* in the city of Venice, according to what the aforementioned *G. Génébrard* said above.

### How and why the Hebrew, Syriac, Chaldean, Greek, and Latin languages have always been used in public prayers and divine offices.

IT IS a most certain and indubitable thing that it was not without great reason and mystery that throughout the entire universal earth, through a very long succession of centuries, it has always been observed by the sole will of God that mortals have used in their public prayers and divine offices the languages mentioned above. Some reduce these to three, in this manner: first, Hebrew, under which they include the Syriac and Chaldean languages—both of which, to tell the truth, are almost one and the same language, although they differ entirely in their letter characters, as I have clearly demonstrated before. The second is Greek; and the third is the Latin language. This is because, to tell the truth, no other languages have ever been found, nor can be found in the future, more proper and significant for expressing and signifying most clearly and vividly, and with less ambiguity, the divine offices and mysteries, on account of the elegance and emphasis of their words and phrases, and the rules of grammar by which everything is orderly held as if by a bridle. This prevents wandering into many doubts and equivocations, to which other languages are prone to stray easily because of the similarity of cases, numbers, and tenses, which can bring many doubts and uncertainties—and for many other infinite reasons amply deduced by us above in the chapters on the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, and Greek languages. In short, at all times in the communion of the Churches of God, only the three aforementioned languages have been used in public prayers and divine offices: namely, Hebrew, sanctified from the beginning of the world, and the others from the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the Title <note>Referring to the *Titulus Crucis*, the sign placed above Jesus on the cross.</note> that was placed upon the Cross in the Chaldean or Syriac language in these words:

> Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews. <note>original transliterated Syriac/Chaldean: "Iefua Notheraá Malca dihudae"</note>

Where in the Hebrew language there was:
->Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.<- <note>original transliterated Hebrew: "Iefua Hamotferi Melech, haiehudim"</note>

And in the Greek and Latin languages:
> Jesus the Nazarene, the King of the Jews. <note>original Greek: "Ιησοῦς ναζαραῖος ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων"</note>
> Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews. <note>original Latin: "Iefus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum"</note>

And this was not without a mystery relating to what had been promised prophetically by the Seventy <note>The "Seventy" refers to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> regarding Psalms 56, 57, and 58:
->Do not corrupt or alter the inscription of the Title.<- <note>This refers to the Latin "Ne dappas" or "Al-tashcheth" in the Psalm headings, interpreted here as a prophecy regarding the preservation of the Titulus on the cross.</note>

This prefigured that of the cross, as Pope Nicholas I <note>Pope from 858 to 867 AD.</note> wrote to the Emperor Michael of Constantinople: for although the Evangelists state that this Title was written in the Hebrew language, we must nevertheless understand that it was in the Chaldean language.

...or Syriac, which is still used today by all the Christians of Mount Lebanon—those called "of the Girdle" <note>French: *de la Ceincture*; a historical term for Christians in the Levant, referring to the *zunnar* belt they were often required to wear</note>—the Maronites, Mesopotamians, Assyrians, and the infinite Nestorians spread throughout Asia on both sides of the lands under the obedience of both the Sophy <term>Sophy: a historical title for the Safavid Shah of Persia</term> and the Turk [the Ottoman Sultan], as well as the Jacobites in Egypt and Arabia. This is despite the fact that each of these groups has their own particular vulgar [vernacular] language in their respective regions, and that the Arabic language is current almost everywhere in the Levant and the South, even reaching as far as Ethiopia. There, the Ethiopians and Abyssinians, who have a language of their own, nevertheless use the Tangic language <note>Likely referring to Ge'ez, the liturgical language of the Ethiopian Church, which the author classifies as a "Chaldean" dialect</note> in their liturgy and the rest of their divine service; this is a dialect of the ancient Chaldean tongue, as I have already noted previously. St. Augustine, in his discourse *On the Miracles of Scripture*, mentioning the Christian Church—which from its beginning spoke all languages through the mission of the Holy Spirit—used these words concerning the three aforementioned languages: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: <note>original Latin: "Harum omnium linguarum noui Testamenti tempore tribus linguis Hebraicæ, vtiq; Græcæ & Latinæ principatus committitur, quia in eis crucis Christi Titulus literis Hebraicis, Græcis & Latinis scriptus, Euangelica auctoritate perhibetur."</note> "Of all these languages, in the time of the New Testament, the pre-eminence is entrusted to three: namely, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin; for it is testified by Gospel authority that the Title on the Cross of Christ was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters." And Theodore Bibliander <note>A 16th-century Swiss linguist and reformer</note>, in his *Commentary on the common reason of all languages and letters*, interpreting these words, says:

> And indeed, in my consideration of languages, it seems worthy of admiration that while all languages possess at least some certain seat and have an empire—and those which are now abolished, such as the Egyptian and old Persian, once had empires when they flourished—the principal languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin (in which the cause of Jesus Christ dying on the cross was written), do not have a certain dwelling place of any one nation, not to say they have no empire as they once did. For the Greek speech is seen in Greece today [as a different dialect], and the Latin in the provinces of Italy, in Latium, and in the city [Rome] has turned aside from its first origin. The Jews, moreover, do not possess [Hebrew] as a vernacular now, but use it as Germans use Latin or Greek, or even Hebrew; and the Jews are resident aliens among all nations. In this wonder, nothing more probable has come to my mind than that Christ, King of Kings, to whom the Heavenly Father gave all nations and the possession of the ends of the whole earth, consecrated those languages for His city, His kingdom, and His empire. Through these He even now preaches in the glory of the Father through faithful ministers, so that Christian Philosophy may be spread everywhere among the nations, whose supreme axiom is this: that Jesus the Nazarene, crucified under Pontius Pilate, is the Messiah, the King both of the Jews and of all nations, true God and at once true man, the one Savior and mediator between God and men. So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of the Father. For that will be to remove, by divine auspices, the confusion of tongues introduced at the building of Babylon [the Tower of Babel], and from so many languages to make, in a certain way, one. That will be to happily tear away the obstacles and impediments of human society, and having removed hostility from souls, to institute, reconcile, cherish, and confirm a holy society and commerce. That will be to lead back the men of all lands to one fold and one eternal shepherd, who gave His life for His sheep. So that one God, who created all things through the Son with the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both, may be worshipped with one language and mouth, and with one shoulder, as the holy Prophets of God once prophesied.

The learned Gilbert Génébrard <note>A 16th-century French Benedictine, Hebraist, and archbishop</note>, in Book 1 of his *Cosmography*, regarding these words, *Sacred matters are not to be performed in the vernacular*, said the following, which is worthy of great notice:

"Thus far, the holy and Hebrew language has held its place in divine matters, not because it was the vernacular, but because it was holy and prophetic. From which it follows that even in this sixth age <note>A reference to the "Six Ages of the World," a periodization of history common in Christian theology</note>, it continues to be used by the Jews, even if it is now less of a vernacular and popular language for them, and is not understood by any of them who have not studied it, just as Latin and Greek are for us. Therefore Ezra and the Scribes handed down and established the formula for divine service in Hebrew—which was then unknown to the common people—according to Maimonides <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> in Part 1 of the treatise *Tephilla* and *Bircath Cohanim*, that is, *On Prayer* and *On the Blessing of the Priests*. And for this reason, they use prayer books written in the Hebrew language in their synagogues, such as the *Mahzor*, the *Siddur Tephillot* (which Rabbi Amram sent from Babylonia to Spain around the year 900 AD), the *Seder*, etc. And it is considered a sacrilege to do so in any other language, according to Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A celebrated 12th-century Spanish-Jewish scholar</note> on Ecclesiastes 5:1, where he also rebukes some lyric poets of his nation for mixing Medical <note>The language of the Medes</note>, Persian, and Spanish words into their hymns, teaching that not even Syriac and Arabic should be used, even though they are related to Hebrew. This is what the Church observes by not using common and profane languages, but only the four holier and more universal ones, which are also grammatical, learned, and better suited for mysteries and disciplines to foster the communion of saints (which a diversity of local dialects would tear apart). She solemnly uses these for divine service: one is holy from its primary origin, which is Hebrew, and three others are sanctified and dedicated by the title on the Cross: Syriac, Greek, and Latin, according to Jerome in the *Epitaphs of Nepotian and Paula*. Lest the title on the Cross, proclaiming Jesus the Nazarene as King of the Jews, be forgotten. For it is written by divine inspiration in the Book of Psalms: *Do not destroy the inscription of the title* (Psalm 56, 57, 58, first verses), as Pope Nicholas the Great wrote to Emperor Michael. For this same reason, Pope Gregory VII, more than 500 years ago <note>The text reads "plus 50," likely a printing error for "plus 500," as Gregory VII reigned in the 11th century</note>, did not grant the request of Vladislav, Duke of the Bohemians, who asked that he and his people be permitted to perform the divine office in Slavonic, because it was less fitting to Christian institutions..."

[Published] at Christopher Plantin's. <note>Christophe Plantin (c. 1520–1589) was a major Renaissance printer based in Antwerp.</note>

Among all languages, Reader, three especially have always been held in the greatest admiration and highest esteem: namely, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. This is both because the monuments of both divine and human sciences have been preserved within them and transmitted from our ancestors to posterity as if by hand, and also because they have attained a certain eminent dignity above other languages, being honored by the memorable title of the glorious Cross of the King of kings and Lord of lords, Jesus Christ our Redeemer. Furthermore, each of these, like a tree divided into three branches, has spread into three other dialects of speech. Hebrew has spread into Babylonian or Chaldaic, into Syrian or Hierosolymitan <note>Jerusalem-style Syriac</note>, and into Arabic, which the Jews call the language of Ishmael. Greek, or Ionic, into Attic, Doric, and Aeolic. Roman, which is also Latin, into Italian, Spanish, and French. Thus, in these three languages—as in most other things of this world, whether they are perceived by the intellect or fall under the sight of the eyes—that divine and adorable Trinity of infinite power, wisdom, and goodness shines forth. Moreover, all these collected together reflect for us once again the mystic twelve <note>Original: 'dodecadem'. The author links the 3 main languages and their 3 sub-dialects (3x3=9) plus the original 3 to reach 12, or perhaps simply refers to the 12 total dialects mentioned.</note>. Therefore, in those three most powerful languages, the thrice-great and thrice-blessed One willed to reveal His divine will to us, and to hand down His holy statutes and precepts which were to be for us a certain rule for living well and blessedly in the public and most ample city of this world, so that we might finally reach eternal and immortal life and enjoy the sight of the one divine essence and the Trinity of persons. It is, therefore, in this thrice-triple kind of languages that the holy and sacred Books have come down to us; these are indeed secret monuments, far more precious than any treasures, preserved by divine providence in great integrity and purity throughout the ages of so many centuries, etc.

Raffaele Volaterrano <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a humanist scholar from Volterra</note> writes in Book 22 of his *Anthropology* that in the time of Pope Innocent VIII in the year 1492, the title of the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was found in the Basilica of the Holy Cross in the middle of the temple, hidden in a wall, written in the 3 aforementioned languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—in these words alone:

->*Jesus of Nazareth, Ki[ng].*<-
<note>original: "Iefus Nazarenus Re." — 'Re' is likely an abbreviation of 'Rex' (King).</note>

The rest of the words being gnawed away or erased.

A great Poet of this time <note>Likely referring to Pierre de Ronsard or Guillaume de Salluste Du Bartas, common sources for such linguistic reflections</note>, speaking of the different kinds of world languages, says these words of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages:

> *Every language changes, whether it be that commerce,*
> *By communicating to us from the Persian Amphitrite* <note>Amphitrite is a Greek sea goddess; the "Persian Amphitrite" refers to the trade routes of the Indian Ocean and the East.</note>
> *Precious treasures, and those from land to the waves,*
> *Happily and boldly trades word for word;*
> *Whether the eloquent man in a graceful fashion,*
> *Curling his golden words and refining his style,*
> *Desirous of glory, strikes new coins*
> *For things and deeds, or at least gives*
> *Currency to decried names, and restores to nature*
> *The superannuated, moldy ones, spoiled by woodworm.*
> *It is just like the leaves of a wood:*
> *One falls, another is born. Words which in times past*
> *Shone here and there in eloquent oratory*
> *Like Lilies in the green countryside...*

[They] are no longer in style: instead, banished from the court,
They dwell in shame beneath the roofs of a lowly hamlet,
And those which the morose judgment of olden times
Had cast aside <note>original: "mis au billon" — a term for demonetizing old currency</note>, are now in high demand.
A fine mind, guided by fortune and judgment,
Can give passport to words that freshly
Emerge from his workshop <note>original: "boutique"</note>, adopting foreign ones,
Grafting the wildlings <note>a metaphor for incorporating "uncivilized" or rustic words into refined speech</note>, making by these mixtures

A language has no law other than usage,
Running without a bridle, without eyes, where the fickle common people
Go rushing headlong; the other kind of speech, enclosed
Within the barriers of art, arranges its words well.
One, already aging upon the threshold of its infancy,
Has the verse for its tomb; the other resists
The passage of the years: one lives unfortunately,
Confined forever within a narrow valley:
The other, bold among the learned, makes itself heard
From the coast of Fez <note>modern-day Morocco</note> to the altar of Alexander <note>likely Alexandria, Egypt</note>.
Such are, for today, Hebrew, Greek, and Roman:
Hebrew, insofar as we still hold from its hand
The sacred Word of the thrice-Eternal,
And because it is the original record <term>protocol|the original draft or foundational text</term> of Divine Law:
The Greek, as having in its learned writings
Every genre of knowledge eloquently comprised,
And the masculine Roman <note>Latin</note>, insofar as its eloquence
Was planted by the sword in every corner of the World.

...matters pertaining to customs are explained with gravity and abundance, and spoken of magnificently. Thus, gravity can be ascribed mostly to the Romans and the majesty of the Empire; to the Greeks, genius and wit; and to the Hebrews, a more secret doctrine and a kind of divinity (as Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a celebrated Italian Renaissance philosopher</note> used to say). The volumes of Moses himself and the prophecies of the Prophets prove this greatly. This was the opinion of our Pico regarding the disciplines and geniuses of the ancients. But even Marcus Cicero <note>The Roman statesman and orator</note> elegantly brought forth these points regarding the Greeks themselves in his *Oration for Lucius Flaccus*:

I will say this regarding the whole race of the Greeks: I grant them literature, I give them the training in many arts, I do not take away the charm of their speech, the sharpness of their minds, nor finally their abundance of speaking—even if they take other things for themselves, I do not object. But that nation never cultivated the sanctity and good faith of legal testimonies <note>original: "testimoniorum religionem & fidem"</note>. Indeed, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, noble among the Platonists, accuses the Greeks themselves of levity and inconstancy; meanwhile, he asserts that the Egyptians or Hebrews (whom he calls barbarians) are constant and outstanding in the worship and observance of the gods. But I will record his words below, as he has expressed all this gravely and copiously in his *On the Mysteries*:

"It is right," he says, "in the worship of the Gods to always guard the ancient rites as sacred and the best, and to keep them untouched and inviolate, so that nothing at all is added or even taken away. For from this," he says, "it happened that the deities themselves and the prayers appear diminished and weakened, because many things were changed out of a desire for perversion and religious innovation, and are changed more day by day. For the Greeks themselves, by their own nature fond of new things, are easily turned in any direction at every moment; being light, and like a ship in which no ballast <note>original: "sabuli," literally sand or gravel used for stability</note> has settled, they preserve nothing at all of what they received from their ancestors. Instead, changing everything repeatedly, they cast out the old and, out of innate levity, exchange one thing for another, constant in nothing. But the Barbarians," he says, "as they are firm and upright in their customs, so they also persevere with the greatest constancy in the same speeches and sentiments; by which it happens that they have deservedly remained closer to the gods than others, and offer them prayers that are most acceptable, which can in no way be changed by others."

Rudolph IV <note>Likely referring to the 14th-century Duke of Austria, though the legal requirement for Electors to be multilingual is traditionally associated with the Golden Bull of 1356 issued by Charles IV</note>, Emperor, ordered that the electors of the Roman Empire should know and learn five languages besides their own mother tongue: namely Greek, Latin, French, Italian, and Spanish. This is something the Germans have always observed very well, so that the Emperors—at least the greater part of them—have known how to speak various languages. The Emperor Otto could respond to all the Ambassadors sent to him, each in their own language. Charles V <note>original: "Charles le Quint"</note>, Emperor and King of the Spains, was accustomed to say that it was a great shame for a person of honor to know how to speak only one language.

### *Of the decline of the Latin language.*

Those who have read the Latin histories and the fragments of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law, dating to the 5th century BC</note> know well enough—as I have amply remarked in the preceding chapters—that if the first and oldest Roman writings survived until the present, we would see that Evander and Turnus <note>Mythological figures representing the earliest inhabitants of Italy in the Aeneid</note>, and the other Latins of that time and of the first centuries, spoke differently than did afterwards the last Roman Kings and the first Consuls and Latins of that era. The verses that the Salian Priests <note>An ancient college of priests who performed ritual dances and songs (the *Carmen Saliare*) for Mars</note> used to sing were understood by those later Romans only with great difficulty. But for having been thus ordained by the first founders, they were not changed out of reverence for Religion. Polybius <note>A Greek historian of the 2nd century BC</note> on this subject writes that the Latin language was so changed from the First Punic War until the second that with great pain and difficulty one could understand the treaties made previously between the Romans and the Carthaginians. And this language remained for nearly five hundred years rude and unpolished, having had no writer in it who was worthy of memory. From then onwards, the Romans and Latins devoted themselves to letters and sciences, and some became learned, though remaining harsh and rough in their speech, praised only for having been the inventors and first masters of Latinity.

This is very well verified by the discourses of Verrius Flaccus <note>A Roman grammarian of the time of Augustus</note>, of Marcus Varro’s *On the Latin Language*, by Nonius Marcellus, and Festus Pompeius <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century grammarian</note> on the same matter, and in F. Quintilian, the Latin orator, and P. Crinitus’s <note>Pietro Crinito (1475–1507), an Italian Renaissance humanist</note> books on the Latin Poets.

This language was rendered very elegant and perfect by Cicero, Caesar, Sallust, and Virgil, mentioned above, and by other eloquent

...men who flourished then in great number, in whom truly the purity of that Latin language is recognized. For afterward, the Roman Republic being transformed into a Monarchy, and morals becoming corrupt, that language similarly changed and was corrupted, losing its previous naturalness and eloquence under the Emperors. Then, the Empire being transferred from Rome to Constantinople, several foreign nations arriving in Italy altered that language so much that people ceased to speak it, and it remained in books alone, which were neither read nor understood for more than eight hundred years: some lost, others eaten by worms, and spoiled by age, until certain Italians and Greeks, through study, brought back to life these two ancient languages—namely, Latin and Greek—which were almost dead or lost, describing, publishing, and correcting the books remaining in libraries protected from the fury and rage of the Barbarians. 

This succeeded so fortunately for them that these said languages recovered great light along with the arts and sciences written in them, which we see restored with them, along with several inventions added to antiquity. Therefore, as the Roman Empire declined in the West, as the Goths, Ostrogoths, Lombards, and other Northern peoples had occupied Italy; the Visigoths and Saracens Provence, Languedoc, Aquitaine, and Spain; the Burgundians and Franks Belgic and Celtic Gaul; the Vandals Baetica <note>A Roman province in what is now southern Spain (Andalusia)</note> and Africa, through their conversation <note>In this context, "conversation" refers to the mixing and social interaction of different peoples living together.</note> the Latin language was corrupted.

From which corruption were born and emerged Italian, French, and Spanish: Italian having remained unpolished for a long time because there was no one who took care of it or sought to give it polish, until Dante, Petrarch, Boccaccio, and Ariosto, who greatly embellished it through their ingeniously expressed conceptions and elegantly laid out in verse and prose, in which they were followed by others no less learned and eloquent who have similarly enriched this language with several beautiful works and traditions. The same happened to Spanish and to French, which has been rendered more copious and elegant for fifty or so years than it was before, by the diligence of certain excellent persons who have translated and transferred a great number of Greek and Latin books, indeed even Italian, Spanish, and others, showing that all doctrines and sciences can be appropriately treated therein.

Several other beautiful and excellent discourses concerning this matter are amply detailed by Louis Le Roy <note>Loys Le Roy (c. 1510–1577), a French humanist professor and writer known for his works on world history and culture.</note> in the sixth book of the *Vicissitude of Things* <note>original: "de la Vicissitude des choses"</note>, in the chapter on the *Decadence of the power, knowledge, and eloquence of the Romans*. Petrarch, opening the Libraries closed before, and removing the dust and filth from atop the good books of ancient authors: for being a man of great understanding and excellent doctrine, he did not only embellish the Italian language, for which he is revered with J. Boccaccio his disciple as the principal author and illustrator, but also laudably stimulated Latin Poetry and Prose.

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE

<note>The following section provides a dense etymological and historical survey of the various names for Italy in antiquity.</note>

Cato, in his *Origins* <note>original: "in originibus"</note>, divides [the geography of the Apennines] according to Hebrew roots. Arias Montanus writes in his *Biblical Appendix* that Italy is called *Kityn*; the Seventy Interpreters <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> of Isaiah 61 seem to call it *Mosoch*. Dionysius of Halicarnassus in Book 1 indicates that the Italians were also sometimes called *Morgetes* <note>original: "μόργητες"</note>. The Slavs call Italy *Vuloska*. Regarding the names of Italy, see Chapter 22 of Hadrianus Iunius’s *Observations* and the *Chorography* of Caspar Varrerius. For why it was named "Italy," read Festus. Dionysius of Halicarnassus in Book 1 calls Eastern Italy that which stretches from the Iapygian promontory <note>The "heel" of Italy</note> to the Strait of Sicily. Diodorus in Book 11 mentions "Ligurian Italy," by which I believe he means Cisalpine [Gaul]. For "Gallic Italy," see the entries for *Gaul* and *Cisalpine*. See also *Chersonesus*.

Cisalpine Gaul <note>The region of Northern Italy "on this side of the Alps" from a Roman perspective</note> is a region of Italy according to Pliny, who calls part of it "Subalpine Italy" in Book 16, Chapter 11. It is "Gallic Italy" <note>original: "γαλατικὴ"</note> in Appian’s *Hannibalic Wars*. Likewise, it is called "Hither Gaul" by the same author, as well as by Caesar, Hirtius, and Sallust. Ausonius, in his address to the Emperor Gratian, calls it "Ancient Gaul." The ancients divide this into Cispadane and Transpadane Gaul <note>Regions "on this side" and "across" the River Po</note>, as do Pliny and Strabo. Aulus Gellius in Book 5, Chapter 18, calls it "Transpadane Italy." Diodorus in Book 11 calls it "Ligurian Italy." Leandro [Alberti] calls it "Lombardy on this side and that side of the Po," using the same meaning. For the Italians call the [river] Padus the "Po," and interpret *cis* and *trans* as "this side" and "that side." Cispadane Gaul was once called *Bianora*, then *Felsina*, and finally *Aurelia* and *Emilia*, as Cato writes in his *Origins*—if credit be given to the author.

Italy was called Oenotria after the Sabine King Oenotrus. Dionysius [of Halicarnassus] relates that Oenotrus and Peucetius, brothers and sons of Lycaon, King of the Arcadians, migrated to Italy. Peucetius occupied that part of Apulia called Iapygia, from which those people were called *Peucetians*. Oenotrus, however, invaded the western part of Italy, which was held by the barbarian Sicels and is now called Latium; he obtained it and named it *Oenotria* after his own name. His successors were Italus, Morges, and Siculus, from whom the Oenotrians themselves were sometimes called Italians, Morgetes, and Sicels. Regarding the Oenotrians, Virgil says:

> *There is a place the Greeks call Hesperia by name,*
> *Oenotrian men cultivated it; now rumor has it their descendants*
> *Have called the nation Italy, after the name of their leader.*
<note>original: "Est locus Hesperiam Graij cognomine dicunt, / Oenotrij coluere viri, nunc fama minores / Italiam dixisse ducis de nomine gentem." — Aeneid I.530-533</note>

From the fragments of Marcus Varro. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book 1 of his *Roman Antiquities*.

->*On the Italian Language.*<-

Those who wish to read exactly what we have written in the two preceding chapters concerning the greatness of the Roman Empire, its decline, and the various captures of the city of Rome—the capital of that Empire—by the Northern nations and others mentioned above (which Empire had employed and made use of the pure Latin language as its vulgar and familiar tongue), will easily believe that, through the incursions and ravages of those nations in this Empire, the aforementioned Latin language has since been changed and transformed from century to century, and from time to time, into the vulgar and common language [of Italian].

...the common Italian language of today: as is confessed by all those who have written of this language.

But some hold that the Lombards <note>A Germanic people who ruled most of the Italian Peninsula from 568 to 774.</note>, coming into Italy at the persuasion of Narses <note>A prominent Byzantine general under Emperor Justinian I.</note>, Lieutenant of the Emperor, began to abolish the laws, the language, and the proper names of places that existed there previously. For the Ostrogoths <note>Another Germanic tribe who preceded the Lombards; they generally admired Roman culture.</note> never attempted such barbarity, but rather followed the ancient Law of the Romans and took pleasure in learning the Latin language. And following the words of the aforementioned personages, it was the Lombards who bastardized the common language of the Italians, and not the other Northern nations as many have estimated. Therefore, according to the opinion of the aforementioned, the Lombards having invaded Italy, they removed the Latin names, using their own customs, and established principalities which were like magistracies: namely four Dukes—specifically of Benevento, Spoleto, Turin, and Friuli—along with two Marquisates, that of Ancona and that of Treviso. This was the reason that since then, one of the lands has been named the March of Ancona, and the other, the Trevisan March. These Principalities were greater than those of the Dukes, as they were perpetual and hereditary, whereas the office of Duke was determined by election. Furthermore, the word "Marquisate" in the language of the ancient Lombards signified a perpetual Lordship.

Several modern authors, speaking in their writings of the Italians of today and of their Italian language, have written the following:

It is not without great divine providence that when God, the All-Good and All-Powerful, visited the earth by becoming man, the seat of the Empire and the retreat of all the nations of the Universe was in Italy. There, soon after, was to be placed the head and Universal Pastor of the Christian Fold <note>A reference to the Pope and the Catholic Church in Rome.</note>. The Italians are often diverse among themselves, both in color and in stature; for those who reside in Cisalpine Gaul <note>The region of Northern Italy between the Alps and the Apennines.</note> and all along the Venetian lands are ordinarily fair-skinned, and more refined in dress and language. In contrast, the Tuscans, Campanians (or Neapolitans), and those of Basilicata and Abruzzo have a leaden <note>Likely meaning olive-toned or tanned.</note> complexion, black hair, small stature, and are lean and nimble, simple and modest in dress and language. In the March of Ancona, and among all the Italians who reside along the Levant coast <note>The eastern, Adriatic coast.</note> as far as Great Greece <note>original: "grande grece"; refers to Magna Graecia, the coastal areas of Southern Italy historically colonized by Greeks.</note> (excepting the Calabrians and those of Apulia who inhabit the corner of Italy), both the manners and the language remain even now a mixture of Greek and Italian.

Several other modern authors speak of it in this fashion: The dress of the Italians is different according to their lands and provinces. The Venetians wear them long and wide, almost to the point of superfluity; and those of the city are much more sumptuous than those of the fields and villages. # LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE

...superbly dressed, and takes more pleasure in foreign fashions than those of Italy: of which the rest goes simply in order, not that the habits there are not diverse, seeing that in this time we have seen an infinity of changes in dress. Throughout the Bolognese region, and almost through all of Lombardy, the great Ladies take much pleasure in dressing in the Spanish style, and the Gentlemen love the ornamentation of the French. In Rome, until recently, the women dressed in the Tuscan style; it was not long ago that the Ladies of Venice wore the throat, breast, and shoulders uncovered, but at present they cover them, and have very wide sleeves, so that their habit somewhat imitates the Spanish. 

As for the Italian language, it is not what it once was, and yet not entirely different, but it is corrupted and altered because of barbarian words which have been introduced in one place more than another, depending on how long foreigners held the Provinces in subjection. Along the coast of Istria, almost all the people speak Venetian, which is a polished, copious, and grave language, and adorned with the sweetness of several other languages, because it is the place where all the peoples of Italy trade: formerly this Venetian language was more rude and very unpleasant to the ears. The speech of the Carnians <note>A people from the Carnia region in northeast Italy.</note> neighboring the Carinthians <note>A region in modern-day Austria.</note> is composed of various languages, and has I-know-not-what that is contrary to the air of Italian words: yet it is more pleasant to the ear. Toward the Trevisan country, in Padua, Verona, Vicenza, Mantua, and Ferrara, everywhere those of the cities are more graceful in speech than the peasants and villagers. 

The Lombard and Milanese speech has a certain coarse roughness different from the rest of Italy in its speaking; however, there is no country that surpasses this one in the beauty of its cities, the refinement and courtesy of its citizens, nor in the honesty and sobriety of life. Of those of Romagna, Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, Faenza, Bologna, and the lands of the Patrimony <note>The "Patrimony of Saint Peter," referring to the lands under the direct temporal rule of the Pope.</note>, the language is sweet and polished. The Tuscan is brief in speech, imitating the ancient manner of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans of ancient Greece, known for their "laconic" or very brief way of speaking.</note>, and this language suits the foreigner better than the native of the country. 

In Rome, until recently, the speech there was rude, but the frequenting of outsiders enriched and softened this coarse roughness. In the March of Ancona, the land of Sabina, and in the Principality, the people speak more rudely and coarsely than in the Duchy of Urbino, or in Puglia, Basilicata, and Abruzzo, which, like all the rest of Italy, have a hard and constrained language, and little mixed with foreign sweetness, except for the Neapolitans, who study to speak their natural tongue with Spanish gravity: in short, whoever looks at things maturely, and judges them in general, will find no people nor city in this world that is not in some case different from those neighboring them, as Sabellicus <note>Marcus Antonius Coccius Sabellicus (1436–1506), a Venetian historian famous for his works on world history.</note> remarks in *Enneads*, Book 2, Volume 1. 

Among the moderns who have written of the beauty, perfection, and elegance accomplished with all the daintiness and refinement of the Italian language, Girolamo Ruscelli <note>An influential Italian humanist and writer.</note>, in the preface to Giovanni Boccaccio printed by Valgrisi in Venice in the year 1557, has greatly excelled; there, he makes no difficulty in pairing this language with Latin, and sustaining through an ample discourse that it should take lordship of the Monarchy over all other languages of this Universe, even having made a specific treatise on this matter, which I have seen and read in the past. Whoever wishes to see infinite things beautiful and rare concerning this language, let him read Dante *Concerning Vernacular Eloquence* <note>Original: "d'ella volgar eloquentia." A famous 14th-century treatise by Dante Alighieri defending the use of the Italian language in literature.</note>, and Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo (1470–1547), an influential scholar who helped standardize the Italian language.</note> *Concerning the Language*...

->*On the invention of rhymes.*<-

Some authors have written that rhymed verses or poems <note>original: "vers ou carmes Rythmez"</note> were first invented by certain individuals living during the decline of the Greek Empire, when the mixing of foreigners came to spoil and corrupt the dialect, pronunciation, and accents of the Greek and Latin languages. This was such that the Venerable Bede, living around the year of our salvation 730, speaks of it in his book *On the Types of Meters* <note>original: "des genres de mettres," referring to *De arte metrica*</note>, in the penultimate chapter, as a form of composition very much in use and practiced in his time; something which Marius Victorinus <note>A 4th-century grammarian.</note> had remarked upon before him in his works. The authors of the *Ecclesiastical History* composed at Magdeburg <note>The "Magdeburg Centuries," a massive 16th-century history of the Church.</note>, citing the *Chronicle of Holstein*, assert that the ancient Germans recorded their wars and victories in rhyme, and that Charlemagne commanded in his time that a collection be made of the rhymes that were then in use among men. Furthermore, we can learn from what a certain individual named Otfrid—a monk of Weissenburg and disciple of Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda, living around the year of our salvation 870—wrote in his translation of the Gospels, that the "homoioteleuton" <term>Omioteleute: A Greek term for "similar endings," referring here to the origins of end-rhyme.</term> rhyme was already in use in his time among the Teutonic Franks <note>original: "François Thyois," referring to the Germanic-speaking inhabitants of the Frankish Empire.</note>. Some have gone so far as to write that it is a certain fact that the French taught the use of "homoioteleuton" or consonant rhyme to the other nations of Europe, as Claude Fauchet discusses at great length in Book 1, Chapter 6, of his *On the French Language and Poetry*. He bases this primarily on couplets extracted from a certain manuscript written nearly five hundred years ago regarding the *Life of Saint Faith of Agen* <note>A 3rd-century child martyr; her "Chanson" is one of the oldest surviving works in a Romance language.</note>. Lilio Gregorio Giraldi in his *Dialogues on the Poets of his Time*, and Velutello in his *Commentaries* in the Italian language on the *Triumphs* of Petrarch, write that Italian rhymes and the fashion of composing in sonnets and stanzas originated and proceeded, according to some, from the Sicilians, during the time when a certain William Iron-Arm <note>original: "Guillaume Ferrabrach"</note>, brother of Robert Guiscard, and other Lords of Calabria and Apulia...

the language, the children of Tancred, French Normans, carried them from Provence to Sicily, a country in Italy; and at that time, the French utilized this form and manner of composition according to the account of Francesco Petrarch in the preface to his letters. Others say that this way of composing in rhyme, sonnets, and stanzas originated with the Etrurians <note>An ancient civilization in what is now Tuscany.</note>, from whom the first and oldest Tuscan language emanated. Our French writers maintain that this proceeded from the invention of the Provençal poets, who flourished around the year of salvation 1162, as has been well noted by Colocci <note>Angelo Colocci, an Italian Renaissance humanist.</note> and Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo, an influential scholar who helped standardize the Italian language.</note> in their discourses on this matter.

This subject was very well debated and treated by Dante in his works; by Petrarch in the fourth chapter of his *Triumph of Love*; and by Jean de Nostradame and Jean Giudici in their discourses on the lives of the most celebrated and ancient Provençal poets. This moved a certain one of our Frenchmen to write these words in a discourse of his regarding Sicily:

"Due to the greater softness and effeminacy of the Sicilians, poetry by rhymes and cadences is attributed to them; likewise, they were the first to treat of love in the vernacular and in rhyme—if one grants faith to Dante and Petrarch—although there are those who attribute this to our Gauls, and to those of Limousin and Provence. This I believe, if one considers the modern way of rhyming <note>original: "rythmailler"</note> and giving meter to verses by the same ending and termination of sounds at their close, regarding which Dante wrote a book that I have seen in manuscript <note>original: "escript à la main"</note>."

The most learned and scholarly of this century in ancient languages assert that the fashion and manner of composing verses or poems in rhyme proceeds from the invention of the Hebrews and Jews. This is treated quite extensively by Friar Sixtus of Siena in Book 3 of his *Library* <note>The *Bibliotheca Sancta*, a major work of biblical scholarship.</note> and by Friar Luis of Portugal in his "globe of the canons and secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture," Book 9, *On the Poetry of the Hebrews* <note>original: "de poeſi Hebræorum"</note>, chapters 7 and 8. In this regard, one should look at what we have written above concerning the Royal Prophet David and his writings composed in the Hebrew language. Gilbert Génébrard, in his *Chronography*, remarks that Eastern histories record that in the year of salvation 904, Emperor Constantine VII lamented the death of his wife with rhymes and all kinds of verse, according to Zonaras in Volume 5 of his histories. This leads one to believe that the Greeks, as well as the Latins, used rhymes at that time. Whoever wishes to see many beautiful and rare discourses touching on this question should read Pierre Grégoire, Book 19, Chapter 11, of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art*, and Claude Fauchet, cited above, in his *Collection on the Origin of the French Language and Poetry, Rhyme, and Romances*, Book 1, Chapters 6, 7, and 8. What is more, we read in the works of Johannes Magnus <note>original: "Iean le Grand"</note> and his brother Olaus in their *Northern Histories*, that the Northern peoples have since time immemorial been accustomed to singing in rhyme at their balls, assemblies, and banquets, the deeds and gestures of their ancestors and predecessors. Polydore Vergil, in Book 1, Chapter 9 of his book *On the Invention of Things*, treats the origin of poetic meters or measures.

# CONCERNING GIOVANNI BOCCACCIO, ITALIAN, AND
## *his writings composed in the Italian language.*

Giovanni Boccaccio, of the Italian nation and a native of Certaldo in Italy, flourished in his country in the Year of Grace 1342. Being a man well-instructed in many beautiful and high sciences, both the humanities and mathematics, he composed in his Italian language, very gracefully and elegantly, several poems mentioned in his biography compiled by Mr. Lodovico Dolce and Mr. Francesco Sansovino. These he wrote as a pastime, because of which he later burned them out of despair of ever reaching the excellence of the poems of Francesco Petrarch. After these, he set himself to composing his *Decameron* very properly and elegantly in Italian prose, during the time when the plague was so vehement in Florence in the Year of Grace 1348. Into this work, he inserted five or six of the best and most pleasant novellas <note>Short stories or tales.</note> which he drew from certain old French narratives <note>original: "tableaux"; in this context, it refers to "fabliaux" or descriptive tales.</note> and very ancient books by French rhymers and poets, as Claude Fauchet curiously notes in book one, chapter six, of *The French Language and Poetry*, and book two, chapters twelve, seventeen, eighty-four, and one hundred and two, of *Ancient French Poets*. After this, he also composed in the said Italian language *The Philocolo* and *Fiammetta*, for the love of Maria—the sister of Joanna, Queen of Naples, and wife (though others say daughter) of Robert, Count of Artois; likewise the *Corbaccio*, *Filostrato*, and *The Labyrinth*. In addition to these books, he also composed several others, but in the Latin language: namely, the book on the *Genealogy of the Gods*, that of *Famous Women*, that of the names of mountains, forests, fountains, lakes, rivers, and streams, along with a compendium on Roman history, as is well noted by Conrad Gessner and Josias Simler in their historical libraries. This personage died at the age of 62 in 1375, as is confirmed by François Floride in his *Apology for the Latin Language*, Paolo Giovio in his *Eulogy of Famous Men*, Raffaele Volaterranus in book 21 of his commentaries, Mr. Lodovico Dolce in his life of the said Boccaccio, Mr. Francesco Sansovino in the life of the said Boccaccio inserted before the said *Decameron*, and Jean-Papire Masson in his biography. He was buried in the said Certaldo in the Church of St. Philip with this epigram, composed by himself before his death:

> Under this tomb lie the ashes and bones of Giovanni;
> His soul sits before God, adorned by the merits of his labors
> In mortal life. Boccaccio was his sire;
> Certaldo was his homeland, and his pursuit was nourishing Poetry.
> <note>original: "Hac sub mole iacent cineres, ac ossa Ioannis, / Mens sedet ante Deum meritis ornata laborum / Mortalis vitæ genitor Bocacius, illi / Patria Certaldum, studium fuit alma Poësis."</note>

In addition to these verses, the same Paolo Giovio, in the passage cited above, brings forward others composed in praise of this personage, which I shall not report in this place in order to avoid prolixity.
