> <note>original: "...Euandro perueniſſet, expulſiſque Aboriginibus gentem illam rudem mo- res & literas docuiſſet Gothi ſuas literas habuerint..."</note> ...[when he] had arrived with **Evander** <note>In Roman mythology, a hero from Arcadia who brought Greek culture and the alphabet to Italy</note>, and having driven out the **Aborigines** <note>The earliest native inhabitants of central Italy</note>, he had taught that rude people customs and letters, the **Goths** already had their own letters. Evidence of this matter is provided by stones of extraordinary size, fixed to the tombs and caves of the ancient Goths: which, being inscribed with the forms of letters, might persuade one that they had been erected there by Giant-like strength before the universal flood, or shortly thereafter. Expressing their deeds on stones with these characters, they handed them down to the eternal memory of men. Although they lacked knowledge of the Roman speech—which at that time, before the founding of Rome, did not exist—nevertheless, such a great diligence for the study of eloquence and for writing their native poems inflamed them, so that not only modest boys (as **Cato** writes the Romans did much later) were everywhere instructed to sing ancient songs in which the praises of their ancestors were contained, but even grave men sang to the flutes about the virtues of famous men (as is still done today): and so great was the honor and reward of learning, that most people bestowed not only scepters and kingdoms but even divine honors upon the wise.
> cc

**Olaus Magnus** <note>A Swedish ecclesiastic and writer (1490–1557) famous for his descriptions of Northern peoples</note>, brother of the aforementioned **John** <note>Johannes Magnus (1488–1544), Archbishop of Uppsala, who wrote a history of the Goths and Swedes</note>, writes the following in Book 1, Chapter 36 of his histories of the **Northern Peoples**:

> <note>original: "Ab antiquiſſimo tempore cùm eſſent Gigantes in Septentrion. terris..."</note> From the most ancient times, when there were Giants in the Northern lands—that is, long before Latin letters were invented, and before **Carmenta** <note>A goddess of childbirth and prophecy, mother of Evander, credited with inventing the Latin alphabet</note> came from Greece to the mouths of the Tiber and the Roman soil with Evander, and, having expelled the Aborigines, taught that rude and clearly woodland people customs and letters—the Northern kingdoms had their own letters. Evidence of this matter is provided by stones of extraordinary size fixed to the tombs and caves of the ancients. If anyone doubts whether these were produced by Giants and in a most ancient age, let him go there and see things larger and more wondrous to the point of amazement than any writing might promise or provide. Thus, with these (as is held in the history of my dearest brother **John Magnus**, predecessor Archbishop of **Uppsala** <note>original: "Vſpalenſis"</note>, Book 1, Chapter 52), impressing their deeds on stones, they handed them down to eternal memory. Some also used various figures of animals as letters for private accounts, after the fashion of the Egyptians, and they still use them with domestic sagacity, as will be said shortly below: similar ones can still be seen in Rome on ancient obelisks, in which individual letters expressed individual names—for instance, a wolf for a greedy man, a fox for a cunning one, a bee for a King: because it behooves a ruler of peoples to have the honey of mercy mixed with the sting of justice. Furthermore, just as letters inscribed on papyrus are now sent between men, so once the Northern inhabitants sent letters carved on wood as a celebrated kind of paper: indeed, even now when papyrus is not available, in military camps or during the siege of cities, they opportunely use the bark or the inner wood of the birch tree split into sheets—indeed, into thin leaves—for writing letters, and all the more securely because bark of this kind is not destroyed by any injury of rain or snow. **Peter Martyr** <note>Pietro Martire d'Anghiera (1457–1526), an Italian-born historian of Spain's explorations</note> also mentions in Book 8 that the **Chaldeans** now write on the leaves of trees, and that the first **Portuguese** discoverers of the **New World** used them when they were forced to restore mutual defenses to suppress the rebellion of the inhabitants. Northern men are also found of such sagacious intellect that, although they have never learned either Gothic or Latin letters, they compose alphabets for themselves from the figures of things and tools: and for the sake of assisting their memory, on skin, paper...

...or they use bark specifically for writing. <note>original: "vel cortice singulariter scribendo utuntur"</note> They share this secret with no one except those within their own households, ordering that ink be made from crushed charcoal and milk, or simply from common water. Therefore, many magnificent monuments from the men of that most ancient age would be available for the education of our present times, if those men—who were born for great deeds—had left behind writings as extensive as the famous exploits they left to their successors. However, they are found to have taken very little pleasure in letters, and the greatest pleasure in arms and heavy wars. <header>LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.</header>

As for their language, no traces of it are found from which one could speak with certainty; however, the Letters of Cassiodorus <note>Secretary to the Ostrogothic King Theodoric the Great</note>, Secretary to Theodoric, teach us that in their public acts they used the Latin language. It is true that the *Histories of Spain* assert that the Gothic language was entirely similar to the language of the Celts. Others affirm that it was the same Teutonic language, the relics of which corrupted languages are today much more different than they possibly were during their period of greatest purity; this is confirmed by Louis de Mayerne Turquet in Book 5 of his *History of Spain*.

Olaus Magnus, cited above in Book 8, Chapter 2 of his *Northern Histories*, writes that the Goths have a certain book written in their language titled *billagines* <note>A term used by the historian Jordanes to describe the ancient laws of the Goths</note>, which was composed by one of their kings named Deceneus, who in his time was the first to teach his people the Philosophy and Religion of Pythagoras. Now, this word *billagines* signifies, according to the report of the aforementioned Olaus in the Gothic language, the same as in Latin, *according to the laws* <note>original: "iuxta leges"</note>. See what this same author writes in Book 1, Chapter 34 of his same histories concerning certain staffs engraved with Gothic letters, by which the Goths from all antiquity served themselves in the knowledge of Astronomy, and to predict and announce the events of times and seasons, and to know the movable feasts and dominical letters <note>Letters used in calendars to determine the day of the week for any given date</note> of future years.

Furthermore, it seems to me very appropriate to mention in this place that the *Histories of Spain* state that when Don Sancho Ramírez <note>King of Aragon and later Navarre (r. 1063–1094)</note> came to the crown of Navarre, he had already reigned in Aragon for several years; he had married a lady, the daughter of the Count of Urgel, named Lady Felicia, by whom he had three children. Under this Prince, the two kingdoms of Navarre and Aragon were reunited 42 years after their separation. He was a warrior and a statesman, and furthermore was a zealot for the Roman Religion. For he caused the Gothic office <term>office des Goths: The Mozarabic or Visigothic Rite, a Christian liturgy distinct from the Roman Rite that persisted in Spain for centuries</term>, which the Christians used in his lands, to be changed, and put the Roman rite into use; possibly by the Council held at Jaca under this King, when the Bishopric of Aragon was first established. For the adornment and enrichment of this see, besides the tithes, portions of the conquests made against the Moors of Zaragoza and Tudela were ordained; and in place of the Gothic civil laws, he introduced the Common Imperial Law into his jurisdiction. There is even a volume of particular laws given by this King to those of Jaca, which is inserted among the customs and usages of Navarre today.

The same histories continue that at this same time mention is made of a Council assembled in the city of Barcelona at the pursuit of Don Ramon Berenguer the Elder, at the request of Lady Almodis his wife, over which presided Cardinal Hugh, Legate of Pope Alexander II or Gregory VII—for the time of it is not precisely fixed, but it is only said that it was celebrated around the year 1071. At this Council, it was ordained that the clergy should live chastely, for as much as, the history says, several ecclesiastics were married, according to the introduction of King Wittiza the Goth <note>The last Visigothic king before the Umayyad conquest, often blamed by later chroniclers for the moral decline of the kingdom</note>, and following the example of the Aragonese, [the office] was left [behind]...

the Mozarabic rite, and received the Roman rite of Saint Gregory in the lands of Catalonia.

The same Histories continue that in the year 1086, during the reign of Don Alfonso, King of Castile and Navarre, the rite named Gothic—or Isidorean, because Saint Isidore <note>Saint Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar and cleric who helped standardize the Spanish liturgy</note> had introduced it, and afterwards called Mozarabic, because the Christians living among the Moors had retained and celebrated it—was in use until that time, both in Toledo and in Castile and Leon. But this King Alfonso, desiring in everything to show himself an affectionate son of the See of Rome, wanted it to be changed, and in its place received the rite called Gregorian, from its author Gregory. Therefore, he sent for a bull from the Pope then reigning, commanding that the Roman rite should henceforth be celebrated in all the Churches of Spain, just as was done in France, because of which it is called by some Spaniards "Gallican." During the time of the aforementioned King, a Council was held at Leon, in the presence of Rainier, the Papal Nuncio, in which among other ordinances it was decreed that copyists and writers would no longer use the ancient Gothic characters invented, as they say, by Ulfilas their Bishop <note>Ulfilas (c. 311–383) was a Goth of Greek descent who translated the Bible into the Gothic language and created the Gothic alphabet</note> (otherwise called Toledan letters), but rather the letters that are currently used in Castile. Abraham Ortelius, in his *Synonyms* and *Geographical Treasury*, says: <note>original: "Dani Populi sunt hodie Denemarker, aut Denemarcker. Apud vetustissimos auctores horum non est mentio. ### Of the Language of the Franks.

### CHAPTER LXXI.

The Franks—remnants formerly left from the destruction of the Trojans <note>A common medieval legend claimed that European nations were founded by survivors of the Trojan War</note>, some 440 years before the Year of Salvation, or the Incarnation of the Savior—finally came from the large and spacious solitudes of Scythia <note>A vast region in central Eurasia</note>, under the leadership of a Marcomir their chief, to settle in Lower Germany, where their brothers the Saxons granted them a residence toward the mouths of the Rhine, in Frisia and Holland. And from there, making many large incursions into the surrounding lands, they warred against the Romans and Gauls for more than nine hundred whole years. Thus, they extended their domination over the greater part of Europe, as their chronicler Hunibauld <note>A legendary chronicler of the Franks whose work was widely cited in the Renaissance but is now considered mythical</note> amply testifies in the 18 books he left to posterity regarding their conquests. In these, he notes among other things that a certain person named Vuastbal had written their deeds and gestures for 758 years in their own language, and in characters such as we represent hereafter, which feel somewhat like Greek writing: but the order of the letters is transposed, and the rest are a bit doubtful—perhaps because of their great antiquity, which might have caused writers to deprave the true shape, as is confirmed by Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German Benedictine abbot and polymath known for his work on cryptography and history</note> in book 5 of his *Polygraphia*.

## Concerning the region of the Finnonians or Finlanders.

<margin>Abraham Ortelius in his *Synonyms* and *Geographic Treasury*.</margin>
<note>Ortelius (1527–1598) was a famous cartographer who created the first modern atlas.</note>
Tacitus <note>A Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD)</note> doubts whether to assign the Fenni <note>original: "Fenni"</note> to the Germans or the Sarmatians. Althamerus thinks they are Prussians or Lithuanians. Ptolemy <note>A Greek-Roman geographer</note> places the Phinnoi <note>original: "$\phi \acute{\iota} \nu \nu \omicron \iota$"</note> in this region. But it seems to me that the Finni (spelled with an *I* by Jordanes) are rather those who inhabit Finland today. They are in the peninsula of Scandinavia, where there are also the *Scritifini* or *Crictofinni*, though located more toward the North. These are so named from "jumping" in a barbarian tongue, says [Paul] the Deacon. For my part, I derive it from *Scricken* or *Scriien*, a purely Germanic word which signifies to leap or to take great strides with legs spread wide while walking. Indeed, as an eyewitness Olaus <note>Olaus Magnus (1490–1557), a Swedish writer and cartographer</note> testifies, they use wooden soles tied under the plants of their feet: with which they seem to glide through snow and ice with a certain admirable speed, rather than run. The use of these is also found among us during the winter. We call them *Seriekschoenen* <note>An early term for ice skates or skis; original: "Seriekschoenen"</note>, as if you were to say "leaping shoes." It remains to be seen whether, because of this swift running, these same people are those called *Horse-foots* <note>original: "Hippopodes," a mythical tribe mentioned by ancient authors</note> by ancient writers. See under "Vandals."

Modern accounts report that throughout all the provinces of Sweden, Gothia, Norway, and Denmark, there are three different languages in use: namely Swedish (the Saxon language <note>referring to Low German influences</note> closely approaches it in many words, as do Flemish and English, by changing some pronunciation); then there is the Finnish language, which is used not only in the Grand Duchy of Finland (except in one province where Swedish is preserved and practiced, and where "Finland" means as much as "new land"), but also in a good part of the surroundings of Reval <note>modern-day Tallinn, Estonia</note>, a city in Livonia. ->*On the difference between the German, Polish, Livonian, Swedish, and Finnish languages.*<-

### CHAP. LXXIII.

It seemed to me very appropriate to show in this chapter that there is a very great difference between the languages detailed above—German, Polish, Livonian, Swedish, and Finnish—and that they are not alike or similar as some modern figures have believed and asserted. To provide proof of this, we will hereafter include the Lord’s Prayer in each of these languages, by which curious and learned persons may recognize the diversity of each of the aforementioned languages as well as they could through many other discourses in these tongues.

As for what concerns the Finnish or Finlandish language, as it is spoken in the middle of the country, it is in no way aligned with, and shares nothing with the aforementioned Swedish language, nor with the language of the Muscovites <note>The Russians</note>, but it is a language proper to the Lapps <note>The Sámi people</note>, who are a people of the middle of the North.

### The Lord's Prayer in the language of the Lapps and Finns, which is also used by some Livonians.

> Our Father, who art in the heavens, hallowed be Thy name, Thy kingdom come: Thy will be done as in the heavens, so on the ground: give us today our daily bread: and forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who trespass against us: and lead us not into temptation: but deliver us from evil. Amen.

See what has been written on this subject by Sebastian Münster in book 4 of his *Universal Cosmography*, and André Thevet in book 20, chapter 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*. And it should be noted that after the Kings of Sweden had subjected Finland to their kingdom, they placed several bailiffs and governors there: one resides near Vyborg <note>original: "Vibourg"</note> in a castle built within the lake; another in Porvoo <note>original: "Borge"</note>, on the edge of the Finnish gulf; all of whom are Lieutenants of the King, to exercise justice in his name. There are also other castles and small towns near Vyborg, and principally Lappeenranta <note>original: "Legabour"</note>, Kexholm <note>original: "Kexholin", now Priozersk</note>, and Shlisselburg <note>original: "Netabourg", also known as Nöteborg</note>; but the Grand Duke of Muscovy has taken these from the kingdom of Sweden. There are also fortresses built on this side of the river such as Lappeenranti <note>original: "Lappaenſi"</note>, Kivennapa <note>original: "Kiuineb"</note>, Uusikirkko <note>original: "Neukirk"</note>, and others which are still under the obedience of the King of Sweden.

Modern accounts speaking of these Northern nations state that Henry, King of Sweden <note>Likely referring to Saint Eric (Eric IX) and Bishop Henry of Uppsala, who led a crusade to Finland in the 12th century.</note>, and Henry, Archbishop of Uppsala, have fully devoted themselves to converting the province of Finland to the Christian religion. This province is among the most Northern, where days and nights grow to nearly six months. It has embraced Christianity, and its people have become so good and charitable as Christians that they occupy themselves mainly with good works. Those of Bothnia <note>A region surrounding the Gulf of Bothnia between Sweden and Finland.</note> do the same on both sides and have their parishes, in which they maintain priests who have charge over them. And in all the surrounding countries, the people are now somewhat converted; for it is certain that on the borders of Norway and the borders of Bothnia and Finland, men and women come from 30 and 40 leagues within the country, when the weather is suitable, to bring to the churches their children—some carrying them in their cradles or in baskets on their shoulders, others putting them atop pack animals—asking for holy Baptism or instruction for living as Christians. And when they can, they bring their tithes and firstfruits; though ignorant of what they are bound to do as Christians, they conform to the law of nature, doing what seems good and praiseworthy to them and fleeing from what seems evil and vicious. Many other things concerning the lives, customs, behaviors, and religions of these Nations are deduced from John and Olaus Magnus <note>Brothers and prominent Swedish historians/cartographers of the 16th century.</note> in their *Northern Histories*, Saxo Grammaticus in his *History of Denmark*, Sidonius Apollinaris in Book 1, Procopius in his *Histories*, Paul the Deacon and Jordanes in their histories, by André Theuet in Book 19, Chapters 15, 16, and following of his *Universal Cosmography*, and François de Belleforest in Book 3, Chapter 6 of his *Universal History*, and in his discourses from the *Cosmography* of Sebastian Münster.

## OF THE REGION OF THE
### *English.*

**O**rtelius <note>Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598), the creator of the first modern atlas.</note> in his *Synonyms and Geographical Treasury*, notes that it is called *Anglia* [England]; *Albion* by Aristotle, Apuleius, and Pliny; *Aluion* <gloss>original: Ἀλουΐων</gloss> by Ptolemy; which is also called *Britannia* [Britain] by others. Avienus calls it the "Island of the Albions." But more truly, as Humphrey Llwyd <note>A Welsh cartographer and antiquary.</note> teaches from the most ancient annals of that island, it is called *Prydania*. This is the island which today contains the kingdoms of England and Scotland.

England, a more southerly part of the island of Albion, derives its name from the Angles, a people of Saxony whom Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD).</note> mentions, who occupied this region.

...they appear, from which even today it is still called **England** <note>original: "Engelandt"</note> (with only the first letter changed). Winfrid <note>original: "Vuunefidus," referring to Saint Boniface, the 8th-century Anglo-Saxon missionary.</note> calls it "Transmarine Saxony," as Beatus Rhenanus <note>A German Renaissance humanist and historian (1485–1547).</note> noted in the first book of his *German Affairs*. More recent Latin writers call the inhabitants **Anglo-Saxons**.

The **British Isles** is the name given by authors to those which today contain the English and Scottish kingdoms along with Ireland and the surrounding islands. Dionysius of Alexandria calls them the *Bretanides* <note>original: βρετανίδες</note>. The largest of these, which today contains the English and Scottish kingdoms, is called **Albion** <note>original: αλουίων</note> by Ptolemy <note>An influential 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian mathematician and geographer.</note>, and by others it is even called **Britain** by excellence, as if it were the primary one among the British Isles. In Book 60, Dion <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian.</note> reads it as *Brettanica* <note>original: βρεττανική</note>; Appian also uses this in the preface to his history. Stephanus writes it as *Pretanica* <note>original: πρετανίκη</note> with a ‘P’. After the Romans had entirely subjugated this island to their Empire, they divided it into provinces and names. In the *Almagest*, Book 2, the part toward the South is called "Greater" and the part toward the North is called "Lesser." Xiphilinus and Dio divide it into "Upper" and "Lower" Britain. According to Sextus Rufus, who flourished under the Emperor Valentinian, there are **Britannia Prima**, **Britannia Secunda**, **Flavia**, and **Maxima Caesariensis**. The *Book of Notices* <note>referring to the *Notitia Dignitatum*, a document of the late Roman Empire's chancery.</note> adds **Valentia**, which Ammianus Marcellinus also mentions.

Humphrey Lhuyd <note>A 16th-century Welsh cartographer and historian famous for his maps and descriptions of Britain.</note> interprets these provinces as follows: he calls **Britannia Prima** that which stretches from the Thames all the way to the Wall. Today this is almost entirely comprised under the name of England (as the Latin common folk call it). He asserts that **Britannia Secunda**, which he writes is also called "the Lesser," is what is commonly named **Scotland**. From **Maxima Caesariensis**, he identifies Kent and the region of the Atrebates. From **Flavia**, he points to the tract of the **West Saxons** along with the Isle of Wight. He indicates that **Valentia** is **Wales** <note>original: "Cambriam"</note>. 

But we must not omit what Humphrey produced from the letters of Sigebert: namely, that before this island was known to the Romans or foreigners, it was divided into three regions, which the language of the natives (which is still in use today in Wales) called **Lhoegria**, **Cambria**, and **Albania**, and they still call them so; see these in their respective places. The same author teaches from the most ancient monuments of that region that this island was called by the general term **Prydain**, from which it is likely the Greeks and Latins derived their "Britain." In the history of Widukind <note>A 10th-century Saxon chronicler.</note>, they are corruptly called *Bracti*, but I read it as *Bretti* in the same manuscript codex. Ponticus Virunius <note>An Italian humanist who summarized the legendary histories of Britain.</note> thinks that Wales <note>original: "Cambriam"</note> was celebrated by Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet.</note> in his 7th Satire with this verse:

->The repeated lesson of Cambre kills the wretched teachers.<-
<note>In Juvenal's original context, "Cambre" refers to a specific rhetorician, but the author here is attempting to link the name to Cambria/Wales.</note>

**Scotland**, the more northern part of the British Isle (which Hegesippus mentions in chapter fifteen), was formerly called **Albania** by Latin writers, and is still called **Albain** by its inhabitants, as Humphrey Lhuyd says. I would argue with Beatus Rhenanus that this Scotland was called **Caledonia** by Tacitus in his *Life of Agricola*.

The **Scots**, whom Orosius, Claudian, and Ammianus mention among Latin writers, are the northern peoples of the British Isle who, originating from Cantabria in Spain and migrating from there into Ireland, finally fixed their seat in Scotland. In the British tongue <note>referring to Welsh or Gaelic</note>, they are called **Guydhyl**, according to Humphrey Lhuyd.

Ireland is called **Hibernia** by Caesar, **Iuverna** by Pomponius Mela, and likewise in the Aldine edition of Solinus. It is **Iuernia** <note>original: Ἰουερνία</note> to Ptolemy, and **Ierna** <note>original: Ἰέρνη</note> to Strabo, Stephanus, and Apuleius.

Aristotle (who is imitated in his little book *On the Universe* <note>original: *libellulo de mundo*</note>) and likewise Claudian <note>A Latin poet of the late 4th century.</note> call it **Vernia** <note>original: $\iota \epsilon \rho \nu \eta$ (*Iernē*)</note>. Robert Constantin, in his supplement to the Latin language, maintains that it is called **Cerne** by Lycophron. However, I would by no means think that Ireland is described by him under that name, but rather that it refers to the island of the same name which Pliny places in the Ethiopian Sea, opposite the Persian Gulf and facing Ethiopia. For that island lies toward the East, or as Lycophron says, "toward the dawn." Meanwhile, to those like Lycophron who live in Greece or Italy, Ireland lies toward the West. Orpheus also speaks of an island called **Ierne** <note>original: $\iota \epsilon \rho \nu \eta$</note>, but whether it is the same as our Ireland, I leave for others to dispute.

### *Of the English Language.*

All of Great Britain, or the Island of England, is divided into two parts which encompass two Kingdoms. The mountains and the rivers Solway <note>original: *Soluer*</note> and Tweed <note>original: *Tuedo*</note> separate the Kingdom of England from that of Scotland; the Northern part remains to the Scots for a length of four hundred and eighty miles, and the Southern part to the English for 230 miles. That which the English possess is divided into three, and according to some into four principal provinces, distributed into 22 episcopal cities along with two archiepiscopal ones, the names of which, as well as those of the provinces and their characteristics, are described particularly in the histories of this country. And we must say that just as the provinces are different in their customs, so too are they in language, seeing as in the province of **Wales** <note>original: *Vuales ou Galles*</note> they speak differently than in **Cornwall** <note>original: *Cornouialle*</note>, and both of these speak differently than the English. There are also, besides these, two types of languages, seeing as in the farthest part of Scotland, the inhabitants and those who live as savages <note>Referring here to the Highlanders.</note> speak one language similar to that of the English, and another entirely different, which is the **Irish language** <note>Gaelic</note>: a rare and marvelous thing to see various languages in one island.

And to clarify this matter, we shall say that the **English language** is a language composed of the German language and the French language, because of the **Anglo-Saxons** who brought the German language into England, and then the **Normans** <note>original: *Northmans*</note> who occupied this island and also introduced the said French language. The ancient British tongue has remained only in the country of Wales, where the indigenous people retreated when these Anglo-Saxons conquered England: and in fact, the English do not understand

<page-num>876</page-num>
<header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF</header>

English practitioners and litigants no longer use the French—or rather Norman—language (which they had used since the time of William the Norman <note>William the Conqueror, who introduced Norman French as the language of the English court and law after 1066.</note>), but rather the English language. He <note>Likely referring to King Edward III, who passed the Statute of Pleading in 1362, mandating the use of English in courts.</note> decreed that all acts of causes and trials be written in it; since that time, this English language has always been used throughout all the palaces and courtrooms of justice in England, as confirmed by the aforementioned Polydore Vergil in Book 19 of his *History of England*. Regarding this language in general, very few books are found written and composed in it, except for some books of theology. This has only occurred in the last twenty-five or thirty years, as the Lutherans and Calvinists (whom they call Puritans in England) write against the Catholics, or indeed the Catholics against the Puritans. These two sorts of religions are quite hostile to one another; the Calvinists especially desire greatly to abolish the form of policy <note>The ecclesiastical structure or hierarchy.</note> still observed in England, where the Archbishops, Bishops, Curates, and Chapters have remained intact. The Lutherans and Calvinists do not approve of this, and for this reason, the Archbishops, Bishops, Curates, and Chapters—among whom there are some very learned men—and the aforementioned Lutherans and Calvinists write against one another every day, as confirmed by Sanderus <note>Nicholas Sander (c. 1530–1581), a prominent English Catholic polemicist.</note> in Book 5, Chapter 4 of his *Ecclesiastical Monarchy*.

This English language is so little esteemed by foreigners who go to England that there are few who wish to take the trouble to learn or speak it, unless they are servants or agents <term>facteurs</term> <note>Commercial agents or representatives working abroad.</note> for the sake of useful things and the necessities of life, which depend on the common people who know how to speak no other language.

Whoever wishes to see many beautiful and excellent discourses on the English and England should read Caesar in his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, Book 5; Bede, Book 1, Chapter 1; Gildas’s book *On the Ruin of Britain*; William of Newburgh’s *English History*; Albert Krantz’s *Danish History*, Book 1, Chapter 2; Saxo Grammaticus, Book 1 of his *Danish History*; and Polydore Vergil in his books on the *History of England*.

See also Ptolemy in book seven, chapter one, and Pomponius Mela in book 3, who call it *Indike* in Greek <note>original: "$\iota\nu\delta\iota\kappa\grave{\eta}$"</note>. India, in Job chapter twenty-eight, verse nineteen, is called *Ophir* in Hebrew <note>original: "אופיר"</note>, signifying Ash, incineration, or bearing fruit.

### A. Ortelius in his Geographical Synonyms,
India, *Indike* <note>original: "$\iota\nu\delta\iota\kappa\grave{\eta}$"</note>, the largest and most noble region of Asia. Ptolemy divides this into two, namely India within the Ganges, and India beyond the Ganges. India within the Ganges is called *Indostan* <note>Hindustan</note> by the inhabitants, according to João de Barros, an eyewitness and, so to speak, an "ear-witness"—as one who acted as the viceroy for Portugal in this India for several years. India beyond the Ganges is thought to be called *Heuila*, or, as others write, *Hauilath*, or *Euilath* <note>Biblical Havilah</note>, in the Sacred Scriptures. Niger writes that it is called *Macyn*, or *Magyn* by the inhabitants. He adds that for those sailing from Egypt to India, it is divided into three parts: Lower, Middle, and Upper. The Lower, which is from the Indus river to the Bariam river, is called *Caiferat* <note>Gujarat</note>. The Middle, which extends from there to another river named the Chaberis <note>likely the Kaveri</note>, is called *Minibar* <note>Malabar</note>. The Upper, *Maabar* <note>the Coromandel Coast</note>, which stretches from the Chaberis to the Ganges river. Marco Polo the Venetian relates that in his time it was also divided into many parts, but he calls the larger part *Malabar* and the middle part *Abascia* <note>Abyssinia, which was frequently confused with or grouped under "the Indies" in medieval geography</note>. He does not indicate the smaller part with a specific name. Pliny testifies that India was called the third part of the world by the companions of Alexander who had conquered it. It is certain that today a no smaller part of the world is included under this single name. For the Spaniards commonly call these Indies, together with almost the whole of the recently discovered America, the "Indies."

### The same in his Geographical Treasury,
The Indians were first called Sabaeans, and then also Homerites <note>The Himyarites of ancient Yemen</note>, says Nicephorus Callistus in book 8, chapter 35. He places them in *Arabia Felix* <note>literally "Happy Arabia," the fertile southern part of the Arabian peninsula</note>. There are also Indians properly so-called, people in India beyond the Ganges, according to Ptolemy. But translators read *Sindi* in its place, and more accurately so, as I conjecture. In the Greek codex it is read as *Sindoi* <note>original: "$\sigma\iota\nu\delta\omicron\grave{\iota}$"</note>, and I think Ptolemy wrote *Sindois*. But as I advise in many other places in this Treasury regarding Indian words, the scribe did not notice the doubled "S" from the mouth of the reader. My opinion is confirmed by Hesychius, who holds the *Sindi* to be an Indian race, and records a Sindican port in the same place. Curtius, in book 9, calls those "Maritime Indians" who inhabit the coast of the Red Sea in Gedrosia <note>an ancient region along the coast of the Indian Ocean, in modern Iran and Pakistan</note>, placing them on this side of the Indus river, contrary to Ptolemy and other geographers. Arrian also names Indians on this side of the Indus river in his third book. The same author, in his work on Indian affairs, calls these "Western Indians" (to distinguish them from those beyond, whom he calls "Eastern"). At the Arbis river, Pliny and Arrian extend India toward the West, and add that these people once obeyed the Assyrians. It is likely that this is the India mentioned in the books of Esther and the Maccabees. There are also Indians in Ethiopia according to Procopius in book 6 of *On Buildings*; for he calls them the "Mountains of the Indians," from which the Nile takes its origin. See *Ethiopians*, *Memnones*, and *Rhizophagi* <note>literally "Root-eaters"</note>.

India, *Indike* <note>original: "$\iota\nu\delta\iota\kappa\grave{\eta}$"</note>, the largest and most noble region of Asia; Ptolemy divides this into two, namely India within and beyond the Ganges.

» The author João de Barros—an eyewitness and, so to speak, an "ear-witness," having served as the Portuguese Viceroy in this India for several years—asserts that India within the Ganges is called *Indostan* <note>Hindustan</note> by the inhabitants. India beyond the Ganges is believed to be called *Heuila*, or, as others write, *Hauilath*, or *Euilath* <note>original Latin: "Heuila... Hauilath... Euilath"; referencing the Biblical land of Havilah</note> in the Holy Scriptures. Dominicus Niger writes that it is called *Macyn*, or *Magyn* <note>referring to Mangi, a term for Southern China</note> by the inhabitants. He adds that for those sailing from Egypt to India, it is divided into three parts: Lower, Middle, and Upper. The Lower part, which runs from the Indus River to the Bariam River, is called *Caiferat* <note>Gujarat</note>. The Middle part, extending from there to another river named the Chaberis <note>likely the Kaveri River</note>, is called *Minibar* <note>Malabar</note>. The Upper part, *Maabar* <note>the Coromandel Coast</note>, stretches from the Chaberis to the Ganges River. Marco Polo the Venetian relates that in his time it was also divided into these parts, but here he calls the larger part *Malabar* and the middle part *Abascia* <note>Abyssinia/Ethiopia; early geographers often conflated East Africa with India</note>. Pliny testifies that India was called the "third part of the world" by the companions of Alexander the Great who had conquered it. It is certain that today no smaller part of the world is encompassed by that name; for the Spaniards commonly call these "Indies" the ancient Indies along with almost the whole of the recently discovered America. Indians are found in Ethiopia, and conversely, Ethiopians in India. See *Ethiopians*, *Atlantis*, *Memnons*, and *Rhizophagi* <note>original: "Rhiſophagi," meaning root-eaters</note>.

Some modern geographers are astonished that those who once divided the earth into three parts <note>Europe, Asia, and Africa</note> did not take heed of the words of Pliny, who, in Book 6, Chapter 7, considering the grandeur of these Indies, uses these words: *The companions of the great King Alexander have left in writing that in this Indian country which was subjugated by their master, there were five thousand cities, and with likely reason showed that, given the innumerable people there and this great expanse of regions, it is the third part of the world, seeing as the Indians never left their country to go conquer other lands.* And yet Alexander the Great did not see a third of the Indies, and never crossed beyond the Ganges toward the south; the glory of this is due to those of our own time, who have done more than he, and more than all the historians, both Greek and Latin, having given us knowledge of what is rarest in this great and very rich Province. 

If then this India is the third part of the earth, by what consideration shall it be so measured? Since Europe makes up one, Asia another, and Africa another, unless we separate it from Asia—just as it never truly had any community with the Asians, and it would be included there improperly insofar as the Kings who held command over Asia never had any power over this great Empire, as we can see in the writings of the ancient Greek and Latin authors. But you will ask me, what is the point of this discussion? For nothing else but to favor the cause of those who call the newly discovered New World the **West Indies**, which I prefer to include under the third part of the earth rather than otherwise, and give the Africans the rank of the fourth part. And this is not without great reason: for those who know the proportions of the terrestrial Globe cannot ignore that by the doubling of the Zones, the East and West face each other in such a way that in our time the Kings of Spain and Portugal have entered into a great dispute over the Molucca Islands.

Moluccas <note>The Spice Islands in modern-day Indonesia</note>, for this reason alone: that some hold them to be Oriental, others Occidental; and nonetheless all of this is comprised under the name of the Indies. Indian Kings command there, and the people for the most part imitate the customs of the Indians, added to which the same trees and plants grow there, and almost the same animals, except where the Sun already approaches the Poles and the cold causes lions, elephants, tigers, and the like to be unable to live there at all. In short, Religion (such as it is, or an imitation of it) makes them all united, in that it seems the Orientals have given their beliefs to the Occidentals, as is apparent by those of the Island of Zipangu, or Japan <note>original: "Zipangu, ou Giapan"</note>. These are known to be so positioned between the East and West (as we have supposed them) that the Geographers of our time do not rightly know whether they should be named Orientals or otherwise.

This leads us to conclude that the Indies comprise the third part of the earth and are of a different extent than the ancients considered them. Their opinions, however, out of the reverence we owe them, should not be cast aside entirely—not that we wish to dwell on the dreams and ravings of the Greeks, who created a Bacchus subjugating the Indians, and produced a great Hercules as a total conqueror, and an Alexander as Monarch. This is deduced at length by Strabo in Book 15, Diodorus Siculus in Book 3, Pliny in Book 6, Chapter 17, Ptolemy in Book 7, Chapter 1, Table 10 of Asia, Solinus in Chapter 65 of his *Polyhistor*, Philostratus in Book 2, Chapter 15 of the *Life of Apollonius*, Quintus Curtius and Arrian in the *Life of Alexander the Great*, Plutarch in the same life, and several other ancient authors.

Leaving these aside, we shall say—considering the East Indies—that as they are of greater extent than all other Provinces and Regions of this universe, so they are divided into two great parts and Regions, both being known and renowned by the River Ganges. Thus, the part that faces us, and which from our perspective is Western, is called **India within the Ganges** <note>Latin: *India intra Gangem*</note>, because it lies between the aforementioned river and the Indus, which gave its name to the entire land. The part that is further East is named **India beyond the Ganges** <note>Latin: *India extra Gangem*</note> because it lies in that great expanse of country that goes as far as the sea of Cin and Mangi <note>References to China and Southern China</note>, and which spreads toward the Southern parts as far as the Golden Chersonese <note>The Malay Peninsula</note>, now named Malacca. This lies opposite that great Island now called Sumatra, which formerly was known by the name Taprobane <note>While Taprobane usually referred to Sri Lanka/Ceylon in antiquity, many 16th-century writers mistakenly identified it as Sumatra</note>.

These two were named thus according to the words of some Geographers; but in the Holy Scriptures, the Oriental part is denoted by the word *Euilath* <note>Havilah</note>, and the one closer to us *Serian*. The people of the country now call this closer part *Hynd* <note>Hind/Hindustan</note>, and the other which is in the East is now called *Macin* or *Magin* <note>Mangi</note>—so much have things changed, or rather, so little knowledge have we had of foreign history. Some moderns have spoken differently on this matter, holding that the Indies toward the West on this side of the Ganges are called *Euilath* in Holy Scripture and *Indostan* by the Indians, and the Indies beyond the Ganges are called *Seriah* in the aforementioned Holy Scripture and *Macyn* (otherwise China) by the Indians. Moderners who have navigated toward these Indies have divided them for us into three: the High, the Middle, and the Low. ...and Goga, all of which belong to the kingdom of Cambaye <note>Modern-day Khambhat in Gujarat, India</note>. Let us then take the fourth division, which has its entrance at Cape Comorin <note>The southernmost tip of the Indian subcontinent</note>, following all along the country of Chilan <note>Possibly Ceylon (Sri Lanka) or the Coromandel coast</note> and Pulicat <note>A historic port town in Tamil Nadu</note>, which cross from one gulf to the other—namely, from the Indian Sea to the Gulf of Bengal—spanning two hundred ninety leagues in extent; this area is the flower of all the Indies. Then, coming from Pulicat to the gulf and bay of Bengal, where the provinces are densely populated and the cities are beyond number, all the people are devoted to trade; this constitutes the fifth part. At Bengal begins the sixth division, reaching to Catigan <note>Chittagong, in modern Bangladesh</note> and ending at the promontory named Cingapule <note>Singapore</note>, which is only one degree north of the Equator and some sixty leagues from Malacca. From this Cape of Singapore, the seventh division heads toward the river of Siam <note>Thailand</note>; and there begins the eighth division of Asia, extending to the country of China. China is divided into fifteen provinces and contains very large cities within them; it sits at fifteen degrees of latitude, and the length of this land along the coast is two hundred seventy-five leagues. The last division goes toward Mangi <note>A term used by Marco Polo for Southern China</note> and Quinsay <note>Modern-day Hangzhou, famously described by medieval travelers as a magnificent metropolis</note>, beginning at forty-six degrees. It spans at least four hundred leagues of discovered and known country and is, as I have said, the easternmost land running toward the North that is yet known—not counting an infinity of islands, because I have detailed each of those in its proper place.

But let us revisit this league by league, starting from the city of Cambaye, the coast of which extends to the aforementioned Cape Comorin. You will find there at least two hundred ninety leagues, which include the flower of all the Indies. This region is divided by two great rivers that cross it from West to East: one of which separates the kingdom of the Deccan <note>original: "Decan"</note> from that of Gujarat <note>original: "Guserath"</note>, which lies to its North; and the other river separates the Deccan from the province of Canara <note>original: "Canaran," a coastal region in Karnataka</note> to its South. And thus nature, in dividing the borders of these provinces in the flatlands, did not forget the seacoast, where an infinite number of small rivers perform the same duty, serving in many places as limits and boundaries for all these kingdoms. These rivers spring from certain fountains toward the East, located at the foot of the mountains of the Ghats <note>original: "mont de Gathe," referring to the Western Ghats mountain range</note>, distant from Chaul <note>A historic port near Mumbai</note> by some fifteen leagues at eighteen and nineteen degrees of longitude. The river that runs furthest North is called the Crusuar, and the one running South is the Benhora; these, finally flowing East, empty into the channels of the Ganges at 22 degrees, near two places named Angelij <note>Possibly Hijli</note> and Pirolde. The great abundance of water coming from these two rivers joined together has caused the ignorant to think that it was the Ganges itself, whereas there is a great difference in their course, seeing as the Ganges flows from North to South, and the others from West to East. There is also much to be said regarding the differences between their mouths and channels. Moving further, and observing the separation of the provinces of Cannanore and Calicut, you will see it is formed by a small river named the Aliga. ## ->ON THE LANGUAGE OF THE EAST<-
## ->Indians in general.<-

### CHAPTER LXXVI.

Strabo, in book 15 of his *Geography*, citing the words of a certain very ancient author named Megasthenes, wrote that the Indians of his time had no use for letters, nor any written laws, but that they observed many fine things through memory and the recollection of past events, just as they had learned them from father to son; this is repeated by Caelius Rhodiginus in book 18, chapter 31 of his *Various Lessons*. Diodorus Siculus, regarding this subject in book 3 of his *Histories*, maintains that on a certain island found near the South by Iambulus <note>A Greek writer of a legendary utopian travel narrative</note>, the inhabitants did not write horizontally as we do, but drew the lines of their letters straight, from top to bottom. They had twenty-eight letters in total according to the meanings they assigned to them, though they had only seven characters, each of which was explained in four modes and fashions. The Emperor Augustus <note>Original: "Octaue"</note> seemed to have wanted to imitate this in his Latin writing, according to Suetonius Tranquillus in his *Life of Augustus*, in these words: <margin>cc</margin> "I have noted this especially in his handwriting: he does not divide words, nor does he move letters that exceed <margin>cc</margin> the end of a line to the following one, but instead places them immediately <margin>cc</margin> below and circles them." <note>original: "Notaui & in Chyrographo eius illa præcipuè, non diuidere verba, nec ab extrema parte verſuum abundantes literas in alterum transferre , ſed ibidem ſtatim ſubicit, circumducitque"</note> He argues that the term for a line of poetry, *verse* <note>original: "verſus"</note>, proves this was the custom of the ancients, as the word is derived from *turning* <note>original: "à vertendo factum"</note>.

Regarding this, we will repeat here what we have previously written about the Syriac language and Syriac letters in the chapter on the Syriac language: namely, that the characters of the aforementioned Syriac letters, although they are read from right to left like those of the Hebrews, Samaritans, Chaldeans, and Arabs, are nevertheless not formed and written by the Syrians from right to left as the Hebrews, Samaritans, Chaldeans, and Arabs do; rather, they are written from top to bottom toward the chest <note>original: "vers l’estomach"</note>, as this Latin verse denotes:

*From heaven to the stomach, Chaldea rereads the marks.*
<note>original Latin: "E cælo ad stomachum relegit Chaldaea lituras." This refers to the vertical orientation of the script, descending from the sky toward the body.</note>

It seems this is what moved Festus Pompeius <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note> to call this kind of writing **downward-turning**, just as we now say **rightward-turning**; specifically as if it were falling and landing from above. For the letters seem to fall and sit upon one another, one carrying the other on its back, as they are applied in the order of the alphabet or in the composition of a word. Thus, it is not without reason that they are believed by that craftsman to have been sent down from heaven—a view confirmed by Teseo Ambrogio in the 9th chapter of his *Introduction to the Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic languages*; André Theuet in book 18, chapter 14 of his *Cosmography*; and Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie in his epistle on the *New Testament in Syriac*.

> Father Luis of Portugal, in book 1, chapter 1 of his *Globe of Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*, confirms this, saying: "Moreover, those first people from whom the Jerusalem Syriac language flowed, holding a middle position between both <note>meaning between those who write left-to-right and right-to-left</note>, write toward the chest—a matter which the legal scholar Andreas Masius and we ourselves discuss at length and with great care in our aforementioned elementary preface. To which is added what Poggio Bracciolini records in book 4 of *On the Vicissitudes of Fortune*: that the Indians write by drawing the pen from the top to the bottom, a practice also observed by the Sinae, or Sinnae, or Chinese."
<note>original Latin: "Primi autem illi, à quibus lingua Syra Hierosolymitana effluxit, medium inter vtrosque tenentes, versus pectus scribunt... Indos à summo ad imum calamum ducentes, scribere, id quod & Sinæ... obseruant."</note>

Modern travelers and navigators assure us that the East Indians, Cathayans <note>People from Northern China</note>, Chinese, and Japanese of today, in following this fashion of forming the characters of the letters of their languages, write from top to bottom. In this, they claim to follow the order of nature, which has given men their heads at the top and their feet at the bottom.

To be brief, these Indians generally write upon the leaves of certain trees growing in their countries, and principally on the trees they call **Tals** <note>The Palmyra palm, *Borassus flabellifer*</note>, from which they make books. These people do not use the method and fashion of forming and writing their letter characters from right to left like the Hebrews and Arabs, nor from left to right like us Christians; rather, they form and write them from top to bottom. However, in the country of **Cambay** <note>A region in Gujarat, India</note>, the inhabitants use paper to form and write their letter characters, which is confirmed—following the aforementioned modern travelers and navigators—by André Theuet in book 11, chapter 23 of his *Cosmography*. Regarding this, Niccolò de' Conti, in his travels in Asia, mentions the inhabitants of the said country of Cambay, maintaining that they do not write like us, nor like the Hebrews and other older peoples descended from them, but indeed like the other East Indians: all along the leaf from the top to the bottom, and that they use three different languages among themselves. Jerónimo Osório, in book 2 of his *History of Portugal*, confirms this, saying that all the reports of the Portuguese sent by them to their King from the Indies stated that these Indians used neither paper nor parchment as we Europeans do, but that they marked their letters with a stylus on the leaves of wild trees they call **palms**, because these trees resemble true palms. He adds that they have very ancient books written on these leaves, made to be of a uniform length, in which they write their annals and memorable histories; then they pierce these leaves through the sides and flatten two wooden covers which they attach quite neatly to these...

### LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

**Gujarati** <note>original: "Guzerathienne"; referring to the language of the Gujarat region of India</note>: And that the language of Goa is different from the language of **Deccan**, and of **Narsinga** <note>The common European name for the Vijayanagar Empire of South India</note>, and that the kingdom of Narsinga contains within itself five great provinces, each of which has its own diverse language, and yet the Indians can understand one another; and this language is called **Tamil** in the Indian tongue. It is said that the inhabitants of the kingdom of **Canara** <note>original: "Canarin"; referring to the Kannada-speaking region or the Konkan coast</note>, who are subjects of the King of the aforementioned Narsinga, have a King different from the others and use a language different from the people of Narsinga. Furthermore, the inhabitants of the kingdom of **Malabar** or **Mylapore** <note>original: "Maliapur"; a historic neighborhood of Chennai</note> use a similar language, named by them **Malcama** <note>likely a reference to Malayalam</note>; if it differs, it is only in small things, inasmuch as all the subjects of this kingdom—which is of a marvelous extent and contains several diverse provinces speaking together—can understand one another, just as all Italians do among themselves, even though the **Lombards** have a different way of speaking than the **Tuscans**, and these different from the **Romans**, **Neapolitans**, and others included in the body of Italy; and just as in our **Gaul** <note>France</note> there is a certain community of languages among the nations subject to one and the same King of France.

Modern accounts report that a Father **Henriquez** <note>Henrique Henriques (1520–1600), a Jesuit missionary known for his linguistic work in India</note> reduced this language to a formal system <note>original: "reduisit en art"</note>, just as we have the **Latin** language, with the declensions of nouns, conjugations of verbs, genders, past tenses, and other rules of Grammar. This seemed almost impossible to a man who had only just arrived from Europe, but nevertheless, in less than six months, he understood this language very well and knew how to speak it; in short, in a short time he had completed the Grammar, along with a Dictionary of all the words, not without great profit for those who wish to learn it. Indeed, some hold that in this kingdom of Malabar there were, when the Portuguese landed there, eight types of nations, all diverse in ceremonies and **idolatry**, and so distant in affection from one another that they would rather die than approach or ally with one another. Such differences exist among them only because of their idols, and the power and dignity thereof, as reported by the aforementioned **Barbosa** <note>Duarte Barbosa, a Portuguese explorer who traveled to India in the early 1500s</note> in his travels to the Indies. He says further that the inhabitants of the Island of **Ceylon** <note>original: "Zeilan"; modern Sri Lanka</note> use a language which seems like that of the aforementioned Malabar, and partly resembles that of **Coromandel**, because the inhabitants of the mainland come to live on this Island for the pleasure and liberty found there.

->HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE<-

<meta>catchword: yet never-</meta>

...nothing in common together: the people of Malacca <note>original: "Malacquois"</note> form and write the characters of their letters like the Jews, from right to left; their language is understood throughout all the islands and surrounding countries as the most courtly of all, just as the French language is in the Northern countries here. The people of Siam <note>original: "Sianois"</note>, in the manner of Europeans, form and write the characters of their letters almost like Latin letters, from left to right, which is greatly worthy of wonder seeing as these kingdoms are so close and contiguous to one another. Furthermore, the aforementioned navigators and travelers report that the histories of the city and kingdom of Malacca <note>modern Melaka, Malaysia</note> contain that this city was, from its beginning, inhabited by several fishermen from the kingdoms of Pegu <note>an ancient kingdom in modern-day Myanmar</note>, Siam, and Bengal <note>original: "Bengala"</note>. In building this city, they established new laws there and formed a language specific and particular to themselves, so that they would have nothing in common with their neighbors. This language they formed from the most excellent words and speech of the languages of their neighboring peoples; they are accustomed to using it to compose very excellent verses and poems on love, and with it, one can trade and converse in all the surrounding regions, as it is the most beautiful, delicate, and eloquent of all others in the Indies.

Whatever may be the case regarding these diversities or variations of Indian languages, we shall hold as certain what we have deduced before in the chapter on the Egyptian language: namely, what we have recently learned from this very embassy from Japan <note>original: "Giapan"; referring to the Tenshō embassy, the first Japanese legation to Europe</note> which, in the year 1585 in the month of March, came from as far as five or six thousand leagues to offer obedience to the Holy Apostolic See of Rome. In the aforementioned East Indies, and even two thousand leagues beyond in China and Cathay <note>a medieval name for Northern China</note>, from whence the art of printing first proceeded, there are two types of writing, just as Apuleius <note>original: "Apulee"; a 2nd-century Roman author who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> previously cited relates regarding Egypt. That is to say, one is of hieroglyphic <note>original: "Hieroglyphiques"</note> letters, and the other of common letters which, by their assembly, can form all the words one wishes to express; both proceed not across—as with the Hebrews in one way and ourselves in another—but rather from top to bottom.

The first, which they call the writing of China, is generally common to all the regions of the Indies, both of the islands and the mainland, but used only for spiritual matters and non-vulgar doctrines by the **Bonzes** <note>a term used by early European travelers to describe Buddhist monks</note>. These are the younger children of Kings, Princes, and great Lords and other principal figures who are placed into monasteries with great revenues and great respect and authority, to prevent the dismemberment of the state and internal disputes. To these **Bonzes** belongs the administration and conduct of everything depending on the spirituality and religion of their country, according to their ancient idolatrous traditions of infinite kinds, and they themselves are almost infinite in number. Although most are vicious and ignorant people, there are found...

...yet nevertheless there are always some of greater understanding and knowledge than others, not through a doctrine acquired by them in schools, nor by the reading of books: for notwithstanding that paper and printing are not unknown to them, they do not have the same convenience as we do, but rather by an ingrained routine and meditations so constant that there are some who have devoted themselves for 30 or 40 years straight without communication with any person who might challenge their ideas. By this means, these <term>Bonzes</term> <note>A term used by early European travelers to describe Buddhist monks or priests in East Asia.</note> forge strange and very bizarre fantasies in their brains, being restrained in this by no bridle of religion nor reprimand from a magistrate, so that each might abound in his own sense, possessed by a vain and slight inconstancy. But they agree unanimously among themselves concerning the eternity of the world and the perishing of the soul along with the body, persuading themselves that what has come from nothing must also return to nothing; indeed, they have infinite other fantasies entirely contrary to the Christian religion, just as I deduced in the chapter on the Egyptian language cited above. 

These <term>Hieroglyphic</term> <note>Western scholars of this era often characterized Chinese characters as "hieroglyphs" because they viewed them as ideograms representing things rather than sounds.</note> letters of the said China and of the said Cathay <note>Cathay was the medieval name for Northern China; the author treats them as overlapping or related regions.</note> used in the aforementioned East Indies are very difficult to learn to read and to form, because they consist of various figures of beasts, birds, trees, herbs, and in short, everything that nature produces, which serve as their marks. Some are used alone and by themselves, and others are joined and coupled several together to create a character that represents more than one word—much like Centaurs, Chimeras, Sphinxes, and similar monstrosities composed of different natures—so that these Bonzes, however sharp their minds may be, consume the better part of their lives before they can become masters of them. This is according to the modern reports sent from the Indies, which maintain that from the general marks of this entirely hieroglyphic writing, by disguising and coupling them in various ways, entirely new composite characters can be formed, just as in <term>Ciceronian Notes</term> <note>Also known as Tironian notes, a system of shorthand used in ancient Rome.</note> and in our devices and name-ciphers. 

Regarding the matter of religion, they are marvelously attached to their idolatry and superstition, and have so vividly imprinted in their minds many fables told to them of their idols and false gods, that it is very difficult to tear them from their souls. This is principally because all these things are set in verse and in the rhythm of their language, which they value so highly that this alone is enough to persuade them of the greatest falsehoods imaginable; the devil having found this invention to make them believe so many follies that they relate concerning their false gods, even things contrary to their laws and to natural reason. Now they learn these verses or rhythms from their tender youth and sing them with a singular pleasure; for although <note>original: "iaçoit que"</note> their verses are very different from Greek and Latin verses regarding the number of syllables (because each contains 72 syllables), they nevertheless do not lack their own grace and beauty, as confirmed by <term>P. du Jarric</term> <note>Pierre du Jarric (1566–1617), a Jesuit historian who compiled accounts of missionary travels in the East.</note> in book 1, chapter 4 of his history of the East Indies.

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [LANGUAGES]

### CHAP. LXXVII.

->*Of the language of the Chinese in general.*<-

Several modern travelers and navigators, speaking in their voyages and navigations of this very great and ample country of China in the easternmost lands of the Indies, have asserted that Ptolemy, in Book 7, Chapter 3 of his *Geography*, had knowledge of it when he spoke these words:

<note>original Latin: "Sinae..." translated here as Chinese.</note> The Chinese are divided on the North side by a part of the country of the <term>Seres</term> <note>A classical name used by Greeks and Romans for the people of North China, famous for silk production.</note>; on the East and South sides by an unknown land; and on the West side by India, which lies beyond the Ganges according to the line described, as far as the Great Gulf, which likewise bounds them along with the other adjacent regions where the <term>Ichthyophagi Ethiopians</term> <note>Literally "Fish-eating Ethiopians"; a term used by ancient geographers for various coastal populations across Africa and Asia.</note> dwell according to the present description. Then, toward the end, coming to speak of the capital city of the Chinese, he speaks thus: "And the metropolitan city of the aforementioned country is <term>Thinae</term>." <term>Stephanus</term> <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary.</note> mentions it in his *Onomasticon* of cities, saying: "Sina is the metropolitan city of the Sinae, of whom Marcian speaks in his navigations." From this it is presumed that this word *Thinae* in Ptolemy is corrupted—and likewise in the first book of Strabo, where the same name is also read—and that for Θινα <note>Greek: Thina</note> one should read Σινα <note>Greek: Sina</note>, as the aforementioned Stephanus calls it in the previously cited place. 

With him agrees Father Xavier, a Jesuit, in an *Indian Epistle* of the year 1552, where he informs the Father General Loyola that three of his brethren have set out toward the Royal city of China, called Sina or Sinar. After the aforementioned Ptolemy and Stephanus cited above, we find some mention of this Kingdom of China in the Persian and Arabic physicians, who, speaking of the drugs that come from the East Indies, use these names *Seni* and *Sini*. This appears in <term>Avicenna</term> <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> Book 2, Chapter 124, when he speaks of Cinnamon, which he calls in his language *Darseni* and *Darsini*, which is "Chinese wood." Consistent with him are Serapion, <term>Rhazes</term> <note>Al-Razi (865–925), a Persian physician and chemist.</note> in his *Continent*, <term>Mesue</term> in his *Confection of Alkermes*, and <term>Averroes</term> in his *Colliget*. The same Avicenna, in the aforementioned book Chapter 578, speaking of Rhubarb, calls it in his language *Rauedseni* and *Rauedsini*, which is "Chinese root," thus calling Rhubarb by excellence because it comes from China. 

Upon these passages, Gerard of Cremona, commentator on the said Avicenna, interpreting the word *Seni* or *Sini*, says that it is a place name. And <term>Bellunense</term> <note>Andrea Alpago of Belluno, an Italian physician who translated and commented on Arabic medical works.</note> interpreting the word *Sinir* in Chapter 172, says that it signifies everything coming from the country of Sini. Also, Serapion in his *Simples*, speaking of <term>Zerumbet</term> <note>A type of aromatic ginger (Zingiber zerumbet).</note>, says by the authority of Isaac that it comes from the country named Sini, which is none other than China. Consequently, it results from these authorities that the country of China is situated in the East of Asia in the East Indies, beyond the Ganges, and is named by the name Sina and Sini, as it still is at present throughout the Indies, according to the testimony of moderns. Among others, Father de la Croix in his *Portuguese Voyage* Chapter 1, and Bernardino Escalante in his *Navigation* Chapter 6, note that from there it has come about that the Portuguese and Spaniards frequenting that country, and hearing it called Sini or Sina, have retained the same name, and have

[They] have called it China, by changing the letter *S* to *Ch*, as often happens in their language, as well as in others like Hebrew, where the word *shibboleth* is changed to *schibboleth* in the Book of Judges, chapter 12; in the German and Flemish languages in the word *Visch* or *Vuisch* derived from the Latin *Piscis* <note>meaning "fish"</note>; and similarly in our own language with the word *Chifre* <note>modern French "chiffre" meaning digit or code</note>, taken from the Hebrew word ספרה, *sephira* <note>original Hebrew: ספרה, meaning "counting" or "numbering"</note>. This happens because of the similarity in sound between these two letters, both in Hebrew and Arabic, where there are two "S" sounds, one named ש *Sin*, and the other ס *Schin* <note>The author likely refers to the Hebrew letters *Sin* (שׂ) and *Shin* (שׁ), which share the same character form but differ in sound, though the OCR identifies the character *Samekh* (ס) as well.</note>, as in German and English where *st* and *th* are pronounced like the *Sch* or the *Ch* of our language in words like *Fasten*, *Schall*, and other similar ones; and finally in Spanish, which pronounces the *Ch* with a sound leaning toward that of the letter *S*, which is why they turned the ancient name *Sina* into their modern *China*, as has been said.

This being established, we shall say that Duarte Barbosa <note>original: "Odouard Barboſſe," a Portuguese explorer and writer (c. 1480–1521)</note>, a Portuguese traveler in his voyages to the Indies, divided and partitioned the country and region of the Sinae into two great provinces: one stretching toward the Southeast, and the other toward the Northeast. The first is Cin, Sin, or China; and the other is <term>Mangi</term> <note>A term, famously used by Marco Polo, for Southern China; here the author uses it to describe a northern or eastern region containing several kingdoms.</note>, containing within it the lands and kingdoms of Chequan, Tainfu, Nanqui, Xauton, Quinzi, and Quinzay. Then, speaking of the Chinese, he says that they have their own language, using almost the same accent and manner of speaking and uttering their words as the <term>Tudesques</term> <note>An old term for Germans or people of Germanic tongue.</note> or Germans—not that their words and languages are in any way similar, which André Thevet <note>A 16th-century French explorer and writer.</note> mentions in passing in Book 11, chapter 25 of his *Universal Cosmography*. And speaking of the people of Mangi, he continues by saying that their language is entirely different from that of the Tartars <note>Central Asian peoples, including the Mongols, who had previously ruled China.</note> who rule them, just as the inhabitants are different in their ways of life from the aforementioned Tartars. This country of China, or rather kingdom, consists of fifteen provinces of very great extent, each having its own metropolitan city from which it is named. There are five maritime provinces, namely: Canton, Fujian, Zhejiang, Chequan <note>Possibly a duplicate or variation of Zhejiang</note>, Nanjing, and Beijing; the others are inland, namely: Shaanxi, Sichuan, Shanxi, Henan, Shandong <note>labeled here as Saucium</note>, Yunnan <note>labeled Olamum</note>, Huguang <note>Oquianum</note>, Guangxi, and Anhui.

Some say that there are in this kingdom as many as 240 cities or towns situated on great navigable rivers. Jan Huygen <note>original: "I. Hugo," referring to Jan Huygen van Linschoten, a Dutch traveler.</note> maintains that there are in these provinces large and renowned cities or towns up to the number of 591, and of small ones as many as 1,593, without counting the boroughs, villages, and hamlets.

The Reverend Father Juan González de Mendoza <note>An Augustinian friar whose 1585 book was the primary European source on China for decades.</note>, of the order of Saint Augustine, in his *History of the Great Kingdom of China* situated in the East Indies, divided into two parts—in Book 1, chapter 1 of his first part—speaks of it as follows: "This great kingdom of China, of which we speak here, was discovered and truly well-recognized ten years ago by the Spaniards inhabiting the Philippine Islands, distant from it by two hundred leagues. Although something was known of it through the reports of the Portuguese who trade at Canton and Macau <note>original: "Malan"</note>, cities of the said state, their variety of accounts had almost obscured the truth. Nevertheless, in the year 1575, Father Martín de Rada <note>original: "Martin Henança, ou Herrade"</note>, Provincial of the Augustinians, and Jerónimo Marín..."

By this means, the Japanese, the Ryukyuans <note>original: "Lechiens," referring to the people of the Ryukyu Islands (modern Okinawa)</note>, the Cochinchinese <note>inhabitants of what is now central Vietnam</note>, those of Sumatra, and other neighboring and adjacent peoples all communicate by writing with the aforementioned Chinese, and yet in speaking to one another they understand each other no more than the Greeks and the Germans do.

As for their schools and studies, the King <note>Referring to the Emperor of the Ming Dynasty</note> maintains them in all the cities at his own cost and expense, as much for learning to read, write, and count, as for teaching moral and natural philosophy, astrology, the laws of the kingdom, and many other singular and curious things. To the great studies <note>higher education or universities</note> arrive a great number of scholars, who strive to study well and profit, especially as it is the means by which they most quickly acquire the name of <term>Loytias</term> <note>From the Hokkien "Ló-tia," a term of respect for a magistrate or government official</note>, or knights, and other titles of dignity: as will be said more clearly in the chapter which follows, where it is spoken of the form and manner they maintain in granting the degree of **Loytias**, similar to that of Doctor, which is given among us. To these studies, both small and great, the King sends visitors every year to see and hear how one profits there, and to know who the masters and superiors are, and such other things that concern the conduct of scholastic government. These visitors, in making such visits, honor with words and praises those who study well, exhorting and encouraging them to continue: and on the contrary, they have the others put in prison and punished, whom they see to be unfit for letters and not doing their duty. And as for those who are not suited for it, or who do not want to study, they immediately remove them from the studies, so that they may make room for others who will better benefit. They have a great abundance of paper which they make from the fibers of canes and reeds <note>likely referring to bamboo paper</note> very easily, by which means it is very cheap, and printed books as well: but in the majority of these, one can only write on one side, because it is too thin and delicate. They do not write with such pens as we do, but they are reed pens, the tip of which is made like that of a painter's brush; and notwithstanding this, there is no lack among them of brave and excellent writers, who achieve their status through the pen. When they write to people of distinction, they gild the entire margin of the paper and illuminate it, and once the letter is written, they put it in a pouch and seal it; afterward, because the letter is merely folded. And they use such letters among themselves so much that even if someone goes to visit another person, he always carries a letter that he presents to them himself, by which he says that he comes to kiss their hands, so that it often happens that there are no more than ten characters written on the whole sheet.

**Father Maffei <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei (1533–1603), an Italian Jesuit historian</note>, book 6 of his *History of the Indies*:**

> >> To write, the Chinese use very narrow and long small pages of a soft and thin paper. They do not write from the left moving toward the right like the Greeks, nor from the right moving toward the left like the Hebrews; rather, they draw their writing from the top of the page toward the bottom. In this manner, I remember having seen a book printed in that country and sent to Rome to the Vatican, and another in the Laurentian Library of King Philip <note>The library at El Escorial, founded by Philip II of Spain</note>. They use characters like the Egyptians, which the Greeks called Hieroglyphics; each of them serves for a name, and indeed sometimes they serve for an entire meaning. By this means, it happens that although the Chinese use various languages—as they have so many and such separate regions—nevertheless, all that is written is understood equally by everyone. In addition to the specific language of each province or nation, there is a certain common language for the learned which corresponds to the Latin language among us. They commonly name it the Mandarin. This is used by courtiers, secretaries, judges, and magistrates, and they study it very carefully.

They have had their rights and written laws for more than 2,000 years, and as they say, these were never changed (folio 329).

**José de Acosta <note>Spanish Jesuit missionary and naturalist (1540–1600)</note>, book 6 of his *Natural and Moral History of the Indies, both East and West*, chapter 5:**

> >> There are many who think, and it is indeed the common opinion, that these writings used by the Chinese are letters, like those we use in Europe, and that through them one can write the words of speech, and that they only differ from our letters and writing in the diversity of the characters, just as the Greeks differ from the Latins, and the Hebrews from the Chaldeans. From which it follows that since things themselves are innumerable, the letters or figures used by the Chinese to denote them are almost infinite: so much so that he who must read or write in China, as the Mandarins <note>The term "Mandarin" refers to the scholar-officials of imperial China</note> do, must know and retain at least eighty-five thousand characters or letters, and those who are perfect in this reading know more than one hundred and twenty thousand—a prodigious and strange thing, indeed, which would be unbelievable if it were not attested by people worthy of trust, etc.
