# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE <note>Although the header mentions "Languages," the text on this page focuses on the physical agility and natural habits of different nations, a common structural quirk in early modern encyclopedic works.</note>

...others, participating more in the nature of fire than those who are distant from it. This is why Pliny, speaking of the Gorgons and the Gorgonides Islands (which are those of Cape Verde), says that the men there are so light in flight that one can hardly follow them with the eye, so much so that Hanno the Carthaginian <note>A Carthaginian explorer (5th century BC) famous for his naval expedition along the African coast.</note> was unable to catch any of them. He even gives an account of the Troglodytes <term>Troglodytes</term> <note>Literally "cave-dwellers," a term used by ancient writers for various tribes in Africa and the Red Sea coast.</note>, a nation of Guinea, whom he says are called "Therotoeans," because they are as swift at hunting on land as the Ichthyophages <term>Ichthyophages</term> <note>Literally "fish-eaters," a name given by ancient Greeks to various coastal peoples.</note> are quick at swimming in the sea, where they tire almost as little as a fish. And Maffei <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei (1533–1603), a Jesuit historian who wrote about the Portuguese missions in the Indies.</note>, in his histories of the Indies, reports that the Nairs <note>The Nairs (or Nayars) are a military and noble caste from the Malabar Coast of India (modern-day Kerala).</note> of the Kingdom of Malabar are so agile, and have such a promptness that it is incredible, and they handle their bodies so well at will that they seem to have no bones, so that it is difficult to engage in a skirmish against such people, especially since with this agility they advance and retreat at their pleasure. But to make themselves such, they assist nature; they stretch their tendons from the age of seven years, which they afterwards fatten and rub with sesame oil. What I say can even be recognized in animals: for a Spanish jennet <note>A small, agile breed of Spanish horse.</note> or a Barb is more gallant and light in the race than a nag or a short-tailed horse from Germany, and an Italian horse more so than a French horse.

Now, although what I have said is true, there are still nations outside the Tropics who, through exercise and artifice, acquire this agility. For Holy Scripture makes mention of an *Israelite named Hazael*, of whom it testifies in *2 Samuel, chapter 2*, that he was light of foot as a wild roe in the fields. And to come to the Northern peoples, the *Heruli* <note>An East Germanic tribe who migrated across Europe during the 3rd to 5th centuries.</note> are celebrated for being swift in the race, by this verse from *Sidonius* <note>Sidonius Apollinaris (c. 430–489 AD), a Gallo-Roman poet and bishop.</note>:

> *The Herulian in the race, the Hun in the javelins, and the Frank in swimming.* <note>original: "Cursu Herulus, iaculis Hunus, Francusque natatu."</note>

And by this lightness, the Germans formerly gave much trouble to *Julius Caesar*. Likewise, our *Armouchiquois* <note>An Indigenous group encountered by early French explorers in the coastal regions of modern-day Maine and New Brunswick.</note> are as well-disposed as greyhounds, as we have said above, and the Savages <note>As noted previously, "Sauvages" refers to people living in a natural, forest-dwelling state.</note> yield very little to them, without however violating nature or using any artifice to run well. But like the ancient Gauls, being devoted to hunting—for it is their life—and to war, their bodies are nimble and so little burdened with fat that it does not prevent them from running at their ease.

Now, the dexterity of the Savages is recognized not only in running, but also in swimming. This is something they all know how to do, but it seems that some do it more than others. As for the Brazilians, they are so born to this craft that they will swim for eight days in the sea if hunger did not press them, and they fear more that some fish might devour them than perishing from exhaustion; it is the same in Florida, where men will follow a fish into the sea and catch it if it is not too large. *Joseph Acosta* <note>José de Acosta (1540–1600), a Spanish Jesuit missionary and naturalist who wrote "Natural and Moral History of the Indies."</note> says the very same of those of Peru. And as for breathing, they have a certain trick of inhaling water and rejecting it, by means of which they easily remain within it for a long time. Women likewise have a marvelous disposition for this exercise: for the *History of Florida* reports that they can cross great rivers by swimming while holding their children on one arm; and they climb very nimbly to the tops of the highest trees of the country.

See what the same author cited above writes in chapter 11 regarding the paintings, marks, incisions, and body ornaments of these West Indians, and in chapter 12 following, regarding the external ornaments of the body, such as bracelets, carcanets <note>A carcanet is an ornamental collar or necklace, often made of gold or jewels.</note>, earrings, etc.

In this, he writes that the Indians of Brazil, having no care for clothing like other Indians, take pleasure in decorating and variegating themselves with bird feathers. They take the downy feathers that we use for bedding and chop them as finely as mincemeat; they then dye these red with their Brazil wood <note>The brazilwood tree (Paubrasilia echinata) produced a valuable red dye and gave the country of Brazil its name.</note>. After rubbing their bodies with a certain gum that serves as glue, they cover themselves with these feathers, creating a garment all of one piece. According to Jean de Léry <note>Jean de Léry (1534–1613) was a French Protestant pastor and author who wrote a famous account of his time in Brazil.</note> in his *History of America*, this led the first explorers who went there to believe that the men called "savages" were naturally shaggy or hairy, which is not the case. For it is certain that these people, in whatever part they may be, have less body hair than we Europeans.

Those of Florida also use this method with down feathers, but only on their heads to make themselves appear more terrifying. In addition to what is mentioned above, the aforementioned Brazilians also make headbands of feathers which they tie and arrange in all colors. These headbands resemble, in their fashion, those "raquettes" or "ratepenades" <note>The term "ratepenade" is an old word for a bat; here it likely refers to a bat-wing shaped headpiece or fan popular in European fashion at the time.</note> used by ladies in our regions, the invention of which they seem to have learned from these people. As for those of New France <note>The French colonial territory in North America, primarily along the Saint Lawrence River.</note>, on their solemn days of rejoicing and when they go to war, they wear a crown around their head made of the long hair of the Moose <term>Ellan</term> <note>Original: "Ellan." The French term "élan" refers to the moose (Alces alces).</note> dyed red, glued or otherwise attached to a leather band three fingers wide, such as Jacques Cartier <note>The French explorer (1491–1557) who claimed what is now Canada for France.</note> says he saw on the King or Lord of the savages he found in the town of Hochelaga <note>A fortified Iroquoian village on the site of present-day Montreal.</note>. However, they do not use as much featherwork as the Brazilians, who make robes, caps, bracelets, belts, cheek ornaments, and bucklers <note>Small round shields.</note> for their lower backs in all colors.

The people are divided by language: indeed, within the same province there are different languages, no more and no less than in Gaul where Flemish, Lower Breton, Gascon, and Basque do not agree with one another. For the author of the history of Virginia <note>Likely referring to Thomas Harriot or the accounts found in Theodor de Bry's "Great Voyages."</note> says that there, each *Wiroan* <note>An Algonquian term for a leader or commander.</note> or Lord has his own particular language. For example, let it be that the chief or Captain of Quanton <note>This may refer to a specific settlement or perhaps a corruption of a name like Agouhanna's territory; the text notes that Jacques Cartier and René Goulaine de Laudonnière frequently used European titles like "King" for these leaders.</note> (whom our historians Jacques Cartier and Laudonnière qualify as King) is called in Canada, *Agohanna*; among the Souriquois <note>Now known as the Mi'kmaq.</note>, *Sagamos*; in Virginia, *Wiroans*; in Florida, *Paraousti*; in the Islands of Cuba, *Cacique*; the Kings of Peru, *Incas*, etc.

I have left out the Armouchiquois <note>A term used by early French explorers for Indigenous groups in present-day New England, likely the Abenaki.</note> and others whom I do not know. As for the Brazilians, they have no Kings, but the elders whom they call *Pcoreroupicheh*, because of their experience of the past, are those who govern, exhort, and order everything. Languages themselves change, just as we see that here we no longer have the language of the ancient Gauls, nor that which was in the time of Charlemagne (at least it is very different); the Italians no longer speak Latin, nor the Greeks ancient Greek—especially on the maritime coasts—nor the Jews ancient Hebrew. Thus, Jacques Cartier <note>Jacques Cartier (1491–1557), the first European to map the Gulf of Saint Lawrence.</note> left us a sort of dictionary of the language of Canada, which our Frenchmen who frequent it today do not understand at all: and for that reason I did not wish to insert it here; I only found this word *Caraconi* for "bread," and today they say *Caracona*, which I believe to be a Basque word <note>Basque whalers were very active in the region, leading to a "Basque-Algonquian pidgin" used for trade.</note>. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE #

Regarding the similarity of languages, words are occasionally found in this part of the world that mean something in the other. For instance, Jean de Léry <note>Jean de Léry (1534–1613) was a French explorer and author of "History of a Voyage to the Land of Brazil."</note> says that *Lery* signifies an oyster in Brazil; however, few words are found that share the same meaning. In the *Oriental History* of Maffeus <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei, an Italian Jesuit whose "Historiarum Indicarum Libri XVI" (1588) covered Portuguese discoveries in the East.</note>, I have read the word *Sagomas* used with the same meaning as our Souriquois <note>The Mi'kmaq people of the Atlantic provinces and Maine.</note> use it: to mean a King, Duke, or Captain. Similarly, those who have been to Guinea say that *Bohougie* signifies a small child or the fawn of an animal there, just as the Souriquois use the word. In France, we likewise have several words drawn from the Greek, such as "Mustache," which comes from *mystax* <note>original: "μύσταξ", meaning upper lip or mustache.</note>, and our expression "drinking like a *tire-larigot*" <note>A French idiom meaning to drink a great deal; *larigot* was a type of flute or pipe.</note> comes from *larynx* <note>original: "λάρυγξ, λάρυγγος", referring to the throat.</note>, and so on; and the Greek words *sympherousi* <note>original: "συμφέρουσι", meaning to contribute or be useful.</note> and *baros* <note>original: "βάρος", meaning weight or burden.</note> come from the Hebrew *parash* <note>original: "פָּרַשׁ", to distinguish or spread out.</note> and *mispar* <note>original: "במספר", in number or by count.</note>.

But as for the cause of the change of language in Canada, of which we have spoken, I believe it resulted from the destruction of a people. For several years ago, the Iroquois assembled as many as eight thousand men and defeated all their enemies, whom they surprised within their enclosures.

I add to this the trade they now conduct with their pelts since the French have begun to seek them out. In the time of Jacques Cartier, no one cared for beavers; the hats made from them have only come into use since that time. This is not because the invention is new, for in the old ordinances of the hatmakers of Paris, it is stated that they shall make hats of fine *bieures* (which is the beaver); but whether because of the high cost or otherwise, the practice was long interrupted.

As for pronunciation, our Souriquois have the *u* or *upsilon* [$\upsilon$] of the Greeks <note>The author is noting that the Mi'kmaq pronounced the 'u' sound in a way similar to the ancient Greek vowel, rather than the standard French 'u'.</note>, and they willingly end their words with the letter *a*, such as calling themselves *Souriquoa* instead of Souriquois; *Capitania* for Captain; *Normandia* for Norman; *Basquoa* for Basque; *Martra* for a marten; and *Tabagia* for a banquet, etc.

But there are certain letters that they cannot pronounce well, namely the consonant "V" and "F"; in place of which they use "B" and "P," saying *Pebre* for *Feure* <note>Referring to "Fèvre," an archaic term for a blacksmith or smith.</note>. For "Savage," they say *Chabaia*, and call themselves such, knowing in what sense we use the word. Nonetheless, they pronounce the rest of the French language better than our Gascons, who, besides the inversion of "V" into "B" and "B" into "V," were recognized and mistreated in Provence during the recent troubles because of their pronunciation of the word *Cabre* <note>Occitan/Provencal for "goat."</note>, in place of which they said *Crabe* <note>Crab.</note>. In the same way, the inhabitants of the Euphrates <note>This is a biblical error in the original text; the author refers to the Ephraimites in the Book of Judges 12:6.</note>, having lost the battle against the Gileadites and thinking to flee, were recognized at the passage of the Jordan by their pronunciation of the word *Shibboleth*, which means an ear of grain, in place of which they pronounced *Sibboleth*, which means a river's ford, while asking if they could safely cross. The Greeks also had diverse pronunciations of the same word, because they had four distinct dialects separate from the common tongue. And in Plautus, we read that the inhabitants of Praeneste, not far from Rome, pronounced *Kouia* instead of *Cicouia* <note>Latin "ciconia," meaning stork.</note>. Even today, the good women of Paris still say "my *coutin*" for "my cousin" and "my *mazy*" for "my husband" [*mari*]. Now, to return to our Savages, although by...

> Through trade, several of our Frenchmen understand them; nevertheless, they have a particular language known only to themselves. This makes me doubt what I said previously—that the language used in Canada <note>In this context, "Canada" refers specifically to the region around the St. Lawrence River explored by Cartier.</note> in the time of Jacques Cartier <note>Jacques Cartier (1491–1557) was the first European to map the Gulf of Saint Lawrence.</note> is no longer in use. For to accommodate us, they speak to us in the language most familiar to us, in which there is much Basque intermingled. It is not that they care much for learning our French languages—for there are sometimes those who say they do not come looking for us—but through long association, they are forced to retain some words. I will say further here regarding numbers (since we have spoken of them) that they do not count distinctly as we do—days, weeks, months, and years—but rather declare years by "Suns." For example, for one hundred years they will say *Cachmetren achtek*, which is to say, "one hundred Suns"; *Bitumetré nague achtek*, "one thousand Suns," meaning one thousand years; *Metren Knich Kaminau*, "ten Moons"; and *tabo metren quenak*, "twenty days." And to demonstrate something innumerable, such as the population of Paris, they will take their hair or handfuls of sand. This manner of counting is occasionally used in Holy Scripture, comparing, by hyperbole, armies to the sand upon the seashore. They also signify the seasons by their effects; for instance, to give it to be understood that the Sagamos <term>Sagamore; a title for a chief or leader among the Indigenous peoples of Acadia.</term> Poutrincourt <note>Jean de Biencourt de Poutrincourt (1557–1615), a commander in French Acadia.</note> will come in the Spring, they will say *Nibir betour Sagmo* (using *Sagmo* as a shortened word for *Sagamos*) *Poutrincourt betour Kedretch*, which is to say, "the leaf having come, then the Sagamos Poutrincourt will certainly come." Having therefore no distinction of days or years, they are also not persecuted by creditors as people are here; nor do their Autmoins <term>A medicine man, shaman, or priest among the Mi'kmaq people.</term> trim or lengthen their years to gratify tax collectors and bankers, as the idolatrous Priests of Rome anciently did through corruption, to whom the regulation and disposal of times, seasons, and years had been attributed, as Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman grammarian and compiler of "The Wonders of the World."</note> says in his *Polyhistor*, chapter three.

The same Lord Lescarbot <note>Marc Lescarbot (c. 1570–1641), a French lawyer and writer whose "Histoire de la Nouvelle-France" is a primary source for this period.</note> in the following chapter 8,

> Everyone knows well enough that these Western peoples have no use of letters <note>Meaning the use of a written alphabet or literacy.</note>; and this is what all those who have written of them say: that they greatly admired seeing that, by a piece of paper, I could make my will known from one world to another, and they thought there was enchantment in this paper.

> But one should not marvel so much at this, if we consider that in the time of the Roman Emperors, several nations on this side [of the ocean] were ignorant of the secrets of letters, among whom Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian.</note> places the Germans (who today swarm with studious men); he adds a notable trait: that good morals have more credit there than good laws do elsewhere. For from the ancient centuries of the Golden Age, they had the use of letters, even before the Greeks and Latins (and may it not displease those fine Doctors who call them Barbarians). ## Of the Diviners & Masters of Ceremonies among the Indians of the New Lands of New France & the Country of Canada. ##

The same Marc Lescarbot <note>Marc Lescarbot (c. 1570–1641) was a French lawyer and writer who lived in the Port-Royal settlement in Acadia; his *Histoire de la Nouvelle-France* is a primary source for early Canadian history.</note> in the aforementioned Book 3, Chapter 6 of the said history [writes]:

> I do not wish to use the name of "Priests," as some have done, for those who perform the ceremonies and invocations of demons among the Western Indians—except insofar as they make use of sacrifices and gifts which they offer to their gods. This is because, as the Hebrew Apostle <note>Referring to the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews in the New Testament.</note> says in chapter eight, verse three: "For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices." Such were those of Mexico (where the greatest was called *Papas*), who offered incense to their idols. The principal idol was the God they named Vitzilipuztli <note>Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec deity of war and the sun.</note>. Nevertheless, the general name for the one they held as the supreme Lord and author of all things was Viracocha, to whom they gave excellent qualities, calling him Pachacamac <note>An Incan deity; the name translates roughly to "Earth-Maker."</note>, which is "Creator of Heaven and Earth," and *Usapu*, which is "Admirable," and other similar names. They also had human sacrifices, as do those of Peru, whom they sacrificed in great number, as Joseph Acosta <note>José de Acosta (1540–1600) was a Spanish Jesuit missionary and naturalist who wrote extensively about the customs of the Aztecs and Incas.</note> describes at length in Book 5, Chapters 20 and 21. These, therefore, may be called Priests or Sacrificers. But regarding those of Virginia and Florida, I do not see what sacrifices they make, and thus I shall qualify them as Diviners, or Masters of the ceremonies of their religion. In Florida, I find these are called *Iaruars* and *Ioanas*; in Virginia, *Wiroances*; in Brazil, *Caribs*; and among our own people—I mean the Souriquois <term>Souriquois; the historical name used by the French for the Mi'kmaq people.</term>—they are called *Aoutmoins* <term>Aoutmoin; a Mi'kmaq term for a shaman, healer, or spiritual leader.</term>. Laudonnière, speaking...

Florida: they have said that their priests, in whom they place great trust, are powerful magicians, great diviners, and summoners of spirits <note>The original French uses *diables* (devils), reflecting the common European bias of the period which interpreted Indigenous spiritual practices through a Christian lens.</note>. These priests serve them as doctors and surgeons, and always carry with them a bag of herbs and drugs to treat the sick, most of whom suffer from the pox <note>Original: *verole*. This likely refers to syphilis, which many early modern writers believed originated in the Americas.</note>; for they are very fond of women and girls, whom they call "daughters of the Sun." If there is some matter to be negotiated, the King calls the **Iaruars** <note>A term for the priests or shamans of the Timucua people of Florida.</note> and the elders, and asks their advice. See, moreover, what I have written above in the 6th chapter of the 1st book. As for those of Virginia, they are no less cunning than those of Florida, and gain credit and make themselves respected through religious feats such as those we mentioned in the last chapter, speaking of certain dead men who were brought back to life. It was by this means, and under the pretext of religion, that the **Incas** <note>Original: *Ingas*. The rulers of the Inca Empire in Peru.</note> formerly made themselves the greatest Princes of America. And this same ruse has also been used by those on this side of the world who wished to bamboozle the people, such as **Numa Pompilius**, **Lysander**, **Sertorius**, and others more recent who acted—as **Plutarch** says—like tragic actors who, wishing to represent things that surpass human strength, have recourse to the superior power of the gods.

The **Aoutmoins** <note>A Mi'kmaq term for a shaman, healer, or medicine man.</note> of the furthest land of the Indies <note>Referring here to the coastal regions of modern-day Canada and Maine.</note> which is closest to us, are not so dull-witted that they do not know how to make the common people believe in them. For with their deceptions they make a living and render themselves necessary, practicing medicine and surgery as well as the Floridians do. For example, consider **Membertou**, a great **Sagamos** <note>A title for a chief or leader among the Mi'kmaq and neighboring peoples.</note>: if someone is sick, they send for him; he makes invocations to his spirit, he blows upon the aching part, he makes incisions there, and sucks out the bad blood. If it is a wound, he heals it by this same means, applying a slice of beaver testicles <note>Original: *roüelle de genitoires de Caſtor*. Castoreum, produced by beavers, was a highly valued medicinal substance in Europe and North America for centuries.</note>. In short, he is given some gift of game or skins. If it is a question of getting news of distant things, after having questioned his spirit, he renders his oracles, which are usually doubtful and very often false, but also sometimes true. For instance, when he was asked if **Pannoniac** <note>A Mi'kmaq individual whose death in 1607 led to a significant conflict with the Armouchicois.</note> was dead, he said that if he did not return within fifteen days, they should wait no longer, and that the **Armouchicois** <note>A term used by the French for the Indigenous peoples living south of the Mi'kmaq, likely the Abenaki or Massachusett.</note> would have killed him. And to obtain this answer, it was necessary to give him some gift; for among the Greeks there is a common proverb which says: *Without money, the oracles of Phoebus are silent.* <note>original: "Sans argent les oracles de Phœbus ſont muets." Phoebus is another name for Apollo, the god of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> The same man gave a true oracle regarding our arrival to the **Sieur de Pont** <note>François Gravé, Sieur de Pont-Gravé, a prominent French merchant and explorer.</note> when he departed from **Port Royal** to return to France, seeing that the 15th of July had passed without having any news. For he [Membertou] always maintained and affirmed that a ship would come there, and that his spirit had told him so.

Likewise, when the Savages are hungry, they consult the oracle of **Membertou**, and he tells them: "Go to such a place, and you will find game." It sometimes happens that they find some, and sometimes not; if it happens that they do not, the excuse is that the animal is wandering and has changed its place; but also very often they do find it. And this is what makes them believe that this spirit is a god, and they know no other; to whom, nevertheless, they render no service nor adoration in a formal religion. When these **Aoutmoins** perform their antics <note>Original: *chimagrees*, likely a variant of *simagrees*, meaning affected gestures or grimaces.</note>, they plant a stick in a pit, to which they tie a cord, and putting their heads into this pit, they make invocations or conjurations in a language unknown to the others who stand around, and this—

Then they dance in their fashion, as we will describe hereafter, with songs that I do not understand, nor did those of our people who understood their language best. 

But one day, while walking in our meadows along the river, I approached the cabin of **Membertou** <note>Membertou (c. 1510–1611) was the Grand Chief of the Mi'kmaq and the first Indigenous leader to be baptized by the French.</note>, and wrote down on my tablets a portion of what I heard, which is still written there in these terms: *Haloet, ho ho he he, ha ha, haloet ho ho he*, which they repeat several times. Having made the customary exclamation, they began another which sang: *Tameia alleluia tameia douyeni hau hau he he.* The melody of this was: G, G, G, F, F, D, D, D, F, F, G, F, F, D, D. I listened attentively to this word *Alleluia* <note>original: "Alleluia"</note>, repeated several times, and could never hear anything else. This is what makes me think these songs are in praise of the devil, if indeed this word means to them what it means in Hebrew, which is: "Praise the Lord" <note>Early explorers often looked for linguistic similarities to Hebrew to support theories that Indigenous Americans were descended from the Ten Lost Tribes of Israel.</note>. And being one day at such a festival, he reports that they said: *he he he he he he he he he he*, with this melody: F, F, G, F, F, G, G, G, G. And that done, they cried out in a way and with a terrifying howling for the space of a quarter of an hour, and the women jumped in the air with such violence that they foamed at the mouth, then began the music again saying: *Heu heurau ré, heura, Heuraure heura, heura cuech*. The melody is F, E, D, G, G, G, F, E, D, E, D, C, D.

This author says that in this song they had lamented their deceased fathers, who were so valiant, and yet they consoled themselves that after their death they were certain to go find them behind the high mountains, where they would dance and rejoice with them. Likewise, they had utterly threatened the **Ouetaca** <note>The Goitacá people, known as fierce enemies of the Tupinambá.</note>, their enemies, with being soon captured and eaten by them, as their **Caraibes** <note>A term used here for their shamans or priests.</note> had promised them, and they had also made mention of the flood of which we spoke in the preceding chapter. ### several languages.

Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC known for his monumental universal history.</note> in his writings mentioned certain peoples who <unclear>had</unclear> the tongue split and divided into two parts, by means of which they formed, articulated, and spoke several and different languages at the same instant: just as Johann Boemus the Teuton <note>Johann Boemus (c. 1485–1535) was a German humanist who compiled a famous ethnographic work on the customs of various nations.</note> repeats in the book of manners and customs of all the peoples of this Universe, according to the report made long ago by a certain ancient navigator named Iambulus, <note>Iambulus was a Greek writer of a utopian travel romance, often cited as historical fact by later authors.</note> who boasted and bragged of having been to a certain Island inhabited by these people with [split] tongues

split and divided in two, in such a way that they seem to be double; for this reason, they use them to express various thoughts all at once, and to say different things. Furthermore, the said Iambulus <note>Iambulus was a Greek merchant and writer of the 2nd century BCE known for his semi-mythical travel accounts, often cited in ancient geographies.</note> said that these people imitate all the birds of the fields, and what is even more marvelous, they speak all together to two men—to one with one part of the tongue, and to another with the other—and even while questioning one, they answer the other as if the two tongues were different and in two separate mouths. Antonio de Torquemada repeated this story in the first day of his *Hexameron* <note>A work titled *Jardín de flores curiosas* (1570), popular for its collection of wonders.</note>, and after him François de Belleforest in book 3, the final chapter of his *Universal History*.

A certain other very ancient author named Timosthenes has left in writing in his works that in former times, in a certain city of the country of Colchis <note>An ancient region on the coast of the Black Sea, in modern-day Georgia.</note> called Dioscorias, or Dioscuria—situated near the Attamonte river, currently named Trebizond—there were at times as many as three hundred sorts of different peoples and nations of this universe who all used different and dissimilar languages. It was such that a good one hundred and thirty <term>interpreters: Often referred to as "truchements" in the original French, these were essential intermediaries for trade in multilingual regions.</term> were needed for the merchants and others who wished to negotiate and trade with these peoples and nations, as reported by Strabo in book 11 and Pliny in book 6, chapter 5 of his *Natural History*. After them, Theseus Ambrosius in his appendix on several and diverse languages, S. Nozenus in his dedicatory epistle on his *Grammatical Questions* <note>original: "erotemates"</note> of the holy language, and François de Belleforest in volume 2, book 3, chapter 5 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

The Greeks maintain in their histories that Cecrops <note>The legendary founder and first king of Athens.</note>, living in the time of Moses—which Cecrops first brought to the Greeks the ceremonies of sacred things, and principally the manner of sacrificing an ox—was nicknamed *double-natured* <note>original: "διφυής" (diphuēs)</note>, as being composed of a double nature because he understood and spoke both the Egyptian and Greek languages.

The Latins attribute to the Latin poet Ennius three hearts, because he understood and spoke the Greek, Oscan <note>An extinct Indo-European language of southern Italy.</note>, and Latin languages.

Mithridates, King of Pontus in Asia, spoke twenty-two entirely different languages without any middleman or interpreter, as recounted by Pliny in book 7, chapter 24, and book 25, chapter 2; Valerius Maximus in book 9; Aulus Gellius in book 17, chapter 17; and Fabius Quintilian in book 11, chapter 2. In memory of this King, Nicolaus Erythraeus, a Venetian, titled one of his books on the names and words of all the people and nations of the earth *Mithridates*; likewise, Conrad Gessner, a German, composed a book of observations titled *Mithridates: On the differences of languages, both ancient and those currently in use among various nations throughout the whole world*, printed in the year 1555 at Zurich <note>original: "Tigurini"</note>.

Among the Christians, Origen of Alexandria was one of the most excellent in the knowledge of languages, for knowing five perfectly: Hebrew, Syriac, Egyptian, Greek, and Latin, according to the report of St. Jerome in volume 3 of his works against Rufinus, and of Epiphanius in the life of this personage.

The histories of Germany record that Emperor Charles IV spoke five languages perfectly.

Porchetus <note>Porchetus Salvago, a 14th-century monk.</note> and Johannes Reuchlin (known as Capnio) demonstrated that they knew several languages in what they wrote in their works titled *Victory against the Jews*, *On the Kabbalah*, and *On the Miraculous Word*. Sixtus of Siena <note>A converted Jew and celebrated biblical scholar (1520–1569).</note>, in book 4 of his *Sacred Library*, speaking of Agostino Giustiniani <note>original: "Augustinus Nebiensis." > "Agostino Giustiniani, Bishop on the island of Corsica, a Genoese by birth from the illustrious Giustiniani family, a Professor of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note> and a most observant theologian, sincerely learned and most skilled in all the languages dispersed throughout the whole world, was the first of all, with a new and immense daring, to bring together both testaments <note>original: "vtrumque sacræ legis instrumentum"; literally, the two instruments of the sacred law, referring to the Old and New Testaments.</note> of the sacred law into five principal languages—Hebrew, Chaldean <note>In this period, "Chaldean" usually referred to Aramaic.</note>, Greek, Latin, and Arabic—into a single body titled the *Octapla*. He did this with such craftsmanship that he arranged eight columns on each page, in which all the aforementioned languages, expressed in their own characters, could be seen at one and the same glance, corresponding to one another line for line and word for word, in this specific order:
> 1. In the first column, he placed the Hebrew version.
> 2. In the second, the Latin translation corresponding to the Hebrew word for word.
> 3. In the third, the common and Vulgate Latin edition.
> 4. In the fourth, the Greek.
> 5. In the fifth, the Arabic.
> 6. In the sixth, the Targum in the Chaldean language, but in Hebrew letters.
> 7. In the seventh, the Latin translation corresponding to the Chaldean.
> 8. In the eighth, scholia, or certain very brief little notes scattered and separated by intervals, with which he primarily refuted the errors of the Jews."

### Of the first usage of Writing among the Ancients, and at what time paper, parchment, and Tablets were invented.

### CHAP. LXXXIII.

**P**olydore Vergil <note>An Italian humanist priest (c. 1470–1555) whose work *De inventoribus rerum* was the first modern history of discoveries and "firsts."</note>, in the second book of *On the Invention of Things*, speaking of this matter, has written as follows:
> "Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), the Roman author of the massive encyclopedia *Natural History*.</note>, in book 13, chapter 11 of his natural history, maintains that before people made
> " sheets from a certain tree named *Papyros* [Papyrus] by the Greeks—Paper, by which
> " and in which life is understood and the memory of men preserved—
> " they wrote on palm leaves. This is why Aeneas, in the
> " third book of Virgil <note>The *Aeneid*, the Roman epic poem.</note>, says to the Sybil <note>A prophetess in Greek and Roman mythology who wrote her oracles on leaves.</note>,
> " *I only pray you, that to the flying leaves*
> " *You do not throw or scatter your verses and writings.*
> <note>original: "Tant seulement te pry, qu'aux fueilles voletantes / Tes vers & des escrits ne iettes & efuentes." These lines translate the Latin: "Foliis tantum ne carmina manda, ne turbata volent ventis rapidis ludibria."</note>

Then they began to write legal instruments and public acts on the thin bark <note>The author uses "escorce subtile," referring to the inner bark or *liber*, which is the root of the Latin word for book.</note> of certain trees, then on sheets of lead, and that which was private was put on fine linens, and later still on wax. For before the Trojan war, they did not use the Tablets called in Latin *Pugillares* <note>term: <term>Pugillares</term>; small writing tablets made of wood or ivory coated with wax, small enough to be held in the fist (*pugillus*).</note>, as that great poet Homer testifies. Now, before the use of Sheets [paper], after Alexander the Great had conquered the country of Egypt and built the rich city of Alexandria, as Varro <note>A prolific Roman scholar and writer (116–27 BC).</note> is the author [of this claim], the aforementioned King found the means to write on the bark of a shrub growing in parts of Egypt, which (as I have said) is called *Papyros*. But at present, this fashion of writing is so common that there is no Prince nor citizen who does not have his own Cipher and private characters.

Before we depart from Egypt, however, something must be said about the nature of papyrus; since the use of paper is essential to the civility of life and to memory. Marcus Varro is the authority that this was discovered following the victory of Alexander the Great, when Alexandria was founded in Egypt. Before that time, there was no use of paper; at first, people wrote on palm leaves, and then on the barks of certain trees. Afterward, public records began to be made on lead volumes, and soon private ones on linens or wax. For we find in Homer that the use of writing tablets existed even before the times of the Trojan War. Yet he also points out that the very land which is now understood to be Egypt did not then exist in its entirety, since all papyrus grows in the Sebennytic nome <note>A district of ancient Egypt in the Nile Delta.</note>; and that land was later built up by the silt of the Nile. Indeed, he reported that the land was once a day and night’s journey by sailing ship from the island of Pharos, which is now joined to Alexandria by a bridge. Soon after, due to the rivalry between the kingdoms of Ptolemy and Eumenes regarding their libraries, when Ptolemy suppressed the export of paper, the same Varro records that parchment was discovered at Pergamum. Afterward, the use of this material, by which the immortality of men is established, became widespread. Papyrus, then, grows in the marshes of Egypt or in the stagnant waters of the Nile, where the overflowing waters sit at a depth not exceeding two cubits; the root is as thick as an arm and grows obliquely, with triangular sides, and is no more than ten cubits in length...

...absorbent, with the letters barely forming without spreading: there is so much potential for failure. Another labor, therefore, follows in the weaving of the sheets. A common glue is prepared from the finest flour mixed with boiling water and a tiny splash of vinegar. For carpenter's glue and gums are too brittle. A more careful <margin>“</margin> method involves boiling water mixed with the crumb of leavened bread; in this way, the paper is least prone to blotching, surpassing even the smoothness of the Nile. All glue <margin>“</margin> should be neither older than one day nor too fresh. Afterward, the paper is thinned with a mallet and <margin>“</margin> brushed again with glue, and once more the wrinkles are pressed out and it is stretched with the mallet. <margin>“</margin> Thus there are long-lasting monuments in the hands of Tiberius and Caius Gracchus <note>Famous Roman populist reformers of the 2nd century BCE.</note>, which I saw <margin>“</margin> in the possession of Pomponius Secundus—the poet and most illustrious citizen—nearly 200 years <margin>“</margin> later. Indeed, we still see the manuscripts of Cicero, the Divine Augustus, and Virgil today. <margin>“</margin>

### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

<margin>»</margin> **Amphitheater paper** <note>original: *Amphitheatricæ*</note>, Wieland <note>Melchior Wieland (1520–1589), a Prussian botanist also known as Guillandinus.</note> substitutes the word **Athribic** <note>original: *Athribicæ*</note> here, after the Athribic district mentioned by Strabo, Ptolemy, and Stephanus. The author mentions Athribis as its capital in Chapter 10, section 5. Some suspect it was named "Amphitheater paper" because it was manufactured in the amphitheaters of Egypt—and especially Alexandria—when they were empty of crowds; just as manual laborers are accustomed to practicing their craft in public places when not occupied by the common masses. Perhaps this was also done in Rome in some amphitheater, hence the name.

<margin>»</margin> *All the layers are woven while wet with Nile water* <note>original: *Textuntur omnes tabulæ madentes Nili aqua*</note>; here Wieland accuses Turnebus <note>Adrianus Turnebus (1512–1565), a French classical scholar.</note> and Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel (1474–1537), a French physician and botanist.</note> of ignorance because they did not understand this passage, nor did they see that "layers" <note>original: *tabulas*</note> here refers to the strips of papyrus which are joined together, and not to a wooden board placed beneath the <term>philurae</term> <note>The thin, inner strips or "ribbons" sliced from the papyrus stalk.</note> upon which they are glued. With all due respect to him, I believe they understood it correctly, as will become clear from the following clause (*when first the supine layer of the sheet is smeared*) in which Wieland thought Pliny's speech should be understood thus: when first the <term>scheda</term> <note>A leaf or sheet of paper.</note> (that is, the <term>philura</term>) is smeared and spread out as a **supine layer** (using the ablative case), meaning that same strip is stretched out lengthwise. This kind of tasteless repetition hardly suits the succinct gravity of Pliny, when it could have been said more precisely and aptly: *when first the sheet is smeared.* Furthermore, while the paper was being made, it was necessary to place a **board** <note>original: *tabulam*</note> underneath, upon which the vertical and horizontal strips could be stretched out to be joined by glue or the turbid water of the Nile: Pliny indicates this here in passing. Moreover, the meaning of "board" <note>original: *tabulæ*</note> differs greatly from the concept of a "strip" <note>original: *philuræ*</note>. For this reason, I believe we should follow the authority of the manuscript codex, which has: *all the layers are woven with the Nile water wetting them* <note>original: *texuntur omnes tabulæ madēte Nili aqua*</note> and again *when first the supine sheet is smeared onto the board* <note>original: *cū primo supina tabulæ scheda adlinitur*</note>; words which could not be clearer or more consistent. 

He explains the **supine sheet** as one placed in an upright position, just as Livy described **supine hands** <note>Hands held palms upward.</note> as being "raised," when the matrons in public mourning stretched them toward heaven and the gods. It is well known by physicians that a **prone hand** is one whose palm faces the earth, and a **supine** one is when the same is turned toward heaven, in the manner of suppliants—a gesture by which the Franciscans <note>A Catholic religious order; the author uses them as a contemporary visual reference for the gesture.</note> still pray today, silent and murmuring. I believe "supine sheet" should rather be interpreted as that part which turned inward on the <term>scapus</term> <note>The cylinder or roll of papyrus.</note> but, when stretched over the board, is turned outward and does not touch the wood of the board. Positioned thus, because it is softer, wetter, and more tender, it more easily embraces and holds the second strip thrown over it. He thinks we should also read *it is afterwards finished with a transverse skin* <note>original: *trasuersa postea cute peragitur*</note>. But the integrity of the manuscript codex suggests nothing should be changed.

One could not call the "weave" of the papers more conveniently or elegantly than by the name of a **lattice** <note>original: *cratis*</note>, on account of the vertical and horizontal strips lying upon one another, which is the shape of a lattice or crate. Furthermore, whether the papers were dried in sunny places or in shaded, breezy spots is a matter worth considering, as it pertains to either emending or confirming Pliny's text. It is true that those things glued only by the moisture of water tend to pull apart; however, they are joined more tenaciously by steam, the warmth and heat of the sun, and even the heat of fire. Thus, those who make thick paper for binding books or for covering merchandise, once they have sufficiently pressed the square sheet of paper in the press, dry it by **insolation** <note>Drying by exposure to the sun.</note>; and booksellers and those who stitch together volumes either bring the backs, smeared with glue, near a fire or expose them to the sun so they may dry more quickly. Therefore, it is not unlikely that in ancient times, papers were also accustomed to being hardened and dried by the sun. But since the variety of vocabulary Pliny used to explain the history of papyrus and paper may delay a reader unskilled in this matter, I shall...

...for which reason it was established, with several things having been set forth. The **stalk of the Papyrus** <note>original: *Scapum Papyri*</note> was generally four cubits—that is, six feet—long, consisting at most of twenty "tunics" or membranes. Once pulled from the water, they would trim it at the top, or the summit, because that part was thinner and weaker; they also trimmed it at the root, because that part was tender and too soft, still soaked with moisture, and would otherwise wither and lack the firmness necessary for gluing, the pressure of the press, the strikes of the mallets, and the smoothing process. The exact amount cut off from each end is not recorded. I conjecture about one foot was cut away, so that four feet of the truncated stalk remained. This they then finally divided down the middle with a iron tool designed and adapted for the purpose, which they perhaps called a "needle," separating the membranes. By placing these in vertical and horizontal positions, they would manufacture the paper. These membranes or tunics torn from the stalk are called **strips, leaves, or shavings** <note>original: *philuras, schedas, ramenta*</note> by Pliny. When they are arranged in a vertical position on the board, they are called **the warp** <note>original: *stamina, siue statumina*</note>; when horizontal, they are **the woof** <note>original: *subtegmina*</note>—terms borrowed from the weaver's workshop. A series or stack of these joined together, whether vertically or horizontally, is called a **layer** <note>original: *corium*, literally "hide" or "leather"</note>. Up until the time of the Emperor Claudius, this was only double-layered: one layer with vertical fibers, the other with horizontal. By his command, however, a triple layer was used in that paper which he called **the Claudian** after his own name. For they wove this with the first and third layers being vertical, and the second horizontal. Pliny never uses the word "Papyrus" to mean these thin strips. In the writings of the jurist Ulpian, in the third book on legacies, "papyrus prepared for paper" is understood not so much as the strips, but the stalks of the papyrus, because the strips were not usually sold separately so as to be ready at hand unless the time for construction was imminent. We shall declare a little later what **the ribbon** <note>original: *Tenia*; a defect in the paper</note> is to Pliny. Certainly, that word is never found in his work to mean a strip, although I do not deny it could be used in that sense, just as neither "page," "tablet," nor "sheet" <note>original: *plagula*</note> is used. For a **sheet** is a piece of finished paper, woven from its strips like a thin plate, which the common people call a "leaf" in our own linen papers. It has two faces: the back and the front—or the anterior and posterior page. We have previously discussed the board which supported the strips as they lay there until the framework was finished and the weaving was complete. There remains the name "skin" <note>original: *cutis*</note>, which I do not think should be used in place of the finished framework; ancient manuscripts argue against it, and the meaning of "skin" does not fit, as skin is always the outermost and visible part, whereas many of the strips are hidden deep within the layers, especially the finer and better ones. If any strip were to be called a "skin," only the outermost and worst of them all would deserve that name.

Nor is it enough to use a mallet. Either the paper is so narrow that it does not match the wider part of the mallet where it strikes, or it is so fragile that it breaks when struck by the mallet. It was the custom to flatten and stretch wrinkled papers with the stroke of mallets. See the 32nd book of the Digests by **Ulpian** <note>Domitius Ulpianus (c. 170–223 AD), a celebrated Roman jurist.</note>; and the "hammered books" of **Guillandinus** <note>The Latinized name of Melchior Wieland, the botanist mentioned on the previous page.</note>.

**The front of the paper** <note>original: *Adversa charta*</note> is the anterior side, set before our eyes, which we look upon while writing and upon which the pen hurries; **the back** <note>original: *auersa*</note> is the posterior side, placed at the rear. A **blot** <note>original: *Litura*</note> is a stain of poured or spread ink on "thirsty" <note>absorbent</note> paper, similar to the mark we make when erasing writing with a pen. It certainly appears more on the back face of the paper, as the ink sinks in; thus, when something is already written on the front, the back is so defiled with black spots that nothing else can be painted there. However, these verses of **Juvenal** <note>Decimus Iunius Iuvenalis, a Roman poet of the late 1st century AD.</note> testify that the ancients wrote on both faces:

> Written on the back as well, and yet the Orestes is not yet finished.

» They call those commentaries written on both sides "opisthographs" <note>original: *opisthographos*</note>; rough notebooks <note>original: *adversaria*</note> have some similarity to these, namely haphazard tablets and many things jotted down carelessly which are then transferred into proper, permanent books arranged in order. Cicero mentions this in his speech for Roscius regarding contracts, manuscripts written on both sides <note>original: *opisthographis*</note>, original autographs, and signed documents. See Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 2, Chapter 30.

» Therefore, the stays <note>original: *statumina*; refers to the structural supports</note> were also made for the second layer. In an ancient manuscript, it reads: (*Therefore the warp-threads were made for the second layer as the woof-threads were for the first:*) there is no difference in meaning if we also read "stays": the warp <note>original: *stamen*</note> is that which women spin wrapped around a distaff; it is also the straight thread of the web in weaving, within which the woof <note>original: *subtegmen*</note> or cross-thread runs transversely. A stay <note>original: *statumen*</note>, however, is a stake or pole by which a vine is supported. The author's meaning is therefore not at all obscure: in the "Claudia" paper <note>A premium brand of papyrus named after the Emperor Claudius</note>, just as in the first layer made of upright fiber-strips <note>original: *philuris*</note>, a second layer was added like a woof or cross-thread from transverse sheets; then, upon this, a third layer was placed, whether called warp or stays, again composed of upright fiber-strips, just as in the first layer.

» The measure was a foot wide. (When the tearing away of one strip would ruin the larger pages) in the ancient manuscript it is called **Macrocolla** <note>Large-format paper</note>. Guillandinus thinks this is named <term>from the Greek for long limbs</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀπὸ τῶν μακρῶν κόλλων*</note>, as if from a long back; I prefer to think it is <term>from the Greek for long limbs</term> as if from long joints and members. Whether the measure of a foot or a cubit—that is, a foot and a half—of these papers refers to the length or the width, Pliny does not specify. I believe it refers to the width, since the subject here is width; the recorded length of the papyrus stalks <note>original: *scapi*</note> from which the sheets were pulled was about four feet, which could not be contracted to the measure of a foot or a cubit, even though the name <term>macrocollon</term> indicates length rather than width. Furthermore, the fact that several pages or larger areas could be ruined by the tearing of a single strip teaches us that the small sheets of finished, dried, hammered, and smoothed paper were usually folded into pages, as happens in our own books; the larger these were, the more the writing would be disturbed and damaged if someone removed a single fiber-strip, whether through malice or because it was corrupt and defective. Martial, in his last book of Epistles, praises the "Augusta" paper and calls the "greeting-paper" in Book 9:

-> *Marcus Antonius loves our Muses, Atticus,* <-
-> *If only the greeting-paper reports the truth.* <- <note>original: *Charta salutatrix si modo vera refert.*</note>

» As for the fact that Guillandinus replaces "Liviana" with "Fanniana," and never ceases to assert that the Augusta, Liviana, and Hieratica papers are the same, it has been stated above that this was decided against the authority of ancient manuscripts and is not approved by us. From this, we can indeed count the papers and review them by their classes, according to their ranking in value and price, and the variety of their width (since the length of all was almost equal): in the time of Augustus, the first were the **Macrocola**, a foot or a foot and a half wide; the **Augusta** and **Liviana** were the best, at thirteen inches; the **Hieratica** <note>Priestly paper</note> was eleven; the **Fanniana** was ten; the **Amphitheatrica** was nine; the **Saitica** and the **Tanitica** (which the author omitted) were fewer, namely seven or eight; and the **Emporetica** <note>Shop or wrapping paper</note> was six. The **Claudia** paper surpassed all of these in both quality and prestige, having been woven during the reign of Claudius from two warps (or stays) with one woof placed between them; it was made of the best materials, namely Augusta and Liviana, and was somewhat wider, as I suspect, at fourteen or fifteen inches.

->Roughness is smoothed by a tooth or a shell.<- <margin>cc</margin>

Our author mentions four defects of papers: roughness <note>original: *scabritiem*</note>, rebellious defiance <note>original: *rebellem contumaciam*; referring to warping or lack of absorption</note>, freckling <note>original: *lentigenem*</note>, and one or more streaks <note>original: *tæniam*</note>. The remedy for roughness is polishing with a tooth or a shell, though moderation must be applied so it is not rubbed too forcefully. For although it may shine more from such smoothing and removal of wrinkles, and please the eye with a glowing luster, if the rubbing is too vigorous, the paper does not soak up the ink but rejects it; and if any letters are drawn upon it, the writing remains unstable and fleeting. The second defect is rebellion. Those who were once subdued by arms and pacified, but move to war again, are said to rebel. Here, moisture rebels when applied carelessly, stubbornly resisting the care and effort of the craftsman; it does not wet and coat every space of the hide <note>The author uses *corij* (leather/hide) metaphorically for the papyrus layer</note> equally, but settles more heavily in some places and is poured more sparingly in others, making both the surface and the drying of the sheets unequal. For when the craftsman thinks the paper is properly treated, worked, and handled, and requires no further labor, then, contrary to his hope, that defect is uncovered and, as if breaking out anew, creates more work for his diligence. Thus, the paper must be unmapped and subdued again with the same labor and overcome as before. This defect is detected with a mallet, because the mallet strikes the more prominent bumps and the lower hollows of the sheets with an unequal blow, revealing the bruised spots as an unpleasing deformity. This flaw is also betrayed and proven by the smell—especially if the paper was compressed and dried in the press too negligently—becoming moldy, poisonous, and foul-smelling from the rotting and stagnant moisture which was neither squeezed out by the press nor dissipated by the sun. Freckling <note>original: *Lentigo*</note> is a blemish scattered across the sheets of paper, reddish or brownish in color, such as is seen on a person, called *phanos* <note>original: φανός; literally "lamp" or "bright spot"</note> by the Greeks. Because of the many such spots on his face, Dioscorides was nicknamed *Phanos*, according to Suidas. In paper, therefore, Pliny calls these moles, grime, discolored marks of dots, and spot-like splatters "freckles." These occurred while the layers were being joined if any impurity fell in that stained the natural color, or if anything twisted or balled up in the sheets darkened the paper. This was recognized by the eyes, either by inspecting the paper immediately if the spots were on the surface, or by holding it up to the sun if they sat deeper within. The fourth and last defect is the Streak <note>original: *Tænia*</note>, which is not, as Guillandinus <note>Melchior Guillandinus, a 16th-century botanist</note> thinks, a fiber-strip or a sheet, but a long and narrow path in the sheets, coated and covered by no glue or fatty moisture. In this spot, the porous and absorbent rarity of the papyrus alone meets the pens of the writers without any protective coating; as it drinks in the ink or the painting of the letter, it spreads it, which is explored neither by the stroke of the mallet nor by the sight of the eyes, but only by writing, as the painted letter melts away and is soaked through on both sides, staining both the back and the front face. <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>cc</margin> <margin>sc</margin>

We also use parchment, which is firmer and more durable than paper; this is made from the skins of goats, sheep, and calves, tanned and prepared by tawers and parchment-makers. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [BOOKS]

> "They wish to write: in full those [pages] that are intended to last a long time, such as the affairs of their religion or histories; others of less weight are written in quarter or half-quarter sizes, on both one side and the other. And when they have written a great number and wish to join them into books, they secure them between two wooden boards <note>The original French uses "ais," referring to the thick wooden planks used in medieval and early modern bookbinding before cardboard became common.</note> in place of the covers we use. Then, just as we sew our leaves with a needle and thread, they attach them with cords to the said tablets. As for missives [letters], it suffices for the leaf to be written upon and rolled up, and for a seal, they tie it with a small thread from the Palm tree itself. They use a pointed instrument of iron or wood for writing, passing lightly over the leaf without piercing it, and imprinting the characters of their letters so that they can write on both sides. Other more permanent writings, such as the foundations of temples, are engraved in stone or copper. Pierre Martyr of Milan, <note>Peter Martyr d'Anghiera (1457–1526), an Italian-born historian for Spain who wrote the first accounts of the explorations of the Americas.</note> historian of the discovery of the new lands made by the Castilians, relates that the inhabitants of Collacuane brought to Spain, among other gifts, certain books written on thin inner barks found between the wood and the thick outer bark. And these are sometimes taken from beech or alder trees, which they cover with thick cloth and secure with cement, then rub with finely ground plaster. And when it is dry, they write upon it whatever they please. Their books are not made of leaves, but rather they extend them in length by several cubits and reduce them into square parts, so joined with sticky cement—easy to turn—that they seem to be made of wooden tablets. And from whichever side they are opened, two written faces are offered, and two pages appear. There are just as many underneath, if one does not extend them lengthwise, because beneath one leaf are several written leaves. The letters and characters resemble hooks, loops, stars, and other such forms, which they arrange in lines in our fashion, somewhat representing the ancient manner of Egypt and Ethiopia; and they paint between the lines figures of animals, especially of men who lived before, such as Kings and Lords reciting their deeds. They also write their laws, sacrifices, ceremonies, observations of the stars, and of farming; the top and bottom are of pleasing craftsmanship, such that when they are folded, they seem in no way different from our own. They also make books from tablets of the fig tree, which they can easily erase. The same Martyr says that in Darien <note>A region in present-day Panama and Colombia.</note> they found books made of tree leaves sewn together, and that in Mexico they use figures by which they declare their affairs, no more nor less than by writing. Furthermore, in Hispaniola <note>original: "l'Heſpagnolle"</note> there is a tree named *Coppeia*, <note>The Copey tree (*Clusia major*), known for its thick leaves that can be scratched to leave permanent marks.</note> whose leaf is suitable for writing like paper, with a needle or pointed wood; and it is believed that this is the tree on whose leaves the Chaldeans, the first inventors of letters, wrote their concepts before the use of letters was invented. The leaf receives writing on both sides, like our paper. It is about twelve fingers wide and almost round, thicker than double parchment and very durable. When wet, it shows white letters against its green; when dry, it whitens and hardens like a wooden tablet, but the letters turn yellow. It is never corrupted nor erased by getting wet, unless it is burned. Marco Polo <note>original: "Paule Venitien"</note>..."

### *On the first books of the world.*

## CHAP. LXXXV.

There is great debate and dispute among the ancient Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and other authors concerning the first inventor of books, and who first brought them to light in the universe to be seen and read by posterity. The most ancient Hebrews have written that Adam, our first Father, from the beginning of the world composed books in ancient Hebrew characters and the Hebrew language, treating of divine laws. Saint Augustine <note>A pivotal theologian and philosopher of the early Christian Church (354–430 AD).</note>, in the thirty-eighth chapter of the eighteenth book of his *City of God*, reports that these were seen and read in the primitive Church, though they were not very well received or approved by the Christians because of their excessive and remote antiquity. The learned Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop known for his "Panarion," a catalog of heresies.</note>, in his first letter to Panarius, makes mention of an ancient Hebrew book titled *The Revelation of Adam, when God cast a deep sleep upon him* <note>original: "Adæ reuelatio, Quando Deus immisit soporem in illum."</note>. And the aforementioned Saint Augustine, in his work against Faustus, mentions a Hebrew book titled *Concerning the Genealogy of the sons and daughters of Adam* <note>original: "de Genealogia filiorum & filiarum Adæ."</note>. Pope Gelasius <note>Gelasius I (Pope from 492–496), associated with the Gelasian Decree which listed authorized and apocryphal books.</note>, in the fifteenth distinction <note>A reference to a division within the "Decretum Gratiani," a collection of canon law.</note>, declared this book apocryphal along with another certain Hebrew book titled *Concerning the Penance of Adam* <note>original: "De Pœnitentia Adæ."</note>. These books, as well as those by Adam himself, are entirely lost or missing today.

> Since it is so that the mere abundance of books is that which from day to day increases and exercises the spirits and understandings of men better and better, and since by this means everyone is drawn, and as if enticed, to the knowledge and learning of good letters and liberal sciences, and since also the study of good disciplines flourishes everywhere at present: I would think myself to be committing a great fault if I passed over in silence such a necessary invention—for the advancement of which, according to the capacity of our spirit, we have also undertaken this labor—seeing especially that such books are the true image of our understandings, and the eternal memory of our acts, as Saint Jerome says to Marcella. ...we have demonstrated very clearly the falsity of this opinion in a discourse previously published by us regarding the truth of the causes and effects of the decays, mutations, changes, conversions, and ruins of Monarchies, Empires, Kingdoms, and Republics, printed at Lyon by Benoît Rigaud, 1598. <note>Benoît Rigaud (c. 1520–1597) was a prominent printer in Lyon known for publishing a wide variety of works, including political treatises and popular literature.</note>

Theodore Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander (1506–1564) was a Swiss linguist and theologian who wrote one of the earliest works on comparative linguistics.</note>, in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, wrote on this subject the following words, which are worthy of being repeated.

> Because speech is based on popular use and consensus, and therefore changes from time to time for many reasons—just as the common people are fickle—no one can truly give laws to the people on how they must speak. It is more difficult to prescribe laws of speaking to the common people by command than it is to impose and maintain laws of living, since they feel that language is a common possession. I cannot pass over in silence in this place the saying of Pomponius Marcellus the Grammarian. When he had criticized something in a speech by Tiberius <note>Tiberius Caesar Augustus (42 BC – 37 AD), the second Roman Emperor.</note> as being poorly Latin, and Ateius Capito defended it as Latin—or if it were not then, it would be in the future, implying the power of Caesar Tiberius—Pomponius, turning to Tiberius, said: "Capito is lying now. For you, Caesar, can give citizenship to men, but you cannot give words to them." <note>original: "Tu enim Cæsar ciuitatem dare potes hominibus, verba dare non potes." This famous anecdote emphasizes that linguistic authority belongs to the community, not the sovereign.</note> Pomponius was implying that not even Kings can dictate speech to the common people, which remains within their own judgment and consensus. But it will be all the more profitable for a certain and stable doctrine to exist, both for judging correctly the speech already received and approved by the common people, and for using it correctly, as well as for preserving speech which the common people change rashly over the years, and almost by the day, condemning some things without judgment and accepting others. For since all public and private matters are usually entrusted to speech as if to a public treasury, it would be best to transmit it to the knowledge of posterity through a certain method and order, so that judgments can still be made about old speech that has already ceased to be used among them. Otherwise, when knowledge of the old language is lost, knowledge of the things themselves will perish at the same time. Anyone who considers civil affairs, laws, treaties, and the form of divine worship a little more diligently will clearly understand that this happens with great misfortune.

The same author, in the chapter on the *Mutation of Languages*, continues with these words:

> The fact that the Greek and Latin languages underwent significant change even during the time they flourished most is proven by so many terms of the arts of Grammar and Rhetoric, such as: *Latinitas* <note>Pure Latin usage</note>, *Hellenism* <note>Greek-style usage</note>, *Barbarism* <note>Foreign or corrupt phrasing</note>, *Solecism* <note>Grammatical errors</note>, *Archaism* <note>Old-fashioned speech</note>; and terms like foreign, new, ancient, primitive, obsolete, and forgotten words. Certain ages of speech are also established, so that one sees a different Latin language in the times of Cato the Elder or Ennius, another in the time of Cicero, another in the age of Caesar, and another in the times of Pliny and Quintilian. <note>These authors represent the evolution of Latin from its "archaic" period (Cato, Ennius) to its "Golden Age" (Cicero, Caesar) and its "Silver Age" (Pliny, Quintilian).</note> In how many ways and for what reasons this happens will be better discussed elsewhere. Here, only some passages from good authors will be added, from which this mutation of languages can be better weighed.

...are forgotten, because they now use other names for them, and many are unaware that the Greek word they now call *ennoia* <note>original: "ἔννοια" (thought or notion)</note> [corresponds to an older term]; that a "well" is what they call *phrear* <note>original: "φρέαρ"</note>; and a "hare" is what they call *lagon* <note>original: "λάγων", a variation of the standard Greek *lagōs*</note>. In this, I do not blame the talent of Lælius <note>Gaius Laelius, a Roman statesman known for his refined speech</note>, but rather I praise his industry. For success follows fortune, but praise follows experience. These things Varro wrote in the first book of his *On the Latin Language* most skillfully regarding the logic of words and most expertly regarding the use of both languages <note>meaning Latin and Greek</note>, and most kindly regarding Lælius himself. But in the later part of the same book, he says that a "thief" (*fur*) is so called because the ancient Romans called the "black of night" *furvus*, and thieves steal more easily during the night, which is black. Does it not seem that Varro erred regarding the thief just as Lælius did regarding the hare? For what is now called *kleptēs* <note>original: "κλέπτης"</note> by the Greeks was called *phōr* <note>original: "φῶρ"</note> in the older Greek tongue. Hence, through the affinity of letters, what is *phōr* in Greek is *fur* in Latin. Whether this fact escaped Varro’s memory at the time, or if he instead thought it more apt and coherent for a thief to be named from *furvus* (that is, "black"), is not for me to judge regarding a man of such excellent learning. 

However, that variety and change of individual idioms is observed in all those things in which property, power, elegance, wealth, and abundance, as well as the virtues, vices, and all qualities of speech and languages are placed. This is seen especially in words, as we judged a little earlier from the examples brought forth from the poet Horace and Aulus Gellius—that "hare" and "thief" (*phōr*) were words of the ancient Greek language. Of this kind is what Aristotle first called *selachē* <note>original: "σελάχη"</note>, those aquatic animals which have cartilage instead of a spine <note>sharks and rays</note>. And again, *mintha* <note>original: "μίνθα"</note>, which among the ancient Greeks signified "mint," was abolished when a new term was introduced, namely *hedyosmos* <note>original: "ἡδύοσμος", meaning "sweet-smelling"</note>, as Pliny teaches. Thus, not only in the age of Donatus, but even in that of the poet Terence, *actutum* was an ancient word for "immediately." And *cascus* was used for "old," and *creperum bellum* for a "doubtful war." Again, Pliny interprets as "cartilaginous" those things which Aristotle called *selachē*. For he could not do otherwise. Many things of this kind occur in the writings of Sidonius Apollinaris, and especially in Apuleius of Madaura. Although not even Sallust escaped the mark of being an "innovator of words." 

Variation is also observed in the affection of words—for instance, in the change of gender, declension, derivation, composition, and similar things. Such as *rapseris* for *rapias* or *rapueris* <note>archaic future perfect forms</note>, *sepelibo* for *sepeliam* <note>archaic future tense</note>, or *gladiola* for *gladiolus*. Nonius Marcellus collected many such examples. In syllables, too, the change of accent is observed, as well as the addition or attachment of syllables. It is also seen in the "Elements" <note>letters/sounds</note>, as the ancients said *olli* for *illi* <note>meaning "to them"</note>, and indeed especially in formulas of speaking, as was previously judged from Quintilian. Of this kind are the things Sallust brought forth unusually: *ductare exercitum* <note>to lead an army</note> and *patrare bellum* <note>to finish/achieve a war</note>. Finally, it is observed in the joining of words, in rhythm, abundance, figures, tropes, and the whole manner of speaking.

### LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE

“ ...nor shall a deceitful tongue be found in their mouth; for they shall feed and lie down, and no one shall make them afraid <note>original: "uēnietur in ore eorum lingua doloſa: quoniā ipſi paſcentur & accubabūt, & nō erit qui exterreat," from Zephaniah 3:13</note>. Concerning this sacred exchange of languages and religion, Paul also speaks to the Romans (chapter 14) and to the Philippians (chapter 2), writing in the words of Isaiah (chapter 45), that most excellent prophet. For speaking of the liberation of the Israelites from Babylon by Cyrus, and of the entire human race from the tyranny of Satan through Christ, he prophesies thus: "Am I not the Lord, and is there any other God besides me? There is no just God and Savior except me. Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is no other. I have sworn by myself. The word of justice shall go out of my mouth, and it shall not return: for to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear." Therefore, he shall say, "In the Lord are my justices and Empire." To him they shall come, and all who resist him shall be put to shame. In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified and praised. 

“ Furthermore, the Lord Christ promises in Mark 16 to those who believe in his name that they shall speak in new tongues. He fulfilled the promise of this matter by sending the most abundant Holy Spirit into the assembly of the disciples. For as he was about to send legates <note>A "legate" is an official messenger or representative, here referring to the Apostles.</note> to the kings and peoples of all languages and nations—not to build Babylons, nor to seize for themselves the seats of kingdoms and empires, nor to plot or devise anything against the knowledge of God, but rather to draw the whole world into the consensus of the Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or "whole" church, from the Greek *katholikos*.</note> religion, and to build the city of the living and true God—he equipped them perfectly for that task. 

“ The foundation, head, cornerstone, and prince of this city is Christ himself, the Lord of Glory. He equipped them not with hammers, trowels, plumb-lines, axes, or iron; nor with the sword, the javelin, the pike, or bronze engines of war; but with the Holy Spirit, with knowledge of divine things, with holiness of life, with virtues of every kind, and with skill in languages <note>original: "linguarum peritia"</note>. Thus, it is a wonderful and stupendous thing to say: men who were previously unrefined and illiterate, and who were almost like infants in their own native speech, suddenly spoke in the languages of all peoples and nations among whom they were to preach the Gospel. 

“ Making a beginning at Jerusalem, the city situated on Mount Sion (as Isaiah and Micah predicted in chapters 2 and 4), they announce that Christ—the Son of God, the Word, Wisdom, Power, and Justice—has come to earth, conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of a virgin from the house of David, died on the cross, and has risen and ascended into heaven, from whence he shall come as the Judge of the living and the dead. He whom the Israelite Church heard preaching on Mount Sinai is now heard by the whole world (contracted, as it were, into a compendium at Jerusalem) preaching on Mount Sion through the Apostles, now clothed in the true flesh of man. Thus, in that multitude which had flowed together from the entire world, each person heard the legates of Christ discoursing in their own native and vernacular speech. 

“ Truly, the early times of the Christian Church required that miraculous and stupendous work. This abundantly proves that the knowledge of languages is a tool that is both useful and necessary for preserving and enlarging the Christian commonwealth, and is a gift of divine munificence that is by no means trivial. The Apostle Paul teaches this in his First Epistle to the Corinthians, and the Church confesses it in its solemn prayer, praying in this manner: "Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love. You who, through the diversity of all languages, have gathered the nations into the unity of faith." This is the first and foremost thing to be sought with holy vows from the heavenly Father, from whom proceeds whatever is rightly judged as good; and the doctrine and instruction of languages should not be despised...

» ...keen study must be applied, along with diligent practice.
