->Voices of Birds.<-

> "You shall say, moreover, that Eagles scream <note>original: "clangere"</note>, Cranes crunk <note>original: "gruere"</note>, and of both the sound is a clangor <note>original: "clangorem"</note>. Hawks peep <note>original: "pipare"</note>, Roosters crow <note>original: "cucurrire"</note>, Cuckoos 'cuckoo' <note>original: "cuculare"</note>. Hyperides <note>An Athenian orator of the 4th century BCE.</note> and Demosthenes, however, said that Roosters 'cuckoo' <note>The author highlights a rare usage in Greek oratory where roosters are described with the sound of cuckoos.</note>. Partridges cackle <note>original: "cacabare"</note>, Quails chirrup <note>original: "gryllissare"</note>, Swans sing <note>original: "canere"</note>, Turtledoves moan <note>original: "gemere"</note>, pigeons flap <note>original: "plausitare"</note>, Jackdaws twitter <note>original: "fringulare"</note>, Witwalls <note>Likely the golden oriole.</note> cluck <note>original: "glocitare"</note>, Blackbirds shriek <note>original: "stridere"</note>, Cicadas chirp <note>original: "fritinire"</note>, Bees hum <note>original: "bombilare"</note>, Hoopoes hoot <note>original: "popissare"</note>, Owls hoot <note>original: "cucubare"</note>, Guinea hens cackle <note>original: "caccissare"</note>, Bats screech <note>original: "stridere"</note>, Dragons <note>original: "Draconites"; likely referring to large serpents.</note> hiss <note>original: "sibilare"</note>, [unknown] <note>original: "picari"</note>, Swallows twitter <note>original: "trinfare"</note>, Nightingales warble <note>original: "cantillare"</note>, and Geese gaggle <note>original: "gratitare"</note>. Connected to these is the human voice: Clamor, voice, talkativeness, sound, shouting, and speech, regarding which one may shout, call, chatter, sound, exclaim, and speak. Indeed, the names for voice, clamor, sound, talkativeness, and speech have already been mentioned: but let there be added to these, from shouting, 'shouter' <note>original: "clamator"</note> and 'fellow-shouter' <note>original: "conclamator"</note>."

Most of these Latin and Greek names and verbs cannot be conveniently turned or rendered word-for-word into our French language, which is less copious and abundant in these words, and others, than the Latin and Greek languages, as I have demonstrated previously when speaking of the Greek language compared with the Latin.

Whatever the case may be regarding these sounds, voices, noises, or languages of animals, we shall say in this place that it is a most marvelous thing to see the docility of certain birds, and principally of Parrots, who alone among those of their kind are very well-suited to imitate and mimic human voices, words, and languages, as the great Aristotle well noted in book 8, chapter 12 of his *History of Animals*. Pliny, in book 10, chapters 40 and 43, writes that these birds, in his time, pronounced the greetings of the Roman Emperors in the Latin language; this is confirmed by Solinus (his imitator) in chapter 55 of his *Polyhistor*; Aelian in book 13, chapter 18 of his *History of Animals*; and Suidas after him in his works; and Plutarch in the treatise *On the Cleverness of Animals*.
The Poet Martial, on this subject:
> *I, a parrot, shall learn from you the names of others;*
> *I have learned by myself to say, "Hail, Caesar!"* <note>original: "Psittacus à vobis aliorum nomina discam / Hoc didici per me dicere Cæsar, aue."</note>
Persius:
> *Who enabled the parrot to say his "Greetings" <note>original: "χαῖρε" (chaire)</note>,*
> *And taught magpies to attempt our words?*
Statius, in book 7 of the *Silvae*:
> *Parrot, leader of birds, eloquent delight of the gods;*
> *Parrot, skillful imitator of the human tongue.*
Julius Caesar Scaliger, in *Exercise 236* to Girolamo Cardano <note>A famous 16th-century Italian polymath.</note> regarding the *Book of Subtlety*, writes of having seen a Parrot jump and mimic its master who was dancing in time with the same gestures. Girolamo Cardano, in book 15, chapter 82 of *On the Variety of Things*, asserts having seen one sing the musical notes *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*. ...description of the parrots of the West Indies which learn in those regions to ask in the Indian tongue for flour, for food, and for drink, and that it is necessary to go to war against their enemies to capture and eat them. Ambroise Paré <note>A famous 16th-century French royal surgeon.</note>, in Book 1, Chapter 20 of his works, recounts wonders of one he says he saw. Those who frequented the court during the time of King Henry II know well that a great Prince of this Realm had a Parrot, which pronounced very distinctly and articulately several Psalms of David in the French language. Caelius Rhodiginus, in Book 3, Chapter 32 of his *Lectionum antiquarum* <note>original: "diuerses leçons"; a massive encyclopedia of classical knowledge published in 1516.</note>, asserts that he saw in his time a remarkable miracle: namely, the Parrot of Cardinal Ascanio <note>Ascanio Sforza (1455–1505), a powerful Italian cardinal and diplomat.</note>, bought in Rome for one hundred crowns, which distinctly and continuing without any intermission all its words, pronounced entirely the Creed of Christian Truth <note>original: "symbole de la verité Chrestiene"; referring to the Apostles' Creed.</note> just as if it were a learned and scholarly man. Jean de Léry, in Chapter 11 of his *History of the Indies* <note>Jean de Léry (1534–1613) was a French explorer who traveled to Brazil and wrote extensively about the Tupinambá people.</note>, speaks of a Parrot that spoke the language of the Savages most excellently. André Thevet also speaks of this in Book 11, Chapter 21; Book 21, Chapter 13; and Book 22, Chapter 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*. Those who wish to see the excellence of an infinity of other birds that have spoken and can speak should read Aelian, Book 2, Chapter 50 and Book 5, Chapter 36 of *On the Nature of Animals*; Pliny, Book 10, Chapter 42 and 43; Plutarch in the treatise *Whether Land or Sea Animals are Cleverer*; Macrobius, Book 2 of the *Saturnalia*; Girolamo Cardano <note>original: "Hieron. Cardan"; a polymath known for his work in mathematics and medicine.</note> in the place cited above, following the aforementioned Scaliger, *Exercitation* 237; Barthélemy de Chasseneuz <note>original: "B. Chassanee"</note>, Book 12 of his *Catalogus gloriae mundi* <note>Catalogue of the Glory of the World.</note>, number 80, page 86; Johannes Stoeffler <note>original: "Stofler"</note> in his commentaries on the *Sphere of Proclus*, chapter on Sagittarius. The same Rhodiginus, in Book 29, Chapter 26 of his aforementioned *Lectionum antiquarum*, speaking of Partridges that have spoken; Pierre Grégoire <note>original: "P. gregoire"</note> in his *Prolegomena of the Admirable Art*, Chapter 5; and André Thevet, Book 3, Chapter 15 of his *Cosmography*, speaking of the bird Rabiac, or Josabia, which speaks very well everything it is taught. See Cesare Maucini <note>original: "Cæsar Maucini"</note> treating the manner of raising, feeding, healing, and teaching birds to sing and speak.

What has been considered above has moved a very great dispute among the most learned Hebrew, Greek, and Latin personages: namely, to know and understand if these birds have certain and assured judgment, reasoning <note>original: "ratiocinations"</note>, understanding, and speech. Porphyry, in Book 3 of *On Abstinence* <note>original: "des sacrifices"; Porphyry's work "On Abstinence from Animal Food" argued for the rationality of animals.</note>, writes that every soul—which we can more properly call life—being endowed with sense and memory (functions which are indubitably in these birds, because they learn human voices so accurately, and the things that are taught to them), is by the same means reasoning and accompanied by internal and external speech. This author asserts that birds participate in this, as do other animals whose speech, he says, if not commonly understood by men, is no wonder, seeing that men think foreigners—whose mother tongue is not known to them—do nothing but moo, bray, or babble. In fact, this Author asserts that there were men in ancient times who perfectly understood the voices, warbling, sounds, and words or languages of these Birds: namely Melampus, Tiresias, and Apollonius of Tyana <note>original: "Apollonius Thianelis"; a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note>, of whom Philostratus recounts wonders in his biography in these words.

The Lord of Pimpont <note>A 16th-century French scholar and commentator on Virgil.</note> in his commentaries on this poet reports several fine Greek passages concerning this matter, which I will not report in this place to advance my subject. Cicero, in his first book *On Duties* <note>original: "Offices"</note>, speaking of these things says: *Insofar as they are moved by sense, they adapt themselves only to that which is near and present, feeling very little of the past or future; man, however, since he is a participant in reason, etc.* <note>original: "tantum quantum sensu mouentur ad id solũ quod adeſt, quodque præſens eſt ſe accommodat, paululum admodum ſentientes præteritum aut futurum, homo autẽ quoniã rationis eſt particeps &c."</note>

To make it short, we will say that Plutarch, in the treatise on which animals are the most clever, reports that Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, Plato, and Diogenes asserted that brute beasts participated in reason, but that they did not use this reason freely because it was weak and clouded within them—neither more nor less than an eye that is darkened and tarnished—and this because of their bad temperament, called by the Greeks <term>dyskrasia <note>original: δυσκρασία; a medical term for an imbalance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which was thought to affect character and health.</note></term>. This author repeats this in Book 5, chapter 20 of his *Opinions of the Philosophers*. Porphyry, in Book 2 of <term>On Abstinence from Living Things <note>original: περὶ ἀποχῆς τῶν ἐμψύχων; a Greek work advocating for vegetarianism and discussing animal souls.</note></term>, concerning the difference between animate things, has left in writing that Aristotle, Empedocles, and Democritus said and asserted as much in this regard, affirming that these brute beasts have <term>participation in the rational power <note>original: μετοχὴν τῆς λογικῆς δυνάμεως; the idea that animals share in a basic form of logic or reasoning.</note></term>, and that Tiresias, Melampus, and Apollonius of Tyana asserted in their lives that birds could be understood in their languages, which Pliny confirms in Book 10, chapter 49, under the authority of Democritus, as I noted above; which will seem at first glance to many to be entirely impossible. But so that I may repeat here what has seemed so to many great and excellent persons: it is a great and strong argument to prove that these brute beasts use some reason to see that they have memory of past things, know present ones, and seem to predict future ones. In fact, the Peripatetics <note>Followers of the philosophy of Aristotle, who often walked while teaching.</note> attribute memory and imagination to brute beasts, except for insects, but not long-lasting memory—as if most men did not also have memory that is just as unstable and fleeting! Truly, did the dog of Ulysses not show that he had a firmer and more stable memory than that of his servants, by recognizing his master even though he had been absent from him for the space of twenty years? This his domestic servants could not do. ...fugitives and escaped from the hands of their Portuguese and Spanish masters, as is contained in the voyages and histories of the West Indies; and the elephants, according to the report of Pliny, <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist. He often attributed high intelligence and even moral virtues to elephants in his *Natural History*.</note> did they not trace or write in the earth or dust in former times in the Greek language, certain words and speech, and perform most marvelous actions which can only depend upon <term>ratiocination</term> <note>The process of logical reasoning.</note>? This was also done by the <term>Cynocephales</term> <note>Literally "dog-headed" creatures; usually referring to baboons, which were sacred in Egypt and believed by some ancient writers to be able to write.</note>, animals of Egypt, according to Caelius in book 28, chapter 28 of his *Various Lessons*. The ancients demonstrated through their auguries and <term>haruspices</term> <note>Ancient diviners who interpreted the will of the gods by inspecting the entrails of animals or observing their behavior.</note> that brute beasts could know temporal vicissitudes and mutations; therefore, we shall hold the aforementioned opinion of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who argued for the intelligence of animals in his treatise *On Abstinence from Animal Food*.</note> to be sustainable, according to "more or less," or as the Greeks say, <term>κατὰ τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ τὸ ἧττον</term> <note>original: "kata to mallon kai to hetton"; meaning a matter of degree rather than a difference in kind.</note>. For this reason, we will not believe that these brute beasts have no reason simply because men seem to have more of it. Furthermore, what would cause dogs, horses, foxes, and other brute beasts to go mad, if there were not in them some part of reason that was spoiled and corrupted? For there can be no privation of a thing in that which has no capacity for it. <note>A philosophical argument: you cannot "lose" reason (go mad) unless you possessed reason to begin with.</note> And it is a certain and assured thing that when this happens, these brute beasts are not only destitute of "common sense," which we call <term>phantasy</term> <note>In the psychology of the time, "phantasy" or "imagination" was the faculty that processed sensory data.</note>, but it is necessary that some other spiritual part be altered in them—namely the "ratiocinative" power which the Greeks call <term>λογικὴν δύναμην</term> <note>original: "logikēn dynamin"; the power of logic or reason.</note>. This power is vitiated and corrupted by an imbalance of humors, yet when it is healthy and whole, it seems not even to be lacking in insects and ants. As Theophrastus says, ants gnaw the germ of the grains they gather for food through a certain natural instinct they have, knowing that they might sprout through rot in their burrows; however, Aphrodiseus <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note>, under the authority of Aristotle, did not hesitate to write the opposite, completely stripping these insects of imagination and memory.

Yet if we judge that brute beasts perform all their actions by the sole force of nature, why then—nature being their guide—do they not build cities, castles, and houses, seeing as that same nature has shown them the way to construct their nests, dens, and lodges? It is for this reason that the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their belief in the kinship of all living things.</note>, contemplating so many wonders of the ratiocinative virtue in animals, did not hesitate to persuade themselves that the souls of men went into the bodies of said brute beasts after the separation from their own bodies. This occurs through <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>The transmigration of souls from one body to another, whether human or animal.</note>, which was supported and embraced by the Brahmins of the Indians, the Magi of Persia, the Gymnosophists <note>Literally "naked philosophers"; a group of ancient Indian or Ethiopian ascetics.</note> of Ethiopia, the Chaldean and Egyptian priests, and the entire school of the Pythagoreans and Platonists, according to the report of Porphyry in his book *On Abstinence from Animals*, and of Plotinus in book 2 *On the Soul*. But leaving aside this metempsychosis as being contrary to our Christian religion, I will not hesitate to assert that these brute beasts have a certain force of reasoning together with imagination and memory—these spiritual parts proceeding from the same corporeal seed of their species. ...[would be wrong to believe] that the souls of these brute beasts are immortal; but I truly believe that they die and are entirely extinguished after the separation from their bodies, without anything remaining after their death: for in man, beyond the reasoning part, I have no doubt that the soul proceeds to him divinely by infusion from on high, and according to the opinion of Aristotle <gloss>that it enters from the outside</gloss> <note>original: "θύραθεν ἐπεισιέναι" (*thurathen epeisienai*); a famous Aristotelian phrase suggesting the intellect has a divine origin external to biological generation.</note>; in explaining this, Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle.</note>, the most prudent among the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, used these words <gloss>from whence</gloss> <note>original: "πόθεν" (*pothen*)</note>, <gloss>and from heaven</gloss> <note>original: "καὶ οὐρανόθεν" (*kai ouranothen*)</note> divinely and not from here below, and <gloss>through the seed</gloss> <note>original: "διὰ τοῦ σπέρματος" (*dia tou spermatos*)</note>: in such a way that if everything died in man, according to Aphrodisias <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a celebrated commentator on Aristotle who argued against the immortality of the individual soul.</note> in his 10th [book], <gloss>how could it be separable, impassive, and eternal</gloss> <note>original: "πῶς χωριστὸς καὶ ἀπαθής, καὶ ἀΐδιος" (*pōs chōristos kai apathēs, kai aidios*)</note>, etc. The soul—separable, unmixed, incapable of suffering, and everlasting—would not fail to fly away; and because the great Aristotle in many places seems to confound sometimes <gloss>reason</gloss> <note>original: "λόγον" (*logon*)</note>, sometimes <gloss>a part</gloss> <note>original: "μόριον" (*morion*)</note>, at other times <gloss>intellect</gloss> <note>original: "νοῦν" (*noun*)</note>, and at other times <gloss>the power of reasoning</gloss> <note>original: "λογιστικὴν δύναμιν" (*logistikēn dunamin*)</note>, it is nevertheless certain that he did not fail to distinguish the parts and functions of the soul, as Suidas <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedic lexicon.</note> also did after him in his writings. Although the <gloss>active</gloss> <note>original: "ἐνεργητικός" (*energetikos*)</note> intellect, operating and effective, is so <gloss>naturally</gloss> <note>original: "συμφύως" (*sumphuōs*)</note> joined <gloss>passively</gloss> <note>original: "παθητικῶς" (*pathetikos*)</note> to the passive [intellect] that it cannot truly be disjoined from it, it is nonetheless separated from reason, according to the report of Hammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a philosopher and commentator.</note>. Long before Aristotle, Plato had written this in the *Timaeus*, but in an obscure fashion, making one part of the soul <gloss>divisible and mixed</gloss> <note>original: "διαιρετὸν καὶ μικτόν" (*diaireton kai mikton*)</note>, and the other <gloss>indivisible and unmixed</gloss> <note>original: "ἀδιαίρετον καὶ ἀμιγῆ" (*adiaireton kai amigē*)</note>, calling one the Point and Unity, and the other the binary and the line: and by the same means making this divisible part of the soul extend through all parts of the World; and the indivisible or unparticipated intellect not be mixed at all; for which reason Anaxagore called it the <gloss>unmixed intellect</gloss> <note>original: "νοῦν ἀμίκτον" (*noun amikton*)</note>. This is what Abumaron the Chaldean <note>Likely referring to a source from the Near Eastern tradition, possibly a corruption of a name like Abu Ma'shar or a similar sage.</note> called "God," Orpheus "Wisdom," the Kabbalists "Matarton" <note>Metatron, a high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical tradition often associated with the divine mediator.</note>, Hermes Trismegistus "Son of God," Themistius "the only illuminating Intellect," Saint John the Evangelist "Light," Saint Augustine the "superior portion," and others "the Father of Lights." Therefore, the rational soul is endowed with an intellect not mixed with the body, which Intellect is called by Aristotle the "Agent," joined to the power of the intellect, and this to the <term>phantasy</term> <note>In ancient psychology, the faculty that produces mental images; a bridge between the senses and the intellect.</note> which some call the "passible Intellect." In this, many have erred greatly by not distinguishing the phantasy from the Intellect of power, even though Themistius, according to the authority of Theophrastus, places a double Intellect in the soul (beyond the phantasy or common sense), which he says is transmitted to the body <gloss>from the outside</gloss> <note>original: "θύραθεν" (*thurathen*)</note> from on high. This cannot be understood as the phantasy; and the same Themistius cites the philosopher Theophrastus saying the Intellect of power is entirely sequestered from the body and is immortal, along with the agent intellect. This was denied by Aphrodisias, who said it was not a part of the soul; these are functions that do not belong to the aforementioned brute beasts, beyond the phantasy and memory by which they reason, having—according to the opinion of Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a Christian philosopher and scientist in Alexandria.</note>—a <gloss>shadow-outline</gloss> <note>original: "σκιαγραφίαν" (*skiagraphian*)</note> of forms, yet not shining with the light of the Intellect, of which they are entirely deprived and destitute. This is why the divine Plato calls this Intellect <gloss>mind</gloss> <note>original: "νοῦν" (*noun*)</note>, Aristotle <gloss>light</gloss> <note>original: "φῶς" (*phōs*)</note>, and Simplicius <gloss>actuality</gloss> <note>original: "ἀνέργεια" (*energeia*)</note>, because just as light does not cause colors but makes them seen, likewise the agent Intellect does not give form to the <term>species</term> <note>The mental concepts or "forms" of things.</note> in the passive Intellect, but causes them to be seen, which were latent and hidden in darkness.
